10078-plain-words-from-america-a-letter-:
Professor Douglas W. Johnson of Columbia University wrote this letter in February 1916, answering a German professor who had pleaded Germany's cause, with newspaper clippings enclosed. The letter appeared in the Revue de Paris in September 1916 and was published as a pamphlet in 1917.

Johnson answers plainly, as an American scholar, on the war, its causes, and America's view of them. His tone is firm but courteous, and his argument rests on facts rather than insults. Readers get a wartime document of unusual clarity: one professor's honest reply to another across the lines.
10128-the-great-events-by-famous-histori:
Volume seventeen of The Great Events by Famous Historians, edited by Rossiter Johnson with Horne and Rudd, covers the middle nineteenth century in master historians' words. Its pages note that in 1844 electricity, last and mightiest of man's servants, changed the age.

Longer narratives treat the Mexican War, vast in territorial results, and the uprising of the peoples in 1848, when nations that had risen in 1830 rose again. Brief introductions connect the narratives, with indices and courses of reading. Readers get 1840s history from writers close to its events. Johnson's editorship kept the series steady across many volumes.
10143-punch-or-the-london-charivari-volu:
London readers bought this issue of Punch on July 11, 1917, in the middle of the First World War. Punch, long the chief British comic weekly, mixed jokes, cartoons, and verse with sharp comment on war, food, and home life. Many writers and artists shared each number, so no single author owns it.

Short items mock tram tickets, baby week, penny dreadfuls, and rumors about Charlie Chaplin, while war news colors the humor throughout. The jokes are light on the surface and pointed underneath. Readers get a funny, telling snapshot of wartime London wit and worry.
10450-punch-or-the-london-charivari-volu:
London readers bought this issue of Punch on August 22, 1917, during the third year of the First World War. Punch, the long-running comic weekly, filled each number with jokes, cartoons, and verse by many hands. War, food, and home shortages color the humor, but the jokes stay light and sharp.

A poultry fancier who disguises his hen-house as a fort opens the number, while short items mock dogs, coal controllers, and the Stockholm Conference. Lost children at New Brighton and sprouting corn in Essex add domestic comedy. Readers get a funny, wartime snapshot of British wit under strain.
10594-punch-or-the-london-charivari-volu:
London readers picking up Punch on September 12, 1917, found a wartime issue full of short jokes about soldiers, shortages, and home-front life. Its "Charivaria" column teases the German press, a conscientious objector before a magistrate, and Charlie Chaplin's new American citizenship. Many writers and artists shared the work, as in every number.

The jokes lean on wordplay and dry understatement, turning bad news into brief laughs. A periodical giving away a bicycle and a newspaper giving away a Kaiser are typical of its light touch. The issue now reads as a small, funny record of British spirits in the third year of the First World War.
10595-punch-or-the-london-charivari-volu:
London readers bought this issue of Punch on September 19, 1917, in the third year of the First World War. Punch, the classic British comic weekly, filled each number with short jokes, cartoons, and verse by many hands. War news, food, and transport color the humor, but the tone stays light and sharp.

Short items mock the national anthem, the Stockholm Conference, a stolen church clock, tube fares, and the Thames as a holiday resort. An undertakers' union joke and a note on Mr. Morel add wartime bite. Readers get a funny, telling glimpse of London wit under strain.
10614-punch-or-the-london-charivari-volu:
Punch, or the London Charivari, was a weekly British magazine of jokes, verse, and satire, and this entry holds its issue of September 5, 1917. Britain was then deep in the First World War, and the issue looks at wartime life through short comic notes, mock news, and sharp one-liners. No single author stands behind it; many hands supplied its jokes and drawings.

The opening "Charivaria" column pokes fun at the Kaiser, food shortages, rumors, and daily annoyances in London. Other pieces in the issue keep the same tone, turning war news and home-front hardship into brief laughs. For a modern reader, it works as a snapshot of how Londoners joked about the war while it was still going on.
10663-punch-or-the-london-charivari-volu:
September 26, 1917, brought another wartime number of Punch, the London weekly of satire and jokes. Its "Charivaria" column mocks bandits in Mexico, a campaign against cabbage butterflies, and a Chatham boy who spent a pound on cakes, fish and chips, and ginger pop and then felt unwell. Paper shortage jokes and literary teasing fill the same pages.

The humor is quick and topical, aimed at readers following war news each week. No single author owns the issue; it is the work of the magazine's staff and contributors. As a historical record, it shows what Londoners laughed at while the war dragged into its fourth year.
10711-punch-or-the-london-charivari-volu:
October 3, 1917, brought Punch readers another wartime weekly, with its "Charivaria" column leading the fun. Jokes target rumors about German prisoners escaping on Sundays, the Bishop of London's sermon on fighting another year of war, and Berlin crowds angry at an officer. A captain back in Quebec reports Eskimos who had not heard of the war at all.

The issue keeps Punch's habit of turning grim news into dry, quick jokes, with many contributors sharing the pages. Its satire bites both enemy and home authorities. As history, it records British humor in the autumn of 1917, when the war's end still looked far away.
10721-punch-or-the-london-charivari-volu:
Punch's issue of October 10, 1917, opens its "Charivaria" column with Colonel Roosevelt telling a New York interviewer he cannot be in France and America at once. The magazine dryly doubts he has really tried. Other jokes touch a church conference, a rude Berlin coal merchant, food control in Ireland, and a Belfast woman chewing banknotes.

The number keeps the weekly's wartime mix of short jokes, verse, and satire from many hands. Its targets range from German officials to British churchmen and officials at home. For later readers, it preserves the quick, topical humor Londoners read while the war entered its fourth autumn.
10903-punch-or-the-london-charivari-volu:
London's Punch for October 17, 1917, offers wartime satire at the height of the First World War. Charivaria jokes target the Kaiser, a mutiny of German sailors at Kiel, and the shortage of flour, sugar, and petrol at home. A Shakespeare translation into Turkish, a prize potato contest, and steel helmets for police all become material for short, sharp jokes.

Cartoons and verses add to the mix, including wounded soldiers listening to an excitable lady describe a bomb crater. The humour is topical and confident, assuming readers know the week's news. For modern readers, the issue is a lively record of how Londoners joked about rationing, danger, and enemy blunders while the war continued.
10923-punch-or-the-london-charivari-volu:
London's weekly comic paper for August 29, 1917, catches Britain in the middle of the First World War. Short jokes under the heading Charivaria poke fun at German leaders, wartime shortages, and daily life on the home front. Cartoons, verses, and mock letters fill out the issue, all in the magazine's familiar teasing voice.

Wartime strain runs through the humor, from food rules and munitions work to soldiers on leave and politicians in Parliament. The jokes assume readers follow the news closely, and they turn official claims and enemy boasts into targets. As a snapshot of 1917, the issue shows how satire helped readers laugh at hardship while the war dragged on.
11076-punch-or-the-london-charivari-volu:
London's Punch for October 24, 1917, offers wartime satire with its usual mix of short jokes, verses, and cartoons. Charivaria notes the Duke of Connaught drinking two glasses of government ale at a canteen, a Basuto soldier offering the Lord Mayor's coachman a cigarette.

A long verse follows Mariana, a lethargic girl who throws herself into cooking for the Voluntary Aid Detachment, sacks her gardeners, hires a lady gardener. The humour turns war work into comedy of character. The issue shows how Punch kept London laughing in the war's fourth year, at generals, officials, and itself.
11169-punch-or-the-london-charivari-volu:
London's Punch for August 15, 1917, carries wartime Charivaria. Count Reventlow claims God gave Germany daily bread and daily victory in the heroic days of 1914, and Punch credits the able assistance of the Wolff Bureau. Mr. Winston Churchill's car was run into in a motor collision, which Punch calls not the Antwerp spirit the Munitions Department is waiting for.

A movement honours Dundee for returning Churchill to Parliament after a morning paper asked it not to. Lord Curzon, on the sale of titles, says a wealthy man gives his wealth, very often his only asset, for his country. German sixpenny paper notes, Punch notes, can patch the new paper trousers if nothing can be bought with them. The issue keeps up Punch's wartime habit of puncturing generals, ministers, and enemy propaganda alike.
11425-punch-or-the-london-charivari-volu:
Punch's December 5, 1917 number opens with Charivaria jokes: Justice Bray's warning that bigamy is rampant. answered by the Food Controller refusing sugar rations for more than one wife; a loaf baked in 1821 disposing of claims nobody anticipated the war except Blatchford. lug-worms at Deal as macaroni substitute; a chicken for sixpence in China, return fare to Shanghai extra; and a tramp in three overcoats, two coats, and enormous boots, fit for music hall.

A cow straying onto the line at Acton Bridge supplies another joke. The number shows Punch finding humor in rationing, courts, and wartime absurdity. Its jokes are short, topical, and unsentimental, aimed at readers enduring the war's third Christmas.
11428-punch-or-the-london-charivari-volu:
Punch's November 14, 1917 number opens with Charivaria jokes on wartime Britain: a hidden brain in the Foreign Office, a German posing as a Swiss sentenced as a spy. three men charged with the pot-of-tea trick, bread consumption blamed on the ninepenny loaf. parsnips at their best in taste if not flavor, and seventy tons of blackberries gathered by Buckinghamshire schoolchildren for soldiers' plum-and-apple jam.

A Chertsey woman listing Home Ruler as her occupation on a sugar card supplies another joke. The number shows Punch keeping morale up with small absurdities amid rationing and war news. Its humor is topical and domestic, aimed at readers living the restrictions it mocks.
11443-punch-or-the-london-charivari-volu:
Punch's November 28, 1917 number opens with Charivaria jokes on the war's third winter: how Germans never got wind of the Hindenburg Line attack. perhaps because MPs did not ask about it first; horse chaff composition fixed as pantomime season approaches. Christmas plum-puddings not to be kept, enforced by a Young Patriots' League; another birthplace of St. George captured in Palestine; and a Camberley man deserting the Navy for the Army, tired of waiting for Tirpitz.

A Bronze Age skull on Salisbury Plain and fallen ostrich-feather imports supply further jokes. The number shows Punch mocking bureaucracy, shortages, and military news alike. Its topical humor, read now, maps what ordinary Britons found funny, or at least bearable, in late 1917.
11444-punch-or-the-london-charivari-volu:
Punch's December 12, 1917 number opens with Charivaria jokes: a Hamburg company for oversea enterprises unconnected with the High Sea Fleet. rabbits in the Isle of Wight holding back for a war bonus at a guinea a dozen. a Newcastle man missing eleven months, excusing himself by a long tea queue; brewery workers threatening to down beer. food ships rumored to torpedo themselves rather than fall to profiteers; and Northcliffe refusing, or not refusing, the health ministry.

Double-headed matches, a Norfolk fisherman fined for neglecting seven of twenty-six children by oversight, and Dublin's Lord Mayor on Irish food supply further jokes. The number shows Punch in the rationing winter, finding comedy in queues, controls, and official statements. Its humor is brisk and unsparing.
11466-punch-or-the-london-charivari-volu:
Punch for 19 December 1917 opens with Charivaria, its run of short jokes on the news. Allenby's pledge over holy places in Jerusalem leads the jokes, with the Kaiser planning a manifesto to Turkish subjects. The Sinn Fein leader and a Food Controller pamphlet on cheese follow close behind.

Wartime shortage and ration talk fill the pages, with a painful story from the north of England about a man seeking a pound. Cartoons and verse come next, including a Clyde-built clipper in the Australian wool trade. A sergeant-major puzzling over a barrow man claimed as an archaeological society member adds a final laugh.
11491-punch-or-the-london-charivari-volu:
Punch's October 31, 1917 number opens with Charivaria jokes: the Ministry of Food ruling a doughnut is not a bun, allaying Twickenham unrest; grocers asking Monday orders for delivery within a week. while telegrams arrive as fast without restrictions; no more London hotels to be commandeered, though a spectacular spring offensive is prepared. and escaped German internees recaptured easily, supposedly unable to bear Britons' sacrifices for their feeding.

The Globe's End of the World article, Churchill's unannounced air appointment, and a Daily Telegraph scoop dating Hastings to October 14, 1066, at nine a. m. , supply further jokes. Allotment pumpkins, including a six-foot Burwash specimen, close the column's humor. The number shows wartime Punch at its most domestic and wry.
11570-punch-or-the-london-charivari-volu:
Punch for 7 November 1917 opens with Charivaria on the news. The Berliner Tageblatt praises Chancellor Michaelis, and then he goes. A Daily Mail quarrel with a neutral country follows.

A Highgate man is fined for feeding a pleasure horse on oats. A ratcatcher is granted sugar for his poisoned rats. The joke turns on rats refusing to forego poison in wartime. Verse follows on sticking to rations, with Sir Arthur Yapp as the man who must be obeyed. A cartoon shows England and France at bay. The issue is wartime Punch at its most topical.
11619-punch-or-the-london-charivari-volu:
Punch for 21 November 1917 opens with Charivaria on the news. More than a million pounds of concealed sugar was found in New York. Lenin's rush for leadership in Russia is mocked with revolvers. Colonel House calls for action, not talk.

Restaurant keepers agree to stamp beefsteak prices on the sole, the joke runs. Parliamentary notes follow in the same number. The House of Lords falls back on sugar substitutes for jam. Barley for beer is discussed as well. The Duke of Marlborough reports care over arsenic in glucose. Lord Rhondda promises barley for cakes and ale.
11629-punch-or-the-london-charivari-volu:
Punch for 26 December 1917 opens with Charivaria on the war. Von Tirpitz speaks of keeping cool, and a long-suffering Fatherland agrees. A Berlin message says Jerusalem was evacuated lest battles be fought over sacred ground.

An American picture sixty feet by nineteen is called the largest miniature ever painted. A tribunal applicant asks six more months of exemption. He has a wife and a place in a butter queue to maintain. Parliamentary notes follow, with Lord Burnham defending proportional representation. He fears the press may grow too powerful without it. A queue for the Commons is drawn as well.
11638-punch-or-the-london-charivari-volu:
Punch for 18 July 1917 opens with Charivaria on the war. The Emperor of China, it reports, has joined the Boy Scout movement. Charlie Chaplin is said to be joining the Army on the Allied side.

Other jokes follow fast. A baker is fined for selling overweight war bread. German cigars are now made of cabbage or hay with strawberry leaves. Lord Selborne notes six small farmers sending six small carts to one station. Metropolitan magistrates, the magazine fears, are losing their edge. Parliamentary notes close the number, with air raids still echoing in the House.
11704-punch-or-the-london-charivari-volu:
Punch for 25 July 1917 opens with Charivaria on the Admiralty and paper yarns. A music-hall comedian is said never to have joked about the mess in Mesopotamia. A tope of thirty-nine pounds caught at Hastings stands in for the sea serpent, absent that year.

The Food Controller calls for strict economy in the use of ice. Parliamentary notes follow in the same number, with Mister Ginnell returning to Westminster. He plans to watch over the growth of the Sinn Fein republic after weeks away. The issue is wartime Punch in full voice, turning shortages, Parliament, and rumour into short jokes for readers at home.
11910-punch-or-the-london-charivari-volu:
Dated August 8, 1917, this wartime Punch opens with a Charivaria joke that no amount of War Office approval will make hens lay. The issue keeps its humor close to home-front life, where shortages, official notices, and everyday absurdities supplied the jokes.

Private Tiddy, a former plumber turned soldier, provides one comic thread: besides his wife, his great passion is letter-writing, pursued at every possible and impossible moment. Verses about welcoming a shy young soldier home, and presenting him with a bat, close the picture of a magazine sustaining morale with jokes rather than solemn editorials.
11992-a-residence-in-france-during-the-y:
This portion of A Residence in France, letters from an English lady prepared by John Gifford, was printed for Longman in 1797. It opens with preliminary remarks by the editor and the letters of 1792. Gifford writes that the letters were submitted to his inspection by an author of high principles and abilities. Her important facts might throw light on France. Early letters include a visit, by municipal order, to the gardens and palace of an emigrated bishop. His garden, large and laid out in the old style, had once been open for public enjoyment.

The volume's value lies in such firsthand detail: a foreign resident watching revolution remake gardens, palaces, and daily life in France.
11993-a-residence-in-france-during-the-y:
A Residence in France, prepared for the press by John Gifford and described as letters from an English lady, covers the revolutionary years 1792 to 1795. It adds remarks on French character and manners. The second edition carries a French epigraph: the more I see the foreigner, the more I love my country.

Early letters reflect on vanity uncorrected by sound judgment, prompted by the Anglo-Gallican legislator Thomas Paine and a speech he lately composed. Through the lady's eyes, Parisian politics, social life, and the habits of a nation in revolution appear as daily experience. They are not a historian's summary, which gives the volume its value as contemporary testimony.
11994-a-residence-in-france-during-the-y:
This portion of A Residence in France, letters from an English lady prepared by John Gifford, opens with a letter dated January 6, 1794. In it, the English lady confesses that following the French revolution through all its absurdities and iniquities has become too difficult and laborious a task. Events, she writes, are now too numerous and complicated for occasional remarks, and a narrator of no more pretensions than herself may shrink from the abundance.

Later passages record the repeal of the law of the twenty-second of Prairial, while the Revolutionary Tribunal is preserved. The old jury, as creatures of Robespierre, is suspended. The letters thus track the Thermidorian reaction from inside France, as terror's machinery is dismantled piece by piece, but not yet abolished.
11995-a-residence-in-france-during-the-y:
This portion of A Residence in France, letters from an English lady prepared by John Gifford, continues the account of revolutionary France through 1792 to 1795. The volume shares the series' second-edition form and its epigraph on loving one's country more the longer one lives abroad.

Its pages dwell on the machinery of revolution. They note that a fourth part of the members of the committees changed every month, a regulation more advantageous to the Convention than to the people. Such rotation kept animosities alive and stimulated ambition. It left the country in anxiety, since no one could guess what system the next month might adopt, a precise, contemporary observation of unstable government.
11996-a-residence-in-france-during-the-y:
This long portion of A Residence in France, letters from an English lady prepared by John Gifford, was printed in 1797. It runs to some two hundred thousand words, far longer than the separate yearly portions. Its editor's preliminary remarks present letters submitted by an author of high principles and abilities, whose facts might throw strong light on revolutionary France.

Midway, the writer contrasts French and English domestic life, noting that gilding, painting, glasses, and silk hangings disguise apartments. Those apartments often lack a single room an Englishman would find tolerably convenient, while solid comforts are sacrificed to vanity. The length allows a fuller picture: manners, houses, politics, and daily life across the revolutionary years, in one continuous correspondence.
12043-punch-or-the-london-charivari-volu:
Punch's August 1, 1917 issue opens Charivaria with the imperial aspirations of King Ferdinand, discussed by a Frankfort paper in an article entitled What Bulgaria Wants. Punch notes, significantly, that the ground covered is almost identical with its own unpublished article, What Bulgaria Won't Get.

A cow that walked down sixteen stairs into a cellar supplies one wartime absurdity. Ariding lesson gives another: shorten your reins, heels down, heads up, hollow your backs, four feet from nose to croup, and get off that mare's neck, Number Seven. Notes on ministers' salaries, including a thinking part at five thousand a year, close a number that laughs at war, bureaucracy, and Bulgaria together.
12567-the-mirror-of-literature-amusement:
A February 1831 Mirror number, volume seventeen, number 476, leads with Lord Byron's palace at Venice, illustrated. Scores of readers journeying through Moore's concluding Life of Byron will thank the Mirror for the view, showing the palace Byron occupied during his Venetian residence.

After an unfortunate marriage, Byron left England in search of peace of mind never destined to be his. Venice, loved from boyhood, offered poetry in situation, habits and history, exciting imagination and curiosity. The article follows Byron's Venetian years through Moore's biography. The number shows the Mirror feeding Byron fever, a palace pictured for readers of a life.
12568-the-mirror-of-literature-amusement:
Dated 19 February 1831, this Mirror number leads with Mount St. Michael in Normandy, illustrated in print. The Mount, at the southern end of ancient Normandy, is one mass of granite. Geologists call it a fine specimen of primary rock, widely spread in the lowest situation and holding no remains of a former world.

Popular interest, the editor says, fully justifies its place in the pages, joining natural curiosity to history. Short articles and engravings around it keep the weekly's twopenny mix. The number shows the Mirror turning a famous rock, abbey and tide into a brief, pictured lesson for London readers.
12575-the-mirror-of-literature-amusement:
A January 1831 Mirror number, volume seventeen, number 471, leads with the Castle of Vincennes, illustrated. Readers versed in recent history, the editor says, will appreciate the choice. Its pictorial and historical interest cannot be matched except in contrast: a gloomy, wretched-looking building against a beautiful landscape of dancing life and bustle.

Spectators may reflect on damning deeds of cruelty and ambition inside the castle, then turn for relief to gaiety outside, and confess the composition abounds in lights and shadows. The article then explains Vincennes more fully. The number shows the Mirror using a French castle to teach recent history in a single engraving.
12576-the-mirror-of-literature-amusement:
Dated 26 February 1831, this Mirror number leads with autographs of eminent persons, selected from an engraved plate of forty-three signatures. The plate came with the Edinburgh Literary Journal, prefixed to a chapter on the connection between character and handwriting, from which the Mirror selects anecdotal traits.

A Shenstone motto from earlier volumes frames the piece: the writer wants to see Mrs. Jago's handwriting, to judge her temper. Anne Grant and other names appear among the hands. The number shows a popular belief of the age, that a signature betrays character, turned into a parlour game for readers.
12597-the-mirror-of-literature-amusement:
A March 1831 Mirror number, volume seventeen, number 480, leads with Swan River in Western Australia, illustrated from a hill intended as a fort site. The view, a mile and a quarter from the river mouth, shows Garden Island on the left in distance and Pulo Carnac to its right. Between them lies the only known entrance for shipping into Cockburn Sound.

Anchorage lies off the island, and the Swan River mouth stands on the right. The article guides London readers through a new colony's geography, in picture and text. The number shows the Mirror reporting empire as scenery, a distant river made familiar by engraving and careful description.
12598-the-mirror-of-literature-amusement:
Dated 19 March 1831, this Mirror number leads with relics of Ariosto, poet of Orlando, preserved at Ferrara. An inkstand and a chair, illustrated, are kept with reverential care at the poet's favourite residence, though not his birthplace. The Ferrarese claim him exclusively as their own, Byron notes in Childe Harold, as the Homer, not of Italy alone, but of romance.

Trivial, fond relics become consecrated memorials in the Mirror's telling, letting readers touch a poet through his things. Short pieces around them keep the weekly mix. The number shows literary tourism in print, a shrine described for readers who might one day make the pilgrimage themselves.
12599-the-mirror-of-literature-amusement:
A March 1831 Mirror number, volume seventeen, number 482, leads with Bray Church, illustrated with a goodly tower. Who has not heard of the Vicar of Bray, and his turning, turning and turning again, the article asks, presenting his church to the Mirror's pages in turn.

No sinister motive guides the choice, the editor says. If the piece hits the white, or rather black, of such variableness, let the galled jade wince and pay the Mirror its stale compliment, veluti in speculum. Bray, a small village a mile from Maidenhead, gives the proverb a place. The number shows the Mirror turning a byword into topography, a church pictured for readers who knew the song.
12618-the-mirror-of-literature-amusement:
A January 1831 Mirror number, volume seventeen, number 472, leads with Christ Church, Doncaster, illustrated from the Gentleman's Magazine. Doncaster, long celebrated for beauty and cleanliness, a striking southern approach, grand stand, race course, public buildings, venerable Gothic church and stately tower, gains a new Gothic church with an elegant spire.

Founded and endowed by a benevolent individual named Jarrett, whose ancestors long connected with the town, the church adds a feature from every approach. A monument in the old church notes a founder's brother as alderman. The number shows the Mirror praising a provincial town's new church, in the language of civic pride.
12619-the-mirror-of-literature-amusement:
Dated 29 January 1831, this Mirror number leads with the Strand, ancient and modern, illustrated from Arundel House, with Strand Cross, Covent Garden and a procession of Edward VI in 1547. Inscriptions copied from the engravings frame the article, which looks northward past maypole and garland.

Earlier volumes had touched Covent Garden and the Strand, and this number continues that antiquarian topography. Readers meet a London street across three centuries, in picture and note. The Mirror's method shows here at its best: a familiar street made strange by history, told briefly for a twopenny audience.
12634-the-mirror-of-literature-amusement:
A May 1831 Mirror number, volume seventeen, number 489, leads with St. George's Hospital at Hyde Park Corner, illustrated in elevation. All who enjoy doing good, the editor says, will welcome a splendid monument of British benevolence, already built. It is only part of an original plan that will add another front toward Hyde Park.

St. George's was set on foot soon after Michaelmas 1733, by gentlemen before concerned in a like charity in lower Westminster. They chose the house for air, situation and nearness to town. The article mixes charity history with architecture. The number shows the Mirror praising a hospital as civic art, and benevolence as a London virtue.
12645-the-mirror-of-literature-amusement:
An April 1831 Mirror number, volume seventeen, number 483, opens on a grotto at Ascot Place, illustrated as a picturesque contrivance of art embellishing nature. The writer has seen many such labours, but none with more satisfaction. Ascot Place lies in Surrey, five miles south-east of Windsor, beside Ascot Heath near Winkfield.

Andrew Lindergreen built the residence, later sold to Daniel Agace, who showed taste in arranging grounds. A brick house with wings stands on a lawn, where a circular Corinthian temple pleases the eye. The grotto, gem of the estate, sits at the end of a canal through the grounds, a labour of leisure on which much expense and good taste were spent.
12650-the-mirror-of-literature-amusement:
A May 1831 Mirror number, volume seventeen, number 488, opens on St. George's Chapel, Windsor, illustrated as a venerable structure in the lower ward of the castle. An earlier number had explained its place: it stands in the centre, dividing the court into two parts.

North and inner side houses hold the Dean and Canons, minor canons, clerks and officers. South and west sides of the outer court hold houses of other officers and residents. The article continues a series on Windsor, pairing picture with description. The number shows the Mirror guiding readers through a royal chapel, court by court, in its accessible antiquarian style.
12676-the-mirror-of-literature-amusement:
A May 1831 Mirror number, volume seventeen, number 490, leads with an old house in Southwark, illustrated. The crazy but not unpicturesque building was taken down in autumn of the previous year, forming an approach to the new London Bridge. It stood on the eastern side of High Street, worthy of record among pleasing relics of antiquity.

Its style, that of Henry VII, shows florid picturesqueness in carvings on first and second stories, probably once extending to upper stories later covered with plaster. The writer remembers the house for twenty years, tracing no other change in its front. The number shows the Mirror rescuing a doomed house from oblivion, in print, just as the bridge approach erased it.
12685-the-mirror-of-literature-amusement:
This supplementary number of the Mirror, from the spring of 1831, leads with a long review of Thomas Moore's second volume of Byron's letters and journals. The reviewer admits that letters resist summary, since their charm lies in manner and wit more than in matter. Byron's gay, anecdotal style draws praise throughout.

The number also prints extracts chosen to show Byron among friends and rivals, including sharp, drunken scenes with figures like Porson and Sheridan. Readers get gossip, judgment, and literary talk in the magazine's usual easy mix. The issue shows how Byron's private voice reached the public only a few years after his death.
12766-the-mirror-of-literature-amusement:
Dated Saturday, April 9, 1831, this issue of a cheap London weekly mixes history, travel, and short essays for general readers. Its lead piece gives the early history of Corfe Castle in Dorset, from its roots before the Norman Conquest to its later grants to princes and favourites. Notes on towns, customs, and natural curiosities fill out the number.

Other items turn to questions of daily life and morals, including a sharp protest against cruelty to animals in sport and show. The tone is plain and chatty, aimed at readers who wanted a little learning with their weekend reading. As a single issue it gives a good taste of what a penny miscellany offered in 1831.
12781-the-mirror-of-literature-amusement:
Dated Saturday, April 16, 1831, this weekly number opens at Mocha, the Red Sea coffee port in Arabia Felix. White houses, flat roofs, and mosque minarets frame a town whose trade in fine coffee gave the drink its famous name. Lord Valentia's earlier visit supplies much of the detail.

The rest of the issue ranges widely, from notes on old hunting and forest roads to short questions and answers on history and custom. Like its sister numbers, it packs a lot of light learning into a few pages at two pence. Readers get a snapshot of what curious Londoners read for pleasure in the spring of 1831.
12965-the-mirror-of-literature-amusement:
Dated Saturday, April 23, 1831, this Mirror number opens a series on Windsor Castle, starting with George IV's gateway from the quadrangle. The writer hopes to show how recent renovations improve the old splendour of the pile, just as summer visitors are expected to double. Under the late king the castle had resembled one vast solitude, broken only by occasional banquets.

A painting review follows, praising a small canvas where sun, guard-ship sail, and quiet water stir deep feeling, with Byron's ode to Napoleon in exile flitting through memory. The issue blends royal architecture with art criticism. It gives a pleasant taste of the weekly's range.
12966-the-mirror-of-literature-amusement:
The Mirror of Literature, Amusement, and Instruction, volume 17, is the April 30, 1831 issue of a cheap weekly miscellany, priced at two pence. It opens at Wrington in Somersetshire, where John Locke was born on August 29, 1632. The cottage by the churchyard is now split into tenements, one room used as a school.

Short pieces follow on science and daily life, such as why some bodies float more easily than others and why ice cools wine best at the top of the bottle. The mix of biography, natural fact, and useful hints gives a clear picture of what a popular 1831 reader met each Saturday.
13090-the-mirror-of-literature-amusement:
Number 494 of The Mirror of Literature, Amusement, and Instruction, dated Saturday, June 18, 1831, cost two pence and mixed fact with fun. Its opening piece describes Exeter Hall in the Strand, a new home for philanthropic societies, praised as a model building with a modest Corinthian doorway. Short essays, anecdotes, and verse follow in the magazine's usual miscellany.

One essay gives blunt rules for social calls, warning late guests and urging a card the day after a party. A grim comic poem haggles over the price of digging a grave, man by man, shilling by shilling. The number is a small window on early Victorian taste: earnest improvement, polite manners, and a taste for odd facts, all sold cheap to a wide readership.
13108-the-mirror-of-literature-amusement:
Number 492 of The Mirror, dated June 4, 1831, opens with three boroughs marked for disfranchisement by the Reform Bill: Dunwich, Old Sarum, and Bramber. The editor calls the ground ticklish, yet gives their topographical history with help from Oldfield's History of the Boroughs. Parliamentary history is touched, but their future fate is left to the movers of government.

Other pages trace Paul's Cross, a timber pulpit cross on stone steps, in use as early as 1259 when Henry III made boys swear before him. A closing life praises a man who died at ninety-two, his grave watered by tears of those his bounty fed. The number mixes reform politics, old London, and moral biography in the Mirror's usual cheap miscellany.
13113-the-mirror-of-literature-amusement:
Number 495 of The Mirror, dated June 25, 1831, again sells for two pence and mixes pictures, history, and tales. Its opening piece describes the Hermitage at Frogmore, a royal retreat bought by Queen Charlotte in 1792, with grounds laid out by Uvedale Price. Short items follow on books, wealth, and odd facts of the past.

One tale follows Osmyn, a writer who waits years at Baghdad for notice, until his pastilles at last draw eyes. Another note reckons Henry VII's hoard at near 1,800,000 pounds, kept under his own key at Richmond. The number is typical of the Mirror's charm: cheap, varied, and eager to feed a reader's curiosity in a single sitting.
13199-the-mirror-of-literature-amusement:
Number 469 of The Mirror, dated January 1, 1831, opens with Petrarch and Arquà, Ariosto, Tasso, and Ferrara, names linked in Italian poetry. Byron, the piece notes, halted at those consecrated spots on his pilgrimage through the land of song, where Laura's lover lies in a tomb reared in air. An engraving by Prout fronts the number.

Other pages describe copper country scorched by sulphur smoke, with a canal of sixteen miles, thirty-six locks, and millions of tons of slag. A review contrasts a didactic pilgrim's guide, heavy with instruction, with Bunyan's lively Pilgrim's Progress. The number is a New Year's miscellany, literary, industrial, and curious in equal parts.
13382-the-mirror-of-literature-amusement:
The Mirror of Literature for June 27, 1831, opens with a portrait of Baron Brougham and Vaux. Lord High Chancellor, and promises original essays, historical narratives, biographical memoirs, sketches of society, topography, novels, anecdotes, and poetry. Published by J. Limbird in the Strand, it sold for two pence a week.

Inside, a narrator weighs duty to country against the dazzle of high office, seeking a field where honesty and consistency can work. A long sketch of Brougham judges him a powerful but alarming debater, whose flood of detail loses the spirit of the question for listeners. The number shows a cheap miscellany serving readers who wanted news, learning, and entertainment together.
13495-the-mirror-of-literature-amusement:
The Mirror of Literature for January 8, 1831, opens at Chichester, a city of higher antiquity than most in Britain. Ella destroyed it in the fifth century, and his son Cissa rebuilt it and named it for himself. Its cathedral, churches, and Cross draw antiquaries, and the Cross is described at length from the Beauties of England and Wales.

Later pages follow Scott at Abbotsford, receiving two tiny Shetland ponies from a northern chieftain. A traveller's Alpine journal rises at six and journeys at nearly three thousand feet above the sea. The Mirror keeps its usual blend: town history, literary anecdote, and travel notes, all for two pence on a Saturday.
13829-the-mirror-of-literature-amusement:
The Mirror of Literature, Amusement, and Instruction for February 5, 1831, offers cheap weekly variety at twopence. Its lead piece describes Princess Elizabeth's cottage at Windsor, a modest home for a royal resident. Readers learn how rural ease contrasted with court pomp. Other items mix tales, history, and curious facts.

A story of Thomas and a farm family by the fireside follows, with talk of night rules and local custom. The Mirror aimed to entertain and instruct working and middle-class readers. Short articles, pictures, and anecdotes fill each number. This issue captures early Victorian popular publishing. It shows what ordinary readers enjoyed before cheap novels spread.
13903-punch-or-the-london-charivari-volu:
Punch for January 3, 1917, opens with More Discipline, a soldier's tale of drill. Sergeant Wally, accepting a cigarette and readjusting a wounded leg, praises discipline as the making of a reliable soldier. He recalls a recruit week on the square, called out by a drill sergeant for standing about. The joke turns on smartness and folly.

Other pieces debate war schemes, with evening talkers claiming more knowledge than they supposed. Casualty allowances grow as pet schemes gain merit. Punch's wartime humour mixes barrack talk with home-front satire. The issue captures Britain in the middle of war. It offers laughs and a record of public feeling.
13935-the-mirror-of-literature-amusement:
The Mirror for May 28, 1831, opens with Ampthill House, seat of Lord Holland. The writer calls it a delightful retreat for a statesman and man of letters. Ampthill's romantic beauties, sung in verse, surround the house. The issue costs twopence and mixes pictures with short articles.

An album piece follows, noting varied minds on its pages: Hood's comic strain, Campbell's pure taste, and another writer's fire. The Mirror aimed to amuse and instruct a wide readership. Short, varied items suited weekly reading. This number shows early Victorian magazine culture at its most polite. It offers a pleasant glimpse of literary society.
13966-punch-or-the-london-charivari-volu:
Punch for January 17, 1917, opens its Charivaria with wartime jokes. An evening paper announces time to deal finally with Tino, King Constantine of Greece. The Berliner Tageblatt grants the king as much right to be heard as a common criminal, and Punch agrees, noting few friends put it so bluntly. The Lokalanzeiger praises the blockade as a refiner of German figures.

Later dialogue jokes about court-martial and jumping up rigid when Fred enters a room. Punch's wartime satire targets enemies and home absurdities alike. The issue shows Britain laughing under strain. Short pieces and cartoons carry the humour. It offers a sharp sample of 1917 Punch.
14022-the-mirror-of-literature-amusement:
The Mirror for March 5, 1831, leads with the ancient palace of Holyrood at Edinburgh. Holyrood sheltered fallen royalty, a haven where flattery's plain reproof asked how a king could claim his title. The palace's history of queens, exiles, and courts fills the sketch. An illustration pictures its old walls.

Other pieces in the number touch ancient slavery in England and London streets, where Chancery Lane gapes for unwary travellers. The Mirror mixed topography with anecdote at twopence a week. Its short articles suited family reading. This issue shows Edinburgh and London in popular print. It offers a pleasant antiquarian sample.
14093-punch-or-the-london-charivari-volu:
January 24, 1917, opened Punch with Greenland jokes and food control. A Dane reports that Greenland knows nothing of the war, while its governor learns of a hymn called From Greenland's Icy Mountains and plans to tell the local publicity committee. Lord Devonport sets up his own press bureau, and the American Line advances its prices. Wartime absurdity gets the full Punch treatment.

Classical spoof crowns the number. Stop-press news reports Horatius cut off at the bridge, with Lartius and Herminius withdrawn and casualties counted: enemy seven killed, Roman one wounded, a lictor having sliced himself with his own axe. A later edition saves Horatius, who swims the river. A Gallipoli mother's tale closes the run, as Le Havre becomes Leeharver in her telling. Satire, schoolroom Latin, and home-front talk blend into one wartime weekly.
14135-punch-or-the-london-charivari-volu:
January 10, 1917, found Punch in wartime mood, joking about curtailed trains and new Treasury notes. Charivaria notes that some southern lines run no trains except those started before New Year's Day. Treasury notes may soon carry the House of Commons, with the Crystal Palace and Imperial Institute to follow. Germany, the jokes add, now enrolls criminals for service.

Soldiers' humor anchors the number. An Irishman drags a goat mascot, reeking of scent, before enemy dogs, and the beast outruns them to the rabbit holes before being bayed. Press cuttings mock raised fares, a civic cat for sale, and Asquith's modest admirer. Short, sharp, and topical, the issue shows a magazine keeping spirits up while war narrows daily life to trains, prices, and rumors from the front.
14230-the-mirror-of-literature-amusement:
June 11, 1831, brought Mirror number 493, priced at two pence, opening at Virginia Water's boat-house. Lakers and lovers of the picturesque flock to its banks, now open to the public, though prize-fighters once trained in secluded alleys and profaned the lake. Rides and walks invite summer visitors, with a warning not to abuse the privilege as of old.

Cholera news fills the graver pages. A Cossack buying food at Doubooka dies after returning to Katchalinskaia, and disease spreads through Cossack villages to Novitcherkask and Taganrog. Fugitives carry it toward Persia and Moscow, where a student from Saratoff, whose servant died on the road, becomes the capital's first victim. Goods never traced the spread, the report stresses; only the presence of sick individuals did. A Fleet Street tale closes the number, as Frank meets a pompous, kindly gentleman and a drunken man struggling to say obligated.
14450-punch-or-the-london-charivari-volu:
Wartime London fills this Punch issue of February 7, 1917, where jokes about the Kaiser, food shortages, and the trenches sit beside cartoons of home-front life. The magazine's short Charivaria column fires off one-liners on German politics and Allied news.

Longer pieces include a comic dialogue about servants, verses on food production, and letters from Macedonia. The tone is defiant rather than despairing, mocking the enemy while nudging readers to endure rationing and cold. As a weekly record, the issue shows British humor under strain, still sharp after two and a half years of war.
14455-punch-or-the-london-charivari-volu:
By March 21, 1917, Punch was joking through shortages, and this issue turns food, fuel, and the Kaiser into steady targets. Its Charivaria notes report a convict said to resemble the Kaiser, a turnip wounding a policeman, and an opera singer paid in eggs.

The Mud-Larks series returns with trench humor, while other pieces offer children's tales for grown-ups and verses on herbs and home life. The laughter is pointed but humane, aimed at keeping spirits up. The issue reads as a morale bulletin in comic form, from a nation deep into total war.
14516-punch-or-the-london-charivari-volu:
January 31, 1917, brought Punch readers another wartime bundle, with Charivaria joking about Berlin's falling birth rate, German films of the Somme, and bathless days the army declined to order. The jokes bite without cruelty.

A comic playlet sends a rich suitor and a soldier rival after the same heroine, while heart-to-heart talks and government satire fill other pages. The issue balances home-front grumbling with trench humor. It shows a magazine keeping its nerve in the war's third winter, laughing at the enemy and at Whitehall alike. Readers then relied on Punch for a weekly laugh.
14639-punch-or-the-london-charivari-volu:
February 28, 1917, brought Punch readers Charivaria jokes on the Kaiser's horror of premature burial and Hindenburg blaming a Bavarian prince. A paper shortage left a news editor begging for spring flower notices, and the shortage itself became a running joke.

Other pages ask what a certain Somebody is doing, in verses on ploughing, verse, lecturing, and holy orders, while broken soldiers and a tragedy of the sea add gravity. The issue balances wartime satire with home-front detail. It shows Punch in its third war year, still finding jokes in shortages and generals.
14767-punch-or-the-london-charivari-volu:
Punch for 21 February 1917 offers wartime satire at full stretch, in a short weekly number from the middle of the First World War. Its Charivaria column fires off jokes on Count Bernstorff's departure from America, shots fired at Count Tisza in the Hungarian Diet, and a liquorice factory changing hands in despatches from Kut.

Other items mock German clothing rules, soup-coloured waistcoats and the claims of the Cologne Gazette about the Western Front. Cartoons and verses, in the magazine's usual mix, carry the same targets. The issue shows Punch doing what it did best in wartime: turning grim news into pointed, topical laughter for readers at home.
14769-punch-or-the-london-charivari-volu:
April 1917 finds Punch still at war, and its Charivaria column still finding jokes in hard news. How America's army will assist the Allies is undecided, so President Wilson will welcome suggestions from halfpenny morning papers, the magazine notes with a straight face.

A military absentee who dined well in London and did not mind returning to the trenches wisely keeps the restaurant's name secret. Reports place Venizelos in London, then deny it, while revue managers, asked to shorten shows, sacrifice both jokes in despair. The British Association cancels its meeting for travel reasons. Wartime Britain, in short, laughs to keep steady.
14856-punch-or-the-london-charivari-volu:
Punch for 28 March 1917 opens with a torpedoed mine-sweeper telling his pal that submarine men face a less risky job than boys in aeroplanes. Charivaria follows with a Kingston man charged as an absentee who said he did not know the country was at war, and grew interested on learning the enemy was Germany.

Hamburg hotel keepers abolish extra charges for meals without wine or beer, for the simple reason that there is no wine or beer to consume. A judge remarks that lawyers live because laymen hold such queer ideas. The issue mixes service humour, home-front jokes and courtroom wit, all in Punch's wartime shorthand.
14966-punch-or-the-london-charivari-volu:
Charivaria in Punch for 7 March 1917 quotes Mr. Justice Bray. A motor car repairer is like a plumber, he says. Once you get him into the house you cannot get him out, unless you show him a burst bath pipe. Then he goes out to fetch his mate.

Herr Wildrube of the Reichstag urges Germans to rejoice at the departure of Mr. Gerard and his pro-Entente espionage bureau, and Punch notes America has rubes but nothing quite so wild. An historical film called The Discovery of Germany is exhibited widely through France, or so the joke runs. The issue is wartime Punch at its shortest: one-line jokes on repairmen, politicians and propaganda.
14974-punch-or-the-london-charivari-volu:
Charivaria in Punch for 4 April 1917 notes the Kaiser has conferred the Order of the Black Eagle on the Turkish Grand Vizier, who has had persistent bad luck. A few weeks earlier, Mr. Robert Blatchford asked what manner of man the Tsar is, and now the Tsar has abdicated, absolving Blatchford from blame.

An Amsterdam rumour that eighty thousand German soldiers had surrendered is followed next day by a report that it was really ninety thousand, a recount having been demanded. The Evening News, ever ready with news, completes the column. Punch's wartime jokes turn abdication, honours and rumour into short, sharp paragraphs for readers following a confusing war.
15012-punch-or-the-london-charivari-volu:
London's famed comic weekly turns its wit on the First World War in this March 1917 issue, printed while the fighting still raged. Short jokes, mock news items, and sharp cartoons take aim at German leaders, wartime shortages, and home-front fuss. The humor is brisk, topical, and firmly on Britain's side.

Charivaria opens the number with one-line cracks about food prices, the Kaiser, and rumors from the front. Longer comic pieces and drawings follow, poking fun at politicians, profiteers, and everyday wartime life. For a modern reader, the issue works both as comedy and as a record of how London laughed through a hard spring.
15021-punch-or-the-london-charivari-volu:
Another wartime number of London's comic weekly, dated April 1917, keeps its jokes aimed squarely at Germany and at British life under strain. One-line squibs, mock reports, and cartoons fill the pages, with food prices, drink rules, and home-front grumbles as steady targets. The tone stays jaunty even as the war drags on.

Items mock the Kaiser's allies, new German trench lines with grand mythic names, and the small vanities of daily life. A child's boast about his illnesses draws a laugh of a different kind. Read now, the issue shows how satire helped London readers bear shortages, rumors, and bad news week after week.
15064-punch-or-the-london-charivari-volu:
Late April 1917 finds Punch still joking through war, with this issue's squibs aimed at occupied France, German boasts, and London life. Short items mock a German paper's claim that German grows popular under occupation, and answer a claim that the British offensive has stalled. A zoo visit supplies a sharper joke.

Longer comic pieces and cartoons round out the number, keeping the weekly's mix of news parody and social satire. The humor leans hard on wartime feeling, and some cracks now read as cruel. Even so, the issue shows how a famous comic paper kept its readers laughing in a grim year.
15121-punch-or-the-london-charivari-volu:
May 1917 brings America freshly into the war, and Punch greets the new ally with jokes about flag days, Ireland, and Mexico. Charivaria notes that New York will hold its first flag day in June, and it teases the notion of swapping problems across the Atlantic. The Kaiser's court architect gets a dry obituary joke.

Other squibs take up mice eating whole haystacks in Australia and the need for a state cat in each rural area. The humor stays loyal, light, and topical, even as the war grinds on. Read now, the issue shows how London welcomed America with laughter rather than solemn speeches.
15313-a-full-enquiry-into-the-nature-of-:
Thomas Purney's Full Enquiry into the True Nature of Pastoral, first printed in 1717, appears here in an Augustan Reprint Society edition of 1948, with an introduction by Earl Wasserman. The essay belongs to a series on poetry, priced at a dollar, and edited by scholars at Michigan and California.

Purney asks what pastoral poetry truly is, how shepherds should speak, and what subjects suit the form. His answers shaped Augustan debate on simplicity and artifice. Students of eighteenth-century criticism will find the enquiry short, clear, and valuable for its period theory.
15330-punch-or-the-london-charivari-volu:
Punch's May 9, 1917 issue opens Charivaria with a Rome report. Hindenburg wants royal princes removed from the West Front, since moving the front further west to shield them has been dropped. A German paper calls the late Bissing an angel of mercy, to the Kaiser's wonder at who started the scandal.

Other squibs take up the Mercantile Marine, bread tickets, and Highland sheep raisers, with cartoons to match. The humor stays sharp and loyal, even as war news stays grim. Modern readers can see, in one weekly number, how London joked through a hard spring of war.
15358-the-great-round-world-and-what-is-:
Dated March 4, 1897, this seventeenth number of The Great Round World, a weekly paper for boys and girls, costs five cents. Publisher Harison, at West 18th Street, offers prize competitions open to subscribers only, for the best commercial maps of the United States. Klemm's relief map serves as the base.

Five prizes, each a book costing no more than two dollars fifty, await winners who draw maps without help. News and school notes fill the rest. The issue shows a children's paper teaching geography through prizes and play. Young history buffs will enjoy its bright, earnest style.
15377-punch-or-the-london-charivari-volu:
This Punch number, dated May 16, 1917, comes from the middle of the First World War, and its jokes bite at the German enemy. The opening Charivaria notes mock counterfeit bread tickets found in Berlin, vanished pigs in Germany, and boastful quotes from Bavarian and German princes. Each item lands in a few sharp lines.

Later pages review books, including a volume of short stories by Marjorie Bowen set in the eighteenth century, praised for costume detail and one haunting tale. The mix shows Punch in wartime form: short satire, verse, and reviews, all aimed at keeping British readers amused and confident. Its humor now reads as a record of home-front feeling, confident, mocking, and very much of its moment.
15512-punch-or-the-london-charivari-volu:
This Punch number, dated May 23, 1917, opens with Charivaria, short wartime jokes in the magazine's brisk style. William Watson's new verse book is mocked as an intermittent commentary on the war, with a jab at the Dardanelles Commission. Weeds puzzle the amateur gardener, who is advised to pull them out and see if they return.

Other items tease a revue producer, confuse an explosives committee with an expletives committee supplied with sulphur from the front, and note a water board appeal against waste. Later pages follow Jeanne and little Polish children sharing toys, a tender wartime scene amid the jokes. The number shows Punch in 1917: satire, wordplay, and small human touches, keeping readers amused while war filled every other page.
15657-punch-or-the-london-charivari-volu:
Punch, or the London Charivari, volume 152, for June 6, 1917, opens with Charivaria, its column of short wartime jokes. A press campaign against young men of military age in offices is said to cause sleepless days. A correspondent reports record heat by his thermometer, and Punch supposes the censor's example over the Folkestone raid explains why nobody can keep a secret.

A movement is on foot to present Italy with a monument to Shakespeare in Rome, though sending George Bernard Shaw to become a naturalized Italian seems less well received. Lord Cowdray presided at a lecture on flying after the war, and most people will wait till it comes by again. Kennedy Jones declared beer a food, which should help those who mistook it for a pigment. An artist was arrested for sketching on the East Coast, since mapping is dangerous in these times. The number jokes through war's third year.
15688-punch-or-the-london-charivari-volu:
Punch, or the London Charivari, volume 152, for June 13, 1917, opens with Charivaria, its column of short wartime jokes. Count Tisza declares he will go to the front for the duration of the war, but denies he caught the idea from Winston Churchill. The Germans announced Cherisy impregnable, yet the British captured it, so Sir Douglas Haig cannot have read the announcement.

Owners of babies are asked to hang out flags for Baby Week at Croydon, and parents with only a little bunting should hang that out instead. A parrot at Ipswich makes poll scratchers from soft wood, and has asked to do war work. A Battersea fitter stole jewels worth two thousand three hundred fifty pounds, though the public has been asked not to buy expensive jewellery. The number shows Punch joking through war, rationing, and official advice.
16113-punch-or-the-london-charivari-volu:
Punch for June 27, 1917, volume one hundred fifty-two, jokes its way through wartime news in the Charivaria column. The Sultan of Turkey, readers learn, favors criminal literature, and a new Life of the Kaiser is on its way to him as a gift book. King Alexander of Greece, who vowed to carry out his father's sacred mandate, tries again when told what following in his father's footsteps might mean.

Air raids, wartime shortages, and home-front grumbles fill the rest of the column in Punch's dry, teasing style. Cartoons and verses would have sharpened the same targets across the weekly. The issue captures British humor holding steady in the third year of the First World War.
17471-punch-or-the-london-charivari-volu:
For February 14, 1917, Punch, or the London Charivari, volume 152, offered a weekly dose of British wartime satire. The issue opens with Charivaria, short jokes and jabs. A German shipping magnate vows to hold up the world's commerce, while his countrymen on the Western Front are content to hold up their hands. A rumour that the Kaiser will honour Count Bernstorff sparks mock alarm in official circles.

Cartoons, verses, and comic pieces follow in Punch's familiar mix, turning the news of the third war winter into humour. Readers get a direct taste of how London laughed at its enemies and at itself in early 1917. The issue works both as light reading and as evidence of home-front mood in the Great War.
17629-punch-or-the-london-charivari-volu:
A June 1917 number of Punch, volume 152, dated June 20, opens its Charivaria with a wartime joke on waste. A man who bought sandwiches at a railway restaurant and threw them into the road was fined five shillings at Grimsby Police Court. His explanation, that he did not know they might injure the road, was not accepted by the court.

A second joke holds that too much fuss has been made about stopping Ramsay MacDonald and Jowett from leaving England. Cartoons, verses, and comic pieces follow in Punch's familiar mix. Readers get a topical snapshot of Britain in the summer of 1917. The issue works as light reading and as evidence of wartime humour.
17634-punch-or-the-london-charivari-volu:
A May 1917 number of Punch, volume 152, dated May 30, opens its Charivaria with a wartime joke on prices. Will Thorne declares that a hotel in Petrograd charged him twelve shillings for four small custards, proof, Punch suggests, that the war spirit of Russia is not wholly dead. Food Ministry officials add that domestic pastry may still be baked, a kind of pastry that tends to decrease the total number of food consumers.

Cartoons, verses, and comic pieces follow in Punch's familiar weekly mix. Readers get a topical snapshot of Britain in the third war year, when food, prices, and allies filled the jokes. The issue works as light reading and as evidence of home-front humour.
18967-the-bastonnais-tale-of-the-america:
John Lespérance published this historical novel in Toronto in 1877, under the title The Bastonnais. It tells of the American invasion of Canada in 1775 and 1776, when rebel forces marched on Quebec and tried to win French Canadians to their cause. The book is organized in three parts, beginning with the gathering of the storm.

Chapters follow blue lights, river crossings, a chateau, Cathedral Square, despatches, and a hermit of Montmorenci, mixing invented lovers and plotters with real events. Pauline's tears and a beautiful rebel give the war a personal face. Readers get a Canadian view of the Revolution's northern campaign, written a century later, when the invasion still stirred local memory.
19349-punch-or-the-london-charivari-vol-:
A November issue of Punch, the London comic weekly, dates from mid-November of nineteen twenty. Its Charivaria column jokes about motor shows, cats, hats, and cab whistles, while longer pieces poke at gossip writers, the League of Nations, and the Irish question. Cartoons and short verse fill out the number.

Read today, the issue is a snapshot of Britain just after the Great War: tired of grand talk, quick to laugh at officials, and unsure about new world bodies. For readers of period humor, it shows Punch's house style at full strength, light on the surface and sharp underneath.
20206-the-agony-of-the-church-1917:
The Agony of the Church, from 1917, weighs the state of the church in wartime. Its writer grants that churches have kept Christ as the world's treasury. Even rote prayer, he argues, lifts them above the secular world. They at least know who the Lord is, while the world does not.

That defense sits beside sharp grief over the church's weakness and pain. War in 1917 forced hard questions on faith, peace, and national pride. The book speaks to believers who felt their church failing its hour. Readers get a tense, searching tract from a year of crisis.
20752-the-journal-of-negro-history-volum:
Volume two of The Journal of Negro History, from 1917, lists a rich table of work. Articles treat Haiti and Liberia, three Negro poets, and Catholics and the Negro. Documents print letters of George Washington that bear on Black life.

Carter G. Woodson founded this journal to prove Black history had real depth. Scholars here use records, wills, and petitions, not mere opinion. Book reviews and notes close the volume, with news of the field's first big meeting. Readers see a new field of study being built in public, one solid document at a time.
2117-history-of-friedrich-ii-of-prussia-:
Carlyle begins the Seven Years' War in Book Seventeen, covering the first campaign of 1756 to 1757, when Frederick broke out into a third Silesian war and kindled all Europe. The world asked whether the war was of his beginning. The Menzel documents, secret papers Frederick had read, convinced him that attack was coming.

Carlyle, drawing on the Menzel documents Frederick had studied for four years, sets out what the king knew and feared. The volume argues the case for Frederick's action, in prose that is partisan, learned, and forceful. Carlyle uses them to settle the old quarrel over who began the Seven Years' War.
22103-with-a-highland-regiment-in-mesopo:
With a Highland Regiment in Mesopotamia 1916–1917 records a Scottish battalion's part in a hard campaign. One of its officers wrote the book, and a senior commander supplied warm praise. The regiment served in the land now called Iraq. British and Indian forces there fought the Ottoman Turks for rivers, oil, and the road to Baghdad.

Heat, disease, and flood plagued the troops as much as enemy fire. The writer follows the battalion's marches, trenches, and attacks month by month. His foreword insists that all ranks did well and suffered much. Such plain unit histories kept the memory of forgotten fronts alive when public attention stayed on France.
26962-wilson-s-tales-of-the-borders-and-:
Volume 17 of Wilson's Tales of the Borders and of Scotland was revised by Alexander Leighton and published in 1884. It gathers historical, traditional, and invented tales from the Scottish Borders and beyond. Its contents run from Roger Goldie's narrative and a Hogmanay tale to gleanings of the Covenant and the Surgeon's Tales.

Other pieces include a Highland tradition, a legend of Calder Moor, and tales of the East Neuk of Fife, including a robbery at Pittenweem. Told in Scots flavor and period detail, the stories mix real border history with fireside invention. The volume closes with a glossary for readers new to the dialect.
31012-the-works-of-robert-louis-stevenso:
Volume seventeen of the twenty-five-volume Swanston Edition of Robert Louis Stevenson, printed in 1912, holds two very different works side by side. The first is A Footnote to History, subtitled Eight Years of Trouble in Samoa, an eleven-chapter account of rival chiefs, foreign consuls, and war in the islands from 1883 into the 1890s.

The second part, Island Nights' Entertainments, collects South Seas stories including The Beach of Falesá, The Bottle Imp, and The Isle of Voices. In them, traders, missionaries, and islanders meet magic, taboo, and moral bargains. Together the two halves show Stevenson both as a reporter of Pacific politics and as a teller of island tales.
3597-essays-of-michel-de-montaigne-volum:
This seventeenth volume of Montaigne's Essays holds a single long essay from Book Three: Of Vanity. Montaigne opens by noting that no vanity is more plain than writing about vanity so vainly, and he quotes Ecclesiastes, that all is vanity. He says the saying ought to be meditated by men of understanding, then proceeds to meditate it at length.

The essay wanders through travel, writing, reputation, and the author's own habits, showing vanity in high and low places alike. Montaigne confesses his own share with humor rather than preaching. The volume suits readers who enjoy one sustained Montaigne meditation, where digression itself becomes the argument.
5291-tales-and-novels-of-j-de-la-fontain:
La Fontaine's seventeenth volume gathers The Progress of Wit, The Sick Abbess. The Truckers completes the trio, opening with a diverting play that resumes its fascinating sway by night or day. The play delights the sex, ugly, fair, or sour, and its chief charm. The author notes, is unknown to husbands, excelling only with the lover.

The tales that follow turn wit, sickness, and trucking into comedy, with abbesses and lovers in their usual La Fontaine roles. Readers get three stories in which cleverness is itself the game, told in verse that invites the reader to guess the play's name and enjoy the joke.
5919-the-history-of-don-quixote-volume-1:
Chapter fifty alone fills this Don Quixote installment, on the shrewd controversy between Don Quixote and the canon, with other incidents. Quixote answers with a good joke, defending books printed with the king's licence, approved by those who examined them, and read with universal delight. The canon's learned objections meet the knight's joyful faith in chivalry, and neither yields easily.

Cervantes gives his debate about fiction itself, staged as a roadside argument. The chapter favors wit and rhetoric over adventure, letting Quixote defend romances that made him mad. It suits readers interested in the novel's self-reflection, since the controversy asks whether delightful books can also be true, and whether madness can argue well.
7603-the-caxtons-a-family-picture-volume:
Part seventeen of The Caxtons moves the family's drama to a larger theatre, under a cloudless horizon. Beyond Lytton's stage frame lies the new land itself. A broad, fair river rolls through wide grassy plains. Vast evergreen forests stand in the distance, and Arcadian pastures hold sheep in hundreds and thousands. The emigrant story gains scale here, and the landscape carries the hope.

The stage frame itself is the narrator's device, dropping the scene to address the audience directly. Good audience, settle yourselves, he says in effect. Chat with your neighbor and take up your opera glass. Treat Tom and pretty Sal to fine oranges, and let the prentice boys cat-call as they will. Solemn gentlemen in the front seats, practiced critics who shake their heads at new actors, are invited to judge as well. Theatre and emigration meet in one farewell gesture.
8209-poems-1817:
John Keats published his first volume, Poems, in 1817, dedicating it to Leigh Hunt. Its epigraph, from Spenser's Fate of the Butterfly, asks what greater felicity can fall to a creature than to enjoy delight with liberty. The dedication sonnet laments that glory and loveliness have passed away, that no nymphs now bring roses and violets to Flora's shrine. Yet insists that delights as high remain, and that the poet feels a free, leafy luxury under pleasant trees.

The volume introduces Keats at twenty-one, already musical and sensuous, with sonnets, odes, and the famous poem on first looking into Chapman's Homer. It sold poorly at the time, but it announced a major poet. For Keats readers, this first book shows the young writer finding his voice, before the great odes of 1819.
8643-punch-or-the-london-charivari-volum:
Punch, or the London Charivari, volume 153, for July 4, 1917, catches Britain in the third year of the Great War. The opening piece, Mentioned in Despatches, gives voice to an old inhabitant bragging about his Billy, praised by Sir Douglas Haig himself. Who used to come whistling round the bend and stop for anyone who held up a hand. The dialect humour is Punch's wartime staple: pride, gossip, and understatement.

Cartoons, jokes, and short sketches fill the rest of the issue, mocking shortages, officials, and the enemy while keeping up civilian spirits. Punch had been London's comic weekly since 1841, and its 1917 numbers show a magazine balancing laughter with loss. Historians and casual browsers alike will find a vivid weekly record of how Britain joked, grumbled, and carried on mid-war.
9546-georgian-poetry-1916-1917:
Georgian Poetry 1916-1917, the third book in its series, carries the survey of young English poets to a seventh year. Published in late 1917 and dedicated to Edmund Gosse, it holds eighteen writers, nine of them new to the series. Names include Siegfried Sassoon, Robert Graves, Robert Nichols, and James Stephens. The editor reversed the name order to give newcomers more prominence.

War now shadows many poems, as young soldiers write from the front and from home. Older poets get less room, so new voices can be heard at length. A reader gets a wartime anthology of high craft, and a record of a generation writing verse while its world broke apart.
adler-neurotic-constitution-1917:
Alfred Adler published The Neurotic Constitution in German in 1912. The English text here is the 1917 translation by Bernard Glueck and John E. Lind. Adler, a former colleague of Freud, founds here his individual psychology. The feeling of inferiority, he argues, drives people to strive and compensate.

Neurotics, in his account, set fictional goals of superiority they cannot reach. Their symptoms serve those goals as excuses and safeguards. Adler stresses social feeling and conscious purpose over Freud's drives. Organ inferiority and childhood experience shape the striving style. The book is the founding text of Adlerian therapy. Its ideas on inferiority entered common speech.
arxiv-2509-00017:
Ophélia Miralles, Daniele Nerini, Jonas Bhend, Baudouin Raoult, and Christoph Spirig present a graph neural network for sharp, fast weather nowcasts in Switzerland in 2025. Nowcasting covers the next few hours. Swiss terrain is steep and varied, so fine maps at one kilometer and ten-minute steps are hard to compute with grid methods.

Their model blends live surface readings with picked past and future states from a numeric weather model. That guided blend boosts short-term accuracy while keeping results in line with physics. Two versions, one trained on local analyses and one not, are checked on many surface traits. Both are compared with the live Swiss forecast and nowcast systems. Local data prove key to fine Alpine forecasts.
arxiv-2509-00117:
Jared Perlo, Alexander Robey, Fazl Barez, Luciano Floridi, and Jakob Mökander map risks and policy needs for embodied AI in 2025. Unlike screen-bound AI, embodied systems live in, learn from, and act on the physical world. Gains in models and hardware widen what they can do, and widen the harms they could cause, from injury to mass surveillance.

Current rules for factory robots and self-driving cars do not cover the full risk range. The paper sorts risks into physical, informational, economic, and social kinds. It then checks how United States, European Union, and United Kingdom rules address each kind. Gaps found in that check point to where new policy must act soon.
arxiv-2509-00317:
Fulvio Mastrogiovanni and Antony Thomas present a task and motion planning framework for space robots in 2025 based on expanding AND/OR graphs. Space work brings high perception and motion uncertainty, strict kinematic limits, and few chances for human help. Task and motion planning joins discrete action sequencing with checks that each motion is actually feasible.

Their framework, TMP-EAOG, encodes task-level abstractions in an AND/OR graph that expands step by step as the plan runs. Motion planning checks run in the loop to test feasibility of each branch. The design gains robustness to a degree of uncertainty from that feedback. Tests show the frame adapts to distinct scenarios, from servicing to surface operations.
arxiv-2509-01217:
Aligning medical scans of the same body part, called registration, underpins many clinical tasks, yet fair tests of competing methods are rare. Lasse Hansen, with fifty-three co-authors, reports the 2024 edition of the Learn2Reg challenge. Earlier editions from 2020 to 2023 set shared data sets and scoring rules for the field.

The 2024 round adds three new tasks, covering large-scale registration across imaging types, unsupervised alignment of brains from different people, and the challenge's first microscopy benchmark. The new data spurred fresh methods, including constraints that keep alignments reversible, pyramid features, keypoint matching, and per-case tuning. Hansen and the large team present the edition as a broader, harder yardstick for tracking progress in medical image registration.
arxiv-2509-01317:
Self-driving cars rely on LiDAR, laser scans that map the scene, but cheap sensors give sparse data that weaken scene labeling. Alexandros Gkillas, Nikos Piperigkos, and Aris S. Lalos present a framework that sharpens LiDAR data and labels the scene in one joint process. It is described as the first end-to-end system to join these two tasks.

Joint training lets the sharpening step use semantic cues, keeping fine detail for small object classes. A new loss function steers the network toward regions that matter most. The model-based design uses far fewer parameters than prior sharpening methods and fits easily with segmentation networks. In tests, results matched models fed with costly sixty-four channel LiDAR, pointing to safer perception on cheaper hardware for cars.
arxiv-2509-01817:
Yonatan L Ashenafi and Peter R Kramer model how colonies of single cell swimmers respond to chemical and air cues. A colony answer blends the answers of its member cells through their linked motion. Two response types are studied: taxis, steering toward a cue, and kinesis, changing random motion by cue direction. Math analysis in a limiting regime drives the study, checked against lab data on protozoa.

Steering by each cell backfires at colony scale, pushing the colony down the gradient in part. An upward drift remains but weakens as the colony grows, tied to uneven oar placement. Under kinesis, where noise rises when a cell faces away from the cue, the colony drifts up at a size free speed. Even symmetric oar layouts work under kinesis.
arxiv-2509-01917:
The Belle II Collaboration, with I Adachi as the first listed member among four hundred thirty-eight authors in total, reports a new particle process and searches for two others. Their data come from electron and positron crashes near a known resonance peak. Final states mix photons, charged pions, and leptons, meaning light charged particles. One target is a hypothesized partner state in the bottom quark sector.

A clear signal appears for a process yielding an eta particle plus an excited Upsilon state, passing a strict significance bar. The pattern does not fit production through known resonances alone. A new state near a meson pair threshold or broad continuum output fits better. No signal appears for the other two targets, so upper limits on their rates are set.
arxiv-2509-02117:
Andrew Duncan, Murray Elder, Lisa Frenkel, and Mengfan Lyu prove a substitution lemma for multiple context-free languages. Multiple context-free grammars extend classic grammars to capture more complex language patterns. A substitution lemma gives a necessary condition that any infinite such language must satisfy. Prior pumping style tools famously fail to generalize to this class, leaving a gap.

Their lemma shows a sample of languages are not multiple context-free. The word problem of a direct product of two free groups is a headline example. Groups whose word problem is multiple context-free gain a decidable rational subset membership problem as a corollary. The result sharpens the boundary of this grammar class. It also links formal language theory with group theory questions.
arxiv-2509-02217:
