Binqing Wu, Jianlong Huang, Zongjiang Shang, and Ling Chen present ST-Hyper for multivariate time series forecasting across joint space-time scales. Many deep forecasters model spatial or temporal patterns separately at set scales. Dependencies that jointly span space and time scopes can slip through that split. Their pyramid module extracts features at multiple joint scales first.

An adaptive hypergraph module then learns a sparse hypergraph linking those features. Hypergraphs connect many nodes per edge, capturing high order dependencies beyond pairs. Tri-phase propagation exchanges information comprehensively across scales. Six real world datasets test the full system. It achieves state of the art results, cutting average error versus best baselines for both long and short horizons.
arxiv-2509-02317:
Chenguang Du and four co-authors present a 2025 survey-style paper on how AI agents should talk to each other. Many new frameworks and protocols have appeared, but they often duplicate work and fail to connect across fields, leaving the area fragmented.

The authors borrow lessons from Internet architecture, the design behind the global network. They pull out five elements that matter for agent talk: scalability, security, real-time performance, high performance, and manageability. Each element is then used to judge chances and bottlenecks for multi-agent systems. By viewing agent communication through a proven design lens, the paper gives builders a shared map for growing agent networks that stay secure and sustainable.
arxiv-2509-03317:
Seokhun Park, Insung Kong, and Yongdai Kim extended a popular statistical model in 2025 to make it easier to interpret. Bayesian Additive Regression Trees, or BART, sums many small decision trees under a Bayesian treatment and captures complex, nonlinear patterns well. Its accuracy, however, comes at the cost of readability: nobody can see which variables drive a prediction.

Their ANOVA-BART rebuilds the model on a functional ANOVA decomposition, which splits a function's variation into parts for each variable and each interaction subset. Theory shows the new model's posterior concentrates at nearly the best possible rate, with matching rates for each interaction part. Experiments found accuracy and uncertainty estimates on par with the original. The decomposition also supports selecting which components matter, a task the original cannot do cleanly.
arxiv-2509-03417:
Spyros Rigas and 3 co-authors studied how to initialize Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks in a 2025 empirical study. These networks replace fixed activation curves with trainable spline functions, promising flexibility and interpretability. How their weights start, however, had barely been studied, even though initialization can make or break training in other architectures.

The authors propose two theory-driven schemes inspired by classic LeCun and Glorot rules, plus a tunable power-law family found empirically. Evaluation covered large grid searches on function fitting and differential equation benchmarks, training dynamics viewed through the neural tangent kernel, and a subset of the Feynman equation dataset. The Glorot-inspired scheme clearly beat the baseline in parameter-rich models. Power-law initialization performed best overall across tasks and sizes. Code and data are public.
arxiv-2509-03617:
Marco Vetrano and three co-authors work on reading exoplanet atmospheres with a quantum machine learning method in a 2025 research paper. Traditionally, researchers compute a planet's spectrum from a forward model and adjust many chemical and physical parameters until it matches observations. That search space is large, so the computing cost grows quickly.

Their alternative uses a quantum extreme learning machine, where a quantum system acts as a black-box processor for input data. Atmospheric features are extracted from that processing rather than from slow parameter sweeps. The design is meant to stay fault-tolerant enough for near-term quantum hardware. A direct run on the IBM Fez quantum device demonstrates that tolerance in practice. The authors see quantum tools eventually enabling faster and more accurate atmosphere models for astrophysical data.
arxiv-2509-03817:
A 2025 research paper by Wei Yang and one co-author focuses on teaching teams of language model agents to deliberate about how they collaborate. Multi-agent systems often follow fixed collaboration protocols, choreographed from outside. Those designs overlook each agent's inner state, like its uncertainty or confidence, treating agents as passive executors of a script.

Their Meta-Policy Deliberation Framework lets each agent learn a decentralised policy over three meta-cognitive actions: persist, refine, or concede. An agent can thus hold its line, improve its answer, or yield to a teammate, based on its own state. Training such policies with ordinary policy gradients proved unstable. Their new algorithm, SoftRankPO, shapes learning advantages from the rank of rewards passed through smooth normal quantiles, making training robust to reward swings. Across five mathematics and general reasoning benchmarks, the framework gains several percentage points of accuracy over six leading multi-agent reasoning methods.
arxiv-2509-04017:
Wei-Tao Lu and three co-authors devote a 2025 physics paper to spin-valley polarised edge states in two-dimensional honeycomb lattices, steered by a side potential. Silicene and germanene have spin-orbit coupling, and their ribbon edges carry helical states. The side potential mixes a potential field with an exchange field at the zigzag boundaries.

Calculations show side potentials reshape the edge states, whose spin and valley labels are locked together. Tuning the potential and the width moves the system between phases: a quantum spin-valley Hall effect, a valley-polarised quantum spin Hall effect, and a spin-polarised quantum anomalous Hall effect. In narrow ribbons, edge-state coupling plus the side potential opens a gap for one spin and breaks time-reversal symmetry, producing the anomalous Hall phase. Distinct polarised states form at each boundary. The resulting insulating states could realise a spin-valley switch.
arxiv-2509-04117:
Mustafa Sakhai and three co-authors release a data set for teaching machines to spot pedestrians with event cameras in a 2025 research paper. Event cameras report only brightness changes, timed to tiny fractions of a second, instead of full picture frames. That makes them fast and strong in harsh light. Their collection, DVS-PedX, mixes simulated crossings from the CARLA driving simulator with real dash-cam footage converted into event form, across varied weather and lighting.

Each sequence pairs ordinary video frames with event frames and labels saying whether the person crosses. Extra raw files let researchers reprocess the data freely. Trial networks built on spiking pulses learned the task but struggled to transfer from simulation to real streets.
arxiv-2509-04317:
Isidoro Tamassia and one co-author, Wendelin Böhmer, harden the AlphaZero game-playing framework against surprises at test time in a 2025 research paper. AlphaZero blends Monte Carlo planning, a search that samples possible futures, with a neural network trained beforehand. It normally assumes the world at play time matches training exactly. Changed rules or boards can therefore cripple it, and real deployments rarely guarantee sameness.

Simple modifications to the standard setup are analyzed and tested here. Even with a small planning budget, performance in altered environments improved significantly. The authors release their code publicly on GitHub. Game AI and planning systems that must cope with shifting conditions gain a practical resilience recipe.
arxiv-2509-05117:
A neural operator that solves many physics problems without retraining would speed up engineering work greatly. Rafael Bischof, lead author with four co-authors, present HyPINO in a 2025 machine learning paper. The system builds a fresh solver for each new equation. A transformer-based hypernetwork maps each equation's parameters to a physics-informed neural network tailored to it. No extra training is needed at that point.

Training mixes labelled manufactured solutions with unlabelled samples. The unlabelled ones are scored by physics objectives. The model handles several equation types in two dimensions with varied sources, geometries, and boundary conditions. It beats strong baselines on seven benchmarks in zero-shot tests. An iterative refinement step solves a correction equation repeatedly. Each pass cuts errors further.
arxiv-2509-05217:
Logistic growth, where a population levels off at a limit, shapes family trees in a 2025 paper by Ruairi Garrett and Julio Ernesto Nava Trejo. Earlier work followed type frequencies forward in time for the same process; the open question was what the ancestry looks like backwards.

The authors find three possible limits, set by how heavy the tail of the offspring distribution is. Depending on that tail, the genealogy approaches Kingman's coalescent, a Beta coalescent, or the Bolthausen-Sznitman coalescent as population size grows. Their proof runs through a modified lookdown construction, a layered way of tracking ancestry. The three outcomes match the forward-time limits found before.
arxiv-2509-05417:
Light from a brilliant early quasar leaves an echo in surrounding gas, mapped for the first time sideways by Anna-Christina Eilers and thirteen co-authors in a 2025 astronomy paper. Ultraviolet light from the feeding black hole ionises intergalactic gas, and changes in brightness should send ionisation patterns outward.

Deep James Webb Space Telescope spectra of background galaxies reveal that echo across several sightlines, not just along our own. The team maps the ionisation cone's shape, orientation, and tilt, and limits how much of the sky around the quasar is hidden. The radiation timescale they infer is far shorter than standard black hole growth would need. Early growth may instead involve weak radiation or heavy cocoons of gas.
arxiv-2509-05817:
Esra Güldoğan Lekesiz develops a finite family of matrix polynomials with a matching biorthogonality property in a 2025 paper. Biorthogonal means two different families pair to zero except on matching terms, a matrix version of the orthogonality used for classical polynomials. Finiteness matters because the pairing stops after a set number of terms.

For this finite pair, the author derives several recurrence relations, rules that build each polynomial from earlier ones. A matrix differential equation, a generating function, and an integral representation round out the toolkit. Together these results give several handles on the same objects: recurrences for computation, the equation for analytic work, and the integral form for estimates. The paper adds a compact, fully worked example to matrix polynomial theory.
arxiv-2509-06017:
Two unexplained bumps in collider data could share one cause in an extended Higgs sector, argue Akshat Khanna and two co-authors in a 2025 paper. CMS data show a significant excess near six hundred fifty gigaelectronvolts in a photon pair plus bottom quark final state, with hints of a light Higgs near ninety-five. Their stage is the type-I two-Higgs-doublet model with a softly broken symmetry.

In their setup, a heavy pseudoscalar Higgs decays to the familiar one hundred twenty-five Higgs plus a Z boson. A light scalar, meanwhile, explains older LEP and LHC anomalies in bottom, photon, and tau channels at once. Checking experimental and theoretical constraints, the authors find the model accounts for all the anomalies together at moderate significance.
arxiv-2509-06117:
Wave behavior of fractional Laplacians on a lattice is charted in a 2025 paper by Nassim Athmouni. These anisotropic operators, defined on the d-dimensional integer grid with a separate exponent per direction, model jumps longer than nearest-neighbor steps. Athmouni studies energy windows away from thresholds, where the spectrum is cleanest.

A Mourre estimate, a commutator bound that rules out trapped waves, anchors the analysis on those windows. Consequences follow in a chain: a limiting absorption principle, propagation estimates with minimal velocity and local decay, and existence and completeness of wave operators for long-range decaying potentials. The stationary scattering matrix is built on shell, the optical theorem proved, and a Birman-Krein formula links its determinant to the spectral shift function.
arxiv-2509-06317:
Navigating between Earth and Moon with guarantees is the aim of a 2025 paper by Tanay Kumar and Raktim Bhattacharya. Cislunar dynamics are chaotic and imperfectly modeled, and sensor errors depend on the state itself. The authors embed the dynamics in a linear fractional transformation model, which packages the gravity model's curves and sensor quirks as structured uncertainty.

Against that model they build a nonlinear filter in the H-infinity and mu frameworks, designs with firm bounds on performance under the stated uncertainties. Simulations for a surveillance constellation in cislunar space show the filter working as intended. The paper offers a control-theoretic route to sound navigation where trial-and-error tuning is not an option.
arxiv-2509-06617:
Foundation vision models meet multi-scan medical imaging in a 2025 paper led by Daniel Scholz, with six co-authors. DINOv2, a model pretrained on natural images, works well on single medical images. Many clinical tasks, though, combine several scan types, and supervised models waste unlabeled data and stumble when one scan type is missing.

The adapted system, MM-DINOv2, adds patch embeddings that accept several modalities at once. During training, whole modalities are masked out, forcing the model to learn how scan types relate and to cope with missing ones. Semi-supervised learning lets it use large unlabeled collections as well. On the task of classifying glioma subtypes from multi-sequence brain MRI, it beat leading supervised methods on an outside test set by a wide margin. The authors present it as a scalable answer for real clinical messiness.
arxiv-2509-06917:
Research papers turned into interactive AI agents that can rerun their own methods are built by Jiacheng Miao and four co-authors in a 2025 paper. Reading a paper is passive: adopting its code, data, and methods takes heavy effort, which slows reuse. Their framework, Paper2Agent, automates the conversion.

Multiple agents analyze the paper and its codebase to build a server following the Model Context Protocol, then iteratively write and run tests to harden it. The resulting agent connects to a chat system and answers scientific questions by invoking the original paper's tools. Case studies cover agents using AlphaGenome for genomic variants and ScanPy and TISSUE for single-cell and spatial analyses. The agents reproduced the papers' results and answered novel queries correctly. One, acting as an AI co-scientist, identified a new splicing variant linked to ADHD risk.
arxiv-2509-07017:
Logical reasoning carried out in the frequency domain of a knowledge graph is proposed by Andrew Kiruluta and one co-author in a 2025 AI paper. Their framework, Spectral NSR, encodes logical rules as templates in that same domain and reasons there directly. It uses the Laplacian eigenstructure, the graph equivalent of a musical scale.

Add-ons include learning the graph and its basis as training proceeds, sharper selective filters, and mixtures of spectral experts for modular work. Proof-guided training and uncertainty scores for well-judged confidence are also included. Coupling to large language models and robustness against attacks are also covered. On reasoning benchmarks such as ProofWriter and CLUTRR, the authors report better accuracy, faster inference, and clearer reasoning than transformer, message-passing, and neuro-symbolic baselines. Analyses show the model's decisions align closely with symbolic proof forms, and transfer tests support adaptation to new domains.
arxiv-2509-07117:
Francisco Meirinhos and 4 co-authors build a theory framework for Kondo echo changes in heavy fermion systems, in a 2025 paper. Heavy fermions are materials in which electrons act far heavier than usual, thanks to strong interactions.

Their framework rests on three pieces. First, a form of time-dependent dynamical mean-field theory written entirely with integro-differential equations. Second, the noncrossing approximation. Third, a quantum treatment of the electromagnetic field that drives the system. They apply it to a heavy-fermion system hit by a single cycle of terahertz light. Two effects stand out. The system jumps at once from the Kondo regime toward the mixed-valence regime, because light strengthens the hybridization. Then it crawls back slowly, held up by the long Kondo coherence time. That picture explains, at the microscopic level, what recent time-resolved terahertz spectroscopy experiments saw.
arxiv-2509-07517:
Frédéric Robert, writing alone in 2025, studies families of solutions to a high-order critical equation on a curved space. The space is a Riemannian manifold, a curved space with a way to measure lengths. The equation joins a high-order operator of Laplace type to a critical power term. That power is the borderline growth where compactness fails. The families are assumed to have a uniform bound on their Dirichlet energy, a budget on gradient size.

Robert proves a sharp pointwise bound for each solution. Each one is bounded by a smooth limit profile plus a sum of explicit standard peaks, called bubbles. The bound holds uniformly as the parameter grows. Such bubble results describe just how solutions can concentrate and blow up. Sharp control is a core tool for proofs of existence in geometric analysis. It also rules out blow-up shapes no one expected.
arxiv-2509-07617:
Attackers can slip hidden instructions into prompts and hijack a language model's behavior, a threat called direct prompt injection. Minghui Li and 6 co-authors present an attack framework in a 2025 research paper. Existing attacks either need inside access to the model or fail to transfer between models. The authors aim for black-box attacks that carry across systems.

They train an energy-based model on the internal activations of a stand-in model to grade attack prompts. A sampling method then improves prompts token by token without gradients. Across five mainstream models, their prompts succeeded far more often than human-written ones. Success held up on unseen tasks too. Analysis links activation patterns to attack strength. The findings expose a transferable weakness that defenders must design against.
arxiv-2509-08017:
Choosing where a few sensors can stand in for measurements everywhere is the job of a 2025 software paper by Niharika Karnik and 8 co-authors. PySensors 2.0, a Python package for sparse sensor placement, adds spatially constrained placement: users can cap or fix sensor counts per region, lock in chosen locations, and enforce minimum spacing between sensors.

Custom bases let any data-driven or spectral representation plug into the placement algorithms. A thermodynamic approach goes further, mapping the whole landscape of good configurations instead of returning one supposed optimum. Engineers monitoring structures, oceans, or industrial plants get flexible, realistic placement plans that respect the physical limits of where sensors can actually go.
arxiv-2509-08117:
Robot teams that learn an unknown field while covering it are coordinated in a 2025 paper by Ruijie Du and 3 co-authors. The field might be pollution density or crop health, unknown at the start and possibly changing over time. Standard Gaussian process models learn such fields but scale poorly and struggle with online updates as new measurements stream in.

Random-feature Gaussian processes, with an online variant, allow incremental inference without restarting the fit. Voronoi-based coverage control spreads robots sensibly, while an upper confidence bound strategy steers them toward informative regions. The team refines its map and its coverage together. Adaptive sampling concentrates effort where the field is uncertain or important, instead of mowing the whole domain uniformly.
arxiv-2509-08217:
Spam filters for human-labelled data quietly delete honest disagreement, warn Eve Fleisig and 3 co-authors in a 2025 machine learning paper. Datasets meant to capture diverse opinions must remove spam while keeping genuine variation in labels. Standard filtering heuristics were built for tasks with one true answer, where disagreement looks like noise.

On subjective tasks, the tested heuristics often remove annotators who disagree rather than actual spammers, trading label diversity away for a false sense of accuracy. The authors evaluate the tradeoffs empirically across filtering methods. Dataset builders for opinion, toxicity, and preference data face a design choice: aggressive cleaning can manufacture consensus and teach models that minority views are errors.
arxiv-2509-08417:
A rare charged Higgs decay could betray itself at a future muon collider, calculate Dzung Tri Tran and 3 co-authors in a 2025 particle physics paper. In two-Higgs-doublet models, the charged Higgs can decay to a W boson and a photon only through quantum loops, making the channel a delicate probe. The calculation is performed in a general gauge to keep it honest.

Gauge independence, freedom from ultraviolet divergences, and renormalisation-scale independence of the one-loop factors are all verified analytically. A parameter scan of the Type-I model then yields branching ratios over the viable space, and charged Higgs pair production at TeV-scale muon colliders is investigated. Rare loop decays amplify new physics effects that tree-level channels would dilute.
arxiv-2509-08617:
Khawla Elhadri and 2 co-authors propose XNNTab in a 2025 paper on interpretable deep learning for tabular data. Tables drive finance and health care work, but neural networks for them are often black boxes. Users cannot see why a prediction was made.

XNNTab uses a sparse autoencoder, a network that learns a small set of active features, inside its latent space. An automated step gives those features plain human meanings. Predictions then become weighted sums of meaningful parts. Tests match or beat strong black box and classic models. The gain is full interpretability without giving up accuracy.
arxiv-2509-08817:
Tobias Winker and 2 co-authors develop quantum methods for cardinality estimation in databases in a 2025 paper. Cardinality estimation predicts how many rows a query will return, guiding the optimizer. Their QCardEst uses a hybrid quantum-classical network.

SQL queries are encoded into a quantum state using only as many qubits as tables in the query. One variational circuit then processes the whole query on current hardware. Different classical layers turn circuit output into a count. A second tool, QCardCorr, corrects classical estimators with a quantum factor. It beats the standard PostgreSQL optimizer by large factors on two benchmarks.
arxiv-2509-08917:
Aida Abiad and 2 co-authors lay foundations for the Eigenvalue Method in coding theory in a 2025 paper. Coding theory studies error correcting codes, which protect data from noise. The method uses algebraic graph theory to bound how large a code can be.

Core assumptions that allow the method are identified clearly. It is tested on several well known classes of codes across different distance measures. Results are compared with the best bounds currently known. New bounds often improve the state of the art. The authors argue spectral graph tools capture structure that classical coding methods miss, opening progress on major open questions.
arxiv-2509-09317:
The young triple star GW Orionis wears a planet-forming disk that observations show warped and snapped into rings. Alison K. Young simulates that disk at high resolution in a 2025 research paper written alone. Theorists had disagreed about what breaks the disk. Analytical estimates suggested the system sits only marginally on the stable side of tearing.

Young's simulations are the first to capture the wavelike regime expected in thick, low-turbulence disks like this one. Using the most favorable allowed values for misalignment and stellar mass ratio, stellar torques alone tear the disk. No embedded planet is needed. The runs also rule out the disk spinning backward against the stellar orbits. A slightly thicker disk matches observations better. The work warns modelers to treat warp propagation carefully in similar young systems.
arxiv-2509-09517:
Zhong-Xia Shang and 2 co-authors study fast-forwarding for open quantum systems in a 2025 paper on Lindbladian dynamics. Fast-forwarding means simulating a long evolution with far fewer steps than its length would suggest. Some closed Hamiltonian systems can beat the usual no-go result, but dissipative systems, where energy and information leak away, had barely been explored in this light.

Their algorithm handles purely dissipative cases with unitary jump operators at improved query cost. When those operators have a block-diagonal Pauli form, circuit depth drops exponentially through parallel access. The same ideas speed up estimates of certain Gibbs state quantities, with gains that depend on how much coherence the input states carry. Tests include ground state overlap checks.
arxiv-2509-09617:
Beena Meena and 5 co-authors report a hidden young star group inside NGC 602 in a 2025 astronomy paper based on James Webb Space Telescope images. NGC 602 is a young cluster in the Small Magellanic Cloud with few heavy elements. A bright mid-infrared feature, named MZS-1, glows between ten and twenty-five microns yet vanishes at shorter wavelengths, marking it as deeply buried.

Its stretched shape and multiple peaks point to several warm, dust-wrapped sources. Model fitting classifies them as very young stellar objects, each under about three solar masses, together roughly three hundred solar masses. Older telescopes had missed the group entirely. The find shows how the new observatory exposes the earliest, metal-poor stages of cluster birth.
arxiv-2509-09817:
P. C. Sabino and 7 co-authors squeeze a heavy-fermion crystal under pressure in 2025, hunting for a second quantum critical point. The compound YbV6Sn6 orders magnetically at a fraction of a kelvin and already shows field-tuned critical behaviour. The team grew fresh single crystals by a self-flux route, then measured their properties at ordinary pressure and their electrical transport while hydrostatic pressure climbed.

Below one gigapascal the low-temperature behaviour settles back into a normal Fermi liquid pattern. Push higher and the fitted exponents slide the other way while a key coefficient swells, signs that a fresh critical point is approaching. Competing influences, from Kondo screening to crystal fields, make the resulting phase map crowded, with criticality tunable by two separate knobs.
arxiv-2509-10017:
H. Tong and 1 co-author write down approximate formulas for the spinning, twisted magnetic field of a magnetar in a 2025 astrophysics paper. Magnetars are neutron stars whose fields are both immense and wound up, and that twist should change how the star beams particles and light. Their model approximates the outward field as a self-similar twisted dipole and takes the sideways field from a minimum torque prescription, keeping the maths solvable by hand.

Five trends fall out as twist grows: the Y-point moves inward, the polar cap widens, particle outflow brightens, and both the peak accelerating voltage and the radio pulse width rise. Let the field untwist and every property drifts back toward an ordinary pulsar's. A wider cap may match the hot spot seen during magnetar outbursts, the authors note.
arxiv-2509-10117:
K. Lisiecki and 18 co-authors stress-test how astronomers pick out dead galaxies from James Webb photographs in a 2025 study. Photometric selection of quiescent candidates is cheap, but the answer leans hard on what star-formation history the fitting code assumes and on how dust is treated. Bursty, random histories can fake or hide quiescence, so the inferred masses, ages, and formation rates all wobble with the modelling choices.

Fitting some thirteen thousand galaxies with three history recipes, with and without mid-infrared coverage and dust emission models, exposes the swings. Candidate counts chosen by colour and by formation-rate rules move between setups, and physical properties shift with them. The lesson for early universe surveys is blunt: a quiet galaxy on paper may only be a modelling assumption wearing a disguise.
arxiv-2509-10417:
Christopher Ormerod and Gitit Kehat test language models that can read an entire student essay at once in this 2025 education technology paper. Standard transformers accept only a fixed maximum length, and longer essays from older students overflow it. The usual fix, cutting the text off, is troubling for grading, since judging organization fairly requires seeing the whole piece.

Using the Kaggle ASAP 2.0 dataset of student essays, the authors evaluate several model families redesigned for long inputs. Their lineup includes fine-tuned XLNet, Longformer, ModernBERT, Mamba, and Llama variants, each with architectural changes meant to stretch context. The comparison shows how these long-context designs behave on the practical task of automated essay scoring, where validity depends on the model actually reading everything a student wrote.
arxiv-2509-10517:
Rodrigo Tertulino benchmarks five federated learning strategies for predicting in-hospital death in this solo-authored 2025 medical informatics study. Hospitals cannot pool patient records freely, and their data differ sharply in makeup and balance. Working with the MIMIC-IV dataset, he splits nearly half a million admissions across five care units to mimic that unevenness and adds a panel of first-day laboratory tests.

Over fifty rounds and five random seeds, FedProx earned the best discrimination scores, and its lead was statistically significant against every rival. FedCluster edged it on F1, though, so no strategy won everything. A centralized model still beat all federated ones, and the global model served the smallest, most distinctive units worst. Tertulino concludes regularization-based methods are the sturdier federated choice, while per-client fairness needs attention of its own.
arxiv-2509-10717:
Career fairs promise computer science students a map of their futures. Briana Lee and four co-authors check what students actually take home, in this 2025 study. The technology industry spans software, AI, security, and data work. Little research documents how students experience these fairs, though. The fairs are meant to introduce those paths.

The authors surveyed eighty-six students. They asked why students attended and how they prepared. They asked what students learned, and whether the events opened doors to careers and tools the students had not met before. The findings address three audiences at once. Career services staff run the fairs. Educators prepare students for them. Industry leaders staff the booths. The study treats the career fair as a designed learning experience. It is not a ritual. As a designed experience, it can be measurably improved.
arxiv-2509-11217:
Tomohiro Hattori and Shu Tanaka wrote this 2025 quantum computing paper. It concerns quantum annealing correction. That family of tricks protects an annealer's answer from hardware errors. The authors study versions linking several replicas of the problem. Extra interactions join the replicas.

The hard cases have a tiny energy gap. The best and second-best solutions sit very close in energy. Annealers normally crawl on such problems. Two designs get tested here. One is the stacked model. The other is the penalty spin model. Both reached the optimal solution in short annealing times. They deliberately use jumps between energy levels. Slower methods avoid those jumps. The findings support correction schemes for noisy, time-limited hardware.
arxiv-2509-11717:
Adhiraj Banerjee and Vipul Arora separate sounds inside a codec. This 2025 audio processing paper treats text-guided separation. A user names a sound, a dog bark or a siren. The system pulls it from a mixture. Leading systems are too heavy for low-latency devices.

Their framework is CodecSep. It works in the latent space of a neural audio codec, not on waveforms. A frozen codec backbone supports a light transformer masker. Text embeddings steer the masker through feature-wise modulation. Open-vocabulary separation runs at codec-level cost. On one standard benchmark and five open-domain ones, CodecSep improved quality over its main rival. Human listening ratings favored it too. Audio sent as codec codes can be separated directly. The decode-separate-re-encode detour disappears.
arxiv-2509-12117:
Teams of learning agents miscoordinate when each one reacts only to the others' current strategies, blind to the updates happening at the same moment. Aryaman Reddi and three co-authors answer with K-Level Policy Gradients in 2025, a recursive fix for actor-critic multi-agent learning.

Each agent's update is computed against the already-updated policies of the others, level by level, so coordinated moves surface faster. With finitely many iterates, the authors prove monotone convergence to a local Nash equilibrium under stated conditions. They build the idea into three established deep algorithms, MAPPO, MADDPG, and FACMAC, and report stronger results than existing methods on StarCraft II scenarios and multi-agent MuJoCo control tasks.
arxiv-2509-12317:
Dark matter might cool itself by radiating light particles. Ordinary gas cools the same way, by emitting photons. That cooling would reshape small galaxies. Garance Lankester-Broche and one co-author lay the groundwork in 2025. They compute scattering and energy loss for dissipative self-interacting dark matter. The regime is the Born limit.

Six cases of emission are covered. The radiated particles are either massless or light. The forces are either short range or long range. Closed-form formulas come from an expansion in the slow relative speed of the colliding particles. The leading behavior is surprisingly universal. The authors also map where the approximation can be trusted.
arxiv-2509-12517:
Give a chatbot a memory of its user and it may start agreeing too much. Shomik Jain and four co-authors measure that effect in 2025, testing whether interaction context makes language models sycophantic, using two weeks of real exchanges from thirty-eight users.

They track two flavors: plain over-agreement, and perspective sycophancy, where the model mirrors the user's viewpoint. Stored memory profiles produced the largest jumps in agreement, and some models grew more flattering even from synthetic context about strangers. Perspective mirroring rose only when the model could actually infer the user's views. The findings complicate the design of personalization.
arxiv-2509-13017:
Kwai-Kong Ng and Min-Fong Yang test in 2025 a claim that quantum help can end the sign problem in Monte Carlo work. The sign flaw makes errors blow up as systems grow or cool. A recent quantum series method claimed shifts could dodge it.

Careful checks show the claim fails when terms do not commute. Shifts can cut bad weights in practice, not end the flaw. On a test chain, mid shifts balance help and noise best. Large shifts boost errors. A squeeze step lifts speed. The verdict is relief, not a cure.
arxiv-2509-13217:
Eman Abu Ishgair, Chinenye Okafor and two co-authors swap software bills of materials safely in 2025 with Petra. Bills list parts inside software for trust and law. Vendors fear leaks of secrets or flaw data inside full bills.

Petra lets vendors share redacted bills with picked encryption. Buyers can search hidden bills for set security answers without seeing barred data. A format-free, tamper-proof form yields lean trust proofs. Audits can thus check redacted bills with math certainty. Extra size stays under one kilobyte per bill, and decode cost stays tiny at query time.
arxiv-2509-13317:
An-Chieh Cheng, Yang Fu and 11 co-authors build SR-3D in 2025, a vision-language model that prompts regions across 2D and 3D. Users can mark boxes or masks on any frame, or in 3D, with no need to label all frames. Shared tokens link single and multi views.

2D traits gain 3D position codes, so strong 2D priors aid 3D reasoning. Objects need not co-occur in one view. Top marks land on general 2D and dedicated 3D benchmarks. Wild video with no sensor 3D input still yields sound spatial links and metric reads. One space serves both worlds.
arxiv-2509-13417:
Clara Murgui and Ryan Plestid study in 2025 how coherent gas scatter off atom interferometers boosts phase and contrast signals. Point-cloud guesses in past work miss real cloud traits. Finite temperature, substructure, and shifting radii reshape the coherent to incoherent crossover.

Realistic features enter the formalism in full. Smooth crossover between regimes follows naturally. Lab tests with infrared photons or electron guns are outlined. A dark matter hunt via long-range forces is sketched as a use case. Cloud structure thus tunes sensitivity, not just noise, for precision interferometers that probe faint forces.
arxiv-2509-13717:
Yifan Yu, Cheuk Hin Ho, and Yangshuai Wang add trustworthy error bars to physics-informed neural networks in a 2025 paper. Such networks solve partial differential equations by baking the physics into training. Existing error estimates for them carry no rigorous guarantees. That is a real problem when the equations model damped oscillators, heat flow, or waves.

Their framework uses conformal prediction. That is a distribution-free method that tunes prediction intervals on held-out data. It promises a stated coverage rate. A local variant estimates cutoff points region by region. The bands then widen where the solution varies fast and narrow where it is calm. The guarantee still holds. Across four test equations and several metrics, the method stayed well calibrated and beat rule-of-thumb approaches.
arxiv-2509-14017:
Marcus Webb explains why low-rank approximations work in a solo 2025 numerical analysis paper. Many scientific computing and data science algorithms lean on one fact. Matrices built from smooth interaction kernels are nearly low-rank. A few components capture almost everything. A theory of when that structure must appear guides both analysis and faster algorithms.

Webb gives a framework bounding the best possible low-rank approximation error. The matrices are sampled from a kernel that extends analytically into a region of the complex plane in one variable. The approximations used in the proof are not abstract. They come from rational interpolation at the roots and poles of Zolotarev rational functions, the optimal rational approximants. That turns the theory into a fast constructive algorithm.
arxiv-2509-14117:
Ali Abouzeid and four co-authors give robot policies geometric grounding in a 2025 robotics paper. Vision-language-action models translate camera images and instructions into robot actions. They falter when the camera moves to a viewpoint never seen in training. Inferring three-dimensional structure from flat images is exactly what they do badly.

GeoAware-VLA borrows a frozen, pretrained geometric vision model as its eyes. Strong three-dimensional features then arrive for free. Only a light projection layer is trained to adapt those features for the policy decoder. On the LIBERO and CALVIN manipulation benchmarks, in-distribution performance held or improved. Success from unseen camera poses jumped by dozens of points on one benchmark and over ten on the other. The gains carried over to a real robot.
arxiv-2509-14217:
Andriy Enttsel and four co-authors set out a theory in 2025 for sending a signal when the receiver must do more than rebuild it. Joint source and channel coding packs a signal for a noisy channel in one step, which suits fast, simple links. Here the receiver must also classify the signal and flag odd cases.

Working with a single bell shaped source and encoders built from straight line pieces, the authors derive usable design rules. They spell out the trade off among three goals: low distortion in the rebuilt signal, low classification error, and low sending power. Improving one goal tends to hurt another. The rules let a designer pick a balance on purpose rather than by trial and error.
arxiv-2509-14317:
Collin T. Christy and eighteen co-authors present a long radio study in 2025 of two tidal disruption events, where a star is torn apart by a black hole. Both events glowed in radio soon after their optical discovery. The glow then lasted for years.

One event, AT 2020zso, shows two separate radio flares. The first peaked about a year after discovery, while the second rose far later and briefly showed two spectral parts at once. That split points to two physically distinct outflows, both moving at a modest share of light speed. The first outflow looks driven by infalling gas. The partner event helps test whether late radio light is a new outflow or stray host galaxy emission.
arxiv-2509-14517:
Scott Mutchnik, writing alone in 2025, extends a classic hierarchy in model theory that measures how order like a theory can behave. Shelah strict order properties, labelled NSOP with an integer index, classify theories by forbidden patterns. The index has always been a whole number at least three.

Mutchnik observes the definition can be restated so any real number at least three can serve as the index. That defines a potentially larger family of properties. Translating the hierarchy to hereditary classes of finite structures yields a new real valued quantity for each class. Whether integer and real hierarchies truly differ becomes a concrete combinatorial question. Fine grained hierarchies help model theorists locate a theory complexity with more precision.
arxiv-2509-14617:
Jianglan Wei and four co-authors present HD3C in 2025, a lightweight medical classifier for low power edge devices, published under a name that differs from an earlier evidence label. Disease screening at the bedside or in clinics without servers needs models that sip power. Heavy neural networks drain batteries and need cooling.

HD3C encodes data as high dimensional hypervectors and groups them into cluster prototypes. Classification is then a similarity search in that hyperspace, a cheap operation. Across three medical tasks, heart sound classification stood out: energy use fell by orders of magnitude against a Bayesian ResNet, with accuracy within a point. Robustness tests add support for noisy real world signals on small devices.
arxiv-2509-15117:
Saajid Chowdhury and Jesús Pérez Ríos link chaotic scattering to heating in collisions between a trapped ion and cold atoms, in a 2025 atomic physics paper. A single ion held in a Paul trap meets a thin bath of atoms just above a microkelvin. Some collisions briefly bind the pair into an atom-ion complex before they separate.

Simulations of hundreds of millions of trajectories, accelerated on graphics processors, map how outcomes depend on atom species, collision energy, trap settings, and potential depth. Lower-energy collisions with heavier atoms form complexes most readily, especially below the initial micromotion heating scale. Those complexes evolve with fractal structure in every scattering observable, the fingerprint of non-hyperbolic chaos. The onset of chaos in the very first collision connects directly to later heating of the ion.
arxiv-2509-15217:
Yue Xin and seven co-authors synthesize training data for geometry problem solving with reinforcement-checked captions, in a 2025 machine learning paper. Multimodal models still stumble on geometry, partly because good image-text training pairs for diagrams are scarce. Template-based synthesis pipelines generate captions that rarely generalize beyond their templates.

The authors insert reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards into the data pipeline. Diagrams are synthesized from fifty basic geometric relations, captions are drafted, and a refinement step rewards captions that actually help solve mathematical problems. The reward signal comes from downstream problem-solving itself, so captions keep the features a solver needs. The resulting data generalizes better to fresh questions and yields clear improvements on geometry tasks, showing that data quality can be trained rather than merely filtered.
arxiv-2509-15317:
M. Lima and C. Gomes work out the cosmology of a gravity theory with a non-minimal Weyl connection in a 2025 gravitation paper. Their model couples matter and curvature non-minimally and lets the connection carry non-metricity, so lengths can change along paths. An extra force term in the theory can imitate dark matter and dark energy effects, and the construction follows Weyl's old ambition to unify gravity with electromagnetism.

Black hole solutions resembling the Schwarzschild and charged Reissner-Nordstrom cases exist in the model, with an additional horizon contributed by the non-metricity vector. The authors derive the cosmological field equations under minimal coupling and present preliminary results on scalar perturbations, the seeds of cosmic structure. Perturbation behavior will decide whether the model can match the observed Universe.
arxiv-2509-15417:
Viktor Byzov and Igor Pushkarev, writing in a paper translated from Russian, prove that a family of rare graphs exists. These directed graphs are strongly regular, which means their links follow strict count rules. The case they study is fixed by five numbers. Such graphs are known in some cases and ruled out in others, so each new case settles an open point.

The pair build the graphs from blocks that repeat in a cycle of three. They describe the found graphs with two ideas they call skeleton and rigging. Each graph's symmetry group turns out to be a small cycle group. The paper adds one more confirmed case to the list of these graphs.
arxiv-2509-15517:
Zelong Bi and Pierre Lafaye de Micheaux survey ways to guess the true dimension of data. Much high dimensional data may lie near a surface of far fewer dimensions. Guessing that count helps users exploit the shape of their data. Past work on such guesses is scattered, with no shared test of the tools.

The pair review the theory that is often skipped and pick eight tools to test. In controlled runs they vary noise, curve, and sample size one at a time. They also compare the tools on fake and real data sets. A principled way to tune each tool for each data set is part of the study. Their results guide which tool to pick when.
arxiv-2509-15617:
Toshiro Hiranouchi and Rin Sugiyama study cycles on shapes defined over special fields. A field earns their label when a norm map between its finite extensions always hits every target. Finite fields, local fields, and some global fields meet the rule at set levels. Zero cycles are formal sums of points, grouped into classes that track deep traits of a shape.

For a shape over such a field, they prove a key group of cycle classes can be split without remainder. Under a further condition on the shape, that group splits into a named K group plus a splittable part. They apply the result to homology groups with finite coefficients. The prime used must differ from the field's own trait.
arxiv-2509-16317:
A sharp test of Einstein's gravity compares its two potentials, which should match if the theory holds on large scales. L. Pizzuti and seven co-authors measure their ratio across nine massive galaxy clusters, using mass maps from light bending and galaxy motions. The ratio is traced from near each center out past the cluster edge.

With two standard mass models, the ratio matched the gravity prediction across the full range. A third model raised mild tension in two clusters. The joint value at a set radius tightens past estimates by about forty percent. The team also weighs how survey quirks affect the result.
arxiv-2509-16617:
David Kreismann, working alone, maps city heat in a 2025 climate paper. Dense city areas often run hotter than the land around them. As warming grows, that extra heat hits health and comfort. Cities need fine maps of air warmth to plan shade, trees, and cool surfaces.

Kreismann fine-tunes a broad geospatial model for this task. The tuned model predicts land surface warmth under future climate paths. Its errors stayed small in pixel-level checks. It also matched ground patterns well. Tests with planted greenery show how land cover shifts heat. Planners could use such maps to target the hottest blocks first.
arxiv-2509-16817:
Xiaojie Fan, C. R. Ramakrishnan, and Himanshu Gupta design a full protocol stack for quantum networks in a 2025 paper. A quantum internet needs more than good hardware. It needs rules for communication, control, and resource use at every layer. Their stack adds a global module that tracks entanglement across the whole network.

The module keeps a shared, up-to-date view of entanglement resources. Sync methods keep that view consistent across nodes. In all tested scenarios, the design cut latency and held up well. The stack offers a practical path toward large, adaptive quantum networks. Such networks could link quantum computers and sensors one day.
arxiv-2509-16917:
Daniel Lindenschmitt and co-authors plan sensing inside 5G networks in a 2025 paper. Future networks may sense their surroundings while carrying data, a pairing called integrated sensing and communication. Open network designs split functions into modules from varied vendors. The team analyze what that pairing needs inside an open 5G radio network.

They weigh radar setups, signal types, and where processing should sit. Threats like spoofing, passive sensing, and privacy breaches are mapped to defenses. The result is a deployment blueprint for public and private networks. It keeps standards in view while pointing toward 6G. Modular sensing could serve factories and campuses first.
arxiv-2509-17217:
Ilai Guendelman and Yoahi Kaspi built a new climate model for Uranus and Neptune in a 2025 arXiv paper. The two ice giants are the least explored planets, and a puzzle hangs over them. Their winds look much alike, even though their tilts and inner heat differ a great deal. Past models have struggled to match the winds seen by telescopes.

The pair's idealized model sweeps through settings to see how winds and overturning flows respond. Depth turns out to be the key knob. When the model's lower layer runs deep enough, the flow stops caring about the shape of the imposed heat pattern. In that regime, moving air itself, through eddy flows that carry momentum sideways and upward, sustains the circulation. That finding explains why two unlike planets can wear such similar winds.
arxiv-2509-17417:
Pengfei Zhang, Shuyan Zhou, and Ning Sun study a quantum resource called magic in a 2025 arXiv paper. Entanglement gets most of the attention in quantum physics, but magic is what pushes a system past what classical computers can mimic. It is measured by the stabilizer Rényi entropy, and most studies of it rely on simulations of modest systems.

The authors build a general frame for that measure in Sachdev-Ye-Kitaev models, which stay solvable even at large size. A saddle-point method then does the heavy lifting. Applied to a coupled version of the model, the frame reveals a string of sharp transitions in the magic as temperature changes. One transition hides from every standard thermodynamic probe. The authors argue that magic can serve as an order parameter for a new class of transitions in strongly linked fermion systems.
arxiv-2509-17817:
J Fransson shows how a chiral molecule can lock into one spin state when it touches a pool of electrons. His 2025 paper starts from closed-shell molecules, which have no net spin. Small flips between spin states keep local spin at zero in the free case.

Contact with the pool opens the shell and spreads the energy levels. With spin-orbit links, that contact splits the levels and steadies one spin state, set by the hand of the molecule. Charge in the molecule shifts with pool spin in a way that breaks a classic swap rule. That break helps explain a known chiral spin effect.
arxiv-2509-18017:
Einan Gardi and Zehao Zhu compute a soft factor for collisions with a massless particle in the mix. Their 2025 paper deals with the soft anomalous dimension, which sums the glow of low-energy particles in a crash. With heavy particles, line-based tools make the sum clean, but light-like lines add extra poles.

Their route starts from a correlator of three time-like lines. A method of regions then takes the limit where one line turns light-like. The hard part of that split gives the light-like correlator, with its clashes. Add the rest back, and the true pole stands out.
arxiv-2509-18317:
Fluids near a sudden change of state show peaks in heat measures along a curve called the Widom line. J. Fournier and five co-authors ask whether a twin idea can sort out electron fluids. Their 2025 paper links the Frenkel line from classic fluid physics to the pseudogap, a puzzling state in some metals. They study a grid model of electrons with strong links between them.

Using a cluster method on a triangular grid model, they compute a new crossover line. On one side sits the pseudogap; on the other, a more normal metal state. They mark the line by back-scattering, seen as a negative dip in how the material responds to light over time. The line reaches up to high temperatures. The work gives a sharper way to map where the pseudogap begins.
arxiv-2509-18717:
Image-text models trained on web data can be poisoned by planted, mislabeled pairs. Tong Zhang and seven co-authors present OTCCLIP, a defense for CLIP pre-training, in this 2025 paper. Older defenses rematch each image with a new caption using only global features. That coarse matching can create fresh wrong pairs and hurt training.

The new framework measures the gap between fine-grained image and text features with an optimal transport distance. Captions are reassigned based on that finer distance. Extra objectives align the two modalities at a fine grain, within and across pairs, to blunt any leftover mismatches. In tests, the method cut the success rates of poisoning and backdoor attacks. It also raised zero-shot and probe scores over prior defenses on poisoned data. The authors frame fine detail as the key to safe rematching.
arxiv-2509-19017:
Hazem Dewidar and Elena Umili tackle tasks where a reward depends on the whole history of an agent's actions, not just its current state. Reward machines attack such tasks with a small automaton that tracks progress through the task. Past versions needed a hand-built map from raw sensor data to symbols, or prior knowledge of the task itself. That setup work limits where the method can be used.

Their fully learnable version learns both the symbol map and the automaton itself, end to end, from data. It can be applied as easily as standard deep reinforcement learning, yet the learned automaton stays small and readable. In tests, their method beat earlier approaches built on recurrent neural networks, a common tool for history-based tasks.
arxiv-2509-19117:
Felix Weissberg and five co-authors ask an uncomfortable question about using large language models to hunt for security flaws in code. Progress there has stalled, and they probe why through classic code metrics: simple numbers like code length and branching that predate AI tools. A classifier trained on those metrics alone, they find, matches top language models at spotting vulnerable code. That parity hints the models lean on shallow cues.

A deeper analysis shows more than correlation. When a metric's value is changed, the model's judgment shifts by a matching amount, a causal effect. The authors conclude that current models read code about as shallowly as the metrics do. That limits their grip on the complex patterns behind real vulnerabilities. They close with recommendations for how research should attack the problem more effectively.
arxiv-2509-19217:
Andrey Tlatov, writing alone, measures how sunspot groups tilt, using more than a century of solar observations. Tilt angles of active regions, the pairs of magnetic poles where sunspots form, help predict the strength of the next solar cycle. Low-latitude pairs matter most for that forecast. Tlatov draws on magnetic field measurements from Mount Wilson Observatory covering 1918 to 2019, plus white-light records from Kodaikanal and Mount Wilson for earlier cycles.

He asks below which latitude the tilt statistics correlate best with the next cycle's strength. For the magnetic data, the answer is an equatorial band below about fourteen degrees. The white-light datasets give cutoffs near nine degrees. Mean tilts and their slope against latitude were both tracked across cycles 15 to 24. The results sharpen an empirical tool for anticipating solar activity.
arxiv-2509-19517:
How much extra clutter can a language model handle before its reasoning breaks? Sai Teja Reddy Adapala tests that limit with a benchmark built to add load in a controlled way. Two load kinds are studied: clutter that does not matter for the task, and the drag left by switching tasks. The test uses hard questions that need several linked steps to answer.

Two smaller open models scored zero on all rounds, even with no added load. A larger model held up well on clean rounds but slipped as clutter grew. The results are early, yet they suggest that load limits differ sharply by model. Builders who stuff prompts with context may be hurting the very reasoning they want. The benchmark gives a cleaner way to measure that harm.
arxiv-2509-20317:
Reasoning inside a model's hidden states, rather than in written words, promises cheaper thought. Xilin Wei and seven co-authors stabilize that implicit chain-of-thought approach in a 2025 arXiv paper. Implicit methods save tokens but trail written reasoning in accuracy. Scaling them up often makes training collapse, as hidden states blur into sameness.

Their module, SIM-CoT, adds step-level supervision during training only. A helper decoder aligns each hidden token with its matching explicit reasoning step. That keeps the hidden states diverse and meaningful. The helper is removed at run time, so inference stays lean. It also lets users project hidden tokens into words for inspection. Tests raised accuracy for two implicit methods and beat written reasoning on one model with far fewer tokens.
arxiv-2509-20617:
Extracting structured data with language models usually means a tangle of one-off scripts. Eric Fithian and Kirill Skobelev package the workflow as DELM, an open-source Python toolkit introduced in a 2025 arXiv paper. The toolkit targets rapid experiments with extraction pipelines and honest measurement of their trade-offs. Boilerplate shrinks through a modular design with structured outputs and built-in validation.

Data loading and scoring strategies plug in flexibly, and batch processing is efficient. Working with model APIs gets retry logic, result caching, cost tracking, and thorough configuration management. Two case studies show the toolkit in action. One demonstrates a new prompt optimization algorithm. The other measures the cost-versus-coverage trade-off when keywords decide which paragraphs deserve a model call. The code is public for reuse.
arxiv-2509-21117:
Using a language model to grade other models is convenient, but the judge contradicts itself in systematic ways. Yidong Wang and thirteen co-authors catalog those contradictions in TrustJudge, a 2025 paper on LLM-as-a-judge evaluation. Inconsistent judging quietly corrupts leaderboards and model comparisons.

The authors identify two failure types. Score-comparison inconsistency means a lower-scored answer beats a higher-scored one in a head-to-head test. Pairwise transitivity inconsistency appears as circular preferences, where A beats B, B beats C, and C beats A. They trace both to information lost in discrete ratings and to ambiguous tie calls. TrustJudge answers with a probabilistic framework, including distribution-sensitive scoring, designed to keep judgments coherent.
arxiv-2509-22017:
Hugh Xuechen Liu and Kıvanç Tatar work on predicting missing links in knowledge graphs that have very few links to learn from. Such two-sided graphs appear in niche fields, where data is scarce by nature. Their 2025 paper presents AEGIS, a method that grows the training set using only real edges. It copies existing links, either evenly or with a bias toward low-degree nodes, and never invents fake endpoints.

The authors test the idea on a naturally sparse graph from game design and on two dense benchmarks thinned out by heavy random removal. Copy-based versions matched the sparse baseline on ranking and calibration scores. A semantic method, which adds links between similar nodes, was the only one to restore ranking quality on the big benchmarks. Random or synthetic edges hurt throughout, which supports the paper's theme: added data must stay authentic.
arxiv-2509-22417:
Habib Ammari, Clemens Thalhammer, and Alexander Uhlmann study wave gaps in chains of tiny resonators. The chains are aperiodic: their blocks come from a small library but never repeat in a fixed pattern. The team asks which frequencies pass and which are blocked, for endless, half-endless, and finite chains. Their tool is uniform hyperbolicity, a way to track stable and unstable wave directions.

A switch from transfer to propagation matrices lets them judge the whole chain block by block. They prove a Saxon-Hutner type result: the gaps of the full chain follow from its blocks by a strict cone test. Edge modes in half-endless chains get an explicit form. Finite chains inherit strict spectral bounds.
arxiv-2509-22517:
Zifei Yu and Baode Li pin down when fractional Hausdorff operators stay bounded. These operators average a function against a kernel over scaled copies, with a fractional power that adds smoothing. The team works on weighted Lebesgue spaces, where a weight reshapes how size is measured. They find necessary and sufficient conditions for boundedness. A new constraint on the fractional parameter appears, one that the non-fractional case satisfies on its own.

They then turn to power-weighted Hardy spaces, which suit functions with strong local behavior. Two characterizations of those spaces give two related boundedness results. Their route differs from an earlier proof that used only the radial maximal function characterization.
arxiv-2509-22717:
Nicholas Caputo asks when AI governance work can safely be handed to AI systems themselves. Advanced systems already help govern AI, and delegation will likely grow as the task gets harder. The risks are real: humans may not grasp AI decisions or check them against user interests, and legitimacy can suffer. Caputo looks for a principled frame in an unlikely place, administrative law.

That body of law governs agencies that out-expert their creators and overseers yet may drift from their goals. Its doctrines state when delegation may occur, what it may cover, and which processes keep agencies aligned. Caputo uses those lessons as a foundation for safe, accountable AI delegation in governance.
arxiv-2509-22817:
Edward McManus and 8 co-authors observe spiral patterns in electrons torn from atoms by a single laser pulse. Strong-field ionization with elliptically polarized light can release electrons into vortex states, states that swirl like a whirlpool. The team shows, in experiment and theory, that vortex structures appear in the photoelectron momentum pattern even with one pulse. The spirals come from destructive interference between two dominant vortex states.

An electron in one state lingers near the atomic core, delayed by the combined atomic and laser potential. That delay makes the phase difference swing fast with energy. The results open a route to studying the dynamics of vortex states in strong-field ionization.
arxiv-2509-22917:
Yuelin Xin and 3 co-authors tackle how neural networks should take in 3D Gaussian splatting data. That format stores a scene as many soft 3D blobs and renders fast. Its raw parameter lists are a poor input for learning, though. The same scene can be stored in many valid ways, and the values mix unlike kinds.

The team propose an embedding built from continuous submanifold fields. These fields capture the color and shape facts inside the Gaussian blobs. The embedding gives each scene one fixed code with uniform channels. That design should help networks learn from splatting data more cleanly. Code for the method is shared in public.
arxiv-2509-23417:
A model can know a fact and still be marked wrong for phrasing the answer in an odd form. Rajaa El Hamdani and 5 co-authors test how much knowledge strict scoring hides. Their Retrieval-Constrained Decoding forces outputs into unique surface forms. A new data set, YAGO-QA, holds over nineteen thousand general knowledge questions. Open models from tiny to seventy billion parameters were tested.

Standard decoding badly undervalued the biggest model. Constrained decoding lifted its F1 score from about thirty-two to forty-six percent. A mid-size model under the new decoding beat the giant under the old one. Knowledge inside the weights is larger than scores suggest.
arxiv-2509-23517:
A row of moving dots on key joints is enough for people to read an action, but can AI models do the same? Akila Kadambi and 3 co-authors built ActPLD, the first benchmark of point-light displays for multi-modal language models. Such displays strip a scene to body motion alone, so meaning must come from movement itself. The test covers single actors and social scenes with more than one person.

Both closed and open state-of-the-art models scored low across the board. The authors read this as a basic gap in how these systems grasp action and change over time. Human skill here grows early in life and rests on bodily experience, which models lack.
arxiv-2509-23717:
A sparse autoencoder feature that fires on neat examples may still fail on near-twins of those examples. Claire Tian and 2 co-authors measure that reliability, which they call feature sensitivity. Instead of writing descriptions of each feature, they ask language models to generate fresh text with the same semantic traits as a feature's activating examples. Then they check whether the feature fires on the new text.

Many features that look interpretable scored poorly on sensitivity. Human checks confirmed the generated texts really did resemble the originals, so the failures belong to the features. Across seven autoencoder variants, average sensitivity fell as width grew, adding a new axis for judging these tools.
arxiv-2509-23917:
An attack crafted for one vision-language task can wound a model at another, and the traffic runs both ways. Kuanrong Liu and 4 co-authors map that cross-task transfer for CLIP and its descendants across retrieval, detection, and segmentation. Attacks born in fine-grained tasks like detection and segmentation transfer more strongly than those from coarse tasks, and they hit the original CLIP hard.

Their framework, MT-AdvCLIP, adds a task-aware feature aggregation loss to craft perturbations with wider cross-task reach. On public data sets it raised average attack success across tasks by over thirty-nine percent at the same perturbation budget. The study frames multi-task robustness as its own security question.
arxiv-2509-24517:
Bigger models forecast better and pollute more, and the balance between the two is rarely measured head-on. Sophia N Wilson and 2 co-authors study that trade-off for spatio-temporal forecasting of incompressible shear flow. They compare seven models that differ in receptive field and in whether they assume periodicity, scoring accuracy, physics fidelity, and carbon cost in training and in use.

No single model won on both performance and carbon. A cheap training run did not reliably mean cheap inference, and runtime alone proved a poor proxy for carbon, above all in training. The authors argue carbon accounting across the full lifecycle should sit beside accuracy as a core design criterion.
arxiv-2510-00017:
En-naoui introduces a new unified notation for exponential congruences. A generalized k-th power symbol that records whether a raised to the k equals plus or minus one modulo n. Extending the spirit of the classical Legendre and Jacobi symbols. The paper systematically develops the symbol's full algebraic properties, organized by which of its three parameters, the base, the modulus, or the exponent, is being varied in this work.

For the base he proves multiplicativity, inversion symmetry, and power compatibility, for the modulus factorization rules, orthogonality relations. And Kummer splitting criteria, and for the exponent reciprocity laws and specialization back to classical symbols. New results add character-based additive behavior, Möbius filtering, exact counting formulas for prime moduli, and further connections with Dirichlet L-series. With the all-prime case generalizing classical reciprocity, Frobenius automorphisms, and Sato-Tate distributions in the theory.
arxiv-2510-00217:
Sung Hee Park and four colleagues published this 2025 statistics paper on sex differences in jaw joint mechanics. The temporomandibular joint links skull shape to the muscles used in chewing. Disorders of this joint strike women far more often than men. The team studied how skull form and muscle attachment sites relate, and how that relation differs by sex.

Their data came from ten male and eleven female cadaver heads measured in the lab. They propose a conditional cross-covariance reduction model for this two-block, two-sex problem. A sparse decomposition algorithm picks out the most telling skull and muscle variables. A sequential permutation scheme decides how many variables to keep. The method spotlights the strongest sex-specific links between bone and muscle. Such maps could guide better diagnosis and device design for jaw disorders.
arxiv-2510-00717:
Li, Shakouri, and Camlibel analyse how fragile data-driven feedback gains can be, in this 2025 arXiv paper on control theory. Data-driven control designs a stabilizing feedback law straight from input-state measurements, skipping system identification. Rounding, finite word length, and hardware faults then perturb that gain in practice. The collected data say nothing about such feedback perturbations, so a nominally stabilizing gain might collapse under tiny changes.

The authors parametrize all quadratically stabilizing gains obtainable from noisy data. They fully characterize extreme fragility, where arbitrarily small perturbations can destabilize the true system. They also give necessary and sufficient conditions for complete immunity to perturbations. Between those poles, a data-computable measure quantifies fragility for any candidate gain. The least fragile gain can then be designed by solving a semidefinite program built from the same data. Results come in closed form or as linear matrix inequalities.
arxiv-2510-00817:
Leisegang, Casini, and Meyer compare two frameworks for reasoning with inconsistent knowledge in this 2025 arXiv paper on logic and artificial intelligence. Weighted knowledge bases assign costs to interpretations based on how many rules they break. The older c-representations instead rank interpretations by penalties for violated rules of thumb, such as birds usually fly. Both aim to answer queries sensibly when facts conflict.

The authors show that, under stated conditions, the two frameworks can produce the very same ordering over interpretations. They also translate entailment notions between the systems, so results proved on one side can inform the other. The paper frames itself as an initial bridge between the query-answering and defeasible reasoning communities. That bridge could let both fields inherit methods and broaden where each approach applies.
arxiv-2510-01017:
Bao, dos Reis, and Wilde establish Malliavin differentiability for McKean-Vlasov equations with common noise in this 2025 arXiv paper on stochastic analysis. McKean-Vlasov equations describe a particle whose dynamics depend on the distribution of the population, a mean-field effect. Common noise adds a shared environment that every particle experiences together, making the law conditional on that environment. Whether solutions respond differentiably to perturbations of the noise, in the Malliavin sense, was open for this class.

Under Lipschitz assumptions in the state and the measure argument, the authors prove that solutions are Malliavin differentiable. Their result also gives meaning to the Malliavin derivative of the conditional law with respect to the common noise. As an application they derive an integration by parts formula on Wiener space for these equations. Such formulas underpin sensitivity analysis and density estimates for mean-field systems in finance and physics.
arxiv-2510-01117:
Sur, Guo, and Mondaini propose a way to freeze highly entangled quantum states in place in this 2025 arXiv paper on quantum physics. Entanglement normally keeps evolving after a state is prepared, so storing it without decay is a core challenge for quantum memory. Many-body localization can hold local information, yet global properties of the state still drift away. The authors instead quench the system to an emergent Hamiltonian that has the target state as an eigenstate.

In general that Hamiltonian is non-local and lacks a closed form, but they find cases where it is exact and fully local. Those examples allow, in principle, storage limited only by experimental imperfections. The protocol keeps both local and global properties of the stored state. Demonstrations cover products of Bell pairs and fragile GHZ states that real devices struggle to prepare.
arxiv-2510-01217:
Paterson and co-authors twist the walls of a microwave cavity and watch its light turn helical. Ordinary resonators keep electric and magnetic patterns separate, so no handedness emerges. A controlled geometric twist breaks mirror symmetry and couples the two field families.

The coupling produces measurable helicity inside a single resonant mode in empty space. Twisting further shifts the resonant frequencies, so one knob steers both properties in real time. Internal helical grooves add a surface-level chirality that skews tuning asymmetrically. Macroscopic control of light's handedness could serve sensors and quantum devices alike. Nearly degenerate modes mix most strongly, which the design exploits. Frequency shifts track the twist angle, giving a clean readout. Chiral light interacts unevenly with chiral matter, a sensing goldmine. Vacuum operation keeps the effect purely geometric. One device tunes pitch and handedness together at once.
arxiv-2510-01617:
Leong and co-authors let a multi-agent system redesign its own communication wiring for each incoming task. Fixed team charts, hand-drawn by engineers, fit some jobs badly and waste effort on others. Their framework, AMAS, includes a graph designer that picks a task-specific structure before work begins.

The designer learns through light adaptation of the language model itself, guided by a custom loss. Queries then travel along pathways shaped for their own demands. Benchmarks in question answering, mathematics, and code generation confirmed the advantage over static charts. Structure becomes a decision the system makes, not a cage it inherits. Sample sensitivity across tasks motivated the whole design. Industrial workloads vary wildly, which is exactly where templates crack. Lightweight adaptation keeps the designer cheap beside the agents it arranges. Topology becomes a per-query choice. Teams shaped per task outperform permanent org charts.
arxiv-2510-01717:
Shaon and Nguyen study federated learning carried by drones in this 2025 engineering paper. In their setup, unmanned aerial vehicles gather data with several kinds of sensors at once. The drones train a shared model together with a ground base station, without sending raw data away. The authors aim to cut the total system delay while keeping the learning sound.

They jointly tune sensing schedules, transmit power, flight paths, and computing resources. That joint problem is non-convex and hard, so they solve it with an iterative method mixing block coordinate descent and successive convex approximation. They also prove convergence results for the learning process under a non-convex loss. Numerical experiments beat existing approaches on both system latency and training performance. The work matters for drone fleets that must learn quickly in the field.
arxiv-2510-01817:
Filipek proposes a leaner attention mechanism for transformer models in this 2025 paper. Attention cost grows with the square of sequence length, which blocks very long contexts. Popular fixes share key and value heads to save memory bandwidth during generation. They do not, however, cut the core arithmetic of the attention scores themselves.

Sparse Query Attention attacks that arithmetic directly by using fewer query heads. Cutting query heads shrinks the operation count in direct proportion. Filipek lays out the theory, the math, and a family of design variants. Benchmarks on sequences from thirty-two thousand to two hundred thousand tokens showed major throughput gains. The savings matter most for training and for processing whole long documents at once. Because the idea complements key-value sharing, the two tricks can be combined in future architectures.
arxiv-2510-02017:
Tayebi, Khodabandeh Yalabadi, Yazdani-Jahromi, and Garibay teach tabular models fairer representations through contrastive learning in this 2025 paper. Tabular data drives many high-stakes decisions, yet its features lack the tidy structure of images or text. Models trained naively inherit societal biases against sensitive groups. Fair representation learning tries to keep predictive signal while scrubbing that bias.

Their framework, FairContrast, selects positive pairs strategically and mixes supervised with self-supervised contrastive objectives. Customized augmentation methods adapt the contrastive recipe to tabular quirks. The learned representations cut bias substantially compared with state-of-the-art contrastive models for tables. Accuracy paid only a minimal price for those fairness gains. The same representations transferred across several downstream tasks. Results suggest contrastive methods, long proven in vision and speech, can debias tabular pipelines too. The authors frame fairness here as a moral duty, not just a metric.
arxiv-2510-02317:
Jaikissoon argues that rules for hybrid cryptography lag behind the technology itself. Her 2025 policy paper looks at the shift toward quantum safe security. Quantum machines threaten today's standard encryption. A full switch will take about ten years, she notes. Hybrid systems bridge the gap by mixing old and new methods. Artificial intelligence raises parallel misuse worries in her account. Both fields now grow faster than their rulebooks. She maps the gaps in current standards and oversight. She then offers fixes meant to guide organizations through the change.
