The authors build HyPerNav, which joins both views with help from vision-language models. Those models link what a robot sees to words for objects and rooms. Tests show the combined view helps the robot search with more sense and fewer wasted moves. Readers get a clear plan for robots that must explore homes or offices on their own.
arxiv-2510-23217:
Alois Thomas, Maya Varma, Jean-Benoit Delbrouck, and Curtis P Langlotz build a reward model that checks radiology reports sentence by sentence. Vision-language models can draft such reports, but they often hallucinate facts that could harm patients. Older detectors lack sentence-level detail or fail to generalize across report generators.

Their process reward model scores the factual correctness of each sentence given the clinical context and prior text. Fine-tuned for this vision-language task, it flags risky lines for review. Sentence-level checks give hospitals a finer safety net for automated reporting tools. The authors present their evidence and methods in full for readers to judge.
arxiv-2510-23617:
Phuong Q. Dao, Mark Roantree, and Vuong M. Ngo work on multimodal sentiment analysis, reading human emotion from text and images together rather than either alone. Two signals usually say more than one, and transformer models give strong tools for each side: BERT for text and the Vision Transformer for pictures. The authors first fuse the two early, so the streams shape each other from the start.

Their extended model, the Dual Transformer Contrastive Network, adds another transformer layer to sharpen the text before fusion and uses contrastive learning to pull matching text and image features closer. On the TumEmo benchmark it reached the best accuracy, about seventy-eight percent, with a matching F1 score. On MVSA-Single it stayed competitive at roughly seventy-seven percent accuracy. The results back early fusion plus deeper context as a sound recipe for emotion reading.
arxiv-2510-23817:
Pedro Cortes dos Santos and two co-authors combine two explanation tools to make fault detection in industrial plants sharper and more understandable. Plants generate tangled data, and machine learning detectors often stay opaque even when accurate. Working with the Tennessee Eastman Process, a standard benchmark with tangled dynamics, the authors first found models limited on both fronts.

They reframe the task using SHAP values, which rank which process features drive each prediction, cutting the problem down to its critical variables. On that reduced set they run causal analysis, building directed acyclic graphs with several algorithms to trace how faults propagate. The causal maps line up with the SHAP rankings, pointing at the same cooling and separation units as the hubs of fault development. The pairing gives operators accurate alarms plus a story about where a fault begins, a combination the authors say is new in this setting.
arxiv-2510-24317:
María Sanz-Gómez and five co-authors present CAIBench, a meta benchmark for evaluating AI agents in cybersecurity. Security spans many linked domains, so existing benchmarks that test isolated skills miss integrated, job relevant performance. The authors also find that a model's stored security knowledge does not imply real attack and defense ability.

CAIBench integrates five evaluation categories with over ten thousand instances, including jeopardy style and attack and defense capture the flag events and cyber range exercises. Its modular design lets teams evaluate both language models and agents across offensive and defensive tasks. The goal is a meaningful measure of how useful these systems are for real security work.
arxiv-2510-24917:
G A Bougas, G C Katsimiga, S Mossman, P Engels, P G Kevrekidis, and S I Mistakidis caught rogue waves in a cold gas of atoms with three parts. Rogue waves are huge, brief peaks that are hard to see in atomic gases, since they need an unstable pull. Their gas parts push each other off and do not mix, yet the scarce parts act as if pulled.

A new scheme shows how that false pull can arise in a mixed set with any signs of push or pull. Instability in and across parts, plus a well trap, then grows wave peaks that can be made again. By use of rubidium states, peak forms could be tuned at will.
arxiv-2510-25317:
Leon Monnier and Frederic Faure study topological index formulas. Their 2025 paper links spectral flow and Chern index. They examine families of pseudodifferential operators, called quantum Hamiltonians. The spectrum of each operator has two energy bands. Those bands exchange a finite number of eigenvalues. An eigenvalue is a special energy value here.

They show that exchanged count equals a Chern index. That index comes from a vector bundle. The bundle is tied to the principal symbol. The symbol plays the role of classical Hamiltonian. The result is a simple case of Atiyah-Singer. That famous formula links analysis and topology. Uses may appear in molecular and plasma physics. Geophysics is another possible application area. They also discuss topological contacts without band exchange. Chern index and K theory cannot detect those contacts.
arxiv-2510-25417:
Petter Tornberg traces shifts in United States social media use. His 2025 paper compares nationally representative survey data. Data come from American National Election Studies. Years 2020 and 2024 are compared directly. Overall platform use has declined since 2020. Youngest and oldest Americans increasingly abstain altogether.

Facebook, YouTube, and Twitter/X have lost ground. TikTok and Reddit have grown modestly instead. The digital public sphere has become more fragmented. Platform audiences have aged over this period. They also became slightly more educated and diverse. Most platforms moved toward Republican users politically. On balance, audiences remain Democratic-leaning in aggregate. Twitter/X showed the sharpest political shift there. Posting flipped nearly fifty points toward Republicans. Political posting links tightly to affective polarization. Most partisan users are also most active posters. Casual users disengage while polarized partisans stay vocal.
arxiv-2510-25517:
Elisabetta Gentili, Tony Ribeiro, Fabrizio Riguzzi, and Katsumi Inoue name predicates with language models. Their 2025 paper addresses logic rule readability. Predicate Invention is a key example producing unnamed predicates. Unnamed predicates hinder readability, interpretability, and reusability greatly.

Giving names to predicates is their target problem. Large language models can process language and code jointly. That ability may suggest semantically meaningful predicate names. They explore model suggestions for unnamed predicates systematically. Testing used hand-crafted logic rules for testing. Results indicate language models hold promise for the task. Better names could make learned theories understandable. Human users could reuse logic theories more easily. Automated naming may reduce manual annotation effort greatly. Logic programming tools could integrate such suggestions. Interpretability of machine-learned rules remains a broad challenge. This work offers a small, useful step forward.
arxiv-2510-25717: Jarmo Makela argues from action-angle variables in quantum gravity. His 2025 paper uses the Bohr-Sommerfeld quantization rule. If a smallest non-zero area exists, he argues, massive particles have a largest observable speed. That speed is a bit less than light speed. The paper is a short theoretical argument for readers interested in quantum gravity and fundamental limits on motion.
arxiv-2510-25817:
Junyu Luo leads ten co-authors in a survey of how to train large language models with less data after their first training phase. Post training is the extra training that helps a model follow tasks and fit a field. Good post training data is costly to label by hand, and adding more data helps less and less over time.

Luo and the team sort data saving methods into five groups, from picking and improving data to making synthetic data and compressing data sets. They sum up leading work in each group and point to open problems and future paths. The survey helps readers see how to use data well at large scale.
arxiv-2510-26217:
Tao Jin and Stuart Florescu, with two co-authors, build a hybrid system for managing collateral under financial contracts. Collateral choice under ISDA Credit Support Annexes must respect integer lots, haircuts, gating rules, and caps by issuer, currency, and class, which creates a rugged, legally bounded search space. Their pipeline starts with a language model that extracts contract terms into normalized data and abstains unless evidence supports each term.

A quantum inspired explorer mixes simulated annealing with small higher order quantum optimization steps to coordinate multi asset moves. A constraint solver certifies feasibility and gaps as the single arbiter. On government bond data, the hybrid beat a strong classical baseline by about nine to eleven percent in their tests.
arxiv-2510-26317:
Hanbing Fang and Yu Li study the rough points of spaces that arise as limits of Ricci flows. A Ricci flow smooths a shape over time, much as heat spreads, and a limit space can have singular points where the smoothing breaks. The pair sort those points into layers, based on how symmetric the flow looks when zoomed in at each point.

Fang and Li prove that one key layer can be covered well by smooth pieces of the right size, a trait called rectifiability. In four dimensions they prove the same for every layer. They also bound the total size of the singular set and add curvature bounds for four-dimensional flows. As a payoff, they settle a conjecture of Perelman about the width of three-dimensional flows.
arxiv-2510-26417:
Kaushiki Mukherjee and Nirman Ganguly study how noise can destroy a quantum resource called network nonlocality. In a quantum network, linked particles can show ties that no local story explains, and networks add new forms of this effect beyond the classic Bell setting. Noise from the surroundings, modelled as quantum channels, can wear those ties away.

Mukherjee and Ganguly define the channels that break network nonlocality, meaning the system loses the resource after passing through them. They work through tests for line-shaped and star-shaped networks, and for the stronger full form of the effect. Examples use common noise types, such as depolarizing and dephasing channels. Their sorting also picks out channels that keep the resource intact, which helps builders choose good links for quantum networks.
arxiv-2510-26517:
Bao-Xi Sun, Ying-Ying Fan, and Qin-Qin Cao study a possible bound state of a phi meson and a proton. A meson is a short-lived particle made of a quark and an antiquark, and the ALICE experiment at CERN has reported an attractive pull between the phi and the proton. That pull is summed up in a scattering length, whose real part is much larger than its imaginary part, hinting that elastic scattering rules.

Sun and his two co-authors model the process with a unitary coupled-channel method drawn from the Bethe-Salpeter equation. They find the measured scattering length comes out only when the attractive pull is included. The amplitude then shows two poles: one may be a resonance state, and the other a bound state of the pair. Neither state yet appears in the standard particle listings.
arxiv-2510-26617:
Marija Bliznac Trebješanin writes on Diophantine triples built from triangular numbers. A triangular number counts dots in a triangular stack. A D(m squared) triple is a set of three numbers where each pair, multiplied and shifted by m squared, gives a perfect square. Such triples are a classic topic in number theory.

She gives a general construction that yields infinitely many families of these triples, all made of triangular numbers. Every triple from the construction contains the same fixed triangular number. Short and focused, the paper adds a systematic source of examples to a topic where explicit families are prized.
arxiv-2510-26917:
Pavel Hernández-Amaro, Maria Durban, and M. Carmen Aguilera-Morillo propose a regression model in 2025. Regression links an outcome to inputs that may help explain or predict it. Their inputs are functions, curves or images, not single numbers alone.

The model handles inputs of one or more dimensions, even when partly seen. It needs no imputation, which means no guessed values are filled into gaps. Curves are built from basis pieces, smooth blocks joined to fit a shape. B-splines, one such block type named in the paper, are used here. Checks use fake data with one-curve inputs and with image-like inputs. A final test sorts air quality in Dimapur, India, from image data.
arxiv-2510-27517:
Zherui Yang leads five co-authors in learning sparse approximate inverse preconditioners that run well on graphics processors. The conjugate gradient solver handles large symmetric positive-definite systems, and a good preconditioner is crucial for fast convergence. Factorization-based learned preconditioners force triangular solves that hinder GPU parallelization and create long-range dependencies graph networks model poorly.

Their graph neural network instead builds sparse approximate inverse preconditioners, which need only two matrix-vector products per solver step and match the local propagation style of graph networks. A statistics-based scale-invariant loss fits the fact that convergence depends on condition number, not absolute scale. On PDE-derived and synthetic datasets it beats standard and learned rivals, cutting GPU solution time substantially with better generalization.
arxiv-2511-00517:
Shuochuan Li and five co-authors automate a tedious expert task: writing code review comments. One model asked to spot every kind of issue tends to produce vague comments, especially on complex changes such as bug fixes. Their framework, RevAgent, instead organizes the work around issue types, with specialist agents for each category of problem.

Five commentator agents draft candidate comments from distinct issue perspectives. A critic agent then picks the best issue-and-comment pairing. Finally, all agents are fine-tuned on curated, category-specific data to sharpen their specialties. RevAgent beat leading language-model baselines on standard text metrics by clear margins and identified issue categories more accurately in hard scenarios. Human judges also rated its comments accurate, readable, and context-aware, with a favorable balance of quality and cost.
arxiv-2511-00617:
Eric Bigelow and six co-authors unify two popular ways to steer a language model's behavior: prompting it with examples, and steering its internal activations directly. Accounts of each method have lived apart, yet both aim at the same target: controlling what the model does. The authors propose both are really belief updates about latent concepts inside the model.

In their Bayesian picture, steering changes the model's prior belief about a concept, while examples in context accumulate evidence for it. The result is a closed-form model that predicts model behavior across both interventions in several domains drawn from many-shot learning studies. It explains familiar sigmoidal learning curves and predicts new effects, such as additivity in log-belief space and sudden behavioral flips from tiny control changes. Control becomes something to compute, not just to try.
arxiv-2511-01717:
Gabriele Columba and ten colleagues image the planet-forming disks around two young stars in the Corona Australis region, V721 CrA and BN CrA, using the SPHERE instrument on the Very Large Telescope. The near-infrared, polarized scattered-light images come from DESTINYS, a survey of nearby young stars, and reveal both disks resolved, extended, and structured.

Fitting analytical disk models, rendered with the RADMC-3D code including polarized scattering, the team measured dust mass, height profile, and inclination. V721 CrA's disk is thicker, brighter, and smaller, about 120 astronomical units across, with spiral arms in its inner regions. BN CrA's disk stretches to about 190 units and shows a dark circular lane, either a real dust gap or a self-cast shadow. The contrast matches their subgroups: V721 CrA sits in the younger, denser on-cloud part, BN CrA in the older off-cloud outskirts.
arxiv-2511-01817:
Sagi Eppel and Alona Strugatski assemble SciTextures, a dataset that pairs visual patterns with the processes that generate them. Cloud textures, waves, growing cities and forests, forming materials: each pattern in the collection comes with the model and the code that produces it. The pairing connects appearance to mechanism across science, technology, and art.

The collection covers more than 1,270 models and 100,000 images drawn from physics, chemistry, biology, sociology, technology, mathematics, and art. It was built by an agentic AI pipeline that autonomously collects, implements, and standardizes generative models, and even invents new pattern-generating methods of its own. SciTextures doubles as a test for vision-language models. Can they link a pattern to the code behind it? Can they recognize different patterns from one process? Or can they infer and recreate an unknown mechanism from its picture?
arxiv-2511-02017:
Aditya Sridhar, Nish Sinnadurai, Sean Lie, and Vithursan Thangarasa tune speculative decoding. It is the trick that lets a small draft model race ahead of a large language model. The draft proposes tokens. The big model then verifies them in parallel. Draft too few and the speedup shrinks; draft too many and verification wastes work. Existing dynamic methods use hand-tuned thresholds, like token entropy cutoffs, that are costly to set and travel poorly across models.

Their algorithm, TapOut, treats the choice among several parameter-free drafting strategies as a multi-armed bandit problem. It learns online from past rewards. It learns which strategy to trust, while still exploring. It needs no training and no hyperparameter tuning, and drops into existing pipelines. Across diverse model pairs and datasets, TapOut matched or beat well-established dynamic speculation baselines, delivering competitive or superior speedups out of the box.
arxiv-2511-02117:
Stephen Henrich, Yann Mambrini, and Keith Olive revisit a dismissed idea for how dark matter was made in the early universe: ultra-relativistic freeze-out. This is the mechanism by which neutrinos separated from the hot early radiation bath while still moving near light speed. Freeze-out of that kind was long rejected for dark matter because it seemed to leave the matter too hot to match the observed universe.

Dropping the simplifying assumption that reheating after inflation was instant changes the verdict. With a gradual reheating period, ultra-relativistic freeze-out can leave dark matter cold and produce exactly the observed abundance. The span of masses runs from below an electron volt to the PeV (peta electron volt) scale. For many interactions, the path from weakly interacting to feebly interacting dark matter passes through this regime by necessity.
arxiv-2511-02217:
Manonmani Sekar and Nasim Nezamoddini tackle traffic lights at multi-lane intersections where human drivers and connected autonomous vehicles mix. Coordinating the two is difficult because their behaviour differs, and signal timing must balance delay, safety, and fairness between the groups. Their controller combines graph attention networks, which model how lanes and signal phases influence each other over space and time, with a soft actor-critic reinforcement learning algorithm.

Trained and tested in a SUMO simulation of a four-way intersection under varying traffic densities and autonomous vehicle shares, the system adapts signal timing and vehicle movement together. Average delay fell by 24.1 percent and traffic violations by up to 29.2 percent compared with traditional methods. The fairness ratio between human-driven and autonomous vehicles also improved, which the authors cite as evidence for real-world potential.
arxiv-2511-02317:
Evyatar Matmon and Daniel Zelazo figure out how to unmask the hidden leaders in a network of agents that are drifting toward consensus. In semi-autonomous networks some nodes lead and others follow, but an observer sees only the motion, not the wiring diagram or the roles. The analysis uses the grounded Laplacian, the network matrix with leader rows removed, and its Fiedler vector, a classic spectral summary of connectivity.

The authors derive conditions under which the Fiedler vector's entries for leaders and followers are guaranteed to differ. A quantity called relative tempo, readable from the agents' steady-state velocities, turns out to be tied to that vector. Their data-driven algorithm therefore reconstructs the Fiedler vector, and with it the leader set, from velocity measurements alone. Numerical examples confirm the method can reveal leadership structures that were not directly observed.
arxiv-2511-02517:
Yang Shen and Yunhui Wu confirm a conjecture about the vibrations of a typical curved surface. Take a random hyperbolic surface built by the Brooks-Makover construction, gluing together idealised pieces at random. Its Laplace spectrum has a gap above zero, and the size of that gap controls how quickly heat, waves, and random walks spread and mix across the surface. The best gap any such surface could hope for is bounded by the one-quarter threshold.

The authors prove that a random surface in this model has a spectral gap exceeding one quarter minus a small term. That term shrinks like a constant divided by the logarithm of the surface's size parameter. In other words, random surfaces come arbitrarily close to the optimal gap as they grow, which is exactly the nearly optimal spectral gap conjecture for this model. The proof runs to fifty pages, with an appendix.
arxiv-2511-03017:
Kaustav Chatterjee and five colleagues study a proposed power macrogrid linking North America's eastern and western grids through a multi-terminal DC network. Earlier studies praised the plan for sharing capacity and propping up frequency, but the risk of slow, poorly damped swings between regions went unexamined. Their 2025 paper builds a custom dynamic model of the DC link and joins it to industry-grade models of both big grids.

Oscillation analysis showed how the link shifts the natural swing modes of each side, and flagged modes with too little damping. The team then designed extra controllers for the DC stations, using wide-area feedback to adjust power set points and calm the swings. Tests under planned conditions and fault scenarios showed the controllers worked as designed.
arxiv-2511-03117:
Yibo Meng, Ruiqi Chen, Zhuoran Lu, Shuai Ma, and Chengxi Zang followed seventeen Chinese digital painters for five years as generative AI entered their field. Their 2025 study uses mixed methods to track how attitudes and working habits changed over that span. Long views of artists adapting to AI are rare, and this one catches the full arc rather than a snapshot.

The painters moved from resistance and defensiveness, through pragmatic adoption, to a reflective rebuilding of their practice. Peer pressure and shifting emotions drove much of the change. Worries about copyright and creative labor never faded, and the authors frame the story as a negotiation of identity and values. They close with design lessons for human-AI creative tools.
arxiv-2511-03417:
D S Bhattacharya and a large team describe the light-sensing modules built for BUTTON-30, a neutrino detector test bed deep underground in north-east England. The project trials a gadolinium-loaded water-based liquid that glows faintly when neutrinos strike, ahead of a possible huge observatory. Watertight optical modules must catch that glow while surviving long submersion.

Design and build details cover sealing, materials, and assembly for the underground setting. Success would clear a path toward large detectors that can also watch nuclear reactors from afar for treaty checks. Remote reactor watching is a prized nonproliferation goal, since it needs no inspector on site. The modules are a small but vital proving step for that vision.
arxiv-2511-03517:
Wencheng Ye and Yan Liu propose U2F, a multi-agent system that pushes software agents to hunt for novel fixes without losing workable ones. Language model agents for coding mostly attack well-defined problems with standard methods, missing fresh paths in open settings. U2F is built to surface unknown unknowns, solution routes absent from the first problem statement.

A discovery, exploration, and integration team uncovers candidate paths and merges the best of them. Cognitive boosts help agents hold onto uncertainty as a resource rather than a flaw. Tests in open software settings check whether novelty survives contact with feasibility demands. The aim is agents that invent when templates run dry, yet still ship code that runs.
arxiv-2511-03717:
Shakil Ahmed designs a quantum-assisted system that predicts blockages in wireless links helped by smart reflecting surfaces. Reconfigurable surfaces bounce signals around obstacles, but knowing a blockage is coming lets a network reroute early. Camera views from the user device are encoded into quantum states by amplitude, while channel readings enter as rotation features.

Variational quantum circuits sort the link into one of three states. Noise from today's imperfect quantum hardware is modeled openly, covering two main error channels on both direct and surface-assisted paths. A fidelity-aware training goal steadies learning under that noise. The design is framed as forward-looking, testing what quantum links could add once hardware matures.
arxiv-2511-04017:
Wenxiang Ying and Abraham Nitzan revisit electron transfer in confined electromagnetic fields, a setting where nanophotonics and cavity experiments can reshape a basic molecular process. Their unified rate theory rests on Fermi's golden rule with a polaron-transformed Hamiltonian.

Analytic rate expressions hold across all temperatures and cavity timescales. At high temperature the theory recovers Marcus and Marcus-Jortner results, while at low temperature the energy gap law emerges. Cavity loss enters through an effective oscillator spectral density, giving closed forms for lossy cavities. Two effects are demonstrated: strong rate enhancement at chosen cavity frequencies, and photon emission induced by the transfer itself, fed by populated cavity modes.
arxiv-2511-04117:
Yunghee Lee, Byeonghyun Pak, Junwha Hong, and Hoseong Kim propose Tortoise and Hare Guidance, a training-free way to speed diffusion model sampling without losing fidelity. Rewriting classifier-free guidance as a multirate system reveals that its two parts tolerate numerical error very differently, a redundancy standard solvers ignore.

The noise estimate is integrated on the fine time grid, the tortoise, while the guidance term runs only on a coarse grid, the hare. An error-aware sampler picks step sizes adaptively and a guidance-scale scheduler steadies long extrapolations. Function evaluations fell by up to thirty percent with almost no quality loss, beating other training-free accelerators under matched conditions in the reported tests.
arxiv-2511-04417:
Michal Pecho and two colleagues add a new player to the Moran process, a standard model of evolution. In that model, individuals are picked at random for birth and for death. When the same type fills both steps, the event is wasted and nothing changes.

Their new type, the replacer, always places its offspring over a different type when one is available. The team computes its advantage in well-mixed groups and on one-dimensional lattices. Being a replacer sharply raises the chance that neutral or even harmful mutants take over. The finding shows how small changes in replacement rules can steer evolution.
arxiv-2511-04517:
Céline Degrande and her co-author constrain four-light-quark operators in the Standard Model Effective Field Theory. That framework adds small extra terms to known physics and bounds them with data. Ten such operators shape how light quarks interact.

The pair uses multijet events and vector boson fusion with jets to probe them. They generate signal shapes at leading order for several jet counts, then merge and shower them. Comparing observables shows which ones bound which directions in the ten-part space. They also test when quadratic terms rival the linear ones, which checks whether the effective approach itself stays valid.
arxiv-2511-04817:
Chido Onyeze leads four authors allocating shared public goods over time without money. Several shareable goods have limited availability, and agents arrive with values each period. Values are drawn from a possibly correlated distribution across agents.

A global limit, written as a submodular cost, caps which goods the principal can offer overall. The goal is high value for every group of agents, not just the total. Their mechanisms hand each agent an artificial currency budget sized to its group. Spending that currency across periods steers allocations toward outcomes close to core equilibria.
arxiv-2511-04917:
Shadrack T. Asiedu leads five authors modeling distributed energy dynamics with efficient splines for grid studies. Rooftop solar and batteries now sway voltage across distribution networks. Detailed transient models capture their behavior but cannot scale to whole systems.

Data-driven identification avoids the detail, yet solving its equations is still heavy. That cost blocks real-time use where operators need answers fast. Their spline-based approach simplifies the learned dynamics into a cheaper form. The goal is transmission-level voltage stability checks that keep pace with a grid filling with small, fast-changing energy resources.
arxiv-2511-05017:
Aakriti Agrawal and co-authors aim to cut false claims in large vision-language models by fixing their text vectors. Such models may name things that are not in a photo, as when an empty counter gets a bowl of fruit that is not there.

Their study shows a root cause: models lean too hard on text and too little on the image, since sight data is just tacked onto a language core. Attention drifts toward words and away from visual proof. By refining the text side, the authors seek output that stays tied to what the image shows.
arxiv-2511-05117:
J. Guo and a co-author extend a theory of normal forms for operators that do not commute, in the second part of a two-part work. Normal forms give a clean standard shape for such operators, which makes hard algebra far more tractable.

As a use case, they get a test for when two operators in the Weyl algebra commute, and for operators in the wider ring of ordinary differential operators. They prove the test when the operators have a normal form that meets a top-line rule. The result sharpens tools for symbolic work with differential operators.
arxiv-2511-05417:
Stephon Alexander and co-authors propose a fix for a long snag in quantum gravity. The snag concerns the Chern-Simons-Kodama state. That state is an exact solution for a universe with a positive cosmological constant. Yet it looked non-normalizable and broke a key symmetry. That cast doubt on its use as a real state of de Sitter space.

Starting from a non-perturbative inner product drawn from reality terms of the self-dual variables, they revisit the state's norm. Their route aims to restore the state as a sound, finite-norm solution. If it holds, a classic candidate state of quantum cosmology stands on firmer ground.
arxiv-2511-05717:
Diba Hadi Esfangereh and co-authors build a system to recognize Persian musical instruments in real recordings. Instrument recognition feeds music search and generation tools, but non-Western traditions are understudied. Persian music in particular lacked a solid labeled resource.

The team recorded solo samples of seven classic Persian instruments, plus violin, piano, and vocals. From those clips they built lifelike mixes with many parts at once, guided by the culture's own rules. A pretrained music model with a sorting head then learned from the mixes. Tested on hand-labeled parts of real old songs, the approach scored best among those tried. The authors offer it as a base for music tools that cover more cultures.
arxiv-2511-05917:
Tuan Nguyen characterizes certain maximal families of sets in combinatorics, called left-compressed intersecting families. Intersecting families are collections where every two sets share an element. Left-compressed means the family stays closed under pushing elements toward smaller labels, a symmetry that simplifies their study.

Nguyen shows that maximal left-compressed families correspond exactly to a special kind of generating set, the small seed sets from which the whole family grows. He then fully describes the maximal intersecting families of this type that have exactly two maximal generators, calling them rank two. For each subset of labels he compares such a family with the classic star family, where all sets contain one fixed element. The result tightens the map of extremal set theory.
arxiv-2511-06317:
A. Damas-Segovia and colleagues point the MeerKAT radio telescope at the spiral galaxy NGC 2997 using its new S-band receivers. That frequency band suits magnetic field studies because it suffers little Faraday depolarization, the twisting that scrambles magnetic signals. Full-polarization observations let the team map the galaxy's regular magnetic field in fresh detail.

Rotation measure synthesis revealed the field direction along the line of sight across the whole disk. A sector-based Fourier analysis, applied to such data for the first time, found three large-scale field modes in the disk. Even multiples of the first mode also appeared after a geometric adjustment, matching dynamo theory predictions for symmetric spiral galaxies.
arxiv-2511-06617:
Bjørn Kjos-Hanssen proves a counterintuitive fact about the hydrophobic-polar model of protein folding. Proteins become binary strings, one letter for water-fearing and one for water-loving, folded onto a lattice and scored by energy. Longer chains ought to fold at least as well as their parts, or so intuition suggests.

That intuition fails: joining two chains can produce a best possible fold strictly worse than one part alone achieves. The result holds on two- and three-dimensional rectangular lattices and on hexagonal and triangular ones. For closed chains under a graded hydrophobicity model, proper knots and links can even appear as the unique best folds, tying this toy model to knot theory.
arxiv-2511-06917:
Xin Zhang and sixteen co-authors simulate the slitless spectroscopy mode of the China Space Station Telescope, a wide-field space telescope still in development. Slitless spectroscopy spreads every object's light into a spectrum while imaging a wide field at once. With no real observations yet available, pipelines and science planning must be built and tested on realistic mock data.

The team's simulation system models the instrument's dispersing optics and structure, then measures how well different targets would be detected. Nearly all first-order spectra come with a matching zeroth-order image, which helps identify each source. Among the spectral bands, the GI band proved most efficient, marking it as the primary band for future stellar and galactic studies with this mode.
arxiv-2511-07117:
Alberto De Marchi, Tim Hoheisel, and Patrick Mehlitz analyze augmented Lagrangian methods for fully convex composite optimization. These problems minimize a sum of a smooth function and a structured nonsmooth term under constraints. The classic theory ties these methods to the proximal point algorithm, but useful versions run inexactly and use safeguarding to stay stable, which the classic analysis does not cover. The authors extend the relationship to the inexact, safeguarded scheme.

Their convergence results distinguish the regular case, where a stationary minimum exists, from the irregular case, where every minimum is nonstationary. They also propose an elastic modification of standard safeguarding that keeps primal convergence while guaranteeing the dual sequence converges to a multiplier in the regular case. Standard safeguarding, valuable for nonconvex problems, actually weakens guarantees in the convex setting, and the elastic version recovers them.
arxiv-2511-07317:
Zhiyuan Zeng and sixteen co-authors scale reinforcement learning for language models by making practice problems adjust themselves. Training on static problem sets wastes signal: problems that are too easy or too hard teach almost nothing. Their approach, RLVE, uses verifiable settings that procedurally generate problems and check answers algorithmically, while continuously adapting the difficulty distribution to the model's current ability.

To run it they built RLVE-Gym, a suite of four hundred hand-built verifiable settings. Joint training across all four hundred improved a strong 1.5-billion-parameter reasoning model by 3.37 points on average across six benchmarks. Simply continuing its original training gained only 0.49 points despite using over three times the compute. The authors release the code, arguing setting scaling is a reliable axis for improving generalizable reasoning.
arxiv-2511-07517:
Popovic, Shah, Kenworthy, and many collaborators rework the Dark Energy Survey supernova cosmology from scratch. Type Ia supernovae serve as standard candles for measuring cosmic expansion. Small calibration errors can shift answers about dark energy, so the team rebuilt the five-year sample with fresh cross-checks.

New white dwarf observations tie surveys together, the light-curve model was retrained, and a host-galaxy color flaw was fixed. The recalibrated set holds about sixteen hundred survey supernovae plus two hundred nearby ones. Matter density shifts slightly, and hints of evolving dark energy sharpen. Cosmologists get a cleaner test of whether dark energy changes over time.
arxiv-2511-07717:
Yifan Liu, Fangneng Zhan, and Wanhua Li estimate a robot full configuration from one ordinary photo. Knowing joint pose from a single camera view helps robots work beside people, but labeled training images are scarce and two-dimensional shortcuts ignore three-dimensional structure. Simulators help, yet the gap to real scenes persists.

RoboTAG aligns a topological graph of the robot across two branches, one working in image space and one carrying three-dimensional priors. The branches evolve together, reducing dependence on labels. Graph nodes track robot parts and their connections explicitly. Better pose from cheap cameras could widen where robots safely operate outside staged labs.
arxiv-2511-07917:
Søren Eilers and Efren Ruiz prove that several open statements across algebra and topology stand or fall together. The statements involve the Cuntz algebra with its diagonal, graph algebras and their diagonals, Leavitt path algebras over various rings, topological full groups, groupoids, and a sign map on algebraic K-theory.

Logical equivalence means settling any one settles all, focusing effort where tools are strongest. The shared truth value governs classification of diagonal-preserving isomorphisms between graph algebras, echoing a hindrance Cuntz met earlier. Equivalence webs like this are progress in themselves: they reveal that separate communities have been circling one core obstacle.
arxiv-2511-08317:
Shuaimin Li and co-authors propose ReViewGraph, a system that automates paper reviewing by reasoning over simulated debates between reviewers and authors. Direct language model scoring of manuscripts suffers from hallucination, biased grades, and shallow reasoning. Real peer review, by contrast, is an argument: claims are accepted, rejected, clarified, or compromised across several rounds of exchange.

Language model agents simulate those multi round debates, and typed relations from each exchange become edges in a heterogeneous graph. A graph neural network reasons over the debate structure to reach a review decision. On three data sets, the method improves over strong baselines by a clear average margin.
arxiv-2511-08417:
Xiyuan Wei, Chih-Jen Lin, and Tianbao Yang propose NeuCLIP, a more efficient way to train CLIP models that match images with text. Contrastive training needs an accurate normalization term for each sample, and standard methods approximate it with huge batches that consume heavy resources. Earlier per sample estimators update in blocks each epoch, but their error grows when data sets are large or batches small.

NeuCLIP reformulates each sample loss through convex analysis so its log normalizer becomes an auxiliary variable. Variational analysis then replaces millions of separate variables with one compact neural network that predicts them. An alternating algorithm trains CLIP and the helper network together, with tailored architecture and acceleration for accurate estimates.
arxiv-2511-08517:
Florin Teleanu and co-authors report nuclear spin relaxation measures in zero to ultralow field magnetic resonance, where spins interact strongly without a large guiding field. In that regime, varied resonances relax at surprisingly varied rates. The rates depend on the prepolarizing field and the path taken to the detection region, on the measure field strength, on the detection method, and even on the excitation pulse angle.

Tests use a carbon labeled formic acid sample with an atomic magnetometer based setup. A theoretical setup explains the detected effects and extracts molecular traits from them. The authors note uses for spectral assignment, identifying motion regimes, image contrast, and characterizing relaxation at extremely low fields.
arxiv-2511-08617:
Ricardo Alonzo Fernández Salguero reviews what research says about the social costs of International Monetary Fund programs. Following PRISMA guidelines, the review searches five large archives plus grey literature and keeps fifty-three studies that pass a screening, each checked for risk of bias.

Studies using weaker designs, often propensity score matching, tend to report no clear pattern of harm. Work with stronger research designs, especially instrumental variable methods, tells a darker story. Those studies link the Fund's terms to higher income inequality, worse health results including tuberculosis and child deaths, and a larger informal economy. Salguero concludes that austerity-centered programs carry real social costs and that the Fund's terms should be redesigned to protect social spending.
arxiv-2511-08817:
Nicolas Bouchot studies a random walk that is trapped forever inside a finite domain, never allowed to step outside. Conditioning a simple walk on survival reshapes its step probabilities through the first eigenvector of the domain's Laplacian, producing a confined walk with rich behavior in three or more dimensions.

The questions are how long the walk takes to visit every point of an inner subset, and which points are visited last. When the subset has enough late points, the cover time follows a sharp asymptotic expansion with a Gumbel random variable in the final term. The late points then scatter like a Poisson process. For ball-shaped subsets the leading term alone is established. The method adapts earlier work on walks on a torus and leans on tilted random interlacements to approximate the confined walk's trace.
arxiv-2511-08917:
Kapil Garg and six co-authors measure how photo quality quietly decides whether blind and low-vision people get useful answers from vision-language models. These models now narrate everyday products for their users. Yet the photos users take often suffer blur, bad framing, or rotation. Nobody had charted the damage.

A survey of eighty-six blind and low-vision participants shaped an annotated dataset of one thousand eight hundred fifty-nine product images drawn from their real use. The best model tested captions ninety-eight percent of clean images correctly. But accuracy falls to seventy-five percent once quality issues appear. It worsens steeply as problems compound. The authors, quoting a participant who noted the technology is trained by non-disabled people, argue that evaluation must center disabled users' experience from the start.
arxiv-2511-09617:
J. S. G. Mombarg and eight co-authors ask whether a cheap 1D approximation can be trusted for reading the insides of pulsating stars. In beta Cephei stars, asymmetries in rotational splitting patterns encode the rotation profile and internal magnetic field. Extracting them demands theoretical predictions more accurate than the tiny effects being measured.

The team couples 1D pulsation codes to a 2D rotating star model and benchmarks them against a full 2D pulsation code. Frequencies agree well overall, but asymmetry differences between methods usually swamp the magnetic signal, they find. Accurate field measurements look possible only for higher-order modes, slow rotation, and strong fields of a few hundred kilogauss. Rotation itself, though, can still be modeled reliably with the simpler tools.
arxiv-2511-09817:
Abdelhay Benmoussa works on a formula in operator theory built around the Volterra integration operator. The paper derives a normal ordering formula for a power of a combined object built from multiplication by the variable and the Volterra operator. Normal ordering rewrites such expressions in a standard arrangement, and the coefficients that appear turn out to have a combinatorial identity.

Those coefficients are shown to coincide with the Bessel numbers, a known counting sequence. Beyond the main identity, Benmoussa presents two applications of the formula and a generalization of the central result. In short, the paper links two fields that look far apart, and shows that a counting sequence sits at the heart of both.
arxiv-2511-10117:
Hossein Kavianirad and five co-authors run a hybrid rehab system that pairs electric muscle stimulation with a robotic exoskeleton. Both tools can give the same help at the same joint, so the control system must choose, each moment, how much work each one does. The two tools have unlike limits, and a clinician may favor one tool over the other for a given patient.

Their setup splits the choice in two. A top-level unit sets the total help, and an allocator hands the torque load to the two tools in real time, within each tool's limits and the user's stated taste. Lab runs and tests showed the split working cleanly. The team sees clinic trials, on patient uptake and health gains, as the next step.
arxiv-2511-10217:
Huimei Wang and seven co-authors investigate changing-look active galactic nuclei, whose broad emission lines dramatically appear or vanish over time. Using five years of high-cadence Zwicky Transient Facility light curves, they assembled 152 such objects confirmed by eye to show spectral transitions and large optical variability. Ninety were analyzed in depth against matched control samples of ordinary type one and type two nuclei plus extremely variable quasars.

Color variability, structure functions, and a damped-random-walk score were compared across the groups. Changing-look objects differed from both control types in luminosity and Eddington ratio, and their on and off states varied alike, unlike the controls. The authors conclude these nuclei are not simply flipping between the two standard types, but sit in a critical state where moderate accretion changes trigger spectral switches.
arxiv-2511-10317:
Arpit Kottur, Jui Mahajan, and Raka Dabhade propose a dark energy model meant to ease the Hubble tension, the mismatch between early- and late-universe measurements of the expansion rate. Their model uses a canonical scalar field with a hybrid potential mixing an exponential term and a power-law term. Eleven parameters are constrained jointly by microwave background spectra, baryon acoustic oscillations, supernovae, local distance ladder data, and the matter power spectrum.

The fit is excellent and yields a Hubble constant near seventy-three in the usual units, shrinking the tension. Data favor a thawing quintessence picture with a small potential slope and a present-day equation of state around minus eighty-five hundredths. A Bayesian comparison still slightly prefers the standard cosmological constant model for its simplicity.
arxiv-2511-10617:
Oem Trivedi and Robert J. Scherrer propose that dark matter might not be a particle at all, but a consequence of the holographic principle. Earlier holographic models aimed at dark energy; this one instead derives dark matter from an infrared cutoff set by the horizon scale of the universe.

Using the Ricci cutoff in a universe containing only ordinary matter and radiation, the model accounts for the observed dark matter. It also explains why the ordinary and dark contributions to the cosmic density are comparable. It also flips the sign of a pre-existing vacuum energy density, which the authors note is interesting because many string theories predict a negative vacuum energy while observations require a positive one.
arxiv-2511-10717:
Samuel Schneider and Torsten Ueckerdt contribute a proof in graph theory concerning forest cuts, vertex separators whose removal leaves a forest. A conjecture in the area holds that every graph with fewer than a certain number of edges has such a cut, mirroring an older theorem of Chen and Yu.

As a step toward that conjecture, other researchers had asked how many edges a 3-connected graph on n vertices must have before every vertex neighborhood contains a cycle. Li, Tang, and Zhan settled the question, showing the threshold is fifteen-eighths times n and that the bound is tight. Schneider and Ueckerdt's contribution is a much shorter proof of that result.
arxiv-2511-10817:
Domingos S. P. Salazar proves a structural result about the measures physicists and information theorists use to tell quantum states apart. His objects are the Petz f-divergences, a family that includes relative entropy and several distance-like quantities, each generated by an operator convex function.

Salazar shows every such divergence can be written as a positive mixture of simple quadratic contrasts, with weights he derives in closed form from the generating function. He also gives closed forms for the canonical cases. Mapping those contrasts onto a classical chi-square statistic lets him import a classical variational bound. The result is a tight, universal thermodynamic uncertainty relation: any f-divergence is lower bounded by a function of the means and variances of quantum observables. Known and new results in quantum thermodynamics fall out as applications.
arxiv-2511-11017:
Dimitar Peshevski, Riste Stojanov, and Dimitar Trajanov present a fully automatic system that turns loose online product text into structured knowledge graphs. Online shops hold vast amounts of product detail in free text, which is hard to search and study. Graphs give that detail a clear shape, but building them by hand is slow and costly.

Their system uses large language models split into agents that each handle one stage. One stage drafts and grows the category scheme, one refines it, and one fills the graph. On real air conditioner listings, the system covered almost all product traits with little repeat, which shows the approach can work in practice.
arxiv-2511-11417:
Alessandro Bosso, Marco Borghesi, and their colleagues compute stabilizing controllers for continuous-time linear systems directly from one noisy input-output record, with no model identified first. Linear time-invariant systems are the workhorse of control theory, but noise in the record corrupts any design built on it. Their output-feedback design joins an observer built on a non-minimal realization with a feedback law from a data-only matrix inequality.

Under an interval excitation condition and a known bound on noise energy, that inequality is feasible exactly when it stabilizes every realization matching the data. A signal-to-noise condition, guidance for the noise bound, and simulations complete the work.
arxiv-2511-11817:
Zhongde An and six co-authors propose FreDN, a forecasting network that untangles a time series in the frequency domain before predicting. Frequency methods capture global patterns well, but for non-stationary series the trend, cycles, and noise smear across the spectrum, a problem the authors call spectral entanglement, worsened by spectral leakage.

A learnable frequency disentangler separates trend from periodic components instead of applying a fixed decomposition, and the design avoids the heavy cost of complex-valued learning. Cleaner separation should mean forecasts that respect both slow drift and repeating rhythms. Finance, energy, and weather forecasting all live on non-stationary data, so the entanglement problem is widely shared.
arxiv-2511-12417:
Yushen Liu, Yanfu Zhang and Xugui Zhou design TSODE, a safety-aware controller for automated insulin delivery in type 1 diabetes. The controller must keep blood glucose in range despite uncertain meals and body variation. Reinforcement learning can personalize dosing, but it has struggled to guarantee safety, with risks such as overdosing before meals or stacking corrections.

TSODE pairs an adaptive reinforcement learning method with a neural differential equation forecaster that predicts near-term glucose for a proposed dose. A conformal calibration layer measures forecast uncertainty and can reject or scale back risky actions. In an FDA-approved simulator's adult cohort, the system reports strong time in range and low time below the safe threshold.
arxiv-2511-12717:
Max Lellmann and six co-authors present HadroTOPS, a software generator for a rare kind of particle collision. When electrons and positrons collide, two photons from the beams can fuse and create hadrons, and studying those events helps map the structure of mesons. HadroTOPS simulates such two-photon events with exact leading-order quantum electrodynamics coupling, letting the hadronic state decay into any number of final particles the user selects over flat phase space.

The code folds in experimental and theoretical knowledge about how hadrons couple to two photons. Motivated by work at the BESIII experiment, it already includes several pion, kaon, and eta channels, plus one multi-step decay chain. New final states can be added easily. For analysts doing partial wave analysis, the generator offers a flexible way to test how higher-multiplicity events should look across energies and photon virtualities before comparing with real detector data.
arxiv-2511-12817:
Shasha Zhou and six co-authors test whether medical knowledge graphs can fact-check answers written by large language models. Medical answers need verification before clinical use, but human review is slow. Their framework, FAITH, needs no reference answer. It breaks a response into atomic claims, links each claim to a medical knowledge graph. Scores the claim by the evidence paths that support it inside that structured web of medical facts.

Across varied medical tasks, FAITH's scores matched clinician judgments far better than competing automated checks, and it separated stronger models from weaker ones. Its scores also held up when the wording of answers changed. Because each score rests on visible evidence paths, users can see why a claim was doubted and act on the model's limits. The authors note remaining limitations, but present knowledge graphs as a leading route to automated factuality checks in healthcare.
arxiv-2511-13017:
Steven M. Girvin and Leo Radzihovsky review the case for a clock that ticks with a nucleus instead of an atom. Atomic clocks define modern timekeeping, and the authors first survey their technology, physics, and limits. A nuclear clock would use an unusual transition in thorium-229, only eight point four electron volts above the ground state. Low enough for lasers to reach, with a lifetime of hundreds of seconds when the thorium is doped into calcium fluoride crystals. 

Realizing one means confronting questions across nuclear, atomic, and solid-state physics at once. The central obstacle the review identifies is inhomogeneous broadening: strains and electric field gradients from the dopants and from crystal defects smear the transition differently for each nucleus, blurring the tick. Minimizing that broadening is the path to a working clock.
arxiv-2511-13217:
G. Makrakis and 4 co-authors ask whether the Helmholtz equation can be tied to a clear variational principle. The equation models waves with absorbing edges, a classic setup that stays hard to solve well at high wave numbers. They look for energy functions whose steady points match true solutions.

Starting from Hamilton's principle for the wave equation, the authors derive time-harmonic energies with a plain physical sense. Those energies can be indefinite, so they build stronger versions that keep the same meaning. They then show how the principles lead to workable methods that use finite elements and neural networks.
arxiv-2511-13717:
Xunjie Wang and 5 co-authors design TZ-LLM, a system that shields on-device language models inside Arm TrustZone. Phones that run models locally gain privacy and low delay, but the valuable model itself sits in hostile hands. Running it inside the trusted zone creates two problems: tight secure memory fights fast inference, and the neural accelerator must be shared safely between worlds.

Pipelined restoration prefetches model weights on demand, hiding loading and decryption behind compute by exploiting predictable access patterns. A minimal co-driver inside the trusted zone shares the accelerator without rebuilding control state at each switch. Built on OpenHarmony with llama.cpp, the system cut first-token delay sharply against a plain baseline.
arxiv-2511-13817:
Osase Omoruyi and 16 co-authors present a deep Chandra X-ray view of the galaxy cluster Abell 2597 and its central black hole feedback. Radio activity from the black hole has blown seven cavities into the hot cluster gas. It has also driven weak shocks far into the core, signs of outbursts repeating over tens of millions of years. A narrow brightness deficit hints at a plasma depletion layer shaped by sloshing gas.

The black hole pours in energy at a rate matching the cluster's cooling glow, yet gas still cools and refills a billion-solar-mass cold reservoir. Steady Bondi feeding from hot gas falls an order of magnitude short of the needed power. Radio and millimeter evidence instead favors chaotic cold feeding, where condensing clouds rain inward and sustain the cycle.
arxiv-2511-14117:
Agamdeep Singh, Ashish Tiwari, Hosein Hasanbeig, and one co-author argue classifiers should be trained on distributions, not single labels. Standard training collapses several annotators into one majority vote, throwing away real disagreement on ambiguous tasks like natural language inference or politeness judgments. Soft-label training instead targets the full spread of human answers.

Across three data sets spanning vision and language, soft labels matched or beat hard labels on accuracy. The models also landed much closer to the true annotator distribution, and their uncertainty lined up with human uncertainty far more strongly. The authors' point is simple: where disagreement is genuine, the distribution is the correct target.
arxiv-2511-14417:
Paolo Victor Redondo, Raphaël Huser, and Hernando Ombao set out a new gauge of how brain zones move as one, aimed at marks of dementia. Both Alzheimer's disease and frontotemporal dementia change the links between brain zones. EEG is a cheap, non-invasive way to hunt for those marks. But probes that sit side by side act much alike, so a probe-by-probe view is the wrong grain.

Their gauge, nonlinear vector coherence, picks up links past the plain linear kind between the waves of two whole zones. A rank-based route gauges it fast, with no need to name the data's spread, and a free-form test checks if the zones are in fact free of each other. The frame treats links zone to zone, as the brain is built.
arxiv-2511-14717:
Benedikt Peterseim and Milan Lopuhaä-Zwakenberg give attack trees a unified mathematical treatment. Attack trees are diagrams that break a system break-in into smaller steps, and metrics on them turn the diagrams into risk numbers. Many metrics exist, yet past frameworks either missed important ones or stayed too abstract to define concrete new ones.

The authors build a compositional theory in which trees are read as string diagrams inside a special category. Parts of a tree form what they call a channel category, and metrics then arise in a systematic way. The payoff is a principled recipe for defining and comparing security metrics instead of inventing each one from scratch.
arxiv-2511-14917:
Nicolas Zucchet, Qianqian Feng, and four co-authors show how brain-like networks can keep teaching signals in step with delayed activity. Working memory needs neurons that hold a trace of the recent past, but stacking such slow neurons layer on layer delays their signals. Feedback about right and wrong answers then arrives aimed at the wrong moment in the activity stream.

The authors give neurons an adaptive current that makes them respond ahead of time, predicting their coming inputs. With that prospective behavior, slow layers can still learn from late feedback. The mechanism mirrors a known trait of real neurons and offers a design rule for memory-capable artificial networks that learn online.
arxiv-2511-15417:
Ward Struyve closely tests whether being derived from an invariant action defines substantive general covariance in space time theories. Einstein used general covariance as a guide, but Kretschmann argued any theory can be written in covariant form. That critique sparked a lasting debate about formal versus substantive covariance. One proposal needs a diffeomorphism invariant action as the distinguishing mark.

Struyve examines covariant reformulations of special relativistic theories as test cases. Those seemingly merely formal versions can always be derived from invariant actions, he shows. The actions use auxiliary terms, but those terms are trivial in a precise sense. The result undermines the action based proposal as stated. Philosophers of physics must look elsewhere for the substantive content of covariance.
arxiv-2511-15917:
Austin E Schumacher and Jon Wakefield build methods to estimate several health indicators at once in small areas. Sound local estimates guide policy for the most disadvantaged groups. Yet nations with the heaviest disease burden often rely only on household surveys with sparse local data. Small area estimation borrows strength across regions, and joint modeling can borrow strength across outcomes too.

They build area-level and unit-level multivariate shared component models made for complex survey data. Tests in simulation validate the approach. On a Kenyan survey, the models jointly estimate child height and weight scores, and, in a second use, three types of contraceptive use in women. Both uses beat single-outcome and naive joint approaches.
arxiv-2511-16317:
Zeqiang Lai and seven co-authors present NaTex, a texture creation approach that predicts texture color directly in three dimensional space. Standard pipelines bake textures from multi view images made by diffusion models. That route struggles with occluded regions, mesh boundary alignment, and cross view consistency. NaTex instead views texture as a dense color point cloud attached to geometry.

Latent color diffusion drives the system, built from a geometry aware color point cloud autoencoder and a multi control diffusion transformer. Both parts train from scratch on three dimensional data alone. Precise mesh texture alignment follows naturally from the representation. Reconstruction and creation are handled in one approach. Direct three dimensional texture synthesis could simplify asset creation for games and simulation.
arxiv-2511-16617:
Satyam Gaba uses generative AI to bridge the lab made to real gap for early wildfire smoke detection. Timely smoke plume identification limits large scale fire damage. Deep networks localize smoke well, but annotated real data are scarce. A comprehensive lab made smoke data set is generated with annotations to train detectors. Unsupervised domain adaptation then adapts those models toward real imagery.

Style transfer, generative adversarial methods, and image matting increase lab made realism. Each technique is analyzed for closing the domain disparity. Better realism should yield more accurate and scalable detection in the field. The thesis style study maps a full pipeline from generation to adaptation. Wildfire agencies need detectors trained without waiting for disaster footage to accumulate.
arxiv-2511-16817:
Carl Pomerance and Andreas Weingartner probe the limits of a famous Egyptian fraction conjecture. Erdős and Straus conjectured every fraction four over n splits into three unit fractions; Schinzel generalized this to m over n for all large n, with a threshold depending on m. The question here is how large that threshold must be.

Building on work of Elsholtz and Tao, the authors show that if the threshold exists it is at least exponentially large in a fractional power of m. Some fairly reachable fractions therefore resist decomposition. An explicit version gives, for enormous m, a prime between m squared and twice m squared for which m over p is not a sum of three unit fractions. Extensive computation supports the same phenomenon for m as small as twenty. They also make Vaughan's theorem, that most n work, explicit in m.
arxiv-2511-17117:
Masahiro Tanaka develops faster Bayesian computation for a class of econometric and statistical problems built on linear moment conditions. These quasi-Bayesian methods are attractive when a full likelihood is unavailable, but sampling from the resulting posterior with Markov chain Monte Carlo can be slow. Tanaka modifies the delayed acceptance algorithm, which screens proposals with a cheap surrogate before the expensive exact check.

Two variants emerge. One folds prior information fully into the proposal and squeezes the most from each iteration. The other drops the prior from the proposal, cutting matrix inversions and gaining speed and stability in higher dimensions. Simulations on regressions with uneven error variance show large gains over standard methods, and two instrumental variable applications confirm them. The faster variant scaled to designs where rival methods became impractical.
arxiv-2511-17217:
Chaowei Fang and four co-authors address realistic image super-resolution: enlarging real low-resolution photographs, whose blur and noise follow messy real-world patterns rather than tidy synthetic ones. Models trained on synthetic data know a lot, but real paired training data is scarce. Their Dual-domain Adaptation Networks transfer a pretrained model from the simulated world to real data efficiently, instead of starting over.

One branch adapts in the spatial domain, updating selected parameters and using low-rank adjustments for the rest. A second branch works in the frequency domain, since recovering detail means restoring high frequencies, and merges spectral information with the backbone's features to predict the missing frequency map. On three public realistic benchmarks, including RealSR, the method beat the state of the art. Code is publicly available.
arxiv-2511-17317:
Karthik Subramaniam Eswaran, Ali Emami Kopaei, and Krzysztof Sacha develop a geometric picture of quantum light inside photonic time crystals, materials whose optical properties vary periodically in time rather than space. Their description places each light mode on a curved coherent-state space, where its evolution appears as a Möbius transformation moving points around the Poincaré disk. The shapes of those trajectories sort the dynamics into stable, unstable, and critical regimes at a glance.

The authors also connect the geometric phase accumulated along a cycle to the hyperbolic area the path encloses in the projective Hilbert space. The result is an intuitive framework: stability and topology in these time-varying media become visible features of a picture, rather than conclusions buried in algebra. The short paper offers the geometry as a tool for reasoning about a fast-growing corner of photonics.
arxiv-2511-17417:
Soroush Javdan, Pragash Krishnamoorthy, and Olga Baysal improve how Ericsson engineers find past trouble reports when a new software fault lands. Trouble reports document production faults, and retrieving similar old reports speeds diagnosis, but the reports are numerous and their fields reflect different aspects of a fault, which generic retrieval models handle poorly. Building on an earlier two-stage retrieval workflow at the company, the authors propose CREST, an ensemble of specialized models, one per report criterion.

Each specialist scores reports on its own criterion, and the system aggregates the scores, so users also see why a report was retrieved, criterion by criterion. On a subset of Ericsson's internal reports, criterion-specific models significantly outperformed a single general model on the key metrics, with better calibrated scores. The study shows that honoring the structure of the data beats treating reports as undifferentiated text.
arxiv-2511-17517:
Marco Savarese and six co-authors present RI-PIENO, a system that plans where and when a driver should refuel. Refueling choices trade fuel prices against detours and timing, and earlier tools tended to use either vehicle data or external information, not both, and stayed static. RI-PIENO combines in-vehicle sensor readings with geospatial and fuel price data, processed through cloud and fog services. It models refueling as a directed graph that evolves over time with the driver's habits and live inputs.

The system thereby becomes a continuously adaptive decision engine rather than a one-off recommender. In realistic multi-driver, multi-week simulations of daily commuting, it achieved significant cost savings and more efficient routing than the authors' previous framework. The design anticipates roadside infrastructure and vehicle-to-everything communication, aiming at deployment inside next-generation vehicular networks.
arxiv-2511-17817:
Younggeun Kim, Jordan Gue, Changhao Xu, and seventeen co-authors reuse data from an axion search to look for high frequency gravitational waves. Steady waves at very high frequency could come from clouds of axions around spinning black holes, formed by a process called superradiance.

They reanalyze a cavity experiment tuned near a set radio frequency and find no candidates on a rescan. That null result sets limits on wave strength across the sky. Under stated assumptions it rules out certain tiny black holes very close to Earth. The work shows that cavities built for axions can double as gravitational wave detectors.
arxiv-2511-18017:
G. G. L. Nashed examines the inside of compact stars in a modified gravity theory built from curvature, a Gauss Bonnet term, and the trace of matter's energy and momentum. Massive radio pulsars, heavier than about one point eight Suns, test gravity in conditions no laboratory can reach.

Using a linear form of the theory, Nashed finds an exact solution for a static star whose pressure differs by direction. Matching the mass and radius of one pulsar pins the theory's two parameters to narrow values. The resulting star obeys a causal bound on sound speed, with behavior that differs from general relativity.
arxiv-2511-18117:
Levon Mahseredjian builds a theory bridge between event level models of a financial limit order book, the queue of buy and sell orders at each price. The bridge leads to smoother large scale descriptions used for analysis. Orders arrive in bursts that excite further arrivals, a self exciting pattern captured by Hawkes processes, and liquidity also migrates between neighboring price levels.

Starting from that microscopic model, Mahseredjian derives a diffusion estimate: a reflected stochastic differential equation system for queue volumes. Its drift and diffusion come from a Taylor expansion of the small scale generator, showing how time excitation and space migration jointly shape the book. The work is purely a theory work, with no calibration.
arxiv-2511-18217:
Yana Teplitskaya gathers open questions in the study of short networks in flat space. Two problem types lead the list. One seeks the shortest linked set whose near zone still covers a given shape. The other, the Steiner tree problem, seeks the shortest set that joins a fixed set of points.

For each type she sums up what is known and marks what stays unsolved. Some gaps yield to basic tools that a student can try. Others have stood for years and need deep new ideas. The survey gives a clear map of where work is done and where a fresh push could pay off. It suits readers who want a hard open problem to work on.
arxiv-2511-18517:
Khanh Gia Bui argues that general intelligence cannot grow out of today's neural networks, no matter the scale. The paper draws on philosophy, brain science, computing theory, and learning theory. Classic thought tests, the Chinese Room and Gödel style arguments among them, frame the case.

In Bui's view, networks act as static function fitters inside a fixed code frame. They show rich behavior, he argues, without the inner structure that true understanding needs — a kind of sophisticated sponge that soaks and squeezes patterns. He also faults recent theory the field leans on. The stance is an argued critique, offered as a check on health of the field, not a measured result. Readers get a broad brief against scale as a path to general minds.
arxiv-2511-18617:
Litian Gong and five co-authors help imitation learning focus on what matters in a demo, with no extra human notes. A policy that copies demos can latch onto clutter or false cues and fail in new scenes. Guiding its gaze to key objects curbs that flaw, yet gaze data and hand drawn focus maps cost much to get.

AutoFocus-IL asks a vision language model to find and track the key objects in each demo on its own. The tracks become time based saliency maps that mark true causal cues and mute clutter. Those maps then shape training of the copying policy. Tests in a driving simulator and on real robot arm tasks show better data efficiency and broader transfer. Focus comes free of human labels.
arxiv-2511-19217:
Wanjiang Weng and five co-authors improve text-to-motion generation, which turns a written prompt into three-dimensional human movement for games, film, and robotics. Diffusion models make varied and realistic motion, but the result often drifts from the prompt's meaning. Their method, ReAlign, scores alignment during generation rather than only at the end.

A step-aware reward model judges each noisy intermediate motion for both semantic fit and realism, using one module for text alignment and one for motion quality. A reward-guided strategy then steers sampling toward better aligned results. On generation and retrieval tests, ReAlign beats leading methods in prompt match and motion quality.
arxiv-2511-19517:
Adarsh Kumarappan and Ananya Mujoo automate the creation of multi-turn jailbreak attacks on language models. Such attacks use the foot-in-the-door trick: a small harmless request opens the way to a harmful one, slipping past safety training over several turns. Defenses lag because attack data sets are built by hand and stay small.

Their pipeline turns the psychology into reusable templates and produces fifteen hundred scenarios spanning illegal activity and offensive content. Seven models from three families are tested with and without conversation history. GPT-family models grow far more vulnerable with history, attack success rising by up to thirty-two points, while Gemini 2.5 Flash stays nearly immune.
arxiv-2511-19617:
Frank Petriello and Kaan Şimşek propose a new probe of physics beyond the Standard Model using the Drell-Yan process, where a quark and antiquark produce a lepton pair. Certain angular moments of that process, called naive T-odd moments, had not been used this way. The authors work inside the Standard Model Effective Field Theory, which catalogs possible new effects by dimension.

Two moments, A6 and A7, prove sensitive at high mass and transverse momentum to dimension-eight operators that break CP symmetry and involve a gluon field. With the data expected from a high-luminosity LHC, the method could probe new physics at scales of a few TeV.
arxiv-2511-19717:
Vikram Ramavarapu, João Alfredo Cardoso Lamy, Mohammad Dindoost, and David A. Bader scale up fake network building for testing group-finding tools. Real networks rarely come with true group labels. So researchers judge such tools on made-up networks with known groups. The RECCS tool builds those networks while keeping each group's links and degree patterns.

Two upgrades are presented. RECCS+ keeps the first method faithful while running its parts in parallel across processes and threads. RECCS++ adds further speed tweaks. The work targets large-scale building, so test networks can grow to sizes that match real ones.
arxiv-2511-19817:
Members of the Scintillating Bubble Chamber Collaboration lay out how to calibrate a ten-kilogram liquid argon detector hunting dark matter and reactor neutrinos. The chamber marries a bubble chamber's blindness to electron recoils with the energy resolution of glowing noble liquid. Its target threshold is a very low one hundred electronvolts.

The plan measures detector response by combining photoneutron scattering with two new tricks for making tiny nuclear recoils: nuclear Thomson scattering and thermal neutron capture. Good calibration underpins the detector's promise of leading limits on dark matter near a GeV in mass, plus a high-count measurement of coherent neutrino scattering.
arxiv-2511-19917:
Qin Ren, Yufei Wang, Lanqing Guo, Wen Zhang, Zhiwen Fan, and Chenyu You ask why image generators waste effort at test time. Extra sampling can improve a text-to-image result, but standard methods redo the whole picture even when only one region is flawed. Good regions get needless work, and small defects stay under-corrected.

Their LoTTS framework, the first training-free method of its kind, rescales only the faulty regions. It finds defects by contrasting attention signals under high- and low-quality prompts, then shapes them into clean masks. Only masked areas are disturbed and denoised locally, keeping the rest intact. Tests on three major models show better local and global quality at much lower cost.
arxiv-2511-20217:
Kumano measures how an exotic hadron candidate is built from quarks and gluons. His 2025 paper determines fragmentation functions for the f0(980) particle. Fragmentation functions say how often a quark becomes that hadron. Ordinary hadrons hold two or three quarks. Exotic ones may hide stranger arrangements inside.

Belle experiment data on electron-positron collisions anchor the fit. The analysis extracts separate functions for each parton type. Up and down quark moments came out equal. Both sit far below the strange quark moment. The gluon moment rivals the strange one closely. Strange quarks also carry momentum at larger fractions. Together these facts point to a strange-antistrange core. At high energies the particle looks mainly like that pair. Low-energy studies instead favored a four-quark picture.
