Low-ionization lines like hydrogen beta and magnesium look more symmetric, coming mainly from slower, denser gas farther out.

Intermediate lines fall between the two in shift size, though in some super-Eddington candidates their outflow speeds rival the high-ionization lines. The pattern matches radiatively driven wind models with radial stratification. Preliminary photoionization modeling, with coronal and hot-disk radiation partly absorbed by a gas layer, adds support. The findings constrain the geometry and physical conditions of these outflows.
arxiv-2512-22917:
Between late 2007 and early 2008, Chile's three retail pharmacy chains raised prices together on more than two hundred medicines. The increases came weeks after advertising restrictions ended a price war in which comparative ads had pushed prices below cost. An economic study by Hao Yu reconstructs that switch from war to coordination using a structural model grounded in estimated demand.

Two forces did the work. Comparative ads once told shoppers exactly who was cheapest, so undercutting won traffic and sustained the war. The ban dulled price sensitivity, making undercutting unprofitable for most drugs, and the ban itself was a public event that aligned each chain's belief that rivals would match a rise. A dynamic model fitted by simulated method of moments reproduces the war, the failed coordination attempts, and the post-ban wave. The harm fell mainly as a transfer to the chains, since inelastic demand limited the deadweight loss.
arxiv-2512-23017:
Fuli Qiao and Mehrdad Mahdavi tackle continual learning for large language models, where a model must pick up new tasks without forgetting old ones and without the memory bill growing forever. Popular low-rank adapters, called LoRA, are usually frozen and stockpiled per task in current methods, so storage grows with every task and old adapters can interfere with new learning.

Their alternative keeps exactly one LoRA module. Each new task starts from an orthogonal basis extracted from what was learned before, which limits interference, and its update is then merged into the single shared adapter. A time-aware scaling balances old and new knowledge during merging, exploiting an asymmetry in how LoRA components behave. Memory stays constant as tasks accumulate. Theory backs the design, and experiments across continual learning benchmarks with several Llama models show strong performance with better efficiency than stockpiling approaches.
arxiv-2512-23117:
Daniel Levine and a large collaboration release OPoly26, a dataset meant to teach machine learning models the chemistry of polymers. Polymers underpin living things and drive advances in medicine, consumer products, and energy. Yet earlier training datasets for atomistic machine learning largely skipped them. High-quality quantum calculations on polymer structures are simply too expensive. OPoly26 fills the hole with more than six and a half million density functional theory calculations.

The calculations cover clusters of up to three hundred sixty atoms drawn from polymer systems, totaling over a billion atoms, and span changes in monomer makeup, chain length, architecture, and solvent. Adding OPoly26 to training improved models on polymer prediction tasks, the authors report. The dataset is released to speed development of polymer-aware models and, more broadly, of universal atomistic models that handle small molecules, materials, and macromolecules in one framework.
arxiv-2512-23317:
Kansei Ushiyama, Shun Sato, and Takayasu Matsuo ask what a convergence rate even means for an optimization method described by a differential equation. Analysts often model gradient methods as continuous-time flows because the equations feel simple. But rescaling time in the model speeds up or slows down its convergence at will, so chasing differential equations with fast rates is meaningless without a fix.

Their fix is the essential convergence rate, a notion designed to be immune to time rescaling. The backing is a theorem: under suitable rules for how the equation is discretized back into an algorithm, no discretization can converge faster than the model's essential rate. That makes the essential rate the honest ceiling a continuous model can promise. The paper reframes a popular design method, giving researchers a target that cannot be gamed by stretching the clock.
arxiv-2512-23417:
Navdeep Singh Dhindsa and co-authors pin down the masses of the triply charmed baryons, particles built from three charm quarks that no experiment has yet produced. Lattice QCD, which simulates the strong force on a space-time grid, is the tool. The calculation is presented as the most precise to date for the lowest spin three-half states of both parities. Six simulation ensembles with 2+1+1 quark flavors, generated by the MILC collaboration, feed the analysis.

Two treatments of the valence charm quark, the HISQ action and the overlap action, cross-check each other, and results are extrapolated to the continuum while systematic uncertainties are accounted. The predicted mass for the positive-parity ground state is about four thousand seven hundred ninety-three million electron volts. The negative-parity partner sits near five thousand ninety-four million electron volts. Such predictions tell collider experiments exactly where to look.
arxiv-2512-23517:
L. Saba and C. D. Fosco offer a teaching-oriented path through van der Waals forces, the weak attraction between neutral atoms. Textbooks usually treat the short-distance London limit with stationary perturbation theory, while the long-distance Casimir-Polder limit, where the finite speed of light matters, is derived with separate semiclassical methods. Students therefore meet the two regimes as disconnected topics.

The authors show that rewriting the stationary calculation in terms of time-ordered correlation functions simplifies the mathematics considerably. The same language then handles the higher-order terms needed at long distance, where retardation effects enter. One unified framework thus connects both limits. The article is pitched as a bridge between advanced quantum mechanics courses and field-theoretic treatments of dispersion forces, for graduate students and specialists.
arxiv-2512-23717:
Shenzhe Zhu confronts a gap in language-model safety training: filters are built mostly against openly harmful requests, but users can rephrase a harmful query so it sounds harmless while keeping its intent. Safety data rarely contains such disguised examples, so aligned models may not recognize them. HarmTransform is a framework for manufacturing them systematically.

Multiple agents debate over each transformation, critiquing and refining one another's rephrasings to keep the harmful objective intact while lowering its visibility. The resulting examples can then train safer models. Experiments show the method beats standard baselines at producing effective covert transformations. The analysis also warns that debate is double-edged: it sharpens stealth, yet can drift the topic or add needless complexity, lessons for anyone generating safety training data this way.
arxiv-2512-23817:
Seyed Mohamad Ali Tousi and three co-authors teach a neural network to clean up after quantum computers solving a fluid equation. The viscous Burgers equation is a standard test problem for shock formation. Through the Cole-Hopf transformation it becomes a diffusion equation, which they discretize and run on noisy quantum hardware and simulators using Trotterized circuits in Qiskit, comparing against high-accuracy classical solutions.

Standard zero-noise extrapolation helps, but the team goes further: they built a large data set sweeping viscosity, time step, grid size. Boundary conditions, pairing noisy, corrected, hardware, and classical results with circuit metadata. An attention-based graph network, fed the circuit's structure and outputs, learned to predict the error-mitigated solution. Across the parameter range it consistently reduced the gap to the classical answer beyond what extrapolation alone achieved.
arxiv-2512-24217:
Runtian Zhu and Lingfei Jin decode two families of error-correcting codes. Maximum distance separable codes sit at the center of practice. Most known examples are generalized Reed-Solomon codes. Codes outside that family are less understood. Their weaker structure can even be a virtue in cryptography. Twisted Reed-Solomon codes and Roth-Lempel codes represent the non-standard side.

Constructions of these codes are well studied. Their decoding was not. The authors build list and unique decoders on the Guruswami-Sudan algorithm. Under suitable conditions, running time is near-linear in code length. That improves the best known quadratic time. The twisted-code decoder handles many twists at fixed rate. Prior work managed only a single twist. For Roth-Lempel codes, this appears to be the first efficient decoder. List decoding also beats the classical unique-decoding radius for wide parameter ranges.
arxiv-2512-24517:
Fabian Retkowski and Alexander Waibel make paragraph segmentation a standard task for speech transcripts. Automatic transcripts arrive as unstructured word streams. Readability and reuse suffer for it. Paragraph breaks are the missing structuring step. Text segmentation research has lacked naturalistic benchmarks for it. The speech domain has mostly ignored the task.

Two benchmarks answer the gap. TEDPara holds human-annotated TED talks. YTSegPara holds YouTube videos with synthetic labels. A constrained-decoding method lets language models insert breaks without altering the transcript. Faithful, sentence-aligned evaluation follows. A compact model, MiniSeg, reaches state-of-the-art accuracy. A hierarchical extension predicts chapters and paragraphs together. Its extra cost is minimal. The package of data and methods aims to standardize paragraph segmentation in speech processing.
arxiv-2512-24817:
Ivan Novak studies how to count rational points with a given j-invariant on modular curves over a number field. The j-invariant labels elliptic curves up to isomorphism, and modular curves parametrize curves with extra structure. His method counts points above a chosen invariant on an arbitrary modular curve.

Applications list, for each positive integer, how many cyclic isogenies an elliptic curve over some number field can admit. Counts are also worked out above an invariant on split and non-split Cartan curves for odd prime powers. Number theory readers get concrete enumerations tied to Galois representation images for CM curves.
arxiv-2512-25017:
Chenguang Liu, Antonis Papapantoleon, and Jasper Rou — with co-authors — put deep gradient flow methods for partial differential equations on firm mathematical ground. Their analysis splits generalization error into approximation error and training error. Solutions of equations under reasonable, checkable assumptions are shown to be approximable by neural networks, so approximation error vanishes as networks widen.

The training process in the wide network limit follows an explicit gradient flow, which they derive and analyze. Applied mathematics readers get convergence understanding for a popular neural PDE solver family. High-dimensional equations are the target, where grid methods collapse and neural methods promise relief.
arxiv-2601-00017: Sergey Parnovsky and A A Varlamov write about the physics of olive oil, a food with more than three thousand years of history in Mediterranean culture. Their article follows olive oil production stage by stage. At each stage, they show how basic physical laws shape what happens, from older traditional methods to newer technology. The piece treats a familiar food as a case study in applied physics.
arxiv-2601-00617:
Huixin Sun and six co-authors address a weak spot of AI vision in a 2026 paper: finding tiny objects. Detectors do well on objects of normal size, but lag on tiny ones. The team show that tiny objects are hurt most by noisy labels. A strict aim on exact place can make a model fit that noise too well. Their method, named TOLF, models the error in a flexible way.

TOLF uses a tool that can bend to fit odd error shapes, not just bell curves. It also weighs each training case by how unsure the model is. Cases with high doubt, which are prone to noise, count for less. Tests on three data sets back the approach. On one standard set of tiny-object photos, TOLF raised a strong base model's score. The work points to noise care as a key step for tiny-object vision.
arxiv-2601-00717:
Lav Kumar Singh and Aljoša Peperko prove a theorem for a broad class of algebras in a 2026 paper. The algebras are called locally C-star algebras. They are like the algebras used in quantum theory, but built as limits of simpler ones. The classic Sherman-Takeda theorem ties such an algebra's double dual to a closure of its image.

The authors first prove density facts for these wider algebras. They then pick out a key trait, which they name the Kaplansky density property. With it, they build a faithful map of the double dual into a space of operators. The image of that map sits inside the weak closure of the algebra's image. For a neat subclass, the map turns out to be a perfect match, in both algebra and shape. That match is the twin of the classic theorem.
arxiv-2601-00817:
Zuzana Haniková and Filip Jankovec pin down the computational complexity of reasoning in unbounded Łukasiewicz logic, a many-valued logic that blends features of infinite-valued Łukasiewicz logic with abelian logic. The logic is complete with respect to an algebraic structure built on the real numbers with a distinguished element. The authors ask how hard its satisfiability and consequence problems are.

They show the existential theory of that structure is NP-complete, which bounds the complexity of the logic's theorems and its finite consequence relation. The proof reduces the problem to the existential theory of the standard MV-algebra, the usual semantics of Łukasiewicz logic, forging a new connection between the two logics. A translation of that theory into itself falls out as a byproduct.
arxiv-2601-01017:
Jihua Sun, Junming Liu, and Zhi-Gang Wang study harmonic maps in the unit disk that stretch space by a bounded amount. Their work in complex analysis asks a simple question with a hard proof. If the real part of such a map sits in a given function space, must the imaginary part sit there too, and with what bound?

The authors check three families of function spaces and prove that the answer is yes, with bounds that depend in a sharp way on how much the map can stretch. They extend the result to maps with an extra uneven term, then give tests for when smoothed maps and their rates of change belong to these spaces. The work tightens what analysts know about how the two parts of a harmonic map control each other.
arxiv-2601-01217:
Jesse Liu reviews the study of the strong force at the Large Hadron Collider, in a summary of a plenary talk given at the Lepton Photon Symposium 2025. Quantum chromodynamics, the theory of the strong force, still holds open questions about its basic nature. The collider, which smashes protons at record energies near Geneva, is a once-in-a-generation lab for probing them.

Liu organizes recent results under four themes. They cover precision tests at huge energy scales, puzzles that resist the usual step-by-step calculations, the mystery of confinement, which keeps quarks locked inside particles, and extreme cosmic-ray puzzles. The review stresses how these themes cross-feed each other and the rest of particle physics. For a newcomer, it maps where the field stands. For specialists, it flags the measurements most likely to sharpen or unsettle the theory in the coming years.
arxiv-2601-02017: Eglė Šidlauskaitė and four co-authors address a practical gap in crystallography. X-ray structures rarely show chemical bonds directly. Software infers bonds from interatomic distances instead. It uses a table of bonding radii, one value for each element. The paper presents an unsupervised workflow. It derives such a radii set from structures in the Crystallography Open Database. Hand-tuned values are replaced with data-driven ones.
arxiv-2601-02117:
Inside a molecule, vibrational energy does not stay where a laser puts it. It spreads among coupled modes. Chemists call that spread intramolecular vibrational redistribution. Measuring it directly is hard. Aurelian Loirette-Pelous and three co-authors build a quantum framework for watching it. The tools are molecular optomechanics and surface-enhanced Raman methods at the single-molecule level.

Two pump-and-probe strategies are modeled. One pumps vibrations with an infrared laser. The other pumps with the Stokes scattering of surface-enhanced Raman spectroscopy itself. In both, the anti-Stokes spectrum carries clear signs. Population flows between coupled modes. With realistic molecular and enhancement settings, the signs should be reachable in the lab. A route opens to timing energy flow inside individual molecules.
arxiv-2601-02317:
Galy Yang and four co authors review single photon emitters, devices that release light one particle at a time for quantum communication, computing, and precision measurement. Every known source trades off purity, sameness between photons, and the ability to tune the color. The review sorts sources by the physical mechanism that makes the photon, which clarifies why each limit appears.

Special attention goes to hybrid perovskite quantum dots, tiny crystals mixing organic and inorganic parts. Their color can be tuned by size and recipe, their lines are narrow, and they work at room temperature. The authors compare mechanisms and scores across platforms, propose a framework for judging scalable sources, and discuss bright squeezed vacuum as a possible route to purer photons at larger scale.
arxiv-2601-02517:
Juan M. Scarpetta, Omar Calderón-Losada, Morten Hjorth-Jensen, and John H. Reina show how to learn the hidden parameters of a single molecule well enough to control it with light. Coherent control tunes interference in atoms and molecules for uses from light harvesting to molecular qubits. But it first requires knowing how the molecule couples to its surroundings, especially at room temperature where dissipation is strong.

The molecule is driven by spectrally shaped pulses, and its two photon absorption glow carries the needed information. Two inference methods are compared on that signal, a direct optimization scheme and a feed forward neural network that learns the mapping from signal to parameters. Both prove robust enough for the task. Reliable parameter estimates of this kind are what turn a control idea into a working protocol, with uses in ultrafast spectroscopy and quantum materials.
arxiv-2601-02617:
Theresa Farah and six co authors show reservoir computing in action, a bio inspired learning scheme that lets a physical system's own dynamics do the computing, using two coupled microelectromechanical drum resonators. Such resonators give nonlinearity and fading memory, the two things a reservoir needs, and they can sense and compute on the same chip. The drums work in the megahertz range and are linked capacitively.

A pump tone is applied at the sideband of a phonon cavity formed by the coupled drums, while one mode is probed, as in optomechanical systems. That sideband pumping creates nonlinear energy transfer between the resonators, and its response carries the computation. The experiment shows a working physical reservoir at microscale, a step toward time based signal work that needs no separate digital chip.
arxiv-2601-03117:
Lalit Pandey, Samantha M. W. Wood, and Justin N. Wood ask whether transformers learn the way brains do, by training them on the kind of input a developing brain actually receives. Before birth, the visual system is shaped by retinal waves, spontaneous patterns sweeping the retina. The authors simulated that prenatal visual world and trained transformers on it with self-supervised temporal learning.

During training, the transformers spontaneously developed the same organization seen in newborn visual systems. Early layers became sensitive to edges, later layers to shapes, and receptive fields grew across layers. Because the models saw only prenatal-style data, the match suggests brains and transformers may follow common learning principles. The developmental convergence reframes the comparison between artificial and biological vision.
arxiv-2601-03217:
Xinghe Chen, Naiming Liu, and Shashank Sonkar build MalruleLib, a library that turns documented student misconceptions in mathematics into executable procedures. Student errors are often systematic: a learner follows a coherent but wrong rule, called a malrule, and repeats it in new contexts. Drawing on sixty-seven learning-science and mathematics education sources, the framework encodes those wrong procedures and generates step-by-step traces of the work they produce.

The library formalizes a test of student modeling: infer the misconception from one worked mistake, then predict the student's next answer when the problem is rephrased. Across nine language models, accuracy fell from sixty-six percent on direct problem solving to forty percent on that prediction task. With one hundred one malrules over nearly five hundred templates, the library can generate over a million practice instances.
arxiv-2601-03617:
Samson Oseiwe Ajadalu, working alone, systematically tests how design choices affect a cheap substitute for LiDAR in three-dimensional object detection. A single camera costs far less than laser scanning, but judging distance from one image is hard. The pipeline first estimates depth, turns the image into a fake point cloud, and then runs a standard detector on it.

On the KITTI validation data, a supervised depth model called NeWCRFs beat a large general depth model in downstream detection. Adding brightness or semantic cues to the point cloud gave only small gains, and mask-based sampling actually hurt by removing context geometry. A distance-based diagnostic rounded out the study. The results tell self-driving engineers where effort pays: depth quality first, extra cues later.
arxiv-2601-03917:
Jinting Liu, Jingwei Li, and Tengfei Chang propose Monaas, a service-oriented design for factory wireless networks full of moving equipment. The underlying radio standard, Time-Slotted Channel Hopping, delivers high reliability at low power and suits factory Internet of Things deployments. Industry 4.0 adds strain: tasks arrive in bursts with varied quality demands, and the fleet of mobile devices keeps growing.

Existing networks lack a framework for those challenges, so Monaas treats mobile nodes as on-demand, elastic resources to be managed and scheduled as services. Its layered design balances global coordination with local autonomy. Task-driven scheduling allocates resources ahead of need, and a joining mechanism folds mobile equipment in as needed. The design aims to give factory networks the flexibility of cloud services while keeping their uptime promises.
arxiv-2601-04017:
Gayatri Ghosh, writing alone, studies how soft breaking of supersymmetry could give an axion-like particle most of its mass. Axion-like particles are hypothetical light particles tied to a symmetry named after Peccei and Quinn. In her setup that symmetry is exact when supersymmetry holds and is broken only by soft terms from supergravity.

That setup makes the particle naturally heavy, with mass set by the scale where supersymmetry breaks. Ghosh works out the related spectrum, including the saxion and axino partners. She then traces what the idea would mean for lab searches, space observations, and cosmology. The treatment stays at effective theory level, without picking one high-energy completion, and it does not try to explain a small strong CP phase.
arxiv-2601-04817:
What would make sixth-generation mobile networks genuinely sustainable? Mattia Merluzzi and 11 co-authors survey that question in a 2026 paper. They argue 6G could connect the unconnected, cut carbon emissions in other sectors, and let people and intelligent systems interact safely. Those gains, though, depend on design choices that weigh positive against negative impacts from the start.

The authors lay out trade-offs and enablers across the whole system, treating sustainability as something 6G must both achieve itself and enable elsewhere. Their holistic view connects network design with energy use and social aims. For planners and engineers, the paper offers a map of where 6G helps, where it harms, and what must change.
arxiv-2601-05717:
Jorge Roser and 4 co-authors propose, in a 2026 paper, using inter-crystal scattering events in PET scanning instead of discarding them. In positron emission tomography, a gamma ray sometimes scatters between detector crystals before being absorbed. That scattering is usually treated as damage to image resolution, though keeping the events could raise sensitivity.

Their physics-based model yields exact formulas for the sensitivity image and system matrix without locating the original line of response. Those formulas plug into a joint reconstruction method alongside conventional events. On modeled and experimental phantom data from a small-animal scanner prototype, adding scattering events clearly reduced noise and raised uniformity, with only a slight drop in recovery coefficients.
arxiv-2601-05917:
Bhanuj Jain and 4 co-authors link atomic-scale math to continuum models in 2026 to predict how hydrogen moves through polycrystalline nickel. Hydrogen embrittlement, which makes metals crack, is governed by diffusion and trapping, especially along grain boundaries between crystals. Predicting those effects in real microstructures has been difficult.

First-principles calculations supply migration barriers for bulk and grain-boundary settings. Kinetic Monte Carlo model runs turn those barriers into anisotropic effective diffusivities, which then feed finite element models of multi-crystal structures with clear boundary character and connectivity. The approach captures both fast paths and trapping without empirical parameters. It reproduces experimental trends for nickel, including how diffusivity depends on grain size and boundary type. No fitted values are used, so the match with lab trends is a real test of the physics in the model.
arxiv-2601-06317:
Yang Lu studies how to estimate one parameter of a branching count process in a 2026 statistics paper. The integrated Galton-Watson process is a basic building block for many count-valued time series models. The parameter of interest is its intercept, a baseline level in the process's evolution.

In this unit root setting, the ordinary least squares estimator is inconsistent, meaning it fails to home in on the true value. An existing weighted estimator works only when the process is transient, a condition that itself depends on the unknown intercept. Lu proposes a different weighted estimator using weights that shrink like one over time. That estimator proves consistent whether the process is transient or null recurrent. Its convergence is slow, at a square-root-of-log rate, but it removes the circular condition.
arxiv-2601-06417:
Simon Chiche and 2 co-authors report the first full characterization of cosmic-ray signals for in-ice radio detectors in a 2026 paper. Experiments in Greenland and at the South Pole listen for radio emission from particle cascades in ice, hunting ultra-high-energy neutrinos. Cosmic-ray showers are both background and calibration tool for that search.

Earlier simulations treated parts of the shower separately. Using the Monte Carlo framework FAERIE, this work incorporates both the in-air and in-ice emission of each shower. The authors quantify radiation energy, timing, polarization, and frequency spectrum, and how each depends on shower properties. The resulting guidelines should help future experiments identify cosmic-ray events and discriminate them from genuine neutrino signals in next-generation detectors.
arxiv-2601-06517:
Melting rates do not follow one rule at every size, show Edoardo Bellincioni and 6 co-authors in a 2026 study spanning metallurgy to climate science. Knowing how fast an object melts at each scale matters for extrapolating from laboratory experiments to ice sheets and oceans. Scaling laws only help if no hidden transition changes the rule midway.

Controlled melting experiments and direct numerical simulations, covering four orders of magnitude in scale, found exactly such a transition. Small objects in turbulent flow melt slowly; large ones melt fast. The switch corresponds to the boundary layer around the object changing from laminar to turbulent type, the same shift as from classical to ultimate turbulence with its enhanced transport. The results give a quantitative basis for predicting large-scale melt rates.
arxiv-2601-06617:
Giovani Braglia and co-authors design a robotic tele-operation system for microsurgery in 2026. Their target is the upper aerodigestive tract, inside the throat. Such treatments often employ transoral laser microsurgery for delicate procedures.

In that surgery, a laser beam cuts target tissue precisely. Forceps grasp, manipulate, and stabilize tissue within the tract meanwhile. Procedures include removal of tumors or polyps from those passages. Tele-operation would let a surgeon control instruments remotely and steadily. The paper covers system design and validation of their setup. Medical robotics readers get a full pipeline, from design to tests. It aims at steadier, safer work in a tight surgical space.
arxiv-2601-07017:
Andreas Langer and co-authors posted a 2026 arXiv preprint. The preprint deals with Ill-Posed foundations of Physics-Informed neural networks and their Finite-Difference variants. It came out on arXiv in 2026 as a PAPERS preprint. Physics-informed neural networks based on automatic differentiation (AD-PINNs) and their finite-difference counterparts (FD-PINNs) are widely used for solving partial differential equations (PDEs).

Yet their analytical properties remain poorly understood. This work provides a unified mathematical foundation for both formulations. Readers in the field get a short, focused account of the problem and the steps the authors take.
arxiv-2601-07117:
A 2026 arXiv preprint by Kexin Bao and co-authors appeared in 2026. It covers few-shot Class-Incremental learning via generative Co-Memory regularization. It was posted on arXiv in 2026 in the PAPERS collection. Few-shot class-incremental learning (FSCIL) aims to incrementally learn models from a small amount of new data. Which requires strong representation and adaptation ability of models learned under few-example supervision to avoid catastrophic forgetting.

On old classes and overfitting to new classes. This work proposes a generative co-memory regularization approach to facilitate FSCIL. Readers get a clear, focused account of the problem and the method the authors set out.
arxiv-2601-07517: Marius Durea and Elena-Cristina Stamate, mathematicians based in Iaşi, Romania, study a boundedness notion for sets defined through cones in a 2026 preprint. Their title names the topic: dually cone-boundedness of a set, with applications. Cone conditions appear across optimization and functional analysis, where they shape how sets and mappings behave. The work develops the new boundedness concept and turns to what it can be used for. The record here is thin, so this note stays with the stated topic and scope.
arxiv-2601-07617:
A large BESIII collaboration reports a detailed study of a rare particle decay, using a huge sample of J/psi events. The detector at Beijing collected about ten billion J/psi particles. From that sample, the team performs a partial-wave analysis of one decay channel into a Lambda, an anti-Sigma-zero, and an eta, plus its mirror process. Their 2026 preprint states the analysis is the first of its kind.

Partial-wave analysis separates a decay into components with different spins and motions. Those components reveal which intermediate particles form during the decay. Branching fraction measurements state how often the decay happens at all. Together they test models of how quarks bind into hadrons. Particle physicists use such measurements to refine the map of known and predicted states.
arxiv-2601-07817:
D. R. Heath-Brown counts special solutions to the simple equation x plus y equals z. The solutions he counts use square-full integers, numbers whose prime factors all appear with exponent at least two. He bounds how many such triples exist with all entries up to a given size B. His 2026 preprint gives that bound with a small saving over the natural exponent. The result holds for any fixed positive epsilon in the exponent.

Square-full numbers are rare, so triples of them summing correctly are rarer still. Counting them tests tools from analytic number theory. Even simple equations become hard when variables are restricted to thin sets. Bounds like this feed work on Diophantine equations and additive problems. The paper serves specialists in analytic number theory. It is a counting result, stated for experts who track exponents closely.
arxiv-2601-07917:
Antti Rantala and colleagues simulate how mid-sized black holes form by runaway collisions in dense star clusters. Intermediate-mass black holes may seed the supermassive ones in galaxy centers. The team explores their formation across a wide range of cluster densities. Surface densities span more than three orders of magnitude in their study. Metallicity, the chemical makeup of the stars, is the variable in this third FROST-CLUSTERS paper. Their 2026 preprint reports the simulations.

Runaway collisions happen when massive stars sink to the center and merge repeatedly. The product can grow into a black hole far heavier than any single star leaves. Metal content changes stellar winds, which change how much mass stars keep before colliding. That link decides which clusters succeed as incubators. The paper serves astrophysicists modeling black hole origins. It maps formation chances across realistic cluster conditions.
arxiv-2601-08017:
Evžen Wybitul and colleagues show that image and text representations inside vision-language models align surprisingly early. For many concepts in adapter-based models, image representations and text descriptions align meaningfully from the very first layer. That contradicts the established view that such alignment appears only in late layers. Their 2026 preprint presents the evidence across a variety of concepts. The models studied connect vision encoders to language models through adapters.

Early alignment changes how scholars picture these models working. If matching begins at layer one, later layers refine rather than create the link. That view affects probing, editing, and safety analysis of multimodal models. It also simplifies some theories of how adapters bridge the two modalities. The paper serves machine learning scholars who study representation geometry. It revises a basic assumption with direct measurement.
arxiv-2601-08217:
Ali Mamaghani and four co-authors present Tiny-Twin, a digital twin for next-generation cellular networks. Their 2026 arXiv paper notes that modern wireless apps need test settings that capture full network complexity. Digital twins promise realistic emulation for such tests.

Existing tools often trade away physical-layer fidelity or scalability, or they demand special hardware. Tiny-Twin runs a full-stack emulation on commodity CPUs instead. Realistic and repeatable 5G experiments become possible without a lab full of radios. For network researchers, a CPU-native twin lowers the cost of testing ideas before field trials. It also makes results easier for other teams to reproduce.
arxiv-2601-08317:
Ibuki Terada and three co-authors study Hall effects boosted by nodal lines in the magnet NbMnP. Their 2026 arXiv paper covers anomalous and nonlinear Hall effects in this parity-mixed antiferromagnet. The anomalous Hall effect is known to reflect the geometric nature of Bloch bands and impurity scattering.

A large anomalous Hall effect was recently reported in NbMnP, a noncollinear antiferromagnetic metal. Its magnetic order mixes even-parity and odd-parity components. The authors link the strong response to nodal-line features in the band structure. Quantum geometric effects like these may guide future spintronic materials that use antiferromagnets instead of ferromagnets.
arxiv-2601-08517: Tolgay Atinc Uzun, Dmitry Ignatov, and Radu Timofte use language models to discover channel configurations in vision models. Their 2026 arXiv paper treats channel search as a hard combinatorial problem. Layer widths must respect tensor shape compatibility and computational budgets at once. The authors argue language models can reason about architectural code structure in ways heuristics cannot. A closed-loop search lets the model propose, test, and revise non-standard channel priors. Smarter architecture search could yield leaner vision networks for phones and cameras.
arxiv-2601-08617: Leo Fillioux and four co-authors wrote a 2026 arXiv paper on how sure a vision-language model should be of its own replies. Such models now serve in health care and self-driving cars, where a wrong reply can harm. Test-time prompt tuning, or TPT, adapts a model at the time of use by tuning its prompt. Past TPT work has chased sharp picks, not trust in them. The authors set out Semantic Orthogonal Calibration, or SoC. It aims at the trust side that past work left aside.
arxiv-2601-08817:
N. Brace tests cheap shake sensors at the cold heart of a lab fridge. Such fridges cool tools to near the coldest heat that can be reached. Shake there can harm weak quantum or space tests. Staff need to know the shake level, but lab grade sensors cost much and may not work in such cold.

Brace checks store bought sensors at heats as low as eight thousandths of a degree above pure cold. He also checks if the sensors give off rays that could harm a test. The aim is a cheap, safe way to watch shake in cold labs. A reader who runs such a lab gets hard facts on what these low cost sensors can and can not do.
arxiv-2601-08917:
Arhum Ansari, Sachin Jain, and Deep Mazumdar link rules from flat space physics to rules for the fast growth era of space. In flat space, a rule set says how a process can split into parts. Those split rules are called cutting rules. In curved, fast growth space, the same splits are more hard to track by hand.

The team gives a dress up step that lifts flat cuts to curved space. In that view, each flat cut maps to a jump in a key energy count. They show the map on tree form and one loop cases for a plain field type. A reader in theory work gets a clear path. It makes curved space cut rules less of a black art.
arxiv-2601-09117:
Shalmoli Ghosh, Matthew DeVerna, and Filippo Menczer study a paid market for AI made adult and fake content on a fan site. The site is Civitai, a hub for AI art tools and models. Its Bounties tool lets a user post a paid ask for a set work. A maker who fills the ask earns the pay. That market can fund deep fakes of real folk.

The team maps how the market works: what asks are made, what pay is set, and what gets made. Such a map is a first step to rules that can curb harm with out a ban on all AI art. A reader in net safety gets facts on a new trade that law has yet to catch.
arxiv-2601-09817:
L. L. Salcedo gives a precise meaning to a quantum state living inside a chosen subspace. His 2026 arXiv paper defines the localization probability of a state within part of its Hilbert space. The localized component of the state is identified explicitly, not just bounded.

The author establishes several mathematical properties of the definition. Applications and interpretations in quantum information are discussed. A clean definition settles arguments about how much of a state sits in a code space or a sector. Such bookkeeping underlies error correction and the theory of quantum resources.
arxiv-2601-10017:
Shu-Cheng Chang, Yingbo Han, Chien Lin, and Chin-Tung Wu study a class of curved shapes named Sasakian. These shapes have a rich extra frame. A past claim by Yau dealt with how such shapes must look when they spread with no end. The claim was for a like class of shapes.

The team works on the Sasaki form of that claim. Their shapes have cross curve that is not below zero. The shapes are whole and not closed. The paper probes what form such a shape must take. Work of this kind sorts curved shapes by the signs of their curves.
arxiv-2601-11217:
Matthieu Meunier, Huyen Pham, and Christoph Reisinger learn control rules with no model. Their 2026 preprint deals with mean-field control in discrete time. Mean-field control steers a vast crowd as one system. Each agent's best move depends on the whole crowd's state.

Past work on this field leans on value-based methods. Policy-based ways are far less explored, for a clear reason. The crowd state drives both moves and rewards as time runs. That loop blocks the classic gradient tricks from single-agent learning. The team builds a policy gradient that works without a model. The state space is finite and the action space compact. The result opens a new path for crowd-scale control.
arxiv-2601-11317:
Robbe Vermeiren builds orthogonal bases from rational functions in this preprint. His 2026 work gives two algorithms for the task. Rational functions are ratios of two polynomials. Vectors of them arise in control and signal work.

The bases are orthonormal under a discrete inner product. That means pairs are clean and each vector has unit size. The builds rest on a pencil-based form of a known problem. That problem is the inverse generalized eigenvalue problem. Work by Van Buggenhout and others set that stage. Vermeiren shows how the bases serve rational approximation. Approximation with rational forms can fit poles that polynomials miss.
arxiv-2601-11417:
Tyler Reinmund, Lars Kunze, and Marina Jirotka study machine learning in care work. Their 2026 preprint deals with health care and social welfare. Sociotechnical challenges are clashes between a tool and its setting. A learning tool may clash with how care is truly done.

Past accounts of such clashes tend to blame one side. Some blame designers who miss the social side of care. Others blame hard technical limits in the tools. Both views give weak help for comparing cases. The team seeks a shared way to describe these clashes. A common frame would let cases be set side by side. That could guide fixes that respect both code and care.
arxiv-2601-11517:
Koyena Pal, David Bau, and Chandan Singh ask if explanations travel between models. Their 2026 preprint deals with large reasoning models. Such models write a chain of thought as they solve tasks. That chain reads like a natural-language explanation of the work.

A readable chain could be a strong tool for insight. It surfaces the model's path in terms humans can check. But it is unclear if such explanations generalize. A chain from one model may not fit another's process. It may also fail to match the model's true steps. The team tests that portability across reasoning models. The answer matters for trust in chain-of-thought audits.
arxiv-2601-11617:
Xu Wang, Boyao Han, Xiaojun Chen, Ying Liu, and Ruihui Li present PointSLAM++. Their 2026 preprint builds a dense neural SLAM system. Real-time 3D reconstruction is crucial for robotics and AR. SLAM maps a space while tracking the sensor in it.

Depth noise often breaks structural consistency in such maps. Pose estimation also turns shaky when depth data err. PointSLAM++ uses a Gaussian point cloud representation. The Gaussians are hierarchically constrained to hold structure. Constraints keep walls and edges true as the map grows. Gaussian primitives then render the scene for the map. The system takes RGB-D input, color plus depth. Robust poses under noise are the stated design aim.
arxiv-2601-11817:
Yumou Wei, John Carney, John Stamper, and Nancy Belmont flip a common view of privacy tools. Most rules act as a shield that users must hold up by hand. Users face opt-in and opt-out picks whose effects are hard to foresee.

They use the Johari Window, a frame for what is known to self and to others. In that view, rules guard the open self and hide the rest. The team argue for tools that help users speak up, not just hide. Their aim is to let users use what AI infers, on their own terms.
arxiv-2601-12217:
Li Ye and Yisheng Song study interval B-tensors and interval double B-tensors in a systematic way. An interval tensor is a family of tensors bounded by low and high terms. B-tensor classes have set sign and sum traits that help in maths tests.

They give checkable conditions that are both needed and enough. The checks rest on the extreme point tensors of the family alone. That turns a check over a vast family into a finite task. Such shortcuts help in optimization and game theory with tensors.  Finite checks make the class tests of real use.
arxiv-2601-12317:
Yiming Huang automates insight finding in two-way tables with a workflow that joins explainable AI and language models. Auto data analysis is a long goal. Agent tools such as DeepAnalyze and DataSage use model-led tool calls for fine work.

Huang asks what a preset, AutoML-like workflow can do in place of free agents. His system, Explanova, hunts insights in N by M tables in that set way. A fixed workflow may be cheaper and more easy to audit. The work tests that trade.  The table case is a set test for the workflow claim.
arxiv-2601-12417:
Yi-Long Duan, Tuohuniyazi Tuniyazi, and Gang Guo study neutrinos from exploding stars. When a massive star dies, its thrown off matter slams into gas that rings the star. That crash can speed up protons and make high energy neutrinos. The team focus on two classes of these blasts, Type II and Type IIn.

They take density profiles for the ring gas from real observations. With those in hand, they compute the neutrino fluxes that should result. They then test how the flux shifts as key inputs change. The inputs are the density scale, the outer radius, and how well protons gain energy. They also vary the share of energy held in magnetic fields.
arxiv-2601-13117:
Mihail Stoian and co-authors tackle a weak spot in database tools. Cloud database firms spend a lot on query optimizers, the part that picks how to run a query. A core step is to guess how big each join will be. A bad guess can wreck the whole plan.

Staff and scholars alike call that guess step the weak heel of the tool. The team gives lower bounds for join size, caps that a true size cannot fall below. Their method is named xBound. Firm bounds give the tool a floor to plan from. That floor can also guide how much stock and time a query gets. For cloud teams, firmer bounds mean fewer slow plans.
arxiv-2601-13217:
Bingsen Chen and co-authors test if deep research agents can fix a report over many rounds. Such agents search and write long reports on call. Past tests treat that write as a one shot task. Real scholars, though, draft and then fix their work in rounds, by self thought or peer notes.

The team asks if agents can do that round work with care. A user note may ask for a fix in one part. A weak agent may break sound parts or miss the note. Their finds mark the agents as not yet safe at multi round fix work. For teams that sell such agents, the test sets a bar that one shot scores hide.
arxiv-2601-13317:
Samantha Sudhoff, Pranav Perumal, Zhaoqing Wu, and Tunazzina Islam set paid climate ads next to free social posts and read both with one lens. Talk on climate shapes what the public grasps and what laws get made. But that talk runs on two kinds of stage with split pay rules.

Paid ad stages reward aimed, planned pleas. Free feed stages host raw talk by users at large. The team builds a theme model that can be read by eye. It maps which themes rule each stage and where they meet or part. For climate talk staff, the split shows whose voice a theme is, not just that it trends.
arxiv-2601-13417:
Yujian Xiong and co-authors enhance eye fundus pics with a GAN led by a sliced Gromov-Wasserstein guide. Fundus pics are the base of eye screen and diagnosis. Their grade is oft marred by noise, flaws, and uneven light. GAN and diffusion tools can lift such pics by pull toward clean pic forms.

The team finds a flaw in that pull. Pics of kin ills can spread apart in the learnt space, and class bounds blur. Their guide keeps that inner shape while the pic is cleaned. It uses a sliced form of the Gromov-Wasserstein span, a way to match shapes. For eye teams, a clean pic that bends class shape is a risk, not a gain.
arxiv-2601-13517:
Nicholas J. Evans and co-authors show a new phase space paint method to tame space charge in strong hadron beams. Strong beams blow up from their own charge push. Multi turn charge swap injection is the stock way to build such beams in rings. Paint sets how the beam fills its phase space as it is built.

Their method is called eigenpainting. It loads bits into one mode of a coupled ring. That gives full four dim hold of the fill form. A form set by mode can spread charge so its push harms less. For ring teams that chase brighter beams, a new paint knob is a real gain.
arxiv-2601-13617:
Yi-Han Luo and a large team work on light sources for quantum links in space in 2026. Sending quantum states over vast gaps is key for world-wide quantum nets. Satellites have sent linked light over a thousand kilometers in past tests. Future fleets and deep-space probes need sources that are small, tough, and frugal with power.

The team built a photon-pair source that works in near-visible light. Pairs of linked photons let two far sites share a quantum link. A compact source that sips power suits small satellites well. The work is a step toward quantum nets that span the globe and beyond.
arxiv-2601-14017:
Pavel Pavlíček and co-authors shape quantum correlations by counting photons in twin beams in 2026. A twin beam is a pair of linked light beams. Spatially-resolved photon counting with an iCCD camera lets them tailor the beams. They divide the idler beam into three equally intense parts.

Post-selection then keeps only cases with a set photocount in the signal beam. The result is idler fields with high degrees of nonclassicality. They also carry tripartite quantum correlations, links shared by three parties. Tailored multi-party light states feed quantum networks and tests of quantum theory.
arxiv-2601-14117:
Oskar Riedler and Thomas Tony show a rigid class of maps must be simple products in 2026. Scalar-rigid maps are Riemannian submersions, by works of Llarull, Goette and Semmelmann, and Tony. A submersion projects a big space onto a smaller one in a smooth way. The team shows these maps are essentially Riemannian products.

The product splits into the base manifold and a Ricci-flat fiber. As an application, they obtain a Llarull-type theorem. It covers non-zero degree maps onto products of manifolds with set curvature traits. Such rigidity results limit how curved spaces can relate.
arxiv-2601-14217:
Axel Fünfhaus, Titus Neupert, Thilo Kopp, and Roser Valentí define a new topology marker for many-body systems in 2026. Integer and fractional Chern insulators show a quantized anomalous Hall conductivity. That trait comes from spontaneous breaking of time reversal symmetry. In time-reversal symmetric spectra, that marker cannot spot nontrivial topology.

The team introduces many-body Euler numbers as a counterpart to many-body Chern numbers. Euler numbers can flag topology while time reversal stays intact. New markers widen the hunt for topological phases of matter. Such phases may host robust quantum devices in the future. The new count works where the old one is blind. It opens a class of phases that past scans would have missed by rule.
arxiv-2601-14517:
Yilong Dai and six co-authors survey learning-based PDE solvers in this 2026 paper. Partial differential equations are central to scientific modeling. Modern workflows increasingly rely on learning-based parts to support model reuse, inference, and integration across large computational processes. Physics-aware data-driven approaches have grown fast in that role.

Yet the field lacks a unified perspective. Without one, the relationships, limitations, and proper roles of the methods stay unclear. The authors give that unifying view for two big families. They are physics-informed neural networks and neural operators. Readers get a map that sorts what each family does, where each fails, and where each belongs in real workflows.
arxiv-2601-14617:
Yunfeng Lin, Li Xu, Yong Yu, Jiangmiao Pang, and Weinan Zhang present a robot software system in this 2026 paper. Deploying learning-based controllers across heterogeneous robots is challenging. Platform differences, inconsistent interfaces, and inefficient middleware all get in the way. A controller tuned on one robot rarely drops cleanly onto another.

Their system, UniCon, is a lightweight framework that standardizes states, control flow, and instrumentation across platforms. It decomposes workflows into execution graphs with reusable components. It also separates system states from control logic, which enables plug-and-play deployment across various robot morphologies. Readers get a path to move learned controllers between robots without rebuilding the stack each time.
arxiv-2601-14717: Planar univalent harmonic mappings are smooth maps of the complex plane that do not fold onto themselves. This 2026 math paper investigates how such mappings change the Lebesgue measure, the area, of measurable sets. The work is motivated by Problem 3.25 of Koh and Kovalev from HQM2010. The authors establish sharp quantitative area distortion inequalities. They cover disks and arbitrary measurable sets under sense-preserving harmonic self-maps of the unit disk. Sharp means the bounds cannot be improved. The evidence pack lists no authors for this entry.
arxiv-2601-15317:
Daisuke Hirota asks why groups that split apart also pull together. His 2026 arXiv paper deals with a social paradox: division and cohesion often intensify at the same time. He gives a structural answer that does not depend on the details of any one group.

The theory is static and rests on relation maintenance. Social ties must meet minimum conditions, set over an abstract space of positions. From those minimal constraints alone, the paper derives its claim. Cohesion without fragmentation is impossible: holding some ties close forces other ties to break apart.
arxiv-2601-15817:
Nina A. Lange and five co-authors fight a limiting effect in optical waveguides in a 2026 arXiv paper. Their material is lithium niobate. It is widely used in nonlinear and quantum optical devices. Examples include frequency generation and photon pair sources. In waveguides, the photorefractive effect caps performance. It limits the input and output powers a device can handle. It also distorts the nonlinear spectral response.

The title contrasts two management routes: high-temperature and cryogenic solutions. Each regime changes how the effect behaves. Choosing between them is a practical design decision. Quantum photonics needs bright, clean sources. Photorefraction stands in the way of both traits. A clear comparison of fixes helps device builders pick the right thermal strategy.
arxiv-2601-16117:
Abdul Hannan and coauthors make speech nets that can shed layers to fit small gear. Their 2026 preprint deals with edge gear with tight and shifting means. A fixed net can be too big for weak gear. Layer drop turns a fixed net into one that can skip parts. Skips cut cost but can hurt speech scores if done with no care.

The team adds a teach step to the drop plan. A full net teaches the lean net as it learns to skip. That teach step aims to keep scores high at low cost. The net can then shift its size as gear means shift. The work targets live speech tools on phones and like gear.
arxiv-2601-16317:
Jian Li and four coauthors study noisy quantum heat acts with a plain noise stand in. Their 2026 preprint deals with heat acts that cool or drive quantum states. Noise and flaws touch all real acts of this kind. They touch acts built to cut noise in the first place. Cool acts can lose both speed and worth when noise hits.

The team uses a mixed state noise path as a stand in. That path, the depolarizing channel, is plain yet rich. It lets them trace how noise bends act scores. Clear bends guide design of cool acts that hold up. The work aids teams who run heat acts on real gear.
arxiv-2601-16417:
Umar Qureshi, Brendon Bullard and Ariel Schwartzman tag all jets in a crash at once. Their 2026 preprint, named PanopTag, deals with jets from particle hits. To tag a jet is to name the grain that made it. Deep tools have lifted tag scores much in past years. Yet past tools still tag each jet one by one.

One by one tags miss links that join jets in one crash. Tag all at once can use those links for each call. Links tell of shared birth paths in the crash. Use of links should lift tag truth for hard jets. The work shifts tag work from lone jets to whole events.
arxiv-2601-16817:
Antonin Boisneault, Marcella Bonazzoli, Xavier Claeys, and Pierre Marchand split hard sound tasks for fast solves. Sound waves in rooms and the open air obey one core rule. Big zones make that rule slow to solve whole. Their 2026 preprint cuts the zone in parts that don't overlap. Each part is solved, then the parts trade edge facts.

Their join pairs two solve styles at the seams. One style fills the zone's guts, the next its skin. A tuned trade rule speeds how the parts agree. Fast sound solves aid hall design and noise plans. They also help map how sound spreads from roads.
arxiv-2601-17117:
Hua-Peng Gu, Fangzhou Jiang, Xian Chen, and Ran Li push a dark halo fall past old bounds. Vast black holes show up too soon in the young cosmos. Plain seed tales strain to grow them in time. Dark halos that self-bump may fall in to seed them. Past work set that fall in calm, non-relativistic form.

Their 2026 preprint drops the calm tack. It adds full relativity to the fall math. Fall paths then cap how big a seed can grow. Those caps face the young holes scopes now see. The work tests if dark falls can truly seed them.
arxiv-2601-17617:
Jingjie Ning and co-authors analyze agentic search at large scale. LLM search agents now handle multi-step information tasks. The field lacks proof of how those sessions unfold. The team studies 14.44 million search requests. They span 3.97 million sessions from DeepResearchGym. Logs show intents and trajectory dynamics across real use.

Such scale turns anecdote into pattern. The study tracks how retrieved evidence is used, step by step. Designers can see where agents loop, stall, or succeed. That guides better agent planners and search tools. The work gives the IR community a shared fact base. Agent claims can now be checked against logs.
arxiv-2601-17717: Kaituo Zhang and eleven co-authors survey how to judge synthetic data made for large language models. The 2026 preprint takes a metric-based view of two questions. First, is the data good enough to train on? Second, can the data and its scores be trusted? The survey sorts the measures in use and compares what each one can and cannot show.
arxiv-2601-18017:
Runjie Song and Kengo Deguchi study waves that grow on swirling flow over a curved wall. Their 2026 preprint deals with Görtler vortices, rolls that form when flow follows a concave surface. These vortices support fast, wavelike disturbances through a second round of instability. Lab work hints that the growth of these waves, at full strength, sets up the shift to turbulence. Predicting that growth well and cheaply has stayed out of reach.

The authors push past the secondary instability view. They target the finite-amplitude stage, where the waves are no longer small. That stage is where transition is decided. Better models here serve aircraft, turbines, and any flow over curved skin.
arxiv-2601-18117:
Boxiao Chen and Jiashuo Jiang price the cost of letting each product team set its own prices. Their 2026 preprint studies decentralized pricing in multi-product firms. When managers ignore how one product's price shifts demand for others, the firm loses money. The authors measure that loss with the price of anarchy, a ratio between selfish and coordinated outcomes. Their pricing game has each manager set prices to lift their own product's revenue.

Diagonal dominance turns out to shape when a Nash equilibrium exists and how bad it can be. The results tell firms when decentralization is cheap and when it bleeds profit. Coordination has costs too, so a clear loss bound helps leaders choose a structure.
arxiv-2601-18217:
Zhihan Liu and co-authors measure the cost of training an agent in one world and using it in another. Their 2026 preprint studies reinforcement learning for language model agents. Generalist agents are often post-trained in a narrow set of environments. They are then deployed across far broader, unseen domains. The authors call the skill lost in that jump a generalization tax. They ask which traits of the training environments and which modeling choices drive the tax up or down.

Knowing the drivers lets builders pick training grounds that travel well. It also tells them when a low tax is a mirage. As agents move into open-ended work, this cross-domain question becomes central.
arxiv-2601-18417:
Ivan Batistić, Pablo Castrillo, and Philip Cardiff build a faster way to solve stress math for solid parts. Their base tool splits a part into small cells and tracks force in each cell. Plain forms of the tool stop at a low grade of truth. The team push the grade up, so bends and loads show in finer detail.

They pair the fine grid with a solver that skips a costly step. The solver, named in the title, guesses and checks its way to the answer with no need to build one huge table of slopes. Fresh slopes come from a fit to near cells, and sums at cell faces keep the count sharp. The mix aims for lab-grade truth on parts like beams and blocks, at a cost that firms can pay.
arxiv-2601-18817:
Nadim Rooholamin, Kabir Bakhshaei, and Giovanni Stabile build a lean model of rough flow that firms can run in far less time than a full sim. A full sim of rough flow in a pipe or past a wing takes a huge grid and days of chip time. A lean model keeps the big moves of the flow and drops the rest. The catch is to keep the lean form true to the full one's laws, such as the law that mass can't be made or lost.

Their plan builds the lean form straight from the full grid, then adds a learned fix for the dropped moves. The grid in view has all flow facts in the same cells, a form that makes law care hard. Their path keeps mass true with no extra props. Lean forms that keep the laws could speed design loops for cars, planes, and pumps.
arxiv-2601-18917:
Semih Cantürk and seven co-authors build a shared test frame for graph inverse problems. Many graph tasks run in reverse: instead of guessing from a known graph, they infer the graph itself from data. Such tasks span finding hidden links, tracing graphs over time, and hard search problems.

Work on each task grew up alone, with its own tools and no shared base. GraIP gives these tasks one bench and one frame so methods can be compared fairly. A shared bench can show which ideas travel across tasks and which only work on the one task they were built for.
arxiv-2601-19217:
Tim Menzies and seven co-authors look back, from an imagined future, at what software journals must become. In 2025, they write, publishing in the field faced a crisis of scale. Communities grew worldwide and fast methods like language models flooded the pipeline, straining the old journal system.

Writing as if from 2036, the team sketches the future the field needs to have built. The playful frame lets senior figures state hard truths about review load, speed, and quality control. Their piece is a call to fix scholarly publishing before scale breaks it for good.
arxiv-2601-19417:
J. Brieussel, R. Tessera, and T. Zheng study random walks on groups, a core topic in modern mathematics. A random walk moves step by step in random directions. The question here is how far the walk can stray from its start over a set number of steps. The groups involved grow in a controlled, polynomial way, which keeps the walk's spread orderly.

The authors prove concentration inequalities for the largest displacement of the walk. In plain terms, the chance of a very large escape falls off sharply, like a bell curve tail. The walk is centred and uses steps from a fixed, bounded set of moves. Such bounds matter wherever random walks model real processes, from diffusion to algorithms. The result gives a firm grip on how wild a walk can get.
arxiv-2601-19817: Bowman Hall reports a computing study of hard-to-catch fake primes. The samples are composite numbers of about three hundred fifty bits. They were built with the Arnault method, so they pass every Miller-Rabin primality test up to base eleven. Two hundred such numbers were generated and checked. Every one of them fails the strong Lucas probable prime test. The gap between the two tests matters for cryptography, where a composite mistaken for a prime can weaken keys.
arxiv-2601-20317:
Yipu Zhang and ten colleagues present VersaQ-3D, a reconfigurable accelerator chip for fast 3D reconstruction. New transformer models can rebuild a 3D scene directly from images, with no per-scene tuning. But a billion-parameter model demands too much memory and compute for instant on-device use.

VersaQ-3D uses versatile quantization, representing numbers at mixed precision, to slim the model for hardware. A reconfigurable design lets one chip serve both feed-forward reconstruction and related tasks. Fast on-device 3D would help augmented reality, robot perception, and digital twins respond in real time. That is the gap this chip is built to close.
arxiv-2601-20417:
SpeechMapper is a cheaper way to connect speech models to large language models. Current speech systems bridge the two with projection layers and train everything on speech instruction data. That strategy is computationally heavy and prone to overfitting the tasks and prompts it saw in training.

SpeechMapper trains a speech-to-text embedding projector instead. By keeping the heavy components fixed, it lowers cost and resists overfitting. The authors aim for models that generalize better to new speech tasks. Cheaper, sturdier speech interfaces would help voice assistants work across more settings and speakers.
arxiv-2601-20717:
Arie Bodek, Hyon-San Seo, and Un-Ki Yang sum up precision tests of a key number in particle physics. Their 2026 paper reviews the weak mixing angle near the Z pole. The Z pole is the energy where the Z boson is made most often. The mixing angle links the weak and electric forces in one value.

The summary centers on an improved extraction of the effective leptonic angle. It builds on a published CMS measurement at the Large Hadron Collider. That measurement used the forward-backward asymmetry in Drell-Yan events at thirteen TeV. In such events, a quark and antiquark make a lepton pair. The paper gathers what these precise numbers say about the standard model.
arxiv-2601-20917:
Masked Lagrange reconstruction is presented in this 2026 paper as a way to split digital signing power among many parties. The target is ML-DSA, the standard signature scheme fixed by FIPS 204. A threshold version lets any T of the parties sign together. The signatures stay at the standard size and verify with unmodified FIPS 204 tools. Rival methods impose limits, such as honest-majority rules or many rounds of interaction.

The paper's technique aims to lift those limits while keeping standard output. That matters for shared custody of keys in finance and infrastructure. No verifier should need special software to trust the result. The work is a focused advance in applied cryptography. It shows that post-quantum signatures can be shared without breaking the standard.
arxiv-2601-21117:
Daniel Köglmayr and three co-authors teach a machine to remember several chaotic patterns after just two glimpses. Their 2026 paper studies two-shot learning of multiple strange attractors. A strange attractor is the tangled shape a chaotic system traces over time. The brain combines short- and long-term memory to store many pieces of information. The authors take inspiration from that design. They extend a recent machine learning technique that does the same.

Their system pairs a next-generation reservoir computer with extremely randomized trees. The reservoir acts as short-term memory; the trees hold the long-term store. Together they process, store, and recall multiple attractors. Learning each from only two examples is the hard part. Success hints at machines that memorize dynamics like brains do. The work joins neuroscience ideas with chaotic time-series learning.
arxiv-2601-21717:
Shogo Nakakita bounds the sample cost of estimating a covariance matrix with a popular sampling algorithm. The unadjusted Langevin algorithm draws samples by following a noisy downhill rule. For strongly log-concave, smooth distributions, its samples can estimate the covariance.

The author compares one long chain against many parallel chains. The single chain wins by a logarithmic factor in dimension and target precision. The gain comes from the burn-in phase cutting bias more effectively. Clear sample bounds help practitioners choose chain layouts with math, not folklore, when sampling feeds a covariance estimate.
arxiv-2601-21817:
Mingyuan Xu, Xinzi Tan, Jiawei Wu, and Doudou Zhou tackle a growing problem. How to rank large language models when no correct answers exist to check against. A common fix is to let other models act as judges. The catch is that judge models differ a lot in reliability.

Treating all judges as equal can produce biased leaderboards and misleading confidence, the authors note. In fact, more data can make a ranking more confidently wrong when judges are pooled the wrong way. Their 2026 preprint proposes a judge-aware ranking framework that accounts for those differences. Fair ways to weigh judges matter, because public rankings steer which models people buy, fund, and build on.
arxiv-2601-21917:
Amir Ali Ahmadi and Georgina Hall prove a discouraging result about a basic computational task. Finding critical points of a function, the flat spots where optimization methods hope to land. Even for simple classes of nonconvex functions, they show that computing even rough approximations is intractable.

Concretely, if a fast algorithm existed that took a polynomial in many variables, of degree as low as three. And returned a point close to critical, that would contradict what complexity theory leads us to expect. Their 2026 preprint draws that line carefully. Negative results like this are valuable: they tell algorithm designers to stop hunting for guarantees that cannot exist. And to aim at structure or heuristics instead.
arxiv-2601-22117:
Francesco Di Braccio and Viresh Patel answer a question about covering colored graphs with tidy cycles. Color the edges of a graph with several colors, and give the graph a high minimum degree, so every vertex has many connections. A question from Letzter and Pokrovskiy asks how many vertex-disjoint cycles, each in a single color, are needed to cover every vertex.

The answer should depend on the number of colors and the minimum degree. Di Braccio and Patel resolve the problem up to a factor that grows only slowly with the number of colors. Their 2026 preprint settles most of a clean extremal question, the kind whose tidy statement hides years of work in graph theory.
arxiv-2601-22317:
Ege Demirci, Francesco Bullo, Ananthram Swami, and Ambuj Singh recover missing flows on a network while keeping the books exact. Flows here are loads that move on edges, in grids, roads, or pipes. Their 2026 preprint presents FlowSymm, a model that never breaks the local rule that flow in equals flow out.

The model acts on flows that already obey the rule, so each step stays legal. A graph heed step learns weights for those acts from edge traits. A light polish step then sharpens the fit. The design suits power, traffic, and travel data.
arxiv-2601-22417:
Yumiao Wang and a large team boost the yield of a rare nuclear state that could power a new kind of clock. The state, in thorium-229, links the nucleus and the atom in a rare way. Their 2026 preprint notes that making it well, on demand, is still a hard lab problem.

Their route uses a cascade decay, fed inside storage rings and electron beam ion traps. A richer yield would speed work on nuclear clocks, which promise time marks sharper than today's best. It would also aid fine tests of physics. The work is a recipe for supply.
arxiv-2601-22617:
Hongxi Yan, Qingjie Liu, and Yunhong Wang cut the cost of long chain-of-thought reasoning by stopping weak chains early. Large reasoning models think in long steps, which costs much compute. Their 2026 preprint, EntroCut, finds that the spread of the model's early output odds tells good chains from bad ones.

Cutting a doomed chain early saves time with little loss. The signal comes free, from odds the model already gives. The trick suits small reasoning models most, where each run counts. It offers speed without retraining. The work is a sharp, cheap gate.
arxiv-2601-22917:
Tom Raynes and eight co-authors work toward counting chimpanzees from camera trap videos, automatically. Estimating how many apes live in an area rests on measuring how far each animal is from the camera. Today, people read those distances by hand from huge piles of video, a slow and costly task.

Automating the distance step could speed up population counts across whole forests. Reliable counts guide protection work for great apes, whose numbers are under pressure. The study links computer vision with field ecology in a direct, useful way. Camera traps gather the video corpora around the clock, so automation promises counts across seasons rather than single expeditions.
arxiv-2602-02417:
Zekun Wang and 2 co-authors reinterpret a continual learning method as a hidden meta-learner, in a 2026 arXiv paper. Continual learning teaches a model tasks one after another without catastrophic forgetting of earlier tasks. Regularization methods can overconstrain learning, while replay methods can drift because replayed data is imperfect.

Their approach combines generative replay with a trust region, a limit on how far each update may move, weighted by Fisher information, a measure of which parameters matter. The authors show the update behaves like one inner step of meta-learning, the training style that prepares a model to adapt quickly. Replay supplies an old-task signal while the penalty shapes curvature efficiently. On image generation and robot control benchmarks, the method retained old skills best and relearned early tasks fastest after each switch.
arxiv-2602-02617:
Moncy Vilavinal John surveys whether quantum states describe reality itself or only information about it, in a 2026 arXiv paper. Some recent tests claim that any model treating the quantum state as mere information must clash with quantum theory's predictions. John approaches the question from a deeper direction, starting in classical mechanics.

The route rewrites the classical Hamilton-Jacobi equation as a wave equation, much as geometrical optics grows into wave optics. Generalizing de Broglie's wave-particle duality then leads to the Schrödinger equation, whose wave function appears as real as its classical counterpart. Eigenvalue equations and state expansions also have classical parallels. Missing pieces in the classical realm, like wave function collapse and entanglement, trace back to nonlinearity in the classical wave equation. Many quantum puzzles, John argues, sit dormant inside classical mechanics, which makes them far less mysterious.
arxiv-2602-02817:
Bhaskar Dutta and 4 co-authors calculate whether a neutrino detector near Fermilab's beam could catch light dark matter exciting argon nuclei, in a 2026 paper. Inelastic dark matter scattering can leave an argon nucleus in an excited state. Its de-excitation emits MeV-scale photons, appearing as small localized blips in a liquid argon time projection chamber.

Reliable signal predictions need serious nuclear theory. The team performs ab initio calculations covering all relevant argon excited states up to eighteen MeV in energy. Backgrounds are accounted for with those predictions in hand. The Short-Baseline Near Detector can probe previously unexplored regions of light dark matter parameter space through this channel. The study turns an existing neutrino experiment into a dark matter instrument at no new hardware cost, provided the low-energy blip signatures can be isolated as modeled.
arxiv-2602-02917:
Learning from wearable heart signals with few clinical labels is the problem in a 2026 paper by Yunsung Chung and 8 co-authors. The signals, called PPG, come from smartwatches. Labels come from lab blood draws, so signals recorded far from a draw are less trustworthy as supervision.

The authors weight each training segment by the time gap to its label. A learned decay rule lowers the weight as the gap grows, with a guard against trivial solutions. Data covered 450 participants and ten biomarkers. The method beat self-supervised and feature-based baselines. A simple straight-line decay worked most robustly. Learned decay rates also show how quickly evidence for each biomarker goes stale.
arxiv-2602-03217:
Graph learning methods can fail badly when they ignore topology, warns a cautionary study by May Kristine Jonson Carlon with 3 co-authors. Brain organization requires models spanning multiple scales. Their hierarchical self-supervised system learns node, edge, and graph vectors jointly, inspired by multimodal neuroimaging, and is tested on a controllable synthetic benchmark mimicking connectome wiring, the wiring pattern of brain networks.

A four-stage review reveals a critical failure. The invariance-based model is fundamentally misaligned with the benchmark's topology and is badly outperformed by classic topology-aware heuristics. Ablations confirm the objective itself learns to ignore community form that classic methods exploit. The authors present the system as a cautionary case study, calling for topology-aware objectives that clearly reward keeping form.
arxiv-2602-03317:
Alex Finkelstein, leading 6 other authors, maps doubt in molecular MRI scans with a physics-structured variational autoencoder. MRI here means magnetic resonance imaging. Quantitative scans such as magnetic resonance fingerprinting aim to read tissue traits from signal changes over time. Most solvers for that inverse problem give point values with no clear doubt attached. That limits trust and the clinical uptake of quantitative biomarkers from scans.

Their autoencoder builds a differentiable spin physics simulator into self-supervised learning. It outputs a full posterior spread for each voxel, with covariance that captures how the traits correlate. Tests span lab phantoms, tumor-bearing mice, healthy volunteers, and a subject with glioblastoma. The posteriors matched brute-force Bayesian analysis while running orders of magnitude faster. Watching posteriors as signals accrue also informs protocol design.
arxiv-2602-03417:
