Yingli Shen and 9 co-authors introduce FactNet, a knowledge resource meant to keep language models factually grounded. Their 2026 paper describes a graph that links 1.7 billion Wikidata assertions to just over 3 billion evidence pointers. The evidence comes from 316 native-language editions of Wikipedia, far beyond the usual English-only resources.

A deterministic pipeline builds the graph, so every evidence unit traces back to its exact source, down to the byte. The team also releases FactNet-Bench, a test suite for completing knowledge graphs, answering questions, and checking facts, with controls against data leakage. Experiments show the bench separates method families clearly, and that cross-lingual structure helps knowledge move between languages.
arxiv-2602-03517:
Many decisions need a ranking, not a number: which patients get preventive care first, or which customers an ad would sway most. Henri Arno and 4 co-authors introduce Rank-Learner in a 2026 paper. The two-stage method learns the ordering of treatment effects directly from observational data. Estimating each effect precisely first, they show, solves a harder problem than ranking requires.

Rank-Learner optimizes a pairwise objective that recovers the true ordering without ever estimating individual effects. The design is Neyman-orthogonal, giving theoretical protection against errors in the background nuisance estimates. It also works with any machine learning model under the hood. In extensive experiments it consistently beats standard effect estimators and non-orthogonal ranking methods.
arxiv-2602-03617:
Vehicles entering an atmosphere at Mach 6 need rough, ablating surfaces, and that roughness can trip the boundary layer into turbulence early. Sean Dungan and 3 co-authors run the first direct numerical simulation of this process on a blunt cylinder in a 2026 paper. Their setup follows sand-grain roughness experiments, with elements covering the whole surface at about a third of the boundary layer's thickness.

Only the streamwise phasing of the roughness rows changes between runs, yet the transition mechanism changes with it. Aligned rows favor a sinuous streak mode, while staggered and random rows favor two-dimensional Tollmien-Schlichting waves. Grown waves destabilize the steady streaks into hairpin vortices and breakdown. One configuration even excites its own waves through acoustic feedback from the turbulent zone.
arxiv-2602-04017:
Chaplains, not clinicians, are the care experts in Joel Wester and 3 co-authors' 2026 study of conversational AI. Chaplains guide people through grief, crisis, and reflection outside medical settings. Eighteen chaplains built AI chatbots and reflected on what the tools could and could not do.

A few were cautiously optimistic. Most found chatbots weak at everyday emotional support. Their accounts cluster around listening, connecting, carrying, and wanting, themes the authors read through attunement, a relational idea about being genuinely present. The study suggests well-being chatbots fail not on information but on presence, and designs should start there.
arxiv-2602-04417:
A moving anchor steadies policy gradient training for language models. Lunjun Zhang and 1 co-author propose EMA Policy Gradient in a 2026 paper. Standard methods anchor updates to a fixed reference policy; theirs uses an exponential moving average of the policy itself, like a target network in value learning.

A top-k KL estimator joins the anchor, interpolating between exact and sampled divergence while staying unbiased in both value and gradient. The authors derive stability conditions for the moving anchor. Combined with GRPO, the techniques boosted math reasoning scores and improved agentic search tasks substantially across seven datasets. Small, principled tweaks to the anchor beat elaborate redesigns.
arxiv-2602-04917:
Streams of events that carry both labels, such as an IP address, and measurements, such as packet length, are the raw material of network data mining. The paper, presented at the ACM Web Conference 2026, comes from Soshi Kakio and 3 co-authors. Older methods force one type into the other's mold, distorting the data, and they chop time into blocks, which hides group attacks.

Their method, HeteroComp, keeps summarizing the stream into components: latent groups for each attribute plus a picture of how each group changes over time. Gaussian process priors let the method learn the shape of measured values directly from data instead of assuming a fixed distribution. On real datasets, HeteroComp beat leading methods at spotting group anomalies such as denial-of-service attacks, and its running time did not grow with the length of the stream.
arxiv-2602-05117:
Cosmic voids, the vast underdense regions between galaxy filaments, are sensitive probes of how galaxies form. Ignacio G Alfaro and 8 co-authors examine how individual galaxy bias behaves inside voids in this 2026 cosmology paper. Bias measures how strongly a galaxy traces the underlying dark matter, and earlier work found it dips near void centers and rises toward the edges.

The question is whether that profile is an artifact of how voids are found. The team ran five different void finders, from spherical and watershed methods to a free-form density approach, over the same galaxies from the IllustrisTNG simulation. The radial bias gradient proved robust across most definitions. Differences did appear: density-based finders preferentially select negative-bias galaxies, while watershed methods admit more high-bias boundary interlopers. Tightening the underdensity threshold changed purity in a systematic way the authors quantify.
arxiv-2602-05217:
Segmenting a new category from a handful of examples is hard enough; doing it in a new domain, like medical scans after training on photos, is harder. Jiahao Nie and 5 co-authors propose Multi-view Progressive Adaptation for that task in this 2026 computer vision paper, accepted at CVPR 2026. Scarce, narrow target examples and a large domain gap conspire against adaptation.

The method progresses on two fronts. On the data side, hybrid augmentation builds steadily more diverse and complex views of the few target images, creating a curriculum of harder and harder learning scenarios. On the strategy side, a dual-chain prediction scheme learns through sequential and parallel paths over those views, with consistency enforced between them. The combination adapts the few-shot skill both robustly and accurately. Across experiments the method beat the state of the art by a wide margin, reported as about seven points.
arxiv-2602-05717:
Training language models with verifiable rewards can quietly destroy diversity, as the model sharpens on a few answers and squeezes out valid alternatives. Tianyi Wang, Long Li, and 6 co-authors name this failure recursive space contraction, an irreversible collapse of the sampling space. Standard KL regularization fights it by forcing the model to mimic a reference model full density, which conflicts with the sharpening that correctness needs.

Their method, Anchored Policy Optimization, replaces global shape matching with support coverage. A safe manifold is defined from the reference model high confidence support, and inside it the model may sharpen freely. A restorative force switches on during error correction to re inflate valid branches before they vanish. Theory shows the method aligns gradients with maximizing support coverage. On math benchmarks, it improved single answer accuracy while restoring the multi answer diversity that standard methods lose.
arxiv-2602-05817:
Internet of things networks grow tangled fast, and the graph neural networks used to watch them hide their reasoning inside opaque embeddings. Enrique Feito-Casares, Francisco Melgarejo-Meseguer, and 3 co-authors build an interpretable pipeline for IoT traffic flows. High dimensional graph embeddings are projected onto a low dimensional latent manifold that humans can look at directly.

Feature attribution tools then decode which traffic characteristics shape the manifold structure. The framework reached a solid classification score on intrusion detection while exposing phenomena such as concept drift, where traffic patterns shift over time. Security analysts can watch network states evolve on the map instead of trusting a black box score. The authors argue this bridges the gap between graph embeddings and human understandable network behavior. The pipeline is aimed at security critical operations.
arxiv-2602-06317:
Attention in a language model tends to pile onto a few tokens, which suggests most of the context could be skipped. Jorge L Ruiz Williams tests how far that sparse decoding idea can be trusted. Capturing most of the attention mass, he shows, does not by itself guarantee the same next word as full decoding.

He proves an exact identity for the omitted mass and a margin condition that suffices for stability, then studies a block selector based on averaged queries. On a small model, no sparse run matched dense decoding for long, though text quality often stayed close at larger support sizes. A clear warning regime appeared where quality collapsed, tied to weak teacher-forced agreement.
arxiv-2602-06717:
Daniil Plyusov and six co-authors study a flaw in how language models are trained with verifiable rewards. A group of sampled answers is scored and the model is nudged toward the correct ones. With small groups, a rare correct solution may never be sampled, so its probability quietly shrinks even while the model's overall score improves. The paper derives how often such tail-miss events happen as group size changes.

Their fix scales each update by a difficulty-aware factor, inspired by focal loss, that down-weights groups the model already finds easy. On a mid-sized open model, the method lifted math scores across three training algorithms by several points, including on out-of-distribution tests, with no extra sampling or computing cost. Simulations and a maze task confirm the same effect in simpler settings.
arxiv-2602-06917:
Sumit Kumar and three co-authors build tools that spot singing mistakes to help music students learn. Audio analysis by machine learning has opened new doors for music teaching, but a teacher needs to know which mistake a student made, not just a raw score. The team gathered a fresh data set of teacher and learner voices recorded in sync, marked with the kinds of mistakes learners made.

From that data they trained and ranked several deep learning models for mistake spotting, and they propose a new way to judge such systems against each other. Their learning-based models beat rule-based ones, and a close look at errors plus a cross-teacher study yielded lessons about teaching itself. Code and data are out in the open, opening new research paths in tech-aided music teaching.
arxiv-2602-07017:
Thuraya Alzubaidi and four co-authors make explanations for medical image segmentation clearer and cheaper to produce. Segmentation guides diagnosis, treatment plans, and disease tracking. Transformer models beat convolutional ones on score, yet their inner workings are hard to read, which hurts trust in clinics. Old explanation tools cost a lot, need many forward passes, and often yield noisy maps that miss anatomy.

Their system, XAI-CLIP, uses vision-language codes to find anatomical regions that matter for care, then steers targeted perturbations to those regions. The result is saliency maps that follow boundaries and carry fewer artifacts, at much lower cost. On the FLARE22 and CHAOS data sets, run time fell by up to 60 percent. Dice score rose by up to about 45 percent, and overlap for occlusion-based explanations nearly doubled, versus standard perturbation tools.
arxiv-2602-07217:
Scheduling tasks whose start and end times are uncertain is a daily problem in operations, from clinics to machines.  Rui Gong and one co-author study sequential interval scheduling where each task's realized interval is revealed only when it is committed to, knocking out conflicting tasks.

The paper proposes two models that differ in how conflicts are enforced, develops relaxations and bounds for each, and backs them with a computational study.  The goal throughout is to maximize expected weight of a conflict-free schedule.  Operations teams get a careful treatment of a real twist: you learn the timing only by choosing.
arxiv-2602-07617:
Niobium fills nearly the whole volume of a typical 2D transmon device, so pair-breaking in its leads, pads. Resonators can dominate decoherence even though the aluminum junction gets the attention.  A large team led by Amlan Datta studies how metal encapsulation changes bulk superconducting properties of niobium thin films used in qubits.

Films encapsulated with gold and palladium-gold are compared with bare niobium through magneto-optical imaging, magnetization. Related measurements, testing whether a strategy that mitigates surface oxides and absorbed hydrogen also alters macroscopic action.  Quantum hardware teams get a comprehensive check on encapsulation: a proven surface fix, examined for bulk side effects.
arxiv-2602-07817:
Adaptive mesh refinement saves compute by refining only where a simulation needs detail, but repeated interpolation can slowly break conservation laws. Kumar Saurabh and four co-authors design a field-conserving coarsening operator for massively parallel octree meshes that fixes the lossy step when fine cells merge back into coarse ones.

Their method first computes conserving values at quadrature points, then recovers coarse nodal values through a mass-matrix projection that also controls error. Tests on mass-conserving phase-field models, including Cahn-Hilliard systems, confirm the approach. Long-running simulations in fluids and materials science gain accuracy that survives many refinement cycles instead of drifting away.
arxiv-2602-08017:
At CMS, the high-level trigger must decide in real time which collisions to keep, and b-jets, jets from bottom quarks, are central to many searches. Uttiya Sarkar reports the commissioning and performance evaluation of b-jet triggers using proton-proton data from Run 3, collected between 2022 and 2024.

The study covers algorithm optimization, efficiency measurements, and comparisons with offline reconstruction, all while holding the trigger output to a few kilohertz. The results clarify how well the current selection strategy works and where refinements could help future data-taking. Trigger and heavy-flavor physicists get a focused performance record for a critical piece of CMS data-taking.
arxiv-2602-08117:
After a disaster, rapid building-damage maps from satellites guide rescue and recovery, but training data are noisy and severely imbalanced across damage classes. Smriti Siva and Jan Cross-Zamirski evaluate vision transformers on the xBD benchmark, focusing on how models distinguish damage types under those hostile conditions.

They test DINOv2-small and DeiT for multi-class damage classification, with a patch-based preprocessing pipeline that isolates structural traits and cuts background noise, plus frozen-head fine-tuning to keep compute manageable. Results is reported across accuracy, fine, recall, and macro-averaged F1. Disaster-response teams gain usable evidence about which transformer setups survive label noise and imbalance when maps matter most.
arxiv-2602-08417:
Robots that localize with LiDAR need maps that are small enough to store yet rich enough to trust, especially when views are partial or blocked. Wentao Zhao and six co-authors present Graph-Loc, a tracker that matches scans against compact point-line map priors. Their arXiv paper targets long-term autonomy under occlusion and low observability.

Each scan becomes a sparse graph of points and lines, matched to a visible map subgraph through unbalanced optimal transport, which tolerates missing and spurious structure. When constraints run weak in some direction, updates along that direction wait until evidence returns. Tests on public benchmarks, stress cases, and real deployments show stable tracking from kilobyte-scale priors. Readers get a robust recipe for localization in messy, changing scenes.
arxiv-2602-08617:
Scaling federated learning to billion-parameter models forces a painful trade among privacy, scalability, and utility. Dario Fenoglio and five co-authors introduce ERIS, a frame built on federated shard aggregation. Their arXiv paper splits each client update into separate shards that are combined across several client-side aggregators.

Sharding removes the central aggregation bottleneck, limits what any single observer can see, and preserves the central update after the shards are put back together. Optional distributed shifted compression cuts payloads and exposed coordinates further. Theory shows convergence is preserved and leakage is bounded by the visible share, shrinking with more aggregators. Tests match FedAvg utility while cutting bottlenecks and resisting inference attacks. Readers get a cryptography-light path to large-scale federated learning.
arxiv-2602-08717:
Identifying body regions in CT and MR scans usually depends on unreliable DICOM metadata, and supervised models struggle in new settings. Farnaz Khun Jush and three co-authors test whether zero-shot detection works using knowledge in large pretrained foundation models. Their arXiv paper evaluates three training-free pipelines on 887 varied scans with verified labels.

A segmentation-driven rule-based system performs best, with weighted F1 scores of 0.947 on CT and 0.914 on MR, robust across modalities and atypical coverage. A multimodal language model guided by radiologist rules competes in distinctive regions, while a segmentation-aware variant reveals fundamental limits. Readers get a practical route to region detection without retraining.
arxiv-2602-08817:
Running a large language model takes a lot of power, and Chenyu Wang and four co-authors look for savings in brain-like hardware. Spiking neural networks send short pulses instead of steady numbers, so they use far less energy. But turning a standard network into a spiking one usually costs accuracy or adds delay.

Their system, Kirin, mixes the two styles: small values become spikes, while the rest stay as plain integers. A silence threshold times each spike so the result matches the original model exactly. Under a compact W4A4 and 8-bit setup, Kirin nears full-precision accuracy while cutting energy use.
arxiv-2602-09017:
Robot policies usually take language orders, but words are too vague to guide a hand. Zichen Jeff Cui and eighteen co-authors replace language conditioning with contact points in space: where the robot should touch, and how. Their Contact-Anchored Policies come as a library of modular utility models, not one giant generalist, enabling a real-to-sim refinement loop.

A lightweight simulator, EgoGym, exposes failures quickly before real-world trials. With only 23 hours of demonstrations, the policies generalize to new environments and robot bodies on three core manipulation skills, beating leading vision-language-action models by 56 percent in zero-shot tests. Checkpoints, code, hardware, and data are all promised open.
arxiv-2602-09217:
Chiara M. F. Mingarelli traces a gravitational-wave background that intermediate-mass black holes in active galactic nucleus disks would create as they spiral into central supermassive black holes. Treating the disk channel as a mass-flow pipeline from the stellar-mass population seen by LIGO, Virgo, and KAGRA up to the supermassive reservoir, she anchors the estimate. It rests on observed merger rates and cosmic black-hole mass density.

For fiducial parameters matching the fourth transient catalog, the background's characteristic strain reaches about 1.2 times ten to the minus twenty-one at 3 millihertz. That sits below the Galactic white-dwarf foreground and the stellar-mass inspiral background, but its non-Gaussian statistics and higher frequency cutoff set it apart. Decihertz detectors could measure it cleanly, constraining how efficiently disks process black holes.
arxiv-2602-09617:
Contact-rich robot touch work demands sensing of time touch feedback, subtle surface bends, and force moves, yet tactile sets and models mostly capture static object traits like stuff. Ruoxuan Feng and eight co-authors offer a ladder of dynamic sensing skills to guide data pool and model design in their 2026 paper. Their dataset, ToucHD, spans tactile atomic actions, real-world touch work, and touch-force paired data at large scale.

Beyond scale, ToucHD plainly supports layered sensing from the data side. Built on it, AnyTouch 2 learns general pictures for diverse optical tactile sensors, joining object-level grasp with fine-grained, force-aware dynamic sensing. The design tracks pixel-level and action-specific bends across frames while modeling physics force moves. Tests across static traits, dynamic marks, and real touch-work tiers show steady strong scores across sensors and tasks.
arxiv-2602-09717:
Spiking neural nets are studied as energy-saving alternatives to convolutional nets, mainly for edge intelligence. Radib Bin Kabir and four co-authors note that prior work stresses large-scale models, leaving light convolutional-to-spiking pipelines underexplored. Their 2026 paper gives the first full benchmark of light spiking nets converted from compact convolutional designs. Activations use leaky-integrate-and-fire neurons trained by surrogate gradient descent in one setup.

Spiking variants of ShuffleNet, SqueezeNet, MnasNet, and MixNet are tested on three image sets for accuracy, F1-score, parameter count, complexity, and energy use. Spiking nets reach nearly sixteen times higher energy efficiency than convolutional rivals while keeping rival accuracy. The SqueezeNet variant leads other light spiking models. Pruning whole redundant modules yields a pruned design improving accuracy and cutting parameters, nearly matching convolutional SqueezeNet accuracy with energy use down near nine-tenths.
arxiv-2602-09817:
Khang Ly and four co-authors offer AnalyticsGPT, a plain fast language model workflow for science-metric question asking, in their 2026 paper. This rare task covers meta-science questions about the science of science. Against old science question asking based on papers, the task poses planning-phase tests. Named-entity spotting of school items and multi-faceted data finding with science-metric indices such as impact factors are needed.

Language models, beyond their power for old language work, show great promise for task splitting, planning, and thought. The paper tests their use for science-metric question asking through an end-to-end system. A stepwise workflow joins boosted writing and agentic concepts, plus joining found data into tidy, set high-level studies. Finding draws on a private research scores checks platform. Tests consult seasoned subject matter experts and language-model judges. Bare code and prompts are shared.
arxiv-2602-09917:
Light data from the Cosmic Origins Spectrograph reaches its users only after a pipeline called CalCOS calibrates the raw photon events. A 2026 report led by Nick Indriolo, with ten co-authors, sums up a large repair job behind that pipeline. In 2024, three early corrections to far-ultraviolet data were improved, shifting photon events into a corrected frame.

Because later calibration steps are defined in that corrected frame, every downstream reference file had to be rebuilt. The team produced new versions of fifty-six files covering six lifetime positions of the instrument. The payoff is better wavelength and flux calibration for far-ultraviolet spectra, sharpening the measurements drawn from the instrument.
arxiv-2602-10117:
Language models often explain themselves with plausible reasoning traces that hide the biases actually driving their choices. A 2026 paper led by Iván Arcuschin, with three co-authors, introduces a fully automated, black-box system for finding such hidden biases. Given a task data set, the system uses model raters to propose candidate bias concepts, then tests each on growing samples with positive and negative versions.

A concept counts as an unverbalized bias when it shifts performance a lot yet never appears as justification in the model's reasoning traces. Across seven models and three decision settings, hiring, loan approval, and university admissions, the system found previously unknown biases and confirmed hand-found ones, including gender, race, religion, and ethnicity.
arxiv-2602-10217:
Machine unlearning asks a generative model to forget set data, but standard classifier guidance can fail when the forget set is sharp and narrow. A 2026 paper led by Jacob L. Block, with three co-authors, reframes unlearning as estimating a density ratio to a goal spread instead of supervised fine-tuning. The team offers Temper-Then-Tilt Unlearning, which freezes the base model and runs a two-step inference routine.

First, tempering flattens high-confidence spikes in the base spread. Then, tilting with a light classifier trained to split retain from forget samples reshapes the tempered spread. Theory links classifier risk to unlearning error with finite-sample guarantees, proving tempering needed for narrow spreads. On the TOFU benchmark, the tool improves forget quality and generative utility while training only a fraction of parameters.
arxiv-2602-10717:
Songen Gu and four co-authors give robots video imagination for manipulation in a 2026 paper. Manipulation demands anticipating how the setting responds to actions, yet most systems lack that foresight, producing errors and inefficiency. Vision-language models guide at a high level but cannot forecast future states, while current world models predict short horizons or inconsistent frames.

Their system selects and adapts a robust video making model for steady future prediction. It distills that model adversarially for fast few-step making. An action model then trains on generated videos plus real views to correct spatial errors. Tests show temporally coherent, spatially consistent predictions that improve manipulation. The system is summarized as say, dream, and act: language instructs, video imagines, action executes.
arxiv-2602-10817:
Naoki Masuda offers a way to detect and forecast tipping points from spread alone in a 2026 paper. Anticipating bifurcations in complex systems is a basic challenge. Older early warning signals based on key slowing down, like rising spread, indicate trouble unreliably and rarely forecast timing.

His system, TIPMOC, exploits the math trait that spread diverges with a characteristic power-law form near codimension-one bifurcations. By sequentially monitoring spread as a control parameter changes, the method statistically adjudicates between linear and power-law divergence at each step. When power-law evidence wins, it forecasts the bifurcation's future place. The approach turns a single noisy statistic into a principled early warning system.
arxiv-2602-11217:
What survives the jump from pretraining to fine-tuning? Simin Fan and five co-authors study knowledge transfer across that edge through four questions about scores, confidence, benchmarks, and scale. They apply link protocols to scores and confidence across data mixes and model sizes.

Transfer trust varies sharply by capability, benchmark, and scale. Scores and confidence sometimes move in opposite ways as models grow, so a benchmark that predicts well at one scale may fail at another. The authors draw practical lessons for benchmark choice, data curation, and fast growth. The paper treats transfer as a measurable, uneven process, not a given.
arxiv-2602-11317:
Tiny iron grains shape how moon dust looks and ages. Ziyu Huang and Masatoshi Hirabayashi use atomistic impact models to compare two origins for nanophase iron: formation in place from native minerals, and delivery by exotic micrometeoroids. Recent mineral evidence suggests the exotic route supplies a large share.

Simulations show distinct fingerprints. In-place iron forms diffusely and radially around impact sites, while exotic iron survives in asymmetric, momentum-aligned clusters. Those spatial signatures could diagnose origin in returned lunar soils. Matching Chang'e-5 sights, exotic production proves large in iron-poor highlands. The findings urge care when reading space weathering and remote-sensing data for the Moon and other airless bodies.
arxiv-2602-11417:
Sharing data without payments invites free-riding, yet payments are often infeasible. Rashida Hakim and two co-authors propose a simple fair-exchange contract for data sharing among strategic agents. For each pair, each agent receives exactly as many points as it provides, equal to the smaller of the two collection levels.

The induced game proves supermodular under a strategy-space transformation, yielding pure Nash equilibria that form a lattice and compute in quadratic time. The maximal balance is truthfully implementable under natural enforcement and globally Pareto-optimal. A graph-restricted variant loses supermodularity but still yields efficiently computable equilibria and Pareto-optimal outcomes. Fair exchange thus offers a tractable, incentive-aligned mechanism without money.
arxiv-2602-11517:
Autonomous shuttles drive differently from ordinary autonomous vehicles, yet few car-following models are tuned for them. Renan Favero and Lily Elefteriadou calibrate a diverse set spanning eight machine learning recipes and two physics-based models on real shuttle path data. Machine learning had not yet been applied to shuttle paths.

They also offer a multi-criteria tests frame joining forecast scores, path balance, and numerical similarity, replacing disparate metrics that hindered match. A tuned gradient boosting model performs best overall. Sequential models capture long-term positional balance but respond less to short-term motion, while traditional and kernel methods trail most machine learning models on scores and balance.
arxiv-2602-11817:
Variational inequalities in Hilbert space model equilibria and optimization problems, but solving their generalized inverse mixed form demands methods with strong guarantees. Nam Van Tran proposes and studies a third-order dynamical system for the task. Under suitable smoothness assumptions, the paths produced by the system exist and are unique. Under strong monotonicity and Lipschitz smoothness, they converge exponentially fast to the unique answer.

The paper also derives an explicit discrete version of the system, yielding a forward-backward scheme with double inertial effects. Its steps converge at a linear rate to the unique answer. Together, the continuous system and its discrete version give both theory and a practical method for a hard class of inequality problems.
arxiv-2602-11917:
Mining trading signals through alpha factors tests quant finance. Current auto methods follow two patterns: decoupled making, treating finds as lone events, and stepwise change, stressing local parent-child tweaks. Both lack a global view, treating factor pools as loose sets or chains, leading to repeat search and limited variety. Taian Guo and eight co-authors reframe alpha mining as travel of a directed acyclic graph.

With factors as nodes and change links as edges, AlphaPROBE treats the factor pool as a live web. Two parts drive it. A Bayesian retriever balances use and search with a belief model. A graph-aware maker uses the full family trace of factors to produce context-aware, fresh outputs. Tests on three major Chinese stock datasets against eight rivals show enhanced forecast scores, return steadiness, and training speed. Using global change shape, the authors argue, is key for lean, robust alpha finding.
arxiv-2602-12017:
Free-floating planets and interstellar objects drift through a sea of stars, and their velocities evolve by gravitational scattering. Jun Yan Lau and one co-author show that equilibrium, where drag friction balances stochastic acceleration, sits above the standard energy-sharing value. It grows only slowly with the mass ratio, as the square root of its logarithm. Reaching that balance takes far too long, however.

Slow floaters, moving no faster than the stellar speed spread, accelerate whatever their mass, doubling their speeds within a few relaxation times. Floaters born with their parent stars' Maxwellian distribution thus develop distinctly non-standard spreads on a settling timescale. Since the Galactic disk relaxes more slowly than it ages, the motions of low-mass floaters in the disk may still carry signatures of their parent stars and exit history.
arxiv-2602-12517:
Mean field games plus RL have spawned many methods for large multi-agent systems, yet testing remains split across bespoke, alone, often simple settings. Lorenzo Magnino led this work with four co-authors, giving Bench-MFG, a full benchmark suite for steady mean field games in discrete time and discrete space. That split makes it hard to judge strength, transfer, and failure modes of new methods.

The suite gives a map from no-play and steady games to possible and motion-coupled games, with sample settings for each. MF-Garnets, a method for making random mean field game cases, enables strict stats testing. A variety of learning methods are tested, including a novel black-box approach, MF-PSO, for loss cutting. Wide results lead to rules for shared future test checks, with code shared online.
arxiv-2602-12717:
Intensity interferometry measures light by comparing flickers across telescopes, a technique that new technology has made far more powerful. Robin Kaiser and colleagues lay out the science it could now unlock in a white paper for the European Southern Observatory. First, its sharp angular vision can size distant supernovae and quasars, and paired with a local physical scale, that gives distances and a new route to the Universe's expansion rate.

Second, tiny dark matter clumps could betray themselves through the small lensing wobbles they imprint on light paths. Third, the method reads second-order coherence of starlight directly, opening a window onto genuinely quantum features of light from space. The paper frames these as near-term chances created by recent technical gains, spanning cosmology, fundamental physics, and quantum optics.
arxiv-2602-12817:
Making a Higgs boson with a top-antitop pair is a key LHC process, and its total rate tests the standard model at high sharpness. Anna Kulesza reports the most exact forecasts to date, mixing next-to-next-to-leading order quantum chromodynamics fixes, with a rough two-loop piece, plus soft-gluon summing at next-to-next-to-leading log level.

The summing is done via two routes, soft-collinear theory and direct QCD, and full next-to-leading order electroweak fixes are added. Match between the two routes builds trust in the numbers. For lab teams matching measured rates against theory, these forecasts set the current bar for top-Higgs linked making.
arxiv-2602-13017:
Bio-inspired neural models come in many flavours, and telling them apart structurally and functionally is hard. Mónika Farsang and Radu Grosu present a unified system for comparing such models, showing that liquid-capacitance-extended models stay clear even in dense, all-to-all looping policies. Adding chemical synapses lifts interpretability further, and combining chemical synapses with synaptic activation gives the most close and clear looping models in their tests.

Testing uses the demanding lane-keeping driving task. Metrics include checks loss weighted by turns, neural activity while driving, activity-trajectory link, and saliency maps with their toughness. The system thus gives researchers a shared lens for bio-inspired design: interpretability need not be sacrificed for closeness, and given mechanisms can be credited with given gains.
arxiv-2602-13417:
Rings without a unit element pose a wrinkle for classical algebra. Many standard results assume a one, and removing it breaks familiar arguments. This paper builds a theory of separable ring extensions and separable functors for such nonunital rings. It works in the setting of firm modules, where the module structure behaves well despite the missing unit.

The theory yields nonunital analogues of classical results on functorial separability and semisimplicity, extending the toolkit to a wider class of rings. As an application, the authors obtain a locally unital version of Maschke's theorem for group rings, a classic result on when group representations split nicely. Patrik Lundström is the sole author.
arxiv-2602-13617: Let theta(n) count the permutations of the numbers 1 through n with no three-term arithmetic progression. That means no three entries form an arithmetic progression. Boon Suan Ho proves that the nth root of theta(n) has no limit as n grows. So 3AP-free permutations have no single exponential growth rate. Their growth cannot be summed up by one constant base raised to n.
arxiv-2602-13817:
Peer review is a high stakes gate for research, yet adding machine help to it divides opinion. Some hope it can ease reviewer load and lift quality, while others fear harm to fairness, trust, and who answers for a decision. At ICLR 2025, reviewers were given an official tool that offered comments after they had written their own reviews.

The authors learned how reviewers used the tool through surveys and talks with reviewers, asking about ease of use and felt effect. What they found mixed promise with strain, in the first close look at such a tool inside a live review round. Their design ideas aim to raise review quality while keeping human skill, choice, and duty at the centre. Shiping Chen leads the work with three co-authors.
arxiv-2602-14417: Miguel Cárdenas, writing alone, offers a wider snowplow model for Z-pinch tests. It counts partial particle entrainment and current loss during contraction. The paper applies the wider methods to a set case. That gives a truer snowplow picture for Z-pinch motion and a base for later Z-pinch work.
arxiv-2602-14517:
Sukumar Kishanthan and three co-authors evaluate a 2026 arXiv question: how well do language models tutor math in low-resource languages? Models show strong math reasoning in English and increasingly serve as tutoring tools, yet reliability for students in non-English languages, especially low-resource ones, remains poorly understood. The study examines Sinhala and Tamil, common tongues in South Asian schools yet thinly covered in AI research.

Six kinds of math problems were used, ranging from plain sums to hard problems where units clash or must be tuned. To dodge translation bias, each problem was written fresh in Sinhala and Tamil by mother-tongue speakers, all strong in math, with the English versions by fluent speakers. Plain sums carried across languages well, while harder thought showed big gaps, marking where multi-language tutoring still falls short.
arxiv-2602-15017:
Szendroi studies a flat degeneration of the classical coinvariant algebra. This is a bigraded Artinian Gorenstein algebra tied to the Segre embedding of the n-fold product of the projective line with itself. Its Frobenius character is found through a refined Lusztig-Stanley formula for the old algebra.

Young invariants in the new algebra are tied to rings of general Segre products of projective spaces. Their Hilbert polynomials are expressed through major-descent generating functions of words in multisets. Links to the diagonal case, quantum cohomology readings, and Garsia-Stanton-style bases are also explored.
arxiv-2602-15117:
Iwai and colleagues close the viable window for MeV-scale QCD axions using kaon decays. A recent proposal kept alive an axion coupling to up quarks, down quarks, and electrons at a mass near 10 MeV. The team reexamines that proposal with new bounds from kaon decays, analyzing the KTeV measurement in detail and reinterpreting decay measurements from E949 and NA62.

Those experiments constrain both the diphoton decay mode and the effectively invisible decay mode of the axion. Combined with prior bounds, the viable window is excluded, mainly by the KTeV bound. Chiral Lagrangian uncertainties are examined as well. The scenario stays excluded even after accounting for them, except for a tiny parameter region. There, higher-order corrections must finely cancel the leading term, suppressing the branching ratio by three orders of magnitude.
arxiv-2602-15317:
Duprey and Bobashev provide a full guide to tuning NetLogo, a widely used tool for agent-based models, for hosting large-scale models on Amazon Web Services and other clouds. Growing size of agent-based models needs lean compute plans to meet growing need for compute power and RAM. The guide lists tips in RAM handling, Java flags, BehaviorSpace runs, and AWS box picks.

By using these tweaks and picking right AWS boxes, the team got a 32 percent cut in compute costs and better speed calm. Through side-by-side study of NetLogo runs on varied AWS boxes using the wolf-sheep hunt model, they show the speed wins won through these tweaks.
arxiv-2602-15517:
Henríquez and Schlottbom devise a lean model for wave problems with zero start state and a source that pairs a Ricker wavelet in time with a spatial profile. Such problems cover both acoustic and elastic wave equations, and they matter for seismic modelling. Working in the Laplace domain, the authors build reduced bases that track the time-domain solution with exponential accuracy.

They prove error bounds that stay explicit and robust as the wavelet shape and width vary, and they pin down a hard accuracy floor set by the wavelet value at time zero. Crucially, the bound does not hinge on the fine Galerkin grid used underneath, which yields clear, computable rules for when exponential convergence should show up. Seismic modellers gain a reduced model with honest error control.
arxiv-2602-15717:
Barbero Lucas and colleagues ask whether a known implication for Artin-Schreier curves runs in reverse. It is known that, for curves X and Y of a special form over the field with p elements, if n divides m, then a nonconstant morphism from X to Y exists. Here X is defined by y to the p plus c y equals x to the m, and Y by the same form with x to the n. The question is whether a morphism forces n to divide m.

The paper answers yes under certain hypotheses for the case m equals p to the k plus one and n equals p to the l plus one. Both Galois and non-Galois morphisms are treated. The result gives a partial converse to a classical construction, pinning down when maps between these curves can exist at all.
arxiv-2602-15817:
So and colleagues address a mismatch between deep reinforcement learning and reachability problems. Reachability aims to enlarge the collection of states where a system can stay safe for good. Reinforcement learning instead optimises expected returns over a user-specified distribution. That mismatch can yield policies that fail on low-probability states still inside the safe set. A natural alternative frames the problem as robust optimisation over initial conditions. But whether that problem has a solution depends on feasibility of the specified set, unknown in advance.

Their Feasibility-Guided Exploration method, or FGE, identifies a group of feasible initial conditions that admit a safe policy. It also learns a policy solving reachability over that set. Tests show FGE learning policies that cover over 50 percent more ground than the best existing method on hard initial conditions. The tasks run across the MuJoCo simulator and the Kinetix simulator, using pixel observations.
arxiv-2602-15917:
Singh and colleagues built ROIX-Comp, a region-of-interest extraction frame that trims X-ray computed tomography data while keeping key traits. In high-performance computing sites, above all synchrotron labs, vast X-ray image sets are made. Their size strains storage and transfer, and curbs real-time work and workflow pace.

ROIX-Comp keeps only the essential parts of each scan. At pre-processing, error-bounded quantisation shrinks the data load and lifts compute pace. At compression, object extraction joins several top lossless and lossy compressors, giving far stronger compression. Tested on seven X-CT data sets, the frame lifts the relative compression ratio by 12 point 34 times over standard compression, while keeping the traits downstream tasks need.
arxiv-2602-16117:
Vicente Chomali-Castro leads a team of four researchers who solve relativistic BDNK diffusion with physics-informed neural networks. They recast the BDNK diffusion equation in flux-conservative form and solve it in one space plus one time dimension. Two solvers are compared: a second-order Kurganov-Tadmor finite volume scheme and neural network solvers. Their SA-PINN-ACTO framework pairs a self-adaptive network technique with exact enforcement of initial and periodic boundary conditions through an algebraic transform of the raw network output.

That design lets the network focus solely on shrinking the equation residual. Tests cover smooth and jagged initial data, plain and evolving backgrounds, and two characteristic speeds. The neural method matches the converged finite volume solutions for smooth profiles. For jagged profiles errors grow, a known limit near sharp gradients. The comparison shows where neural solvers can stand in for classical schemes.
arxiv-2602-16317:
Maksim Elistratov and coauthors present CADEvolve, a pipeline and data set for creating realistic computer-aided design models via program evolution. Computer-aided design delivers rapid, editable modeling, yet progress is bottlenecked by data. Public corpora mostly contain sketch-extrude sequences, lacking complex operations and design intent. Attempts to bypass data scarcity with frozen vision-language models often yield simple or invalid programs.

CADEvolve starts from simple primitives and, via vision-language-model-guided edits and validations, incrementally grows programs toward industrial-grade complexity. The result is thousands of complex parts expressed as executable CadQuery parametric generators. After post-processing and augmentation, the team obtains a unified data set of over a million scripts paired with rendered geometry. A vision-language model fine-tuned on CADEvolve achieves state-of-the-art results on the Image2CAD task across DeepCAD, Fusion 360, and MCB benchmarks.
arxiv-2602-16417:
Bendegúz Sulyok, Sámuel G. Balogh, and Gergely Palla study Drosophila geometry. The recent reconstruction gives a large network. The authors examine its geometry with embedding techniques applied to the graph of synaptic connections. Earlier analysis revealed an inhomogeneous degree spread, so they first use a hyperbolic embedding as points in hyperbolic space.

Hyperbolic methods exploit the exponentially growing volume of hyperbolic space with distance from the origin, allowing uniform node distribution in small-world networks. By multiple quality metrics, the network structure is captured by the embedding, fitting it better than original neuron coordinates in Euclidean space. The authors also apply Euclidean Node2vec, whose dimension can be set freely. In three dimensions that embedding scores lower than original coordinates, but scores improve with dimension, passing that level near sixteen and peaking at sixty-four. Since embeddings feed downstream tasks, the results offer new perspectives on this network.
arxiv-2602-16517:
Jean-Christophe Mourrat, writing alone, gives a counterexample: a function meeting a two-sided Polyak-Lojasiewicz condition. Its gradient descent-ascent flow fails to converge to the saddle point, circling it instead of settling there.

The example can even be made strongly convex in one variable while meeting the PL condition in the other variable. The paper thus shows that PL conditions, even with strong convexity in one variable, do not guarantee convergence of gradient descent-ascent dynamics. That is a caution for readers who might assume such conditions settle the question of convergence.
arxiv-2602-16617:
Hiroki Uratani and Hirofumi Sato study exciton transfer between the two ligands of a bis(dipyrrinato)zinc complex. Transfer depends on excitonic coupling, set by the relative orientation of the chromophores. Coupling is often treated as static, but structural motion can make it time-dependent, and that effect was scarcely understood. The authors combine non-adiabatic molecular dynamics, exciton density analysis, and a simple two-state model.

A reaction coordinate is recovered by regression on diabatic energy gaps and atomic displacements. The results suggest that dynamical angular fluctuation between the ligands breaks symmetry and incidentally raises coupling, speeding transfer between them. Photochemists get a concrete mechanism showing that molecular wobble can accelerate energy transfer rather than merely blur it.
arxiv-2602-16817:
Debabrata Mondal, Lea Santos, and S. Sinha show that loss can serve as a tool in quantum dynamics, not just a foe. Loss tends to bring decoherence and one-way change, yet in a lab-ready Bose-Josephson junction with two bosonic kinds, it reshapes motion in striking ways. Tuned values pick among synced phase-locked swings, short-lived chaos with long-time coherence regained, and steady chaos.

At weak links, the two parts sync despite loss, showing long-lived coherent swings akin to a boundary time crystal. Stronger links drive a loss-led shift into a self-trapped zone with chaotic motion. Loss sets chaos lifetime and enables coherence regained at long times, and a controlled tilt turns short-lived chaos into steady chaos. Standard spectral checks fail to split the two chaotic zones, showing spectra mainly track short-time instability.
arxiv-2602-17117:
Yicheng Cao led a six-author team coupling realistic 3D rendering with stable physics simulation. Current reconstruction-based simulators update step by step in explicit fashion, which makes them sensitive to step size and prone to fast accuracy loss for stiff materials or near-static motion. The paper introduces i-PhysGaussian, which pairs 3D Gaussian Splatting with an implicit Material Point Method integrator.

Instead of marching forward step by step, the method finds each end-of-step state by minimizing a momentum-balance residual through implicit Newton-type optimization with a GMRES solver. That design cuts time-step sensitivity and keeps the physics consistent. Tests showed stability at far larger time steps than explicit baselines, with structure and smooth motion kept even through complex shifts. The framework suits engineering risk work built on visual reconstructions.
arxiv-2602-17217:
Enrique Crespo-Fernandez led a four-author team teaching agents to build their own causal world models while they act. Navigating complex settings demands grasping the world's hidden logic, yet standard world models suffer from sample hunger, opacity, and poor scaling. The paper builds symbolic causal models fully online, weaving continuous learning and repair into the agent's decision loop.

Meta-Interpretive Learning plus predicate invention supplies meaningful, reusable abstractions, letting the agent grow a hierarchy of disentangled concepts from its own observations. A lifted inference approach then scales to domains with rich relational dynamics, where propositional methods explode combinatorially, while beating a standard neural baseline on sample efficiency by orders of magnitude. The result is a transparent, sample-thrifty route to causal world models.
arxiv-2602-17317:
Thomas Courant, writing alone, proves instability for two-pulse periodic waves in Hamiltonian partial differential equations. The setup covers quasilinear versions of the Korteweg-de Vries equation and spreading disturbances of the Euler equations for squeezable fluids, in Lagrangian or Eulerian frames. It includes fluid forms of the nonlinear Schrödinger systems. Each period carries two pulses, one tending to a bright soliton and one to a dark soliton, as waves lengthen.

For large enough periods, the author shows such waves fail the spectral test, using two routes. The first route expands the Hessian of the action sum at large scale and ends via prior work, for cases where both limiting lone waves are stable. The second route tracks spectrum convergence as period grows, handling cases where one end-state lone wave is unstable, via the approach of a rescaled Evans function for periods.
arxiv-2602-17417:
Maarten Derickx led a two-author paper giving practical algorithms for computing divisor class groups and gonalities of algebraic curves over finite fields. The approach achieves several orders of magnitude speedup over existing methods for sufficiently large genus or residue field. The key is a precomputation step involving power series expansions, enabling efficient amortized computation of large numbers of Riemann-Roch spaces.

The paper thus turns class group and gonality work from a slow, specialized chore into a routine fast calculation for large genus or residue field cases. Practitioners gain methods that handle many Riemann-Roch spaces efficiently through one shared pre-step, rather than paying full cost per space.
arxiv-2602-17517:
Hanyuan Zhang led a nine-author team on depth-augmented, finite-element-free 3D-2D liver registration for laparoscopic liver augmented reality. Laparoscopic liver AR guidance needs exact matching of preoperative models to live video, despite partial views and tissue shift. Older methods use contour-based rigid starts and finite-element models. The team offers a depth-augmented, finite-element-free pipeline joining rigid starts with patient-specific non-rigid refinement.

Rigid matching adapts RefineNet from FoundationPose to laparoscopic liver scenes, using contour maps and depth to refine pose. Deformable matching uses a statistical deformation model, patient-specific, from non-rigid ICP correspondences, tuning pose and shape. On a public liver set, mean target registration error is fourteen point seven three millimetres under manual contours. Depth beats contour-only inputs, while good surface matching need not cut localization error. On an outside set without ground truth, overlays look plausible.
arxiv-2602-17917:
David I. Spivak models systems with interfaces through polynomial functors: each polynomial lists outputs a system can produce and, for each output, inputs it accepts. An earlier two-level system of dynamic organizations let interaction patterns evolve, yet each system's ports stayed fixed. In many real systems, outputs and inputs reshape the ports themselves: a cell gaining receptors, a sensor losing a channel, a network growing output resolution during training.

Spivak introduces polynomial trees, self-feeding trees whose nodes carry polynomials, where each round of output and input picks a child tree, hence the next ports. He builds a tensor-closed frame of polynomial trees with self-feeding maps, tensor product and internal hom, plus a broader two-level system on the earlier one. Constant trees, whose interfaces never change, embed the old system. He closes by sketching growing generative adversarial networks whose image ports grow with gradient feedback.
arxiv-2602-18217:
Kohei Kajikawa and two co-authors propose a new way to measure the memory load of reading sentences. Their 2026 paper notes that real-time reading forces listeners to hold context in mind to guess what comes next. Older measures score that load with fixed, symbolic grammar rules that give every prediction the same discrete cost.

The new measure counts, in information terms, how much past words reveal about future context under uncertainty. It is continuous, chance-based, theory-neutral, and can be read off pretrained language models. Three English tests back it: it recovers known asymmetries in nested clauses, tracks a grammar-based cost in an annotated corpus, and predicts reading-time variation in two large natural datasets beyond standard predictors. The code is public for reuse.
arxiv-2602-18317:
Édouard Bonnet and four co-authors give a near-efficient approximation scheme for maximum weight independent sets in a restricted graph family. Their 2026 paper treats graphs with only a bounded number of pairwise disjoint, non-adjacent long induced cycles. For every fixed pair of bounds, the team proves a quasipolynomial-time approximation scheme for the weighted independent set problem.

Combined with known results, the scheme also finds largest induced subgraphs of bounded treewidth with any hereditary property expressible in counting monadic second-order logic, for these same graph classes. The work advances toward a conjecture of Gartland and Lokshtanov, which claims polynomial-time algorithms for such problems in graphs excluding any planar graph as an induced minor. That conjecture remains famously open, confirmed only in very restricted cases.
arxiv-2602-18417:
Joshua Nunley derives recurrent and transformer designs from subgroup shapes. His 2026 paper builds sequence models whose hidden states live on closed subgroups of the unitary group, from a minimal set of axioms. Subgroup choice acts as a drop-in stand-in for state space, tangent projection, and the update rule, yielding both recurrent and transformer templates from one shared skeleton.

Specializing to the orthogonal group, Nunley tests orthogonal-state recurrent and transformer nets on Tiny Shakespeare and Penn Treebank with matched sizes. A linear-mixing extension in tangent space, general across subgroup choices, improves finite-budget scores in the orthogonal experiments. The work offers a clean route from symmetry choices to sequence designs.
arxiv-2602-18517:
Arya D. Keni and eight co-authors grow ultra-thin light-emitting crystals for photonic chips. Their 2026 paper notes organic molecules in an organic matrix show lifetime-limited optical coherence and bright emission below three kelvin. The team presents a simple vapor-phase growth method for optically thin DBT-doped anthracene crystals fit for integrated nanophotonics.

The crystals are about two hundred nanometers thick with sub-nanometer roughness and tunable width up to two hundred micrometers. Molecular transitions stay narrow and stable, with broadening below one hundred gigahertz, comparable to DBT in bulk anthracene. Dopant density can be tuned up to several hundred molecules per square micrometer, placing emitters near nanophotonic structures. The team shows the crystals can be placed precisely onto integrated photonic devices with molecular dipoles aligned to the optical mode. The approach opens a path to on-chip single-photon sources and collective emitter effects.
arxiv-2602-18717:
Spotting what changed between two satellite images is a core remote sensing task, and recent state space models have set a strong bar. Yufan Wang, with two co-authors, tests whether modern convolutional and attention designs can match them in 2026, with NeXt2Former-CD, an end-to-end change detection framework.

A Siamese ConvNeXt encoder started from DINOv3 weights feeds a deformable attention module that fuses the two time points, followed by a Mask2Former decoder. The design aims to tolerate small misalignments, tiny spatial shifts, and ambiguous meaning in the image pair. On three standard datasets it beats recent Mamba-based baselines on both F1 score and overlap, while keeping inference speed comparable despite a larger model.
arxiv-2602-18817:
A robot that must place a shoe needs to know a toe from a heel. Yet purely geometric policies often lack that part-level meaning. Chongyang Xu, with five co-authors, presents HeRO in 2026. It is a diffusion-based policy that couples geometry with semantics through hierarchical semantic fields for pose-aware object manipulation.

Dense semantics lifting fuses fine-grained, geometry-sensitive features from DINOv2 with smooth, globally coherent correspondences from Stable Diffusion. That gives features that are both detailed and spatially consistent. Those features are split into a global field and local fields. A hierarchical conditioning module feeds both to the generative denoiser through a permutation-invariant design, avoiding order bias. Tests show a new state of the art, with clear gains on dual-shoe placement and across six challenging pose-aware tasks.
arxiv-2602-19017:
Training neural networks is usually analysed in a model where real numbers cost nothing. In that Real-RAM setting, even simple training is existentially real-complete, harder than NP. Ilan Doron-Arad, with one co-author, asks in 2026 what changes under a bit-level model, where parameters and inputs are rational numbers with bounded bit-lengths.

A dichotomy governed by activation function emerges. For deep networks with any polynomial activation of degree at least two and rational coefficients, deciding bit-level empirical risk minimisation is counting-hard, harder than NP-complete. Determining the sign of a partial derivative is intractable, and deciding a gradient bit is counting-hard. That gives a complexity view of exploding and vanishing gradients. For piecewise-linear activations such as ReLU, by contrast, bit-level training lies in NP, specifically NP-complete, and backpropagation runs fast. Finite precision is thus fundamental to learnability.
arxiv-2602-19117:
Vision-language models think well from their own viewpoint, but falter from an object's viewpoint. Jaeyun Jang, with three co-authors, fixes that object-centred weakness in 2026 with SymPL, Symbolic Projective Layout. Self-centred thought comes naturally to these models. Object-centred thought demands inferring relations from inside the scene.

SymPL recasts object-centred questions into symbolic-layout forms. Four factors drive the switch. Projection, abstraction, bipartition, and localisation each play a role. Models handle the resulting structured forms far better. Tests show large gains on object-centred and self-centred tasks alike. Robustness improves under visual illusions and multi-view settings. Each component proves critical. Perspective-aware thought thus becomes tractable through symbol reformulation.
arxiv-2602-19317:
A personal answer should draw on a user's own history, not just match the question's words. Maryam Amirizaniani and two co-authors argue that most retrieval-augmented generation methods for personalized question answering stop at surface-level personalization, because they retrieve with the raw query alone. Their framework, PR2, short for Personalized Retrieval-Augmented Reasoning, weaves reasoning and retrieval together with reinforcement learning.

PR2 learns when to retrieve, what evidence to pull from a user profile, and how to fold it into intermediate reasoning steps. Training rewards reasoning paths that fit user-specific preferences and context signals. On the LaMP-QA benchmark with three large language models, it beat strong baselines by about 9 to 12 percent in relative terms. Readers get a recipe for deeper, multi-step personalization.
arxiv-2602-19717:
In several complex variables, an analytic disc is a holomorphic map of a disc into complex space. Stationary discs are those that meet a real surface in a special extremal way. A 2026 arXiv paper by Mohammad Tarek Al Masri and four co-authors studies discs of a generalized stationary kind. These discs attach to a surface whose defining geometry is degenerate in a precise sense.

Under suitable geometric assumptions on the surface, the authors show that the family of such discs forms a finite-dimensional real submanifold inside the Banach space of all analytic discs. That finding gives the family a clean, finite structure rather than an unruly infinite one. Readers get a rigorous footing for studying discs attached to degenerate surfaces, a setting where standard tools for non-degenerate cases do not apply.
arxiv-2602-19917:
Offline reinforcement learning trains from logged data rather than live interaction, but it suffers when the learned policy strays into regions the data never covered. A 2026 arXiv paper by Thanh Nguyen and four co-authors introduces a Q-network framework that tracks uncertainty, built on a rank-one multi-input multi-output design, to tame that extrapolation error.

Existing fixes penalize out-of-distribution values or constrain the policy to stay near the behaviour policy, but they can be overcautious, imprecise, or expensive. The new framework quantifies data uncertainty and folds it into training losses, aiming for a policy that maximizes a lower confidence bound on value. Its rank-one architecture matches an ensemble's uncertainty ability at nearly a single network's cost. Tests on the D4RL benchmark show leading performance with computational efficiency, balancing precision, speed, and memory.
arxiv-2602-20017:
Real-world tables are messy: schemas disagree, value formats vary, and relationships hide implicitly, degrading question answering. A 2026 arXiv paper by Gaurav Najpande and five co-authors proposes QuIeTT, a transform-first framework that cleans tables before any question arrives.

Existing methods normalize and restructure at query time, repeating work for every question and producing representations that fail on unseen queries. QuIeTT instead converts each raw table once into a single SQL-ready canonical form, under three constraints: no access to evaluation queries, preservation of information, and reuse of one table. A three-stage pipeline probes issues with synthetic queries, generates a plan, and executes it structurally. Tests on four benchmarks and five model families show steady gains over strong baselines. Gains are largest on a hand-labelled challenge set of structurally diverse unseen questions.
arxiv-2602-20117:
Reasoning models improve with reinforcement learning from verifiers. Writing a checker is often easier than annotating solutions. Yet most synthetic data methods stay centred on solutions, while verifier-based methods use a few hand-built rule-based environments. A 2026 arXiv paper by Andre He and six co-authors scales the verifier route with ReSyn, a pipeline that builds diverse reasoning environments, each with an example generator and a verifier.

The tasks span constraint satisfaction, algorithmic puzzles, and spatial reasoning. One test used a Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct model trained with reward-based learning on ReSyn data. It gains steadily across reasoning benchmarks, including math benchmarks outside the training domain. Its improvement on the challenging BBEH benchmark exceeds a quarter. Removal studies show checker-based supervision and greater task diversity each contribute greatly. Building reasoning environments at scale can strengthen thinking ability.
arxiv-2602-20217:
To speed up a language model, draft tokens with a cheap, shallow version of itself, then check them with the full model. Picking which layers to skip has relied on fixed rules that miss how costs shift as context grows. A 2026 arXiv paper by Seongjin Cha and four co-authors treats that choice as a packing problem: choose layers to maximize tokens gained per unit time. Their method, KnapSpec, needs no training.

Attention layers and MLP layers are handled apart, since their costs on hardware grow differently with context length. A parallel dynamic programming method then picks the best draft setup on the fly, adapting as the bottleneck moves. The paper also proves, with full rigor for the first time, that a measure of how alike two internal states are is a sound stand-in for acceptance rates. Tests use Qwen3 and Llama3 models.
arxiv-2602-20417:
Imaging with only a few detected photons is a basic challenge in computational imaging. Single-photon avalanche diode sensors promise quality where ordinary cameras fail, but their quanta frames hold only sparse, noisy, binary photon detections. Aryan Garg and two co-authors adapt large text-to-image latent diffusion models to this photon-limited world, handling Bernoulli photon statistics and combining latent-space restoration with burst-level spatio-temporal reasoning.

The method is tested on synthetic benchmarks and new real-world datasets, including the first color single-photon burst dataset and a demanding deforming-video benchmark. Across all settings it substantially improves perceptual quality over classical and modern learning-based baselines, staying photometrically faithful and perceptually pleasing even under fast motion. The work shows that large generative priors can serve extreme photon-limited sensing.
arxiv-2602-20517:
Human-AI teamwork needs agents that show human-like conduct and adapt as contexts change. Copying learning struggles with the range and non-memory-free nature of human conduct, and cannot steer conduct at use time. Rakshit Trivedi and two co-authors draw on the theory that inner speech guides action choice before action. Their setup, MIMIC, uses language as an internal form of conduct intent.

Vision-language models provide word support to train a gated variational net. That net makes inner speech from sights. A diffusion-based conduct cloning policy then acts, tuned to sights plus made inner speech. Tuning to conduct-set speech enables fine-grained steering at use time without training on extra demos. Tests on robotic handling and human-AI teamwork games show MIMIC greatly lifts conduct range and match to human demos.
arxiv-2602-20817:
The p-adic general linear group and its metaplectic covers carry Hecke algebras that standard p-adic methods struggle to describe. Valentin Buciumas and Chun-Ju Lai develop a new algebraic toolkit for them in this 2026 arXiv paper: quantum wreath products of skew polynomial type. Their framework gives clear descriptions of the pro-p Iwahori-Hecke algebra and its Gelfand-Graev modules, which had resisted direct treatment.

The paper introduces spherical and antispherical modules, plus Kashiwara-Miwa-Stern modules, for these quantum wreath products, and reads the p-adic Gelfand-Graev modules through them. As an application, the authors work out structure theory for the related pro-p Schur algebras, with an explicit basis and multiplication rules. They also give new algebraic proofs of several known results, including a basis theorem and the failure of the local Shimura correspondence at the pro-p level.
arxiv-2602-21317:
Language models are closing in on a single hive mind, falling into one variety of views that fresh thought and finding need. Guancheng Tu, Shiyang Zhang, Tianyu Zhang, Yi Zhang, and Diji Yang counter that fall in this 2026 arXiv paper with PRISM, many-sided thought through in-context structure model work. Use-time nurture means one-by-one knowledge paths: explore, take in, and express.

Dynamic on-the-fly knowledge graphs build the frame in a model-blind system. Three fresh-thought trials show state-of-the-art novelty with greatly wider spread variety. A rare-disease finding trial confirms the split is real: PRISM finds correct long-tail findings standard models miss. The work moves many-sided AI beyond single-block shared view toward varied mind views.
arxiv-2602-21417:
Cristian Cobeli and two co-authors build a statistical model for sequences tied to a bijective involution. Take a set with M elements and a map that pairs elements with each other and is its own inverse. The sequences studied are those whose second half mirrors the first half through that map.

When M is even, the authors prove a limit probability density exists for the count k of appearances of set elements in such sequences. The number of fixed points of the map shapes that density. It splits into two pieces with complementary factors, and the smaller piece appears only when k is even. Applied to modular-style sequences, the model yields a threshold beyond which almost all sequences hold related terms at prescribed frequencies.
arxiv-2602-21717:
Tabular data drives industrial analytics, but its growing scale strains storage and training. Dataset condensation shrinks training sets to small yet informative samples, yet current methods rely on costly gradient-based optimization and ignore tabular quirks like mixed feature types and class imbalance. Sijia Xu and four co-authors present C2TC, the first training-free tabular condensation framework, which jointly tunes class allocation and feature representation.

The method recasts condensation as a class-adaptive cluster allocation problem. A heuristic local search solves it by alternating soft allocation with class-wise clustering, plus a hybrid encoding that preserves meaning across mixed discrete attributes. On ten real-world datasets, C2TC ran at least 100 times faster than leading rivals while beating them downstream.
arxiv-2602-22117:
Quantum acoustic devices store quantum information as sound, but their promise hinges on how long mechanical vibrations stay coherent. Raquel Garcia Belles and sixteen co-authors study acoustic loss in high-overtone bulk resonators coupled to superconducting circuits. The catch is the piezoelectric film needed for coupling: it can open new loss channels through surface scattering and two-level defects.

Measurements show the film's defect density and its interface with the bulk limit coherence, even as modes reach lifetimes of hundreds of microseconds and coherence times near a millisecond. Coupled to a superconducting qubit, the system forms a hybrid quantum device. The findings point makers toward cleaner films and interfaces for longer-lived quantum sound.
arxiv-2602-22217:
Retrieval-augmented generation usually demands a heavy stack: cloud vector databases, GPU frameworks, and embedding servers. Ahmed Bin Khalid argues that bloat locks out edge devices, air-gapped sites, and privacy-sensitive users. He introduces RAGdb, a single portable SQLite container that unifies varied input handling, ONNX-based extraction, and hybrid vector search with no outside dependencies.

A fixed hybrid scoring rule blends sublinear TF-IDF vectors with exact substring boosting, so queries need no GPU inference at all. The single-piece design trades distributed scale for portability and data sovereignty. For edge and offline use, RAGdb offers grounded language-model answers without the cloud stack.
arxiv-2602-22317:
Reversibility means different things in thermodynamics and in integrable dynamics: entropy preservation in one, conserved action variables in the other. Rohan Banerjee and three co-authors study the murky middle ground, where systems are nearly integrable and neither idealization quite applies. They use toy models to ask how far reversible processes are even possible there.

The paper then explores fighting the dissipative losses of rapid driving with approximate counterdiabatic driving, a technique that steers systems to mimic slow, gentle changes. Numerical evidence suggests much of the same phenomenology should hold for quantum many-body systems with large degeneracy under integrability-breaking perturbations. The work maps where reversibility survives and where it frays.
arxiv-2602-22517:
Thiago H. Moreira and one co-author ask what gravity does to quantum superpositions, states in which a particle sits in two places at once. Gravity cannot be shielded, so it matters for the shift from quantum to classical behaviour. Earlier work suggested graviton effects touched only large systems. But a system's own inner motion can strengthen the effect.

Adding a classical Newtonian potential to the picture, the authors show the graviton bath rules at short times. Yet contact between gravitons and the system's inner parts makes decoherence certain in the long run, even for tiny masses. Decoherence means the loss of superposition. The Newtonian pull slightly slows the process. For systems with no moving inner parts, it can even mimic recoherence, a partial return of quantum behaviour, at least in principle.
arxiv-2602-22617:
Hai Huang and two co-authors challenge the data-efficiency limits implied by language-model scaling laws. Those laws fit how loss falls with compute, data, and size, but they describe typical training, not the best possible training. Few studies have beaten the data term, and it takes aim at exactly that bound.

The Geodesic Hypothesis claims token sequences trace geodesics, locally straight paths, on a smooth semantic manifold. From it comes Semantic Tube Prediction, a JEPA-style regularizer that keeps hidden-state paths inside a tube around the geodesic. The constraint raises signal quality and stops paths colliding during inference. On the NL-RX-SYNTH dataset, models matched baseline accuracy with sixteen times less training data, a direct break from Chinchilla-style data scaling.
arxiv-2602-22817:
Shuo He and five co-authors fix a bias in stepwise group-based reinforcement learning for long-horizon agent tasks. Stepwise methods treat each rollout step independently while a memory module holds history, but steps grouped together may carry different historical contexts. That context inconsistency skews relative advantage estimates and degrades policy learning.

Hierarchy-of-Groups Policy Optimization assigns each step to multiple hierarchical groups matched by context consistency, computes distinct advantages per group, and merges them with adaptive weights. The design wins a better bias-variance trade-off with no extra models or rollouts. On the ALFWorld and WebShop tasks with Qwen instruct models, it significantly beat existing agent reinforcement learning methods under equal compute budgets.
arxiv-2602-23417:
Filippo Camilloni and one co-author explore whether the Blandford-Znajek mechanism works the same across different black hole spacetimes. The mechanism is the leading process for tapping spin energy from a feeding black hole to power fast jets. Using a general model of black hole spacetimes, they test whether jet power is the same in all cases.

The first-order share of Blandford-Znajek power stays the same across spacetimes, while the next term differs between them. The consequence is sharp. Slowly rotating black holes cannot be told apart by jet power measurements. Fast-spinning ones could reveal strong-field spacetime traits, if jet brightness and black hole spin rate are both measured on their own.
arxiv-2602-23617: Samuel Quirino and one co-author classify all topological vector spaces with linear topology in which every algebraic automorphism is continuous. The short paper gives a complete classification of spaces with this automatic continuity trait. It also proves further traits of these spaces, mapping exactly which linear-topology spaces force algebraic automorphisms to be continuous. In plain terms, the result says when algebra alone forces maps to respect limits.
arxiv-2602-23817:
Pratibha Kumari and five co-authors present a continual learning system that writes pathology reports from whole-slide images without storing past slides. The 2026 paper addresses clinics where new organs, sites, and reporting styles arrive over time, and repeated fine-tuning wipes out earlier skills.

The core is a compact domain footprint built in a frozen patch space: a small codebook of typical tissue patterns, slide-level co-occurrence summaries, and light count priors. Footprints drive generative replay, making synthetic slide codes that mirror each domain, while a teacher snapshot supplies synthetic reports for training. A compact style descriptor captures each domain's wording and steers output; at test time the model picks the best descriptor from the slide alone. Tests across continual benchmarks beat exemplar-free and limited-buffer rivals.
arxiv-2602-24017:
