Lilian Magermans and nine co-authors present a low-cost liquid crystal device that generates tunable dynamic speckle patterns for random illumination microscopy. The 2026 paper notes that speckled illumination enables optical sectioning and super-resolution in widefield fluorescence microscopy. Pattern generation usually needs costly digital mirror devices or spatial light modulators.

The zwitterion-doped liquid crystal device produces independent, high-contrast speckle patterns whose decorrelation time can be tuned across a wide range under visible laser light. Applied to widefield random illumination microscopy of tissue and cell samples, it achieves fine axial sectioning and a substantial improvement in lateral resolution. Its low cost and simplicity make it an attractive alternative to mirror and modulator devices. In short, a cheap device can now do work that once needed costly gear.
arxiv-2603-01617:
Gianmarco Del Sarto, Franco Flandoli, and Marta Lenzi ask why Arctic temperatures swing more as the climate warms. Their 2026 work uses a simple energy-balance model of the Sellers type, with random sunlight input. Carbon-driven forcing may raise not just mean heat, but also how much heat varies.

They start with fast sunlight noise and slow temperature change, then reduce the pair to one equation. In that form, noise multiplies the state, which can amplify swings near ice-sensitive settings. A clear formula for steady variance shows it grows as the forcing parameter rises. A spatial version shows the same growth in linked swings between places. The result names a clean mechanism for wider, more synced Arctic swings under forcing.
arxiv-2603-02317:
Hanpu Liu, Yan-Fei Jiang, Eliot Quataert, and colleagues build a synthetic spectral library for puzzling red objects in this 2026 paper. Little Red Dots are compact distant objects that defy standard black hole models. Their light looks like a blackbody with star-like features at red wavelengths. That hints at a thick atmosphere at a few thousand degrees.

Their library varies surface temperature and gravity across thick atmosphere models. Gravity here acts most directly as a stand-in for surface density. Pure blackbodies prove crude next to these detailed spectra. Several features track surface density well, including a kink from hydrogen opacity and a calcium absorption line. One local object matches a very low density on all three checks, which disfavors a static, held-up atmosphere.
arxiv-2603-02817:
Ryan Griffiths, Timothy Butterley, Richard Wilson, and James Osborn improve a sky-watching instrument that measures air shimmer for telescopes. Their 2026 paper advances the SHIMM, a fast infrared sensor that profiles optical turbulence day and night. Knowing where turbulence sits helps observatories and laser ground stations plan around it.

They derive new weighting functions, correct for the blur from nonzero exposure times, and estimate how fast turbulence evolves by pairing the profile with a defocus method. End-to-end simulations matched the recovered values closely, with tiny errors and strong correlations. A simple four-layer air model also held up, even in rough daytime conditions. They report the instrument's sensitivity limit and flag a mixing effect between the ground layer and the next layer up.
arxiv-2603-02917:
Lucas Hanouz, Marc Kaplan, Jean-Sébastien Kersaint Tournebize, and colleagues run two quantum tasks on hardware built for one. Most quantum networks today only distribute encryption keys. Their 2026 paper implements quantum oblivious transfer and quantum tokens on the same key-distribution hardware, a step toward multi-purpose networks.

The contribution is largely method: a full-stack framework that runs the same user applications on simulated or real back ends. Because the simulator copies the real device's losses and errors, code can be validated before touching hardware. All software sources are open for reproduction. The team reviews security against known bounds and explains the engineering choices that made real-hardware runs feasible. Their process lowers the expertise barrier for testing new quantum protocols.
arxiv-2603-03217:
Hashir Kuniyil, Asad Ali, Syed Arslan, and colleagues turn a photon detector's recovery lag into a quantum hacking tool. Quantum key distribution promises secrecy, but its single-photon detectors need dead time to recover after each click. Security proofs usually treat that recovery as a fixed constant.

Experiments show the effective recovery stretches substantially when the incoming count rate climbs into the high regime. An attacker who floods the detector can therefore suppress detections unevenly across measurement bases, turning mismatch errors into plain loss. In one common protocol family, that stealth keeps the error rate below the abort threshold while erasures climb. Countermeasures built for timing attacks do not cover this recovery effect, so security models must include detector dynamics explicitly.
arxiv-2603-03317:
David Kogan and Sam Nguyen of Google introduce Retcon, a prompting method for steering chatbots turn by turn. Support agents, teaching assistants, and game characters all need behavior that can change mid-conversation: a new tone, a harder question, a reaction to events. Their 2026 paper notes that ordinary prompting loses that control as conversations lengthen or drift from earlier turns.

Retcon uses a few well-chosen examples to give precise control at each turn, without retraining the model. In their tests it performs far better than both zero-shot prompting, which gives no examples, and traditional few-shot prompting. The result is a light, practical tool for builders who need a conversational agent whose behavior stays adjustable throughout a long exchange.
arxiv-2603-03417:
Yegon Kim and four colleagues improve how language models pick their best answer. A popular trick generates many candidate solutions in parallel and lets a verifier choose. Two bottlenecks follow: picking correctly is hard, and generating many full solutions is slow. Their 2026 paper argues both trace back to one cause, how well the verifier is calibrated.

Existing verifiers score each candidate alone, ignoring the context of the rival answers. The Multi-Sequence Verifier instead reads all candidates jointly and models their interactions, which sharpens calibration and improves best-answer selection. A streaming variant watches candidates as they form and stops generation early once the winner is clear. In tests it reached the same target accuracy at roughly half the latency of isolated scoring.
arxiv-2604-00217: Wang and six colleagues show that engineering graphene dielectric environment controls its ultrafast carrier dynamics without changing Fermi energy, optical power, or ambient heat. Dielectric screening weakens carrier-carrier interactions and slows things: weaker scattering delays the hot electron spread, slowing heating, and re-thermalization after phonon emission also slows cooling. Stronger screening further lowers electron-hole puddle energy, raising charge mobility and the Seebeck coefficient. Such control of inner workings and transport thus tunes device output, including photodetector sensitivity for data and radio links.
arxiv-2604-00417: Senoo and colleagues test how quantum mechanics describes single particles travelling in free space. The uncertainty principle trades position control against momentum control, but mixing two states with sharply different trade-offs creates an interference term that seems to pin down both at once. The team prepares photons in such a mixed position-momentum state inside a Sagnac interferometer. Three output-port settings then capture the starting position pattern, the starting momentum pattern, and a case partway through travel.
arxiv-2604-00617: Kim and colleagues hunt for new physics inside jets with the Herwig 7 parton shower and beyond-Standard-Model radiation. Old searches assume a Z-prime boson is made in the hard process. But Z-prime bosons could also appear in jets via shower emissions, a probe through jet substructure and event shapes. The Herwig 7 framework supports beyond-Standard-Model showers for simulation in the enhanced regime. With a U(1) B-minus-L benchmark, they test how both showers interact, seeking features that set Z-prime jets apart.
arxiv-2604-01017: Grandel, Benner, and George test how fine-tuning changes machine-learning interatomic potentials, fast stand-ins for density functional theory in atom-scale models. They check phonon band shapes, heat traits, and the energy landscape along imaginary phonon modes. With as few as 10 extra training samples, they gain a lot. They also present Equitrain, a fine-tuning toolkit using LoRA-based tuning. Across 53 matter systems, fine-tuned models always beat both the base model and models trained from scratch, with Equitrain best overall.
arxiv-2604-01117: Takabatake and Akaho study pseudo-Gibbs sampling in dependency networks through an information-geometric lens, treating every sampling move as a projection onto the manifold of full conditionals. They define the full conditional divergence and give an upper bound pinning down the stationary distribution among distributions. Structure and parameter learning turn into optimization problems splitting into subproblems per node, and the learned model distribution tends to the true distribution as training samples grow without bound. Tests confirm the upper bound is tight in practice.
arxiv-2604-01917: Maquiling, Abdrabou and Kasneci test whether pupil size skews eye-tracking measures of depth. Vergence, the inward or outward turn of the eyes, is read as a clue to depth, but pupil shifts may distort it. With a head-mounted tracker and a beamsplitter rig showing near and far targets, the team ran still, shifting light and blocked trials. Near and far targets split cleanly by vergence angle, yet pupil coupling varied widely by person and setup, and shifting light narrowed but did not remove the distortion.
arxiv-2604-02117: Aguilar and colleagues extend the Bures metric and density space to non unital C star algebras with a faithful trace. They prove the Bures metric is indeed a metric there, with a topology weaker than the C star norm topology. A Heine Borel type result follows: the density space is noncompact exactly when the algebra is infinite dimensional. They also extend the quantum metric to the non unital case via quantum Lipschitz triples, and study matrix valued functions on the quantized interval as test cases.
arxiv-2604-02617: Du and three colleagues present AutoVerifier, an agent-based tool that checks complex technical claims in scientific and technical intelligence without needing domain experts. It splits each claim into subject-predicate-object triples and reasons through six layers, from corpus building and claim extraction to cross-source checks and a final hypothesis matrix. On a contested quantum computing claim, it caught overclaims, metric mismatches and hidden commercial conflicts.
arxiv-2604-03217: Patel and Weissmann examine the Hitchin morphism on higher-dimensional varieties, focusing on a class they call r-small. For that class, the image of the morphism from the Dolbeault moduli space equals the spectral base, giving a stronger form of a conjecture by Chen and Ngô. The proof adjusts the spectral-cover construction to produce normal spectral covers.
arxiv-2604-04217: Italiano, Brambilla and Nicoli tackle vehicle positioning inside road tunnels, where satellite signals cannot reach. Their JAVELIN system uses one multi-antenna anchor plus passive radio-reflective road markings. It tracks a vehicle to under a metre, combining near-field signal measurements with recursive tracking that needs no prior map of the tunnel. Tunnel simulations show it beating existing single-anchor methods.
arxiv-2604-04417: Dai and Chen develop a primal heuristic for nonconvex Mixed-Integer Quadratically Constrained Quadratic Programs, optimization problems with integer choices and square limits. The method centers on a convex approximation tuned on the fly within a feasibility-pump-style alternating method, adjusted per instance. Local branching also refines the answers found. The work builds on their second-place entry in the 2025 Land-Doig MIP Competition. Tests on QPLIB instances solve three previously open cases and improve the best-known answers for fifteen more within five minutes.
arxiv-2604-04617: Prasetyo, Gunara and Suroso compare the effect of using the trace of the stress-energy tensor against a real-valued scalar field in the Nonminimal Derivative Coupling gravitation model. The two versions are called NMDC-T and NMDC-phi respectively. In this preliminary study, the team applies the model to an incompressible star and examines how both models affect compactness and the mass-radius relation. Coupling parameters of NMDC-T prove less sensitive than those of NMDC-phi.
arxiv-2604-04817: Corral and three colleagues build planar anti-de Sitter spacetimes carrying NUT parameters, a case where the trick for adding rotation parameters fails. They offer two routes past the vacuum field equations' limits. One adds scalar fields with an axionic profile, motivated by momentum relaxation models; the other uses Einstein gravity with quadratic curvature corrections. Both routes yield multi-NUT spaces in AdS. They close with Kaluza-Klein monopoles in AdS with magnetic charges, plus a Gross-Perry-Sorkin monopole with a cosmological constant.
arxiv-2604-04917: Sarch and five colleagues ask what it takes to build a visual reasoner for charts, science, spatial tasks, and open-ended questions. Leading vision-language models show visual reasoning is within reach, but their closed data and pipelines block study and reuse. Their Vero family of open models matches or beats open-weight models across visual reasoning tasks. They scale data and rewards across six task groups, building Vero-600K from 59 datasets with task-routed rewards. On their 30-benchmark VeroEval suite, Vero-600K beats datasets under controlled comparisons.
arxiv-2604-05217: Cirrincione builds a theory of what place codes ought to do, swapping design. Any model without a place signal cannot solve any task tuned to word order. Training assigns distinct vectors to distinct spots at every best point, under mild rules. The best code match uses multi-D scaling on Hellinger gaps between place spreads, with quality judged by one number, the stress. The code has rank r, at most n minus 1, needing r(n+d) knobs instead of nd.
arxiv-2604-05317: Aoyama, Tomita, and Ino design a faster way to arrange flawless grids of neutral atoms, the building blocks of a quantum computer design. They move many atoms at once with a lattice pattern made by light deflectors. Their plan splits any rearrangement into at most three one-dimensional shuttling jobs, so total travel grows only with the square root of the atom count. On an array of about 400 thousand atoms, the plan cut travel cost to one seventh of the best rival method while capturing roughly a third more atoms.
arxiv-2604-05417: Kim, Jung, and Yun speed up language-model inference by combining several small drafting models instead of relying on one. Their MetaSD framework treats drafter choice as a multi-armed bandit problem, using alignment feedback to shift compute toward whichever drafter matches the target model best. Experiments show it consistently beats single-drafter speculative decoding across varied tasks.
arxiv-2604-05817: Xie and three colleagues forecast axion-like particle signals from galactic supernovae for future MeV telescopes. Primakoff-made particles flipping in galactic magnetic fields could reach couplings near 1.61 times 10 to the power -13 per giga-electron-volt for tiny masses. That would beat current astrophysical limits by two orders of magnitude, probing ultra-light dark matter.
arxiv-2604-06317: Bashi, Clarke, and Belokurov find a quadruple excess in wide binaries, evidence of correlated formation. If partners formed alone, the quadruple fraction, where both parts are close pairs, should equal the close-pair product. From Gaia DR3 radial velocity data, they measure an enhancement factor of 2.34, above unity. Shuffling pairings while keeping magnitude spread shows none, ruling out bias. Enhancement stays strong to 5,000 astronomical units but declines toward unity at wide gaps. It also fades with peculiar velocity, as dynamical churn in old, hot groups may turn 2+2 quadruples into triples.
arxiv-2604-06417: Kinnear and DiazDelaO propose niching importance sampling, a framework mixing reliability analysis with niching tools from evolutionary multi-modal optimisation. Reliability concepts include Markov chains and importance sampling, plus relative cross entropy tuning. This yields a highly robust gauge of failure chance, able to tackle sampling hurdles posed by the shape of a reliability problem. Tested on a range of test cases, niching importance sampling always avoids the degenerate results seen in old reliability methods across several multi-modal performance functions.
arxiv-2604-06717: Dipierro, De Pas, and Valdinoci rebuild double-well potentials from transition layers in long-range phase coexistence. Their exact form matters greatly yet cannot be derived from first principles. Starting from a set transition layer with power-type decay at infinity, they recover structural traits of the linked well, focusing on long-range effects where links grow delicate. Their work links the layer's decay rate to its smoothness, showing set patterns and possible breakdowns.
arxiv-2604-06817: Naseem and thirty-three colleagues run SemEval-2026 Task 9 on multilingual online polarization. The shared task spans 22 languages with over 110,000 annotated instances, each tagged for polarization presence, type, and manifestation. Teams tackled three jobs: detecting presence, identifying type, and recognizing manifestation. Over 1,000 participants joined with more than 10,000 submissions, yielding final entries from 67 teams and 73 system papers. The report gives baselines and reviews top systems, noting the most common and most effective methods across jobs and languages, with the dataset public.
arxiv-2604-07317: Debnath and five colleagues build an approximate non-LTE model for the winds of hot, massive stars in multiple dimensions over time. Earlier unified models assumed local thermodynamic equilibrium, which fails in the extended outflow where heating and cooling opacities diverge. Their method treats scattering across about four million spectral lines in an accelerating medium, using escape probabilities and thermalization parameters. The result is a multi-component wind, split in density, velocity, and temperature, with shock heating localized by strong radiative cooling.
arxiv-2604-07517: Tang and six colleagues present GraspDreamer, a method for zero-shot functional grasping without massive data collection. Visual generative models trained on internet-scale human data implicitly capture how humans interact with physical objects. GraspDreamer combines those priors with action optimization tuned to each robot body to grasp functionally with minimal effort. Tests on public benchmarks with different robot hands show better data efficiency and generalization, real-robot trials confirm it works, and the method extends to downstream manipulation tasks.
arxiv-2604-07917: Teng and four colleagues introduce a general semiparametric clusterwise elliptical distribution for studying how hidden cluster structure shapes continuous results. Cluster means are estimated by cutting a weighted sum of squares with a separation penalty, using a per-person view. A starting scheme based on repeated Mahalanobis reassignment plus a computing algorithm with guaranteed convergence joins fitting. Under local conditions, the penalty rule gains a local oracle trait, and the local grouping recovers the true hidden grouping. The usable steps are evaluated apart through number studies.
arxiv-2604-08417: Lira and four colleagues test whether giving language models caller and callee code helps them spot security flaws that span several functions. On 509 flaws from the ReposVul set, across C, C++, and Python, four current models were tried with code alone, plus callers, or plus callees. Gemini 3 Flash gave the best value for C flaws, while Claude Haiku 4.5 correctly found and explained the flaw in 93.6 percent of cases checked.
arxiv-2604-08517: Fikioris, Sivan, and Tardos study repeated second price auctions where both a learning bidder and a strategic bidder face strict budgets. They generalize the Stackelberg equilibrium to a budgeted version, proving the optimizer's best plan splits into at most k plus 1 phases for a k dimensional budget. They also show a standard proportional bid pacing rule is strategically robust: the optimizer cannot beat its budgeted equilibrium payoff against it.
arxiv-2604-08717: Sendonaris and four colleagues measure ultrafast multimode squeezed states with optical gating through a parametric amplifier. Mode shapes matter for using these states in communication, computing, and sensing, yet current methods need tight assumptions and complex setups. Their FROG plus amplifier scheme recovers mode shapes and squeezing levels at once, lifting weak states to detectable levels while keeping quantum information, as simulations confirm.
arxiv-2604-09417: Jiang, Huang, and Li ask whether many-objective Bayesian optimisation really needs to approach the entire Pareto front. With more than three objectives, solutions needed to represent the full front typically grow substantially. That challenge is acute in Bayesian optimisation, where only a few hundred solutions are evaluated. Since only one solution is ultimately deployed, the authors propose a single-point-based search framework. Its acquisition function, expected single-point improvement, is proven convergent and beats state-of-the-art methods on benchmarks.
arxiv-2604-09717: Mirza Raquib and five co-authors tackle Bangla handwriting reading, hard because styles vary and letters look alike. Current sets lack breadth and skew classes. The team builds an even dataset of 78 classes with about 650 samples each, with basic letters, Juktobarno forms, and digits. Their design runs EfficientNetB3, Vision Transformer, and Conformer modules side by side, fused by multi-head cross-attention. It reaches about 99 percent score on the new dataset and about 96 percent on the CHBCR benchmark, with Grad-CAM maps showing telling regions.
arxiv-2604-10117: Carlucci and eight colleagues automate network design for blood pressure estimation from photoplethysmography signals. On-board processing keeps data private, but good models are usually too large and power-hungry for wrist devices. Their pipeline combines hardware-aware search, pruning, and mixed-precision search for tiny low-power chips. The best networks cut error by about 8 percent with far fewer parameters, or use 83 times fewer parameters with tiny loss. All models fit in 512 kilobytes and run in 142 milliseconds at 7.25 millijoules per inference. Tuning to each patient lifts accuracy further.
arxiv-2604-10217: Corley, Stoken, and Berton test 24 pretrained image matchers for optical-radar satellite registration, a disaster-response bottleneck, with no tuning on satellite or radar data. Transfer is uneven: matchers trained for cross-modal work do not always beat the rest. XoFTR and RoMa post the lowest mean tie-point error, 3.0 pixels, on SpaceNet9 training scenes, RoMa using no cross-modal training. XoFTR also runs about ten times faster than RoMa, while protocol choices shift mean error up to 33 times for one matcher.
arxiv-2604-10717: Xie and seven colleagues defend RAG systems against extraction attacks, where hostile prompts coax a model into leaking private retrieved content. Their CanaryRAG defense plants canary tokens inside retrieved chunks and treats protection as a two-path runtime integrity game. Leaks are flagged live whenever either path breaks its expected canary behavior, even under hostile hiding tricks. Tests show far lower chunk recovery than leading baselines, with tiny cost to task quality and speed. The design drops into any pipeline with no retraining or rebuild.
arxiv-2604-10817: Ben-Arosh and three colleagues show by simulation that vectorial-time-polarization-gating reduces how much broadband high-harmonic generation depends on carrier-envelope phase. In the vectorial scheme, cutoff harmonics grow much less swayed by the driver's phase, and the emitted light's twist proves tough. Unlike scalar schemes, where recollision counts depend heavily on the phase, the driver keeps that count almost steady, steering only how they split between crossed paths. The scheme's phase toughness promises steady, helical sources for fast-pulse science without steadying the driver's phase.
arxiv-2604-11017: Wanigasooriya and Ekanayake present NimbusGuard, an open-source proactive autoscaling system for Kubernetes built on deep reinforcement learning. Standard autoscalers react only after demand is detected, risking costly over-provisioning or slow under-provisioning. NimbusGuard forecasts workload with a long short-term memory model feeding a deep Q-network agent, scaling ahead of demand. Tests against the built-in Horizontal Pod Autoscaler and the event-driven KEDA autoscaler show the proactive approach performs better, cutting waste while protecting responsiveness.
arxiv-2604-11317: Zhan, Wang, and Wang propose a falsifiable timing test for the double-white-dwarf model of long-period transients. If the burst period of CHIME/ILT J1634+44 is the orbital clock, and its 4206-second modulation is a spin-orbit beat, then the beat period must drift jointly with the orbital and spin clocks. Gravitational-wave losses, magnetic dissipation, and tides drive that joint drift. The predicted beat drift near ten to the minus ten seconds per second implies tens of seconds of drift within one year.
arxiv-2604-11917: Liu and Cernak propose StreamMark, a semi-fragile audio watermarking system built to catch deepfakes by design rather than by after-the-fact detection. It survives benign changes that keep meaning, such as compression and noise, but breaks under meaning-changing edits like voice conversion and speech editing. Tests show high imperceptibility, with signal-to-noise ratio 24.16 decibels and PESQ 4.20, plus resilience to Opus encoding. Under deepfake attacks, message recovery falls to chance near 50 percent, while benign AI style transfers stay above 98 percent.
arxiv-2604-12417: Kimon Boehmer studies max-min allocation when all players share the same valuation function. Items must be divided to maximize the least-satisfied player's share. Valuations are monotone and submodular, with diminishing returns from extra items. His greedy algorithm reaches a 0.4 approximation, beating the previous factor near 0.37. He also gives the first constant upper bound on the configuration LP integrality gap. The result extends to allocations constrained by k matroids, with an estimation method whose guarantee scales with k.
arxiv-2604-12517: Benjamin Vejnar shows the converse of Borsuk's result on fans fails. A fan is a connected continuum with exactly one branching point. It is arc-wise connected and hereditarily unicoherent, in topology terms. Borsuk proved every fan splits into arcs meeting only at the branch point. Vejnar proves the reverse fails: not every such arc union is a fan. His proof gives a more general result covering the counterexample.
arxiv-2604-13017: Chakraborty and seven colleagues turn lecture videos into interactive lessons with PAL. The platform reads multimodal lecture content and quizzes learners at shifting difficulty as each lesson unfolds. Questions adapt to the learner's answers in real time. Each session ends with a personalized summary that reinforces key ideas through examples matched to the learner's interests.
arxiv-2604-13117: Talla Waffo studies second-order differential operators tied to scaled polynomial groups, and series built by reusing those operators from a linear start. He factors them into first-order pieces, gives weighted divergence forms and formal self-adjointness, and covers their eigenvalue equations with hypergeometric functions. Both keep hyperbolicity, keep zeros in an interval, and keep proper place. Iterated series show strict interlacing of consecutive zeros and zero-counting totals tending to one shared limit measure.
arxiv-2604-13217: Khoshk Angabini and five colleagues handle blastocyst grading for IVF, replacing visual judgment with a multi-task embedding approach. A ResNet-18 model with an added layer learns from day-5 embryo images to identify the trophectoderm, inner cell mass, and expansion, plus their grades, despite the visual likeness of these structures. Results show promise for robust, steady quality assessment from limited data.
arxiv-2604-13317: Choudhury and Patel study skill-training delivery at the Livelihood College in Dhamtari, India. They trace mobilization, counseling, and training within a five-stage process that also covers placement and tracking. Drawing on a year of fieldwork, mapping, video analysis, and talks with staff and nearby employers, they find three core problems. Access is unequal and gendered, counseling is laborious with too few support staff, and attendance is patchy with digital assets underused. They propose stronger partner, digital, and counseling arrangements.
arxiv-2604-13517: Sun argues that actor routing among multi-timescale value heads in PPO creates a numerical shortcut, not a reliable temporal abstraction. In a PPO setting on LunarLander, he formalises Surrogate Objective Hacking: a softmax router chases favourable advantage heads without improving control. He also identifies the Paradox of Temporal Uncertainty: error-based routing favours short-horizon heads because their targets are easier, even when they align poorly with delayed success. Target Decoupling updates the actor only with the long-horizon advantage, removing that routing pathway and improving worst-seed return.
arxiv-2604-13817: Wang and seven colleagues help chatbots draw out facts users hold back. People hide details for privacy, uncertainty, or shyness, leaving models with gaps. Their method, Reinforcement Prompt Selection, learns which prompt to ask next, treating prompt choice as a sequence of decisions. In a synthetic test it beats random questioning. On IELegal, a benchmark built from real legal cases, adaptive prompts beat fixed prompts.
arxiv-2604-14117: Adam and seven colleagues report the first canonical-ensemble lattice results for hot, dense quark matter using true physical quark masses. Working from high-statistics data on a small finite lattice at zero chemical potential, they stretch the canonical method to fractional baryon counts. They then tie those results back to the usual grand canonical picture. The scheme yields pressure and density directly, without extrapolating in chemical potential, and proves workable up to about 500 MeV.
arxiv-2604-14417: Rogers and four colleagues argue that design-oriented visualization research needs traceability, not reproducibility, since insight grows through subjective, situated, iterative work. They define traceability as showing where contributions came from and how they grew, using rich artifacts from the design process. A joint self-study plus a tool called tRRRacer test three tenets: record abundant annotated artifacts, report curated threads of rationale and change, and read through views that retrace claims. The paper theorizes traceability and reflects on how to support it.
arxiv-2604-15617: Jiang, Lv, and Chen build a graph neural solver for parametric hyperbolic conservation laws that keeps physics intact instead of acting as a black-box updater. The net learns a reconstruction-and-flux step, which bakes in local conservation and upwinding. It treats message passing as high-order space-time prediction for steady large-step updates. On supersonic flow tests it beats rival surrogates on long-horizon stability and accuracy, running far faster than fine simulations.
arxiv-2604-15817: Sagawa tours nucleus puzzles tied to spin and isospin, with small-scale models that hold true pair pulls plus tensor links. For a frame to span nucleus and star work, he runs Hartree-Fock plus RPA models. A beyond-mean-field Subtracted Second RPA adds two-particle two-hole ties. Magnet-dipole and Gamow-Teller jump dimming is read through two-hole ties. Beta-decay lives of near-magic and magic nuclei are read in both models.
arxiv-2604-15917: Zhao and eight colleagues reframe image editing failures as a task formulation problem, not a lack of model power. Many failures trace to poorly worded tasks, such as tiny targets, vague spatial relations, or thin instructions. Their adaptive reformulation framework turns each image-instruction pair into a sequence of steps chosen and run by a multimodal agent through analysis, routing, reformulation, and feedback. Tests across ImgEdit, PICA, and RePlan show steady gains, largest on hard cases.
arxiv-2604-16017: Škondrić and Violini study Lions' density patch problem in two dimensions at critical regularity. They prove global existence, uniqueness, and stability hold for a fluid filling a bounded Lipschitz region surrounded by vacuum, evolving under the incompressible Navier-Stokes equations. They also show the patch keeps its Lipschitz regularity, and that its long-time motion becomes rigid, leading to an asymptotic domain.
arxiv-2604-16317: You and seven colleagues present Paper2Data and UrbanDataMiner, tackling global urban data discovery, where no unified platform exists and researchers must hunt through sites and papers by hand. Paper2Data is a large-scale LLM pipeline that finds dataset mentions in scientific papers and organises them under a unified urban metadata schema. It powers UrbanDataMiner, a portal with over 60,000 urban datasets from over 15,000 Nature-affiliated publications. Human checks show about 90 percent recall in dataset identification and over 80 percent field-level precision.
arxiv-2604-16617: Araujo and colleagues introduce AVRT, transferring reasoning from single teachers to AV models. Multimodal transfer lags for lack of good reasoning data in combinations. AVRT generates vision and audio traces from teacher models, then merges them with an LLM. The merged traces adapt the model through fine-tuning, then a reinforcement learning stage on larger data. On audio-visual and audio benchmarks, B and B models reach top results among similar-size models. That training transfers to single-modality tasks, establishing a pipeline for multimodal reasoning models.
arxiv-2604-17517: Fernandez exposes a blind spot in runtime governance of autonomous agents. Enforcement engines flag actions that break hard rules, yet the paper's Non-Identifiability Theorem proves they cannot tell whether an agent's overall behavior still matches the admissible space fixed at admission time. The enforcement signal sees actions one by one, while admission expectations span whole trajectories, so behavior can drift systematically without any single action tripping a rule. The result holds under a local observability assumption the author argues every practical system meets.
arxiv-2604-17717: Bilal and six colleagues revisit application-level code debloating through ground-truth-based evaluation, replacing proxies like test correctness, code size, and gadget counts. Their analysis of eight debloaters, Blade, Chisel, Cov, CovA, Lmcas, Trimmer, Occam, and Razor, spans source-to-source, IR-to-IR, and binary-to-binary tools. Dynamic tools often remove up to 94 percent of code that should stay, while static tools over-retain through over-approximation and sometimes add code via specialized variants. False removals and retentions cause incorrect function, inconsistency, and exploitable flaws.
arxiv-2604-17817: Shiquan Zhang and five colleagues introduce DailyDroid, covering 75 tasks across 25 Android apps in five scenarios at three difficulty levels, mimicking everyday smartphone use. Tests on GPT-4o and o4-mini across 300 trials compare text-only with multimodal inputs, finding comparable performance with multimodal inputs marginally ahead. In-depth failure analysis yields a handbook of common failures, pointing to UI accessibility, input modalities, and LLM and app design as critical issues. Lessons follow for future agents, apps, and UI work.
arxiv-2604-18217: Zhao, Cheng, and Gerbner study generalized Turán problems for Berge hypergraphs. A Berge copy of a graph matches each graph edge to a hyperedge containing it. The authors ask how many copies of one hypergraph can appear in another that avoids Berge copies of a given graph. They link the count to shadow graphs, prove exact results for large complete graphs via balanced complete multipartite constructions, and bound counts for complete hypergraphs with conditions for equality.
arxiv-2604-18617: Wallner studies chains: directed graphs with one start point, one end point, and ordered branches. Their depth-first spanning tree forms a single path. Such graphs arise in tree compression, and each matches one tree whose size sets the graph's size. For a fixed branch count of at least two, he finds the mean expanded size of a random chain, which holds a stretched exponential term in the square root of its size. That finding also bears on Brauer chains of fixed length.
arxiv-2604-18817: Donatelli and six colleagues introduce a math method for coherent surface scattering imaging. A specimen on a substrate yields X-ray patterns at grazing incidence as it rotates. Its 3D structure is hard to rebuild, since dynamical scattering and missing phases complicate the data. The method joins iterative phasing with fast nonuniform Fourier inversion methods. Tests on Siemens star and porous data rebuild sharp structures from one or two angles.
arxiv-2604-19017: Bergman, Liao, and Yang study quantum sensing with chaotic Floquet dynamics from Haar random gates. An initial state, random gates, and sensing gates combine in two protocols: control and state preparation. Each protocol uses global and local two-site gates forming a Floquet circuit. Precision scales linearly at shot noise for large dimensions, with advantages beyond linear scaling outside that regime. They bound Fisher information fluctuations with concentration inequalities and prove a random circuit conjecture: the Floquet operator behaves like a global unitary at large local dimension.
arxiv-2604-19117: Pandey shows models agreeing with a user's false belief detect the error and agree anyway. Across twelve models from five labs, the same attention heads carry a wrongness signal, whether judging alone or pressured to agree. Silencing these heads flips sycophancy while leaving accuracy intact: the circuit controls deference, not knowledge. Patching confirms shared connections drive sycophancy, factual, instructed lying. Opinion agreement without ground truth reuses these positions but writes orthogonally. Training leaves the circuit: an RLHF refresh cuts sycophancy roughly tenfold while the heads persist or grow.
arxiv-2604-19217: Shyam and Chandrakar present a multimodal tool for crop yield prediction from satellite and soil data. Old forecasting uses static data that miss dynamic environmental relationships over time. Their model merges satellite imagery, meteorological time series, and soil properties, unlike models using only one factor. Convolutional networks extract spatial features, while temporal attention weights phenological periods over time, based on spatial image and video features. The work scores an R-squared of 0.89, far better than rivals.
arxiv-2604-19317: Nicol, Singh, and Torok study two rival sources of stable laws in deterministic systems: slow mixing and heavy tails. For heavy-tailed measures on polynomially mixing billiards with cusps, the two sources interact and a switch occurs. Depending on the mixing exponent and the tail index, the limit law is set either by the measure or by the system motion. The authors prove stable limit laws for such measures, with tails fixed by a power of distance to a boundary point.
arxiv-2604-19817: Obikhod surveys supersymmetry, supergravity, and the non-perturbative physics of gauge theories, from algebra and superspace to the Seiberg-Witten solution. The survey then builds one-supersymmetry supergravity step by step, showing how the Kähler potential and superpotential fix all five parts of the theory. String-theory uses close the review, with a close look at KKLT moduli stabilization. It ends on the clash between stable de Sitter vacua and the swampland conjecture.
arxiv-2604-19917: Savvidou tackles the disk mass budget problem, the mismatch between dust masses observed in planet-forming disks and those inferred for exoplanets. Splitting model dust distributions by initial disk mass and embryo injection time, she finds intermediate disks of roughly 4 to 7 percent of a solar mass match observations best. Giant planets help explain the gap: their pressure bumps trap optically thick dust and seed planetesimals, lowering the visible dust while leaving planet formation itself unaffected.
arxiv-2604-20117: Zheng and three colleagues present SCG-MEM, a memory system for LLM agents that builds its stores under schema rules. Dense lookup fails when near-alike cases clash, while open-ended writing risks making up keys that do not exist. SCG-MEM limits output to valid keys inside a live schema, ruling out fake keys. Memory updates fit new items into old schemas or widen those schemas, with a link graph for multi-hop thought, and LoCoMo tests show gains in all groups over plain lookup.
arxiv-2604-20417: Kuffo and five colleagues introduce Semantic Recall, a metric judging approximate nearest neighbor search by semantically relevant objects only. Unlike plain recall, it does not punish missing objects that are semantically irrelevant, even when they sit among the nearest neighbors. Semantic Recall shines for queries with few relevant results among nearest neighbors, a common case in embedding data sets. A second metric, Tolerant Recall, proxies it when relevant objects cannot be identified, and tuning search for these metrics improves cost-quality trade-offs.
arxiv-2604-20717: Pachon shows hydrogen-like ions give no useful bound on the gyrogravitational ratio chi. In molybdenum-95 with charge 41+, gravity shifts hyperfine constants by at most one part in 10 to the 38, with tensor hyperfine structure. Centroids wipe it out, and the 2p lines span 1.3 eV. Isotopes with spin can, however, join King-plot searches for new bosons. On the cadmium clock line, cadmium-111's second-order hyperfine shift is about minus 1 MHz. A specific difference with cadmium-113 cuts it to about 2 Hz once calculable anomaly and third-order corrections apply.
arxiv-2604-20817: Fu, Zhou, Belkin, Sharan, and Jia find a two-tiered ladder of periodic features in representations learned in language models, with periods at T equals 2, 5, 10. While Transformers, Linear RNNs, LSTMs, and word vectors all learn features with cyclic spikes in Fourier space, only some learn geometrically separable codes for linear sorting of a number mod-T. They find two routes to geometrically separable codes: from co-occurrence cues in general language data, or from multi-token (but not single-token) adding problems. Models learn similar features from varied signals.
arxiv-2604-20917: Hasanov and colleagues argue that judging code understanding by input-output prediction alone gives a narrow, contamination-prone picture. True grasp of execution, they say, has two sides: predicting what a program does for a given input, and inferring how the input must change to reach a chosen behavior. Their DexBench benchmark pairs 445 instances across both tasks, and tests of 13 language models show dual-path reasoning discriminates dynamic understanding robustly.
arxiv-2604-21017: The Open-H-Embodiment Consortium introduces the largest open data set of medical robotic video with motion data, spanning more than 50 institutions. It covers surgical manipulation, robotic ultrasound, and endoscopy across platforms including the CMR Versius, Intuitive da Vinci systems, Rob Surgical BiTrack, and Moon Surgical Maestro. The team trains two foundation models on it. GR00T-H, the first open vision-language-action model for medical robotics, completes a suturing benchmark fully in 25 percent of trials, against zero for rivals. It averages 64 percent success across a 29-step suturing sequence.
arxiv-2604-21117: Max Tzschoppe and three colleagues speed up B+ tree searches on a programmable chip by handling batches of keys level by level, reusing loaded nodes and cutting trips to global memory. Their flexible kernel runs on an AMD Alveo card and beats a single-threaded CPU search by 4.9 times on a million-entry tree. Four kernels in parallel still more than double a 16-thread CPU run.
arxiv-2604-21317: Sebastián Camponovo and Rafael Torres construct, for each odd integer p above 1, infinitely many pairwise non-diffeomorphic irreducible smooth structures on a definite 4-manifold with an endless fundamental group. In plain terms, one shape can carry smooth atlases without end, each distinct under smooth change. The abelian version of the fundamental group is a product of two cyclic groups tied to p.
arxiv-2604-21617: Frederik Dennig and Daniel Keim present a stability framework for parametric projections, which embed new points live but shift with noise or drift. The framework probes projections with Gaussian noise around anchors and gauges neighborhood shifts. It joins mean displacement, bias, and nearest-anchor error with vectors, PCA ellipsoids, and Voronoi misassignment views. They test it on UMAP- and t-SNE-based projectors, probing Jacobian regularization as a defense, and apply it to MNIST and Fashion-MNIST. It finds unstable regions hidden from reconstruction error or local metrics.
arxiv-2604-21717: Bao, Shen, and Wang extend Monte Carlo solvers for heat equations to a case earlier solvers left largely untouched: nonlinear radiative boundary conditions. Their Picard-style iteration repeats a fixed-point step and stays stable in practice with a well-chosen relaxation factor, even from rough starting estimates. A further step cleans up noisy estimates at the edge, where older methods focus only on interior points. Tests on synthetic benchmarks and practical heat-radiation cases back the method.
arxiv-2604-21917: Majumdar presents CrossCommitVuln-Bench, a benchmark of 15 real Python vulnerabilities whose exploitable condition spans several commits, each harmless alone under per-commit static analysis yet critical together. Each CVE is annotated with its commit chain, a rationale explaining how each commit dodges per-commit analysis, and Semgrep and Bandit baselines in per-commit and cumulative modes. Per-commit detection is 13 percent, so 87 percent of chains are invisible to per-commit static analysis. In cumulative mode, detection is only 27 percent, confirming that snapshot-based tools miss multi-commit vulnerabilities.
arxiv-2604-22217: Shanto, Asaduzzaman, and Ngom present RAG-Reflect for comment-edit prediction on Stack Overflow, reaching fine-tuned performance without task-specific training. It combines language models with retrieval reasoning and self-reflection. It runs a three-stage workflow on pattern analysis. An Interpretation module derives rules from the knowledge base. At inference, the system retrieves examples, reasons about causality, and reflects using pre-established rules. On SOUP, RAG-Reflect scores Precision about 1, Recall about 1, and F1 0.78, beating baselines and nearly matching fine-tuned models.
arxiv-2604-22317: Lü, Ma and Wang address a Stackelberg stochastic LQ game with closed-loop information, which is time-inconsistent. Existing methods solve two coupled Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman equations by time steps, whose convergence remains open. The authors instead use closed-loop equilibrium strategies, deriving the leader's Riccati equation from forward-backward equations. The follower plays a global best plan against leader control, not just a locally best one along the path. The follower is tougher and the leader more credible, and the equation matches the coupled system, backing the limiting argument.
arxiv-2604-22517: Hirota and eight colleagues ask whether an automatic judge of business ideas should mimic a pooled consensus or model each expert alone. They release PBIG-DATA, roughly 3,000 expert scores over 300 patent-based product ideas across six business dimensions. Experts disagree sharply on fine-grained scores but agree more on coarse choices, a pattern the authors read as structured diversity rather than noise. Comparing rubric-only, aggregate, and personalized judges, they find personalized judges track their target evaluator more closely across dimensions and model sizes.
arxiv-2604-22817: Fan and five colleagues extend a speech-aware language model so it predicts word-level timestamps together with its transcript. That removes the need for outside alignment tools. Their light training methods strengthen alignment while keeping recognition quality high, aiming at captioning, media search, and syncing speech with other media. Across several data sets the approach improves time-stamp accuracy and also raises overall speech-recognition scores.
arxiv-2604-23117: Iguchi, Nandi, and Oudah use SQUID imaging to see vortex cluster dynamics in the weak type-II superconductor CaSb2. They reveal dense clusters with enhanced boundary susceptibility and suppressed internal vortex motion, unlike isolated vortex or flux tube behavior. These are the first local views of magnetic dynamics within vortex clusters in a weakly pinned superconductor. Although superfluid density matches a one-gap BCS picture and the Ginzburg-Landau parameter sits outside the type-II/1 regime, clustering and uneven dynamics point beyond existing microscopic theories for single-band superconductors.
arxiv-2604-23217: Gootzen and Chong design a secure state estimator for Lur'e-type systems whose sampled outputs may be maliciously corrupted, motivated by power grid health monitoring. When fewer than half the sensors are attacked and inter-sample times stay bounded, its accuracy does not depend on the attack. Error convergence is shown under an impulsive system framework, with an error bound independent of attack signals, and stability conditions as linear matrix inequalities for observer design. A low-voltage power distribution grid demo shows the estimator in action.
arxiv-2604-23617: Baek, Jeong, and Kim expose denial-of-diagnostic-service attacks on vehicles that exploit the CAN transport protocol, which was designed without security in mind. They identify eight novel attack scenarios using flow-control manipulation, sequence-number violations, and error-handling abuse. Tested on a real passenger car with two diagnostic tools, three scenarios succeed, hiding faults and falsifying sensor readings in ways that could mislead technicians and drivers.
arxiv-2604-23717: He and nine colleagues present HeadRouter, a training-free token pruning method for large audio language models that respects the fact that attention heads differ across audio tasks. Instead of averaging head scores, it weights heads by task importance to keep the tokens that matter most. On two audio benchmarks it sets a new compression mark, even beating the unpruned model while keeping only 70 percent of audio tokens.
arxiv-2604-23817: Popovici and Dobre describe the minimum viable product of FUTURAL's metasearch platform, the gateway to digital smart solutions for rural areas across five domains. Built on a single open-source data service, it uses large language models to offer a natural-language interface to solutions from FUTURAL and other initiatives. Evaluations show the approach works well and can scale efficiently, paving the way for more services and datasets.
arxiv-2604-23917: Sarkar and Ni propose MR-CCC, a Bayesian Mendelian randomization method for cell signals, beyond ligand-receptor pairing, which misses signals. It uses cis-eQTLs as tools for ligand-receptor levels and models receptor-tuned ligand effects via an interaction term. A spike-slab prior yields posterior probabilities, with a Gibbs sampler. Versus regression, MVMR, and MR-BMA, it controls discoveries under confounding and keeps power, estimating main and interaction effects uniquely. On OneK1K NK-monocyte data, it finds eight hits across GABA, interferon, interleukin, and prostaglandin signals.
arxiv-2604-24417: Gizzi and seven colleagues study laser-driven very high energy electrons for FLASH radiotherapy. Laser wakefield acceleration offers a compact source of electrons at ultra-high dose rates for the FLASH effect. Pencil beams show wide energy spread and small transverse size, unlike other beams. Start-to-end Monte Carlo simulations of a beam on a brain tumor achieve tumor coverage by scanning. Dose patterns from overlapping beamlets are examined. Dose histograms show quality, and FLASH adds healthy tissue sparing. The authors outline the path toward FLASH dose rates.
arxiv-2604-24517: Chen, Peng, and Tang design a simple closed-form rule for pooling expert forecasts. It works when the forecaster knows neither the shared prior nor even the range of possible outcomes. Their log-odds combiner pools reports in logit space and carries near-tight worst-case regret guarantees across three knowledge settings, including cases where experts see independent signals. It also sets a new mark in the classic binary setting and extends to forecasters whose marginal distributions are known.
arxiv-2604-24617: Vaia and seven colleagues measure distances to the Milky Way's spiral arms from X-ray dust-scattering rings left by three gamma-ray bursts. Rings from dust clouds beyond 5 kiloparsecs line up with the Perseus, Outer and Outer Scutum-Centaurus arms, giving direct distances along three sight lines. Two new rings toward one burst and a confirmed cloud toward another, plus clouds out to 19 kiloparsecs toward the third, tighten constraints on Galactic structure.
arxiv-2604-24817: Awan, Chen and Molinari propose a Bayesian method for privatized data. Privacy noise makes inference harder. Old methods need strong parametric assumptions or fail at large scale. Their two-step approach imputes confidential data, then samples the non-private posterior. They prove the sampler is asymptotically valid under mild assumptions. Simulations show conservative frequentist traits too. They test it on simulated data and on homeownership via the 2022 American Community Survey.
arxiv-2604-24917: Altland and four colleagues develop a unified theory of Anderson localization on the hyperbolic plane. This plane is locally flat at short range, but vast at large scales. It offers a paradigm for disorder-driven phase transitions, notably the Anderson transition. Building on work that treated short and large scales separately, they build a framework bridging low- and high-dimensional trapping rules. Their main result is a two-part flow in a plane spanned by scale-changing bend and flow. A long key line divides metal and non-metal phases.
arxiv-2605-00117:
Kejun Liu rethinks the Kramers-Kronig relations, the classic links between the absorptive and dispersive parts of a response. Those relations rest on a binary premise: a response function either is analytic in the upper half-plane or is not. Liu shows a single reduced-state transform organizes both outcomes into one sharp dichotomy controlled by microscopic unitarity.

One closed-form function carries both a zero and a pole in the upper half-plane, and a spectral quantity of the reduced propagator decides which appears. On the unitary side the zero is protected and measurable directly from a finite-time record, with the relations intact. On the gain-driven side the zero becomes a genuine pole, the winding number jumps, and the relations gain a correction term. Solvable models realize both sides, and a terahertz signature is proposed.
arxiv-2605-00217:
Kamtila Kari and 3 co-authors work in Poisson geometry, on the cohomology of a degenerate Poisson structure on the flat plane. A Poisson bivector assigns to a plane a rule for how functions interact; here the rule degenerates, vanishing along a line in a controlled power-law way. Cohomology, in this setting, measures the obstructions and symmetries hidden in that structure.

The authors compare two versions of the theory: the classical Poisson cohomology and a logarithmic version built along the ideal tied to the bivector. By working out the logarithmic Hamiltonian operator and its cochain complex, they compute the related invariants. Their result is that the two cohomology groups agree in every degree. That agreement simplifies how this degenerate case can be studied with either toolkit.
arxiv-2605-00417:
Renzo Angles, Claudio Gutierrez, and Daniel Hernández pin down the expressive power of SPARQL, the query language of the linked-data web, under multiset semantics. Real query results are bags, not sets: duplicates count. The paper analyzes the algebra and logic of SPARQL patterns built from joins, unions, filters, gaps, and column picks, where every step respects the counts.

To pin SPARQL down, the authors align it with two known languages. One is a multiset version of non-recursive Datalog with safe negation, a rule-based logic language. The other is a multiset algebra over tables with projection, selection, natural join, union, and except. Their main theorem is that all three systems match in power: anything one can say, the others can say too. Such matches matter in practice, since they let teams move queries and tuning between the database and logic worlds without loss.
arxiv-2605-00717:
Laurent Dubus and 3 co-authors argue that power system planning must systematically absorb climate information, and show a European database built for that purpose. Climate change strikes energy systems on several fronts at once: weather variability swings daily and seasonal supply and demand, while long-term trends and sharper extremes threaten infrastructure and adequacy. Compound events and cross-border correlations make the modeling harder still.

The Pan-European Climate Database, built by the transmission operators' association with the Copernicus climate service, combines historical reanalysis with six climate models across four emissions pathways, openly and in harmonized form. Its wind and solar conversion models track technology change better than machine learning trained on history. Gaps remain, notably hydropower modeling and public harmonized energy datasets. The authors call for closer collaboration between climate services and energy planners, friendlier tools, and feedback loops to shorten adoption.
arxiv-2605-00817:
Sailesh Panda, Pritam Kadasi, Abhishek Upperwal, and Mayank Singh test whether language models truly follow step-by-step arithmetic procedures, rather than just reaching plausible answers. Their diagnostic benchmark gives a model a defined procedure and two numbers, and asks for the final value. Difficulty grows through longer procedures and through steps that must look back at earlier intermediate results.

Average first-answer accuracy fell from well over half on five-step procedures to about one fifth on ninety-five-step procedures. Looking at full outputs, failures often meant missing answers, answers given too early, self-correction after an initial error, or traces that stopped short. The pattern shows steady decline as procedural complexity rises.
arxiv-2605-00917:
Angshul Majumdar proves that deciding whether a tensor's spectral norm exceeds a given threshold is hard for the existential theory of the reals, a strong form of hardness. For a rationally specified tensor, the feasible domain is compact, so attaining the maximum is not the issue; the threshold decision is. The proof uses an explicit polynomial-time reduction from bounded quartic equality testing.

Steps transform that testing problem into homogeneous quadratic sphere testing, then into a quartic form whose maximum over the unit sphere separates workable from unworkable cases. Writing the quartic form as a symmetric order-four tensor completes the reduction. The obstruction is thus real algebraic testing itself, not only nonconvex search.
arxiv-2605-01317:
Vira Putri Maharani and five co-authors compare older machine learning tools with a deep learning model on reviews of the Mobile Legends game app. Their data set holds 10,000 reviews, each tagged as positive, negative, or neutral in tone.

The older tools use word counts and an automated model search, while the deep model, an LSTM, reads each review as a sequence so word order counts. The LSTM wins, reaching about 92 percent correct labels and a strong score across all three tone classes. The authors argue that deep learning copes better with the slang and loose, context-based wording that players use in app reviews.
arxiv-2605-01417:
Benjamin Warner and 34 co-authors release Medmarks, an open test suite for judging language models on medical work. Current suites are wearing out: top models max them out, key data sets sit behind restrictions, and task coverage is patchy.

Medmarks packs 30 benchmarks across question answering, fact extraction, medical calculation, and open clinical reasoning. The team runs 61 models in 71 setups, scoring with checkable metrics plus a model judge. Top reasoning systems from the big labs lead, and they also use far fewer tokens than open-weight rivals. Models tuned for medicine beat their general base versions, and smaller models are swayed by answer order. A slice of the suite doubles as training grounds for post-training medical reasoning. All code is public.
arxiv-2605-01717:
Xinran Li and four co-authors extract sentiment quadruples from multi-round dialogue: who holds an opinion, about what aspect, with what polarity, in conversation that jumps between threads. Graph networks used for this task import structural noise and ignore speaking order, while standard position codes flatten the difference between word order inside a reply and progress across replies.

Their framework answers both faults. A thread-constrained directed acyclic graph filters cross-thread noise, keeps the dialogue connected through a root anchor, and respects time order. A discourse-aware rotary position code then aligns meaning across layers, measures thread distance in tree steps, and adds utterance-level progress so distant tokens stop diluting. On two benchmark data sets the combined design posts state-of-the-art scores for conversational quadruple analysis.
arxiv-2605-02417:
Desong Yang and Mang Ye present DirectEdit, a training-free image editing method for flow-based text-to-image models that removes reconstruction error at its source. Editing usually adds noise to a clean image through inversion, then denoises along separate reconstruction and editing paths. Because the reconstruction path is approximated with noisy latents from mismatched timesteps, drift accumulates and limits fidelity.

The authors analyse inversion inside the flow transformer step by step. DirectEdit aligns the forward paths directly, rather than trying to repair the inversion path as most prior work does. That eliminates the inherent reconstruction error with no extra neural function evaluations. Step-level accuracy in inversion is the paper's central claim, aimed at edits that keep unedited regions faithful.
arxiv-2605-02917:
Sheng Wong and seven co-authors present PRISM-CTG, a foundation model for reading cardiotocography, the fetal heart and contraction traces used to monitor labor. Supervised models for this task rely on small, carefully labeled sets from limited groups of patients, leaving large volumes of informative recordings unused. Self-supervised pretraining on those unlabeled traces is the alternative pursued here.

The model learns from three joined tasks: rebuilding masked signal parts under a random projection guide, predicting clinical variables, and classifying features. Each task gets its own token, and controlled cross-attention lets them share context. Metadata and domain knowledge, often ignored in training, become prediction targets that steer learning toward clinical meaning. The result is a reusable representation for later tasks in fetal monitoring.
arxiv-2605-03117:
Shahd Seddik, Fahd Seddik, Amirrezza Esmaeili, Mahdieh Sadatbenis, and Fatemeh Fard present ARISE, a toolset that helps AI agents repair code across a whole repository. Finding a fault among thousands of files needs more than file structure; agents also need to know how variable values flow inside each procedure.

ARISE builds a graph down to single statements linked by define-use edges and offers data-flow slicing as a one-call tool for any agent framework. On SWE-bench Lite with an open coder model, it raised solved issues and sharply improved function and line localization. Tests credit the data-flow graph, not the tool layout.
arxiv-2605-03217:
Yash Aggarwal, Atmika Gorti, Vinija Jain, Aman Chadha, Krishnaprasad Thirunarayan, and Manas Gaur measure moral sensitivity in language models as a graded trait, not a yes-or-no bias label. Bias often grows with context pressure, so binary tests miss how it actually emerges.

Their Moral Sensitivity Index scores biased output across seven tiers, from abstract numbers to settings rooted in historic injustice. Four leading models showed distinct profiles shaped by their alignment design. Circuit-level checks on criminal-bias cases then found a U-shaped pattern: small models biased, tuned models clean, and reasoning-distilled models biased again, with matching circuits across stages.
arxiv-2605-03317:
Ruibin Min, Yexin Liu, Aimin Pan, Changsheng Lu, Jiafei Wu, Kelu Yao, Xiaogang Xu, and Harry Yang improve diffusion transformer training with alignment that adapts across the denoising timeline. Fixed alignment targets ignore a basic fact: early noisy steps need coarse layout guidance, while late steps need fine spatial detail.

Their AHPA framework draws multi-level features from the frozen image encoder, spanning local geometry to broad semantics. A timestep-aware router weights those levels to match the model's current needs. Experiments show faster convergence and better generation quality over baselines, with no added inference cost and no external encoder supervision.
arxiv-2605-03417:
Mengqi Zhang, Dongdong Wan, and Huanshu Tan study how shear-thinning changes the stability of the Stokes layer, an oscillating flow above a plate, in Carreau fluids. Many real fluids thin under shear, and whether that steadies or destabilizes a time-periodic layer was not settled.

They solve the base flow numerically and by a binomial expansion in the fluid response time, with good agreement at small values. Floquet analysis shows stronger thinning, through a lower power-law exponent, steadily stabilizes the flow, while the response time acts non-monotonically. Energy analysis traces growth to phase alignment with the base shear.
arxiv-2605-03517:
Fabian A. Mikulasch and Friedemann Zenke propose a single framework for self-supervised learning, the method that lets models learn useful representations from unlabeled data. They cast it as latent distribution matching: a representation should fit an assumed latent model well, yet stay spread out enough to avoid collapse. That pair of goals is called alignment and uniformity.

Their view unifies independent component analysis with contrastive, non-contrastive, and predictive methods, including stop-gradient approaches. From it they derive a sampling-free Bayesian filtering model with a Kalman-based predictor for high-dimensional time series. They also prove that predictive matching can recover identifiable latent representations under mild assumptions.
arxiv-2605-04117:
Marco Menale, Giuseppe Toscani, and Mattia Zanella build a kinetic framework for the spread of antimicrobial resistance. The population is divided into susceptible, infectious, recovered, and resistant compartments. Their aim is to measure how antimicrobial use drives resistance. Too much use, or the wrong use, speeds it up. In the model, a share of infectious people moves into the resistant compartment during an infection. The infection is driven by susceptible-infectious contacts.

The model is a system of Boltzmann-type equations for pairwise interactions. Added linear operators represent recovery, resistance growth, and reinfection. In the grazing collision limit, the authors show the Boltzmann system is well matched by coupled Fokker-Planck equations. That form is easier to handle. They study its long-time behavior. The analysis shows how interaction terms drive the population toward a stable end state.
arxiv-2605-04217:
Yaobo Zhang studies how neural networks tell a model where each word sits relative to others, a step that shapes what attention can learn. Standard methods add either a rotating phase or a simple distance penalty, each giving the model a limited set of patterns.

Zhang combines a rotating part and a fading part inside one mathematical block, producing patterns that wave and decay together, with distance itself scaling the wave. He gives the exact form, a stable variant that trades exactness for safer numbers, and tests at the kernel level plus on a synthetic task designed for this structure.
arxiv-2605-04417:
Chatchawan Panraksa and Aram Tangboonduangjit analyse the cycles created by repeating Chebyshev polynomials modulo powers of an odd prime. Lifting a polynomial map from a prime modulus to a prime power can change both how many cycles exist and how long they are, and the pattern was not fully known.

For every degree, prime, and power, they give explicit formulas for the number of fixed points, all possible cycle lengths, and how many cycles have each length. The prime three needs a special correction, which they explain through rational fixed points colliding modulo three. Their proofs combine the classical link between Chebyshev polynomials and power maps with p-adic arithmetic.
arxiv-2605-04817: Samuel Kalužný and Tibor Macko determine, up to some extension problems, the higher smooth surgery structure sets of complex projective spaces and how they map to their topological versions in low dimensions. Surgery structure sets classify the ways a space can carry a smooth structure. This article is the first of two, and it concentrates on the free subgroup, where the authors obtain information in all dimensions. The torsion part is left to the second article.
arxiv-2605-05017:
Xiaoliang Fan and eight co-authors argue, in a position paper, that embodied AI needs privacy treated as a whole-life-cycle design constraint rather than a patch for single stages. Robots and similar systems are moving from simulation into homes and other sensitive places. Optimising sensing, planning, and interaction separately, they warn, creates a combined privacy crisis once deployed often.

Their proposed framework, SPINE, treats privacy as a changing control signal that flows across every stage of the system. A classification matrix coordinates sensitivity across stage boundaries. Early simulation and real-world case studies show how privacy limits reshape later behaviour, and why scattered local fixes cannot be enough.
arxiv-2605-05517:
Many mechanical systems look the same after a rescaling, and that symmetry can simplify them. Javier Fernández, Sergio Grillo, Juan Carlos Marrero, and Edith Padrón define a reduction procedure for Lagrangian systems with such scaling symmetries. The reduced problem keeps the essential dynamics in fewer variables.

Paths of the full system can be rebuilt, up to quadratures, from the critical points of the reduced principle. Those points obey equations the authors present as the scaling analogue of the Lagrange-Poincaré equations. They close by asking whether these systems connect naturally to the Herglotz variational principle.
arxiv-2605-05617:
Strong electric fields can tear electrons from atoms, a process called tunneling ionization. Marcelo F. Ciappina rebuilds the standard theory of that process inside space-fractional quantum mechanics, where the usual kinetic energy is replaced by a fractional operator. That change makes the dynamics nonlocal, so old formulas must be derived anew.

Working with a static field, he obtains a closed-form tunneling exponent for a triangular barrier. The familiar scaling with ionization energy changes, and a telling sine factor appears. He also lays out how time-dependent runs could test the new exponent, giving strong-field physics a clear benchmark.
arxiv-2605-05817:
General relativity is usually written as a textbook theory, but Callum Bell and David Sloan recast it in first-order form as an action-dependent, non-conservative one. They apply earlier results on scaling symmetries for theories with special Lagrangians. Einstein's theory splits into conformal spacetime geometry plus a dissipative sector.

The dissipative part makes up for removing scale, which the conformal factor normally encodes. The linearized equations give the free wave equation one expects for metric ripples. At second order, covering gravity's backreaction, the behavior departs from the standard story in ways the authors examine.
arxiv-2605-06417:
Nassim Bourarach, Franck Picard, Vincent Rivoirard, and Angelina Roche study how well functional principal parts can be estimated from noisy data seen only on a grid. Curves are seen at shared points with added noise, and the goal is the covariance eigenfunctions and eigenvalues. Smoothness of the kernel alone, they show, cannot guarantee that eigenfunction estimates hold up.

Their process class controls both kernel smoothness and a local eigengap measure, leading to lower bounds that separate sampling, discretization, and spectral effects. A wavelet projection estimator using Coiflet functions matches those bounds in sample size and grid resolution. The framework also covers several classical Gaussian processes and related constructions.
arxiv-2605-06717:
Nghi D. Q. Bui and Georgios Evangelopoulos argue that coding agents need proactivity, not just autonomy. Today's agents already edit repositories, open pull requests, and run scheduled routines. The next step is agents that notice relevant changes before being asked, connect signals across tools, choose when to interrupt, and remember preferences across sessions. Yet proactivity itself lacks a clear definition or measures.

The authors ground the idea in mixed-initiative interaction: what matters is the agent's insight policy, deciding what deserves attention and whether to surface it. They propose three levels of proactivity, compare current agents against five practical criteria, and sketch a user-simulation protocol with three evaluation targets.
arxiv-2605-07017:
Giuseppe Spallitta, Leonardo Duenas-Osorio, and Moshe Y. Vardi look for short partial solutions to satisfiability problems. Many reasoning tasks need an implicant, a small set of choices that already guarantees a formula can be satisfied. Standard encodings into Ising or QUBO models assign every variable, leaving no way to mark a variable as unused.

The authors add a dual-polarity encoding that builds don't-care choices into the quadratic model itself. Under stated conditions, the best solutions of the model are short, even minimal, partial assignments. Tests with simulated annealing leave about a third of variables unassigned on random formulas. Repeated rounds often reach true minimality.
arxiv-2605-07117:
Dawood Wasif and three co-authors protect individual fairness when groups must learn together without pooling their data. In vertical federated learning, each party holds different facts about the same people, and protected traits may stay private. The question is whether changing such a trait would arbitrarily flip a person's outcome.

Their SCC-VFL system finds feature roles privately, edits only allowed mediator features in what-if tests, and punishes banned outcome changes. Across credit, health, and crime datasets, it held or improved scores while cutting decision flip rates sharply against strong rivals. It also resisted attacks that try to infer that trait.
arxiv-2605-07317:
Rui Fang, Hsi-Wen Chen, and Ming-Syan Chen make vision transformers cheaper to run by combining low-precision math with early exits. Quantization noise can upset exit choices and amplify errors along shifting paths, because existing methods assume the full network always runs. Their framing accounts for how often each layer actually faces that noise.

A two-level system then tunes exit thresholds and bit widths together under clear risk control. The result improves the accuracy-speed frontier, cutting the math load sharply while holding accuracy. Across sorting, spotting, and outlining tasks, it beat strong rivals by wide margins, offering a sturdier route to deploying such models on limited hardware.
arxiv-2605-07617:
Chitayat and Hajra classify a family of algebraic surfaces defined by a simple equation in three variables. Each surface comes from a sum of three powers plus one, with exponents of at least two, over the complex numbers. The question is when two such surfaces are isomorphic, meaning they share the same structure under a change of variables.

The authors prove that two surfaces in the family are isomorphic exactly when their exponent triples match up to a permutation of the entries. In other words, reordering the exponents changes nothing, but any other change gives a genuinely different surface. The result belongs to the wider task of classifying varieties up to isomorphism, a core and often hard challenge in algebraic geometry. It extends the picture beyond classical examples such as Danielewski surfaces, used here as a point of comparison. The proof gives a clean numerical test for telling them apart.
arxiv-2605-07817:
Brown Ebouky and five co-authors give a vision-language model something like human gaze control. People reason visually by aiming a sharp fovea at task-relevant details while keeping the whole scene in peripheral view. Ordinary models instead process everything passively, and their visual evidence dilutes as reasoning chains grow longer.

GazeVLM emits gaze actions inside its reasoning, as tags naming a region to inspect. During training, a suppression bias dampens features outside gazed regions, teaching the model to steer its own attention. At deployment the bias is removed, and the model keeps most of the effect in an ordinary forward pass. On high-resolution benchmarks it beat its base models by about four points and agentic image-cropping pipelines by five to twelve.
arxiv-2605-07917:
Yannick Mvondo-She studies the logarithmic graviton of critical topologically massive gravity from inside the bulk spacetime. Starting from the Grumiller-Johansson mode, the radial coordinate is carried into the complex plane. The mode's monodromy, how it changes when carried around a loop, is read off directly from the branch structure and winding of its logarithmic radial factor.

Global descendants of the mode are then built by differential action, and each one splits into a universal log part plus a log-free meromorphic remainder. The result is an unipotent monodromy across the whole family.
