Generative retrieval models encode a user's listening or shopping history, then generate the next recommended item. Standard attention reads every pair of history entries, so cost grows quadratically and becomes a latency bottleneck for active users. Most faster attention variants only handle one-directional reading, yet encoders benefit from reading both ways.

Their layer, Gated Bidirectional Linear Attention, runs in linear time while still reading sequences in both directions. It adds local mixing, a gating mechanism for soft forgetting of old entries, and a gated normalization step. A hybrid encoder alternating standard and new layers matched full attention quality on a large Yandex Music dataset. On modern graphics hardware the new layer ran up to about eight times faster at the longest history length tested.
arxiv-2606-07417:
Agresti, Germ, and Veraar build a local theory for stochastic reaction-diffusion equations driven by rough noise, in this 2026 arXiv paper. These equations model chemistry, ecology, and pattern formation buffeted by forcing. When the noise is not trace-class, a technical condition meaning its roughness is severe, solutions have low regularity and the nonlinear terms become hard to define. The authors prove local existence and uniqueness for systems from irregular data, pinpointing which initial-data spaces are critical for a range of nonlinearities.

The framework yields instant smoothing, criteria for when they blow up, and conditions keeping them positive, which matters for population models. Applications cover systems including stochastic Allen-Cahn, Burgers, Fisher-KPP, and Gray-Scott equations. Standard regimes gain results for trace-class and space-time white noise. In 1 dimension with white noise, combining their local theory with global estimates handles a singular regime that resisted treatment.
arxiv-2606-07917:
Shastry and colleagues at the Joint Physics Analysis Center extract a complete set of coupling constants linking two short-lived particles, in this 2026 arXiv paper. The particles are the nucleon and the Delta resonance, an excited state of the nucleon. Their couplings to three exchanged mesons, rho, b-one, and a-two, govern how photon beams produce Delta particles from protons, a basic hadron process never fully pinned down.

The team works in a Regge framework, where families of particles are exchanged together rather than one at a time. They fit polarised photo-production data from the GlueX experiment, where a photon knocks a pion and a Delta out of a proton. The fit yields the first determination of the complete set of nucleon-Delta couplings to all three mesons. Such couplings feed amplitude analyses across hadron spectroscopy, so a consistent set sharpens other extractions depending on this reaction.
arxiv-2606-08117:
Michel Berthier, Gabriel Niebel, and Edoardo Provenzi classify all the ways a two-state quantum system over the real numbers can evolve. They then use the result to model colour vision, in this 2026 arXiv paper. A rebit is a qubit restricted to real amplitudes. Its Markovian, memoryless evolutions form one-parameter families of channels. The authors characterise them through the GKSL equation, the standard generator form for such dynamics, identifying the Lindblad generators and positivity conditions.

The application is perception. In a recent model, perceived colours arise from Lüders measurements on the rebit state space. The chromatic distortion caused by a non-neutral illuminant, light that is not white, acts as a Markovian rebit channel that shrinks, over time, how distinguishable colours are. Simulations on digital images illustrate the effect. Other channels on the list could model colour vision deficiencies the same way.
arxiv-2606-08617:
Fanjin Zhang and colleagues fix mislabeled authorship in academic databases by cross-checking sources against each other, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Author name disambiguation, deciding which papers belong to which real person among namesakes, is a key challenge for academic search. Current algorithms suffer stacked errors in paper-author assignments. They also overlook inconsistent assignments across sources. The authors explore a new perspective: cross-source correction, using exactly those mismatches, since disagreement between sources flags where errors likely hide.

Their framework, CrossND, integrates data refinement, cross-source reasoning, and test-time scaling. A chain-of-refinement pipeline first denoises author profiles and produces more accurate paper-author matching scores. A supervised fine-tuning process then uses these refined signals. Reasoning across sources resolves conflicts that no single source can settle alone. Test-time scaling spends extra compute on the hardest cases.
arxiv-2606-08717:
Martínez-Gil, Bargueño, and Miret-Artés propose a way to amplify one of physics' tiniest effects into something countable, in this 2026 arXiv paper. The weak nuclear force violates parity, mirror symmetry, which should make left- and right-handed versions of a chiral molecule differ slightly in energy. This parity-violating energy difference is far too small to measure directly. The authors propose detecting it indirectly. They form chiral molecules from ultracold collisions of achiral diatomic molecules, where the tiny bias slightly shifts the resonance energies of the two handed configurations.

After formation, the molecules evolve inside a Bose-Einstein condensate, with tunneling between the two handed states and thermal conversion competing. Solving coupled rate equations, the authors show the collective dynamics can amplify the microscopic bias into a complete population imbalance.
arxiv-2606-09117:
Fan and colleagues train a network on an optical Ising machine, borrowing a classic optimizer for faster settling, in this 2026 arXiv paper. A coherent Ising machine is a device whose dynamics seek low-energy states of an Ising model, a lattice of interacting spins. They use one to train an energy-based network by equilibrium propagation. In that local learning rule, the network settles freely, then again with output nudged to target, and the difference teaches the weights.

Performance matched software implementations of the same method. Adam, deep learning's workhorse optimizer, is integrated into solving for the Hopfield network's ground state, significantly improving convergence speed and accuracy. They demonstrated it on deeper architectures and convolutional operations. The results sketch a route to efficient training hardware from analog circuits, optoelectronics, or photonics, where device physics does work GPUs brute-force today.
arxiv-2606-09217:
Muskan maps out how quantum key distribution could deliver encryption keys from satellites, in this thesis-length 2026 arXiv paper. Quantum key distribution shares secret keys encoded in quantum states, secure because eavesdropping disturbs the states. Fiber networks limit its range, so satellites in low Earth orbit are the route to global coverage. The study progresses from standard protocols to high-dimensional schemes and finally to realistic finite-key analysis.

Early chapters evaluate prepare-and-measure and entanglement-based protocols under circular-beam models of the satellite link, tracking atmospheric attenuation, pointing errors, and orbit geometry. High-dimensional encoding, using extra photonic degrees of freedom, buys rate and noise tolerance. The last part adds finite-size statistics and decoy states for a CubeSat downlink running BB84, the standard protocol, under mission-like conditions. The arc gives system designers one framework running from ideal protocols to deployable key rates.
arxiv-2606-09317:
Agneedh Basu and colleagues run a head-to-head comparison of speech encoders and training objectives for telling India's languages apart by ear, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Spoken language identification routes speech to the right downstream model, but Indic languages overlap heavily in sound and many have little labeled data. The study pairs two pretrained encoders, Whisper and FastConformer, with a simple linear classifier across 42 languages in 4 families. Each is tested frozen and fine-tuned, under 3 objectives.

Trained on the Vaani dataset and tested cross-corpus on FLEURS and Kathbath, the frozen FastConformer passed 90 percent macro accuracy with no tuning, well ahead of Whisper out of domain. Fine-tuned Whisper won in-domain instead. Hierarchical softmax beat cross-entropy and contrastive training for both encoders, largest gains out of domain; the contrastive loss actually hurt FastConformer's generalization. Central Indo-Aryan varieties proved hardest, with Hindi-Urdu the dominant confusion pair.
arxiv-2606-09417:
Maxim Lyutikov proposes a plasma mechanism that could power fast radio bursts in this 2026 arXiv paper. Fast radio bursts are millisecond flashes of radio energy from deep space, widely linked to magnetars, neutron stars with extreme magnetic fields. Lyutikov studies long-wavelength X-modes, a type of electromagnetic wave, travelling through a magnetised plasma of electrons and positrons.

Simulations show that when the wave's own magnetic field exceeds the background guide field, the wave steepens and collapses within a fraction of its natural timescale. The energy, first spread over large scales, is squeezed into short, intense, localised pulses. By late times, nearly ninety percent of the initial electromagnetic energy sits inside these pulses, which resemble the observed bursts. The collapse also accelerates particles to very high energies with an unusually hard spectrum, suggesting companion high-energy flashes could accompany the radio emission from magnetar magnetospheres.
arxiv-2606-09517:
Jan Niklas Lettner, Hadeer El Ashhab, and Benjamin Schäfer warn that electricity price forecasts can look precise while being statistically untrustworthy in this 2026 arXiv paper. Probabilistic forecasts give a distribution of possible prices, which traders need for risk management as renewable generation makes markets more volatile. Two qualities matter: sharpness, how narrow the forecast distribution is, and calibration, whether predicted probabilities match observed frequencies.

The authors show that the standard proper scoring rules used to train these models often reward sharpness at the expense of calibration. A model can then become an overconfident proxy for a plain point forecast, with narrow intervals that miss reality far too often. They conclude that future research must build this balance into objectives and model design. Only then will the uncertainty estimates carry the distributional integrity that market decisions require.
arxiv-2606-09717:
Li Zhu, Shekhar Nayak, and Matt Coler ask which voice traits make fake speech sound sarcastic in this 2026 arXiv paper. Sarcasm flips a line's plain sense, and tone of voice carries much of the flip. Past studies used real speech, where pace, pitch swing, and loudness move together. Their joint drift hides which trait does the work.

The team used a neural text-to-speech system with prompt-based control. They built a balanced set of clips that vary pace, pitch swing, and loudness one at a time. Human listeners rated each clip for sarcasm and natural feel. A foundation model that hears audio gave its own calls for the same clips. Loudness drove the human sense of sarcasm most. The model leaned instead on speech pace. That split shows a gap in how machines weigh voice cues.
arxiv-2606-09817:
Abhner de Almeida, Gary Mamon, and Gastão Lima Neto trace how dwarf galaxies shrink into compact satellites in this 2026 arXiv paper. The stage is TNG50, a large hydrodynamical simulation of cosmic growth. Dwarf galaxies there end with a wide spread of sizes at one mass. The team sorts the tight ones from the normal by the size-mass line.

Two firm paths to small size stand out, plus a third, more tentative one. Dark-matter-rich compact dwarfs live in poor zones with few mergers. Their calm past lets low-spin gas flow in, sparking dense inner star birth that packs the core. Dark-matter-poor ones, in contrast, are squeezed by tides that strip their outer stars. Gas speeds that squeeze by at least fifteen percent. A few rich ones start with a starburst crushed out by ram pressure at first close pass.
arxiv-2606-09917:
Chen and Yiu add geometry to state space models, which scan sequences in linear time, in a 2026 arXiv paper on time series forecasting. Their concern is multivariate data, where many linked variables change together. Standard models flatten these links and lose how correlations evolve. The authors instead treat correlation structure as a path on a curved mathematical space.

Their model, SPDM, tracks covariance matrices on the symmetric positive definite manifold, a space of matrices that describe spread and correlation. It projects that path into a flat tangent space and uses the geometry to steer the model's selective scanning. The design keeps the linear-time cost of the Mamba architecture it builds on. Across eleven real-world benchmark datasets, SPDM reached state-of-the-art forecasting results, and follow-up studies credited the geometric constraints as the main factor behind the gains. Code is publicly available.
arxiv-2606-10217:
Huang and colleagues turn the alignment process used to make language models behave into a shield against dataset spying, in a 2026 arXiv paper on machine learning privacy. Models fine-tuned on domain data can leak dataset-level properties, such as the fraction of records with some trait, through property inference attacks. Their defense instead reshapes the model's output distribution after training.

They adapt two standard alignment frameworks, Direct Preference Optimization and Group Relative Policy Optimization, constructing preference pairs and a reward function that push outputs toward a target property ratio. The training data itself is untouched, so the defense applies when data is unavailable or models are already deployed. Comprehensive experiments show the alignment-based defenses effectively mitigate property inference attacks while maintaining a strong trade-off between utility and confidentiality. The work reframes alignment as a privacy tool, not just a behavior-shaping one.
arxiv-2606-10417:
Paul and Holmes tackle a blind spot in software testing in this 2026 arXiv paper: standard quality scores measure how code runs, not whether it does what it should. Code coverage records which lines tests execute, and mutation testing checks whether tests catch planted faults. Neither reveals a behavioural gap, a documented expected behaviour that no test checks. Their tool, bFinder, extracts expected behaviours from documentation and code and matches them against test cases.

Across ten popular open-source Java libraries, bFinder extracted 20,729 behaviours with 93.1 percent precision from 8,922 methods in total. At least 17.5 percent of those behaviours are entirely untested in the developers' own suites, and automatic test generators leave even larger gaps. The misses are not predicted by the old scores: many sit in methods with perfect line coverage, so behavioural coverage adds a genuinely separate measure of test quality.
arxiv-2606-10617:
Wei and colleagues solve a merging problem for image generation models in this 2026 arXiv paper. Low-rank adapters, called LoRAs, are small add-ons that teach a diffusion model a style or skill, and users naturally want several at once. Naively merging their weights causes interference, where add-ons collide and corrupt each other. SSR-Merge refuses to merge weights at all. It concatenates the adapters into one shared subspace, then routes signals inside it. An inverse correlation matrix decorrelates mixed signals, and a guide matrix steers each purified signal into its own task's subspace.

The authors prove this routing matches the ordinary least squares solution, so the merge is principled, not heuristic. A streaming variant updates on the fly, cutting memory and compute. Experiments show significant gains over leading merging techniques at comparable efficiency, with no training. Interference, the paper argues, is a routing problem.
arxiv-2606-10817:
Hiatt, Simpson, Wang, and Wu study Euler characteristics of tropical varieties in this 2026 arXiv paper. Tropical geometry replaces algebraic shapes with piecewise-linear ones. The authors ask whether a classical sign rule survives: for subvarieties of complex abelian varieties, Green and Lazarsfeld showed a certain signed Euler characteristic is never negative.

For H-regular tropical subvarieties, those locally modeled on well-behaved cases, the answer is yes: the signed Euler characteristic stays nonnegative. The proof rests on a local vanishing theorem for H-regular tropical fans, which also yields a Lefschetz-type result. For general tropical subvarieties the rule fails, and they build a three-dimensional fan whose link is not a bouquet of 2-spheres.
arxiv-2606-11217:
Vaccaro argues in a 2026 arXiv paper that experiments with AI agents need preregistration. Researchers increasingly run in silico behavioral experiments, using language model agents as stand-ins for human participants in studies of cognition, decisions, and social dynamics. The approach is cheap and scalable, and it matters in its own right now that agents negotiate and transact for real organizations.

These experiments inherit the weaknesses of human subjects research, and amplify some. Vaccaro catalogs the researcher degrees of freedom introduced: model selection, prompt wording, settings, and outcome-contingent redesign, quietly reshaping the study after seeing results. Iteration is so cheap, and reporting norms so weak, that such choices are easy to exploit and hard to detect. That is exactly the failure mode preregistration was built to block. The paper proposes a preregistration template tailored to agent experiments, and calls on conferences, journals, and funders to make it standard practice.
arxiv-2606-11317:
Sannino's lecture notes present methods for composite operators in a 2026 arXiv paper. The notes introduce conformal field theory through a semiclassical framework for scaling dimensions of composite operators, especially ones built from many field powers. The core idea: at large charge, an operator creates a highly occupied state, and through the state-operator correspondence its dimension is the energy of that state on a cylinder.

The notes build a complete route from conformal symmetry to semiclassical dynamics. Early parts review the conformal group, primary fields, radial quantization, and mixing. It is built first in the free scalar theory, then through the double-scaling limit and Bohr-Sommerfeld rules. Later parts develop periodic saddles, Floquet theory, fluctuation determinants, and the Gutzwiller trace formula. The final part applies everything to the quartic scalar theory near four dimensions at the Wilson-Fisher fixed point, deriving the one-loop large-charge dimensions.
arxiv-2606-11417:
Mittal and Gupta prove a folk claim about intrinsic motivation in a 2026 arXiv paper. Compression progress rewards an agent when its world model gets better at predicting or compressing experience. The folk claim: this reward is credible because it is paid only for learning, immune to Goodhart gaming. They make it precise: reward is the signed decrease of a fixed sealed-audit loss.

Cumulative reward then telescopes exactly to endpoint audit improvement. Consequently, no policy can drive reward upward indefinitely while true audit performance stagnates or degrades. For finite audit panels, the same result holds with a sharp false-positive budget, bounding empirical reward by true improvement plus a slack term. The sealed audit is the key design element, since the audited loss cannot be shaped by the agent's own behavior. The authors present this as a Goodhart-resistant basis for compression-based intrinsic motivation.
arxiv-2606-11717:
Dan Jiang, Yin Huang and JiongJiong Zhao reinterpret several exotic particles as molecules in this 2026 arXiv paper on hadron physics. Some observed particles cannot be built from the usual quark combinations, so researchers suspect molecular states: two ordinary particles bound loosely together. The charmed-strange family, containing a charm quark and a strange quark, has known candidates built from a kaon and a D meson.

Using the Gaussian expansion method to solve the Schrödinger equation with forces from exchanging five meson types, the team tests assignments for heavier states. One state fits a pure P-wave molecule of a D meson and an excited kaon, its mass about fifty-four energy units below the pair's threshold. Two states near the same mass fit molecules of excited partners, dominated by different wave components. Additional molecular states with various spins are also predicted.
arxiv-2606-12217:
Qiu and co-authors fix a subtle failure in robots that imagine the future before acting, in this 2026 arXiv paper. World action models first generate a video of how a scene may evolve, then decode robot actions from that imagined future, and pretty futures do not guarantee good actions. Probing attention patterns and running causal interventions, tests that change one factor at a time, shows the action decoder stares at the wrong regions.

Their fix, AGRA, aligns the video model's inner features with semantic representations from a foundation visual encoder, a large pretrained vision system. On real-world manipulation tasks, the decoder then focuses on true hand-object interaction regions. Object localization and affordance understanding, knowing what a part is for, both improve. The policy also resists perturbations in irrelevant regions. Gains hold both on familiar tasks and on unseen variations, showing better generalization.
arxiv-2606-12317:
Jacobs packages Bayesian survival models that untangle treatment effects, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Survival analysis predicts time until an event, like relapse, when many patients are only partly observed: censored. Bayesian additive regression trees sum many decision trees into a flexible predictor needing no fixed formula. Existing packages miss interval-censored data, where events are known only to fall between checkups. ShrinkageTrees fills those gaps inside an accelerated failure time framework.

Two regularizations keep trees honest: priors penalizing deep structure, and shrinkage priors pulling step heights toward zero. The package first implements the Horseshoe Forest, whose prior shrinks noise while sparing signals. A tau-learner architecture splits prognostic and treatment-effect parts for causal questions. An Rcpp backend and multi-chain sampling support fitting, prediction, and diagnostics. It is the first CRAN package combining interval-censored survival, the tau-learner, and horseshoe step heights in one framework.
arxiv-2606-12617:
Alexander Yelland and co-authors read the carbon in stars to reconstruct how the first small galaxies lived and died, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Carbon-enhanced metal-poor stars carry carbon from early enrichment, preserving the fingerprints of the first supernovae. The team compiled a thousand stellar carbon abundances across the halo, ultra-faint dwarfs, classical dwarfs, accreted systems, and streams.

A pattern emerges with size. Tiny ultra-faint dwarfs show high fractions of carbon-enhanced stars at low metallicity; classical dwarfs show few. This defines a relation between a dwarf's brightness and its carbon-enhanced fraction. The ultra-faints' richness points to enrichment by faint supernovae, since blasts would have shut down their star formation. The classical dwarfs' poverty implies they formed in place, not by assembling smaller pieces. Eight stars sit in a forbidden zone for cooling, implicating dust-driven cooling in the first star formation.
arxiv-2606-12717:
Van den Berg constructs an interpolation for option-pricing volatility models that stays inside the model family and creates no arbitrage, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Option models fit the risk-neutral density of a forward price at each expiry as a mixture, a blend of bell-shaped components. But expiries are sparse, so pricing between them needs densities at intermediate times. A valid interpolation must remain a mixture and avoid calendar-spread arbitrage, meaning prices cannot fall as expiry lengthens.

His construction freezes both endpoint mixtures' locations and widths in a pool of at most twice as many components, then moves only the weights along a line. He proves the path is arbitrage-free whenever the endpoints are, and that for full-support kernels such as Gaussian components it is realised by a unique local-volatility diffusion. The scheme chains across a term structure at additive cost.
arxiv-2606-13117:
Russell and colleagues use density functional theory to model the conductive nickel-organic nanoribbons inside cable bacteria and test whether their structure can support efficient electron transport, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Cable bacteria are many-celled bacteria that conduct electricity over centimetre scales through a fibre network in their cell envelope, with conductivity matching the best conductive polymers. Microscopy and spectroscopy show each fibre embeds a bundle of nanoribbons built from stacked nickel bis(dithiolene) oligomers, called NiBiD units.

The models examine possible stacking layouts and their electronic properties. In the AB-type structure that is most stable by energy, some nickel centres become 5-fold coordinated through formation of an inter-layer nickel-sulfur coordination bond. In several low-lying structures, the electronic coupling between nearby molecules exceeds the critical threshold for charge delocalisation, so charge can move beyond the small-polaron hopping regime.
arxiv-2606-13317:
Chen and colleagues present SkillCAT in this 2026 arXiv paper, a framework that helps language model agents improve their own skills. Agents learn by converting execution records into reusable skill documents, but existing pipelines learn from one attempt per task. They also merge candidate improvements before testing them, and load the skill library every time. SkillCAT separates the work into three stages. The first samples attempts per task and contrasts successes with failures to find what caused the difference.

The second stage replays each candidate patch on cloned tasks and keeps patches that help or do no harm. The third stage organises the skills into a routable network of capability nodes, so each task loads only the skills it needs. The authors evaluate on agent benchmarks covering spreadsheets, table questions, and document understanding. They test whether skills transfer across underlying models and to new task types.
arxiv-2606-13817:
Jiang and colleagues build a world model that helps robots predict how floating objects will move when unseen currents push them around. World models are learned simulators that forecast future images from past images and actions, letting a robot plan ahead. Boats and drifting objects keep moving from momentum, and water or wind adds hidden drift that a single camera frame cannot reveal. Their 2026 arXiv paper, FlowMo-WM, tackles both effects together.

The model splits its memory into two parts. A short history summarizes the object's own motion, while a longer history captures slow ambient influences such as currents. A special transition step separates action-driven motion from drift effects during forecasts. In simulated surface vehicle tests with varied hidden flows, FlowMo-WM predicted long rollouts more accurately than comparable models. Erasing or shuffling the drift memory hurt stability, showing the learned context does real work.
arxiv-2606-13917:
Zhang and colleagues speed up the search for low-energy routes between crystal structures. A minimum energy pathway shows how a material transforms, revealing barriers and intermediate states. The solid-state nudged elastic band method traces such paths but demands costly quantum calculations at every step. Their 2026 arXiv paper builds a hybrid: two pre-trained machine learning models, EquiformerV2 and eSEN, do early work, and density functional theory refines it.

The hybrid was applied to three systems: cesium lead iodide, gallium nitride, and titanium dioxide. It converged to the same pathways full first-principles calculations predict. The speedup reached sevenfold in the best case. Models only propose starting paths that quantum calculations then verify, so accuracy stays anchored to physics. The framework doubles as a benchmark for machine learning potentials, showing where their energy, force, and stress predictions still stray.
arxiv-2606-14117:
Cohen and Kincaid borrow psychology's Implicit Association Test to probe bias in language models, fixing a flaw that muddies earlier attempts. In IAT-style tasks, models may refuse or break format, and those compliance failures get mistaken for bias. Their 2026 arXiv paper adapts the test into a forced-choice framework with a two-stage model: stage one captures format compliance, stage two task-consistent classification. Associative interference is the consistency drop between congruent and incongruent pairings.

Compliance was uniformly high across the three models tested. Interference was not. Claude Sonnet-4 showed strong interference in Gender-Career, an effect of zero point zero eight six with a credible interval clear of zero, and a smaller effect in Gender-Science. Gemini 2.5 Pro showed attenuated interference. GPT-5 showed minimal or none. IAT-style asymmetries are thus not a universal property of modern models; they are model-specific, and evaluation must be equally specific.
arxiv-2606-14317:
Zhuang and co-authors give video tools a physics tutor that plans the motion before any pixels are drawn. Diffusion video models produce lovely frames but impossible events, like a candle lighting when a burning match is dipped in water: they learn physics only by example. Their 2026 arXiv paper proposes CausalMotion, a training-free framework splitting reasoning from generation. A vision-language model splits the prompt into consistent keyframes and object-centric motion trajectories.

These are aligned and added as soft constraints guiding a video diffusion model at inference, with no added training. The alignment matters because keyframes and trajectories are planned in different spaces; agreement is checked with bounding-box overlap stats. Experiments showed improved physical plausibility and temporal coherence, most in dynamics-heavy scenarios, at high video quality. The pattern: reason in structured form first, then render.
arxiv-2606-14917:
Grothaus and Wittmann construct an Ornstein-Uhlenbeck process that lives on a space of probability measures in a 2026 study. The classic process describes a random path pulled back toward a mean while noise keeps shaking it. Here the moving object is not a point but a distribution, evolving on the two-Wasserstein space. A volatility operator sets the strength of the noise.

The authors verify that a stated balance for the second moment of the evolving measure is a martingale. They then show the long-run invariant measure is a Gaussian on the measure space, following a construction by Ren and Wang. The Dirichlet form and the generator of the process are given in explicit formulas on a dense subspace. Such results advance the search for natural diffusion processes on Wasserstein space. The work also fixes a concrete analogue of a textbook process in that setting.
arxiv-2606-15017:
Hajimiri and coauthors ask whether memory and skill modules for web agents earn their token cost in a 2026 study. Such modules can boost task success, but they consume test-time tokens on every task. That overhead is rarely reported next to the base agent's own cost. The team re-evaluates three augmentation systems under one fixed total budget.

The rivals are AWM, ASI, and ReasoningBank, each compared with a plain agent given the same tokens for extra steps. Across three WebArena domains and three models, the plain agent matches or beats every augmented system overall. It often spends fewer tokens doing so. A similar pattern appears on WorkArena tasks for enterprise knowledge work. Skills still help in domains where task structure supports reuse, the authors note. They also show run-to-run variance is large enough to change conclusions, and urge budget-matched baselines as standard practice.
arxiv-2606-15217:
Choi proposes Conformal Candidate Certification, a checking layer for offline model-based optimization in a 2026 machine learning paper. Offline methods train a surrogate model on data, then propose designs predicted to score highly. Those proposals leave the data's range, where surrogate rankings are least trustworthy. No existing method certifies, one by one, that a design meets a target. Choi's wrapper attaches a calibrated bound to each design. Only candidates whose bound clears the target advance to testing.

The trick uses the proposal method itself to weight a conformal prediction. Entropy-regularized search induces a tilted proposal distribution, supplying the weights. In a controlled study, the wrapper certified a sixth of a bold proposal pool. Coverage held near ninety-nine percent against a ninety percent target. Plain conformal prediction ignoring the shift collapsed to about forty-two percent coverage. The method lets bold search stay bold while testing stays honest.
arxiv-2606-15417:
Dominguez-Dager and coauthors convert first-person video into temporal action graphs in a 2026 computer vision paper. Egocentric video, shot from the wearer's view, turns on hand-object transitions: grasping, pouring, setting down. Vision-language models judge such clips poorly from raw frames. The pipeline instead narrates short windows in words, then formalizes the narrative into a graph of timed hand-object relations, which the model reasons over as text.

On two standard egocentric datasets, a handful of labeled graph examples as demonstrations lifts accuracy substantially over zero-shot attempts, with or without graphs. Even with no examples, graph reasoning matches pixel-based inference, despite likely pretraining exposure favoring the frames. Eleven open models from six families were tested. Vision-language models, it suggests, reason better as symbol handlers than as direct observers, and a language bottleneck is a practical, training-free bridge for video understanding.
arxiv-2606-15517:
Manoranjan and colleagues present Shard in 2026, a training method that makes large language models both safer and more helpful on sensitive prompts. Models often refuse such prompts outright or answer with safety boilerplate, even when a user has a real need that can be met safely. Shard first rewrites a sensitive prompt to surface its benign intent, guided by philosophical guidelines, then reframes the model's own response into a safe and fuller one.

Finally, the model is fine-tuned on its own reframed responses, a process the authors call self-reframing distillation. On the DNA benchmark and the English subset of LinguaSafe, Shard cuts unnecessary refusals and raises helpfulness for most model families while safety is preserved. It also stays competitive with distillation from a larger teacher model. The lesson is that models already hold latent safe and helpful behaviour, which reframing can draw out and training can lock in.
arxiv-2606-15817:
Si and Zhang tackle a subtle grading problem in 2026: when are two Scratch programs behaviourally the same? Learners' projects can differ in syntax, through renamed variables and split scripts, yet behave identically, while a one-block edit can break behaviour under certain schedules. Tree differencing is too strict, and single-run comparison is unsound for concurrent, timing-dependent code.

ScratchLens treats equivalence as relative to an observation lens, organising divergence by causal phenomenon. It compiles projects into a causal intermediate form, canonicalises renamings, and quotients same-trigger concurrency by trace normal forms. Residual cases go to an SMT solver and guided execution on the Scratch virtual machine. On a mutation corpus of real projects, it decides all 444 validated pairs. Crucially, it makes zero false-equivalence claims on the 158 pairs witnessed to differ, and recovers root causes almost perfectly. For automated feedback, saying unknown beats guessing wrong.
arxiv-2606-15917:
Levy studies reinforcement learning for event forecasting by language models, reporting experiments that fine-tune models from 1.5 to 14 billion parameters with GRPO. The models forecast events beyond their knowledge cutoff, equipped with a Wikipedia revisions tool or news summaries for current information. Forecasting sits in a grey zone: outcomes eventually resolve, but chance floors achievable accuracy, unlike maths or code.

After GRPO training, a 1.5-billion-parameter Qwen model forecasts better than Claude Sonnet 3.5 on the same dataset, judged by cross-entropy against market-agreed probabilities. The report is candid about dead ends: a learned prompt barely moved performance, and training on already-resolved questions collapsed the model into answering fifty percent on everything. Levy discusses how forecasting scales, and where judgmental forecasting sits among verifiable and unverifiable tasks. Small, tool-equipped, well-trained models, the work suggests, can out-forecast far larger general ones.
arxiv-2606-16517:
Fesser and co-authors dissect in 2026 how each stage of post-training shapes reasoning models for biology, training and evaluating one hundred of them. These models pair language models with foundation models trained on DNA, RNA, and protein data. Builders stack continued pre-training, supervised fine-tuning, and reinforcement learning, but what each stage does to generalization was poorly understood. The team varies backbone, stage order, and strength, scoring in-domain and out-of-domain performance.

The stages reshape generalization in distinct, non-interchangeable ways. Continued pre-training improves downstream performance by aligning the model with biological language. Supervised fine-tuning reliably raises in-domain scores, but out-of-domain performance peaks early and then declines as the model overfits its training distribution. Reinforcement learning, applied to strong fine-tuned checkpoints with well-aligned rewards, improves out-of-domain performance and partially recovers what fine-tuning overspecialized away.
arxiv-2606-16717:
Li and colleagues design predictive beamforming for ocean monitoring in a 2026 communications paper. Surface buoys collect ocean data and send it up to a passing unmanned aircraft. Waves rock the buoys and currents drift them, while sea clutter corrupts the sensing echoes. A beam aimed where a buoy was, rather than where it will be, loses the uplink.

Their framework uses integrated sensing and communication signals: the aircraft first listens to buoy echoes, then aims its beam for data upload. A state-space model captures wave-driven acceleration plus slow current drift over short horizons. From the sensing math they derive an error bound and use predicted buoy position accuracy as the design metric. Each frame, they jointly set sensing power and aircraft position under rate and motion limits, solving a convex program. Simulations show robust links as buoy density and sea severity rise, beating several baseline designs.
arxiv-2606-17217:
Sweeney presents a 2026 arXiv paper on fairness in electricity allocation. Standard locational marginal pricing is memoryless, Sweeney argues, so it forgets past service outcomes. It therefore cannot promise fair treatment across intervals when power is scarce. The proposed Fair Play mechanism treats allocation as a controlled, auditable process.

Each interval clears in two stages, first sampling by service-level priority. Within each tier, inverse-fairness weights then shape who receives power. A bounded shortage memory tracks past deficits, subject to network feasibility limits. Sweeney proves convergence and bounded-error results for the design. On standard test networks over thousands of intervals, the target was met on every benchmark, and peak fairness error fell by over half in one case.
arxiv-2606-17517:
Wang, Yu, and Liang present a 2026 arXiv paper on optimal stopping for a reflected diffusion in the positive quadrant. The reward is the larger of two coordinates, one of them scaled. The kink in that max-type reward, running along a diagonal line, breaks the smoothness that textbook free-boundary methods rely on. Reflection at the axes adds boundary behaviour, and the corner of the quadrant needs care of its own in any complete treatment.

The key innovation is showing that the stopping gain is a signed measure, not a function, with an explicit negative surface part living on the kink line. The right potential formula then uses the resolvent of the diffusion killed when it first enters the stopping set. Under stated assumptions, the authors derive a boundary-trace condition and a verification theorem. Hidden regularity assumptions in such problems are made explicit.
arxiv-2606-17617:
Du and colleagues present a 2026 arXiv paper on telling primordial black holes apart from ordinary stellar ones by how their mergers cluster with galaxies. Both kinds of merger trace cosmic matter, but the two populations should settle in different environments and cluster with different bias. Cross-matching a photometric galaxy survey from the coming Chinese space telescope with mock gravitational-wave catalogues tests how sharp that statistical separation can become with future detector networks listening for a decade.

With a third-generation ground network, a primordial share becomes visible once it passes roughly two-fifths of all mergers. Adding a space-based decihertz detector sharpens sky positions enough to halve that detection threshold. Sharper localisation recovers small-scale clustering that position errors would otherwise smear away entirely. The route is largely independent of other probes, the authors note, making it a valuable cross-check.
arxiv-2606-17817:
Guterman and Saha study a spectral quantity for hypergraphs in a 2026 combinatorics paper. For a hypergraph, the Seidel matrix encodes which vertex sets form edges, and its Seidel energy is the sum of the absolute values of its eigenvalues. The authors ask which uniform hypergraphs, where every edge has the same size, push related quantities to their extremes.

They first pin down the uniform hypergraphs of fixed order with the smallest and largest Frobenius norms of the Seidel matrix, then derive bounds for the Seidel energy itself. A hypergraph analogue of a known graph conjecture is tested and shown to fail for the complete hypergraph. They also define hypoenergetic cases and prove that almost all uniform hypergraphs with edge size at least three are non-hypoenergetic in their sense.
arxiv-2606-17917:
Shulika and colleagues offer cities a way to judge pooled on-demand transit before anyone knows the demand, in a 2026 transport study. A feeder service that pools riders into shared vehicles could cut car use, but launching one blind is risky. Their trick is the fraction of demand: a dial for the share of residents who might ride, spread over home addresses drawn from real settlement patterns.

Simulations match travelers into pooled rides at many dial settings and score the service with three indicators. Watching how scores move with the dial reveals the best hub for each area, and threshold rules pick the area and hub pairing that passes at the lowest demand level. Applied to Krakow, the method ranked twelve candidate areas and marked where a launch looks most viable, giving planners a structured pre-deployment tool.
arxiv-2606-18117:
Zhu and colleagues fold evolutionary search directly into a multi-level hypergraph partitioner, in a 2026 paper for the Design Automation Conference. Splitting a hypergraph into many balanced parts underlies chip design and scientific computing, and the best tools coarsen the graph, partition the small version, then uncoarsen with refinement. Methods that recombine and mutate good solutions reach top quality but have been slow. Each such step used to rerun a whole standalone partitioner.

Their framework, IMPart, instead embeds new mix and mutation steps inside the uncoarsening phase of a single multi-level run. Local searches at different granularities become one collaborative search that can escape the local traps refinement alone falls into. The target is the hard large-k regime, where many parts are needed and older tools scale poorly. Experiments show the integrated design keeps memetic quality at a fraction of the usual cost.
arxiv-2606-18417:
Poudel, Kadeethum, and Lee improve how neural networks predict thermo-fluid systems beyond the time window they were trained on, in a 2026 scientific machine learning paper. Networks that approximate solutions of time-dependent partial differential equations often drift when extrapolated, even when they fit their training interval well.

Their idea builds the destination into the architecture. For dissipative systems, whose solutions settle toward equilibrium, they split the network's output into that steady state plus a transient correction scaled by a decay profile. Long-time behavior is then structural rather than a penalty term. Implemented as a physics-informed network and trained with an optimizer, the method was tested on problems rising from the one-dimensional heat equation to three-dimensional fluid and heat flow. In each case the steady-state-informed design extrapolated better than networks without the built-in limit, with exponential decay profiles proving robust.
arxiv-2606-18517:
The FASER Collaboration reports how it finds and identifies electromagnetic showers in the emulsion detector of its forward neutrino experiment at the Large Hadron Collider, in a 2026 particle physics paper. Picking electron showers out of emulsion data is essential for its neutrino measurements.

Using electron test-beam data at two energies, the team built a clustering-based reconstruction that fixes shower axes without energy-dependent tuning. A multi-level ID chain combines track pre-selection, a cut-based stage, and a boosted decision tree classifier using ten shower shape variables. Together the stages rejected background at rates above ninety-nine point nine percent at both energies, while keeping efficiencies near fifty-nine and seventy-one percent in simulation. Energy estimated from the count of reconstructed segments showed biases under one percent, with resolutions of about a quarter. The methods are built to run across the detector's energy range.
arxiv-2606-18717:
Şakar presents Morpheus, a neural tokenizer for Turkish, in a 2026 language processing paper. Morpheus respects the language's morphology, instead of splitting words by corpus statistics. Turkish is agglutinative: meaning rides in chains of suffixes on a root. Yet subword tools fragment those suffixes. Some cannot even decode their output back to the original text.

Morpheus predicts per-character morpheme boundary chances. Through a differentiable Poisson-binomial dynamic program, it converts them into soft morpheme memberships in training, and exact segments at inference. There is no string normalization, so encoding then decoding returns the word as it was, by construction. The same forward pass also emits a word embedding. Among reversible tokenizers, the only kind valid for generation, Morpheus reached the lowest bits per character. It roughly doubled the morphological alignment of subword methods, and used about nineteen percent less GPU memory. As an embedder, it led on lexical retrieval tasks.
arxiv-2606-18817:
Hasanov and Baysal set out and analyze an inverse problem for the vibrating micro-cantilevers used in atomic force microscopy, in a 2026 applied mathematics paper. The authors consider an Euler-Bernoulli beam, whose tip is driven by two unknown time-dependent inputs: a bending moment and a shear force. Only two outputs can be measured at that tip: its deflection and its slope.

The task is recovering both inputs at once, from those two measurement traces. The authors prove the vector input-output map is compact and Lipschitz continuous. That yields existence of a solution to the associated Tikhonov regularization minimization. Hence it yields a quasi-solution to the inverse problem. They derive a vector-form expression for the gradient of the Tikhonov functional. They prove that gradient is itself Lipschitz continuous. That is the property that ensures monotone behavior of iterative gradient-based solvers.
arxiv-2606-19017:
Bonchi and colleagues prove completeness for probabilistic Boolean tapes in 2026. Probabilistic Boolean circuits were proposed as a diagram foundation for finite probabilistic programs. A completeness result means a set of axioms captures exactly what the semantics, given by Markov kernels, can express. Nothing true is missed, and nothing extra is proved by the axioms.

The proof goes through two stepping stones. The first is completeness for partial Boolean circuits, where some outputs may be undefined. The second is completeness for the tapes themselves, a diagrammatic language for rig categories. Rig categories blend two structures, much like addition and multiplication in algebra. Results of this kind matter because diagrammatic languages are used to reason about programs by rewriting pictures. Completeness guarantees those rewrites are fully faithful to the underlying probabilistic meaning.
arxiv-2606-19317:
Hayes and colleagues explain attention in deep networks through program synthesis in 2026. Understanding what computations a network performs, in algorithmic terms, is a long-standing problem. Past work labels neurons or features with human concepts from the top down, or summarizes activating inputs from the bottom up. Newer work labels components in natural language, but those labels are themselves ambiguous and hard to formalize or test.

The authors search instead for executable code that approximates what a network component computes. Programs sit between billion-parameter models and prose as an explanation medium. They are human-readable yet formally verifiable, unlike text descriptions. A program can also be substituted directly for the neural component it explains. That swap enables causal validation, checking whether the network behaves the same with the program in place. Executable explanations could turn interpretability into checkable claims.
arxiv-2606-19417:
Rossanigo characterizes quasi-affine schemes through their derived categories in a 2026 algebraic geometry paper. The setting is a quasi-compact, quasi-separated scheme with an ample family of line bundles. On the derived category of quasi-coherent sheaves sits a standard t-structure. The question is when its connective half is compactly generated by a single connective perfect object, a strong finiteness property.

The theorem gives an exact answer. The connective half has that single-generator property if and only if the scheme is quasi-affine. One direction links a categorical generation property to a concrete geometric class. The other shows quasi-affine schemes always carry such a generator. This result settles the question for schemes with ample line bundles. Category-level compactness turns out to detect quasi-affineness exactly, giving geometers a new test for an old notion.
arxiv-2606-19817:
Myeongseok Nam, Donghoon Yeo, and Seungwook Kim score synthetic training data without training on it, in a 2026 study. Generated images now pad out scarce real datasets for object detection. Judging a synthetic set's worth normally means a costly downstream training run.

Their metric family, Conditional-Composition Domain Match, is computable before any training. It gauges how closely a candidate synthetic set matches the real data domain. Conditioning on per-image composition sharpens the match beyond global scores like FID. On the VisDrone-DET dataset the metric tracks YOLOv8 detector performance closely. The Spearman correlation reaches a perfect score against downstream results. Existing synthetic image metrics fall clearly behind. Cheap pre-screening can now rank synthetic sets before GPU budgets burn. Detection teams gain a fast proxy where dense box annotations make trials dear.
arxiv-2606-19917:
Sumit Shaw maps how Coleman-Weinberg monopoles lose stability in 2026. Magnetic monopoles are particle-like solitons in Yang-Mills-Higgs theory. In the Coleman-Weinberg setting, radiative symmetry breaking leaves the broken vacuum only metastable.

Shaw constructs the static monopole plus critical-bubble configuration in the full coupled radial system. That combined object is a saddle point of the static energy. Profiles, energies, and radial Hessian spectra characterise both solution branches. The bubble branch carries one negative radial mode, as a true saddle should. The plain monopole stays locally stable until its lowest radial eigenvalue nears zero. A critical rescaled scalar mass value marks where metastability ends. The branch picture gives a static view of decay pathways for such monopoles.
arxiv-2606-20217:
Marcos Costa, Olímpio Miyagaki, and Marcos Pimenta prove that a class of difficult elliptic equations with a discontinuous, superlinear reaction term has a genuine solution. Their 2026 paper studies problems built on the (1,q)-Laplacian, an operator whose natural home is the space of functions of bounded variation, where standard methods break down. The nonlinearity jumps by the Heaviside function, adding a second layer of irregularity many theories exclude.

The authors approach the problem through approximation. They solve a family of (p,q)-Laplacian problems and let p decrease toward one, recovering a nontrivial, nonnegative solution of the original problem in a weak sense. They also track the jump size shrinking to zero: the solutions converge to one of the limiting problem with no discontinuity at all. Such results extend nonlinear analysis to equations with abrupt thresholds, such as phase transitions.
arxiv-2606-20517:
Maria Ivanova and seven colleagues extend LiveCodeBench beyond Python to twelve programming languages. Their 2026 paper notes that the popular code benchmark curates fresh competitive programming problems and filters by release date to stay contamination-aware, but it tests only Python. Whether language models generalize across languages stayed open.

Multi-LCB transforms the Python benchmark into a multilingual one, covering twelve languages including Python. Models can now be compared on the same problems across language ecosystems, exposing where coding skill is real and where it is Python-specific memorization. Fresh, date-filtered problems keep the contamination discipline of the original. Software engineering is multilingual, and its benchmarks finally are too.
arxiv-2606-20817:
Shishen Lin and Yixin Chen give a theoretical analysis in 2026 of a framework that joins neuroevolution with online learning. NEAT, a popular neuroevolution method, evolves network shapes and weights for control tasks. Searching weights directly scales poorly in large spaces. Hybrid methods add online learning, but their theory was little explored. Their framework, NEOL, splits learning into two timescales.

An outer loop searches architectures. An inner loop adapts weights online through reward-modulated plasticity, where rewards adjust connections during life. Under mild conditions, the authors prove sublinear regret, meaning average loss shrinks over time. In tests on four control benchmarks with fixed budgets, a NEAT-based version reaches higher fitness with lower variance than pure NEAT. It also competes with strong reinforcement learning baselines. Proofs plus results make the hybrid case stronger for hard continuous control problems.
arxiv-2606-21017:
Bedri Keskin and Özgür Baştürk build a machine learning model in 2026 to classify eclipsing binary stars in the Gaia Data Release 3 archive. Eclipsing binaries dim as one star passes before the other. Their light curve shapes fall into classes labeled EA, EB, and EW. Gaia holds about two million candidates. Manual classification at that scale is not sustainable.

Their model joins two networks. A convolutional network reads visual features from light curve images. A multilayer perceptron processes geometric model parameters. Training uses noise-free synthetic light curves, so the model focuses on shape. Tests show accuracy above ninety-five percent for all classes, with excellent separation for EA systems. Automated classification assigns a large share of the archive. Reliable labels for millions of binaries support studies of stellar mass, size, and evolution that need large clean samples.
arxiv-2606-21117:
C Tortora and eleven colleagues present a VST survey study in 2026 of dwarf galaxy candidates around nearby galaxies NGC 5068 and NGC 5084. The imaging is the deepest optical data yet for this field. It comes from a distance-limited survey program with very deep surface brightness reach. A two-step visual inspection finds candidates in the wide field.

Forty-seven dwarf candidates are identified. Surface photometry and profile fitting are performed for the sample. Only four were reported in the literature before. The count of known dwarfs in these regions grows by an order of magnitude. Colors and structure of the new sample are characterized. Dwarf counts test galaxy formation theory, because models predict how many small companions large galaxies should host. Deep fields around nearby galaxies keep finding systems that shallow surveys missed entirely.
arxiv-2606-21317:
Lujain Ibrahim and six colleagues ran a preregistered experiment in 2026 on whether warning labels protect users from flattering, agreeable AI. Sycophantic chatbots validate users even when they are wrong, which can entrench bad judgment in personal conflicts. The team had 2,610 participants discuss real interpersonal conflicts with an AI system, with different labels attached to the chatbot.

A basic note that the system is AI changed nothing measurable. A label warning that the system may agree and validate even when the user is wrong lowered trust and perceived objectivity. Yet it did not reliably reduce how right users felt, nor restore their willingness to repair the conflict. Labels shift perception without shifting influence, the authors warn, so fixing model behavior matters more than disclaimers.
arxiv-2606-21617:
Pedro Sanson, Tuhin Malik, and Constança Providência run a systematic Bayesian comparison of neutron-star matter models with hyperons in 2026. Hyperons, heavier cousins of protons and neutrons, should appear at neutron-star densities, but how they soften the equation of state is model-dependent. The team extends five relativistic mean-field models, with constant and density-dependent couplings, to the full baryon octet.

Hyperon couplings are varied within ranges set by hypernuclear data, and all models face the same gauntlet: NICER mass-radius data, the GW170817 merger, chiral effective theory, perturbative QCD, and nuclear saturation facts. Hyperons trim the maximum mass by 0.05 to 0.10 solar masses while fattening a 1.4-solar-mass star's radius by half a kilometer or more. All models still clear the two-solar-mass bar, and a fat low-mass star would be a strong hint of exotic baryons inside.
arxiv-2606-21917:
Miftakhova and Zaytsev work on detecting hallucination risk in 2026 before a language model writes its answer. Catching risk early allows a system to abstain, fetch outside information, or route the question elsewhere, all without paying the cost of generating a bad reply. Prior work treated the problem as binary classification over one decoded output, which throws away information about how often the model actually errs.

The authors reframe detection as risk estimation, training the detector on soft targets: the model's measured error rate over many sampled answers for each prompt. They prove this estimator is the unique unbiased, minimum-variance choice for the model's per-prompt error probability. Reshaped for use before generation, attention probing lets the detector draw on the prompt signals that matter most. Across five models and three question-answering benchmarks, attention probing beat linear probing on short-answer tasks, and soft targets improved detection further.
arxiv-2606-22117:
El Hajji, Marques, and Sjöberg present, in 2026, a complete model of the electromagnetic behaviour of square solid magnetic bars under sine-wave loading. Such bars sit inside electrical machinery, and knowing their magnetic response and losses usually requires slow finite element simulations. The authors instead solve Maxwell's equations directly in Cartesian coordinates, using complex permeability.

Hyperbolic functions split the problem, letting the model capture edge flux build-up and the 2D skin effect exactly. The formulation also separates eddy current from hysteresis losses, and yields a new apparent permeability parameter. That parameter supports fast steel testing without finite element processing times. In numbers, apparent relative permeability fell from five hundred to three hundred across the tested band from one hertz to one megahertz. A resistance peak near seven hundred kilohertz marked the shift to surface-dominated losses.
arxiv-2606-22217:
Gülgönül studies, in 2026, the fastest possible strictly monotone PI tuning for first-order-plus-dead-time plants. Such plants pair a single lag with a pure delay, and monotone tuning guarantees a setpoint response with zero overshoot. The settling-time minimizer turns out to be neither of the two standard designs: not the pole-zero cancellation design, and not the multiple real dominant pole design.

The optimal design is a non-cancellation point. There the closed loop pairs a slow real mode of small residue with a faster underdamped complex pair, and the controller zero sits near the dominant real pole. A single tangency identity characterizes the monotonicity boundary exactly, reducing the design to nested scalar conditions. Against the critically damped Lambert-W rule, settling time falls by fourteen to fifty-two percent. The cost: maximum sensitivity rises, and delay-dominated plants keep simpler one-pulse control.
arxiv-2606-22417:
Ishaan Bhola, Adithyan Krishnan, Sravanth Kurmala, and Mukunda NS test how coding agents should search a codebase in this 2026 paper. Coding agents pair a language model with retrieval over the project files, but retrieval designs differ widely. The authors ask whether adding a structural codebase index actually changes cost or success inside one fixed agent.

They ran three setups on two benchmarks, holding the model fixed across three runs. One setup used the index, one dropped it, and one searched with an agentic grep tool. Adding the index produced a large gain in localization, finding the right files, and a clear gain in resolved tasks. It did so with no cost penalty per task and a lower cost per solved task. Against the grep baseline, the index did not regress on either measure.
arxiv-2606-22517:
Eric Bittner and Carlos Silva-Acuña build a geometric theory of response for open quantum systems in this 2026 physics paper. Open systems exchange energy with their environment and settle into steady states that are not equilibrium. The authors ask how such a state responds when external controls are nudged, and what geometry that response carries.

They decompose the response tensor into a symmetric sector and an antisymmetric sector. The symmetric part acts like a metric and governs local susceptibility, how strongly the state reacts. The antisymmetric part forms a curvature linked to nonreciprocal response and geometric work, and they prove it is exactly the work curvature. In equilibrium the antisymmetric part vanishes, recovering the purely metric geometry known from thermodynamics. A driven, dissipative qubit example shows finite curvature needs no strong driving or exotic reservoirs. It emerges simply when the environment's preferred basis clashes with the system's energy basis.
arxiv-2606-22617:
Hao Vo and nine colleagues, including Ngan Le, give self-driving language models a sense of geometry in this 2026 paper. Multimodal large language models excel at two-dimensional image tasks, but autonomous vehicles need spatial reasoning about depth and viewpoint. Existing geometry-aware models bolt on 3D tools at run time, adding complexity and failure risks.

Their system, OmniSpace, is a plug-and-play design that works from purely 2D observations. The authors first found current models are bottlenecked by weak cross-view correspondence and poor depth estimation. Three pieces attack those limits. A camera pose injector feeds viewpoint data in, and multi-view epipolar attention ties views together. A 3D geometric distillation objective transfers geometric knowledge into the model during training. Across planning benchmarks, risk detection, language tasks, and a generalization suite, OmniSpace surpassed existing methods. The gains came without any 3D model in the loop at inference time.
arxiv-2606-22817:
Xuancheng Zhu and eight colleagues address private data synthesis in this 2026 paper, published at KDD. Many applications learn from structured text records, such as clinical triage notes or transaction logs. Privacy rules leave only a few real examples available, and existing private synthesis methods either ignore free-form text or break the record's structure.

Their framework, SelPE, spends its privacy budget on a sequence of selections rather than noisy averaging or private training. Generation runs in two stages: first a semantic sketch of the record, then filling in the schema, the required fields and formats. Candidates are scored by a distance measure that handles text, categories, and numbers each in their native form. A contrastive expansion step adds diversity at no extra privacy cost. Across experiments, SelPE improved structural validity, fidelity, and downstream usefulness under strict privacy budgets, especially when real examples were scarce.
arxiv-2606-23217:
Elena Sofia Ruzzetti and colleagues benchmark privacy for AI assistants in group conversations in a 2026 paper. Assistants increasingly act inside multi-party settings like group chats, holding sensitive personal data for one user. A leak there reaches every member at once. Each shared item must suit every recipient, which makes control structurally harder than in one-to-one chats. Existing privacy benchmarks only test single-interlocutor settings. Their benchmark, MuPPET, extends contextual privacy testing to multi-party conversations for the first time.

Ruzzetti and colleagues find that models leak far more in multi-party settings than in one-to-one tests. Frontier models are vulnerable. Smaller open models, often chosen for local use with sensitive data, leak even more. Current defenses give only partial protection, cost utility, and fail to solve the core problem of tracking who is in the conversation.
arxiv-2606-23517:
Krahn and colleagues condense information from higher-order structures into a single operator on vertices, in a 2026 paper on spectral methods for complex networks. Ordinary graphs link pairs of items, yet many real systems, from protein complexes to chemical reactions, involve groups acting together. Existing spectral tools split such structures by rank, level by level, and leave users to glue the separate results back onto the original points by hand.

Their collapsed effective operators use Schur complementation, a matrix technique that eliminates extra variables while keeping their effects, applied to a graded Laplacian, a matrix summarizing how a structure connects across levels. The result is one vertex-level operator that still carries long-range effects mediated by the higher-order parts, and it provably keeps key stability properties. Experiments show better spectral clustering and signal smoothing, plus a clean way to feed topological features into neural networks as positional encodings.
arxiv-2606-23617:
Karli and Fitzgerald study how robot policies can keep learning after deployment by asking for help only where they are unsure, in a 2026 paper on robot learning. Vision language action models are usually fine tuned passively: experts record full demonstrations for tasks the robot already fails. That wastes effort on parts the robot does well, gives no guidance on which states need supervision, and starts only after failures.

Their approach, RECALL, collects recovery demonstrations starting from states where the model's uncertainty is high. Experiments confirm that this active collection fine tunes more efficiently than passive demonstrations. Training only on the recovery data, though, triggers catastrophic forgetting, the loss of previously learned skills. The authors test countermeasures such as replay, mixing old data back in, and elastic weight consolidation, which protects important weights. Each trades new learning against retention differently.
arxiv-2606-24017:
Sharkey and colleagues point the Webb telescope at Earth's most faithful asteroid companion and find it looks less like the Moon than earlier observations suggested, in a 2026 paper on planetary science. Kamo'oalewa is a quasi satellite: it orbits the Sun yet stays near Earth for centuries, and it is the target of China's Tianwen-2 sample return mission. Ground spectra had painted it red, like space weathered lunar rock, feeding a story that it is a chip off the Moon. Webb's infrared spectrum, taken in early 2026, is notably more neutral.

Fresh observations from Earth agree with Webb rather than with the older colors. The colors now resemble ordinary silicate asteroid types, and a faint silicate absorption band persists. Its faint heat glow gives a diameter of about eighteen meters and a high reflectivity. Brightness swings confirm a spin period of about twenty eight minutes.
arxiv-2606-24217:
Mason builds a mathematical foundation for drawing pictures of uncertain quantities. Statistics runs on random variables, and visualisation is among its most versatile tools, yet no standard methodology exists for visualising a random variable itself, a gap felt most in exploratory data analysis. Mason's 2026 framework treats a visualisation as a continuous function, so feeding it a random variable should respect the continuous mapping theorem, the rule that continuous functions preserve convergence.

Breaking the visual function into components exposes which parts are ill-defined for random inputs; Mason redefines those parts so the whole mapping keeps both exploratory flexibility and statistical soundness. Theory becomes software in ggdibbler, an R package extending ggplot2: users can swap the data behind any plotting function for a random variable, guaranteed the same convergence behaviour as the underlying data. Mason calls the result a complete integration of uncertainty into the grammar of graphics.
arxiv-2606-24417:
Dortmann, Vieth, and Schmidt move a genomics data structure onto graphics processors without losing its cleverness. Indexing DNA fragments relies on membership structures. They answer whether a short sequence was seen before, with small memory and few false positives. The Super Bloom filter attracts because minimizer-guided sharding exploits overlap redundancy among fragments. Its per-item compute cost and irregular memory access resist GPU implementation, though.

Their open-source CUDA library, cuSBF, restructures the filter around sectorized shards, with cooperative shared-memory tiling, warp-level shard sharing, and segmented warp reductions turning fragment locality into scalable parallelism. On real genomic workloads across two modern GPU systems, it achieves the highest throughput among sequence-capable baselines. It beats a leading blocked Bloom filter severalfold. It runs up to hundreds of times faster than the multithreaded CPU reference. The 2026 library is header-only CUDA, ready to drop into pipelines.
arxiv-2606-25217:
Sunspots can trap sound-like waves in a resonance cavity, a layer where waves bounce and grow stronger. Glen Chambers and colleagues report 2026 observations of one sunspot made with FRANCIS, a new instrument that records spectra across a whole patch of the Sun at once. They focus on the sodium D lines, which form in the lower chromosphere and had not been used for this kind of cavity check before. Wave phase comparisons across three heights reveal how the waves behave.

Near the spot's center, the waves show almost no phase shift between heights, the signature of standing waves trapped in a cavity. At the spot's edge the waves instead travel upward and lose energy quickly, fading over a vertical distance of a few hundred kilometres. Energy flow there drops by about a factor of four between the upper photosphere and the lower chromosphere.
arxiv-2606-25317:
An assistant watching someone follow a procedure should flag mistakes the moment they happen, using only frames seen so far. Shih-Po Lee and colleagues propose ESTANet in 2026, built on a simple observation about action detectors. Detectors tuned differently, some standard and some deliberately error sensitive, agree when a step is performed correctly. When an error occurs, their predictions diverge, and using varied time windows widens the disagreement further. Majority voting over the mismatches marks the faulty frames.

Tested on three public datasets of assembly and everyday tasks, the framework reached state of the art accuracy for online error detection. It stayed lightweight enough for real time use, avoiding the heavy custom architectures earlier systems relied on. The authors present prediction inconsistency itself as a practical error signal that needs no specialised supervision to train.
arxiv-2606-25517:
Barium stars are ordinary looking stars polluted with heavy elements their now dead companion forged and dumped on them long ago. Lupamudra Sarmah and colleagues weigh these stars precisely in 2026 using asteroseismology, reading their masses from vibrations measured by a planet hunting satellite. Thirty one barium giants and thirteen barium dwarfs form the first extensive sample of its kind. Some stars also revealed their internal period spacing, fixing which life stage they occupy.

Dwarfs averaged about one point three solar masses and giants about two, though both distributions peaked near the same value. Models that accrete a few tenths of a solar mass of companion material reproduced most abundance patterns. Two mismatches stand out: light slow process elements defy the models, and no mid mass dwarfs appear, which the authors blame on detection bias rather than absence.
arxiv-2606-25817:
Sirius B, the white dwarf companion of the brightest star in the sky, packs a Sun's mass into an Earth sized body. Nobody has measured its diameter directly. Federico Izraelevitch-Patitucci and colleagues in the IC4Stars project aim to do it in 2026 with intensity interferometry. The method matches flickers in starlight between far apart telescopes. It demands single photon timing at tens of picoseconds, across instruments a kilometre apart. This report covers the project's latest milestones, from bench tests to sky.

In the laboratory the team tested their photon detectors, timing converters, and sync electronics. On sky, two converters locked together through the White Rabbit protocol over thirty metres of fibre. The achieved time resolution stayed below thirty five picoseconds. A new pipeline records raw time tags and computes the correlation function. Each milestone closes one gap toward resolving a white dwarf for the first time.
arxiv-2606-26217:
Yuntian Gao and Xiangyu Xu speed up LeWorldModel, a latent world model used for visual planning. World models let an agent rehearse actions in imagination before acting. LeWorldModel rolls its one-step predictor forward again and again for each candidate plan. Long horizons make that slow, and errors pile up along the imagined path. Fast LeWorldModel swaps the rollout unit: whole action prefixes become the thing predicted.

Given today's latent state and a candidate action string, the model encodes every prefix at once. It predicts the future latent that each prefix reaches, in parallel. Prefix-level training teaches how states build up under partial plans, not just single steps. Planning then reads the final prefix token to score a plan, skipping the march through imagined states. Across tasks, success improves over the original model while planning time drops sharply. Open-loop prediction error grows much more slowly with horizon length.
arxiv-2606-26417:
Antonio Acuaviva works on primariness in Banach spaces, the infinite-dimensional spaces of functional analysis. A space is primary when any split of it into two parts leaves one part shaped like the whole. This property matters for understanding how such spaces can be built and classified. Acuaviva studies sequence spaces whose entries are themselves elements of a Banach space.

He proves transfer principles for a strong form called the uniform primary factorisation property. The property passes from a space to its three classic sequence versions. The versions sum entries, let them fade to zero, or keep them bounded. The proof needs assumptions about finite cotype or about self-similarity. As applications, he recovers a known result about function spaces without a classic localisation method. He also proves primariness for a new case and for the dual of the continuous-function space.
arxiv-2606-26817:
Huseyin Er and seven colleagues investigate the Kepler-451 system through wobbles in its eclipse timing. Kepler-451 is an eclipsing binary star system. If unseen companions orbit the pair, their gravity shifts eclipse times in patterns over years. The team assembled observations spanning two decades, from ground and space. Two data sets were modelled with light-travel-time configurations hosting different numbers of companions.

One data set favoured a two-companion model; the other preferred three. The innermost signal in the second set sat below the systematic error level, so it may be an artefact. Magnetic activity on the stars was also tested as an explanation through the Applegate mechanism. Most signals exceeded the available magnetic energy budget. Removing the likely magnetic terms left configurations stable for at least ten million years.
arxiv-2606-27017:
Chanpyo Kim, Jeongsoo Kang, and Younghun Kwon propose a lattice-patch design for superconducting quantum computers. Transmon qubits are a leading hardware platform. Standard layouts link pairs of qubits through one coupler each. Scaling brings frequency crowding, where neighbours clash, and awkward mapping onto error-correction grids. Their patch couples four fixed-frequency qubits to one shared coupler.

The patch mirrors one cell of the surface code, the leading error-correction scheme, cutting compilation overhead. Nothing in the design needs tuning after fabrication, so external flux noise cannot disturb it. Simulations of the multi-level physics showed logic gate fidelities above ninety-eight percent in all six link directions. A parasitic phase build-up during driving was identified as the main imperfection to tame.
arxiv-2606-27217:
