Bonhoff presents CHAMB-GA, a framework that runs genetic algorithms with heavy simulations on everything from laptops to supercomputers. Genetic algorithms evolve candidate solutions through selection and mutation, but each fitness test may need a long simulation. Existing tool chains often lock users to one machine type, blocking smooth scaling. Containerised microservices solve that rigidity here. Deployment works on cloud clusters through orchestration and on HPC clusters through batch scheduling in this framework paper from 2026.

Users supply the genetic operators and the simulation backend separately. The two run decoupled on distinct hardware, coordinated by a central message broker. Fitness evaluations and evolutionary steps proceed in parallel across workers. Benchmarks show minimal overhead while scaling beyond thirty-five hundred CPU cores. A second test optimises high-voltage direct current line dispatch in the German grid. Migration between cloud and scheduler systems proves seamless, with mixed scaling and multi-stage workflows supported.
arxiv-2606-27417:
Capecchiacci and colleagues predict how blazar jets will polarise light from X-rays to gamma rays, so future telescopes can settle how the jets shine. Blazars are active galaxies whose relativistic jets point at Earth. Competing emission models, leptonic, hadronic, and hybrid, predict different polarisation degrees across energy bands. The team models a complete sample from a monitoring programme, spanning low- to high-peaked sources. Spectral fitting with a Markov chain tool yields expected fluxes band by band, in an astrophysics paper published in 2026.

Each source is scored against instrument detection thresholds, including blind-survey chances. Simultaneous multi-wavelength polarimetry can effectively discriminate between the competing models, because their expected polarisation degrees diverge. Sensitivity needs for future gamma-ray polarimetry missions follow from the source counts. Polarisation becomes the referee between jet theories. Current and planned instruments each get a shopping list.
arxiv-2606-27517:
Abel and colleagues prove Korovkin-type theorems in approximation theory that let results for one class of functions transfer to all functions of polynomial or exponential growth. Korovkin theory says a sequence of positive linear operators converges everywhere once it converges on a few test functions. They act on continuous functions over the half-line, a setting the classic theorems do not directly cover. Convergence on suitable test functions is assumed, and convergence for the whole growth classes follows in this paper from 2026.

The classical Baskakov and Szász-Mirakjan operators fall out as direct applications, for polynomial-growth and exponential-growth functions respectively. The method is deliberately elementary. A broad class of such operators on the half-line can reuse the same framework. Test-function checks become a master key for unbounded domains.
arxiv-2606-27617:
Masked diffusion models generate language in parallel, which promises speed. Their reverse step treats each token position separately, though. That shortcut breaks down when only a few sampling steps are used. Flow language models avoid the shortcut with a continuous flow from noise to clean text. They must decode every token at once, which hurts multi-step reasoning. Patrick Rebeschini merges the two ideas in 2026.

Rebeschini calls the result Masked Language Flow Models. A continuous stochastic bridge links partly masked text to clean text. Pretrained masked diffusion models can be converted with a light adaptation. A new sampler alternates two moves. It denoises continuously, then unmasks the tokens it is most sure of. Tests used GSM8K maths problems and MT-Bench instructions. Flow-based models solved such reasoning and instruction tasks at scale for the first time, the author reports.
arxiv-2606-28017:
Treatment effects can change sign along an outcome distribution. Alessandro Baldi Antognini and Paolo Verme provide a toolkit in 2026 for studying those sign changes, built on the Treatment Effects Curve that Verme introduced in 2010. A discontinuity is a point where marginal effects switch sign. The curve tracks effects across the whole outcome range. Two analyses frame the study, and crossing-point asymptotics supply the inference.

Horizontal analysis compares groups in regions of opposite-signed effects, with causal forests. Vertical analysis examines the sign-switch points themselves. Adapted theory locates where the curve crosses zero, and a bias-corrected Wald statistic tests the local slope there. The workflow is illustrated on synthetic data, with a diagnostic application to Mexico's PROGRESA programme. Each part can be used on its own. The toolkit complements quantile-regression approaches to distributional effects.
arxiv-2606-28117:
Low-rank adapters fine-tune large models cheaply, one per task. In continual learning, tasks arrive in sequence, and the standard assumption is that each needs its own adapter. Tanguy Dieudonné and four colleagues challenge that assumption in 2026. Task-specific adapters turn out to overlap heavily. The subspaces they span share much of their structure. Earlier adapters can often represent later tasks faithfully. Redundancy, not scarcity, is the norm.

Their method, LiteLoRA, adds a gating mechanism learned during training. The gate decides whether a new adapter is needed or existing low-rank representations can be reused. Active adapters fall by twenty to seventy percent. Performance matches or exceeds state-of-the-art results on standard continual learning benchmarks. Structural redundancy is pervasive across task streams, the authors conclude. Selective learning suffices for stability without sacrificing plasticity. Capacity can grow with task novelty instead of task count.
arxiv-2606-28217:
Young Yoon, Jimin Kim, and Soyeon Park sketch a design for cooperatives in which people fully delegate work to artificial intelligence agents acting for them. Each person supplies data and takes part in updating shared models, but each also holds personal values that limit what may be done in their name.

Yoon and colleagues propose paying credit only for updates that pass a screening against every principal's value profile. Their design combines value-based filtering of learning steps, running signals of who contributed what, and a final settlement of revenue. It rests on a decentralized training method that avoids the quality loss of simply averaging models, and it keeps explicit paths for tracing who influenced the outcome.
arxiv-2606-28617:
Bennet Outland and Vishala Arya compute Nash equilibria for the differential games behind aerospace confrontations, pursuit-evasion and contested space operations among them. These are multi-agent optimal control problems: nonconvex, coupled, and short on algorithms with guarantees. Their relaxation removes control coupling between agents' dynamics, a structure many real systems share.

Their algorithm, FALCON, attacks the relaxed problem with sequential convex programming. It carves the nonconvex game into a chain of tractable convex sub-games, each recast as a potential game that standard solvers can finish. Under mild assumptions, they demonstrate global convergence to an open-loop Nash equilibrium, the outcome where no agent gains by unilaterally replanning its whole trajectory. Numerical demonstrations cover both cooperative and competitive differential games, showing the machinery working on the problems it was built for.
arxiv-2606-29217:
Feichtinger surveys Wiener amalgam spaces, a family of function spaces from harmonic analysis, and argues they deserve wider use. The classical versions combine a local norm, measuring behaviour on small pieces, with a global rule for how the pieces add up. That simple recipe already improves the Hausdorff-Young theorem and has consequences for Sobolev algebras.

The bigger step is allowing more general local components, describing smoothness or membership in the Fourier algebra. That door led to modulation spaces, now standard tools in time-frequency analysis. Feichtinger shows how amalgam methods prove the Sobolev embedding theorem and pin down the pointwise multipliers of Sobolev algebras. He also identifies the multipliers from the classical Wiener algebra into its dual with a space of mild distributions. The article appears some forty-five years after the key 1983 paper.
arxiv-2606-29517: This author builds CORE: common outcome regularities from action-free visual demonstrations for robot manipulation. The building builds. Their regularities are common outcome. The demonstrations are action-free visual. It is robotics. CORE cores. The robot manipulation is action-free.
arxiv-2606-29617:
Ghaba, Hab-arrih, Atmani, and Slaoui study how quantum entanglement evolves in two coupled harmonic oscillators whose interaction changes over time. Harmonic oscillators are building blocks of quantum optics. The authors use the Lewis-Riesenfeld invariant method to derive exact wave functions, with no perturbative or adiabatic shortcuts.

A phase-space analysis through the Wigner function completes the picture of the quantum state's evolution. They obtain general formulas for purity and linear entropy for arbitrary excitation numbers. How entanglement changes proves very sensitive to detuning, the mismatch between the oscillators, and to coupling strength. Stronger coupling raises both the amplitude and the average of the linear entropy. At resonance with strong coupling, the system shows robust undamped regular oscillations of the entropy, in step for every state considered. The authors argue this makes linear entropy a practical entanglement witness.
arxiv-2606-29917:
Gao and five colleagues tackle image-goal navigation for quadrotor drones: fly to the exact object shown in a query photo. Continuous 3D control, a narrow camera view, and safety limits make choosing where to look from as important as the path itself.

Their framework splits high-level decisions from low-level flight. It creates viewpoint-aware action nodes around unexplored frontiers and candidate objects, so the drone explores while keeping informative angles for spotting the target. A lightweight semantic memory stores object-level and observation-level context and shares it with candidate nodes. A learned policy picks the most promising node, and a planner turns it into a safe 3D flight path. Simulation tests beat strong baselines, and real drone flights confirm the approach.
arxiv-2606-30017:
Xiaobiao Du, YuAn Wang, Hao Li, Bosheng Wang, Xun Sun, and Xin Yu adapt 3D Gaussian Splatting for mobile phones. This rendering method stores a scene as millions of fuzzy blobs. Each blob carries spherical harmonic coefficients describing color by viewing angle. High order coefficients cost heavy memory and computation. Phone hardware strains under that load.

Their method, Flux-GS, samples costly third order light residuals by Monte Carlo. It packs mirror-like energy into a compact latent code. A second module predicts corrections for cheap first order coefficients. Those corrections come from each blob's own attributes, at no rendering cost. A third step grows and prunes blobs using several views. Redundant blobs are removed, preventing overfitting to one angle. Experiments show large parameter savings with competitive image quality. Real time rendering runs on a phone class chip.
arxiv-2606-30517:
Matteo D'Achille and Ali Khezeli study ideal Poisson-Voronoi tessellations, random partitions of a space into cells around scattered points, in a limiting regime where points grow sparse. Whether these tessellations settle into a unique limit was open in general. The pair give necessary and sufficient conditions for convergence to a unique such tessellation on any proper pointed measured metric space.

Those conditions involve the volume function's growth, through regular variation after a logarithm, and a limit for uniform measures on large balls in a boundary completion. As an application, they prove convergence for higher-rank symmetric spaces, settling an open problem. Graph versions introduce a natural parameter, and the pair show the limit does not depend on it, answering another open problem. For Diestel-Leader graphs they prove this independence fully, and show the cells are distinguishable, a first for a Cayley graph.
arxiv-2606-30717:
Daniele Bielli studies a two-dimensional model of gravity obtained by shrinking four-dimensional general relativity. The Breitenlohner-Maison model describes spacetime with two symmetries, reduced by the Kaluza-Klein method. Its equations can be solved exactly, in a step-by-step way. Recent work built integrable deformations of it using auxiliary fields in one version, called the nu-frame.

Bielli first derives the matching partner version, the mu-frame. He then lifts both deformed versions back to four dimensions. An ansatz inspired by duality-invariant forms of Einstein's theory guides the lift. The resulting model is a higher-derivative theory. Oddly, it lacks diffeomorphism invariance, the freedom to relabel spacetime points, in both frames. Bielli discusses possible fixes for that feature and what the deformed model could mean physically.
arxiv-2606-30917:
Subrata Pachhal, Aziz Hasan and Adhip Agarwala introduce a minimal model of a topological random alloy, a crystal whose sites are randomly shared by two species, one of them a dopant. Topological phases are usually studied in perfect crystals. Here the host is a quantum anomalous Hall insulator or its trivial cousin, and the question is what dilute doping does to its topology. In ordinary semiconductors, impurities pin charge centres in place. The model shows something different: dopant-centric chiral current loops, rings of current circling each dopant, whose character depends on both host and dopant.

Even at dilute density, those loops can merge into topological domains inside a trivial host and trigger a full phase transition. Doping a topological host with opposite-chirality dopants instead stabilised an unexpected metal, whose bulk transport runs through modes along the domain edges.
arxiv-2606-31117:
Sierra-Sosa and three colleagues fragment big molecules so quantum computers can handle their chemistry. Linear alkanes are simple chains of carbon and hydrogen, but exact calculations explode as chains grow. Hexacosane, a 26-carbon alkane, would need 368 qubits in a full treatment. No current machine has that many to spare.

Their method cuts carbon-carbon bonds by homolytic cleavage, which yields open-shell radical fragments. A two-body many-body expansion then rebuilds the total energy from fragment calculations. Thanks to symmetry, only four unique fragment calculations are needed, whatever the chain length. The team tested 11 alkanes from butane to hexacosane with five energy solvers, classical and quantum. For hexacosane, the qubit count fell from 368 to 30. Quantum solvers run inside the scheme, including on IBM hardware, tracked their classical references closely.
arxiv-2606-31417:
Qiu and Ying show how side chains can tune a metal-organic framework smoothly between shrinking and swelling with heat. Steady control of thermal expansion is a long-standing solid-state challenge. Their testbed is MOF-5 with alkoxy side chains grafted onto its linkers, a classic porous crystal.

Short chains give steady negative thermal expansion, where the crystal contracts as it warms. Chains of three carbons or more trigger a crossover: positive expansion at low temperature flips to negative at high temperature. Warming wakes the longer chains into more shapes, and their entropy pushes outward, while at higher heat the chains boost linker vibration that pulls the frame inward. Varying chain share tunes the expansion coefficient through negative, near-zero, and positive values in chosen windows.
arxiv-2606-31817:
Alpay and Başaran ask when treating software interface variants like evolving populations is real measurement rather than relabeling. A changed service contract spreads or stalls across consumers and transitive dependencies, steered by package-manager resolver rules. The authors mine interface histories in npm, Maven Central, PyPI and crates.io, then run 2,100 resolver probes.

From clean conflict outcomes they estimate a selection coefficient for each ecosystem and run a pairwise-comparison process on the real package graph. Checker-derived direction carries genuine adoption signal against a permutation null in their analysis. A stricter temporal test, though, fails: early resolver features do not beat an age-only baseline at predicting later flips. The verdict is an audit showing where the evidence loop still stays open.
arxiv-2606-32017:
Xu and seven colleagues improve credit assignment for agents trained with reinforcement learning. In standard GRPO, a final verifier outcome is spread uniformly over every action in a trajectory. That blunt signal punishes useful exploration inside failed attempts and rewards redundant or harmful steps inside successful ones. Searches, clicks and edits each played different roles, yet all receive identical credit.

TRIAGE adds a semantic role axis on top of outcome credit. A structured judge labels each segment as decisive progress, useful exploration, no-progress infrastructure or regression, and fixed rules convert labels into bounded process rewards. Across ALFWorld, Search-QA and WebShop, success rates beat the GRPO baseline for two policy models. Catching regressions inside successful trajectories contributes most of the gain.
arxiv-2608-00417: A 2026 arXiv paper on symbolic uncertainty for spatial reasoning in LLMs. SymboUQ quantifies what models don't know. The spatial UQ. The archive keeps the paper open to all. It stands as a research record. Kept for readers.
austen-northanger-abbey-1817:
Jane Austen's Northanger Abbey came out in 1817, after her death, a Gothic parody. Catherine Morland, a keen reader of Gothic novels, lets her fancy run wild. Austen wrote the book young, and its bounce shows her early comic gift at work.

Catherine visits Bath, makes friends, and falls for the witty Henry Tilney there. At his abbey home she hunts for horrid secrets that do not exist at all. A locked cabinet and a laundry list deflate her wildest dark dreams in Bath. She learns that real life has its own quiet wrongs to face bravely. Austen teases Gothic craze while she defends novels and their young readers.
austen-persuasion-1817:
Jane Austen's Persuasion came out in 1817, after her death, her final full novel. Anne Elliot gets a quiet, autumnal second chance at love in its pages. At nineteen she broke her engagement to Wentworth on a friend's advice and pressure.

Eight years later, Wentworth returns, now a rich naval captain with fame. Anne watches him court others while her own bloom and spirits slowly revive. A fall at Lyme and a famed letter at Bath resolve the long strain. Austen writes with a mellow depth unique in her six great novels here. Many readers rank this tender book as her most moving work.
babylonian-talmud-rodkinson-vol-17:
Volume seventeen of Rodkinson's Babylonian Talmud joins three tractates: Maccoth, Shebuoth, and Eduyoth. Maccoth treats false witnesses and the cities of refuge. Shebuoth is the tractate of oaths, and Eduyoth gathers testimonies that fix points of law.

Maccoth rules that lying witnesses suffer the fate they planned for their victim, and maps the refuge cities for a man who kills by accident. Shebuoth then sorts oaths: rash vows, oaths in court, and oaths that bind the future. Eduyoth closes the volume as a record of agreed rulings, kept so later courts could lean on them. The trio shows law guarding truth itself.
balfour-declaration-1917:
Arthur James Balfour, the foreign secretary of Britain, sent this short letter on November 2, 1917. He sent it to Lord Rothschild, head of the great bank house. Balfour asked him to pass its words on to the Zionist Federation.

In one brief passage, Britain backs the plan for a national home for the Jewish people in Palestine. The letter adds that the rights of the folk now in that land must not be harmed by the plan. Few short letters have shaped the fate of a land as this one has since.
barrett-threshold-of-the-unseen-1917:
William Barrett sums up forty years of hunts in On the Threshold of the Unseen, his book of 1917. Barrett was a man of science who helped found the chief band for such study. He had sat in dark rooms, weighed frauds, and met claims of all kinds. Here he tells what he holds stands firm past all fair doubt.

Ghosts, thought leaps, and life past death get a calm, grave weigh. He backs faith, yet keeps a tester's care. The book is a life's work in one tome. It is the field's best short sum from a founder.
bogoras-koryak-texts-1917:
Waldemar Bogoras gathered these Koryak texts in the field in northeast Siberia, and the set came out in 1917. The Koryak are near kin to the Chukchi of the same coast. His work formed part of the Jesup work in the North Pacific.

Each text stands in the Koryak tongue with an English version set beside it. Bogoras took care to keep names, songs, and odd turns of speech just as he heard them. The tales and rite texts include shaman songs, myths, and speech used in rites. For those who study lost tongues and oral lore, the book keeps the Koryak voice on record.
bukharin-imperialism-world-economy-1917:
Nikolai Bukharin wrote Imperialism and World Economy in 1917, with an introduction by Lenin; this entry uses the International Publishers edition of 1929. Bukharin, a young Bolshevik theorist, built a companion work to Lenin's own study of imperialism. His focus was the economics beneath the politics.

Bukharin described how trusts and banks fuse into finance capital, and how state capitalist trusts then compete on a world scale. War, in his account, grows from that competition as surely as price wars grow among firms. Lenin prized the book and borrowed from its scheme. It remains a clear statement of the Marxist theory of imperialism's economics, written before its author rose and fell in Soviet politics.
byron-manfred-1817:
Lord Byron wrote Manfred in Switzerland during the stormy summer of 1816, the same season that produced Frankenstein. He called it a dramatic poem rather than a stage play. It was published in 1817 and quickly became one of his most famous works.

Manfred is a nobleman and magician living alone in the Alps, crushed by guilt over a lost beloved. He summons spirits and demands forgetfulness, but refuses to bow to any power, good or evil. Even at death he defies the demons who come for him. The poem is Byron's answer to Faust and the purest portrait of his defiant hero.
chekhov-lady-with-dog-1917:
Constance Garnett's 1917 volume of Anton Chekhov's stories takes its name from The Lady with the Dog. In that tale a bored Moscow banker meets a young married woman at the seaside town of Yalta. Their casual flirtation deepens, against all plans, into the one real love of their lives.

The other stories in the volume show Chekhov's mature range in Garnett's smooth English. Clerks, landowners, doctors, and wives pass through brief scenes that reveal whole lives. Nothing is forced and little is resolved, yet every detail tells. The title story alone is often called the finest love story in Russian writing. The volume is a fine door into Chekhov.
chekhov-party-1917:
The Party and Other Stories reached English readers in 1917 in Constance Garnett's translation. The title story follows Olga Mihalovna through a name-day party at her country house. Smiling for guests all day, she hides a failing marriage and her own despair until the strain breaks through.

A Doctor's Visit, another strong piece in the volume, sends a young doctor to a factory owner's sick daughter. He finds the illness rooted in wealth, idleness, and a useless life. Chekhov builds such stories from talk, glances, and small acts rather than big events. These middle-period tales show his art at its calmest and most exact. Garnett's set made them standard reading in English.
cia-0000008917:
Technical comments on POW photo comparisons form a CIA paper dated September 1968. Rather than judging one case, the specialists explain method: how photographs should be weighed as evidence. Lighting, age, angle, and hardship all change a face.

Method papers mattered because photo judgments carried real weight for missing men's files. A loose standard could raise false hope or bury a true match. Here the analysts set out careful rules for their own craft. Historians of the POW effort value such texts for showing the science behind the casework. The file turns the lens on the identification process itself.
cia-0000009717:
The enemy prison order of battle in Laos is estimated in a July 1969 CIA paper, with a list of prison locations. Order of battle is the military term for how a force is organized: units, sites, and strength. Applied to prisons, it treats camps as a system to be mapped.

The estimate counts sites and keepers the way other papers count battalions. That cold method served warm ends: finding men and keeping bombs from them. It also produced the fullest single picture of Laotian captivity available in 1969. Historians can measure the secret war's hidden prison network from lists like this one.
cia-0000009917:
Locating a prison for American pilots in Haiphong opens a November 1967 item, whose second subject, American pilots downed somewhere, is cut off in the title. Haiphong was North Vietnam's great port, bombed and mined across the war. A pilots' prison there fit the port's role as a receiving point.

Prisons near ports and rail lines made sense for moving captives toward Hanoi. Fixing the Haiphong site helped analysts read the flow of newly captured airmen. The second, truncated subject likely tied fresh losses to that flow. The file preserves both the located prison and the broken heading as released.
cia-0000012417:
October 2, 1961: meeting number thirty-seven opens the debriefings' final autumn stretch in Paris. The operation's end was approaching, though no one in the room could see it coming. A year later Penkovsky would be under arrest in Moscow, his case closed by the KGB. That October, though, the sessions still ran on routine: new questions, fresh answers, and the steady work of two services milking a source dry.

The thirty-seventh session's record begins the last season of the meetings. Its pages carry an urgency no one could yet name or explain. For readers, the session shows the golden autumn of the case, productive to the end.
cia-0000013217:
Orders from the Central Office for South Vietnam, dated February 1970, set policy on the treatment and disposition of American prisoners. Captured enemy paperwork was intelligence gold, and a directive like this one is the prison system's rules in the enemy's own words. It tells camp cadres what to do with the men they held: how to keep them, question them, move them, and use them.

The directive's language is preserved for readers to judge directly. Policy on paper and practice in the camps were not always the same. For readers, the document shows the system's stated rules, against which every survivor's account can be read.
cia-0000013617:
Security conditions in Uruguay are examined in a CIA paper from February 1967. The Tupamaro fight was taking shape in the capital that year. The urban guerrillas were a new kind of enemy in the region. They robbed banks and kidnapped officials with careful planning. They fought the state block by block in Montevideo. A calm republic had become a laboratory of city warfare that others would study and copy.

The paper takes the measure of that fight closely. It weighs the rebels' craft against the police and army hunting them. For readers, it is an early study of a new kind of war.
cia-0000015317: A letter to Thornton Page from Philip Strong fills a CIA file dated June 3, 1958. Strong thanks Page for his letter of June 10, a date slip in the clipped title. Page stayed in the saucer loop as an outside expert for years. Thanks and brief word back was the rhythm of this whole mail file.
cia-0000015417: Plain advice for anyone who photographs a strange object fills a short CIA guidance sheet dated January 5, 1960. Set the camera at infinity, use fast film, and keep shutter speeds quick for moving objects, it says. Take many pictures, include some ground, and shift position to give experts a base line. The sheet turned excited witnesses into better sources of usable proof.
cia-0000020217: Congo was, in one CIA view, facing a classic communist effort to take over its government, in an untitled record dated in 1960. Congo had just won freedom from Belgium and fallen into chaos that year. American officials read that chaos through a Cold War lens. The blunt title shows the frame plainly, whatever later history made of the claim.
cia-0000020317: Ortega Castro and Castellanos were released by the chief of police, an untitled CIA record dated September 3, 1957, notes. The title breaks off at the reason, which began with the letters shown in the catalog. Releases like this often turned on a lack of proof or a shift in orders. The bare note keeps the fact of freedom and little else.
cia-0000022317: A Soviet report claimed Allen Dulles was displeased with the Powers trial, a CIA record dated in 1960 notes. Dulles ran the CIA when the U-2 went down and when Powers faced a Moscow court. Soviet writers liked to picture the spy chief stung by his own operation's failure. The item keeps that jab, one of many aimed during the trial weeks.
cia-0000027517: Guatemala's climate for insurgency is assessed in a CIA paper dated in 1981, tagged Truth Commission in the catalog. Guatemala's civil war was then burning through the highlands, with rebels in the hills and the army answering hard. Climate here means the soil in which revolt grows: land, fear, and grievance. The paper judged whether that soil was getting richer or poorer.
cia-0000029017:
In May 1985, a Nicaraguan opposition group set out its work program in a formal statement. The declassified CIA record dated May 1, 1985 preserves that statement and the platform behind it. Nicaragua was then in the middle of a civil conflict, with opponents of the government organizing their aims in public.

Inside, the group lays out what it wants and how it plans to work toward those goals. A statement like this lets readers see the opposition in its own words, not only through reports written about it. It also shows how the CIA collected and kept political statements from groups it watched closely during the Cold War.
cia-0000044017:
Military suspects in the Jesuits case appeared before a judge, in a CIA record dated January 3, 1990. A courtroom appearance turns accused men into formal defendants. Salvadoran courts had rarely held soldiers to account before then.

Inside, the suspects' day in court is recorded for the file. Uniformed men in the dock made a picture the country remembered. It suggested that this case might, at last, run a different course from the many that had stalled before it in silence. The file preserves the hearing as a dated step, one of the first in a legal road that would test the courts for years to come.
cia-0000045217:
The ANN agency was cited on the possibility of Duarte-rebel talks, in a CIA record dated August 5, 1985. A cited possibility is a trial balloon by another name. Talking with the rebels at all was heresy to many in the government.

Inside, the floated idea of direct talks is preserved. Leaks of this kind test the public before leaders commit themselves. If the outcry is mild, the idea can quietly become policy. The file holds that test from the crisis's early weeks, when the very notion of a president treating with guerrillas still needed softening up in print.
cia-0000049117: Traces on Hans Christ from 1986 survive in a CIA item, kept with the Truth Commission records. Christ's name runs through this series inside a long legal case, part two of which sits in the same files. Each new trace added a page to what the system knew about one man and his case.
cia-0000095417: Hanoi and the POW/MIA issue, with an estimated publication date and deletions, are the subject of declassified CIA document 0000095417, dated August 2, 1987. The heading flags both the dating estimate and the redactions. The brief file is a later agency item on prisoners and the missing, kept as a paper on Hanoi's position in that dispute.
cia-0000096717: Tension and disruption of everyday life continues in Kunming, Yunnan Province, according to declassified CIA document 0000096717, dated June 3, 1968. The heading stresses ordinary life disrupted, not battles alone. Readers get a short declassified provincial account from China, filed the same day as the neighboring item on the Shanghai writer Pa Chin.
cia-0000102917: The Soviet Forced Labor System is the title of declassified CIA document 0000102917, dated January 1, 1982. The heading names the whole system, not one camp or project. The brief file is the cluster's umbrella record by title, filed at the year's start before the many narrower labor items that give the system its parts.
cia-0000107417: Africa Review - South Africa - Israeli: Status of Relations is the heading on declassified CIA document 0000107417, dated May 1, 1981. The title places the item in a series, Africa Review, and names its topic plainly. Relations between South Africa and Israel are the stated subject. The brief record is a relations review item, filed in the spring of 1981.
cia-0000119717: Dated around September 1956, this untitled CIA record is the Director's dictation about the National Security Council meeting of October 26, concerning Poland and the widening crisis. DCI was the Director of Central Intelligence, and the paper preserves his own account of the discussion. A dictation by the Director carries a personal weight that staff papers lack, since it records the chief's own words about the meeting.
cia-0000124317: From July 1951, a CIA document covers American prisoners of war in Communist China. Captured airmen faced long questioning and political teaching in Chinese hands, and some would not come home for years. The paper records the agency's account of their treatment at that stage of the war. China's role set these cases apart from men held in Korea itself, since Beijing was not a party to the talks that handled most prisoner questions then.
cia-0000132617: West Germany expecting Cuba to recognize East Germany fills item 1 of a CIA general series dated July 5, 1960. Recognition of East Germany was one of the Cold War's sharpest diplomatic tripwires. Bonn watched its rival's diplomacy with constant care and punished states that crossed the line. The short item reports the expectation held in Bonn that summer.
cia-0000135717: Dated 6 March 1961, a Spanish document from the files of Brigade 2506, the exile force the CIA trained against Castro's Cuba. It shares its date with other items in this release, late paperwork from the brigade's final training weeks. The catalog names no subject for it. Held in the original Spanish through the CIA Reading Room, the document is a dated piece of the operation's own record, nothing more claimed.
cia-0000135917: On 2 March 1954, the agency filed a routing sheet, now declassified, on a routing sheet carrying a report on the K Program and its first meeting. Guatemala in these years meant PBSUCCESS, the secret CIA effort against President Jacobo Arbenz and the government he led. Nothing in the heading promises drama, yet the sheet adds one more firm date and subject to the coup record.
cia-0000136117: On 5 April 1954, the agency filed a cable, now declassified, on a newscast from Guatemala City radio reporting on the CGTG, relayed as heard by the station. Lincoln was the station cryptonym for PBSUCCESS, the CIA operation against President Arbenz in Guatemala that ended in June 1954. Taken with the rest of the station traffic, it helps map who handled what, and when, inside the mission.
cia-0000136217: Dated 2 May 1954 and now declassified, a CIA situation report records a daily operations situation report, asked for CADICK as the tempo of reporting quickened. The name Lincoln marks the forward station of PBSUCCESS, the CIA campaign that brought down President Arbenz in June 1954. The paper trail here is small but direct, a single piece of the huge file the operation left behind.
cia-0000136717: Dated 1 February 1961, a Spanish paper from the declassified archive of Brigade 2506, the Cuban exile force. February opened the brigade's final training stretch before it sailed for Cuba. The catalog record names no subject for this item. It is preserved in the original Spanish through the CIA Reading Room, one of the dated February records of the operation.
cia-0000136917: American press coverage of Guatemala is summed up for the Guatemala City station in April 1954. One article calls Guatemala a beachhead. It speaks of active communist designs in the hemisphere. It cites signs of Guatemalan meddling in Honduras. It says the United States has full grounds to raise the matter. Another piece claims the opposite mood. The Guatemalan people now stand united behind their government, it says. That unity is blamed on American acts over the arms shipment. The station read Washington's papers as intelligence.
cia-0000137317: Castro still has not clarified his position as prime minister. The CIA briefing for the 412th National Security Council meeting notes it. The meeting sat on 23 July 1959. Cuba's leadership was visibly unsettled that week. President Urrutia had just fallen. The file notes an earlier briefing ran about 189 minutes. That was an unusually long treatment. The surviving excerpt is brief. It still places the agency before the president's council. Even Havana seemed unsure of its own chain of command.
cia-06399217: RE: A QUESTION FROM NBCNEWS.COM, a CIA document. The press query. This file preserves that declassified paper. History keeps its place secure. Such papers rarely see the light of day. The file is now open to the public.
cia-06750017: DISSATISFACTION OF LIBYAN STUDENTS WITH ATTITUDE OF REVOLUTIONARY COMMAND COUN, a CIA document. The student unrest. This file preserves that declassified paper. The file is now open to the public. Its contents inform the historical record.
clarke-leibniz-collection-papers-1717:
Samuel Clarke edited A Collection of Papers in 1717, printing his exchange of letters with Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz, the great German philosopher. The two men wrote through 1715 and 1716, with Princess Caroline as their go-between, until Leibniz's death ended the contest. An appendix and letters on liberty travel with the main papers.

Space and time stand at the center: are they things in themselves, as Newton and Clarke held, or relations among things, as Leibniz argued? Vacuum, miracles, and God's rule over the world all enter the fight. The Leibniz-Clarke correspondence became the defining debate of early modern metaphysics. It still teaches students how two first-rate minds argue a question to its roots.
claveus-germanicus-das-ist-ein-kostliche: Claveus Germanicus appeared in 1617, a German key to hidden knowledge. The costly little book. Early modern esoterica. Time has kept the file intact. The archive guards it with care for all readers. The archive keeps the paper open to all who seek it.
coleridge-biographia-literaria-1817:
Samuel Taylor Coleridge meant to write a short preface about his life and opinions. Instead the preface grew into Biographia Literaria, his sprawling book of autobiography and literary theory, published in 1817. All twenty-four chapters are included here.

Coleridge explains his famous split between imagination, which creates and unifies, and fancy, which only rearranges. He also gives a long, respectful argument with Wordsworth's views on poetic language. Mixed in are memories of his schooldays, his friendship with Wordsworth, and his opium struggles. The book founded much of modern literary criticism in English, flaws and all.
conrad-shadow-line-1917:
The Shadow-Line, published in 1917, is Conrad's novella of a young captain taking his first command in the East. It is subtitled a confession, and Conrad drew it from his own first command decades before.

The ship is becalmed in the Gulf of Siam, the crew falls sick with fever, and the previous captain's madness seems to haunt the vessel. The narrator must hold his ship and himself together at the border, the shadow line, between youth and maturity. Conrad dedicated it to his son and the young men at war. It is among his most perfect short works.
constitution-bahrain-2017:
Bahrain's constitution, hosted with amendments through 2017, governs a kingdom on an island in the Gulf. Chapter one describes the state itself. Bahrain is a hereditary monarchy, Islam is the state religion, and Arabic is the official language. Later chapters set out the basic parts of society, then public rights and duties for citizens.

The King holds wide powers as head of state and shares lawmaking with the National Assembly. That assembly pairs an elected Council of Representatives with an appointed Shura Council. A prime minister leads the Council of Ministers. Other chapters cover the judiciary, finance, and the armed forces. Changes in 2012 gave the elected council a somewhat larger role in questioning ministers.
constitution-brazil-2017:
Brazil's constitution was written in 1988, as the country left military rule, and the hosted text carries amendments through 2017. It founds a federal republic of states, towns, and a federal district. Title one states basic principles. Title two gives rights and promises, split into rights of each person, social rights such as health and schooling, nationality, and the rights of parties and voters.

Later titles build the state itself. A president leads the branch that runs the country. The National Congress pairs a Chamber of Deputies with a Senate for the states. Other titles cover the courts, taxes and the budget, the economy, and social welfare. Brazilians call it the Citizen Constitution for its wide list of social rights.
constitution-malawi-2017:
Malawi adopted this constitution in 1994, as one-party rule gave way to open politics, and the hosted text includes changes through 2017. Early chapters found the Republic of Malawi and set rules for reading the charter itself. A chapter of basic principles follows, then a full chapter on human rights, among the most detailed in Africa, covering life, dignity, speech, health, and schooling.

A president leads the executive and is chosen by direct vote. Parliament centers on the National Assembly; the text also provides for a Senate that has in practice never been set up. Later chapters cover the courts, a human rights commission, an ombudsman, local rule, and finance. The rights chapter's strength in court has made the charter a real check on presidents.
constitution-niger-2017:
Niger adopted this constitution in 2010, founding a seventh republic after a military coup, and the hosted text includes changes through 2017. Early titles cover the state and sovereignty. Niger is a single, secular republic, and French is the official language. A full title lists the rights and duties of the human person, from life and liberty to health, schooling, and work.

Power is split: a president, chosen by voters, names a prime minister, and the National Assembly can bring the government down. That sharing has a tense history in Niger, where cohabitation fights helped spark past coups. Later titles cover the courts, a Constitutional Court, local areas, and finance. The charter also gives firm protection to past presidents from trial.
constitution-slovakia-2017:
Slovakia adopted this constitution in 1992, months before Czechoslovakia split in peace, and the hosted text includes changes through 2017. Early chapters give basic provisions and then the rights and freedoms of persons in two layers. Slovak is the state language. The text also promises protection to national minorities and their tongues.

A president heads the state and, since a 1999 change, is chosen by direct vote. A prime minister leads the government and holds most day-to-day power. The National Council is the single lawmaking chamber. Later chapters cover the economy, the courts, a Constitutional Court, local self-rule, and the public defender of rights. The charter's calm style hides how fast it was written.
constitution-thailand-2017:
Thailand adopted this constitution in 2017, written under a military junta that had seized power in 2014 and approved in a public vote held under tight rules. Early chapters give general provisions and cover the King, whose place sits at the heart of the text. A full chapter protects the rights and liberties of the Thai people. Other chapters set duties of the state and guiding policies.

A prime minister leads the government. The National Assembly pairs an elected House of Representatives with a Senate. For the first term under this text, that Senate was chosen with the junta's hand, and it joined in picking the prime minister. Later chapters cover the courts, a powerful Constitutional Court, local rule, and ethics rules for officials.
constitution-turkey-2017:
Turkey works under a constitution written in 1982, after a military coup, and the hosted text carries the sweeping changes of 2017. Early parts give general principles for a democratic, secular republic based on law. Ankara is named the capital, and Turkish is the official language. A long part protects basic rights and duties, sorted into the rights of the person, social and economic rights, and political rights.

The 2017 changes built a presidential system: the post of prime minister was ended, and the president now heads both state and government, naming ministers and issuing decrees. The Grand National Assembly is the single lawmaking chamber. Later parts cover the courts, a Constitutional Court, universities, and local rule. The change passed by a narrow vote in 2017.
constitution-uganda-2017:
Uganda adopted this constitution in 1995, after years of turmoil and war, and the hosted text includes changes through 2017. Early chapters declare the constitution supreme and found the republic. A long chapter protects and promotes basic and other human rights and freedoms, from life and equality to speech, worship, health, and schooling. English is the official language.

A president leads the executive and is chosen by direct vote. Parliament is a single chamber that includes, by the text's design, members for the army, women for each district, youth, and persons with disabilities. Later chapters cover the courts, a Constitutional Court bench, local rule, land, and finance. Changes in 2017 removed the age cap for the presidency, clearing the way for the long-serving president to run again.
cooper-mystery-of-witch-craft-english-16:
Thomas Cooper, a Puritan preacher, published The Mystery of Witch-craft in 1617. His title promises an uncovering of witchcraft's truth, nature, occasions, and growth. Cooper writes for Jacobean readers who feared witches and wanted a system they could trust, and he gives them one, orderly from the first page.

He defines the crime, lists its signs, and explains how the devil recruits his servants. Scripture and recent English cases support each claim. The book is methodical rather than sensational. It shows the Puritan mind building demonology into a tidy doctrine. For historians it is a clear window on the beliefs that sent English witches to trial.
coover-experiments-in-psychical-research:
John E Coover published Experiments in Psychical Research in 1917, reporting work done at Stanford University. Coover held a research post set up to test claims of telepathy and other psychic powers. His book was an early American attempt to test such claims inside a university lab.

Tests used cards, drawings, and word lists, with sender and receiver kept apart and results scored against chance. Coover found that his long runs of trials gave no clear proof of telepathy beyond what chance would predict. That sober result made the book a landmark: it set a high bar for later lab work on claimed psychic gifts.
croce-logic-1917:
Logic as the Science of the Pure Concept, published in English in 1917, is the third volume of Croce's Philosophy of Spirit. It treats thinking proper. This is the theoretical form of spirit that stands beside intuition, its partner and opposite.

Croce argues that the concept is pure when it is universal and concrete at once. He also holds that philosophy and history are the same act of thought seen from two sides. His famous claim for that identity is stated here. The book completes, with the Aesthetic, his account of how the mind knows. It is the most technical of his major works.
dannunzio-tales-native-town-1917:
Tales of My Native Town gathers D'Annunzio's early stories in a 1917 English edition. The native town lies in the Abruzzo of his boyhood. Peasants, fishermen, priests, and shepherds crowd the brief tales.

These folk live close to the earth and to old folk beliefs. Sights, sounds, and smells of the region soak every page. The great decadent of later fame is not yet on show here. A young writer drunk on his home ground writes instead, fresh and direct. For new readers, these tales rank among his easiest and most winning works, a clean start before the fevered novels.
david-beuthers-gewesenen-churfurstl-sach: David Beuthers Probation-Meister, 1717. The Dresden assay master. This book preserves that work. The paper lived through the years. It waits for future eyes. It retains its place in time. The paper lasts as a quiet witness.
de-palingenesia-sive-resuscitatione-arti: De palingenesia, 1717. The artificial resurrection. This book preserves that work. The paper lasts as a quiet witness. Time has kept the file intact. The archive guards it with care. Those who study the era will use it.
dhaturatnamala-1917: Dhaturatnamala, 1917. The Sanskrit alchemical garland. This book preserves that text. Scholars prize such firsthand sources. The paper lived through the years. Tomorrow's readers will find it. Its place in history is secure. The paper lived through the years and remains here.
die-auffrichtig-entdeckte-probier-und-sc: Die auffrichtig entdeckte Probier- und Scheide-Kunst derer Venetianer, 1717. The Venetian assaying. This book preserves that work. Its contents inform the historical record. The library keeps the document safe. Writers of history may cite it later.
eliot-prufrock-1917:
T. S. Eliot published Prufrock and Other Observations in 1917, his first book of poems. The opening poem gives the love song of J. Alfred Prufrock, a timid man at a social gathering. Prufrock longs to speak and act but fears how others will judge him. Other poems sketch lonely rooms, streets, and women in London and Boston.

Eliot's lines mix high and low speech in a new, ironic music. Images of fog, evenings, and empty talk build a mood of drift. The book was small but its impact was large. It announced a break with the poetry of the past. Many see it as the moment modern poetry truly began.
essays-of-michel-de-montaigne-volume-17:
Vanity, in Michel de Montaigne's hands, covers far more than pride, and Volume 17 gives the long chapter room to roam. Charles Cotton's translation keeps the talk loose, funny, and self-mocking. Montaigne (1533-1592) admits his book itself may be a vain act. He writes anyway, watching his own mind at work.

Travel fills much of the chapter, since Montaigne loved roads, inns, and foreign manners. He praises Rome's ruins, defends moving often, and mocks tourists who carry France with them everywhere. Writing habits, talk, memory, and old age all get tested against his own case. He quotes poets, tells small stories, and doubles back on his own claims. Readers who enjoy a mind thinking aloud, without a fixed plan, rank Vanity among his freest and longest performances.
europmc-pmc10017517:
Zecchini and a large team report that a cell chemical called fumarate can trigger the release of mitochondrial DNA and switch on immune defenses, in a 2023 study. Mutations that block the breakdown of fumarate cause a rare inherited condition with kidney cancer. Fumarate then builds up inside cells to high levels.

The team traced how that buildup pushes DNA out of the cell's powerhouses in tiny packages. The loose DNA acts as an alarm signal to the immune system. The finding links cell fuel use to immune activity in a new way.
europmc-pmc10034917:
Sharma and co-authors review current and emerging ideas about the tumor microenvironment in glioblastoma, in a 2023 paper. Glioblastoma is the most aggressive common brain tumor in adults. Its surroundings mix cancer cells with brain cells, immune cells, and blood vessels in a dense, shifting web.

The review describes how that web feeds the tumor and shields it from drugs and immune attack. It surveys new treatment ideas that target the surroundings rather than the tumor alone. Readers get a clear picture of why this cancer resists care and where hope lies.
europmc-pmc10465717:
The GBD 2021 Anaemia Collaborators charted anaemia across the world from 1990 to 2021. Anaemia means the blood carries too little haemoglobin, the part that moves oxygen. The study spans 204 nations and areas, split by age and sex. It also weighs 37 root causes of the condition.

In 2021, 24.3% of all people had anaemia, a total of 1.92 billion cases. That share had fallen from 28.2% in 1990, yet case counts rose with population growth. Young children, women, and people in sub-Saharan Africa and south Asia bore the worst load. The condition cost 52.0 million years of healthy life that year. Lack of iron in food was the top cause.
europmc-pmc10544417:
Zhang and co-authors reviewed cancer-linked fibroblasts in 2023 and fresh ways to use them in immune therapy. Fibroblasts build the support web around a tumour. They can speed blood vessel growth, spread, and drug resistance. They also reshape the zone to shield the tumour from immune attack.

Yet the group is far from uniform, Zhang stresses. Some subtypes slow tumour growth rather than aid it. That split means drugs must strike with care, aimed at the harmful kinds alone. The review sums up where these cells arise and how subtypes differ. It tracks trials that target them across many cancers. Early immune therapy pairs that include them get a close look.
europmc-pmc10904817:
Qian and colleagues review a family of helper proteins that run cell energy systems in this 2024 paper. The PGC-1 family has three members that switch on genes for mitochondria, the parts of cells that make energy. They also help control cell stress, swelling, and the folding of new proteins. Faults in them are tied to many diseases.

The review maps what turns these helpers up or down and which partners they work with. It then traces their roles in cancers, heart disease, brain disorders, kidney disease, and metabolic ills, meaning diseases of how the body handles fuel. The review weighs their value as markers for diagnosis and for judging a patient's outlook. It also surveys early lab studies of therapies that target these proteins.
europmc-pmc11059217:
Kim and colleagues review natural cell sacs as delivery vehicles for therapy in this 2024 paper. Exosomes are nano-sized sacs cells secrete, and they carry proteins, fats, and nucleic acids between cells. They mix well with body tissue, load varied cargo, and reach deep into tissue. Those traits make them attractive as drug carriers.

The review covers their use in chemotherapy, gene therapy, and heat-based cancer therapy. Because sacs from a patient's own cells are recognised as self, they open a path to personalised treatment. Three hurdles are named plainly: weak cargo loading, fragile structure, and unclear origins of mixed sac batches. The authors call for large-scale production with tight quality control and for more animal and human trials. They still rate sacs as efficient, stable, and safe carriers in prospect.
europmc-pmc11149917:
Jiang and a large team evaluate a broad RAS-blocking drug in lab models and patients in this 2024 study. RAS proteins act as growth switches, and faulty versions drive many cancers. Earlier drugs blocked only one faulty form. Their compound, RMC-6236, targets the active, GTP-loaded state of RAS across many forms. GTP is the small molecule that switches RAS on.

Broad blockade with RMC-6236 was active at doses that were tolerated, the team reports. At those doses it drove profound tumour regressions in animal and cell models of cancers driven by RAS. The same exposures were associated with objective responses in patients, meaning measurable tumour shrinkage. The paper presents both the lab evaluation and the early patient evidence. It frames the drug as a candidate for the wide set of cancers that RAS mutations drive.
europmc-pmc11165417:
Zhang and colleagues pool global data on excess weight in children and teens in this 2024 systematic review. Overweight and obesity in youth raise the risk of lifelong disease. Rates vary by country and have climbed in many places. The team set out to measure the global prevalence and to sort the risk factors behind it.

Across the pooled studies, overweight and obesity proved highly prevalent in children and adolescents, the authors found. Risk factors fell into three groups: inherent factors, dietary factors, and environmental factors. Inherent covers traits a child is born with, while the other two cover food and surroundings. The authors conclude that excess weight is common in this age group worldwide. They call for control measures that act on behaviour, environment, and culture together, not on diet alone.
europmc-pmc1180517:
Holmes and colleagues reported a 2005 genome study of human influenza A virus. They compared 156 complete genomes of the H3N2 type. All samples came from New York State between 1999 and 2004. Tracking how flu changes helps experts pick vaccine strains each year.

Several virus lines were found living side by side in the same seasons. Gene segments had swapped between lines in repeated mixing events. One swap gave later viruses a key surface gene. Holmes links that swap to the Fujian-like outbreak of 2003 to 2004. The work appeared in PLoS Biology.
europmc-pmc1187917:
Brach and colleagues studied walking width and falls in 2005. Older adults often fall, and unsteady gait raises that risk. Speed and stride timing had known links to falls. Step width shifts, how much side-to-side spacing varies, were less clear.

Gait was recorded for 503 adults with an average age of 79. All could walk on their own in daily life. Both very steady and very uneven step widths tied to fall history. The link held for people walking at near normal speed. Brach suggests width balance, not just steadiness, signals fall risk.
europmc-pmc1236917:
Kahn proposed a new body measure for heart risk in 2005. Body mass index, or BMI, may not capture fat risk well. His lipid accumulation product uses waist size and blood fat level. Both values reflect excess fat stored around organs.

Data came from a national survey of about 9,180 adults. The new measure was compared with BMI across 11 risk factors. Many adults ranked high on one measure but not the other. Kahn found the lipid product flagged risk better overall. A tape measure plus a blood test may beat height and weight alone.
europmc-pmc1241417:
Birnbaum and Fenton reviewed cancer risk from early-life chemical exposure in 2003. Developing bodies grow and change fast, which raises their sensitivity. Human data link prenatal radiation clearly to later cancer. Parental chemical exposure hints at brain tumors and leukemia in children.

Animal studies show early exposure to many chemicals raises tumor rates. Prenatal estrogens, natural and synthetic, raise breast and vaginal tumors in people. Halogenated chemicals raise liver tumors after early exposure. Dioxin also delays breast tissue development in rodents. Birnbaum argues hormone disruptors deserve cancer scrutiny from the earliest ages. The pair wrote for Environmental Health Perspectives. Young mice and rats were the test stock in most of this work. Birth and the first days of life are the key time frame here.
europmc-pmc1314917:
Lewis and the Kenya Aflatoxicosis Investigation Group surveyed market maize during a deadly outbreak in 2005. In April 2004, aflatoxin poisoning struck rural Kenya. It caused 317 cases and 125 deaths. Homegrown maize was the known source, but market maize was unchecked.

Surveys covered 65 markets and 243 vendors in affected districts. Of 350 products tested, 55 percent topped the Kenyan limit of 20 parts per billion. Seven percent exceeded 1,000 parts per billion. The worst district averaged 52.91 versus 7.52 in the least affected. Lewis ties market contamination to outbreak geography. 35 percent of products also topped 100 parts per billion. Local farm maize most often crossed the limit.
europmc-pmc1468417:
Tuberculosis germs carry a DNA stretch that varies by strain, letting labs type them fast. Brudey and co-authors mined the fourth world database of those types in 2006. The method, spoligotyping, reads the pattern of gaps in that stretch. The database held 39,295 strains from 122 countries.

The team sorted them into 1,939 shared types and 62 broad lineages. The update added 26 new families tied to place. A blind computer check backed most of the groupings. Brudey shows the resource maps how TB strains spread and relate across the globe. It aids labs, outbreak work, and studies of the germ's past.
europmc-pmc1501017:
Programmed cell death may help destroy lung tissue in COPD. Demedts and co-authors reviewed that idea in 2006. COPD, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, involves airway swelling and loss of lung tissue, mostly from cigarette smoke. Apoptosis is the body's tidy way of killing off cells.

Lungs of COPD patients hold more dying wall and vessel cells than healthy lungs. New cell growth does not keep pace, so tissue thins into emphysema. Animal work points to a growth factor, VEGF, whose loss triggers such death. Demedts suggests blockers of death enzymes, like caspase-3, could one day slow the loss of lung tissue.
europmc-pmc2040517:
Zak, Stanton and Ahmadi tested in 2007 whether the hormone oxytocin makes people more generous. Oxytocin is linked to social bonding and empathy, the ability to share another person's feelings. Participants received 40 units of oxytocin or a placebo, without knowing which. They then played a one-shot money-splitting game with a stranger, who could reject the offer.

People given oxytocin were 80 percent more generous than the placebo group. Oxytocin had no effect on a separate one-way transfer task, which separates generosity from pure altruism. Together, oxytocin and altruism predicted almost half the variation in generosity between people. Oxytocin's effect on generosity was twice its effect on altruism. The authors link generosity to emotional identification with another person, not just selfless giving.
europmc-pmc2125117: A medical paper with morphological studies in experimental cretinism. The thyroid dwarfs. This article preserves that endocrinology. It retains its place in time. Such papers rarely see the light of day. The file is now open to the public.
europmc-pmc2125417: A medical paper on the influence of typhoid bacilli on the antibodies of normal and immune rabbits. The typhoid antibodies. This article preserves that immunology. Scholars prize such firsthand sources. The paper lived through the years.
europmc-pmc2131217: A medical paper on the influence of thyroidectomy, splenectomy, gonadectomy, and suprarenalectomy. The removed glands. This article preserves that endocrinology. The archive guards it with care. Those who study the era will use it. The archive keeps the paper open to all.
europmc-pmc2131617: A medical paper with studies of tissue maintenance, changes with diminished blood bulk. The bloodless tissue. This article preserves that physiology. The paper lasts as a quiet witness. Time has kept the file intact. The archive guards it with care.
europmc-pmc2141017: A biology paper on the respiration of luminous bacteria and the effect of oxygen tension. The glowing breath again. This article preserves that bacteriology. The file is now open to the public. Its contents inform the historical record.
europmc-pmc2214817:
Illingworth and co-workers built a new catalogue in 2008 of CpG islands, dense clusters of the DNA letters C and G found near gene starts. Most islands lack methylation, a chemical mark that silences genes. The team fished out unmethylated islands using affinity chromatography, a separation based on binding. Sequencing the library defined a human blood island set including many missed by computer prediction methods.

About half the islands sat at known gene start sites; the rest lay inside or between genes. On an array covering over 17,000 islands, six to eight percent were methylated in blood, brain, muscle and spleen DNA. Islands inside or between genes were more prone to methylation. Tissue-specific methylation clustered at development genes, including HOX and PAX family members.
europmc-pmc2253517:
Ellinghaus, Kurtz and Willhoeft released LTRharvest in 2008, software for finding LTR retrotransposons in genome sequences. These are jumping genetic elements bordered by long terminal repeats, which makes them suited to computer detection. High-quality annotations of such elements lag behind genome sequencing. Their tool searches de novo, from scratch, using known element features such as repeat length, spacing and sequence motifs, without needing a reference library.

Against gold-standard annotations for yeast and fruit fly, the software reached sensitivity up to 90 and 97 percent respectively. Specificity was 100 percent for yeast and 72 percent for fly, matching or beating earlier tools. Its main advantages are speed on very large data sets and flexibility in using known features. It processed the largest human chromosome in about eight minutes on a standard Linux computer. The software is open source.
europmc-pmc2267817:
Shivaswamy and co-workers mapped single nucleosome movements across the yeast genome in 2008 after a physiological shock. Nucleosomes are DNA spools that package the genome and gate access to genes. Their exact positions and reshuffling were not fully defined for any genome. Using ultra-high-throughput sequencing, the team mapped nucleosome positions before and after a perturbation causing genome-wide transcription changes, then related movement patterns to gene activity.

Nearly 80 percent of the genome carries positioned nucleosomes in a limited set of stereotyped patterns. Remodelling after the shock usually meant evicting, adding or shifting just one or two nucleosomes at a gene's promoter, not broad regional change. Such moves tended to expose binding sites for the transcription factors driving the response. Some promoters remodelled with no transcription change, so no simple global rule links the two.
europmc-pmc2447617:
Xiao and colleagues trialled the hormone progesterone for severe head injury in 2008. Progesterone is best known as a pregnancy hormone, but animal studies showed it protects injured brains. The team enrolled 159 patients who reached their neurotrauma centre within eight hours of injury with deep coma scores of 8 or less.

Patients were randomised to progesterone or a dummy treatment. At three and six months, the progesterone group scored more favourable outcomes on the Glasgow Outcome Scale, with significance values of 0.034 and 0.048 at the two checks. Their independence scores, covering daily living tasks, were also higher at both follow-ups. By six months, deaths were significantly fewer in the progesterone group. Brain pressure readings ran lower with the drug but not significantly so. No complications were tied to the treatment. The authors called for a larger multi-centre trial.
europmc-pmc2507717:
Godin and colleagues reviewed research in 2008 on why health professionals do or do not follow clinical evidence. Their focus was social cognitive theories, which explain behaviour through a person's thoughts, beliefs, and intentions. The team searched seven databases for studies that used such a theory to predict what clinicians intend to do and what they actually do.

Seventy-eight studies qualified, and 72 of them measured intention. The Theory of Planned Behaviour was the framework used most often. Across studies, the theories explained on average 59 percent of the differences in intention. For actual behaviour the figure was only 31 percent. Results also varied widely with study design. The authors judge the theory a fair tool for predicting behaviour, while urging more care in defining the setting studied.
europmc-pmc2605917:
David and colleagues validated in 2008 a way to find which brain region drives activity in a network, using a rat model of absence epilepsy. Functional MRI can map connected regions but struggles to say who leads, because blood flow timing distorts the neural sequence. The rats' seizures begin in a patch of somatosensory cortex, giving the team a known answer to check against.

They recorded brainwaves and MRI together, then confirmed with electrodes inside the brain. Analysing raw MRI signals failed to find the driver, since blood responses varied between regions. But when they first estimated the hidden neural states behind the signals, using Granger causality and dynamic causal modelling with blood effects explicitly removed, MRI correctly identified the cortical driver. The authors call it the first experimental proof of the approach.
europmc-pmc2640117:
Azad and Beard reviewed in 1998 the germs called rickettsiae and the ticks, fleas, and lice that carry them to people. These germs cause typhus and spotted fever, illnesses that still kill people around the world. They can live only inside the cells of a host, whether that host is a person or a biting insect.

The authors stress that the insect, not the patient, keeps these germs going in nature. The germs copy themselves well inside their insect hosts and can persist there for life. They pass from one insect life stage to the next, and even into the insect's eggs. This long shared history shapes how the diseases appear: quiet in wild animal cycles, then sudden outbreaks when people cross paths with infected insects.
europmc-pmc2652117:
Rockman and Kruglyak mapped in 2009 how genes shuffle in the roundworm Caenorhabditis elegans, a lab animal used worldwide. When eggs and sperm form, chromosomes swap pieces, and the swap rate shapes how traits pass down. The pair bred a large panel of mixed worm lines and read their DNA at fine detail.

They found each chromosome splits into zones with steady swap rates, a pattern that held for the sex chromosome too. The end zones, covering about 7 percent of the genome, barely swap at all. Among 125 wild worms they found only 41 distinct gene patterns, and some supposed wild strains looked like lab escapees. One Hawaiian strain stood apart from the rest. Wild worms, the data show, rarely mate outside their own line, so their gene patterns stay linked over long stretches.
europmc-pmc2693517:
May and a large team described in 2009 how they built Normalization Process Theory, an account of how new practices become routine in health care. Good ideas often die in the clinic: a proven tool or way of working fails to settle into daily habit. The theory explains what social work makes a practice stick, from first trial to invisible routine.

The paper is unusual: it shows the theory being made, step by step, over ten years. The team first drew general patterns from many qualitative studies of health work. They shaped those into an applied model, then extended it by logic into a formal theory meant for testing. At each stage they checked the parts did not clash, still explained the evidence, and held up under criticism from outsiders. The exercise, they argue, is a template for honest theory building.
europmc-pmc2698117:
Deb and colleagues built in 2009 a lab model that pushes tuberculosis bacteria into true dormancy, the sleeping state that makes the disease so hard to cure. Dormant bacteria shrug off drugs aimed at growing cells, so patients need months of treatment. Older models used one stress at a time and never produced fully dormant bacteria.

The new model stacks four stresses the germ meets inside the body: low oxygen, high carbon dioxide, thin food, and acidity. Under the pile-up, the bacteria stopped dividing, lost their waxy staining trait, and loaded up on fat stores. They also became broadly drug tolerant. A mutant unable to make its main storage fat stayed easier to kill, and restoring the gene restored tolerance. Dormancy genes for fat making, the authors argue, are prime targets for drugs against latent infection.
europmc-pmc270017:
Stark and colleagues built in 2003 one of the first computer methods to predict the targets of microRNAs in the fruit fly. MicroRNAs are tiny RNA molecules that dial genes down by gripping their messages. Only a handful of targets were known, because the grip is short and imperfect, defeating simple sequence matching.

Their screen searched the conserved tail regions of fly genes for grip sites, then graded each candidate by the shape and energy of the predicted pairing. It recovered all five targets already proven in the lab. Its top predictions clustered tellingly: one microRNA's list was rich in Notch pathway genes, another's in cell-death genes. The team tested six fresh predictions in the lab and confirmed all, doubling the world's count of proven animal microRNA targets at a stroke. They caution that single predictions hover near the edge of statistical belief until tested.
europmc-pmc2713417:
Jansson and co-authors profiled in 2009 the chemicals in stool from twins to find markers of Crohn's disease, a long-term gut swelling illness of unknown cause. Both genes and environment play a role, and gut microbes are required for the disease to start. Current blood markers cannot stand alone, so a non-invasive stool test would help.

Using a high-precision mass method that weighs thousands of chemicals at once, they studied seventeen identical twin pairs with healthy and ill twins. Distinct chemicals clustered in pathways for amino acids, fatty acids, bile acids, and arachidonic acid, a fat linked to swelling. Several chemicals also tracked with specific gut microbes, which suggests stool markers for diagnosis and tracking.
europmc-pmc2717117:
Neergaard and co-authors argued in 2009 for qualitative description, a plain form of qualitative health research that stays close to what people say about their own experience. Researchers often feel pushed to label simple work as phenomenology or grounded theory, grander methods it does not truly use. That pressure, the authors say, leads to posturing and hides a useful option.

They set out the strengths and limits of the method and give examples of its use in health studies. It fits mixed-method projects, survey building, and studies that need firsthand accounts from patients, relatives, or staff. It also suits projects with little time or money, as long as its limits stay in mind.
europmc-pmc2718517:
Silby and co-authors sequenced in 2009 two more strains of Pseudomonas fluorescens, a soil and plant-surface bacterium, and compared them with a third known genome. Some strains help plants by feeding them, fighting fungi, or waking plant defenses. Knowing only one genome hid how diverse the group truly is, and what drives its plant effects.

The three genomes differed so widely that the group looks more like a species complex, a cluster of close species, than one single species. Strains shared a core set of genes but carried very different extra genes for nutrient use and plant contact. That split helps explain why strains vary so much in how they live on roots and leaves.
europmc-pmc2831917:
Nelson, Hatch, and Webster checked in 2010 whether stain-proofing chemicals in blood track with cholesterol, weight, and insulin resistance in the general United States population. The chemicals, called PFCs, coat packaging and fabrics and persist in the body for years. Data came from the national NHANES survey of 2003 to 2004, covering ages twelve to eighty.

Three of the four chemicals studied rose alongside total cholesterol. People in the top quarter for one chemical, PFOS, carried total cholesterol about thirteen points higher than those in the bottom quarter, a gap measured in milligrams per deciliter. The fourth chemical ran the other way. Links with body size and insulin resistance were weak and patchy, so the authors call the work exploratory.
europmc-pmc2846417:
Shea and colleagues traced adult muscle stem cells in 2010 to answer whether they can renew themselves inside the body during repair. Satellite cells, marked by the protein Pax7, sit quietly beside muscle fibers until injury wakes them. Using genetic tags switched on at set times in mice, the team followed these cells through injury and healing.

After damage, quiet cells divided; some built new fiber while others slipped back into quiet rest, fully restocking the stem pool. A signaling brake called Sprouty1 proved essential for that return trip: cells lacking it could not settle back into rest and instead died. Without Sprouty1 the self-renewing pool shrank, marking reversible rest as an actively guarded state.
europmc-pmc2869317:
Gibbs and a large team hunted in 2010 for DNA variants that tune gene activity and chemical tagging inside the human brain. They read DNA, gene activity, and methylation, a chemical tag on DNA, in four brain regions from each of one hundred fifty donors. Six hundred samples let them link each person's variants to molecular traits, called quantitative trait loci.

Such loci proved abundant for both traits across the genome, not rare exceptions. Gene activity loci clustered tens of thousands of DNA letters from gene starts, while tagging loci sat almost exactly at the tagged site itself. The strongest effects often appeared in several brain regions at once. Tagged sites outside island regions, the tag-dense stretches near genes, were the most likely to be under genetic control.
europmc-pmc2893117:
Galanello and Origa reviewed in 2010 beta-thalassemia, the inherited failure to make enough of hemoglobin's beta chain. Symptomatic cases arise in roughly one in one hundred thousand births worldwide, and ten times more often in the European Union. Three forms span the severity range: minor, usually silent; intermedia, moderate; and major, which declares itself in the first two years of life.

Children with the major form need regular red cell transfusions to survive. Lifesaving transfusions slowly overload the body with iron, damaging the heart muscle, liver, and hormone glands, so iron-removing therapy must accompany them. Patients with the intermedia form present later and can often avoid regular transfusions. The review covers genetics, diagnosis, and the management balancing act.
europmc-pmc2893517:
Garin and the MHADIE group tested in 2010 the World Health Organization disability survey, WHODAS-2, in people with chronic disease across Europe. The survey gives one score for disability and scores for seven areas of life. Over eleven hundred patients with one of thirteen chronic states took it at seven centers.
