The proteins are useful in several brain and nerve diseases, so the team measured them in ninety patients and forty healthy volunteers, and compared levels with standard severity scores.

Neither protein differed between patients and controls, and neither tracked with disease severity, past crises, or treatments. The authors conclude plainly that these markers should not be adopted for monitoring this disease, despite their value elsewhere. As one of the larger controlled analyses of its kind, the study helps steer the search for myasthenia-specific blood markers in other directions.
plos-pone-0352117:
RETRACTION: The PLOS One Editors have withdrawn a study that claimed a protein called ISL1 can push human stem cells to become heart muscle cells. Concerns were raised after the work came out. Several figures looked wrong in ways that are hard to explain as honest error.

In one chart, the error bars looked far too even across all time points. In gel images, sharp breaks showed between lanes. Bands in different rows also looked too much alike. The first author answered some points, but trust in the data was gone. Readers should not rely on the study's claims.
plos-pone-0352317:
Sibel Balik and five colleagues report this 2026 PLOS One experiment on growing basil microgreens under LED lights in an indoor vertical farm. Light color recipes shape how these young greens grow and how nutritious they become. The team grew basil under three spectra: red-heavy mixes, a full spectrum, and one adding white and far-red light, then measured growth, color, and a long list of nutrients and flavor compounds.

The recipe with far-red produced the tallest plants, best yield, and brightest color, along with the most phenolic compounds. The full spectrum led on vitamin C, flavonoids, and oil content, while the red-blue mix gave the most dry matter and minerals. The authors recommend the far-red recipe for commercial growers, while noting results may differ by crop variety.
plos-pone-0352417:
Vedran Premuzic and seven colleagues ask whether timing matters for a blood-filtering therapy in severe muscle injury. Their 2026 study covers intensive care patients in Croatia. Crushed or starved muscle releases toxins that can shut down the kidneys. Hemoadsorption scrubs some of those toxins from the blood. Thirty patients received it alongside standard dialysis-style support. Twenty-five comparable patients received the standard support alone.

Within the treated group, starting early made the difference. Patients whose filtering began within twelve hours of kidney injury recovered kidney function better. Blood levels of the muscle toxins myoglobin and creatine kinase were tracked for three days. Follow-up ran to sixty days. Because the study was small and retrospective, it cannot prove cause. Its title-stated association still gives intensive care teams a practical prompt: when this therapy is used, do not delay it.
plos-pone-0353017:
Dane Wattle and co-authors documented the sea-floor life of key reefs in Australia's Groote Archipelago after back-to-back disasters. Mass coral bleaching and a tropical cyclone struck in quick succession, yet no formal benthic baseline existed for these waters. The archipelago's Traditional Owners, the Anindilyakwa people, hold deep sea knowledge but had not recorded reef change in survey form.

The 2026 study filmed reef sites and analysed frame composition to describe what covers the bottom now: coral, algae, rubble, and other benthic classes. Site health assessments accompany the inventory. Wattle and colleagues offer the baseline as shared ground for collaborative management, so future change can be measured against a documented starting point.
plos-pone-0353117:
Bewuketu Terefe, Nebiyu Mekonnen Derseh, and Tadesse Awoke Ayele map where young women across sub-Saharan Africa do and do not test for HIV, in this 2026 PLOS ONE spatial analysis. They pooled recent national survey data covering about one hundred and forty thousand women. Overall, fewer than four in ten had been tested — far short of global targets — and the map was strikingly uneven.

Testing clustered high in eastern and southern Africa and low in the west. Education, employment, media exposure, marriage, pregnancy, and wealth all nudged testing upward, while distance to a clinic dragged it down. The authors argue that blanket campaigns waste resources: the cold spots on the map need targeted outreach first.
plos-pone-0353217:
Ali Aligholizadeh and three colleagues published this 2026 agriculture study of two friendly fungi that live inside plants. Isolated from native plants, the fungi Aspergillus micronesiensis and Penicillium momoi were pitted against three Fusarium strains that rot tomato and grain crops. The team also tested them under salty conditions and built a powder product.

One fungus fought by crowding the pathogens out, the other by chemical attack, and together they curbed growth strongly. Both tolerated salt, and their powder stayed viable for over two years. Aligholizadeh sees dual-purpose helpers for stressed fields.
plos-pone-0353417:
Da Zhang and seven colleagues read the map of Hebei Province in China through its place names, in this 2026 PLOS ONE study. They catalogued more than eighteen hundred township names and tracked how names drawn from nature and from culture shifted over centuries. The study focuses on the transition belt where the Taihang Mountains meet the Great Wall corridor.

Nature-based names retreated toward the northeast mountains and coast, while culture-based names moved north. During the Ming and Qing dynasties the border belt shifted from military to civilian names. Slope, vegetation, migration, and ethnic mixing emerged as the main drivers — evidence that place names preserve a landscape's history long after events fade.
plos-pone-0354517:
Rebekah Sullivan, Andrew Gardiner, and Glen Cousquer study health care for homeless people in the United Kingdom who live with companion dogs. About one in ten people seeking shelter own an animal, most often a dog, and that bond can block access to housing and clinics. Their 2026 paper uses deep interviews with homeless dog owners and with health, vet, and housing staff.

Both sides described human and animal health as tangled together, not separate problems. Joint clinics at one site drew interest but also raised worries about space and safety. Sullivan and colleagues favor a looser goal: coordinated care across services that respects the pair as a unit. They argue that ignoring the dog often means losing the person too.
plos-pone-0354617:
Souleymane Abdou and Abdoul Moumouni Iro Sodo published this 2026 field study of quick-maturing cowpea in southeastern Niger. Cowpea feeds people and livestock across the Sahel, but drought, poor soils, weeds, and parasites cap yields. Twenty-one varieties were grown in six environments, and several stability methods judged which gave steady grain and fodder harvests wherever planted.

Environment shaped yields most, yet a set of named lines combined earliness with high, steady output of both grain and fodder. Abdou recommends wider testing across farming zones before release as climate-ready varieties for farmers.
plos-pone-0354717:
Saxton and colleagues, in a 2026 national survey study, estimate how a fairer blood donation rule would change who can give blood in New Zealand. Many countries long barred men from donating for a set period after sex with another man. New Zealand has moved to judging each donor's own behavior instead, and the team asked how many men that change would newly include.

More than three thousand men from this community answered an online survey. Most had donated before or wanted to, and most favored the individual approach. Under the old rule, only about one man in eight was eligible. Under the new individual assessment, that share rose to roughly four in ten. Newly eligible men tended to be in their thirties, more educated, and more connected to gay community life. The authors say the policy widens the donor pool safely.
plos-pone-0354817:
Kelly Holloway, Umair Majid, and Quinn Grundy interview Canadian doctors about prescribing immunoglobulin, a costly blood-plasma treatment whose demand keeps rising, in this 2026 qualitative study. Supply is limited worldwide, so doctors sit at the choke point between patients who need the treatment and a system trying to use it wisely. Twelve prescribing clinicians described how they actually make these decisions.

Three broad orientations emerged. Some doctors felt concern and uncertainty about prescribing at all. Others saw themselves as careful stewards of a scarce resource. A third group acted as advocates, pushing for their patients' access. The authors argue that policies built only on applying evidence mechanically miss these human stances, and that understanding them is essential for managing shortages fairly.
plos-pone-0354917:
Vladislav Soukhovolsky and colleagues modelled the flight and numbers of the conifer silk moth, a major forest pest across northern Eurasia. Foresters use light traps to track the moth, but catches are small when populations are low. Their 2026 paper draws on twenty-one years of trap records to build three linked models.

One model predicts when flight starts each season, using accumulated warmth after vegetation greens up in spring. That warmth total stayed stable year to year. A second model shows this year's catch depends mainly on the two previous years, matching known larval patterns. A third handles within-season catch shape. Together the models support forecasting pest numbers from trap data alone.
plos-pone-0355117:
Keji Shan and colleagues test in 2026 whether giving vitamin B12 together with a blue dye drug can ease septic shock in rats. Both agents alone have shown some promise when blood vessels lose tone badly. Rats were pretreated before a bacterial toxin triggered shock, and artery tissue was checked for gene changes alongside blood pressure, organ damage, and stress markers.

Combined treatment lowered several vessel relaxing signals, eased blood pressure problems in part, and reduced inflammation and tissue injury in lung, liver, and kidney. The authors link the benefit to a vessel wall pathway, while noting proof of cause still needs direct testing.
plos-pone-0355217:
Ivaan Pitua and six colleagues published this 2026 protocol, a detailed plan for a review of gout and high uric acid in people living with HIV. Modern HIV treatment has shifted attention toward long-term metabolic problems, and some widely used HIV drugs may raise uric acid. Nobody has yet totaled the worldwide burden.

Pitua's plan covers observational studies of adults, screened and scored by two reviewers working independently. The team will pool rates of high uric acid and gout, then compare results by drug era, region, and immune status. Registering the plan in advance keeps the later review honest and repeatable.
plos-pone-0355417:
Ameen Chaudry led a team of eight authors taking stock of diversity in orthopaedic surgery, published in PLOS ONE in 2026. Orthopaedics remains one of the least diverse specialties in medicine. The team examined residency applications to ask where diversity currently stands in the pipeline that feeds the field.

Chaudry's numbers show how far the pipeline has come and how far it still has to go. Application data reveal whether diversity efforts fail at attracting applicants or at selecting among them, two very different problems. A specialty that treats patients of every background benefits when its surgeons reflect that range. Honest stocktaking is the precondition for programs that aim to widen the door.
plos-pone-0355717:
Ruiheng Wu, Houmin Xing, and Jeffrey P Townsend re-analyzed whole genomes from 494 Chinese liver tumors, asking not just which mutations recur but which ones actually give cancer cells an edge. Their 2026 study computed, for every recurrent mutation, a scaled measure of the selective advantage it confers, using each gene's background mutation rate as the neutral yardstick.

The usual giants, including CTNNB1, TP53, and a famous regulatory hotspot, showed intense positive selection. More interestingly, several rare candidates, including genes tied to collagen chemistry and immune signaling, carried outsized effects, while some previously nominated drivers looked no better than neutral passengers. The authors stress the rare finds are computational priorities for laboratory proof, not established drivers.
plos-pone-0356617:
Amina Mouhamed, Jim Al-Khalili, and Marco Sacchi published a 2026 theoretical study in PLOS ONE on a quantum puzzle at the heart of psychiatry's oldest drug. Lithium has steadied bipolar disorder for decades, yet nobody knows exactly how it works. Its two isotopes have different nuclear spins, and some studies hint they act differently in biology. They ask whether lithium's spin could steer a radical pair mechanism, a quantum effect where magnetism changes chemical outcomes, in a pairing of flavin with the vitamin C radical.

Using density functional calculations and spin simulations, they model how lithium's nuclear spin might shift the balance of reaction products from these fleeting radical pairs. The vitamin C radical is a plausible partner because it is plentiful in the brain and long-lived. Whether such spin effects matter in patients is unproven, the authors stress, but the calculations make the idea concrete enough to test.
plos-pone-0356717:
Naohiro Wakisaka and six colleagues published this research article in PLOS ONE in 2026. It studies oropharyngeal cancer, cancer of the throat behind the mouth, associated with HPV, the human papillomavirus. The authors map where immune programs sit across the tissue compartments of these tumors.

Spatial organization means which immune activities happen in which parts of the tumor tissue. Where immune cells gather, and where they are shut out, shapes how a cancer behaves and responds to treatment. Head and neck cancer researchers and immunotherapy teams are the readers for a map of immune geography inside these tumors.
plos-pone-0356817:
Hui Zhang and Pengpeng Cai study silicon etching in a 2026 PLOS ONE paper on predicting etched shapes. Wet etching carves silicon at rates that depend on crystal direction, a trait used to build tiny machines and through-silicon holes. Mask shape and conditions make the three-dimensional result hard to predict and control.

Using measured etch rates for a few crystal planes, the authors filled in rates for all planes and built a simulation based on the level set method, which tracks a moving surface. Tests under window, mesa, and double-sided masks matched real etched profiles well. The approach also adapts to other etch systems and to crystals such as quartz.
plos-pone-0356917:
Marika A. de Hoop-Sommen and coauthors published a 2026 modeling study in PLOS ONE supporting guidelines for a delicate switch in children's intensive care. A child is moved from continuous morphine or fentanyl to methadone, then tapered away to prevent withdrawal. Clinicians lack agreed conversion ratios and taper speeds. The team built physiology-based models of how children's bodies handle all three drugs, checked them against published data, and simulated many plans.

The simulations pointed to clear working ratios: a fentanyl-to-methadone ratio of one to ten and a morphine ratio of one to one kept methadone in the therapeutic range. Most published tapering schedules peaked at similar methadone levels, except the gentlest low-risk schedules of two protocols. An expert panel of pediatric intensivists and pharmacists turned the results into recommendations. The models support, rather than replace, bedside judgment.
plos-pone-0357017:
Jung Ah Lim and colleagues argue that the standard yardstick for low muscle mass in older adults quietly measures fat as well. They propose a fix using Korean national survey data. Their 2026 study analyzed body scans from more than three thousand adults over sixty-five. It compared muscle indexed to height squared against a ratio. The ratio sets muscle in the arms and legs against muscle in the trunk.

The height-based index rose with body fat. Paradoxically, people it flagged as low-muscle had less metabolic syndrome. The trunk-relative ratio behaved oppositely. It fell as fat rose, flagged genuinely higher metabolic risk, and tracked insulin resistance even after fat was accounted for. The authors suggest the ratio gives doctors a cleaner read on muscle depletion in aging patients.
plos-pone-0357117:
Philipp Naß and coauthors published a 2026 protocol in PLOS ONE for PRIMA, a German project turning ordinary GP practices into multiprofessional care centers. Germany's primary care is strained by aging patients, chronic disease, and workforce shortages. The model adds specially trained nurses to practice teams. It gives them extended duties and reorganizes who does what inside the practice. Triage software can be added, and chronically ill high-risk patients are the focus.

The evaluation compares patients in twenty intervention practices against matched controls from routine insurance claims, over twelve months. The main measure is how many emergencies occur that good ambulatory care should have prevented. Healthcare use, deaths, continuity, and costs are also tracked. A parallel study follows how the change actually unfolds in daily work. The aim is to show whether nurse-integrated practices deliver better, more productive care, evidence German health policy lacks.
plos-pone-0357917:
Hui G. Cheng and coauthors published a 2026 longitudinal study in PLOS ONE following Americans through a cancer diagnosis to map how health, habits, and finances change together. Using fifteen waves of a national retirement study spanning three decades, they identified several thousand newly diagnosed people, matched each to similar cancer-free controls, and aligned timelines to the diagnosis year.

Diagnosis hit like a step down: self-rated health dropped sharply and functional limits jumped, with only partial recovery afterward. Depressive symptoms spiked and stayed elevated for years, and physical activity stayed suppressed even longer. Some changes were welcome: smoking fell at diagnosis and stayed lower, while weight and drinking shifts faded. Work and money suffered too: employment dropped and out-of-pocket spending jumped by over two thousand dollars a year. Survivorship care, they say, should plan for this whole bundle, not just the tumor.
plos-pone-0359217: Diniz and seven co-authors published a 2026 PLOS ONE study on field research at Fiocruz, Brazil's noted public health institute. They used the ideas of sociologist Pierre Bourdieu to weigh the challenges and chances in clinical field work. Field studies meet real life: transport, trust, and local politics shape results. Lessons from a century-old institute can guide research teams elsewhere.
plos-pone-0359317:
Yong-Han Cha, Jung-Taek Kim, Jin-Woo Kim, Hyun-Bin Kim, and Jun-Il Yoo published this research article in PLOS ONE in 2026. It uses artificial intelligence to profile thigh muscle volume on CT scans. The patients are elderly East Asian people who have suffered a hip fracture.

Muscle volume around the thigh matters because weak muscles slow recovery after hip surgery and raise the risk of further falls. Measuring that volume by hand on scans is slow, so an AI tool that profiles it automatically could enter routine care. Orthopedic teams treating hip fractures in aging populations are the natural readers.
plos-pone-0359417: Liu and seven co-authors published a 2026 PLOS ONE study on how well mumps vaccines protect children in Taizhou, China. The study covered children under fifteen and used real-world records, not a trial. Each sick child was matched with two similar healthy children for comparison. Real-world checks matter because protection in daily life can fall short of trial results, and gaps guide booster policy.
plos-pone-0359517: Sterling and seven co-authors published a 2026 PLOS ONE study on an invasive fish in the Upper Mississippi River. Silver carp, brought from Asia, now crowd parts of the river system. The team described the population's makeup: ages, sizes, and growth. Such basic facts about numbers and age shape how managers try to slow the carp's spread and protect native fish.
plos-pone-0359717:
Ana Tsutsunava and eight colleagues published this research article in PLOS ONE in 2026. It associates genomic variants of Mycobacterium tuberculosis, the TB bacterium, with minimum inhibitory concentrations for two newer TB drugs, delamanid and pretomanid. That concentration is the lowest drug level that stops the bacterium growing.

If gene patterns predict drug potency, laboratories could flag weak drug-bug matches from sequence alone, faster than growing cultures. Both drugs are vital for drug-resistant TB, where every effective medicine counts. TB reference labs and treatment programs are the readers for a genotype-to-potency link.
pmc-13122017:
Yasmin Ibrahim is first author on a 2026 perspective article asking why hepatitis B stays underprioritized in global health. Nearly two hundred and fifty-nine million people live with chronic hepatitis B, yet only a small fraction receive life-saving treatment, and the virus caused most viral hepatitis deaths in twenty twenty-two. Vaccines, tests, and treatments already exist.

Through personal stories of people living with the virus worldwide, the article traces roadblocks including stigma, discrimination, and weak funding. It draws lessons from HIV, COVID-19, and Ebola, where advocacy and sustained money drove progress. The authors call for greater investment, joined-up programs, and patient-reported outcomes in hepatitis B care.
pmc-13191817:
The European Food Safety Authority, EFSA, issued a 2026 scientific opinion on residue limits for the pesticide acequinocyl in berries. A company branch had applied through Germany to modify maximum residue levels, the legal caps on pesticide remains, for cane fruits and other small fruits and berries. EFSA assessed the supporting data under European rules.

The data sufficed to propose new limits, and lab methods can enforce them at a very low detection level. Trials also checked carry-over into honey and found no change needed to the current honey limit, though those trials used higher doses than intended practice, making the judgment conservative. Short- and long-term consumer intake from the proposed uses was judged unlikely to risk health.
pmc-13197317:
Malin Ramne and Eva Lendaro report a 2026 brain wave study of phantom limb pain. Phantom pain is pain felt in a limb that has been removed. Chronic pain often links to stronger slow brain waves at rest, so the team tested whether that pattern holds here.

They recorded dense scalp signals at rest in nineteen controls, six amputees without pain, and thirteen with pain. The study plan was logged before data work began. Across main and check analyses, no firm link tied pain to slow wave power or to peak rhythm speed. Some shifts tied to limb loss itself, not pain. Findings shifted with the measure used, so the authors urge caution.
pmc-13197617:
Döndü Ülker Üstebay and colleagues offer a 2026 case report on a rare inherited disorder with no diabetes so far. Faults in the TRMT10A gene can cause small head size, learning disability, seizures, and short stature. Blood sugar problems often join that list, but not in this patient.

Their patient was a fifteen-year-old boy with those core traits from early childhood. Brain scans were normal, yet brain wave tests showed seizure-like activity needing treatment. Gene sequencing found a harmful variant in both copies of the gene, matching recessive inheritance, where two faulty copies are needed. Early diagnosis lets doctors watch for diabetes and act fast if it starts. Long follow-up is vital.
pmc-13198717:
Omar Taher and colleagues present a 2026 case report on a child's bowel blockage with two causes. A Meckel diverticulum is a pouch on the small bowel left from before birth. In this boy it twisted the bowel, then a second blockage followed surgery.

The eight-year-old had a week of belly pain and vomiting. Scans showed a blocked small bowel with a swirl sign. Keyhole surgery found the dead pouch and twisted bowel, and surgeons removed that bowel segment. After brief recovery, swelling and bile vomiting returned. A second keyhole operation found a single tissue band near the join and freed it. The lesson: early focal blockage after surgery may need prompt re-check by scope.
pmc-13200417:
Chiara Robin Bojarzyn and colleagues studied flu virus growth when cell sugar use is blocked in a 2026 paper. Influenza A virus leans hard on host cell metabolism to copy itself. Blocking glycolysis, the cell's sugar-burning path, curbs the virus, but a TCA cycle fuel called oxaloacetate might rescue it.

Infected cells with blocked sugar burning made far fewer viruses. Adding oxaloacetate reversed that drop, restoring viral proteins, genomes, and titers. The sugar mannose rescued growth to a like degree. Chemical profiling showed pyruvate, a sugar-burning product, piled up with oxaloacetate added. Direct pyruvate rescued almost as well. The virus taps this backup fuel axis when its main path fails.
pmc-13212617:
Xiaohui Lin and co-authors explore in 2026 whether a fat-carrying protein in blood, apolipoprotein E, worsens a mouse model of multiple sclerosis. The protein had been linked to disease progression in people, but its mechanism stayed unresolved.

Mice lacking the protein developed milder disease after researchers triggered autoimmune damage to nerve insulation. Their spinal cords kept more myelin, and immune cells in the tissue showed less activation and produced fewer inflammatory signals. A myelin protein was also better preserved. The pattern suggests the protein helps drive inflammatory damage, making it a possible target for slowing multiple sclerosis.
pmc-13212717:
Aya A. Ibrahim and colleagues characterise in 2026 two cast alloys built from titanium mixed with chromium, molybdenum, zirconium, tantalum, and niobium. Swapping part of the costly niobium for iron could cut price, but the team needed to check what that swap does to structure and performance.

Both alloys, melted under vacuum, formed branching crystal structures dominated by one main phase, with extra compounds appearing between branches. The iron-bearing version proved harder and stiffer, while the niobium-rich version resisted corrosion in salt water better on its own. Adding a mineral coating improved both dramatically. Such tailoring matters for implants and other demanding uses where cost and durability compete.
pmc-13212817:
Ching-Chieh Tzeng and colleagues ask in 2026 whether routine blood tests can warn that a glioblastoma brain tumour is progressing after surgery. Scans remain the standard check, but a cheap blood-based signal could prompt earlier imaging.

Records for 193 patients treated at a Taiwanese hospital fed the analysis, with 150 used to build the score. White cell counts, neutrophil counts, platelet counts, and one ratio all ran higher in patients whose tumours progressed by six months. Four factors, including how fully the tumour was removed, formed a simple four-point score. Higher scores meant higher odds of progression, and the score held up in a small internal check group.
pmc-13213017:
K. Julia Hurry and colleagues publish in 2026 a commentary questioning a review that linked parents' mental health to tooth decay in young children. The review reported higher odds of decay for children whose parents live with such conditions, and urged vigilance.

The commentators argue that conclusion goes beyond what the studies show, because most included studies measured everything at one moment and cannot show direction of cause. Few adjusted properly for poverty, diet, and access to dental care, which themselves drive decay. Parental distress may act through habits such as brushing supervision and feeding, a pathway the review never tested formally. Untangling such routes matters before services are redesigned around the claim.
pmc-13217217:
Elbeltagi and colleagues systematically review whether ultrasound stiffness scans of the liver can flag insulin resistance in children. Insulin resistance sits at the root of fatty liver disease linked to metabolism. Liver elastography, which measures stiffness with sound waves, is painless and quick, and clinics use it more and more in children.

The open question is how well stiffness readings match standard blood-based signs of insulin resistance. The review gathers the scattered studies and weighs their agreement. A clear answer would matter. A scan that truly mirrors insulin resistance could spare children repeated blood draws. It could also catch metabolic trouble earlier. A weak link, instead, would warn doctors not to over-read stiffness numbers.
pmc-13217917:
Lateefat Kalejaye and colleagues describe, in a 2026 paper, a faster way to spot antibody drugs that will become too thick at high concentration. Concentrated antibodies often turn viscous because the proteins attract each other, which complicates making them and injecting them under the skin. The team used small-angle X-ray scattering to detect that self-attraction early, while samples were still dilute.

Synchrotron measurements covered 21 antibodies in a histidine buffer, first across a wide concentration range and then with machine handling for screening. Antibodies that later proved highly viscous showed a distinct upturn in scattering at concentrations of 10 milligrams per milliliter or less, while low-viscosity ones showed a downturn. A rule based on this structure-factor transition sorted every antibody correctly by its behavior at 150 milligrams per milliliter. The dataset, the largest of its kind for one recipe, can also support computer models of antibody solution behavior.
pmc-13218117:
Yi Cai and co-authors compare MRI and CT for judging whether rectal cancer spread to nearby lymph nodes, in a 2026 retrospective study. Node status drives treatment planning, and a standardized scoring system called Node-RADS grades nodes by size and shape. Whether the system works equally well on both scans was untested head to head.

The study covered 97 patients with rectal adenocarcinoma who had both contrast-enhanced CT and MRI before surgery. In all, 148 nodes were scored and checked against surgical pathology. Node-RADS scores rose in step with the pathological stage for both scan types. MRI achieved stronger diagnostic performance, with an accuracy score of 0.883, and reader agreement was also higher for MRI than for CT. The MRI advantage held for small nodes under five millimeters and where images were matched directly to pathology. The authors recommend MRI as the preferred scan for this scoring system.
pmc-13219917:
Bom Soo Kim and colleagues compare two cartilage repair strategies for osteochondral lesions of the ankle's talus in a 2026 study. These lesions, where cartilage and the bone beneath it are damaged, cause ankle pain and disability. Bone marrow stimulation is the fix, while particulated autologous cartilage transplantation, implanting minced cartilage, is newer and its relative value unclear.

Patients treated between 2015 and 2022 were followed for two years: forty-eight ankles with marrow stimulation and sixteen with the transplant. The transplant group started worse on pain and function scores. By one year quality-of-life scores had pulled ahead, and by two years ankle scores were higher. Cartilage quality scores also favored the transplant, and an arthroscopy in some patients supported the same direction. The authors conclude the transplant produced better cartilage and better late function, while noting the transplant group's small size and worse starting point as cautions.
pmc-13222017:
Qing Wang and co-authors use genetic data to probe a possible chain from toothache to Alzheimer's disease, in a 2026 Mendelian randomization study. Their proposed route runs through a brain chemical called NAAG and immune cells carrying the CD33 marker. Summary data came from the United Kingdom Biobank, a large metabolite study, immune trait cohorts, and an Alzheimer's meta-analysis.

People genetically prone to toothache showed lower NAAG levels. Lower NAAG in turn linked to higher CD33 expression on myeloid cells, which linked to greater Alzheimer's risk. Sensitivity checks supported the pattern. The authors call the case preliminary, yet it offers a testable bridge between oral pain and brain disease.
pmc-13222617:
Hae Won Lee and co-authors compare how the diabetes drug dapagliflozin behaves in obese versus nonobese healthy adults, in a 2026 pharmacology study. Twenty-two volunteers took ten milligrams daily for five days. Blood sampling after the last dose mapped drug exposure, and statistical analyses probed whether body weight explains any gap.

Obese participants showed lower overall exposure and lower peak levels than nonobese participants at steady state. No strong direct correlation appeared between single weight measures and the drug parameters, though adjusted analyses were run to test weight as an explanation. Since the drug also trims body weight, knowing that obesity itself shifts its handling helps interpret dosing across patient sizes.
pmc-13223617:
L Winter Mokhwelepa and G Olivia Sumbane set out a protocol for reviewing how clinicians bully medical students in South Africa, in a 2026 scoping review protocol. Hierarchy, power imbalance, and inherited teaching habits may feed mistreatment in local medical schools, yet no systematic map exists for this setting.

Six databases, including African Journals Online, will be searched for qualitative and quantitative work. The review will catalogue forms of bullying, prevalence, contributing factors, consequences, and institutional responses, organized through a socioecological model. The work is scheduled across ten months from November 2025. The authors present it as the first systematic map of this problem in South African training.
pmc-13224017:
Dunyu Chang and co-authors present a 2026 engineering design for harvesting radio-frequency energy and converting it into direct current. Their device is a flat metasurface, a patterned sheet that interacts with radio waves, fitted with a rectifier circuit. Four symmetrical T-shaped slots in each unit cell trap unwanted harmonic signals produced by the rectifying diode.

Because suppression is built into the surface, no extra filter parts are needed, and the single-layer layout keeps the device compact. Simulations reached a conversion efficiency of 75.6 percent across wide arrival angles and varied wave orientations. Small prototype arrays confirmed that the design scales, which suits wireless power delivery for compact electronics and connected devices.
pmc-13224117:
Rebeca Brasil Albuquerque and co-authors write a 2026 letter from a Brazilian blood centre about a counting problem in stem cell transplantation. Collected cell products are dosed by CD34, a surface marker, yet harmless B-cell precursors called hematogones carry the same marker. Their presence can inflate the count and mask a shortfall of true stem cells.

Reviewing 501 collection units processed between 2020 and 2024, the centre found hematogones in about twelve percent of them. In three borderline cases, spotting and subtracting these cells prevented transplanting an inadequate dose, because a second collection could be arranged. The letter argues that laboratories should quantify and report hematogones routinely.
pmc-13227717:
R. Noah Padgett and a multinational team describe a 2026 analytic blueprint for the Global Flourishing Study, a multi-wave survey of human well-being across many countries. Rather than testing one exposure against one outcome, the project runs outcome-wide analyses, relating a single life factor to a broad sweep of later outcomes at once. The article explains how dozens of research teams keep those analyses consistent.

Methods cover compressing many control variables into summary components, respecting complex sampling, filling missing data, probing hidden bias, and pooling results across countries. A worked example links an early sense of mastery to many later outcomes and shows how coding choices change answers. Strengths and limits of the whole design are laid out candidly.
pmc-13229317:
Haiming Liang and co-authors search a 2026 gene study for links between uric acid and diabetic retinopathy, the eye disease that remains a leading cause of blindness in diabetes. Uric acid is implicated in the disease's onset, but the responsible genes were unclear. Public gene-expression data were mined with machine learning and diagnostic-accuracy analysis, and candidate findings were checked in patient blood samples.

Two genes, MMP15 and FOXK1, emerged as potential key players, both clearly raised in patients' blood. Enrichment analysis tied them to distinct signalling and protein-processing pathways. Immune-cell patterns in the tissue also shifted, with natural killer cells and memory T cells among the types most involved. Twelve shared regulator factors targeted both genes, sketching a control network for follow-up work.
pmc-13229917:
Saleh Abualhaj and colleagues describe in 2026 a serious early problem after BariClip surgery for weight loss. A woman in her late forties with obesity and low thyroid function had the clip placed to narrow the stomach while keeping its shape. Two days later she returned with belly discomfort, nausea, and swelling.

Scans showed the clip had slipped downward, and a camera operation confirmed it had moved and torn the stomach wall in several places. Surgeons removed the clip and stitched the holes closed. She then developed a lung blood clot, received blood-thinning treatment, and went home in good shape on day ten after the second operation. Reports of such harms are still few, so each documented case helps define the risks.
pmc-13230317:
Gabriel Stankiewicz and colleagues tackle in 2026 fuzzy edges in a method that designs stiff sheet structures by varying thickness. Filters needed to keep the math well behaved blur the borders between solid and empty regions. Thin leftover zones also make the designs hard to manufacture.

One fix pairs a penalty rule with an updated projection step to remove nearly all unwanted thin regions. The main fix uses local thickness slope to sharpen edges only where the slope is steep, leaving inner areas mostly untouched. Test designs regained a crisp solid to void border while inner shapes stayed intact. Stiffness barely changed, so edge quality improved without a real performance cost.
pmc-13230417:
Tingting Cai and colleagues review in 2026 how small chemical swaps change the behavior of a family of sodium battery cathodes. Sodium batteries appeal for large storage because sodium is cheap and widely available. Two close cousins in the NASICON family differ mainly in how fluorine and oxygen sit in the structure.

Side-by-side comparison shows how those anion differences reshape the crystal and the paths sodium ions travel. Making and coating methods are judged for how they link structure to working performance. High voltage slowly damages the surface where cathode meets liquid, and the review maps how that damage proceeds. Lessons drawn here can guide tougher cathodes for other high-voltage sodium cells as well.
pmc-13233517:
Qingyu Xu and colleagues published a 2026 case series on a custom 3D-printed prosthesis that replaces both the jaw joint and part of the skull base. Combined damage in this area is hard to reconstruct, and no standard protocol exists. Twelve patients treated at one hospital between 2016 and 2024 received implants designed for their own anatomy, then returned for checks over an average follow-up of just under four years.

No infections, spinal fluid leaks, loosening, or fractures occurred, and bite and facial shape stayed stable. Pain, eating, jaw function, and mouth opening all improved significantly after surgery. Opening deviation and sideways movement toward the healthy side did not change. The authors present the device as a safe and accurate option for these complex reconstructions.
pmc-13236817:
Emily Weaver and co-authors mapped the research on harmful chemicals in chemical hair straighteners in a 2026 scoping review. Two product types dominate the market: relaxers and keratin treatments. The reviewers gathered 21 studies and reports that tested products, read labels, measured chemicals in people's bodies, or sampled salon air.

Formaldehyde and chemicals that release it appeared often, especially in keratin treatments, while relaxers more often carried hormone-disrupting chemicals and fragrance ingredients. Metals and volatile organic compounds also turned up across products. Salon workers may face higher exposure than customers. The authors urge newer exposure science and community-led steps to cut the risks, which fall heavily on women of color.
pmc-13236917:
Alfi Raudatil Jannah and colleagues profiled proteins in postmortem brain tissue in 2026 from people with tau diseases: Alzheimer's disease, corticobasal degeneration, and progressive supranuclear palsy. Each group had only four brains, matched by four controls, so the work is exploratory. Mass spectrometry measured thousands of proteins, and network analysis looked for connected changes.

Six proteins formed a tight network tied to mitochondria, the cell's energy producers, including parts of the breathing chain that makes fuel. Follow-up blot tests agreed for four of the six proteins, and tissue staining placed two of them in neurons and support cells. The authors treat the shared mitochondrial pattern as a lead for larger studies, not a settled answer.
pmc-13237017:
Abdelmohsen, Wassif, and Ramadan build a shopping recommender that watches for fake reviews. Online shops lean on reviews to rank products, yet deceptive reviews warp what buyers see. Fake-spotting tools and recommenders have mostly been built apart, so a sly fake can still train the system that ranks for everyone.

Their system feeds a language model's estimate that a review is deceptive straight into the training of a neural recommender. Reviews judged likely fake then count for less as the model learns tastes. The goal is a ranking shoppers can trust more, tested on whether real users still get suggestions that fit them.
pmc-13239017:
Batirbay Torambetov and colleagues determined the crystal structure in 2026 of a small sulfur- and nitrogen-containing ring compound, 5-bromo-1,3,4-thiadiazol-2-amine. Such thiadiazole rings form the core of many drug families, from antimicrobials to anti-cancer agents, and offer grip points for building metal complexes and engineered crystals. The molecule itself is nearly flat, the team found.

Inside the crystal, hydrogen bonds between nitrogen and hydrogen atoms link molecules into ribbons running along one axis. The ribbons pack against each other in a zipper-like pattern, held apart by repulsion between bromine atoms. A surface analysis mapped where the molecule is most likely to touch neighbors. The authors present the structure as groundwork for crystal-engineered materials and bioactive molecules built on this scaffold.
pmc-13239517:
Judith van Zwol and co-authors set out a 2026 trial protocol for major abdominal cancer surgery. The operation combines removing widespread tumour deposits with heated chemotherapy washed through the abdomen, and it often causes heavy fluid loss plus widened blood vessels that invite fluid overload.

Seventy patients at two centres will receive either argipressin, another name for vasopressin, or the standard drug norepinephrine to hold blood pressure steady. Both groups follow a goal-directed fluid plan, and total fluid given during surgery is the main outcome. Recovery quality, kidney injury, lung problems, and hospital stay will also be tracked. The team hopes the alternative drug cuts complications.
pmc-13240117:
Asuka Yamamura and team report a parasitic lung infection caught from restaurant crab in a 2026 two-case paper. A couple shared previously frozen freshwater crab at a Tokyo restaurant. Both then fell ill with paragonimiasis, an infection by a lung fluke passed through raw or undercooked shellfish.

One partner's lung patch was first misread as a kind of eosinophilic pneumonia. The other had fluid around the lung with high counts of eosinophils, a type of white blood cell. Antibody tests in blood proved the parasite in both cases. The drug praziquantel treated them with success. The cases show that freezing cannot always be trusted to kill the parasite, so food history counts in such lung cases.
pmc-13240417: A 2026 correction notice in Case Reports in Endocrinology amends a case report by Kayalvizhi and co-authors on a decade with Sheehan's syndrome, a pituitary disorder after heavy bleeding in childbirth. The notice is a correction only, with no new clinical findings. It states that the brain scan image printed as the patient's own matched an image in another publication, used without credit. The legend now calls it an illustrative example from that source. One sentence in the case text is also rewritten. The authors apologise for the errors.
pmc-13241417:
Addario and colleagues at Maastricht printed a chip built to grow blood vessels into lab-made kidney organoids. Kidney organoids from human stem cells mature poorly without a blood supply. The chip was printed by extruding a sacrificial gel that later melted away. Two channels and three gel compartments resulted.

Endothelial cells lined the channels first, then organoids joined them in a tissue-derived gel. Five days of co-culture ran under gentle flow. Capillary-like sprouts grew toward and through the organoids, reaching their centers. The sprouts overlapped with early kidney markers, suggesting genuine integration.
pmc-13241517:
Yao's team at Zhejiang use deep learning to speed up the design of tiny hemispherical resonators. These devices serve in fine gyroscopes, and their quality factor is limited partly by thermoelastic losses. Modeling those losses the standard way is accurate but painfully slow. The team trained a hybrid network to predict the losses straight from shape.

Their model joins a pattern network with a transformer, fed extra training data fitted from sim results. Swapping part of the network for a second attention stage gave the best scores. Dropout checks showed the error bars were well set. Shape analysis favored squat shells with small anchor radius and thick walls for the highest quality factor.
pmc-13242517:
Theresa Waclawek and co-authors followed couples for ten days to test whether mindfulness shows up as compassion at home. Their preregistered diary study appeared in Communications Psychology in 2026. It enrolled 230 adults in long-term heterosexual relationships, including 114 couples where both partners took part. Each evening, participants reported their own mindfulness and rated their partner's compassion, giving the study an outside view of kindness.

On days when a person felt more accepting and mindful than usual, their partner rated them as more compassionate that same day. People with steadier mindful attention were also seen as kinder overall. Much of the link ran through self-absorption: mindfulness lowered it, and lower self-absorption freed up compassion. The authors say inner attention training can have visible social effects in daily life. Partner ratings, they note, keep the findings honest beyond self-report.
pmc-13243917:
E. Wohlfarth and colleagues updated a head-to-head lab comparison of five modern antibiotics against drug-resistant Gram-negative bacteria. Their study appeared in JAC-Antimicrobial Resistance in 2026. The panel covered 401 clinical isolates collected in Germany in 2019 and 2020. Cefiderocol, a drug that smuggles itself into bacteria through their iron gates, faced four rival combination drugs, with resistance genes checked by sequencing.

Cefiderocol held up best. Against Pseudomonas, its resistance rate sat under two percent, while the rivals failed against a fifth to two-fifths of isolates. Against two other problem germs, the dose needed to stop growth was many times lower than for every rival. A commercial test kit for the drug was also checked against the reference method. The authors conclude that cefiderocol's activity against these problem pathogens exceeds the combinations tested. For hospitals facing the toughest resistant infections, that margin matters.
pmc-13244517:
Xueting Li and colleagues asked whether the amount of protein leaking into urine predicts how kidney patients respond to rituximab. Their study appeared in Annals of Medicine in 2026. All 123 participants had PLA2R-associated membranous nephropathy, an autoimmune kidney disease, confirmed by biopsy or antibody testing. The team split them by starting proteinuria, four to six grams a day versus above six, and followed remission for a year.

The lower-protein group responded faster and more completely at nearly every checkpoint. Partial remissions came earlier, and complete remissions were significantly more common by nine and twelve months. At the extreme, patients spilling more than twelve grams a day remitted least of all. The gradient suggests waiting until proteinuria soars may squander the drug's best window. The authors propose baseline proteinuria as a guide for when to start rituximab. Timing, in their data, is a treatment variable.
pmc-13246017:
Moon, Blumenschein, and Swetz measured broken ankles to guide screw placement, in this 2026 OTA International study. Some shinbone fractures come with a separate small break at the back of the ankle joint, often fixed with screws through the skin. Using CT scans from a trauma center, the team worked out the angle a screw should take to cross that back fragment squarely and hit its center.

They found the fragments in about half of the shaft fractures they reviewed. One standard angle and starting point would land the screw well in only about half of cases in one plane, though it did better in the other. Their conclusion is practical: surgeons should template each patient's screw path from the scan first.
pmc-13246417:
Tin-Yun Ho and co-authors test clove and its main compound against psoriasis-like skin disease in mice in 2026 work. Clove has a folk history for inflamed skin, but its targets in psoriasis were vague. Eugenol makes up about two thirds of clove extract.

Mice with induced skin disease got oral clove extract or eugenol and improved visibly. Scaling eased and skin thickening shrank under treatment. Protein mapping showed the pair calmed two linked inflammation paths and raised a natural brake protein. Bench tests showed they also block a key immune signal from docking with its receptor. The dual action may explain the skin gains.
pmc-13246717:
Jiaru Liu and co-authors probe shared biology between rheumatoid arthritis and depression in a 2026 study centered on fat metabolism. The two diseases often travel together, with inflammation and lipid trouble in common. The exact molecular bridge was unclear.

Joining gene data from ten public cohorts, the team built a nine-gene signature tied to fat and immune work. The signature sorted arthritis cases sharply in fresh cohorts but sorted depression weakly. Its activity tracked immune cell presence in joint tissue. In a dish test, fluid from fat-stressed mouse brain cells switched on human joint cells. That result hints at a brain-to-joint route worth chasing.
pmc-13246817:
Merabtine, Sognigbe, Marcellaud, and co-authors interviewed digestive cancer patients in Benin about their routes through care, in this 2026 Supportive Care in Cancer study. At the national university hospital in Cotonou, the team conducted in-depth interviews with eleven patients who had used complementary or alternative medicine alongside, or instead of, conventional treatment.

Patients described long delays: symptoms first minimized, rounds of inconclusive consultations, and low awareness of digestive cancers, compounded by money problems and scarce medicines. Alternative medicine appealed for cost reasons, frustration with conventional care, relief of side effects, and a search for well-being. Patients asked for holistic care with nutrition and psychosocial support, and wanted doctors involved in supervising alternative treatments rather than ignoring them.
pmc-13247517:
Suenaga and co-authors report an immunologically puzzling diabetes case in this 2026 JCEM Case Reports article. A thirty-nine-year-old Japanese woman had lived fourteen years with stiff-person syndrome, an autoimmune nerve disorder often paired with type 1 diabetes. She arrived in diabetic ketoacidosis and was found to have autoimmune diabetes destroying her insulin-producing cells at speed. This happened despite long-term immune-suppressing treatment, and despite carrying a gene pattern thought to protect against the disease.

All three major islet autoantibodies were positive, and her remaining insulin output collapsed within thirteen months. Her HLA typing mixed a susceptibility pattern with a protective one and lacked the allele most tied to the syndrome in European patients. The authors say stiff-person autoimmunity can overwhelm genetic protection, with profiles differing across populations.
pmc-13248817:
Hichem Moulahoum and co-authors review MXene materials for electrochemical sensing in a 2026 survey. MXenes are two-dimensional sheets of metal carbides and related compounds. They conduct like metals, love water, and wear changeable surface chemistry, a rare mix for sensors.

The review ties sensing power to sheet makeup, surface endings, and layer stacking. Those traits govern charge flow, catalytic action, and how targets stick to the surface. Uses span small molecules, pollutants, body markers, and drugs. Hybrid designs that blend MXenes with other materials show extra gains. Stability and batch sameness remain the chief barriers to market use.
pmc-13249217:
Christopher D Katanski and a large team show how one tRNA tweak rewired codon use across gut bacteria in a 2026 study. Transfer RNAs read codons during protein building, and a chemical edit to one letter widens what it can read. The team studied families of bacteria that live in the human gut.

Families carrying the edited leucine tRNA had shifted their leucine codons genome-wide. Proteins in many metabolism paths carried the new codon choices. Bench and growth tests showed the swaps kept translation faithful and aided fitness. The result casts a small RNA edit as an engine of genome evolution in friendly bacteria.
pmc-13249917:
Stich, Van Inghelandt, and Wu review computer simulation as a plant breeder's rehearsal room, in a 2026 Theoretical and Applied Genetics article. Breeding programs run for years and consume fields, seed, and labor, so every design choice is expensive to test live. Simulations let breeders compare crossing and selection schemes virtually, and check the statistical behavior of new methods before trusting them.

The authors survey every publicly available simulation tool they could find, spelling out what each assumes and where each falls short. Two uses get the deepest treatment: optimizing whole breeding programs, and validating new statistical procedures. They also touch on crop growth models and genotype-by-environment interplay as growing frontiers for the simulators.
pmc-13250217:
Broomand and colleagues grade infection prevention work across hospitals supported by Médecins Sans Frontières. Their 2026 BMJ Global Health study uses a stepwise assessment tool applied in one hundred seventy-three facilities between 2021 and 2023. Clean care is hard to guarantee in low-resource and humanitarian settings, where infections can spread fast.

Across nearly four hundred assessments, the median score sat at an upper-intermediate level of practice. Having a formal infection program and keeping bed occupancy below ninety percent best predicted strong scores. Repeat assessments brought the biggest gains to facilities that started weakest, while top performers barely improved. Weak tracking of surgical site infections stood out as a key gap for future work.
pmc-13253717:
Kamila Kwiecień and colleagues report a 2026 skin study on DGAT1, a protein that handles fats and vitamin A-like compounds called retinoids. Skin cells called keratinocytes form the skin barrier. The team asked what happens to these cells when DGAT1 is missing, in normal skin and in psoriasis, a scaly skin disease.

Without DGAT1, skin cells grew too fast and the barrier failed under normal conditions. Yet in psoriasis-like swelling, losing DGAT1 slowed cell growth instead. The shift ran through retinoic acid signals, which grew stronger without DGAT1. The authors call DGAT1 a context-based regulator, meaning its effect depends on skin state.
pmc-13254017:
Hongye Li and colleagues review dandelion compounds that may protect the brain in a 2026 paper. Dandelion, a common plant first from Europe, is rich in flavonoids, phenolic acids, terpenoids, and sterols. The review covers their chemical structures, brain effects, and how structure shapes activity, plus uses in food and medicine.

These compounds seem to guard nerve cells by calming swelling, cutting oxidative stress, and blocking cell damage. The core skeleton of each compound sets its main activity, while small groups, like added oxygens or sugars, fine-tune it. The authors aim to support wider use of this non-toxic plant.
pmc-13254217:
Hao Luo and co-authors build a risk model for older heart failure patients in a 2026 study. The vulnerable phase after hospital care brings frequent readmission and death. The team trained 18 machine learning models with six algorithms and used SHAP, a method that shows how each factor shapes a prediction.

Eleven models scored above 0.8 on a key accuracy curve measure. The best, Boruta-XGBoost, reached 0.873, with sensitivity of 0.839 and accuracy of 0.769. The top five factors were hemoglobin, a thyroid hormone measure, age, diabetes, and blood potassium. The authors stress the model's clear reasoning as a strength.
pmc-13254817:
Kyohei Otani and colleagues map online harassment of health workers in a 2026 scoping review. They searched three databases through December 2025 and included 24 studies from 12 countries. Digital harassment covers workplace cyberbullying, online defamation, and social media attacks.

Workplace cyberbullying rates ranged from 1.5 to 46.6 percent across studies. Harassment was linked with depression, anxiety, burnout, and stress symptoms, though cause could not be proven. Seven studies covered pandemic-era abuse of health workers. Proof of helpful interventions was scarce, so the authors call for policies, legal protection, and support systems. pmc-13255017:

pmc-13255717:

pmc-13256117:

pmc-13256817:

pmc-13256917:

pmc-13257117:

pmc-13257317:

pmc-13257417:

pmc-13257617:

pmc-13258017:

pmc-13258117:

pmc-13258517:

The piece uses a One Health frame, which joins human, animal, and world health in one view.
pmc-13258817:

pmc-13259217:

pmc-13259617:

pmc-13260417:

pmc-13260617:

pmc-13260917:

pmc-13261017:

pmc-13261317:

pmc-13262317:

pmc-13263217:

pmc-13264317:

pmc-13264617:

pmc-13264817:

pmc-13265017:

pmc-13266017:

pmc-13266217:

pmc-13267017:

pmc-13267517:

pmc-13267617:

pmc-13267817:

pmc-13269017:

pmc-13269317:

pmc-13269617:

pmc-13270417:

pmc-13270817:

pmc-13272217:

pmc-13272317:

pmc-13272517:

pmc-13272617:

pmc-13273217:

pmc-13273317:

pmc-13273417:

pmc-13273717:

pmc-13274817:

pmc-13276217:

pmc-13276317:

pmc-13276417:

pmc-13276517:
Hamada S Salem and co-authors test a milk thistle compound against fungicide poisoning in rats, in a 2026 study. The mixture combined four farm fungicides, including copper oxychloride and propiconazole. Exposure to such chemicals can injure the liver, kidney, and brain through cell stress.

pmc-13276617:

pmc-13277417:

pmc-13278017:

pmc-13278617:

pmc-13278717:

pmc-13279017:

pmc-13279617:

pmc-13280117:

If sport lifts grip in youth, paths like muscle growth, nerve skill and habit carry over could explain later gains. A future follow up study built on sport history may test the chain. pmc-13280917:

pmc-13281317:

They note the tool was built on one hospital's records and needs wider tests.
pmc-13281517:

pmc-13281617:

pmc-13281817:

pmc-13282117:

pmc-13282217:

pmc-13283017:

pmc-13283217:

pmc-13283617:

pmc-13283817:

pmc-13284017:

pmc-13284117:

pmc-13285417:

pmc-13285717:

pmc-13285817:

pmc-13286817:

pmc-13287017:

pmc-13287417:

pmc-13287517:

pmc-13287617:

pmc-13288417:

pmc-13288717:

pmc-13289017:

pmc-13289217:

pmc-13289317:

Tumor-bearing mice got naive or pre-activated tumor-specific CD8 T cells before or after treatment with a radioactive agent called 90Y-NM600. Growth slowed most when active cells were already present before radiation began. A prostate tumor model with vaccination before radiation showed the same pattern, with more memory-type killer cells inside tumors. Blocking type I interferon signals was also tested to probe how the benefit works.
pmc-13289417:
Michelle Mendiola Pla and colleagues report a 2026 trauma registry review on survival after penetrating heart injury at an urban Level 1 center. Such wounds kill often, yet which injury and arrival traits best predict survival stayed partly unclear. Records spanned 2017 to 2025 and captured body signs, wound type, and chambers hit for each case.

Among 18 041 trauma activations, only 57 patients had penetrating heart injury, and overall survival was 25 percent in that group. Gunshots caused 67 percent of wounds and carried higher death risk than stab wounds in the models. Injury to several chambers, chest vessel injury, and belly injury each tied to death. Breathing on one's own and signs of life on arrival strongly favored survival.
pmc-13290117:
Surgery notes at a tertiary hospital fell short of national standards, an audit by Ajay Kamat and colleagues shows, and a simple fix lifted them. The 2026 clinical audit compared orthopaedic operative notes against standards from the Royal College of Surgeons of England and the British Orthopaedic Association.

One hundred notes from early 2023 were scored first: patient identification appeared in 72%, intraoperative findings in 65%, the postoperative plan in 58%, and surgeon details in 70%. The department then introduced a standard note template plus staff training and re-audited another hundred notes. Every domain rose sharply, and overall adherence climbed from 68% to 95%. Kamat and colleagues recommend building note training into induction for rotating staff to hold the gains.
pmc-13290517:
A seed-oil regulator gains a partner in oilseed rape, Zhuang Li and colleagues show in a 2026 study of erucic acid production in Brassica napus. The transcription factor ABI5, known for holding back germination, also switches on the marker gene FAE1 and raises erucic acid levels in seeds.

The team showed that the two genes' activity overlaps in developing seeds and that ABI5 sits in the nucleus and can drive gene expression. The mediator subunit MED25 binds ABI5 in living cells and in test-tube assays, and reporter and DNA-binding experiments place it inside the circuit that controls FAE1. Plants overexpressing ABI5 made more FAE1 transcript and more erucic acid. Li and colleagues present the pair as a mechanism steering long-chain fatty acid build-up, of interest for oil quality and industrial uses.
pmc-13290617:
A bodyweight HIIT module designed for Chinese college students earns strong expert backing in a 2026 development and validation study by Wendi Cui and colleagues. Student fitness has been slipping, and short, equipment-free interval training is a practical answer, but no validated module existed for this group.

Working from 20 published studies, the team collected 48 candidate movements. Ten physical education teachers screened them for feasibility in a first Delphi round, and nine experts then scored what remained with content validity methods. Twelve movements survived screening and eight made the final module, from high knees and burpees to mountain climbers and push-ups. Expert agreement was high, with a scale-level validity index of 0.976. Cui and colleagues offer the module as a ready framework and a base for trials of its fitness effects.
pmc-13290717:
Thirty-five years of research on cervical cancer in women living with HIV are mapped by Lin Sui and Rutie Yin in a 2026 bibliometric analysis. The two pulled 6,137 publications from 1990 to 2025 across several databases and charted who publishes, who collaborates, and where the topics are heading.

Output rose steadily, led by the United States, with China, South Africa, the United Kingdom, and India behind. The International Journal of Cancer and AIDS stood out as the field's core outlets. Attention is now gathering around screening, HPV vaccination across the life course, and deep learning. The authors also foresee precision therapy guided by the tumor immune environment, plus screening that low-resource settings can actually run. They offer the map to policymakers pushing toward cervical cancer elimination.
pmc-13291217: Izabella Skulimowska and co-authors issued this 2026 correction for their Cell Reports paper on polyclonal regeneration of mouse bone marrow endothelial cells after radiation conditioning. The notice is a correction only, fixing one dataset accession number in the methods and adding no new results. Two cited datasets were both printed with the GEO number GSE108892. The number for the Baryawno dataset should instead read GSE128423. Because much time has passed, the paper cannot be updated, so this notice points readers to the right record.
pmc-13291717:
Zhiqian Yang and co-authors report 2026 laboratory work testing whether the antibiotic tigecycline can slow somatotroph pituitary tumors. They used the rat GH3 cell line, which models growth-hormone-secreting pituitary neuroendocrine tumors. Cells received tigecycline doses from 6.25 to 100 micromolar, and the team tracked viability, spheroid growth, cell death, and hormone output.

Tigecycline curbed cell growth in a dose- and time-dependent way and also held back three-dimensional spheroid growth. Treated cells stalled in the G0/G1 phase, showed weaker Akt/mTOR signaling, and died through the intrinsic apoptosis pathway. The drug also cut growth hormone production inside the cells and its release outside them. The authors offer these findings as early support for testing tigecycline against this tumor type.
pmc-13292017:
Faridokht Salahshoori and co-authors appraise a 2026 review of clinical guidelines for telerehabilitation, the remote delivery of rehabilitation care. Guideline quality varies widely, which can ripple into care quality and policy. Searching six databases plus grey sources turned up 2,575 records, and two reviewers scored the qualifying documents with the AGREE II tool.

Only seven guidelines made the cut. The American Physical Therapy Association's 2024 guideline alone scored high across all six quality domains. Three others landed in the middle and were recommended with changes, while three rated low for weak methods and thin stakeholder input. The authors call for rigorous, inclusive, evidence-based guidelines so remote rehabilitation stays safe and effective worldwide.
pmc-13292217:
Sofía González-Núñez, Carlos Amador, and Mariano Martín automate surfactant design in a 2026 study. Surfactants mix a water-loving head with a water-fearing tail, and that split drives behavior. Hand-built measures often blur the two domains. The team's framework first cuts each molecule into head and tail automatically. It then figures clear values for each domain alone.

Those split values feed models for three prized traits: the micelle threshold concentration, surface tension, and adsorption efficiency. The models stayed accurate across a wide surfactant range, including twin-headed Gemini types. Costs fell compared with whole-molecule quantum measures, and reach to new structures improved. Grouping heads and tails apart showed which pairings give the best profiles. Makers can use that map to propose new surfactants before making them. The authors frame the tool as a design aid for cleaners and beyond.
pmc-13292317:
Tomohiro Yasuda and Takashi Suemasu survey a 2026 spintronics topic: making the ferrimagnet Mn4N hit magnetic compensation at room temperature by doping it with impurities. Mn4N needs no rare-earth elements, carries small magnetization near 100 kA per meter, and shows strong perpendicular anisotropy. Near compensation points, magnetization can flip and domain walls can race far faster than usual.

The review compares films doped with copper, silver, gold, and palladium against earlier nickel and chromium work, all grown on strontium titanate substrates. Results cover how each impurity shifts magnetization and angular momentum balance. The authors also present ultrathin platinum films, about 4 nm thick, grown on magnesium oxide for injecting spin current through the spin Hall effect. They frame the package as groundwork for fast spin-torque devices.
pmc-13293417:
Kristina M. Kokorelias and colleagues set out, in a 2026 protocol, a planned review of coronary artery disease and heart failure in older adults who have faced homelessness. This group faces more heart risk and poorer care access, yet pooled data on their heart burden are lacking.

The review will follow standard reporting guides and count how common these conditions are, plus related deaths, in adults aged 50 and older with a history of homelessness. The lower age cutoff reflects faster aging in this group. By pulling scattered studies together, the team hopes to guide care and policy for a group often missed by services.
pmc-13293917:
Yanqiu Li and colleagues report a 2026 case described as the first pairing of smoldering multiple myeloma with activated PI3K delta syndrome, a rare inherited immune disorder. The young patient had repeated lung infections, swollen lymph tissue, genital herpes, autoimmunity, and raised IgM and IgG. Gene sequencing found a heterozygous PIK3CD change, also confirmed in the patient's son.

Bone marrow sampling and serum immunofixation showed monoclonal plasma cell growth, supporting the myeloma precursor diagnosis. No targeted therapy was given. The authors urge early genetic testing when the immune syndrome is suspected, since prompt recognition can improve outlook and family screening.
pmc-13294217:
Tshepo A. Ntho and coauthors survey health science students on HIV prevention pills in 2026, surveying students at one school in Limpopo Province, South Africa. Pre-exposure prophylaxis prevents infection but uptake lags across the region. A structured questionnaire reached 350 students at one institution, with analysis in SPSS and significance set at p below 0.05.

Good knowledge appeared in 88.6% of students, positive attitudes in 79.7%, and strong intention to use or support the pills in 80.3% in the reported shares. Social media was the top awareness source. Gaps persisted on who qualifies and how often to dose, and nearly half worried about risk compensation. Older and senior students scored stronger.
pmc-13294917:
Fatma Demir and colleagues make a fresh set of candidate bone cancer compounds and test them in the lab, in a 2026 medicinal chemistry study. Starting from chalcones, natural-product-like building blocks, they assembled twelve thiocarbamoylpyrazoline derivatives and confirmed each structure with a battery of spectroscopic methods. The goal is chemotherapy that hurts cancer more than healthy tissue, a balance standard drugs often miss.

Two standard assays measured how the compounds affected two human bone cancer cell lines and normal cartilage cells. None of the compounds detectably harmed the healthy cells, while several slowed cancer growth notably, in some cases rivaling the reference drug. Four compounds stood out for tumor selectivity, and two of those combined strength with the cleanest safety profile. Computer docking against four cancer-relevant proteins offered clues to how the best compounds might bind their targets.
pmc-13295117:
Jiaxuan Li and a large team pair a protein degrader with an approved drug against stubborn prostate cancer in a 2026 study. The PARP blocker olaparib helps only patients with BRCA gene faults, leaving most castration-resistant cases without that option. Forcing a BRCA-like state could widen its reach.

Data from 921 patients across six public sets flagged the regulator CDK9 as raised in advanced disease. The degrader D45 lowered repair gene activity, piled up DNA damage, and made cancer cells behave as if BRCA-faulty. Giving D45 before olaparib killed more cells, shrank mouse tumours, and held up in human tissue pieces, with bearable side effects.
pmc-13295517:
Dave Osinachukwu Duru and colleagues review diabetes drugs and shoulder tendon disease in a 2026 scoping article. GLP-1 receptor drugs are widely used for weight and blood sugar control, yet their effect on rotator cuff tears and repairs was unknown. Four databases were searched up to late January 2026.

Six studies qualified, four in people and two in controlled animal work. Human data covering well over a million patients found no extra complications after cuff repair among drug users. Users did show more spontaneous cuff tears needing repair, while animal work found stronger, tidier healing with one drug, prompting calls for careful prospective studies.
pmc-13295617:
Anar Eminov and colleagues ask what makes travelers act on green intentions found online, in a 2026 survey study from Azerbaijan. Social media feeds now steer most trip planning, and user reviews carry the weight. Three hundred fifteen respondents rated how much they trusted user-generated content, their ecological awareness, their attitudes, and their plans for sustainable travel choices. The analysis modeled how those pieces connect, and whether sloppy, shortcut thinking breaks the chain.

Trust in reviews proved the spark: it strengthened attitudes toward sustainable options, and attitude was the strongest single predictor of intention. Trust also worked directly and through ecological awareness in parallel. Cognitive processing bias, the tendency to skim and lean on easy cues, weakened the trust-to-attitude link and shrank the indirect effects. Persuasion, the authors conclude, runs on credibility processed carefully, not on information volume.
pmc-13295717:
Miguel A Rodríguez-Domínguez and colleagues sum up decades of saving two Canarian giant lizards in a 2026 article. Gallotia simonyi of El Hierro and Gallotia bravoana of La Gomera are both critically endangered. Outdoor breeding centres have run since the 1990s and 2000s, feeding reintroduction attempts at natural sites.

Breeding records from 2006 to 2024 cover eggs laid, incubation practice, and hatchlings raised each year. Both measures differed between the species and across years, while health checks found most animals in good shape. Wild groups survive and releases show partial success, with one islet population of the El Hierro species holding steady.
pmc-13295817:
Xing Liu, Li Li, and Huilin Wang study mindfulness and distress in college athlete-students in a 2026 survey. Balancing study with heavy training loads strains mental health in this group. Two inner resources, reframing thoughts and feeling full of life, were tested as bridges in the link.

Four hundred thirty students from five universities in Hunan Province answered the survey. Mindfulness tied to stronger reframing habits and greater vitality, and both resources tied to lower distress. Statistical checks with repeated sampling supported indirect paths running through each resource. The authors frame the results as groundwork for later trials rather than proof of cause.
pmc-13296017:
Alexey P. Ershov and co-authors sequence, in 2026, the genome of a salt-tolerant bacterium taken from a Kazakh oil reservoir. Strain G3 eats oil components and survives salty formation water, traits that could help squeeze more oil from ageing fields.

Its genome carries genes for making protective solutes against salt stress and for breaking down both straight-chain and ring-shaped oil compounds. Other genes support nitrogen handling and production of alginate, plus signs of soap-like substances that could displace oil. The authors present G3 as a hardy candidate for microbe-assisted oil recovery in salty reservoirs.
pmc-13297017:
Yiyan Li and colleagues scan the CAD enzyme gene across many cancers in a 2026 multi-omics analysis. CAD runs the first steps of building pyrimidines, the letter molecules needed for DNA. Data from tumour atlases, cell-line screens, and metabolite studies were combined to judge its biomarker promise.

CAD ran high in seventeen cancer types, with strong diagnostic accuracy in a few of them. High levels tracked with features linked to initial immunotherapy response, yet also with worse long-term survival in pooled patient groups. Metabolite data tied high CAD to pyrimidine build-up and shifted amino-acid handling. The authors call CAD a candidate marker needing mechanistic and clinical validation.
pmc-13297117:
Michela Balconi and colleagues scan two brains at once while pairs of people work through a mock negotiation in a 2026 study. Each pair faced a workplace dilemma in stages: first deciding alone, then talking it through, then reaching a deal. Light sensors tracked blood signals in both partners at each stage, and both also filled in forms on traits and decision habits.

Brain signals in the pair diverged most when one partner spoke and the other listened. Listening seemed to place its own load on the mind at those moments. Traits such as being outgoing, plus a habit of avoiding choices, tracked the brain patterns at set stages. Mixing brain data with such profiles can sharpen the study of teamwork.
pmc-13297917:
Jiayue Li and co-authors review rice bran polysaccharides in a 2026 survey of their structure, modification, and possible uses. These natural compounds come from the bran layer left over from rice milling. The review links extraction and chemical or physical modification to changes in molecular weight, sugar composition, and chain shape.

Those structural changes are tied to reported effects that include anti-inflammatory, antioxidant, immune-modulating, and gut-microbiota actions. Later sections consider processing behaviour and roles as delivery carriers, food additives, and active ingredients. Readers interested in turning an abundant milling byproduct into food or health products get a map of what is known and where applications may develop.
pmc-13299217:
Aristeidis Tsitiridis and others map how integrated care is evolving toward learning health systems, in a 2026 scoping review. Searches across major data banks and policy sources yielded almost two hundred included studies. Synthesis covered care concepts, AI infrastructure, rollout barriers, and digital governance.

Most real services sit at a joined digital stage yet adapt only weakly, held back by maintenance debt, semantic drift, and governance gaps. Progress across nine world regions tracked organisational and payment integration more than digital sophistication alone. The authors argue useful learning systems need longitudinal data, stewarded model lifecycles, accountable governance, and outcome-based contracts, rather than analytics layered onto weak infrastructure.
pmc-13300017:
