A deep circumflex iliac artery to L3 lumbar artery link was found on pre-op imaging and shown on scans as the culprit pathway. Aimed coil embolisation occluded that pathway and resolved sac opacification, though follow-up showed a separate leak from another side without sac growth, consistent with flow redistribution. Vascular surgeons gain a reminder to search beyond usual suspects in lasting leaks.
pmc-13371717:
Daniel García-Gutiérrez and colleagues map evidence on social media and body image among university students in a 2026 scoping review. Studies from 2020 to 2025 in seven databases were gathered, keeping work where at least 70 percent of participants were university students and a body image outcome was measured. Meta-analysis was not done because designs varied too much.

Eighty-one studies covering nearly 20,000 students, mostly aged 18 to 25 and about 70 percent women, met the criteria. Six overlapping themes emerged, led by dissatisfaction, shame, and low physical self-esteem, followed by eating disorders and weight control behaviours and interest in cosmetic procedures. The review gives universities and platforms a map of where harm concentrates and where interventions should focus.
pmc-13373217:
Chambers and colleagues discover a two-protein switch that turns on bacterial immune defenses when DNA is damaged, in 2026 microbiology research. Bacteria arm against invading viruses with immune operons, gene clusters that can kill the host cell to stop an infection spreading, so these weapons need off-switches. Upstream of many operons sit two proteins the team names CapK, a kinase, and CapS, a repressor that blocks the operon's transcription by binding DNA as a dimer.

Single-stranded DNA, a byproduct of DNA repair, directly activates CapK. The kinase phosphorylates CapS, breaking its dimer apart so it falls off the DNA and the immune genes switch on. The same protein pair appears inside an anti-phage toxin-antitoxin system, where DNA damage unleashes a nuclease toxin. Chambers argues the kinase-repressor module is a reusable plug-in for stress control, letting diverse bacterial defenses share one damage sensor.
pmc-13374017:
Aida Rebollar-Zepeda and co-authors dug into a math flaw in solution sums in a 2026 study. Lab sums often pair a bath model with gas-phase heat terms. For steps where molecule counts change, like two parts that join, the gas terms do not cancel out.

A plain test of one liquid's self-join showed the flaw in raw form. The join was a win on the core sums, yet the end sum still read as a loss, much like a gas. Checks on water and a wash fluid groups showed the same false fee. The team traces the root and gives a fix, so joined forms are not wrongly taxed.
pmc-13374217:
Zihan Qin and others link a composite metabolic vulnerability index to chronic liver disease in a 2026 cohort study. The index blends inflammation and metabolism markers, but its relation to liver disease was unclear. The team followed 255,171 UK Biobank people for a median of 13.7 years, adjusting for demographic and health factors.

People in the highest index quarter faced higher risks than those in the lowest. Risks rose for cirrhosis, alcohol-related liver disease, immune liver disease, liver and bile duct cancer, liver-related death, and death from any cause. No link appeared for viral hepatitis. Risk shapes varied, from reverse-L curves for cirrhosis to linear rises for immune disease. The index may help flag patients who need closer liver monitoring.
pmc-13375017:
Kelvin Mupunga and co-authors pooled trials of a vein mineral for fast heart flutter in a 2026 review. The flutter is the most common heart pace ill in old age. The mineral is often added to pace drugs, but past pools split on if it truly helps.

Six trials with 480 patients set the mineral next to a sham drip. A fresh trial was new since the last pools, which spurred the redo. Pooled math weighed pace and rhythm gains in non-surgery adults. A firm read could end years of ward habit split, and guide when the cheap drip is worth its slot in fast care.
pmc-13377417:
Zhou and colleagues build a single-cell atlas of pig development, mapping gene use cell by cell across five tissues, before and after birth, in 2026 livestock research. The atlas profiles 252,033 cells and nuclei, resolving 83 cell types, using single-cell and single-nucleus RNA sequencing. A view of tissue growth was missing for livestock, despite pigs' importance to farming and their closeness to humans as a biomedical model for growth and disease.

Tissues changed in coordinated waves, as stem and progenitor cells multiplied, committed to lineages, and matured into cell types. Immune cells followed a conserved two-branch pattern across the tissues. Combining the atlas with population data pinpointed a muscle enhancer of the MYOT gene that breeding selection targeted, driving divergence in meat quality between Asian and European pig breeds. A cross-species comparison with humans revealed cell types. Zhou offers the atlas as infrastructure for precision breeding.
pmc-13378117:
Kaye Rolls and colleagues improve delirium assessment and communication in a rural hospital in a 2026 study. Delirium detection and prevention are global safety priorities, yet nurses often lack screening skills and knowledge. A repeated audit study across four wards between March 2023 and March 2024 combined the 4Es implementation model with a three-part education programme: face-to-face teaching, self-directed online learning, and a clinical exam.

Bimonthly audits of 378 patient notes against an 85 percent benchmark showed that six key practices reached and held the benchmark through the study and for three months after. Knowledge and self-efficacy surveys from 187 nurses tracked gains before, after, and six weeks after training. The study shows that paired implementation and education can lift delirium care beyond a single training event.
pmc-13379317:
Lin Lin and a large team describe a 2026 biohybrid robot for delivering chemotherapy inside the bladder. Drugs washed into the bladder often fail to reach tumours well or pass through tissue. Their robot is built from algae fitted with magnetic material and loaded with a cancer drug.

Magnets steer the robots, and a computer system using live images guides them on its own. Swarms of robots can change shape, and flowing fluid helps push the drug deep into tissue. In mice with bladder tumours, the method delivered far more drug than a standard wash and shrank tumour burden greatly. The work points toward more precise bladder treatment.
pmc-13379717:
Muhammad A Zahid and colleagues present a 2026 review of cancers of the nose and sinuses that had grown into the eye socket. Such cancers are uncommon and often found late, because they grow deep in the face and cause vague early symptoms. Growth into the orbit changes how the disease is staged and treated.

The team reviewed records at a major hospital in Islamabad, Pakistan, for patients treated from April 2022 to March 2026 whose scans showed spread into the eye socket. They recorded patient details, cancer type, patterns of invasion, and treatments given. The analysis looks for links between those features. The goal is to guide planning for a difficult group of patients.
pmc-13380617:
Daphne Condon asked US experts which wildlife rules belong in solar site screening, in a 2026 Delphi study. Big solar farms compete with protected land, and site screenings aim to steer projects to low-conflict zones. Yet no shared list said which wildlife criteria are essential or whether data exist to use them.

A panel of wildlife and clean energy experts named 16 core rules and 13 secondary ones. Core rules tracked regulation most closely, while secondary ones hinged on local ecology lacking consistent scalable data. Open data covered 14 core rules across 10 databases, but only 10 reviewed US screenings used core rules. The gap calls for finer wildlife data and closer agency teamwork.
pmc-13383017:
Arezoo Dehghan and colleagues search heart valve tissue for hard-to-grow microbes in patients with valve infection in Tehran in 2026 work. Standard blood tests miss some causes of infective endocarditis, a life-threatening heart infection. The team tested samples from 232 patients who had valve replacement surgery between 2021 and 2025.

DNA tests found Brucella species most often, followed by the Q fever microbe, Bartonella, and the Whipple disease microbe. Breathlessness linked to several of these infections, while fever and sweating linked to Brucella. The authors argue that tissue DNA testing should play a larger role when blood cultures stay negative.
pmc-13383217:
Azusa Yamazaki and co-authors show how high lipoprotein(a) levels distort a common cholesterol test in 2026 work. Standard LDL cholesterol assays rely on density separation, and a protein part of lipoprotein(a) can shift where particles settle. The team compared routine assay results with a chromatography method across 1,560 human samples.

Routine values ran higher than the reference method as lipoprotein(a) rose, and the gap grew clearly above a set level. A formula-based VLDL estimate moved the opposite way with rising levels. The authors conclude that density-based assays overstate LDL cholesterol when lipoprotein(a) is high, a caution for labs and clinicians reading results.
pmc-13384517:
Snehalakshmi Kavacheri Subramaniam and colleagues review links between sugar tagging of proteins and cell aging in lung disease in a 2026 article. Cell aging drives lasting inflammation and poor repair in chronic lung conditions. In parallel, faulty fucosylation, the adding of fucose sugar tags, alters airway surface and immune signals.

One enzyme, FUT8, adds core tags that can amplify pathways known to start and sustain cell aging. Those same pathways feed scarring in diseases like COPD, asthma, and pulmonary fibrosis. The authors propose the fucosylation-aging axis as a source of new markers and drug targets for these hard-to-treat diseases.
pmc-13386617:
Farzaneh Saki's team presents a trial plan combining neuromuscular training with pain science teaching for knee arthritis in older women, in a 2026 paper. Existing training programs often target single elements and neglect mental factors and pain science.

pmc-13386717:
Arda Toptaş, Onur Koç, and Semih Demirci link poor sleep before tooth extraction to harder recovery in a 2026 study. Records covered 111 adults aged 18 to 65 treated at Hacettepe University in Turkey. A standard sleep scale split patients into disturbed and sound sleep groups before surgery.

pmc-13389217:
Shuangyue Pan's team traced how loss of the ARID1A gene helps triple-negative breast cancer spread to bone, a lethal turn whose workings were unclear. Patients with ARID1A-mutated tumours showed more bone metastases, and most mutations wiped out the protein.

pmc-13389617:
Kristine Gvinepadze and Marika Toidze describe, in 2026, a 67-year-old woman whose systemic sclerosis appeared together with two rare problems. Systemic sclerosis, also called scleroderma, scars tissue and harms small blood vessels across the gut, skin, heart, eyes, kidneys, and lungs.

pmc-13390317:
Zhong Chu's team reports early results for one-eye three-focus lens fitting in lens-clouding patients, an approach with limited evidence. They were tested before surgery and at one, three, six, and twelve months for distance, mid-range, and near vision plus optical quality and reading.

At twelve months, over three quarters reached 20/20 distance vision unaided and nearly nine in ten with glasses. All eyes managed 20/40 or better at mid-range and near ranges. Focus stayed stable and accurate, backing one-eye three-focus fitting for patients seeking glasses independence in one eye.
pmc-13392517:
Zhao Ge and eight co-authors review coronary microvascular dysfunction, a fault in the heart's smallest vessels that can starve heart muscle of blood even when the large arteries stay open. Studies of traditional Chinese medicine that may act on the same route are covered too, as a possible path toward combined, patient-matched care.
pmc-13392617:
Tosin T Fakiyesi leads a group reviewing how heart damage from anthracycline chemotherapy might be caught earlier, before it hardens into heart failure. Damage tends to grow quietly from cell injury to a weakening heart pump.

Older watch methods, above all the ejection fraction measure of pumping strength, often flag trouble only after it turns hard to reverse. The review weighs scans, magnetic resonance imaging, and blood markers of early injury, then turns to artificial intelligence tools and remote monitoring worn or used at home. pmc-13392917:
EFSA's Panel on Additives and Products or Substances used in Animal Feed weighed a licence renewal for zinc chelate of amino acids hydrate. Maker Zinpro Animal Nutrition sought the renewal, and the panel checked company data showing the marketed product still matches its licence conditions. No new evidence emerged to disturb earlier safety findings.

For handlers it counts as an eye irritant and a skin and airway sensitiser, so contact by any route should be kept low. One question stayed open: the panel could not conclude on environmental safety, deferring to a forthcoming opinion on trace elements that will apply directly here. Efficacy required no fresh assessment for renewal.
pmc-13393917:
Lihong Dang and colleagues map the brain immune response three days after cardiac arrest in a 2026 single-cell study. Most arrest victims are elderly, and brain injury from inflammation drives much of the lasting harm, yet the roles of individual immune cells were poorly understood.

The paper points to age-specific immune targets for protecting the post-arrest brain.
pmc-13394017:
Hannah Jackson, Luke Grzeskowiak, Joanne Enticott, Sarah Wise, and Emily Callander examined who receives subsidised anti-nausea medicines in pregnancy under Australia's Pharmaceutical Benefits Scheme, and whether access tilts by wealth. Spending showed a moderate one, since richer women's use costs the scheme less. The authors frame the pattern as an equity question for pharmaceutical policy on off-label prescribing.
pmc-13394117:
Virginia R Nuckols and others ask whether menopause vessel health is all about estrogen in a 2026 review. Heart risk climbs fast across menopause, long blamed on falling estradiol, yet progesterone also falls while two brain glands' hormones rise.

It reframes menopause as a multi-hormone vessel shift, not a one-hormone tale. Doctors gain a wider base for weighing heart risk in midlife women and for judging hormone care.
pmc-13395417:
Yuan Wei and colleagues model, in 2026, how blue honeysuckle branches shake when a harvest machine vibrates them. Shaking must throw fruit off, yet trunks and roots soak up much of the energy. When the shake runs near a branch's own pitch and angle, unstable parametric shaking can erupt. That wild motion boosts the force on fruit. Computer models and branch tests matched the maths on peak swing across pitches. The authors offer the model as a design base for honeysuckle harvesters. Right tuning could raise fruit drop and save effort.
pmc-13396217:
Fan and co-authors monitor, in 2026, an enzyme molecule at work by listening to its electrical conductance. pmc-13396317:

Nanosuspensions grind or build active ingredients into tiny particles held in liquid, which can make them dissolve better, last longer on the leaf, and release slowly. Some products instead use nanomaterials that kill pests on their own. The authors survey preparation methods and the tests used to check particle size and stability, and cover packaging designs that keep such products usable in the field.
pmc-13397517:
Published in 2026 with no byline shown, the study tracks lawsuits over body contouring surgery across 45 years in the United States. Operations such as tummy tucks and liposuction rank among the most done cosmetic procedures, with about 170,000 tummy tucks in 2024 alone. Infections, fluid build-up, poor scars and unhappy results often end up argued in court.

The review compares what sparked each claim, how cases ended and which problems arose. It also contrasts plastic surgeons with doctors from other fields who offer the same operations.
pmc-13397617:
Tracey Pérez Koehlmoos and colleagues report the fourth annual workshop on fetal alcohol spectrum disorders, held in Washington, DC on 17 September 2025. Published in 2026, the summary centres on conditions that occur alongside these disorders. Alcohol exposure before birth can shape development, behaviour and learning across a whole life, and ranks among the top preventable causes of disability in the United States.

Nearly 100 people from universities, clinics, federal agencies and advocacy groups shared findings from a four-year federally funded initiative. Talks covered prevention, screening, diagnosis, family support and care inside the military health system, which serves about 9.6 million people. Lessons from military families may also guide better civilian care.
pmc-13398517:
Hutchinson and co-authors revisit, in 2026, how the giant Late Triassic predator Postosuchus kirkpatricki actually moved, using three-dimensional musculoskeletal modeling of this crocodile-line archosaur from North America. Whether it walked on four legs or two, and whether it stood flat-footed or on its toes, has been disputed for decades. The team rebuilt its pelvic limb muscles digitally and compared joint ranges under competing anatomical arrangements.

Their reconstruction gives Postosuchus hindlimb musculature roughly three times as massive, relative to size, as a similar-sized Nile crocodile's. The main tail-driven thigh muscle was smaller than expected, though, because the animal's tail was gracile. An earlier collated dataset had estimated an 85 to 100 percent probability of bipedalism from body proportions and center-of-mass position, theirs sitting about 78 percent of femur length ahead of the hips. pmc-13398617:
Yanqiu Zou and colleagues ask whether good sleep habits shield people with type 2 diabetes from vessel damage. Small-vessel risk also dipped, driven by nerve damage rates, while stroke showed no clear link. Blood markers partly carried the effect, and the authors probe whether diabetes severity changes the protection.
pmc-13399217:

Electrode material, operating settings, and the mix of substances in real wastewater all shift how well removal works. The authors flag high energy use, electrode wear, and toxic byproducts as open problems. They propose better electrodes plus standard risk testing as next steps.
pmc-13399317:

Guidelines disagree: some allow clear liquids only, while the World Health Organization lets low-risk women eat and drink as they wish.

Main outcomes include vaginal delivery rate, caesarean section, and newborn measures such as the ten-minute Apgar score. The protocol is registered on PROSPERO as CRD42025630953. No ethical approval is needed, since only published trial data will be used.
pmc-13399517:
R. Mukesh and colleagues built a hybrid forecasting model for disturbances in the ionosphere during volcanic eruptions, reporting in 2026. The team tested their model against six major eruptions.

The hybrid blends a LightGBM machine learning model with an LSTM deep learning network, combined by weighted average. It was trained largely on data from the BAKO station in Indonesia. They benchmarked it against each component alone and against two classical statistical models. For the strongest event, Mount Ruang in 2024, where disturbance peaked around 100 to 110 TEC units, the hybrid's error was 2.841 units. That was clearly below LightGBM at 3.484, the LSTM at 5.084, and the classical models above 5.3 in the reported comparison. The hybrid also led on the other eruptions, from Etna in 2013 to La Soufrière in 2021.
pmc-13399817:
Catarina Reis Rodrigues and colleagues present a hybrid repair for medial meniscus ramp lesions in a 2026 technical note. No single repair method has proven best, so the team combined two: a loop stitch placed from behind, under direct posteromedial vision, plus an all-inside suture delivered from the front.

A high posteromedial portal is placed with a spinal needle about a centimeter behind the joint line. Through it the surgeon refreshes the torn edges and places the loop stitch exactly through the meniscocapsular tissue. The anterior all-inside stitch follows through the familiar front portal, adding a second, easily placed layer of fixation. The authors describe the pairing as each method covering the other's weakness: precision and capture from behind, speed and stability from the front.
pmc-13400217:

CT showed a well-defined ossified lump of about three centimeters in the olecranon fossa acting as a mechanical doorstop.

Old teaching waits twelve to twenty-four months for such lesions to mature before excision, fearing recurrence. The authors argue a defined mechanical block justifies earlier surgery before muscles waste and soft tissues contract around the block. Excision plus structured rehabilitation restored the elbow's full motion. One year out there was no recurrence. The authors present the case as evidence that carefully selected patients can be offered early excision safely.
pmc-13400517:
Pushpa Narayanaswami leads a team measuring, in 2026, how generalized myasthenia gravis affects daily life in the United States beyond clinic scores. The disease weakens muscles and can disrupt work, money, sleep and family roles. Caregivers share much of that burden, so both groups were asked directly.

Interviews first produced 25 specific impacts grouped into eight life areas. A separate survey of 239 patients and 81 caregivers then rated each one. Work, planning and independence, finances, physical limits and sleep scored highest for patients. Caregivers ranked finances and sleep at the top too. The authors argue that judging a treatment value should count these lived effects, not only medical outcomes.
pmc-13400617:

Thirty-nine men were grouped by diabetes status and semen quality, then tested for hormones, sugar control, sperm movement and shape, plus death markers. Diabetic men had worse sugar control, higher pituitary hormones and lower testosterone. Men with both diabetes and abnormal semen fared worst, with the slowest sperm and the highest early cell death rates. pmc-13400717:
Leah Leslie Dias and co-authors follow, in 2026, how memory, exploration and anxiety change across the rat lifespan. Aging alters sensory, emotional and social systems, but which behaviors shift and which hold steady needs careful testing. Two standard tasks were used: recognizing a new object, and exploring an open arena.

Rats aged six, twelve and twenty-four months, spanning early adulthood to old age, were tracked by automated video. Recognition memory dipped only slightly in middle age and stayed largely intact even in old animals. Anxiety-like behavior did not differ by age. Rearing and exploration, however, declined with age, which the authors read as a locomotor and curiosity change rather than a memory failure.
pmc-13401317:
Maria Fueth and colleagues present a 2026 case report of cutaneous angiosarcoma, a rare blood-vessel cancer of the skin, in a woman whose extreme obesity blocked standard cancer care. She weighed about 280 kilograms, with a body mass index above 100, and had stage IV lymphedema in both legs.

A fast-growing purple, ulcerated plaque on her left calf proved on biopsy to be high-grade angiosarcoma of the Stewart-Treves type, which arises in chronically swollen limbs. CT, MRI, and PET staging were impossible because she exceeded scanner opening and table limits at every reachable centre. pmc-13401717:
Wasay Mumtaz Awan and colleagues wrote a 2026 perspective on oral nicotine pouches and youth addiction in Pakistan. The smokeless, flavoured pouches are sold as safer than cigarettes, but teenagers are taking them up fast, and the authors map the market and the rules around it.

pmc-13401917:

Losing substantial weight on these drugs could add to that danger. pmc-13402017:

pmc-13402617:

pmc-13402717:

The authors present uneven composition as a recipe for damage-tolerant soft materials fit for harsh mechanical work.
pmc-13402817:

pmc-13403217:

pmc-13403417:

pmc-13403817:

pmc-13405017:

pmc-13405117:

pmc-13405617:

The team has now restored the correct image, stressing that the counts came from a different panel, so no result or conclusion changes.
pmc-13405717:

pmc-13407017:

pmc-13407817:

pmc-13410517:

pmc-13410817:

The review covers drug carriers, scaffolds, enzyme-like particles, and tissue-like builds that aim drugs at damaged muscle and rebuild its structure. Readers get a map of what works in the lab, what still blocks use in patients, and where the next steps for muscle repair research should fall.
pmc-13411717:
Trung-Loc Ho and colleagues report in 2026 that a plant compound blocks breast cancer's spread to bone by silencing a guidance protein. Ferdinand Otto and colleagues follow patients with secondary progressive multiple sclerosis who stopped anti-CD20 antibody therapy, in a 2026 multicenter study. pmc-13417017:

pmc-13418417:

Chen and colleagues review adiponectin, a hormone made by fat tissue, as an early warning marker for gestational diabetes, the blood sugar disorder arising in pregnancy, in 2026 hormone research. Wenjing Zhao and colleagues tune a jelly-like scaffold that sets inside the body and can hold living cells in three dimensions. Cells grown inside the winning gels stayed alive and spread in space through day 10 of culture, beating flat dish growth. The tuning method can guide scaffold design for other tissues.
pmc-13420717:
Rajamanickam Baskar and colleagues screen a new plant compound from Cassia fistula bark as a possible diabetes drug that blocks starch breakdown. Stepwise filtering cut many candidates down to this one validated lead. The authors stress that animal studies must come before any human claims. A plant-derived blocker with this profile could widen diabetes options where synthetic drugs strain budgets.

Qiu and colleagues report a 2026 study of a skin treatment that pairs fine needles with radiofrequency heat to refresh aging faces. Evidence for the higher 5 megahertz setting was thin. Twenty participants received one full-face treatment, and the team checked skin measures with imaging systems before treatment and over the following month.

Side effects and patient satisfaction were tracked at each visit. A single session thus gave measurable firming within a month, with short-lived early changes that patients should be warned about.
pmc-13421317:
Bing Zhang and eight co-authors chart, in a 2026 study, how thousands of single-letter changes to the immune protein STING alter its behaviour. Their massively parallel assay tested thousands of variants at once, mapping which regions set the protein's signalling strength and which separate its outputs. Some changes made STING respond more keenly to its natural activator; others uncoupled interferon production from a second pathway, autophagy. Structures of overactive variants, solved with cryo-electron microscopy, revealed how the protein flips from its resting to its signalling shape.
pmc-13421717:
Onur Taydas leads a twelve-author team reporting, in a 2026 study, a backward route into the leg arteries for clearing complex blockages. They entered through the popliteal artery behind the knee. The procedure succeeded in all but one case, with no embolic events, deaths or amputations, and one minor access-site bruise. pmc-13422117:
Mahran Mohamed Abd El-Emam leads a ten-author team testing, in a 2026 study, whether packaging a plant antioxidant into tiny carriers protects rat testes from chemotherapy damage. pmc-13422317:

Partner genomes for acetate oxidation and methane making complete the chain the authors chart.
pmc-13422817:
Blanca Collado-González leads a Spanish multicentre team surveying, in a 2026 study, how paediatric emergency departments organise safety work. Extra reporting systems came with more frequent event reports and better feedback, and leadership walkarounds lifted several measures too. pmc-13423317:
Johanna Vikkula and five colleagues use automated registry data to describe what happens at first relapse of multiple myeloma in Finland. After 2018, newer antibody-based therapy and pomalidomide spread quickly among younger patients but stayed limited in the elderly, a gap the authors say needs closing.

Venter and co-authors read the chemistry of starvation in purple sea urchins, in this 2026 study. The urchins live in barrens. They were shoring up cell membranes at the same time. The picture is reproduction sacrificed for survival, which the authors note could frustrate kelp restoration: hungry urchins endure rather than die off.
pmc-13424517:

Understanding ligand distribution gives implant designers a concrete target: shaping surfaces so cell adhesion itself switches on regeneration for complex fractures and large defects. The team could watch cells grip, turn, and line up on each tube size, then link each step to how fast new bone cells formed.

When one arm of the guard cells wakes too soon, the shots that count on it fall short. pmc-13428217:
Liu and colleagues examined in 2026 whether blood zinc levels track with chronic kidney disease in United States adults, using a national health survey. Of 4,192 adults, 685 had chronic kidney disease. Each small rise in blood zinc came with lower odds of disease, and people in the highest zinc quarter had roughly half the odds of those in the lowest. Machine learning models gave zinc real predictive weight. The authors caution that a one-time survey cannot prove zinc protects kidneys. Karine Lamiraud and Radu Vranceanu ask, in a 2026 study, whether French patients actually value doctors who charge above the standard fee. pmc-13429117:
Esteban Daudén and the Inpsight Working Group survey, in a 2026 Spanish study, how psoriasis shadows well-being across a lifetime. pmc-13429217:
Eren Kıymaz and colleagues report, in a 2026 case, a rare and fatal brain infection in a young cancer patient. Fluid pressure built up in his brain, so surgeons placed an emergency drain. Fluid samples grew Klebsiella pneumoniae, a hospital germ known for drug resistance. pmc-13430817:

Kakouris and colleagues published a 2026 review on events that wound a person's moral core. Such events involve doing wrong, failing to stop wrong, or betrayal by trusted leaders. pmc-13432517:
Kole H Buckley and co-authors counted past contact with a stomach germ in 2026 among people who carry inherited faults in two famed cancer guard genes. Non-White race stood out as the trait tied to contact. The authors note that past contact may not equal live infection, so next studies must split the two and weigh what each does to stomach cancer risk in this high-risk crowd.
pmc-13433317:

pmc-13434417:
Feba T Pulikkottil and coauthors use electric current to turn simple amines into prized fluorine compounds in 2026. Two product families come from one pot setup with cheap, shelf stable stock. No dry solvents, no inert gas, and no costly silver agents are needed.

Shifting the mix steers the pot toward one family or the other. Yields range from fair to excellent across many starting amines. Late changes to complex drug like molecules also worked. pmc-13435217:
Bart J Keulen and coauthors sift research on brain wave marks for non motor woes in Parkinson disease in 2026. Deep brain stimulation eases shaking and stiffness, yet mood, sleep, and urge issues linger. The review gathers studies that tie basal ganglia field signals to those other symptoms.

pmc-13435517:
Jiaming Wu's team mapped cell death patterns in stomach cancer in 2026 by joining single-cell and bulk gene data. pmc-13436417:
Karen Fong and coauthors pair a bacteria eating virus with old antibiotics against resistant Salmonella in 2026. The germ causes vast foodborne illness and gains resistance fast. Checkerboard tests mix the phage SeKF_13 with chloramphenicol or tetracycline below killing doses.

pmc-13436917:

pmc-13437617:
Manuel Garcia and co-authors reviewed how cholesterol-lowering agents talk with the gut's microbial community. High cholesterol drives heart disease, and its treatments do more than trim blood fat. pmc-13438417:
Yuan Man, Shifei Zhao, and Kang Li built a new yardstick for a quieter cost of city heat: the shrinking hours when outdoor activity is safe. pmc-13441517:

Attachment priming produced the most consistent and largest benefits across the follow-up points at the end of practice, one week later, and four weeks later. pmc-13441917:
Faisal Alrehily reviews how radiation risk gets explained to patients, arguing that honest conversation is an ethical duty even where science stays unsettled, in a 2026 paper. pmc-13442817:

pmc-13444317:

pmc-13444717:
Olayinka and colleagues use a genetic risk score to hunt for rare Alzheimer's variants in this 2026 study. A polygenic risk score sums many common small-effect variants. The team reasoned about people who develop Alzheimer's despite a low score. They may carry strong rare variants worth finding. Working with the Alzheimer's Disease Sequencing Project, they split European-ancestry participants into high and low score groups of roughly five to six thousand each.

Rare risk variants were indeed concentrated in the low-score group, while protective variants clustered in the high-score group, the opposite of their background risk. Genome-wide significant risk variants spanned a stretch of chromosome 14, and protective variants appeared in three genes, ALDH9A1, BICC1, and PAN3, in the upper group. The authors present stratification by background risk as a lever for discovering rare variants that ordinary scans miss.
pmc-13445517:
Klaas Reglitz and Martin Steinhaus present an automated machine that lifts scent compounds gently out of foods and drinks for lab study, in a 2026 methods paper. Heat can break fragile scent molecules or create false ones, so aroma work needs a cool, mild separation step. Their system updates an earlier solvent-based method with new glassware and controls.

A light valve, a modern controller, and a sensor that spots the end of a run let the device work on its own and shut down safely. Tests stress three gains: true scent profiles with no heat damage, clean extracts with little carry-over of heavy matter, and easy setup. The kit is sold as a full set for aroma labs that run the method often.
pmc-13446317:
Lucas Abreu Dias and colleagues survey how parents and caregivers in southeastern Brazil handle fever in children, and what marks good handling, in a 2026 study. Fever drives a large share of child clinic visits, yet home care often strays from national guidance. A structured survey ran online and in person at primary care units through 2024.

Eight hundred forty-seven caregivers took part, and only forty-two in a hundred met every rule for sound fever care at once. Schooling linked to good care in simple comparisons but faded once other traits were weighed. Waiting some hours before rushing to a clinic, from six up to thirty-six, linked on its own to better care. The authors aim teaching at the decision of when to seek help.
pmc-13446517:
Yada Kunpalin and colleagues chart how severe fetal brain injury unfolds after laser surgery for twin-to-twin transfusion syndrome, in a 2026 case series from the Ontario Fetal Center. The syndrome starves one twin and floods the other through shared placenta vessels, and laser sealing is the standard rescue. Brain harm after the rescue was known, yet its shapes over time were not.

Fifteen fetuses from fourteen pregnancies, treated between June 2023 and March 2025, had serial ultrasound and MRI review. Early scans most often showed bleeding injury near the brain's fluid spaces, plus cerebellar bleeding in a quarter. Later scans showed brain volume loss in most, often in the parietal lobes, with folding faults and fiber decay. Past four weeks the picture froze.
pmc-13446717: Hu and colleagues published a corrigendum in 2026 to their 2015 study of blood microRNAs in children with combined pituitary hormone deficiency. A reader spotted duplicated and previously published blot images in one figure. The authors admitted assembly errors, no longer held the original data, and repeated the western blot experiments. The new results matched the originals closely, and the authors state the study's findings and conclusions stand unchanged.
pmc-13447217:
Tengyan Wu and colleagues measure crushing treatment costs for tuberculosis households in Guangxi, China, in a 2026 survey. TB care is meant to be affordable, yet travel, tests and lost income can overwhelm poor families. Knowing how often costs turn catastrophic, meaning very large relative to income, helps target support.

Two hundred fifty patients who finished drug-sensitive TB treatment across three counties answered detailed cost questions. Median out-of-pocket spending across the whole course ran to several thousand yuan, with direct medical costs the largest share at each stage. Nearly half of households crossed the catastrophic threshold. Very low household income and more than a week in hospital after diagnosis carried the highest risks. Education and insurance type also mattered, shaping the authors' calls for warnings and stronger coverage.
pmc-13449517:
Georgia Herbert and coauthors ran a 2026 feasibility trial of a short water-only fast before chemotherapy for bowel cancer. CAPOX chemotherapy is standard for stage two and three colorectal cancer, but side effects often force dose cuts. Brief fasting may shield healthy cells through differential stress resistance, yet nobody knew whether patients would join or stick to such a trial.

Patients at two English hospital trusts were assigned at random to a thirty-six-hour water-only fast before their first three chemo cycles or to standard diet advice. The team tracked recruitment, adherence, retention, and data completion, with interviews on how patients experienced the fast. The trial answers the practical question first: can this approach even be tested properly in routine care?
pmc-13449817:
Bryce Roberts, Darren Kempton, and Nikifor Konstantinov use a 2026 case to teach a clue for crusted scabies, the severe mite infestation that overwhelms people with weakened cellular immunity. Their patient was a 65-year-old man who had vascular dementia, schizophrenia, and lung disease. He arrived from an assisted living facility red from head to toe, with widespread scaling, scratch marks, and strikingly thickened skin under his nails. His blood also grew MRSA bacteria, and he tested positive for COVID-19.

The under-nail buildup matters doubly, the authors argue: mites concentrate there, so it is prime material for microscope diagnosis, and it shelters mites from treatment, reseeding the skin. He received vancomycin for the bloodstream infection plus permethrin cream and oral ivermectin against the mites, and the rash and itching cleared before discharge. They urge immediate microscopy, combined therapy, and contact precautions whenever this nail sign appears with redness.
pmc-13449917:
Aaron Wan Jia He and co-authors lay out in 2026 a pilot trial protocol. It aims to draw Hong Kong's older adults into community District Health Centers, the primary care hubs the city wants to carry more of its care. With residents over sixty-five heading toward thirty-six percent of the population by 2046, the hospital-heavy system strains. The pilot tests a hybrid push: trained students visit elders at home in an intergenerational format, then a month of artificial intelligence generated messages, videos, and graphics follows through WhatsApp.

The cluster trial will enroll 180 older adults across six clusters, with centers rather than individuals randomized. Feasibility comes first: recruitment, retention, dose delivered, engagement, and satisfaction. The headline outcome is the share of participants who join a District Health Center. Follow-up surveys at one, three, and six months also track service use, health status, risk habits, and digital health literacy.
pmc-13450417:
Ketzel and colleagues combined lab measurements with computer models in 2026 to map the shapes of macrocycles, ring-shaped peptides gaining ground as drugs. Adding flat aromatic rings to these cycles creates new shapes that may reach targets once seen as undruggable. The rings also make the molecules flex between forms in ways standard tests miss.

The team paired nuclear magnetic resonance data, which reports on atom positions and motion, with boosted computer sampling and quantum calculations across several solvents. Measurements of residual dipolar couplings, signals that reveal average molecular alignment, exposed motion that older methods based on atom closeness had hidden. Up to three interchanging backbone shapes were needed to match the data for each ring, each with its own pattern of internal hydrogen bonds. The ring motifs steered which shapes dominated, giving drug designers a firmer map for tuning these molecules.
pmc-13450617:
Jonathan Ong and co-authors write in 2026 on gaps in care for a common heart rhythm fault across four Pacific lands. The fault, atrial fibrillation, touched more than 52 million people in 2021 and drives stroke, heart failure, and hospital stays. The piece covers Australia, New Zealand, Malaysia, and Singapore.

Good care rests on stroke guard drugs, control of rate or rhythm, and care for linked health risks. The authors say old national guides, patchy digital systems, and uneven access to proven drugs hold back that care in the region. They also note that most local proof comes from small single-center work, and they call for fresh population data to shape policy.
pmc-13451817:
Laura Pini and a large team follow in 2026 four years of a biologic drug in severe asthma across nine Italian centers. The drug, benralizumab, targets a cell type that drives a common severe asthma form, and full remission is now a stated goal of care. Records covered 128 adults, many with nasal polyps as well, treated for up to 48 months.

Attack rates fell fast, from over three a year to a third of one, and the gains held. The study tracks lung flow, swelling marks, and patient-rated control, plus how far steroid pills and sprays could be cut. The authors read the long arc as proof that deep control can last, a claim real-world data past three years had not yet shown.
pmc-13451917:
Tongtong Wang, Hanying Bai, and Jinghe Li build in 2026 a stacked learning model that guesses how much a red clay soil will squash under load. That squash rate drives how much buildings settle, yet lab tests take a week or more and disturb the soil. The team trained on 454 data sets from Guilin, China, using plain soil measures such as water content.

A tuned stack of three boost models with a linear top beat each single model, with a test score near the top of the scale. Two inputs, a wetness index and water content, carried near all the weight, and their joint rise drove high squash. Map-style checks and repeat random runs held firm, with most doubt bands narrow.
pmc-13452117:
Xue Chen and a large team review in 2026 a cell switch that may drive the ligament growth behind many cases of narrowed spine. The ligament, the flavum, thickens with age and squeezes the cord space, and no drug yet targets it. The switch, PPAR gamma, is a fat-sensing control that touches swelling, scar growth, blood vessel growth, and cell death.

The review walks each of those paths and the ways drugs might turn the switch. Direct proof in the ligament is still missing, the authors grant, yet the switch shows up in process after process that builds the thickening. They cast it as a prime lead for the first targeted drug work in this disease.
pmc-13452317:
Seburn and Hilton publish a step-by-step laboratory protocol in this 2026 methods paper for studying how injured nerves regrow. Their system exploits a quirk of sensory neurons in the dorsal root ganglia. Injuring the peripheral branch of the neuron flips it into a vigorous growth state. Injuring its central branch does nothing of the sort.

The protocol walks through a conditioning crush injury on the mouse sciatic nerve. Then it waits for the growth program to switch on. Next it dissects the lumbar ganglia, levels L3 through L5. Finally it cultures the neurons so new axons extend across the dish for measurement. It covers surgical tool preparation, culture conditions, and quantification of outgrowth, and it is designed to pair with cytoskeletal imaging and molecular profiling. The authors frame the method as an accessible entry point into regeneration biology's central puzzle.
pmc-13452417:
Conghui Su and four co-authors ask whether weaker language skills go with weaker brain wiring in young children with autism. Their 2026 study scanned 67 Chinese children with autism and 36 children without it, all aged about 20 to 93 months. Brain maps were built from scans that track water flow along white matter, the brain's wiring bundles.

Splitting the autism group by language skill gave 29 children with stronger language and 38 with weaker language. The weaker language group showed less smooth whole brain traffic, fewer hubs, and fewer links between the brain's two halves. In that group only, worse wiring tracked more severe autism traits, and language skill shaped how tight that link was. The authors argue that language level should guide both care plans and how studies group children.
pmc-13453017:
Wattanawongwon and colleagues ask which healthy-feeling people with an enlarged heart shadow actually have structural disease. Their 2026 cross-sectional study at Siriraj Hospital in Bangkok covers 452 asymptomatic adults. Their routine chest X-rays showed a cardiothoracic ratio of at least 0.5, the conventional enlargement threshold. All received an echocardiogram within six months. Known heart disease was excluded.

Just over half, about 53 percent, turned out to have structural abnormalities on ultrasound. Several factors flagged them in simple comparisons, but three survived multivariable modelling as independent predictors: age of 65 or over, hypertension, and left ventricular hypertrophy visible on an electrocardiogram. A systolic murmur, significant alone, dropped out after adjustment. The authors suggest these three cheap findings can triage which incidental X-ray enlargements deserve prompt ultrasound, rather than scanning everyone or no one.
pmc-13453717:
Fanni Küplen and four co-authors reanalyze a public dataset on climate anxiety in American university students. Their 2026 study covers 435 students aged 18 to 22, most of them women, scored on a four part climate anxiety scale. The team asks which parts of that anxiety predict green behavior and which predict seeing barriers to climate action.

One part did nearly all the work: behavioral engagement, the drive to act, predicted both greener behavior and sharper barrier awareness. The distress parts of the scale, troubled thoughts and daily life disruption, showed little link to either outcome. Splitting by sex, engagement drove green behavior in women, while personal experience of climate harm drove it in men. The authors urge care workers and researchers to treat climate anxiety as several strands, not one lump.
pmc-13453817:
Jiahao Yuan and five co-authors sort nursing interns in China into types by their cyberchondria, the anxiety fed by searching symptoms online. Their 2026 study surveys 538 interns at 14 top grade hospitals in Hubei Province between September and November 2025. Interns sit in a sore spot: some medical knowledge, heavy ward stress, and easy internet access.

Four types emerged: a low, detached group at 8.7 percent, a mid, careful group at 44.2 percent, a higher, irritable group at 38.0 percent, and a high, obsessive group at 9.1 percent. Work stress pushed interns away from the low group and toward the irritable one. Health anxiety carried the stress effect along different paths for three types, and fully explained the path into the obsessive group. The authors urge support tuned to each type.
pmc-13454117:
Savitha Dhandapani and eleven co-authors show that a light based scan can measure leaf nitrate without harming the plant. Knowing nitrate status early guides feeding, yet lab assays destroy the leaf they test. Their 2026 study starves two week old pak choi, a C3 plant, and amaranth, a C4 plant, of nitrate for one to three days.

A Raman scan, which reads how light scatters off molecules, gave a peak tied to nitrate at a set position. The peak's height against a neighbor peak tracked leaf nitrate in a straight line for each species. Prediction errors ran near 7 percent of the full level in pak choi and 19 percent in amaranth. The method also exposed species specific nitrate dynamics. The authors offer it for precision feeding and live plant screening.
pmc-13455317:
Zhou and team hunted the root zone of oil-tea camellia, an ammonium-loving woody crop, for bacteria that convert organic nitrogen into ammonium plants can use. They screened 160 grown isolates from rhizosphere soil. Twenty-five made ammonia in first-pass tests, with output ranging from 1.016 to 14.753 units across the active strains.

Four champions were named by gene sequencing as Arthrobacter, Chryseobacterium, Stenotrophomonas, and Bacillus species from the camellia root zone. They grew best at pH 7 to 8, between 20 and 30 degrees, with a 2 percent starting inoculum, and none inhibited the others, making them consortium-compatible for combined use. In pot trials, single strains and the mix all significantly raised rhizosphere ammonium, nitrate, and available nitrogen over untreated controls. Nitrogen-transforming soil enzyme activity also climbed, peaking around 60 days after inoculation in the pots.
pmc-13457017:
Huijie Sun and six colleagues review, in 2026, using bacteria-hunting viruses to control the biofilms behind tooth decay. Cavities grow from a disordered film of microbes on the teeth, and broad mouthwashes wound friendly species alongside the culprits. Viruses called phages offer a sniper's alternative, striking named bacteria and chewing through film structure.

The review first maps the mouth's own virus community and its hand in keeping microbial peace. Named phages against the chief cavity maker, Streptococcus mutans, and its partners get detailed treatment, along with the enzymes phages use to burst cells and dissolve film. Delivery ideas range from mixed phage cocktails to pairings with standard antimicrobials and slow-release carriers. The authors close on the hurdles: narrow targeting cuts both ways, and regulators lack a template for living mouth medicines.
pmc-13457217:
Phyllis N. Muniu and Folashade B. Agusto chart how poor mental health clusters county by county across the Great Plains and Rocky Mountain states. Care in this largely rural region is costly and treatment centers are scarce, so knowing where distress concentrates can guide scarce resources. Their 2026 study uses frequent mental distress, a survey-based measure, across county data from 2019 to 2023.

The pair applied spatial statistics and a ladder of regression models, from plain least squares to versions letting relationships vary by place and year. Distress stayed persistently clustered, running higher in Kansas, Nebraska, Oklahoma, and Texas counties and lower in North Dakota, Wyoming, and Montana. Links with unemployment, poverty, lack of insurance, schooling, and racial composition shifted markedly from county to county. The geographically weighted models fit far better than the plain one, showing that national averages hide sharp local differences in what drives distress.
pmc-13457917:
Nilsen and co-authors chart how heart attack risk unfolds after an atrial fibrillation diagnosis, separately for women and men. Their 2026 paper follows 25,132 participants of Norway's Tromsø Study from 1994 to 2021, none of whom had either condition at the start. The analysis split heart attacks into the two main types and grouped time since diagnosis into bands.

Overall, atrial fibrillation raised heart attack hazard in women but not in men. The patterns diverged sharply by timing. Men's risk spiked within the first six months after diagnosis, more than doubling, then faded. Women's risk grew later, peaking a decade or more after diagnosis at about 1.75 times the hazard. The milder heart attack type drove women's late risk, while men's early spike included the severe type. The authors urge sex-aware follow-up after diagnosis.
pmc-13458217:
Edmund Proper and colleagues audit how quickly a Melbourne hospital network delivers emergency blood pressure control after a brain bleed. Bundled-care trials showed that dropping systolic pressure below 140 within the first hour improves outcomes, a demanding target. Their 2026 retrospective analysis reviews 209 intracerebral hemorrhage patients admitted to Monash Health during 2023, modeling what sped or slowed the clock.

Median time to a CT scan was 33 minutes when a Code Stroke call was activated, which happened for 52 percent of patients, against 121 minutes without one. Among the 74 percent who received active rather than palliative care, pressure fell below target in a median 193 minutes, and only a quarter made the one-hour mark. Higher pressure on arrival, a longer wait for an emergency department bed, and no Code Stroke activation each independently stretched the timeline. The authors argue protocolized rapid-response systems, borrowed from ischemic stroke care, are the lever hospitals control most directly.
pmc-13458317:
Dave Gwun and seven colleagues published this 2026 report on building a case-based learning curriculum in plastic and reconstructive surgery for pre-clerkship medical students in Canada. Such students usually get no exposure to the specialty before rotations. Faculty and residents co-designed five modules, from skin lesions to burns and hand trauma. Each mixed a short lecture, a clinical case and a hands-on workshop. They were aligned with national licensing objectives and matched to the students' coursework.

Across 2023 to 2025, ten sessions drew 453 registrations from 201 students. Forty-one percent reported no prior interest in the specialty. Test scores rose significantly after nearly every session, the exception being the fourth. Over 83 percent of respondents agreed the objectives were met and the sessions effective. Students' feedback praised the hands-on, multimodal format and contact with surgeons. The authors offer the model as a template for early exposure to under-taught specialties.
pmc-13458917:
Jin Ling and co-authors set out in 2026 to test which imaging classification best predicts failure of conservative care in isolated superior mesenteric artery dissection. That condition is a tear in the main artery supplying the bowel, occurring apart from any aortic tear. The study covered 156 patients treated at three Chinese centers between 2009 and 2023.

Eight classification systems were scored against outcomes, since 48 patients did not settle with conservative management alone. Patients who failed had endured abdominal pain longer before admission and had narrower arteries. One system, Tan's classification, discriminated best and gave the greatest benefit in decision analysis. The authors suggest it could help clinicians decide sooner who needs intervention.
pmc-13459117:
Xiaonan Shen and co-authors built in 2026 an eight-gene risk signature for colorectal cancer from genes tied to epithelial-mesenchymal transition, a program that helps cancer cells spread. Using tumor data from The Cancer Genome Atlas, they combined gene activity with survival modeling. Risk scores were then tested against outcomes, immune features of tumors, and likely responses to drugs.

Patients in the high-risk group lived shorter lives than the low-risk group. Lower scores lined up with better predicted responses to immune checkpoint drugs and to the chemotherapy drug fluorouracil. Laboratory and animal experiments singled out one gene, FABP4, which promoted tumor growth, movement, and drug resistance. The signature could help clinicians judge prognosis and pick treatments with more precision.
pmc-13459217:
Sheheryar Shahid and co-authors explored what clinical placements feel like for senior nursing students from private colleges in Karachi, Pakistan, who must train in crowded public hospitals. Their 2026 study ran eight focus group discussions with 59 final year nursing students from three colleges. Students described learning settings shaped by scarce equipment, weak support, and a wide gap between classroom teaching and ward reality.

Five themes organized their accounts. Students reported systemic gaps and unsafe practices born of resource scarcity. They felt let down by instructors and looked down on by hospital staff, in a culture of neglect and hostility. Watching unsafe routines on wards clashed with their training, creating deep discomfort. Many nonetheless built resilience and found peer support and online mentoring to survive. Their closing demand was systemic reform: better oversight, trained preceptors, and real resources.
pmc-13460117:
Xuefang Ren and colleagues pooled in 2026 the randomized trial evidence comparing robotic and camera-assisted keyhole surgery for removable non-small cell lung cancer. Five trials covering 712 patients, including two pivotal recent studies, were combined. Outcomes ranged from blood loss and lymph node counts to pain, complications, costs, and survival.

Robotic operations lost less blood, retrieved about two and a half more lymph nodes on average, and left patients with slightly lower pain scores. Conversion to open surgery, overall complications, operating time, and three-year survival all matched the camera approach. Hospital costs ran significantly higher with robots, driven by equipment expenses. The authors judge robotic surgery safe and effective, with its price the main argument against wider adoption.
pmc-13460217:
Haina Wu, Lina Hao, Honglei Wang, and Yefeng Shen built in 2026 a risk score for sudden worsening episodes in fibrotic idiopathic interstitial pneumonia. This group of scarring lung diseases carries high short-term death rates when episodes strike. Their single-center cohort held 638 patients, 358 with idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis and the rest with related conditions. Six predictors survived the final modeling, mixing age, two breathing capacity measures, lowest oxygen on a walking test, a scan-based fibrosis score, and a blood inflammation ratio.

The simplified score sorted patients into low, middle, and high risk, and it predicted episodes over twenty-four months with good separation of risk. High-risk patients dominated the cohort. It worked better in the non-IPF subgroup, and the score also tracked overall survival, supporting its use for tailoring monitoring.
pmc-13460317:
Piret Hellberg and colleagues test whether p53 status splits clear cell ovarian cancer into distinct subgroups in a 2026 study. A new gene classification proposes TP53 wild-type versus mutated clear cell carcinoma, yet stain-test check was needed. Clinic-and-lab factors, 12 stain-test markers and outlook were analysed in 132 clear cell ovarian cancers.

The p53 abnormal group fared worse in cancer survival and cancer-free survival, largely through higher stage and more frequent left-over tumour. Marker patterns also diverged: ARID1A loss and HNF1-beta presence marked p53 normal tumours, while p16 extra and hormone receptor presence marked p53 abnormal ones, with group-only outlook links. Cancer doctors gain support for two distinct subgroups with different body workings and outcomes.
pmc-13461317:
Zhang and colleagues measured in 2026 sport nutrition knowledge among teenage athletes in the Greater Vancouver area of Canada. Good fuel matters for performance, growth, and health at ages 14 to 18, yet many teens miss dietary targets and know little about their needs. Most past data came from the United States. Fifty-one organised-sport teens, 31 of them girls, completed a validated 35-item knowledge questionnaire online.

Zhang found an average score under half correct, which the authors rate as poor knowledge. Scores were weak on both general nutrition and sport-specific parts. Almost no teens had access to a team dietitian, and only about a quarter had any structured nutrition teaching. Boys and girls scored alike on every part, with no significant sex gap. The authors call for built-in nutrition education in youth sport to support health and development.
pmc-13461417:
Ashleigh A. Kucharski and colleagues tested a gut drug and prebiotics, alone and together, against fattening-season inflammation in ground squirrels and mice. Hibernating squirrels naturally grow inflamed as they fatten, a process driven by gut microbes leaking through the gut wall.

Treatments ran in food for up to eight weeks; mice received them after a transplant of squirrel gut microbes. The two tools acted separately rather than adding up, contrary to the team's hope for a combined boost. In squirrel gut, the drug raised calming IL-10 and cut inflammatory TNF, while prebiotics showed their own mixed pattern. In mice, prebiotics gave the highest IL-10 levels, Kucharski reports, and fat tissue signals stayed unchanged under every treatment.
pmc-13461817:
Xue Du, Liyun Tang, and Lei Tang test, in a 2026 study, a Chinese version of a scale that measures lean management in hospital nursing. Lean methods, born in manufacturing, cut waste and smooth work flow. Nursing services in China have begun using them. A scale built for that purpose needed careful translation and cultural fitting before hospitals could trust its scores.

The team recruited 2,127 clinical nurses from four hospitals in Liaoning Province. After a guided translation, they checked the scale item by item and tested its structure. Five factors emerged, accounting for a share of score differences. A second testing round confirmed the structure fit the data well. Scores were consistent within the scale and steady on retesting. The scale behaved alike across gender, department, and education groups. The authors judge the Chinese version sound for those hospitals, while urging more checks in wider settings.
pmc-13461917:
Jing Tang and co-authors examine, in a 2026 records study, how the lowest blood level of vancomycin relates to kidney injury in patients with sepsis. Vancomycin levels are checked to guide dosing. The team used a multi-hospital intensive care database. Adults with sepsis who received the drug into a vein and had a trough level measured were included, unless already injured.

Among 946 patients, about one in ten developed kidney injury. After accounting for other factors, each rise in the first trough level came with higher odds of kidney injury, in a straight-line pattern with no safe cut-off. The top band carried several times the risk of the lowest band. High lactate, a marker of poor tissue supply, sharpened the link. Risk rose there and barely at all when lactate was normal. The authors advise extra caution with drug levels when lactate is high.
pmc-13462217:
Syed Shaheer Ali and colleagues analyze, in a 2026 national study, throat complications after heart surgery in older adults across the US. Complications include swallowing trouble, weak vocal cords, and voice problems, and are often missed. Earlier reports disagreed on how much they matter. The team used a readmissions database covering 2016 to 2022, sorting patients aged 65 and older who had coronary, valve, or aorta operations.

Over one million patients were counted, and about one to two in a hundred carried a throat diagnosis. Those patients were older and more often women. After adjustment, complications went with higher odds of death, lung problems, and infections. Stays ran over five days longer on average, costs were far higher, and unplanned readmission within thirty days was likelier. The authors stress cause cannot be proven from such data. They argue for early detection and care steps that blunt downstream harm in older patients.
pmc-13463017:
Hana Seo and Nahyun Kim studied intensive care nurses in 2026 to find what drives their use of standard precautions against infection. Intensive care infection rates run about 2.7 times ward rates, since patients there face weak immunity and repeated invasive care. Standard precautions treat all blood and body fluids as risky and cover hand hygiene, protective gear, and safe injections, yet reported use ranges from 60 to 97%.

The descriptive correlational study weighs personal, organisational, and environmental drivers, from knowledge and awareness to ward culture and the supply of gear and guidance. A stubborn gap runs through past work: nurses often know the rules better than they follow them. Pinning down which levers close that gap should help intensive care units turn known rules into daily routine.
pmc-13463117:
Han, Wu, and Hu reviewed in 2026 how the pregnant womb wall, the myometrium, turns stretch into the timed contractions of labour. The growing baby loads the wall mechanically, yet how that force merges with ion channel behaviour was scattered across fields. The review follows stretch, overdistension, hormone signals, and inflammation as they feed calcium entry, wall excitability, and contraction timing.

Han sorts the channels into direct force sensors, force-regulated coupling paths, and nearby excitability controls. The strongest human evidence centres on the sensor PIEZO1, with a second channel, TRPV4, supported in narrower settings. Normal term labour, overstretch-driven early activation, and infection-driven preterm birth share some downstream parts but are not the same process, the authors stress. They close by marking the gaps that must close before channel drugs can be judged for clinical use.
pmc-13463317:
Wang and a large team measure fear of movement after heart stent treatment in this 2026 multicenter study. The fear, called kinesiophobia, can stop patients from exercising after percutaneous coronary intervention, the procedure that opens blocked heart arteries with a stent. Researchers recruited patients from cardiology departments at eight major hospitals in China between November 2022 and December 2023 and assessed fear, mood, and support with validated scales.

Of 970 patients with complete data, about 80 percent showed kinesiophobia, a strikingly high share. Higher physical activity was protective: patients with high activity had far lower odds of fear than inactive ones. Retirement and hypertension were each linked to higher odds. Taking part in cardiac rehabilitation was too. So were rising stress and anxiety scores. Stronger confidence about exercising lowered the odds slightly.
pmc-13463617:
Daisuke Ito leads a team hunting drug targets for amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, a disease that kills motor neurons. Patients differ widely in how fast the disease moves, and the reason has stayed hidden. The team started from body-wide metabolic shifts seen in patients and worked backward to candidate drugs.

Blood fats called N-acyl taurines tracked with how fast patients declined and how long they lived. A drug that blocks the enzyme FAAH raised these fats in patient-derived cells and in a mouse model of the disease. Treated models showed less motor neuron loss, calmer immune cells in the brain, and stronger synapse support. The team presents the drug, PF-04457845, as a candidate worth clinical testing.
pmc-13463917:
Yanjin Huang and six co-authors sort stroke survivors in China into groups by symptoms and daily function. Stroke leaves many people with weakness, pain, fatigue, or low mood that drag on quality of life. The team surveyed 779 patients at three large hospitals with standard patient-reported scales.

Three groups emerged: a low-symptom, high-function group held about a third of patients, a middle group held over half, and a small worst-off group held under a tenth. Older age, living alone, lacking insurance, and low income each raised the odds of landing in the worst-off group. Family burden also tracked with group membership. The authors urge rehab plans shaped for each group, with extra help for poor and isolated patients.
pmc-13464917:
Afifa Aziz and four co-authors review seed mucilage, the slippery gel that seed coats release on wetting. The gel blends several sugar chains with small shares of protein and minerals, and its recipe shifts by plant species. Green extraction methods, from ultrasound to enzyme help, are weighed against old soaking routes.

Green methods cut solvent, energy, and time against matched old methods, though gains vary by seed and setup. Chain length, acid content, and branching shape how the gel thickens, foams, and holds mixtures together. Those traits feed its antioxidant, gut-friendly, and germ-fighting actions. Standard recipes, safety rulings, and human trials still trail the lab interest, the authors warn.
pmc-13465017:
Macias-Muñoz turned in 2026 to a genomic oddity of the freshwater polyp Hydra, an animal that can regrow its entire head. Roughly 60 percent of its genome is made of transposable elements. These are DNA segments that copy and move themselves around. The study reanalyzed public gene-activity data from a time course of head regeneration. It asked which of these usually silent elements wake up during rebuilding.
