pmc-13484517:
Hyeran Chung compares five-year survival among older Mexican-origin adults with diabetes, dementia, both, or neither, in the United States and Mexico. Their 2026 study harmonises two representative longitudinal surveys of adults aged seventy-four and older, one American with linked Medicare data and one Mexican.

Survival fell steadily as conditions accumulated in both countries. In the United States, standardised five-year survival dropped from 73.3 percent with no condition to 36.6 percent with both diabetes and dementia. Mexican survival was higher in every group, from 77.5 percent down to 40.9 percent. Women died less than men in the United States but more in Mexico, though sex did not significantly change the effect of the conditions themselves. The authors argue the cross-national gap reflects overall mortality differences, and call for integrated chronic disease and dementia care tailored to each setting.
pmc-13484917:
Elham Kashafi Jahromi tests whether packaging a protective brain peptide in fat bubbles improves stroke recovery in rats. Published in 2026, the experiment blocks a brain artery for sixty minutes, then restores flow to mimic human stroke treatment. Sixty rats split into sham, untreated injury, empty carrier, free peptide, and packaged peptide groups, with treatment given one hour after flow returned.

Free apelin-13 already shrank damaged volume, improved nerve scores, and cut neuronal loss while quieting two inflammatory relay proteins. The packaged form did all that more strongly, bringing several measures back to sham levels. Only the packaged form suppressed the TLR4 sensor itself and eased brain swelling plus inflammatory cytokines. Packaging a fragile peptide for delivery clearly bought extra protection.
pmc-13486517:
Kwong and co-authors benchmarked eight generations of a popular vision detector on one rescue task: spotting life jackets from aircraft or drones, day or night. Search teams scan huge sea areas under brutal lighting, and no standard dataset existed for this job. Their 2026 study built a custom image set with several jacket types, then crossed eight detectors with twelve image-fixing methods across five simulated lighting conditions.

Preprocessing clearly rescued detection in both overexposed and underexposed images compared with raw inputs. One model, YOLOv10, gave the best overall bargain, holding precision near 0.68 while running at about 44 frames per second on the test hardware. Rival detectors won individual lighting cells but lost on the combined score. Kwong says that speed-plus-reliability profile suits live rescue feeds where every minute counts.
pmc-13487817:
Hye Rin Seo and Do-Young Kim report a 2026 real-world try at slow dose cuts of a hair drug after full regrowth in alopecia areata. The disease makes hair fall out in patches and tends to relapse. Sixty-six patients at a Seoul hospital had held full regrowth on baricitinib at 4 milligrams a day for two months or more. Cuts began from late 2023 to early 2026 on a set step plan.

Steps drop through mixed 4 and 2 milligram days, then 2 milligrams a day. Later steps thin to five days a week, then each other day, then stop. Checks each six to eight weeks gate each next step. Small returns get local care or a held step. Big returns, set by a score of five or more, force a jump back to full dose. That jump is the fail mark for the whole plan.
pmc-13487917:
Adrienn Geiger and co-authors map fungi living in and around grapevines in a 2026 genetic survey in Hungary. Two fungi-driven trunk diseases, Esca and Botryosphaeria dieback, slowly kill vines and cut yields. Samples came from soil, roots, bark, wood, fruit, and ground cover plants at two sites, which DNA barcoding used to identify community members. Groups compared covered disease-causing types, kinds that attack other fungi, and kinds that feed on dead matter.

Soil held the widest fungal diversity, while trunk disease fungi were richest in bark and wood of sick vines. Some harmful types also lived in ground cover plants near the vines. Dead-matter feeders dominated most sample types. The maps point to where disease fungi hide between outbreaks.
pmc-13488217:
Junshuo Zhu and co-authors examine inflammation and depression together after coronary stent treatment in a 2026 retrospective cohort study. Patients had proven coronary artery disease treated with percutaneous coronary intervention, where a balloon and stent reopen a narrowed artery. An inflammation score combined two blood markers, and depression was screened with a nine-question survey, using the standard cutoff for meaningful symptoms. Follow-up tracked major heart events in 487 patients.

About twenty-eight percent of patients suffered a major event during follow-up. Meaningful depressive symptoms alone predicted events after wide adjustment, while high inflammation alone did not reach significance in the reported models. Patients with both problems carried the highest risk by far. The authors urge caution, since the combined effect estimates were imprecise.
pmc-13488317:
Winstone and co-authors review why ovarian cancer resists one-size-fits-all treatment. Their 2026 paper surveys the disease's subtypes, which differ in biology, behaviour, and drug response. It concentrates on high-grade serous carcinoma, the commonest and deadliest form. It also covers low-grade serous, endometrioid, clear cell, and mucinous variants. Late diagnosis at stage three or four drives the poor survival that makes this the deadliest gynaecological cancer.

The review gives equal weight to the tumour microenvironment, the supporting tissue and immune cells around the cancer, which steers progression, spread, and immune evasion. Matching treatments to subtype biology requires biomarkers that distinguish them, and the authors argue the microenvironment is a promising place to find such markers. Their stated aim is earlier diagnosis and subtype-tailored therapy to cut mortality in a disease usually found too late.
pmc-13490517:
Salim and colleagues extended the working life of smart-city sensor networks by rotating which nodes stay awake, using sets of nodes that collectively watch the whole field. Only one such dominating set needs to be active at a time, so the rest can sleep. Their 2026 framework forms many candidate sets, keeps only those not beaten on both size and lifetime, then schedules them with a learning method borrowed from slot-machine strategy, the multi-armed bandit.

Scheduling sorts the sets into four cases by size and remaining lifetime, applying a tailored activation policy to each case. Data collection within the active set also routes energy-aware, avoiding hot spots near the sink. The skyline filtering step prevents wasting time on sets that another set dominates outright. Salim argues the combined design stretches heterogeneous networks, where nodes start with unequal batteries, toward city-scale deployments.
pmc-13491817:
Sumayli and co-authors present a 2026 cross-sectional study of 58 healthy Saudi women students aged 18 to 23 at Jazan University. The team measured chronotype, meaning whether a person naturally prefers mornings or evenings, using a short questionnaire. Blood taken early in each woman's menstrual cycle provided levels of two reproductive hormones, estradiol and testosterone, which the researchers then compared with the chronotype scores.

Women who leaned toward evenings tended to have higher testosterone, with a correlation the authors report as statistically strong, while their estradiol-to-testosterone ratio pointed the other way. The links stayed significant after accounting for age, body mass index, and cycle day, but estradiol alone showed no connection with chronotype. Because all measurements came from one point in time, the authors caution that the study cannot show whether sleep timing changes hormones or the reverse.
pmc-13491917:
Issilbayeva and co-authors compared gut microbiomes in 2026 between obese and non-obese patients with atherosclerosis, the artery-clogging disease behind most heart attacks and strokes. Obesity is known to worsen atherosclerosis, but how it changes the gut bacteria linked to the disease was unclear. Using shotgun metagenomic sequencing, which reads all microbial DNA in a stool sample, they profiled patients and matched controls.

The study covered ninety-three non-obese patients, sixty-eight obese patients, and twenty-seven non-obese controls, and community composition differed significantly across the groups, with obesity exerting the strongest effect among patient factors. Obese patients showed reduced species richness and evenness, and their microbiomes shifted toward a distinct state marked by an expansion of Prevotella bacteria opposing the rest of the community. Several other groups, including Bilophila and Faecalibacterium, rose as disease markers. The authors suggest the Prevotella expansion may flag higher risk.
pmc-13492017:
Jianmeng Zhu and four colleagues test in 2026 whether nanopore targeted sequencing can catch tuberculosis in people who carry the bacteria without symptoms. Subclinical disease spreads quietly and defeats standard tests because bacterial numbers are tiny. Samples from 103 suspected cases, spanning spit, lung wash fluid, and chest fluid, were run through sequencing, culture, and the rapid Xpert test in parallel.

Sequencing found about ninety-one percent of cases under the combined reference standard, against roughly forty-one percent for culture and fifty percent for Xpert. Its overall accuracy and its ability to rule disease out both topped the older methods by wide margins. The authors argue that sequencing could close a dangerous blind spot in tuberculosis control by finding infectious people before symptoms start.
pmc-13493317:
Pierre Hamonic leads a thirteen-author team demonstrating in 2026 single-shot readout of a silicon spin qubit built as a compact unit cell in an industrial chip factory. Semiconductor spin qubits promise long coherence, yet scaling to the millions needed for fault-tolerant computing demands readout that is fast, tiny, and does not need extra sensor structures. Their cell holds two electron spins whose coupling can be tuned.

Instead of a separate charge sensor, the team read the spin through its own gate using a dispersive radio-frequency technique. The cell supported initialization, a two-electron entangling gate, and readout in a single attempt, with spin visibility around eighty percent from exchange oscillations. Performance held at temperatures up to one kelvin with low electrical noise, a practical milestone for foundry-made quantum hardware.
pmc-13493717:
Edouard Raynaud and six colleagues validate in 2026 a simulator that shows people how facial dark spots may spread over fifteen years depending on sun habits. Such spots are a leading sign of skin aging in Asian populations. Unlike social media aging filters, it was built from knowledge harvested from twenty-eight dermatologists through a structured consensus process. It was encoded as causal probability networks and paired with a generative image model trained on six hundred standardized portraits.

It reproduced expert reasoning with a correlation near point nine six against clinical grading. For a thirty-eight-year-old Chinese woman, the chance of a meaningful jump in cheek spot density by age fifty-three reached about seventy-one percent with no sun protection. Daily high-strength sunscreen cut that probability to roughly thirty-nine percent. The authors offer the tool for education and personalized prevention planning.
pmc-13495117:
Kayaaslan and colleagues followed twenty-seven hundred ICU patients to build a score to predict candidaemia, a bloodstream yeast infection, in a 2026 prospective study. Candida infections strike patients and kill often when antifungal treatment starts late, yet giving antifungals to everyone is wasteful and harmful. Patients in hospital over forty-eight hours were followed for thirty days.

Kayaaslan recorded 204 candidaemia cases and found infected patients arrived sicker, with higher severity and chronic-disease scores and more kidney failure, dialysis, cancer, gut surgery, and low white-cell counts. Modeling found risk factors, and duration mattered as much as presence. A central vein catheter's risk climbed steeply the longer it stayed in, reaching a seventeenfold increase beyond three weeks. IV feeding beyond two weeks raised risk. The CanDi-Score performed well in the development and validation groups, giving clinicians an evidence-based trigger for starting antifungal treatment early.
pmc-13495217:
Bin Hu and a large team search, in a 2026 study, for cell-death genes that could serve as drug targets in osteosarcoma, a bone cancer of teens and older adults. Survival has stalled for decades, above all when the cancer spreads. The team mined public tumor data sets for genes that differ in tumors and also belong to the programmed cell death family.

From thousands of differing genes, a few hundred overlapped the death family, and a statistical sieve picked six hubs. Five checked out in real tumor tissue, and one, CIB1, ran high and drew deep study. Turning CIB1 down in tumor cells slowed growth and invasion, triggered cell death, and stalled the cell cycle, with shifts in known guard and growth pathways. The authors name CIB1 a promising target whose blocking might form a new line of attack on this cancer.
pmc-13495317:
Ebru Sevinç, Nur Bahar Kuru Aktürk, and Seyhan Çerçi test, in a 2026 randomized trial in Istanbul, whether creative drama teaching deepens nursing students' professional values. Values such as care, fairness, and duty anchor nursing practice, and lectures may instill them weakly. Sixty students from a foundation university were split between drama-based sessions and standard lectures on the same content.

The drama group met weekly for five ninety-minute sessions using role-play, frozen scenes, forum theatre, case work, and group talk. On a standard values scale, their total and part scores ended clearly above the lecture group's. The drama students gained across every part of the scale, while lecture students barely moved. Having a health worker in the family shifted some part scores. The authors call drama a strong short-term method, since acting values out lets students live them rather than hear them.
pmc-13495517:
Tshepo A Ntho and colleagues survey, in a 2026 study, nursing students' attitudes toward caring for older adults at a university in Limpopo Province, South Africa. Such attitudes shape the geriatric care these students will one day give, and local training gives elder care little dedicated room. The team surveyed 246 undergraduates with a standard attitude scale, drawn by stratified random sampling.

Just over half showed mildly positive attitudes overall. Age and sex stood out as the drivers. Students in their early and mid twenties had far lower odds of strongly positive attitudes than the youngest group, a slide the authors find worrying. Male students showed higher odds than female students of the strongest positive views. Study year, past contact with elders, and plans to work with them showed no tie. The authors urge weaving elder care content through the curriculum.
pmc-13495717:
Hormann and Heiles build a workflow for measuring how much of each fat molecule sits in each spot of a tissue slice. Imaging methods map where lipids are but rarely how much, while ordinary liquid chromatography measures amounts precisely yet loses all spatial information. Their 2026 workflow sprays thirteen isotope-labelled lipid standards onto mouse heart tissue. It images everything with a laser-based technique, then checks the standards and identifications with the chromatography method as quality control.

The sprayed standards landed evenly. The comparison also exposed a quirk: imaging variability depended on both a lipid's amount and its chemical class, unlike the chromatography method where only scarcity hurt. Polar lipids matched well between the two methods, while oily triglycerides overlapped poorly. The authors conclude the control pipeline is not optional decoration but what makes the imaging numbers trustworthy.
pmc-13495917:
Malina Behrens leads a large team profiling, in a 2026 study, how antibodies against Epstein-Barr virus behave in multiple sclerosis. The virus is strongly tied to the disease, and antibodies against one of its core proteins stay raised for life after onset. The team mapped the fine features of these antibodies in sixty people with relapsing MS, followed over time, and fifty-four matched healthy carriers of the virus.

Antibodies aimed at that viral protein carried an inflammatory signature in MS: they gripped immune receptors harder and triggered stronger cell eating, complement attack, and killer cell engagement. Antibodies against other common viruses showed no such pattern. Stronger receptor binding, for this protein and a second viral target, tracked with relapses and active brain lesions on scans. The authors suggest these antibody functions do not merely mark the disease but may help drive its flare-ups.
pmc-13496017:
Tomasz J. Klimczak and others report a hybrid laparoendoscopic full-thickness stomach resection with lymphatic mapping for a gastric neuroendocrine tumour. In 2026, the technical note concerns a grade 2 tumour on the lesser curvature in a thirty-seven-year-old woman with persistent upper belly pain and nausea. Standard surgery would sacrifice much of the stomach.

Endoscopic full-thickness resection merged with laparoscopic lymphadenectomy guided by lymphatic mapping achieved complete removal with clear margins and no nodal disease. Recovery was uneventful with no recurrence found. The authors support further review of organ-sparing hybrid plans for selected localized gastric neuroendocrine lesions.
pmc-13498517:
Baris Afsar and others review how mineralocorticoid dock blockers affect fat mass and fat fuel use. In 2026, the review covers drugs long used for heart and vessel disease, including spironolactone, eplerenone, and the newer non-steroidal finerenone, now also noted for kidney protection. Obesity involves excessive fat accumulation and risks of blood sugar illness, heart failure, liver disease, and cancer.

Across studies, these drugs reduced fat mass in various organs with lower cell damage, swelling, and insulin resistance, independent of blood pressure lowering. They increased browning of adipose tissue and reduced white fat mass, with no safety signals found so far. Mechanisms remain unclear, so the authors call the findings early and urge studies to explain how the benefit arises.
pmc-13498617:
Edoardo Vergani and others build an AI-driven data mart for adult growth hormone deficiency from routine records at a single Italian center. In 2026, the study joins hospital warehouse extraction with natural language processing of medical narratives, identifying patients by finding codes and text mining, with multidisciplinary expert testing. The condition is under-recognized and its data fragmented.

Of 210 found patients, 188 were checked, with findings from dynamic testing, panhypopituitarism with low IGF-1, or AI-assisted identification, and cause retrieved in nearly eighty-eight percent, most often post-surgical. About thirty-eight percent received growth hormone replacement. The first such data mart offers a complementary plan for real-world evidence and future analytics.
pmc-13499217:
Aline D'Angelo Campos and co-authors run in 2026 a randomised trial with Chilean parents on labels for nonnutritive sweeteners, the intense sweeteners used in place of sugar. Chile's sugar warnings pushed makers to swap in such sweeteners, and some countries now label them too, with little evidence on shopper behaviour. Parents of children aged 2 to 14 were assigned to see no label, a child-focused warning, or a plain disclosure on products.

Among 3,523 parents, both label types sharply improved spotting which products contained these sweeteners. Parents in both label groups chose sweetener products less often and unsweetened options more often, without shifting toward sugary products instead. The warning label scored higher on perceived impact, while the plain disclosure was recalled more often, giving policymakers two workable designs with somewhat different strengths.
pmc-13499517:
Manuel Laslandes and colleagues review in 2026 cases of a dangerous heparin reaction seen in a university kidney department, focusing on its autoimmune form. Heparin, a blood thinner used heavily in dialysis, can rarely trigger antibodies that activate platelets and cause clots while platelet counts fall. The autoimmune form keeps activating platelets even without heparin and tends to run a severe course, so the team searched their lab database from 2013 to 2024 for confirmed cases.

Among 64 test requests, seven cases were confirmed, drawn from nearly nine thousand admissions over the period, and patients were followed for up to six months. Ages spanned young adulthood to late old age, and most patients were men. The write-up examines whether immune kidney diseases cluster with this reaction, a question relevant to kidney units where heparin exposure is routine and missing the diagnosis carries high risk.
pmc-13499917:
Nadieh Drenth and co-authors explore in 2026 whether early vessel damage from cerebral amyloid angiopathy, where a sticky protein deposits in small brain vessels, already alters how brain regions communicate. Diagnosis usually waits for late scan markers, while sluggish vessel responses to activity may appear sooner. The team analysed MRI data from 93 older adults, including a subgroup of 46 meeting standard criteria for possible or probable disease. The analysis linked vessel response timing in vision areas with connectivity at several scales.

No links appeared between vessel response and whole-brain or large-network connectivity after accounting for age, sex, and diagnosis. Pair-by-pair analysis instead found a limited set of localised connections tied to each vessel measure, and the pattern held in the disease subgroup. The authors read this as damage beginning in small pockets while broad communication stays intact, with global breakdown reserved for advanced stages.
pmc-13500817:
Yin-Yin Huang leads a five-author team reporting a 2026 study that ranks the sustainability of 103 countries over time rather than in a single snapshot. The team combined a method called Dynamic TOPSIS, which scores each country against ideal and worst cases, with entropy weights that decay so recent years count more. Seven indicators covered economic, social, and environmental dimensions from 2014 to 2024. K-means clustering then cross-checked the rankings by grouping countries spatially.

Countries settled into three stable tiers, and the clustering error fell from 26.34 to 8.06 when moving to the three-group solution. Rankings held up under robustness tests, with no reversals among the top twenty. The lagging tier scored surprisingly well on environmental efficiency because its industries are small, yet weak human capital and institutions held it back. The authors point to education and governance as the barriers that aid money alone cannot fix.
pmc-13501617:
Jingxia Xu leads a nine-author team with a 2026 nanomedicine design against triple-negative breast cancer, a subtype lacking the usual drug targets and prone to resist cell death by apoptosis. In a tumour's acidic surroundings the particles fall apart fast and flood the cancer cell with all three payloads.

Calcium overload in mitochondria drives cells to make extra hydrogen peroxide, and the released zinc converts that peroxide into damaging hydroxyl radicals through a Fenton-like reaction. The resulting burst of reactive oxygen species strengthens shikonin's necroptotic killing. Debris from the dying cells also matures dendritic cells and activates killer T cells, adding an immune attack. The authors present the platform as a combined necroptosis and immune route for apoptosis-resistant tumours.
pmc-13501717:
Rafael Prieto-Moreno and others find what drives rich action and daily-life balance among older adults in care homes. In 2026, the one-year forward-looking cohort follows 144 dwellers across four nursing homes and day centers in Andalusia, Spain. It tests buy-in, balance, working status, frailty, and taking part in daily, mental, leisure, body, sensory, and group pastimes at start and twelve months.

Working status, frailty, and mental buy-in emerged as key drivers, while highly set leisure pastimes ruled current programs and may limit rich buy-in. The authors urge co-built, person-focused programs aligned with dwellers' likes, values, and skills, cutting stiff leisure time in favor of rich moments, with future test and mixed-methods research.
pmc-13502617:
Xuejie Li leads a five-author team with a 2026 route to porous organic polymers that skips the usual Friedel-Crafts knitting chemistry. The team started from ready-made linear polyimines and crosslinked them with m-phenylenediamine, whose amine groups add across imine bonds to form aminal linkages. Four polyimines crosslinked well. The resulting networks reached surface areas up to 650 square metres per gram, against roughly 100 for the uncrosslinked chains, at an estimated cost of only 16 US dollars per kilogram.

Dynamic breakthrough tests, flowing real gas mixtures through the material, confirmed clean separation of the C2 gases from methane. The authors pitch the method as cheap manufacturing for gas purification.
pmc-13503717:

Using cryo-electron microscopy, the team froze the channel in a shut state and in an active state bound by three signals. The pocket that holds the main signal looks much like that of its kin, so gaps in grip strength likely come from flex in a control region. The team also pinned down where ATP, the cell fuel, binds and shifts channel action. Tests with altered channels confirmed the site and its role.
pmc-13503917:

Their method extracts the toxin in one step with a common solvent, with more than 90 percent recovered. The extract is dried, redissolved, and read by a sensitive mass-based instrument. Spiked samples in two labs matched set target values well. When the team ran foods bought at Polish markets, none held detectable patulin. The authors offer the method as a fast, reliable screen for food safety labs.
pmc-13505517:
Bao and colleagues tracked in 2026 how state Medicaid programs paid clinics for methadone treatment of opioid addiction across five years of policy change. The team gathered payment rules from 40 states, covering March 2020 to July 2025, and charted the changes. More than half the states still paid per dose or per day, tying clinic income to how often patients show up. Over a quarter kept an old flat bundle that rewards at most a week of take-home doses. A two-tier bundle modeled on Medicare spread slowly. The authors warn that flexible care will lag until payment matches the new rules.
pmc-13506117:
Mehdi Darmoul, Amine Trifa, Ghassen Elkahla, and Kais Maamri followed 113 patients who had front-of-neck fusion surgery across three or four levels for worn discs pressing on the spinal cord. pmc-13507017:

The team studied 58 fed-batch cultures in vessels from 10 liters to 2000 liters, tracking oxygen taken up and glucose used over time.

Total oxygen use tracked total glucose use in a near straight line once lactate, a waste product cells can later reuse, was counted. The match held across projects, cell lines, and scales. Trials at 200 liters predicted next-day glucose need well. Factories could guide feeding with data they already collect, without new glucose sensors.
pmc-13507217:
Firdissa Sadeta Tiye, Diriba Korecha, Tariku Mekonnen Gutema, and Dessalegn Obsi Gemeda analyze, in 2026 work, past and future climate in Bale Mountains National Park in southeastern Ethiopia. Rainfall varied strongly with height, and most stations trended drier after 2000. Annual rain fell by about 100 millimeters across three decades, while high and low temperatures each rose by well over a degree. Future runs project more rain and more heat, with the sharpest shifts under high emissions late in the century. Adaptive conservation planning is urgent.
pmc-13508117:
Fabien Fayez Jarjour and six co-authors use detailed 3D dental scans to study infection at tooth roots and how it links to root canal quality, in 2026 work. Their group covered people in Lebanon, with 183 scans read by a radiologist with 30 years of practice. Every treated tooth was checked for missed canals and for how well its filling fit. In total the readers found 424 cases of root-tip infection in treated teeth.

Missed canals appeared in about one in twenty treated teeth, and over half of those teeth showed a lesion at the root tip. The most often missed canal was a second canal in upper molars. Fillings that ran too long or fell short also carried high lesion rates. Most fillings, about two thirds, were judged adequate. The authors tie careful canal hunting and filling length to better outcomes.
pmc-13508317:
Tao Luo and five co-authors test frequent online quizzes as a way to build self-directed study habits in anatomy classes, in 2026 work. Anatomy packs in huge amounts of content, and Chinese medical students often study passively. One class year of 369 students took five in-class quizzes on an online platform during their anatomy course, roughly one every three to four weeks. The prior year's class of 386 students, taught without the quizzes, served as the comparison.

The quiz year's final exam average beat the earlier class by a wide margin, and its pass rate was much higher too. In surveys, nearly all students viewed the quizzes positively. Most said the quizzes improved their self-learning, helped them plan study, and spread revision across the term instead of cramming. The authors present light, frequent testing as a cheap lever for active learning in content-heavy courses.
pmc-13508417:
Catharina Savelkoul and Sophie Park study how a fairer funding tariff changed undergraduate general practice teaching in England, in 2026 work. Better pay helped recruit and keep teaching practices, and quality rose. Reporting rules added outside legitimacy and steadier rollout across schools. As oversight shifts to a new home, the authors urge keeping the transparent budget setup that made the gains possible.
pmc-13508517:
Delian Hofman leads a sixteen-author team laying out the design of a trial replacing some clinic visits with home monitoring for lung fibrosis patients, in 2026 work. Pulmonary fibrosis brings constant breathlessness, cough, and fatigue, and checking its course demands frequent hospital trips that burden patients. The SUITS study, run across several centers, will assign patients at random to standard care or hybrid care. Standard care keeps clinic visits every three months. Hybrid care swaps alternate visits for video calls backed by home data.

At home, patients blow into a portable lung meter and check blood oxygen weekly through an app. They also fill regular symptom questionnaires and can read a disease library. The main outcome is change in patient self-management over twelve months, scored on a validated activation scale. Their design also tracks whether care gets more efficient for the health system.
pmc-13509217:
Tomemori and colleagues studied antibiotic eye drops in 2026. The drops are given to prevent infection during eye injections, and the team asked whether repeated use changes drug sensitivity in normal bacteria of the eye and nose. They compared 21 patients before their first drops with 26 patients who had received twenty or more injections.

Two common bacteria, Staphylococcus epidermidis and Corynebacterium, showed reduced sensitivity to quinolone antibiotics in the repeat-use group. Resistance-linked gene mutations were also more common in that group. In four of ten patients, resistant bacteria from the eye and nose shared the same strain type, suggesting the two sites can harbor related germs. Overall nasal microbe diversity did not differ between groups. The authors warn that routine preventive drops carry a resistance cost.
pmc-13510017:
Ondrej Preťo, Bogdan Iaparov, Friedemann Freund, Miloslav Karhanek, and Viktor Stolc use the yeast metabolic cycle to study how breathing rhythm affects the accuracy of gene messages, in 2026 work. Yeast cells here swing between a high-breathing, low-oxygen phase and a lower-breathing, high-oxygen phase. About fifteen hundred genes changed activity between phases, with building and protein-making genes up in the low-oxygen phase and defense genes up in the high-oxygen phase. Mismatch rates also shifted by phase, yet the pattern split by mismatch type, with one class rising and another staying flat. Most mismatches appeared in single samples only, pointing to passing RNA errors rather than lasting DNA change. The cycle offers a simple model for timing and message fidelity.
pmc-13510517:
Shanshan Yu, Rongxue Ma, Yanjin Liu, Yuting Chen, Xinyu Lu, and Yuxi Zhang use a ranking method to map how people treated for lymphoma experience their illness, in 2026 work. Four distinct patterns emerged. One group focused on the hospital setting while coping with strong side effects. A second group adapted actively and faced treatment with a positive stance. A third group was weighed down by lasting symptoms and fear the cancer would return. A fourth group carried heavy money pressure yet kept going with resolve. The authors say naming these patterns can help nurses and doctors tailor support and build better measures of what patients value.
pmc-13511517:
Susmitha Nagula, Nasreen Ahmed, Kryss Shane, and Anthony D. Slonim reframe medical gaslighting in children's care as a safety problem in diagnosis, in a 2026 review. The term covers cases where patients or parents feel symptoms were brushed aside or blamed on the mind without proper checking. In pediatrics the risk grows because clinicians lean on parent reports while children may struggle to describe changing symptoms.

The authors tie the experience to known drivers of diagnostic error: thinking biases, communication breakdowns, and the shadowing of new problems by old labels. They also draw on the idea of epistemic injustice, where a speaker's knowledge is unfairly discounted. Recasting the issue as a safety weakness, rather than a charge of misconduct, opens paths to measurable fixes. Proposed steps include structured re-checks, bias training, and better capture of family concerns.
pmc-13512617:
Shigenori Tanaka builds a quantum-like version of the free-energy framework for cognition that stretches across time, in 2026 work. The classic free-energy principle explains perception and choice with probability models of hidden causes. The new frame swaps in tools from quantum theory, including states defined over time spans, a bridge method for paths between states, and quantum logic for context rules.

Cognitive growth is cast as the shaping of time-extended quantum-like states under a combined cost with three parts: path divergence, a cognitive free-energy term, and context-set logical limits ending in target claims. Context updates arrive as soft projections that do not pick a single outcome, and an inner control field steers the system from within. A two-state toy model shows the parts working together. The author offers the frame as a math base for context-shaped thinking over time.
pmc-13513017:
Li and co-authors studied in 2026 how insecticide resistance builds in the oriental fruit fly, a pest of fruit and crops in more than one hundred twenty countries, under varied spraying regimes. Farmers lack guidance on how often sprays can be applied before resistance takes off. The team tracked it in field populations and screened the fly's genes to find which ones switch on as the trait develops.

Checks across eleven populations showed resistance to insecticides such as alphamethrin, trichlorfon, and abamectin still rising in 2023, after a climb first tracked in 2010. Using suppression subtractive hybridization libraries and cDNA screening, they found genes that switch on or off between resistant and susceptible flies, pointing to candidate mechanisms. The authors frame the work as a basis for setting spray intervals that slow resistance and keep sprays working, for longer lasting pest management.
pmc-13515317:
Jigarkumar Modi, Ruizhi Jin, Kejun Dong, and Gu Fang simulate how self-propelled particles pack inside a boundary in a 2026 physics study. Such active particles, which move under their own power, model everything from bacteria to robot swarms. The team asked how steering toward neighbours' direction, short-range push-back, and the size of the confining circle jointly shape packing density and shared direction of travel. Computer runs varied the sensing range, push-back range, boundary size, and noise level.

Tight confinement jammed the particles into a dense but disordered state where alignment had little say, whatever the noise. Once the boundary passed a critical size, the system unjammed. Alignment then raised both the shared direction and the packing density. Measures of local structure, such as neighbour counts, behaved alike with and without alignment.
pmc-13515817:
Bonventure Juma and six colleagues measure drug resistance in gut bacteria from patients with diarrhoea in an informal settlement in Nairobi, Kenya, in a 2026 study covering 2018 to 2020. Resistant Salmonella and Shigella kill many people where clean water and second-line drugs are scarce. Stool samples were cultured, the germs named, and their drug sensitivity measured by machine, with gene tests for the resistance machinery.

Shigella flexneri dominated the finds, ahead of typhoid Salmonella and other Shigella types. Resistance ran highest against ampicillin, at over eighty percent, then tetracycline and co-trimoxazole at about half. Newer drugs mostly still worked, with little or no resistance found. Gene tests found the matching resistance genes for these drug families. Juma's team calls for steady watching to guide first-choice treatment in such settlements.
pmc-13516017:
Yew Woon Chia leads a ten-author workgroup presenting the Singapore Post-cardiac Arrest Care Guidelines 2026. Care after the heart restarts is the sixth link in the chain of survival, and Singapore's rising arrest rates make it urgent: bystander CPR has climbed, yet discharge survival still lags. The review builds on national workgroup reports from 2017 and 2021 and the newest American, European, and international guidance.

The document gives intensive care teams a practical summary for patients admitted after circulation returns. Its organising device is an A-to-I bundle, a lettered checklist for running the full package of post-arrest care in the unit. Registry figures frame the stakes, with favourable brain outcomes among discharged survivors improving over the decade. Chia's team aims to close the gap between surviving admission and leaving hospital with a working brain.
pmc-13516917:
Luo and co-authors present AbAgKer, a computer model for judging antibody candidates, in this 2026 paper. New design tools can propose large numbers of therapeutic antibodies, but checking how tightly each one grips its target antigen still depends on scarce lab data. The model predicts both binding strength and binding kinetics, meaning how fast an antibody attaches and lets go.

AbAgKer blends learned sequence features with biological knowledge. That knowledge covers the antigen's binding region and the antibody's variable loops. A mixture-of-experts design routes data to specialized sub-models. To cope with limited labeled examples, it learns partly from its own predictions on unlabeled data, a strategy called self-distillation. In tests it beat comparison models, and its learned representations transferred to predicting dissociation rates, which govern how long a drug stays attached.
pmc-13517417:
Neli Vilhelmova-Ilieva leads a seven-author team testing light-activated compounds against a human coronavirus in a 2026 study. Photodynamic inactivation uses dye-like molecules plus light to flood viruses with damaging oxygen species. Two metal-bearing phthalocyanine dyes, one with gallium and one with zinc, faced the coronavirus OC43 under red light. The team measured attacks on free virus particles, on the virus's grip step, and on its copying cycle inside cells.

The zinc dye hit hardest: a four-log cut in free virus and up to complete blocking of the grip step with longer light exposure. Both dyes worked early in the copying cycle, with the zinc compound again ahead on the team's inactivation index. Computer docking added: both dyes bound plausibly to several viral proteins and to the human entry receptor. The authors present light-activated treatment as a promising anti-coronavirus route worth developing.
pmc-13518817:
Shanying Sui and colleagues engineer in 2026 a stiff clay aerogel, modeled on mortise-and-tenon joinery, that can both detect and remove organic pollutants from water. Ordinary inorganic aerogels are brittle and hard to reuse, which limits cleanup work. Their layered double hydroxide design interlocks amino acids and calcium ions inside the structure.

The aerogels reached compressive strength near 40 to 45 megapascals while staying tough. Removal of five test pollutants, including tetracycline and Congo red, ran from 95.4 to 99.9 percent, and 87 percent of performance survived five reuse cycles. Detection reached a limit of 710 nanomolar. The material also resisted liquid nitrogen, open flame, and burning, suiting harsh settings.
pmc-13518917:
Ümmügülsüm Yıldız-Altay and a large team compare skin lupus across mice, dogs, and humans in 2026, focusing on conversations between T cells and hair follicles. Cutaneous lupus brings T cell-rich inflammation and scarring hair loss, yet shared drivers across species were unmapped. Spatial gene profiling charted which follicle neighborhoods switch on immune signals.

Mouse models driven by two T cell types shared 35 percent of their gene changes, with one type uniquely reshaping tissue scaffolding. Follicles in all three species switched on interferon responses and CXCR3-attracting signals. Removing CXCR3 from T cells eased mouse disease, and B cell depletion helped too. Two conserved targets, CFD and the S100A8/9 pair, await trial testing.
pmc-13520217:
Sungkrit Pojmonpiti, Wisunee Witthayawarakul, Todsaporn Fuangrod, and Supakorn Suntornchatchaweach run a noninferiority trial in 2026 on teledentistry follow-up for head and neck cancer patients after radiotherapy. Radiation wrecks oral health, and survivors need close dental monitoring. Remote visits using live video plus patient self-photographs were compared with standard in-person care over six months.

Twenty-seven patients completed the study. Remote follow-up proved noninferior for plaque levels and gum bleeding on probing, the two main outcomes, and also for bone death incidence. Satisfaction ran high in both groups. Results for other complications and quality of life stayed inconclusive. The authors call teledentistry feasible for the first six months after treatment.
pmc-13520317:
Xinyi Gao and colleagues present in 2026 a deep learning system that judges whether tiny lung spots in colorectal cancer patients are spread of cancer or harmless nodules. Spots under one centimetre are hard to judge by eye, yet the answer changes treatment plans.

Data came from several centres, covering more than a thousand patients in the main group plus two outside check groups. The system first outlines each spot, then classifies it. Sorting accuracy stayed high across check groups and across spot sizes, beating radiologist accuracy in the main group. The work suggests software support for a common and anxious scan decision.
pmc-13520517:
Na Wang and colleagues search in 2026 pressure ulcer data for blood-vessel-related genes that could serve as diagnostic markers or drug targets. Wound samples numbered 381 against 391 healthy controls in a public dataset, with a focus on genes tied to new vessel growth.

Analysis found 128 altered vessel-related genes and seven hub genes with strong diagnostic potential, including CDKN1A. Network maps link those hubs to small regulatory RNAs, transcription controllers and candidate drugs. A rat wound model then checked CDKN1A behaviour and the effect of removing it on healing. The layered design moves from data mining toward experimental follow-up in a single study.
pmc-13521017:
Jaszczyk and a large team measure bruise colours on broiler chicken carcasses to standardise a quality defect. Their 2026 research note examines 79 bruises at least a centimetre wide, from breast, leg, and wing, under commercial slaughterhouse conditions. A portable colorimeter recorded each bruise in the standard CIE colour space, and clustering analysis looked for natural groupings.

Bruises differed by body region in their red and yellow-blue components, though not in lightness or overall colour distance. Leg bruises ran stronger in red-yellow tones, while wing bruises shifted toward blue-purple, a pattern consistent with bruises of different ages or depths. The analysis supported three colour profiles, partly tied to anatomy. Bruising also signals how birds were handled before slaughter. The authors therefore argue quantitative colour assessment could standardise it. A subjective judgement would become a welfare and quality measure at the line.
pmc-13522317:
Anwei Wei and colleagues show in 2026 that ginsenoside Rg1, a ginseng compound, forces liver cancer cells into ferroptosis, an iron-driven death route that can bypass standard resistance. Liver cancer often presents late, leaving systemic therapy as the main option.

Rg1 slowed growth and migration of liver cancer cells in laboratory tests. Treated cells displayed hallmark ferroptosis features, linking benefit to that death pathway rather than generic toxicity. A cystine transporter called SLC7A11 fell under treatment, restoring ferroptosis sensitivity, although the authors note that its mediator role still needs functional validation. The findings support ferroptosis-targeted combinations for hard-to-treat liver cancer.
pmc-13522417:
Maki Tanaka studied how Japanese nurses pause on conscience in the press of daily care. Published in 2026, the narrative study drew on twelve nurses in Japanese health institutions, reading their stories for how ethical moments feel and unfold. Modern nursing pairs rising complexity and time pressure with a duty to honor patient vulnerability and dignity.

Pauses took several forms: holding back from snap judgment, acting with care to keep harmony, wrestling with institutional demands, and making meaning over time. Harmony emerged not as a fixed rule but as a relationship renegotiated through practice, often in response to quiet vulnerability rather than loud moral claims. The author argues that ethics lives in these shared moments, which deserve recognition and support.
pmc-13522517:
Xiang Zhang and colleagues test a plant compound against bone loss in a 2026 study of cells and mice. The compound, koumine, comes from a medicinal plant and was applied to bone-eating cells grown from mouse bone marrow. Excess activity of those cells drives diseases such as osteoporosis, where bone thins and breaks more easily.

Koumine reduced formation of the bone-eating cells and their resorption activity in a dose-dependent way, without killing the cells or harming bone-building cells. It dampened a key signaling pathway and lowered several proteins needed for bone breakdown. In mice that had lost ovarian hormone production, treatment prevented bone loss, improved inner bone structure, and reduced cell numbers. The authors propose koumine as a candidate for bone-loss therapy.
pmc-13522617:
Muhammad Sajid and colleagues present a decision method for choosing renewable energy for transport in Pakistan in a 2026 study. Biofuels raise concerns about land use and food security, so solar, wind, and hydropower need a fair comparison under uncertainty. The method uses an advanced fuzzy set framework that can hold expert judgments with optimistic and pessimistic views across many criteria at once.

Expert evaluations were combined with two logical operations to produce a final ranking, demonstrated in a case study guided by recent official advice. The authors argue that the framework handles ambiguity better than simpler scoring methods. For planners, the work offers a structured way to rank clean transport energy options while making uncertainty explicit rather than hiding it in single numbers.
pmc-13523217:
Haonan Ye leads a team studying a mitochondrial protein that helps glioblastoma grow in a 2026 laboratory study. Glioblastoma is a brain tumor with a very poor outlook, driven in part by disordered energy use and resistance to a form of cell death called ferroptosis. Gene data showed the protein MRPL36 is overactive in these tumors and linked to worse survival.

Silencing the protein damaged mitochondria, disturbed fat metabolism, and triggered ferroptosis in tumor cells, slowing growth, invasion, and tumor formation in animals. Two competing chemical tags on a protective enzyme lay at the center of the mechanism: silencing tipped the balance from a stabilizing tag toward a destruction tag. Blocking ferroptosis partly reversed the benefit, confirming the pathway. The authors present the protein as a candidate treatment target.
pmc-13523317:
Shun-Wun Jhan and co-authors build a combined deep learning model to detect shoulder tendon tears from plain X-rays in a 2026 study. Five hundred eighty-seven shoulder radiographs from patients with and without small to medium rotator cuff tears were split into training, validation, and strictly held-out test sets. Three pretrained image networks were fine-tuned and combined by majority vote.

The ensemble beat each individual model on the validation set, reaching accuracy near four fifths with strong sensitivity. On the untouched test set, accuracy rose slightly above four fifths and sensitivity was perfect, although specificity stayed modest. The authors present the ensemble as a low-cost preliminary screen that could reduce unnecessary advanced imaging and speed care, while noting that further validation is still needed.
pmc-13523417:
Kevin Rama and co-authors describe combined hip surgery for a large benign bone growth in a 2026 case report. A forty-three-year-old Italian woman with multiple hereditary exostoses, an inherited condition producing many bony outgrowths, developed severe hip impingement from a large growth on the inner side of her femoral neck. Safe surgical dislocation of the hip through a controlled bone cut allowed complete removal of the lesion.

Removal left an extensive defect in the neck cortex, so a sliding hip screw was implanted preventively to guard against fracture. Recovery began with no weight bearing and a structured rehabilitation program. Tissue testing confirmed a benign osteochondroma. Seven years later she reported lasting pain relief, restored function, and full joint movement, with no complications on imaging or examination.
pmc-13527917:
Annet Aketoko Onzia and nine colleagues report a 2026 cross-sectional study of HIV among men seeking care for urethral discharge syndrome at public clinics in Kampala, Uganda. Between October 2019 and July 2022 the team enrolled 450 men, gave questionnaires on background and sexual behavior, and offered rapid HIV testing on site.

Of the 441 men included in the analysis, 18.4 percent were living with HIV, and a small share learned their status for the first time during the visit. Just over half of those on treatment reported a suppressed viral load. Older age and hazardous drinking were linked with infection. The authors argue these clinics are a strong place to combine testing, prevention, and treatment support.
pmc-13528017:
Yuxin Liang and seven colleagues test a sulfur compound as a partner for immune therapy in liver cancer in a 2026 study. The compound, S-propargyl-cysteine or SPRC, boosts an enzyme that makes hydrogen sulfide gas inside cells. In dish tests it bound that enzyme tightly. It also calmed two signaling switches, NF-κB and STAT3, in vessel-lining cells. New vessel growth slowed as a result.

In co-cultures, SPRC lowered the PD-L1 shield on liver cancer cells. Killer T cells looked more active and released more granzyme B. In mice with liver tumors, adding SPRC to anti-PD-1 therapy shrank tumors better than the drug alone. More killer T cells entered tumors, while regulatory T cells and vessel density fell. The authors say the gas pathway reprograms both vessels and immunity.
pmc-13528117:
Jingwen Shi and eight colleagues build a database of older Chinese patients with many illnesses at once in a 2026 paper. The database, called CECMed, pools records from hospitals in the north, center, and south of China. Over ninety percent of patients had at least one geriatric syndrome. Five machine learning methods were trained to predict bad events during hospital stays.

Two boosted tree methods led the field. Their accuracy scores passed 0.91 on the ranking measure. An explanation method then ranked what drove the warnings. Frailty, D-dimer, illness severity, daily-living scores, and clotting breakdown products topped the list. The authors offer the database as shared ground for aging research. They say early warning models like theirs could help wards act before harm lands.
pmc-13528517:
Jiafeng Wan and eleven colleagues make carbon dots that change glow color with their surroundings in a 2026 chemistry paper. The dots were cooked from citric acid and urea, a classic pairing. Scattered in water they shine blue. Clumped in another solvent they shine red. The team traced the switch to stacking between flat molecules and solvent effects.

Tuning solvent polarity shifts the spacing between dots and thus the color. That trick was put to work in printing. Hidden messages appear only under the right conditions, a guard against counterfeits. Mixed into a soft gel, the dots formed glowing pads that store coded information. The authors say such state-dependent glow widens what carbon dots can do. Security printing and smart labels are the near-term targets.
pmc-13529717:
Mrudula Jeeva and Santhosh Miriala convert a vision network into a spiking one for spotting weeds in cotton fields in a 2026 study. Spiking networks mimic brain pulses and sip power. Six weed classes were the target. A compact network called AkidaNet was first trained the normal way. It was then shrunk by quantization and rebuilt as a spiking model with vendor tools.

Plain quantization dropped accuracy to about eighty-eight percent. Training that anticipates shrinking recovered it to about ninety-one percent. After conversion, the spiking model scored about ninety-four percent on test data. That nearly matches the original network's validation form. The authors say such models fit low-power neuromorphic chips. Those chips could ride on field robots for live weed control. Cotton growers lose yield and lint quality to weeds, so cheap automation matters.
pmc-13530217:
Sadegh Valinejad Bolghan and colleagues ask in 2026 whether ABO blood group shaped how COVID-19 presented in southeast Iran. Records covered 894 confirmed patients admitted to two referral hospitals between April and September 2020. Symptom counts, other illnesses, and outcomes were compared across the four blood groups.

Patients with group AB reported the fewest symptoms on average, a pattern that held after adjusting for age, sex, and other illnesses. Group O patients carried more coexisting illness, especially heart disease, and faced the highest admission rates. Fever, cough, headache, and gut symptoms also varied by group, suggesting blood type tracks illness pattern.
pmc-13531617:
Okumura wrote a 2026 editorial weighing where warfarin, the older blood thinner, still fits in stroke prevention for atrial fibrillation now that four direct oral anticoagulants dominate guidelines. Those newer drugs matched or beat warfarin in trials, roughly halving brain bleeding risk. Yet warfarin remains the only oral option for patients with mechanical heart valves or marked mitral narrowing. It costs a small fraction of the newer drugs.

Okumura discusses a study that clusters patients by risk. In a low-risk cluster, defined by younger age, higher body mass, and better kidney function, warfarin's net clinical outcomes rivaled the newer drugs. The study comes with an interactive prediction tool. He cautions that the cluster cutoffs are not yet defined for everyday practice and need validation. The editorial argues warfarin deserves a deliberate place in care, especially where resources are limited.
pmc-13531817:
Baptiste de Maleprade and colleagues compare in 2026 women whose spinal inflammatory disease began around childbirth with women whose disease began at other times. Hospital records in Rouen covered 154 women with spondyloarthritis and known delivery and symptom dates. Fifty-eight formed the around-birth group.

That group carried the classic gene marker less often, yet showed more chest wall syndrome and psoriasis. Inflammation markers, joint damage on scans, and sacroiliac inflammation all ran lower. Standard tumor-necrosis drugs were stopped sooner, suggesting weaker response. The authors describe a distinct childbirth-linked form centered more on tendon attachments than deep inflammation.
pmc-13532317:
Hironobu Murakami and colleagues report in 2026 on gene changes that help bovine leukemia virus spread in cattle. The virus causes a fatal blood disease and cuts milk yield and farm income. The team tracked one herd of 50 to 68 cows for seven years and took 438 samples.

One change in a viral control region grew more common over time and became the main form. Two changes in the Tax protein also shifted how much virus the cells made. Strains with high output spread with an edge, so tracking these marks may help farms spot risky strains sooner.
pmc-13534417:
Kavyashree N Kalkura and colleagues report in 2026 the first detailed measure of fine airborne particles at Munnar, a high-altitude site in the Western Ghats of India during the southwest monsoon. Particles affect climate, rain, and health, and monsoon winds reshape them fast. Sampling ran from early June to late July 2021.

Organics formed the largest share, closely followed by sulfate. During active monsoon spells sulfate led, carried by fast marine winds, while organics led in mixed spells. Source analysis found four organic types, with aged biomass types dominant, pointing to secondary formation in the air.
pmc-13534617:
Ryan Schildcrout and colleagues built Metab8D, a network linking eight omics layers to the metabolome across cancer cells. Published in 2026, the study used machine learning to predict metabolite variation across about one thousand cancer cell lines with matched data from DNA, RNA, protein, and modification layers. Metabolite levels reflect tangled regulation, yet which layers predict them best was unclear.

Coding and non-coding RNAs emerged as top predictors overall, with the metabolome tightly tied to the transcriptome. Outer metabolites tracked their own enzymes, while central metabolites needed combined signaling and redox predictors and did not mirror pathway expression. YAP1 signaling led global predictions across four layers. Top predictors also enriched for synthetic-lethal pairs and synergistic drug combos. Readers get a regulome map for metabolism-guided therapy design.
pmc-13534917:
Christopher M Goden, Amanda M Agnew, and Angela L Harden study in 2026 whether shin bone shape affects injury outcomes under blunt impact. Reading skeletal trauma depends on outside forces, yet the bone own shape may also steer breaks. Sixty adult human shin bones faced standard four-point bending tests at set speed.

Shape traits, notably front crest form and shaft curve, linked to fracture count and overall injury complexity. Age and sex changed how shape played out, and complexity gave clearer, more meaningful patterns than count alone. Forensic readers should weigh bone shape when judging how an injury formed.
pmc-13536717:
Chengcheng Zhu and colleagues study hormone receptor patterns in aggressive ovarian cancer in a 2026 review of 176 patients. Tumors were grouped by whether they carried estrogen and progesterone receptors, which are proteins that respond to hormones. Survival was compared across groups, with statistical matching to limit other differences. A prediction chart combining receptor status with clinical features was then built and tested.

Patients whose tumors carried both receptors lived longest, while those with neither receptor fared worst. The combined pattern stayed linked to survival after other factors were considered. The prediction chart distinguished risk well for one, three, and five year survival in internal checks. The authors suggest receptor testing plus the chart can support more personal risk estimates for this hard-to-treat cancer.
pmc-13536817:
Changliang Si, Li Li, and Wei Zhang test tailored nutrition for shingles recovery in a 2026 review of 258 patients treated between 2019 and 2023. Shingles brings painful rash and slow healing despite standard antiviral care. One group ate a standard diet, while the other received personal diet plans shaped by lab markers, history, and lifestyle. Blood inflammation and immune markers, healing times, pain, and quality of life were compared.

The tailored group showed larger drops in several inflammation markers and healed faster on every timed step, from blister stop to full recovery. Pain scores fell more, and quality of life, mood, and anxiety scores improved more than in the standard group. The authors conclude that personal nutrition can support standard shingles care.
pmc-13538317:
Solfrid Thunold and co-authors test dual-time-point sugar scans as outlook markers in chest lining cancer under immune therapy in a 2026 trial analysis. Standard scans capture one moment, while paired scans an hour apart reveal how tracer uptake changes over time. Patients from an immune therapy trial received paired scans before treatment and at week five, with most completing both rounds. Uptake change and early uptake were sorted into thirds and linked to survival.

Week-five uptake change sorted survival in a steady stepwise way, with the lowest third faring best for both overall and progression-free survival. Early uptake also linked to survival yet with a less tidy pattern. Responders showed lower values on both measures at week five. Starting values predicted nothing. The authors call the week-five signal promising yet exploratory.
pmc-13540817:
Lingyue Yang and five colleagues analyse, in a 2026 study, whether uneven COVID-19 vaccine coverage across countries shaped how the coronavirus evolved. More than thirteen million viral genomes from 86 countries, collected between March 2020 and September 2022, underpin the analysis.

Before the Omicron variant took over, medium levels of adjusted vaccine coverage were linked with faster protein-changing evolution in part of the spike protein, while high coverage showed no significant link. Once Omicron dominated, the association vanished, possibly because that variant escapes immunity so well. Death rates and viral adaptation also moved together. The authors argue for fast, fair vaccine sharing in future pandemics.
pmc-13542217:
Théophile Bieth and colleagues tested whether dream sleep rewires how the mind links riddle ideas. Published in 2026, the study gave people a riddle before and after a 90-minute rest of dream sleep, non-dream sleep, or waking. Dream sleep is famed for joining weakly tied concepts, a process pitched as key to novel problem-solving.

Versus waking, dream sleep reshaped the leading riddle picture by yoking distant concepts and trimming strong but off-track links. That reshaping tracked brain-wave signs of a richer mental state. Yet dream sleep alone did not lift riddle-solving success, hinting deeper reshaping or extra steps are needed for true breakthroughs. Readers get lab backing for sleep's reshaping role, with its limits laid bare.
pmc-13543517:
Sara Abedini, Shohreh Ariaeenejad, and Azadeh Lohrasbi-Nejad published a 2026 study hunting salt-loving, chitin-eating bacteria in Iran's hypersaline Lipar Pink Wetland as seed treatments to help wheat germinate under salt stress. Salt ruins germination on farmland worldwide. From shrimp shell waste the team extracted chitin, screened forty-five bacterial isolates on it, and kept three strains whose enzyme-rich liquids stayed active across temperatures and acidity. Both living cells and the liquids were tested as seed-priming soaks.

Salt cut untreated germination from about seventy-four percent to about thirty-four percent. Under salt, one strain's liquid given as a three-hour prime lifted germination to roughly seventy-five percent and produced the longest shoots and roots and the strongest seedlings. Two strains belonged to the Bacillus cereus group. A wetland microbe, fed on shell waste, could thus shield a staple crop at its most fragile moment.
pmc-13545317:
Tim S Goldmann retraced the life of Charlotte Pommer, anatomy scholar and resistance fighter, likely the first German woman to lead an anatomy school. Published in 2026, the study draws on archives and her letters to trace her path from 1914 to 2004. Pommer left anatomy in the Nazi era after meeting the regime's victims on the cutting table, alone in doing so.

New papers show Pommer ran the Erlangen anatomy institute as interim head from 1947 to 1949. That places her among Germany's earliest women on record in such a post, though a national survey is needed to prove first place. Her early resistance and young-doctor duties shaped her worldview, and old burdens and moral binds linger. Reading her life as an ongoing war among Germans, she turned private life into a moral verdict on post-war identity. Readers get a witness whose medical and moral self-image bridges a ruptured century.
pmc-13545717:
Koen C van Son and colleagues charted in 2026 how liver cancer is changing in the Netherlands, using the national cancer registry for every new case from 2014 through 2022. The cohort held 6,526 patients. Incidence, adjusted for age, climbed from 3.5 to 4.1 cases per 100,000 people over the period, even though rates fall in some other regions.

Alcohol-related liver disease remained the commonest cause, yet cases tied to fatty liver disease linked to metabolic problems grew fastest, at more than 8 percent a year. Survival stayed poor, with fewer than one in five patients alive at five years. Receiving treatment aimed at cure improved survival more than any other factor, which the authors say argues for better surveillance of at-risk patients.
pmc-13546717:
Md Abu Rayhan and colleagues fed broiler chickens feed fermented with yeast in 2026, testing how much of the ration could be replaced by the moist fermented product. A corn and soy mash was fermented for two days with yeast and water, then fed at shares from a quarter up to the whole diet to 300 chicks over 35 days. Plain feed served as the comparison.

Birds on three-quarter and full fermented diets grew best, reaching the highest final weights with better feed conversion and more meat at processing. The full fermented diet also improved digestion of nutrients, bone mineral content, and meat protein while lowering fat, and it cut production costs enough to raise profit. The authors recommend high inclusion of the fermented feed.
pmc-13547217:
Junfei Yi and co-authors studied in 2026 how pregabalin, a widely used pain drug that leaks into waterways, can harm developing nerves, using zebrafish larvae as the test animal. Computer network analysis first predicted likely targets of the drug, and laboratory gene tests checked those predictions. The concern is that heavy clinical use leaves residues in the environment with unclear effects on wildlife.

Exposure interfered with a receptor involved in glutamate signaling, the brain's main excitatory messenger, and pushed nerve cells toward death. Larvae grew nerve fibers about 9 percent shorter than normal and swam roughly a third less far and less fast. The authors offer the results as evidence for assessing the ecological risk of drug pollution.
pmc-13547417:
Lukas Sempach led an ENIGMA consortium study in 2026 asking whether depression's brain signature is really many different signatures averaged together. The team pooled harmonized brain scans from 5,146 people, patients and matched controls, aged 9 to 82. Instead of only comparing averages, they measured how much individuals scatter around the average, focusing on cortical thickness.

Patients varied more than controls in thickness, especially across the cingulate, insula, frontal, and temporal regions, where variation ran roughly six percent higher. The scatter was widest among patients taking antidepressants. The small share of patients with extreme thickness variability also reported more severe symptoms. The authors suggest this variability map could help split depression into meaningful subgroups.
pmc-13548517:
Li-Min Lei and a large research team examine how cold exposure damages bone through changes in gut bacteria, in a 2026 mouse study. Earlier work had linked cold conditions to bone loss, and the gut is known to influence bone health. The authors asked whether bacteria living at room temperature could protect animals kept in the cold, and which microbe mattered most.

Mice housed with room-temperature partners, or given their gut microbes, kept more bone than mice exposed to cold alone. Sequencing pointed to one species, Bifidobacterium pseudolongum, whose numbers fell in the cold and recovered with co-housing. Giving that bacterium by mouth eased the bone loss. Tiny vesicles released by the bacterium reached bone tissue, supported bone formation, and calmed a cell-death pathway in marrow stromal cells.
pmc-13548617:
Eylül Eyiz and colleagues interview twenty people in Türkiye who fear flying, in a 2026 interview study of causes and coping. Fear of flying touches a few percent of the population and can shrink careers and family life despite flying's safety record. Guided conversations ran from mid-2024 into early 2025. The team read them for themes until no new ones appeared.

Turbulence, enclosed cabin space, and media coverage of crashes stood out as triggers. Underneath sat anxiety conditions, claustrophobia, worst-case thinking, body signals like a racing heart, and habits learned from family or screens. Social media exposure to alarming aviation content fed avoidance. People coped through therapy techniques, relaxation, and prayer, yet few used professional or airline programs. The authors recommend blended help that joins therapy, plain facts about flying, and respect for local culture.
pmc-13548717:
R. N. Hamoo and A. H. Suaan infect male rats with the intestinal parasite Giardia lamblia and track the fallout for blood sugar and the liver over four weeks, in a 2026 animal study. Giardia usually gets attention for gut symptoms and poor absorption, yet its wider metabolic reach is less charted. Infected rats were compared with healthy controls on glucose, insulin, insulin resistance, and liver measures across the month.

Blood sugar climbed steadily in infected rats, peaking far above controls, while insulin stayed lower than in healthy animals. Insulin resistance rose sharply and sensitivity fell, pointing to disturbed whole-body sugar control. Two liver enzymes climbed progressively, signaling stress or damage in liver cells, while the protein albumin edged up without reaching significance. The authors argue intestinal parasites deserve attention for metabolic harm beyond the gut.
pmc-13550417:
Biswajyoti Banik and nine colleagues published this 2026 field study on pairing drip irrigation scheduling with plant hormone sprays to sustain wheat yields with less water. Groundwater decline threatens wheat farming, so the two-year trial tested three irrigation levels set by crop water demand, at 60, 80 and 100 percent. These were crossed with sprays of salicylic acid, gibberellic acid, abscisic acid or water, in a split-plot design.

Deficit irrigation at 60 percent pushed roots longer and thinner, a foraging response to dry soil, but full irrigation kept leaves healthier and yielded most. It beat the deficit by about 8 to 9 percent. Salicylic acid stood out among the sprays, raising root dry weight by about 19 to 26 percent and boosting antioxidant enzyme activity over the water control. The winner was 80 percent irrigation plus salicylic acid, which matched full-irrigation yields while using less water. The authors recommend the pairing for drought-prone wheat regions.
pmc-13550617:
Nasrin Mehrjoyan, Fatemeh Zarei, Fazlollah Ghofranipour, and Fazlollah Ahmadi published a 2026 study of teen girls and food in Khuzestan, Iran. The team spoke with 17 schoolgirls aged 13 to 17. They also spoke with eight parents and three school health staff. Talks ran from February to August 2024. The team read the talks through a theory that weighs the self, the group, and the setting.

The talks yielded 208 codes in six groups. Trust in one's own skill was one group. Hoped-for results, home and school settings, and self-control were others. Knowledge gaps and views of local foods closed the list. Stress made healthy eating hard, and praise from others swayed choices. The team urges teaching plus changes at home and school.
pmc-13551717:
Lei Chen, Hongru Deng, and Lingbing Meng published a 2026 analysis of United States survey data from 2013 to 2023 on sleep, mood, and heart-metabolic health. Short or long sleep and depressive symptoms each track with cardiometabolic problems, and they often occur together. Using the national NHANES survey, the authors defined abnormal sleep as under seven or over nine hours on weekday or weekend measures, and scored depression with a standard nine-item questionnaire.

Weighted regression models related the combined exposures to blood pressure, body mass index, cholesterol, and an inflammation marker, adjusting for demographic, lifestyle, and clinical factors. Interaction terms tested whether sleep and mood amplify each other, and subgroup checks varied by sex and age. The authors frame joint exposure, rather than either factor alone, as the point of the analysis.
pmc-13551917:
Chongyang Yang, with six colleagues, published a 2026 study of seed aging in a medicinal herb. The herb is Saposhnikovia divaricata, used in traditional medicine. Its seeds lose vigor in storage, which cuts germination and limits farm output. Harm from reactive oxygen is a key driver. The team profiled gene activity and proteins across storage years. They focused on the ubiquitin system, which tags worn proteins for removal.

Weakening of a gene family called UBC1 stalled that removal system. Worn proteins then piled up inside the seeds. Genes for building proteins also fell quiet. Germination dropped to about thirty percent by year four. Embryos hollowed out, and membrane harm markers rose. The team presents the first joint gene and protein picture of aging in this herb.
pmc-13553517:
Kungwengwe and co-authors surveyed a 2026 national United Kingdom study, called INSPIRE, on mentorship for aspiring plastic surgeons. Plastic surgery is fiercely competitive, and ethnic minority candidates face extra barriers including scarce mentorship and research access. The survey reached medical students and doctors before specialty training across the country.

Among 2,528 respondents, about a fifth expressed interest in plastic surgery, with similar interest between men and women. A plastic surgery rotation more than doubled interest, and research involvement nearly quadrupled it, Kungwengwe reports. Having a mentor multiplied research engagement roughly nine fold in the adjusted analysis of the survey data. Despite equal interest, men progressed to specialty training more readily than women, and ethnic minority candidates progressed at under half the rate. Mentorship softened perceptions of both racial and gender bias.
pmc-13553717:
Yang Yang and four colleagues review tantalum, a hard metal, as a building block for materials that help body tissue regrow. Their 2026 review links the metal's basic traits to ways it is mixed with other materials for repair work. Pure tantalum is friendly to tissue and very stable, yet it is dense, costly, and hard to shape. Mixing it into other materials keeps its benefits while easing those drawbacks.

Four families of mixed materials receive attention, for both hard and soft tissue repair. The review traces how tantalum helps cells grow and new tissue form. Gaps in proof, plus cost and shaping hurdles, still slow the move into clinics. The authors map those hurdles and point to design choices that could speed safe use in patients.
pmc-13554217:
Haoyan Zhang leads a nine-author team making tiny palladium specks on clay tubes to burn off toluene, a harmful solvent vapour, in a 2026 study. Particle size governs how well such catalysts work. Their support, halloysite, is a natural clay rolled into hollow tubes. A mild vinegar-acid wash prepared the tubes before palladium was laid down by a simple settling method.

The finished catalyst destroyed ninety percent of toluene at a modest heat. Microscope and gas tests showed smaller, more evenly spread palladium specks than usual. More of the metal sat in its active form, with more oxygen clinging nearby. Extra acid sites on the surface also helped the reaction along. The team traced the burn path through several halfway chemicals to carbon dioxide and water.
pmc-13556317:
Wenliang Yu's team issued a correction to their 2026 paper on a sodium-responsive hydrogel that delivers engineered Salmonella bacteria for tumour immunotherapy. The notice fixes figure labels that were garbled during polishing. Several scale bars should read in millimetres rather than micrometres, one treatment label drops a stray letter, and two graph axes should read in cubic millimetres rather than cubic centimetres.

It also restores an omitted animal-ethics approval from Xinxiang Medical University alongside the Nanjing University approval. The authors state the errors have been fixed online and change neither the account, the reading, nor the conclusions of the work. Readers should therefore use the corrected units and the full ethics statement when citing the study.
pmc-13558317:
Zachary D Leslie and colleagues analysed how high-risk illnesses shape outcomes after ERCP, the endoscopic procedure for bile and pancreatic ducts, publishing the national study in 2026. Kidney disease, heart failure, and liver cirrhosis often travel with patients needing ERCP, yet it was unclear whether poor outcomes stemmed from the procedure or the underlying illness. The team studied over 1.17 million ERCP admissions in the National Inpatient Sample.

Nearly a quarter of admissions carried a high-risk condition, and those patients died and suffered complications at far higher rates, stayed longer, and cost more. Adjusted models tied the conditions themselves, not just procedure mishaps, to the excess risk, with cirrhosis predicting death most strongly. The validated risk models should help teams counsel patients, triage cases, and plan peri-procedure care.
pmc-13558617:
