Takayuki Kitahara and eleven colleagues measured in 2026, second by second, where radiation lands on the surgical team during full-endoscopic spine surgery. The technique suits elderly patients because it runs under local anaesthesia, yet its live X-ray guidance exposes staff unevenly across the operation. Wearable dosimeters tracked dose over the protective apron for the operator, assistant, supervisor, and scrub nurse across 28 cases, split into marking, setup, and final check phases.

The operator absorbed by far the most radiation, roughly fifty times the scrub nurse's dose per case. Nearly all of that dose arrived during the setup phase, when the working sheath is placed, rather than during marking or checking. The surgical approach chosen made no difference to totals. The authors name setup as the moment to attack with distance, single-shot imaging habits, and shielding.
pmc-13560117:
Alireza Partoazar, Sima Shahabi, and Shima Afrasiabi load curcumin into ethosome nanocarriers to strengthen light-activated therapy against mature dental biofilm. Their 2026 laboratory study targets Streptococcus mutans, a bacterium central to plaque and tooth decay. Photodynamic therapy often fails because the light-sensitive drug cannot penetrate thick biofilm, and toxicity limits dosing.

The ethosomes formed spheres averaging about 191 nanometers across and trapped most of the curcumin offered during preparation. Tests on human gum fibroblasts showed the carrier was gentle on healthy cells. Once lit by LED light, the loaded carrier cut mature biofilm by roughly forty percent in the reported assay, statistically close to a strong sodium hypochlorite rinse. Microscopy showed bacterial cells breaking apart after treatment. The authors argue the carrier deserves further study, especially for older, stubborn biofilms.
pmc-13560217:
Reza Bergemann and four colleagues simulate core decompression surgery for hip osteonecrosis in three dimensions to learn which instrument suits which lesion. Their 2026 study built CT-based models of one hundred hips from seventy-five patients treated at their institution. Six instruments, from straight drill bits to expandable reamers, were run through each model virtually.

The team scored each tool by resection fraction: necrotic bone removed divided by all bone removed, healthy included. All three expandable reamers beat the straight instruments. The small expandable reamer won for small lesions, while the medium reamer won for larger ones. The largest reamer underperformed both across nearly every size, wasting its extra reach. The authors advise personalizing instrument choice to each patient's anatomy and lesion size. They note the computer metric itself still needs validation against real clinical outcomes.
pmc-13560917:
Denis Ruto and colleagues surveyed nutrient management in lagoon wastewater systems serving small American communities, publishing the study in 2026. Lagoons remain the sanitation backbone for many towns under 10,000 people, prized for low cost and simple upkeep, yet their nutrient performance was poorly mapped. Using federal and state data plus permit reviews, the team assessed thousands of facilities and effluent records from 2020 to 2024.

About 61 percent of lagoons were non-aerated, most plants were tiny, and nitrogen and phosphorus were often monitored but rarely capped by enforceable limits. Organics control was moderate, but ammonia and nutrient levels varied widely and often breached limits for sensitive watersheds. Targeted upgrades, such as biofilm reactors for nitrogen and chemical precipitation for phosphorus, performed best, pointing to permitting reform as the key lever.
pmc-13561517:
Yuan and colleagues introduced MultiDMPcaller, a 2026 software package that finds and visualizes DNA methylation differences between sample groups. Methylation, a chemical tag on DNA, is mapped genome-wide by bisulfite sequencing, but existing analysis tools disagree with each other, so real differences get missed or false ones slip through. The package automates the downstream analysis and draws chromosome maps and enrichment views.

Yuan built in two innovations: a two-step significance adjustment tuned to the methylation habits of plants versus animals, which rescues genuine signals that a single strict correction discards. A voting scheme that compares every control replicate against every test replicate and keeps only sites winning enough votes, with stricter rules where differences are small. Tested on thale cress, apple, and mouse data plus simulated human data, the tool agreed well with existing software while showing higher precision and fewer false discoveries.
pmc-13562317:
Anna Rajtar-Wysocka and four colleagues screen adults getting ready for metabolic bariatric surgery for ADHD, using a structured diagnostic interview rather than symptom checklists alone. Their 2026 study tests seventy candidates during routine pre-surgery mental-health evaluation, adding standard scales for depression, anxiety, and impulsivity. ADHD has lately drawn notice in this group for its links to follow-through struggles.

Thirteen people, 18.6 percent of the sample, got an ADHD diagnosis. That group showed much heavier depressive and anxiety symptoms and higher impulsivity, and met criteria for mood and anxiety disorders more often. In adjusted models, female sex, ADHD, and impulsivity each on its own tracked depression severity, while female sex and ADHD tracked anxiety. The authors urge focused screening for ADHD and impulsivity before surgery, so patients carrying this extra burden can get stronger mental support around the operation.
pmc-13563717:
Deniz Aktaran Bala and five colleagues test whether aspirin can shield the rat brain from the stress of blaring white noise. Noise is a general stressor that ramps up reactive oxygen species, and the amygdala and hippocampus, the brain's alarm and memory hubs, are easily hurt by damage. The 2026 experiment pretreated rats with acetylsalicylic acid before noise exposure, then read chemistry across blood and five brain regions. Measures included a fat-damage marker, vitamin C, stress hormones, blood chemistry, and inflammatory signals.

One result stood out. The damage marker in the amygdala ran lower in pretreated, noise-exposed rats than in every other group. Most other regions and signals barely moved. Vitamin C in whole brain dipped in the pretreated stressed group, and tumour necrosis factor rose with aspirin. Blood chemistry stayed largely flat. The authors report a narrow, region-specific protection, not a broad shield.
pmc-13563817:
Ji Wook Kim and six colleagues compare two drugs for the violent shivering that can follow anaesthesia, a misery that also strains the heart. Meperidine is the traditional fix, but it is an opioid, and interest in alternatives is rising. Their 2026 study reviewed 484 adults who shivered in a recovery unit during 2024 and received either dexmedetomidine or meperidine first. Statistical matching produced 149 balanced pairs. Treatment failure meant needing a rescue drug before leaving the unit.

Dexmedetomidine failed far less often, at 3.4 percent against 10.1 percent for meperidine. Its price was blood pressure: low readings struck 6.7 percent against 1.3 percent. Slow heart rate, nausea, time in the unit, and extra opioid use matched between groups, and neither group showed dangerous breathing depression. The authors offer dexmedetomidine as a strong alternative where blood pressure can be watched closely, not as a universal swap.
pmc-13563917:
Weishen Wang and a large co-author group present a 2026 analysis of pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma that groups tumors by regulators of liquid-liquid phase separation, a process that forms droplet-like structures inside cells. Using data from 176 patients, the group defined three tumor subtypes and built a risk score linked to those subtypes.

The subtypes differed in outlook, immune makeup, and predicted response to immune therapy, and the risk score held up across cohorts. Laboratory work singled out a protein called NRF1, which switched on several risk genes and helped tumor cells grow. Blocking it slowed tumors in experiments, making it a candidate target for further drug work.
pmc-13564117:
Margaret S. Pichardo and co-authors report, in a 2026 secondary analysis of the Women's Health Initiative trial, whether a low-fat eating pattern also lowered intake of advanced glycation end-products. These are harmful compounds formed when foods are cooked at high heat. Diet records from 40,209 postmenopausal women in a trial of 48,835 were scored for these compounds at entry and over five to seven years.

Women assigned to the low-fat pattern had clearly lower compound scores throughout follow-up than the usual-diet group, whose scores stayed near the starting level. The result helps explain one route by which the eating pattern, already linked to lower breast cancer deaths in the trial, might benefit health.
pmc-13569117:
Nirakar Panda, Aline Koch, and Venkata Partha Sarathi Amineni search, in a 2026 study, for gene targets that could kill the brown marmorated stink bug through RNA interference. The bug is an invasive pest of fruit and field crops, and the method silences chosen genes. Five nerve-related genes were silenced by injecting genetic material into adult bugs.

Silencing two widely and strongly expressed genes killed nearly every bug within thirteen days and sharply reduced feeding damage in later tests. Three brain-focused genes had little effect despite their nerve roles. Pest specialists learn that broad, abundant gene expression predicts a good silencing target better than a gene's nerve function alone.
pmc-13572517:
Sherin Rebecca Flavian, with seven colleagues, reports a 2026 lab study of a weed extract against liver cancer cells. The plant, Mollugo cerviana, is known for calming oxidation and swelling, and plant drugs draw interest as gentler options. The team tested an alcohol extract of the whole plant on HepG2 cells, a standard liver cancer line.

Cell survival fell as dose rose, from 98 percent to 44 percent across the range tested, with the half-kill dose near 356 micrograms per millilitre. Treated cells held more reactive oxygen, a stress signal, and showed clear DNA damage in a comet test. Staining showed 54 percent of dead cells died by apoptosis, the tidy route, and 6 percent by necrosis. Chemical scans named the extract's main compounds, and property checks rated their drug-like quality. The authors back the plant as a therapy lead.
pmc-13573417:
John Moriarty, with 17 colleagues, presents a 2026 national review of Streptococcus suis in Ireland's pigs across 2010 to 2024. This bacterium is a top cause of lung and body-wide illness in young pigs after weaning, with losses and welfare costs. No long-term national picture existed for Ireland before this work.

Lab submissions over 15 years were sorted by strain type, drug response, and partner infections. Types 9 and 2 or 1/2 led the list, and in recent years type 9 pulled ahead. The bacterium often arrived with pig viruses and other bacteria in sore lungs. Resistance ran high to two older drug families, yet first-line penicillin drugs still worked well. Wide variety between and within herds makes vaccine choice hard. The authors call for steady watching and gene studies.
pmc-13574817:
T Vujović, with four colleagues, reports a 2026 check of how common lab solvents sway zebrafish larvae on their own. Solvents carry test drugs into fish water, yet the carriers themselves may stir or calm the fish and spoil the read. The team set safe levels for seven of them.

Larvae five days old swam in each solvent at four strengths, from faint to one percent. Cameras tracked distance, speed, turns, and rest under flipping light and dark. Four solvents sped the fish up at half a percent or more. One calmed them at the top dose after speeding them at mid dose, and one slowed them even at mid dose. Two were safe only at the lowest tenth of a percent. Light flips shaped behaviour as much as dose, so the authors urge fixed lighting in such tests.
pmc-13575017:
Rodolfo Rossi and four colleagues map what shapes childhood vaccination in African countries hit by armed conflict, in a 2026 scoping review. Conflict breaks up health services and raises the risk of outbreaks of diseases that vaccines can prevent. The review gathers work on why some children still get their shots.

Twenty-eight studies met the review's rules, drawn mainly from Ethiopia, Somalia, the Democratic Republic of Congo, and Nigeria. Mothers with more schooling, clinic visits during pregnancy, and births in facilities tied to higher uptake. Poverty, remote homes, displacement, and insecurity worked the other way. Stock-outs, weak outreach, and staff shortages added further barriers. The authors argue conflict deepens gaps that already existed in access to care.
pmc-13575117:
Bon Park and five colleagues report a new way lymphoma can resist a key antibody drug, in a 2026 study of diffuse large B-cell lymphoma. Rituximab targets the CD20 protein on these cancer cells. Many patients still fail treatment, and loss of CD20 alone does not explain every case.

The team measured large particles shed by tumours into the blood, which carry CD20 on their surface. Lab work showed these particles soak up rituximab like a decoy, leaving less drug to hit the cancer cells, and they blunted immune killing in cell tests. Patients with high particle levels before treatment had worse survival in two patient groups. The authors propose the blood measure as a marker to guide antibody treatment.
pmc-13576017:
Jacob Edward Hoerter and colleagues reviewed 192 adults whose neck masses turned out to be cancer, tracing how clinical decisions shaped the time to diagnosis. The median time from first presentation to a cancer diagnosis was 21 days. Primary care prescriptions of antibiotics were tied to a 20-day delay, while primary care imaging orders were tied to a 4-day delay.

Fine needle aspiration, used first in most patients, confirmed cancer in only 56 percent of cases, compared with 74 percent for core needle biopsy and 100 percent for excision. Only 18 percent of patients followed the most streamlined path, reaching diagnosis in a median of 6 days. The findings argue for earlier specialist referral and biopsy choices that are more likely to give a firm answer.
pmc-13576317:
Xingyu He and four colleagues explore how exercise links to problem smartphone use in teenagers in western China, in a 2026 multi-centre survey. Phones are a public health worry in this age group, and activity is known to help, yet the inner steps of that help were unclear. Pupils from 34 schools took part, 8,245 in total.

Problem use appeared in 23.97 percent of boys and 19.47 percent of girls in the sample. Modelling showed more exercise tied to less problem use. Two middle steps carried part of that link: stronger self-control and a stronger sense of meaning in life. Together they formed a chain from exercise through self-control to meaning, accounting for 9.17 percent of the total association. The authors suggest activity programmes could work partly by building those inner resources.
pmc-13578017:
Emily E Farah and three colleagues argue for a wider view of care for children with spinal muscular atrophy in a 2026 review. New gene-targeting therapies have changed survival and movement outcomes in this muscle disease. The authors say everyday functioning and participation now deserve the same attention as motor scores.

Their literature review covers work to 2025 on adaptive functioning, meaning how a child manages daily life across mobility, self-care, social, and developmental areas. A World Health Organization framework for functioning offers a structured way to capture those domains. It can shape personal goals, coordinate the care team, and track what matters to families. Most existing studies predate the new therapies, the authors note, and patient-reported measures are especially thin. Fresh assessment in the treatment era is their main call.
pmc-13579217:
Wazir, Vega, and Khaleel argue that fuel cell chemistry is stuck on a scaling law, and they map the exits. Proton exchange membrane fuel cells could power transport, but their cathode reaction, reducing oxygen to water, is slow and leans on platinum. The reaction's steps bind to catalyst surfaces in lockstep: strengthening one weakens another, capping efficiency. Their 2026 outlook gathers strategies to break that lockstep by roughening the interface where the reaction happens.

Strain in the metal lattice, lone atom sites, doping, electric fields, and confinement each bend one step's binding more than the others. Yet none fully frees the steps in practice. The authors contend the design must tune three layers together: the lattice under the surface, the layer of stuck molecules, and the solvent hugging the interface. Durability and gas transport must be co designed too, or lab gains will die inside a fuel cell stack.
pmc-13582717:
S. N. Mladen and colleagues developed and piloted EXCEL, a peer-led group program that builds autonomy, connection, and competence in health sciences trainees. Trainees face heavy distress from the learning environment, yet few programs teach the nontechnical skills to navigate it. Grounded in Self-Determination Theory, EXCEL combines psychoeducation, guided discussion, and skill practice across three parts, tested in a pre-post pilot with stress and need-satisfaction scales.

Average resource gains for autonomy rose and perceived stress fell from before to after sessions. Trainees who started with the lowest need satisfaction gained most, significantly across all three domains, and participants reported feeling heard and able to name self-support strategies. The authors support peer-facilitated, theory-based programs as a practical way to ease trainee stress and strengthen psychological resources.
pmc-13583417:
Sau-Shan Cheng, Wai-Ching Sin, Yuen-Yi Chau, and Hon-Ming Lam profile chemical marks on histones across six plant species in this 2026 study. Histones are proteins that pack DNA, and small chemical marks placed on them help switch genes on or off without changing the DNA itself. Marks linked to stress response in plants remain poorly mapped, in part because antibody tools miss many of them.

The team used a mass spectrometry workflow that can spot many marks at once and compared maize, rice, soybean, pepper, tomato, and Arabidopsis. Their survey found marks, including oxidation and hydroxylation types, that appear shared across these crops and model plants. Because the same marks recur in both cereal and broad-leaf species, the authors present them as a conserved layer of gene control worth deeper study.
pmc-13585417:
Timothy J. Craig and colleagues pool world data on how common hereditary angioedema is in this 2026 review. The inherited condition causes sudden swelling of skin and inner passages and is often missed for years. Reports of its frequency vary a lot between places, so the team screened more than five thousand studies and kept 41 that measured diagnosed cases.

Their pooled figures put the main type at a bit over one case per hundred thousand people each year, with a rarer second type well below that. Europe and North America showed the highest pooled rates, while single reports from other regions ran lower. Ways of finding cases differed so much between countries, though, that the authors doubt the gaps are fully real, and they call for shared diagnostic rules in future counts.
pmc-13587117:
Lilyana Amezcua and fifteen colleagues, for the CHIMES Study Group, published this 2026 report of a two-year single-arm trial of ocrelizumab in Black and Hispanic people with relapsing multiple sclerosis. These groups are underrepresented in MS research. The phase 4 CHIMES trial enrolled 113 Black and 69 Hispanic participants across the US, Puerto Rico and Kenya, most of them women with a mean age of 35.5, and treated them with the antibody drug for two years, measuring relapses, disability progression and MRI activity.

At week 48, 50.5 percent showed no evidence of disease activity across measures. 94 percent were free of disability progression and relapses, and 95.6 percent had no new contrast-enhancing lesions, though 52.7 percent escaped new or enlarging T2 lesions. Serious adverse events affected 8.2 percent and 2.2 percent stopped treatment. Infusion reactions were commoner in Hispanic participants, gut complaints in Black participants. The authors judge the results consistent with the trials dominated by white participants.
pmc-13591217:
Katsuhiro Yasumi leads a nationwide study of suicide among university students in Japan over five school years, from 2020 to 2024. Suicide is the top cause of death for young people in Japan, yet student specific counts were scarce. Reports came in each year from campus offices, covering over nine in ten enrolled students. The team logged 1,526 deaths classed as suicide or suspected suicide.

Rates ran higher for men than for women, though the gap shrank across the period. Deaths peaked in September and March, months of sharp change in the school year. School failure was the most common presumed motive, ahead of career worry. Few students had used campus health services, which Yasumi and the team say argues for active outreach.
pmc-13592317:
Wu and colleagues showed in 2026 that polymer coatings on gold nanorods actively steer how the rods are etched by oxidation. Gold nanorods are tiny rods whose light properties suit them for sensing and photonics. The team used penta-twinned rods, which contain five crystal domains and many defects, with polymer brushes grafted onto their surfaces.

Experiments and simulations showed the brushes gather etchant ions at the rod surface. That lowers the energy needed to remove gold atoms at defect-rich spots, so etching attacks defects first. Corrugations formed along the rods' long faces, a pattern absent in single-crystal rods. By tuning polymer chain length and grafting density, the team gained precise control of the etched rods' light properties. The authors establish polymer brushes as active directors of surface reactions.
pmc-13592417:
Ajit Kumar leads a 2026 team formulating an ionic liquid electrolyte that tames the two big faults of lithium sulfur batteries. Sulfur intermediates normally dissolve and shuttle across the cell, while the lithium metal side corrodes. Their ammonium based liquid, blended with two lithium salts, choked polysulfide dissolving to trace levels and coated lithium with a dense, fluorine rich film.

Cells delivered strong capacity and kept seventy percent after 300 cycles. Performance barely shifted across a wide range of electrolyte amounts, unlike standard ether mixes. A rival cation left its anions half reacted and its film weaker, showing the cation steers film chemistry. Kumar and the team present tailored ionic liquids as a joint cure for shuttle and anode decay.
pmc-13592817:
Andrea Jaramillo-Cerezo leads a team charting chronic lung disease of prematurity in a Colombian intensive care unit. Bronchopulmonary dysplasia hits preterm babies hard, yet data from middle income settings stay thin. Their cohort covered babies born before thirty two weeks between 2021 and 2023, with the disease judged by support needs at thirty six weeks. Records supplied birth, maternal, and treatment factors for statistical modeling.

Of 338 babies enrolled, 299 survived long enough to be judged, and about seventy six percent met the disease mark. Most cases were mild, though roughly five percent reached a potentially fatal grade, and overall deaths ran at thirteen percent. Extreme prematurity, invasive ventilation, diuretics, infection, maternal thyroid disease, and prenatal steroids each linked independently. The team spotlights fixable care factors for similar units.
pmc-13593717:
Saadet Inan and Scott M Rawls asked which receptors make rats pass more urine after a dose of xylazine, a veterinary sedative now turning up as an adulterant in illicit opioids. Xylazine was recently found to act strongly at kappa-opioid receptors, a class known to raise urine output, so their 2026 rat experiments tested two blocking drugs against it.

Xylazine raised urine output in a dose-dependent way over two hours in metabolic cages. Pretreatment with a kappa-opioid blocker cut that increase, and so did pretreatment with yohimbine, which blocks the alpha-2 receptors xylazine was long known for. Neither system alone explains the effect. The authors say anyone interpreting xylazine's actions in the body, especially as its role in overdose cases grows, needs to reckon with both receptor systems at once.
pmc-13595517:
Jie Wang and colleagues built a prediction tool for whether breast cancer has reached the armpit lymph nodes, sparing patients unnecessary node surgery when risk is low. Their 2026 study drew MRI scans and clinical data from 221 patients with confirmed breast cancer, extracting hundreds of image features known as radiomics.

A blood measure, the platelet-to-lymphocyte ratio, topped the list of clinical predictors alongside the scan's own reading of the nodes and its standard severity category. Image models combining two MRI sequences beat either sequence alone. The team blended the best image score with the clinical predictors into a nomogram. A nomogram is a visual calculator. This one was also released in a dynamic online form. It separated patients with and without nodal spread with high accuracy in both training and validation groups. The authors say the tool could guide decisions about node sampling.
pmc-13596717:
Payal Kapur leads a eighteen-author team profiling small kidney tumors that nonetheless spread, a puzzling minority since metastases in kidney cancer usually come from large primaries. Using tissue from several institutions, the team combined microscope examination with whole-exome and RNA sequencing, comparing the metastatic small tumors against similar tumors that stayed put.

Among the clear cell tumors, the spreaders carried multi-hit aggressive genetics: losses of three chromosome regions and at least two driver changes together, including in BAP1 and growth pathway genes. Their gene activity matched a known aggressive subtype and showed rewired metabolism with weakened immune attack. The non-clear cell spreaders included NF2-altered tumors, an ELOC-mutated cancer, and a rare mTOR-driven type. The authors offer the profile as a basis for judging which small tumors can safely be watched and which need treatment.
pmc-13610117:
Amalia Gorzko and six colleagues re-analyze a probiotic trial in polycystic ovary syndrome, asking whether benefit reaches beyond hormones. The syndrome travels with insulin resistance and poor lipids, and earlier probiotic results have been inconsistent. In the parent study, fifty women were randomized to twelve weeks of a nine-strain probiotic or placebo. This analysis compared fasting and post-meal glucose, insulin resistance, and cholesterol, adjusting for starting values.

Forty-three women finished: nineteen on probiotic, twenty-four on placebo. No outcome separated the groups: not glucose control, not insulin resistance, not any lipid measure. An intention-to-treat analysis imputing the seven missing participants told the same story. The authors are careful: with this sample size, estimates were imprecise, so a real but modest effect cannot be ruled out. Twelve weeks of this probiotic showed no metabolic gain; larger trials would be needed to close the question.
pmc-13612417:
Jonathan D Koss, Sule Tinaz, and Hemant D Tagare argue that Parkinson's motor scores are too noisy to reveal how the disease truly progresses in 2026. The standard MDS-UPDRS Part III exam sums dozens of rated items into one total, and rater noise can fake patient subtypes. Their method first denoises the scores to expose the underlying signal, then analyzes items in full dimensionality instead of collapsing them into a sum.

Two patterns emerged. First, progression heterogeneity is continuous: patients spread along a spectrum rather than clustering into tidy subtypes. Second, the variation organizes along two easily read axes, giving clinicians a simple map of a high-dimensional space. A sobering third result followed: baseline scores alone could not predict any individual patient's future course. The authors offer the denoising pipeline as a better foundation for trial design.
pmc-13612517:
Rebeca Moscatel leads a five-author team testing whether an AI chatbot can handle the consent conversation for a clinical trial in 2026. Prospective participants ask hard questions, and research coordinators are stretched thin. The team built a language model fenced in by the trial's own documents and checked its answers two ways: human raters, and a second model acting as moderator. Both graded accuracy, readability, and consistency.

Scores looked strong overall. Humans rated accuracy at 4.8 out of five, the moderator model at 4.7. Both found reading levels near grade seven and near-identical consistency. The catch surfaced in agreement: humans barely agreed with each other, a kappa of 0.1, while the moderator agreed with itself at 0.8. Raters marked down technically correct but toneless, context-blind answers. The authors frame the system as a design tool for trial teams. Their rater split warns that consent is a human interaction, not a quiz.
pmc-13616317:
Mathias Houe Andersen leads a team studying how the ageing brain handles surprises in sound, using a test that separates local from global pattern breaks. Listeners heard tone sequences where a note could break a short local pattern, a longer global one, or both. Brain magnetic signals were recorded from 37 younger and 40 older adults and decomposed into networks active during the task.

The classic view says ageing simply weakens the brain's prediction responses, yet reports conflict. Three overlapping networks carried the work, and ageing touched each one differently rather than muting them all. Early sensory surprise responses actually grew stronger in a network spanning the hearing areas. The finer picture suggests older brains rebalance prediction across systems, which matters for designing hearing and thinking tests that stay fair across the lifespan.
pmc-13617217:
Yoxin Chin and four colleagues report a 2026 systematic review of delivery room breathing support for late preterm and term newborns. The treatment, continuous positive airway pressure, keeps gentle air pressure on a newborn's airway to ease breathing. The team searched four databases through March 2025 for studies comparing babies who received it in the delivery room with those who did not.

Seven studies covering more than one hundred thirty-five thousand infants qualified. In observational data, babies given the support had far higher odds of pneumothorax, a dangerous air leak around the lung, plus more surfactant use and more intensive care admissions. The two randomized trials told a different story for admissions and recorded no pneumothorax events at all. The authors warn that sicker babies may simply receive more support, and they call urgently for stronger trials.
pmc-13617317:
Suchada Wattanaploy, Suchaya Luewan, and Theera Tongsong build a prediction model for miscarriage from routine first-trimester blood counts. The retrospective study covered Thai women with singleton pregnancies who attended a first antenatal visit between January 2020 and December 2025 and had complete blood count results. Inflammatory ratios computed from that standard test were combined with clinical factors.

Among seven hundred ninety-six women, one hundred eighteen later miscarried. Women who miscarried came in earlier in pregnancy. Their lymphocyte counts ran higher, while neutrophil counts and neutrophil-to-lymphocyte ratios ran lower. A simple model using only age and gestational age discriminated modestly, while adding two inflammatory indices improved it significantly, catching about seventy-seven percent of miscarriages at the chosen threshold. Because the indices cost nothing beyond a routine blood count, the authors see them as practical aids once outside validation confirms the model.
pmc-13618917:
Caroline Guimarães and nine colleagues document a heavy burden of depressive symptoms among sexual and gender minorities in Brazil and test what drives it. Their cross-sectional survey, recruited through dating apps, included six thousand two hundred twenty adults who completed the PHQ-9 depression scale. Analyses were stratified by race and weighed discrimination and internalized homonegativity, the absorption of negative attitudes about one's own identity.

Symptom scores ran higher among Black and Pardo participants than White participants. The share screening positive for depression was about thirty-nine and thirty-eight percent in those groups against thirty-two percent among White participants. Higher discrimination scores and younger age predicted worse symptoms in every group. Internalized homonegativity and lower income added risk for Pardo and White participants but not for Black participants. The authors call for policies that attack racism, homophobia, and transphobia together, plus reachable mental health services.
pmc-13619017:
In this editorial for PLOS Medicine, Manpreet Kaur, writing on behalf of the journal's staff editors. She argues that smartwatch data could reinvigorate cardiovascular research, which has stalled even as heart disease remains a leading killer. Biobanks in single countries have powered recent progress, yet their pools poorly represent the world. Roughly a quarter of humanity owns a smartwatch, and these devices record heart rate, its variability, blood pressure estimates, and sleep.

Such streams have surfaced diagnoses like cardiomyopathy and atrial fibrillation early enough to act on. The editorial's focus, though, is the barrier set: consent and privacy ethics, data quality and access logistics, and the danger that device ownership skews toward wealthier populations. That bakes inequity into any global database built from wrists. Kaur's case is that those obstacles must be cleared deliberately, so smartwatch data produces research that is both actionable and fair rather than merely abundant.
pmc-13620917:
Xiaohan Wang and five colleagues tested how squeezing blood flow during heavy training changes the short-lived power boost athletes get afterward. Twelve trained male college athletes each completed four sessions in random order. Sessions covered standard complex training, pairing heavy lifts with jumps, and the same work with thigh cuffs set at three different pressure levels. Jumps, muscle electrical activity, and blood lactate were measured before and at four points after.

The middle pressure level, seventy percent of the pressure that fully blocks arterial flow, gave the most consistent gains. Jump height and relative power rose clearly at eight minutes and power stayed up at twelve, with matching rises in thigh muscle activation. Lower and higher pressures helped only patchily. Lactate spiked early and faded across recovery in all groups. The authors suggest the middle pressure suits warm-up routines built around this boost, pending wider testing.
pmc-13621917:
Alexander Furuya leads a study of food insecurity and sleep among transgender women of color in the TURNNT cohort, a United States health study that followed participants from 2020 to 2023. Food insecurity means not having steady access to enough food. The team asked whether that hardship predicts later sleep problems.

Surveys from 314 women showed that about six in ten had faced food insecurity, and over half slept less than seven hours. Lower income and less schooling made food insecurity more likely. Women who lacked food at the start were about twice as likely to report poor sleep quality six months later, after accounting for age, income, and other factors. Trouble falling asleep showed no such clear link in the headline result. The authors argue that sleep care for this group should tackle food access itself, not just bedtime habits.
pmc-13623117:
Rafaela Soares Rech leads a team building artificial intelligence tools to screen for dysphagia, a swallowing disorder that can cause choking, lung infection, and poor nutrition. Early spotting matters, yet the confirming test, a moving X-ray of swallowing, is not always available. The team asked whether answers to a short screening could predict the X-ray result.

The study included 465 adults and older adults, of whom 153 had confirmed dysphagia on the X-ray test. Eight learning algorithms were trained on personal, health, and mouth-health information, then judged on accuracy and on how many true cases they caught. Four models led the field, reaching fair accuracy while catching most cases, led by logistic regression and a simple probability method. The authors propose a fifteen-item screen built from these results. They stress that outside testing in new settings must come before clinical use.
pmc-13623417:
Kamila A Zub Carlsson and colleagues published a 2026 case report of a scalp skin cancer that outgrew its usual slow pace in a transplant patient. The man, aged seventy-four, had received heart and kidney transplants and took long-term drugs that suppress the immune system. His tumour was a well-differentiated squamous cell carcinoma, a normally slow-growing type.

The lesion on the left side of his scalp measured four centimetres across when seen, with a horn-like surface, and tests showed no spread to bone. Removal was planned but postponed twice, first for team reassessment delays and then for sepsis. Three months later it had doubled in width, and his growing frailty ruled surgery out. Radiation given for comfort shrank it partly, though regrowth months later needed more treatment. The authors stress that immune suppression can speed well-behaved skin cancers, so timely treatment matters.
pmc-13623917:
Albert Yeam and colleagues published a 2026 experiment on how communication delay affects remote teaching of stitching wounds, a problem that matters for spaceflight. On Moon or Mars missions, astronauts with little medical training may need ground experts to talk them through procedures, with signals delayed by seconds. The team simulated that setting with simple interrupted suturing.

Students with no suturing experience were split between near real-time guidance and a four-second delay, and each closed five stitches. The delayed group took longer overall, though the gap shrank by the fifth stitch as they adapted. Instructors reported clearly higher mental workload under delay. Finished stitch quality, however, matched between groups. The authors conclude that remote guidance of simple procedures by untrained hands is workable even with delay, while warning that instructor strain is the hidden cost planners must manage.
pmc-13624417:
Shuo Huang and collaborators build three-dimensional photonic crystals, materials that block a chosen band of light, from gyroid networks with a built-in mirror defect. Their design borrows from twin boundaries found in natural gyroid structures. By changing one distance, the gap between paired mirror planes, they hoped to widen or narrow the blocked band without moving its center.

Calculations and lab tests agreed: as the mirror gap grew, the blocked band widened in a steady, one-way pattern while its middle frequency stayed put. Field maps showed the defect slowly turning split light patterns into smooth ones. That single-knob control could simplify devices that filter or route light at set wavelengths.
pmc-13624817:
Giovanni Landoni and three colleagues, writing in 2026, argue that amino acid infusions should now enter routine care to protect the kidneys. Their narrative review builds on the PROTECTION trial, which gave short, low-dose amino acid drips to more than 3,500 heart surgery patients and cut both mild and severe kidney injury. European guidance for adult heart surgery has already taken the practice up.

Using a who, what, when, and how framework, the authors cover which patients fit, which mixtures studies used, and how long to run the drip, warning against going past forty-eight hours. Early signs of benefit reach beyond heart surgery, and a cost study found shorter bills, which together make the case for quick adoption.
pmc-13625617:
Laura Brunelli, Federico Fonda, Silvio Brusaferro, and Blake Lesselroth argue, in a viewpoint essay, that skill with artificial intelligence should count as a core public health competency. They define AI literacy through knowledge, skills, and attitudes, scaled to each professional role. The essay maps where AI already helps, from outbreak spotting to health campaigns, and asks schools and institutes to teach it on purpose rather than by accident.

For teaching, they sketch personal tutoring, shifting practice scenarios, and immersive simulations built with AI help. For research, they frame AI as a cross-cutting support for the World Health Organization's essential public health tasks. Their refrain is that AI should extend human judgment, not replace it, and that sharing this literacy is a joint duty.
pmc-13625717:
Xingchen Guo and co-authors take the first layered look inside piglets infected with porcine deltacoronavirus, a gut virus that kills newborn pigs and can enter human cells. Working in the small intestine, the virus's main target, they combined gene, protein, and small-molecule readouts in one integrated analysis. The host answered with a strong interferon defense, the front-line antiviral alarm, while fat handling shifted at the same time.

One control network, PPAR signaling, stood out, with fat-moving genes turned up and down in a coordinated pattern. Membrane fats broke down widely, and a prostaglandin branch of inflammation gathered fuel. The pattern echoes metabolic-immune tangles reported in severe COVID-19, which hints that coronaviruses may share tricks and that the PPAR network deserves a look as a treatment target.
pmc-13625817:
Isabel Bestard-Lorigados and colleagues compare five mutations in presenilin 1, the gene behind most inherited Alzheimer's disease. Each mutation tweaks how the amyloid precursor protein is cut, and the pieces, called Aβ40 and Aβ42, differ in how readily they clump. The team placed the mutations into nerve-like and kidney cells stripped of their own presenilin genes, then measured amyloid output, cell harm, and how fast the mutant proteins matured.

Every mutation raised the clump-prone share of amyloid, the Aβ42 to Aβ40 ratio, yet each got there by a different route. A partner cutting enzyme stayed unchanged, all mutants harmed cells, and only those that also disturbed a growth signal called Notch cut cell survival. One gene, five roads to the same toxic tilt.
pmc-13628417:
Juthathip Khongpetch and seven colleagues followed a birth cohort in Benin, published in 2026, asking whether ordinary malaria episodes in infancy leave marks on children's development. The children were enrolled at birth between 2010 and 2011, checked for malaria through their first two years, and assessed for development at ages one and six.

More episodes of malaria with fever during infancy were tied to lower motor scores at both ages, and malaria paired with anaemia showed the same pattern. Blood haemoglobin levels appeared to carry part of the effect. No steady link appeared for cognitive scores. The authors warn that even uncomplicated malaria should not be dismissed as harmless, and they suggest folding anaemia screening into malaria control and routine child health care.
pmc-13628817:
Takumi Takemoto and four colleagues report the case of a woman of sixty-six. Her chest mass was misread before surgery as a benign teratoma. Scans showed a neat, calcified growth beside the left rib arch. It held a fatty part and low activity on scans. Nothing pointed clearly to the nearby rib cartilage as its source.

Surgeons removed the mass with a robot-guided camera operation. They worked through the right chest. The tumour proved joined to the sixth rib cartilage. Lab tests then named it a low-grade chondrosarcoma, a cartilage cancer. Leftover tumour could not be fully ruled out. So a tumour board chose watchful waiting. No return appeared over eighteen months. The authors warn that this rare source belongs on the checklist. It matters for calcified masses at the front of the chest. It changes how wide the cut must be.
pmc-13630217:
Margo Gustina and two colleagues used library funding votes as a hard measure of how much voters value public libraries. Many library budgets are set by direct ballot votes on tax levies. The study could thus model thousands of real choices. It worked at national scale across nearly a thousand library system years. It also worked within Washington state at precinct level.

Physical access dominated all else. A precinct holding a library building was far more likely to vote yes. Support faded steadily with each extra mile to the nearest branch. Extreme heat events also dented support. The authors read the results as hard proof of a simple point. Libraries act as critical local infrastructure. Voters show that value at the ballot box, not merely in words.
pmc-13632017:
A smarter way to read heart scans is proposed by Naghavi and colleagues, aimed at people whose standard calcium score reads zero. A zero score usually signals very low heart risk, but a small share of such people still develop coronary heart disease. The older method uses thick scan slices and a fixed brightness cutoff, so it can miss small, faint, or partly calcified plaque in the coronary arteries.

The team applied an artificial intelligence framework, called Agatston-2.0, to scans from nearly four thousand people who had scored zero in two long-running studies. It found hidden calcium in about twenty-two percent of them, and those people developed heart disease at roughly twice the rate over twenty years as those with no hidden calcium. If further cohorts confirm the pattern, the authors argue, this finer scoring could become the new standard.
pmc-13634617:
Meijia Fu and three colleagues review genetic causes of protein leaking into urine, centering on the podocyte. Podocytes are cells that wrap the kidney's tiny filters and hold back blood protein. When they fail, proteinuria follows and kidneys decline. Sequencing has widened the list of genes involved far beyond the filter's structural parts. Newer finds touch cell shipping routes, nucleus control, energy factories, and the cell's grip on its surroundings.

Despite that spread, faulty genes produce look-alike illnesses. The authors argue the illnesses converge because podocytes run as one connected system across many compartments. Mechanical signals from the filter's base layer, protein delivery to the slit between cells, gene switching in the nucleus, and energy supply all lean on each other. Damage in one layer spreads through the network. Framing the cell this way, they suggest, explains the overlap and may guide future treatments.
pmc-13637717:
Mônica J Rodrigues-Jesus and seven colleagues published this 2026 study of patients carrying more than one strain of a notorious hospital gut bacterium. Clostridioides difficile infection follows antibiotics and causes severe diarrhea. The team cultured stool specimens from infected patients at a Virginia tertiary hospital over about ten months, picking three colonies per patient. Gene tests profiled each isolate's toxins, and a subset went to whole-genome sequencing.

Mixed-strain infection turned up in about a third of the patients. Age, sex, recurrence, severity, and death rates looked the same between mixed and single-strain cases. One twist mattered: among mixed infections, carrying a non-toxigenic strain, one that makes no toxin, paired with clearly less severe disease. Sequencing confirmed the mixes and named the commonest sequence types on each side. The authors suggest the harmless roommate may blunt illness, and that treatment research should test mixed infection directly.
pmc-13641717:
Hsiao-Yuh Roan and thirteen colleagues present a whole-organ cell mapping study of the zebrafish liver, built on a new expansion microscopy method that resolves every liver cell in an intact adult organ. How organs grow cell by cell after the embryo stage has been hard to watch directly.

Counting labeled liver cell nuclei, the team found an adult liver holds on average about 1.27 million hepatocytes, a more than five-hundred-fold rise driven by a concentrated growth burst. Lineage tracing showed a few cells expanded into large clones. Damaging scaffold proteins uncoupled organ shape from cell number, suggesting the two are controlled separately.
pmc-13642917:
Andreas Tiefenbacher and eighteen colleagues present a 2026 study of a fat-burning pathway as a drug target in prostate cancer. Tumors rich in the marker PSMA act more aggressively, and sampling paired high and low regions revealed their metabolic wiring.

PSMA-high regions turned up ATGL, the enzyme that starts fat breakdown, a link confirmed in ninety treated-naive patients. One cell line depended on fat yet could not switch fuels, and blocking ATGL, by drug or gene silencing, hit that inflexible line hardest. A hormone therapy drug itself raised ATGL, showing two-way control. The authors name fat breakdown a targetable weakness.
pmc-13646217:
Lijing Zhu and ten colleagues report, in a 2026 study, that a channel protein called pannexin 1 protects the liver against fatty buildup and insulin resistance. Fatty liver disease tied to metabolism affects more than a quarter of the world's people, and treatments are scarce. The team lowered or raised the protein in mice fed a rich diet and in liver cells bathed in fats. Microscopy, gene tests, and rescue drugs traced the pathway involved.

The protein's level was reduced in human fatty liver samples and in the animal models. Mice lacking it gained more weight, handled sugar worse, and packed far more fat into the liver. Raising the protein reversed that direction, and protection ran through an energy sensor that switches on the cell's recycling system, autophagy. Blocking recycling removed the benefit, which pins down the route. The authors name this channel a candidate target for future fatty liver drugs.
pmc-13646717:
Yuchen Qu and Wataru Yamori published this 2026 review organising what is known about how plants withstand heat into design principles for breeding tougher crops. Rising temperatures already cut yields of wheat, rice and maize, threatening food security. Research on heat responses has been fragmented into separate pathways, the authors argue. They reframe the field around one shared goal: keeping photosynthesis, the plant's carbon-gathering engine, running when temperatures climb.

The synthesis sorts defence strategies into six domains: membrane and structural integrity, photosynthetic regulation, protective metabolites and hormone signalling, scavenging of reactive oxygen, protein quality control, and gene regulation at several levels. Rather than independent tricks, these form a timed hierarchy with real energy costs, the authors show. They then map how mutagenesis, transgenic methods and targeted gene editing could strengthen each node, naming the trade-offs each route brings. The result is a roadmap for high-yielding, heat-tolerant cultivars.
pmc-13646917:
Mathilde Kadouch and six colleagues test whether part of p53, the famous tumor guard protein, can behave like a prion, a self-copying protein shape. Using baker's yeast, they fused the p53 core region to part of a known yeast prion protein. The fused protein formed aggregates that cells passed to their offspring in classic prion fashion. Unlike familiar yeast prions, this one did not need the usual helper proteins to persist.

The prion form could push full-length p53 into clumps, shown by dye staining and by transfer between cells. Most cancer-linked variants behaved like the normal core, yet one notorious variant, R175H, switched into the prion state about eighteen times more often. That matches its known clumping habit in human tumors. The authors offer the yeast system as a measuring tool for p53 inactivation and as a screening bench for switch-blocking drugs.
pmc-13647117:
Luyao Xiang and four colleagues survey 3,466 Chinese college students on how hard childhoods relate to online aggression, and what softens that link. Students reported childhood adversity, cyber aggression, resilience, and exercise habits on standard scales. Models tested whether resilience carries part of the link and whether exercise changes its strength. The authors are careful to treat a one-time survey as association, not cause.

More childhood adversity went with more cyber aggression, and the rise steepened at higher adversity counts rather than climbing evenly. Lower resilience formed one bridge between the two, since adversity tracked with weaker resilience and weaker resilience with more aggression. Exercise strengthened resilience's protective side: where students exercised more, resilience pushed back harder against aggression. The authors suggest campuses pair trauma-aware support with resilience building and regular exercise.
pmc-13648417:
Shiyuan Chen and five colleagues built RNASeek, a large AI model that reads RNA and dreams up new RNA strands. RNA steers how cells use gene code. A tool that both grasps RNA and writes it could speed the craft of new gene switches.

The model learned from RNA of many life forms, with no labels given. It picked up species traits and gene borders on its own. Fine-tuning taught it to guess how fast a self-cutting RNA works and how long a virus message lasts. A reward step then pushed its writing toward prized traits. Lab tests backed the plan: built RNAs cut as well as wild ones, and built tail ends beat their training set. The team frames it as one loop of learn, guess, and tune.
pmc-13649117:
Pavlina Laskova and thirteen colleagues list the germ proteins that helper T cells spot in tularemia, a harsh disease from the germ Francisella tularensis. A weak live strain shields in part, and helper cells drive that shield. Yet their true targets were near unknown.

The team used mass scans on infected sentry cells to list the protein bits those cells display. They found 57 bits from 23 germ proteins. Tests in mice then showed which bits wake helper cells: ten did, and five drew replies in most mice. A shot built from those five bits helped mice rein in a strong strain early, though it did not shield in full. The list also gives tools to track such cells.
pmc-13649217:
Aitor Moruno-Cuenca and three colleagues present singIST, free software for judging how faithfully animal disease models mirror human disease at single-cell resolution. Preclinical models often fail to reproduce human biology, and single-cell sequencing now produces detail that ad hoc comparisons cannot handle systematically.

Built in the R and Bioconductor ecosystem, the package maps genes between species and scores how well pathways, cell types, and individual genes are recapitulated in direction and size. A companion dashboard lets users explore results interactively and generate publication-ready figures without writing code. The workflow is demonstrated by comparing a mouse skin inflammation model with human eczema data, supporting better model selection.
pmc-13649717:
Tran Yen Linh Le and four colleagues tested a mix of three helpful microbes on highbush blueberry plants, watching fruit, soil, and root-zone bacteria at once. Green farming leans more on such mixes, yet their joint effects were unclear. Plants fed the mix by drip lines were set against untreated plants of the same crop type.

Treated plants showed their first fruit about eleven days sooner, and the fruit ran much sweeter. Soil under treated plants held fewer salts and less of most nutrients, though phosphorus rose. Bacteria near the roots grouped apart by treatment in some checks, with richer variety in a treatment-linked subset. The authors note the design cannot prove which change caused which.
pmc-13650617:
Suelen Camargo and two colleagues review how two brain proteins, tau and alpha-synuclein, move between helpful liquid droplets and harmful solid clumps. Healthy cells organize chemistry in membraneless droplets formed when proteins condense out of solution, and both proteins can join such droplets because large stretches of them are naturally disordered.

The review follows the sequence features that let these proteins condense, age inside droplets, and sometimes harden into the amyloid assemblies that mark Alzheimer's and Parkinson's diseases. Droplet formation and amyloid formation overlap but are not the same road, and the authors emphasize that one does not guarantee the other. When protein quality control fails, misfolded proteins also jam transport and energy production inside neurons. Understanding where the reversible process tips toward the irreversible one may reveal intervention points before neurons are lost.
pmc-2253517:
Ellinghaus, Kurtz, and Willhoeft introduce LTRharvest, software for finding LTR retrotransposons in genomes. These jumping DNA elements are plentiful in organisms with nuclei and shape how genes and chromosomes evolve. Many genomes had been sequenced, yet few had high-quality maps of such elements.

LTRharvest searches fresh sequence data for the tell-tale long terminal repeats that mark these elements. It was built to be both efficient and flexible for genome-wide scans. Better maps of jumping elements help researchers understand genome size, gene disruption, and the forces that remodel DNA.  Repeat-rich regions, once skipped over, become visible for study as well.
pmc-3887317:
Ekor reviews the growing use of herbal medicines, focusing on adverse reactions and challenges in monitoring safety. Use of herbal products and supplements grew tremendously over the past three decades. A large majority of people worldwide rely on them for part of their basic health care, he notes.

Although such therapies show promising potential, they can also cause harm and interact with prescribed drugs. Monitoring their safety is hard because products vary and reporting is voluntary. The review urges stronger surveillance and honest labelling so traditional remedies can be used with open eyes.
pmc-4427717:
Jaishankar, Tseten, Anbalagan, and their colleagues reviewed heavy metal toxicity in 2014. Heavy metals pose a major threat to health, the authors argue, with several serious risks. These metals have no useful role in the body, yet they persist in forms that harm it.

The review covers how key heavy metals poison the body and the health effects that follow. Exposure comes from polluted water, soil, air, and some work settings. Damage can hit the nerves, kidneys, and other organs over time. Gathering the mechanisms in one place helps doctors spot metal poisoning and helps officials set safer limits.
pmc-5477817:
Afshin, Forouzanfar, Reitsma, and their colleagues analyzed health effects of overweight and obesity in 2017 across nearly two hundred countries over twenty-five years. The rising pandemic of obesity had received significant attention in many countries. Whether that attention changed trends or the disease burden remained uncertain.

The team analyzed data from tens of millions of individuals to assess trends in obesity and overweight prevalence and the burden they cause. Their scale reveals how fast rates rose in children as well as adults. Obesity drives diabetes, heart disease, and several cancers worldwide. The study gave policy makers a hard measure of a problem that attention alone had not slowed.
pmc-6323917:
Ana Kozomara, Maria Birgaoanu, and Sam Griffiths-Jones reported the state of miRBase in 2018. miRBase names and catalogs microRNA sequences from all species. The release covered hundreds of organisms and tens of thousands of precursor and mature sequences.

The update improves how entries link to evidence and to the genes microRNAs come from. Better confidence flags help users drop entries that rest on weak data. A shared naming system keeps papers talking about the same molecules in the same words. Anyone starting microRNA work checks miRBase first for names and sequences.
pmc-7006217:
Shanika Amarasinghe, Shian Su, Xueyi Dong, and coauthors reviewed long-read sequencing analysis in 2020. Long-read machines now deliver better accuracy and output than their early versions. Their data differ enough from short reads to need dedicated tools.

The review surveys software for assembly, variant calling, and transcript work on long reads. Fast-moving development leaves users unsure which tools are mature. The authors sort options by task and note where benchmarks exist. Anyone planning a long-read project can use it to build a pipeline that fits the data's quirks. A closing section lists open problems, including methylation calling and phasing of whole chromosomes.
pmc-7284317:
The Global Burden of Disease Chronic Respiratory Disease Collaborators published a worldwide accounting in 2020 of long term lung and airway diseases. Earlier efforts had usually counted one condition at a time, such as chronic obstructive pulmonary disease or asthma. This study instead measured the whole group together, using data gathered for the Global Burden of Disease Study covering 1990 to 2017.

The authors estimate how common these diseases are, how many deaths they cause, and how much healthy life they take away, country by country. Their results show a heavy and uneven burden that falls hardest where smoking, air pollution, and limited care combine. Health planners use figures like these to decide where prevention money does the most good.
pmc-9810617:
Alistair Johnson and colleagues described MIMIC-IV in 2023, a freely accessible dataset of electronic health records from hospital care. Hospitals now collect digital data throughout routine practice, and those records capture how patients were treated and how they responded. Such data offer rich material for research, yet they usually sit locked in hospital archives.

MIMIC-IV opens a large collection of de-identified records to approved researchers anywhere. The article explains what the dataset contains, how it was built, and how privacy is protected. Because anyone qualified can use the same data, studies based on it can be checked and repeated, and the dataset has become a training ground for clinical data science.
poems-1817:
John Keats published his first book, Poems, in 1817, a slim volume that introduced one of England's greatest poets to a mostly indifferent public. Keats dedicated it to Leigh Hunt, the editor who had championed him, in a sonnet praising the delights still left in a world where Pan is no longer sought. Many of the shorter pieces and sonnets, a note explains, were written earlier than the rest.

The volume opens with the long, lush poem beginning on a little hill at dawn, full of buds, clouds, and morning freshness, in the sensuous style that became Keats's signature. Sonnets and shorter lyrics fill out the book, written while Keats was still finding his voice. Few first books in English carry this charge of promise: nearly everything Keats became is present here in early form, three years before his death.
punch-or-the-london-charivari-vol-159-19:
Punch for November 17, 1920, in volume 159, opens with Charivaria, its column of short news jokes. The Lord Mayor's Show, small cars, and Ireland pass in review.

A man who bought a tiny two-seater at the Motor Show is rumoured to have found the cat playing with it at home. Westminster council wants night whistling for cabs stopped, a gossip writer expects Mr. Austen Chamberlain to become Viceroy of India, and the Lord Mayor's coachman is reported to have been accompanied by the Lord Mayor himself. A West Ham parrot trained to copy the bagpipes will have its life insured, the column hopes.
punch-or-the-london-charivari-volume-152:
Charivaria fronts Punch, volume 152, for April 11, 1917, with wartime jokes on America, food, and the stage. The United States had just entered the war, and the column wonders how its army will help the Allies.

President Wilson, it says, will still be glad of suggestions from the halfpenny morning papers. A military absentee who dined at a London restaurant and did not mind returning to the trenches wisely hid the restaurant's name. Revue managers, told to shorten performances, cannot choose which joke to keep and in desperation resolve to sacrifice both.

Punch, volume 152, for April 18, 1917, opens with Charivaria and its short war jokes. Germany's widening circle of enemies leads the column this week.

With nation after nation declaring war on Germany, the column fears the supply of interned German ships may run short. An Austrian general is overwhelmed by an avalanche, and patriotic English folk offer to forgo their snow ration at Easter in view of its military use. Parliamentary reform is called a dangerous precedent, since the press had not demanded it first. Spring brings no relief. Spring brings no relief.

Charivaria leads Punch for April 25, 1917, in volume 152, with brief jokes on the occupied lands, bequeathed brains, and the spring offensive. The tone stays dry while the news stays grim.

A German paper claims German grows more popular in the occupied districts; the inhabitants, the column answers, look forward to telling their occupiers in German what they always thought in French. Distinguished Americans bequeath their brains to Cornell, while the German Crown Prince's offer of his headpiece awaits confirmation. A claim that the British offensive has been arrested is read as a speeding case.

Punch for April 4, 1917, in volume 152, opens with Charivaria. The Kaiser has conferred the Order of the Black Eagle on the Turkish Grand Vizier, and the column calls it persistent bad luck for the Vizier.

Mr. Robert Blatchford had lately asked what manner of man the Tsar was, and now the Tsar has abdicated; the ex-Tsar absolves him of blame. A rumour of eighty thousand German surrenders grows to ninety thousand after a recount. Advice on renovating last year's suit ignores the cheap butterfly nets now available to fur-coat owners for moth season.

Charivaria fronts the Punch of February 14, 1917, in volume 152. Herr Ballin's threat to hold up the world's wheat, meat, munitions, and commerce is answered by a picture of his countrymen on the Western front holding up their hands.

The Kaiser is reported ready to give Count Bernstorff the Iron Cross with white ribbon, causing consternation among officials who feel the Count has done his best for Germany. A Berlin paper's discovery that Germany is at war is praised as proof that nothing is hidden from great German minds. Henry Ford's offer of his works to America draws a dry moral.

Punch, volume 152, for February 21, 1917, leads with Charivaria and a joke at Count Bernstorff's expense. Annoyed at Americans who supported President Wilson, the Count decided to teach them a lesson they would not forget, so he left America.

Hungary is settling down, the column adds, since only two shots were fired at Count Tisza in the Diet last week. The liquorice factory at Kut is back in British hands, to the relief of bronchial readers. Berlin dress rules punish garments bearing marks of prodigal eating, and soup-coloured waistcoats are suddenly in demand.

Charivaria opens Punch for February 28, 1917, in volume 152. The Kaiser, it is said, has developed an absolute horror of being buried prematurely, and several experts say the thing is impossible.

Hindenburg blames the Crown Prince of Bavaria for a misunderstood order that lost Grandcourt; the prince retorts that the real culprits were the British. A sketch of Von Bissing praises his execution, which the column thinks only natural. A cartoon shows a news editor handling the paper shortage by sending early snowdrop reports to the advertisement columns. Admiral von Capelle's claim that no submarine has been lost is warmly received.

Punch for February 7, 1917, in volume 152, opens with Charivaria and the Kaiser's birthday theatre. His entertainment, The German Blacksmith, was partly his own work, and the column wonders how his people had offended him.

Greece, long misjudged, has saluted the Entente flags, and King Constantine is rumoured ready even to put out his tongue at the Kaiser. Chancellor Bethmann-Hollweg, accused of selling his countrymen to the Allies, appears from the latest note to have given them away. Wild boars in northern France give the Kaiser a film role as their destroyer.

Charivaria leads Punch dated January 10, 1917, in volume 152. Curtailed train services open the column: on parts of one southern line, no trains now run except those that started before January 1.

New Treasury notes will carry a picture of the House of Commons, and the column hopes other places of amusement will follow on later issues. Germany is enrolling criminals in the army, a step the column calls unnecessary, since criminals have conducted many of its operations already. The week's remaining items keep the war at a joking distance it never quite reaches.

Punch, volume 152, for January 17, 1917, opens with Charivaria. An evening paper announces it is time to deal finally with Tino, King Constantine of Greece, and the column is relieved the matter will not be left to eternity.

A Berlin paper grants King Constantine as much right to be heard as a common criminal, which his friends had put less bluntly. The blockade is praised in a German paper as a refiner of the German figure, though its effect on the German swelled head goes unmentioned. The Kaiser, in true humility, has decided to allow the war to continue.

Charivaria fronts Punch for January 24, 1917, in volume 152, beginning in Greenland. A visitor reports that Greenland knows nothing of the war. The Intelligence Department now wonders if its tab colour was wrongly chosen.

The Governor of Greenland, giving evidence in the Prize Court, is interested to learn of the famous hymn about Greenland's icy mountains. He thinks the local publicity committee will resent the climate reference when next thawed out. Lord Devonport sets up his own press bureau while the press bureau plans its own food controller. American Line fares rise three pounds, discouraging Henry Ford.

More Discipline, a soldier's tale, leads Punch for January 3, 1917, opening volume 152. Sergeant Wally, resting a wounded leg and accepting a cigarette, explains that a man who moves on the word of command without waiting to think becomes a reliable soldier.

He recalls being called out of the ranks as a recruit for standing about until he chose to obey, a rebuke that nearly made him cry and later served him often. His borrowed sarcasm, the narrator reflects, must have had many victims since. Readers get barracks-square wisdom from a man the war had already marked.

Charivaria opens Punch dated January 31, 1917, in volume 152. Berlin's birth rate has fallen considerably this year, and the column understands the reluctance to be born a German just now.

German official films of the Somme are said to prove that, but for the Allies, Germany would have won the battle. The military authorities decline to introduce bathless days, ablution being a habit the Teuton does not pursue to excess. Midland Railway traffic jams follow the Food Controller's praise of the company's cheap luncheon. The column keeps its wartime jokes short, sharp, and close to the headlines.

Punch, volume 152, for June 13, 1917, leads with Charivaria. Count Tisza means to serve at the front for the rest of the war, though he denies copying the idea from Mr. Winston Churchill.

Chérisy was announced impregnable by the Germans shortly before the British took it. Sir Douglas Haig plainly never saw the announcement. For Baby Week at Croydon, parents are asked to hang flags from their houses, or a little bunting where flags are lacking. An Ipswich parrot makes her own poll scratchers from soft wood and has often asked to do war work.

Charivaria fronts Punch for June 20, 1917, in volume 152. At Grimsby a man was fined five shillings for throwing railway restaurant sandwiches into the road. His defence, that he never knew they could injure the road, failed.

Too much fuss, the column thinks, is made about stopping Ramsay MacDonald and Jowett from leaving England, since neither threatened to return. One northern man sticks stupidly to his tale of not hearing the Messines explosion at all. King Constantine's decision to abdicate is praised as humility worthy of true greatness, in the column's driest voice.

Punch, volume 152, dated June 27, 1917, opens with Charivaria. Crime stories are said to be the Sultan of Turkey's favourite reading. A gift is on its way to him: a new life of the Kaiser, shaped as a book.

King Alexander of Greece first proclaimed he would carry out his father's sacred mandate. When it was pointed out that a chance to follow his father's footsteps would doubtless be granted, he tried again. Air raid news fills the next item. Readers get the war's eastern kings handled with the same irreverence as its generals.

Charivaria leads Punch dated June 6, 1917, in volume 152. A press campaign against young men of military age in government offices is said to be causing some of them many sleepless days.

A correspondent reports record heat by his own thermometer, and the column blames the Censor's example, after the Folkestone raid, for everyone's failure to keep secrets. A movement to present Italy with a Shakespeare monument in Rome is weighed against sending George Bernard Shaw to be naturalised Italian instead. Lord Cowdray lectures on flying after the war, which most people will wait to meet when it comes round again.

Punch, volume 152, for March 14, 1917, opens with Charivaria and a punishment for Herr Zimmermann. For mishandling the Mexican affair, Herr Zimmermann is to learn a terrible lesson at the Kaiser's hands: appointment as Food Dictator.

Field-Marshal von Hindenburg says no one can predict when the war will end, which the column calls nonsense, since military experts have predicted it more than once. A French journal thinks the war will end this year; the Germans are less pessimistic. The Kaiser, settling the unemployed question in his own way, will give a dinner to Count Bernstorff.

Charivaria fronts Punch for March 21, 1917, in volume 152. A convict at Pentonville is said to be exactly like the Kaiser, and feels the Kaiser owes it to him to remove his moustache or grow side whiskers.

At a special service for the war's success, the Kaiser is reported to have sung the De Profundis very loudly. All but the top of his voice was, so to speak, under water. At Barmen, rioters seriously wounded the chief of police with a turnip. A famous singer in Berlin was paid in food, including sixty eggs, for a private concert.

Punch for March 28, 1917, in volume 152, prints a cartoon of two minesweeper men comparing risky jobs before its Charivaria column. One sailor, interrupted mid-sentence by events, holds that submarine crews run less risk than the boys in the aeroplanes.

The column then reports a Kingston man charged with absence from military service. He stated he did not know the country was at war, and grew interested on hearing the enemy was Germany. Hamburg hotel keepers drop a food surcharge for guests who take no wine or beer, for the deep reason that none exists to take.

Charivaria opens Punch for March 7, 1917, in volume 152, with a judge's comparison from Mr. Justice Bray: a motor-car repairer is like a plumber, in that once he is in the house he cannot be got out.

Rejoicing in the Reichstag over Mr. Gerard's departure and the end of his spy bureau draws a crack about wild rubes of the American kind. A German government film called The Discovery of Germany tours the fatherland, while the further discovery that Germany was fatally misled awaits imperial approval. German officers warn the public not to discuss military matters.

Punch, volume 152, for May 16, 1917, leads with Charivaria. Berlin factories printing counterfeit bread tickets have been discovered, and the expected defence is that the tickets were only meant to be exchanged for counterfeit bread.

King Ludwig of Bavaria says the enemy's desire will be dashed against troops accustomed to victory; several of the victors now behind British positions profess themselves nauseated with it. Over five million pigs have mysteriously disappeared in Germany in a year. A festival performance of Parsifal will mark the anniversary of Jutland, with a more topical substitute proposed.

Charivaria fronts Punch dated May 2, 1917, in volume 152. America's freshness as a new member of the Alliance is envied. New York will hold a first flag day on June 2.

America wants the Irish question settled, though there is no truth in the rumour that Britain cabled an offer to take on Mexico if America would take on Ireland. Von Ihne, the Kaiser's court architect, is dead, and future changes to the Hohenzollern house will lose the All-Highest's personal taste. Whole haystacks are said to be eaten in a night somewhere in Germany.

Punch, volume 152, dated May 23, 1917, opens with Charivaria. Mr. William Watson describes his new book of war verse in grand terms, as a running commentary on the war and its side effects. People are already asking why a man like this was left out of the Dardanelles Commission.

Weeds trouble the amateur gardener because he cannot always know them; the column advises pulling them up, since weeds are the ones that come up again. Mr. Charles Cochran's plans follow. Readers get poetry, gardens, and show business weighed in the same wartime scale.

Charivaria leads Punch for May 30, 1917, in volume 152. Mr. Will Thorne declares a Petrograd hotel charged him twelve shillings for four small custards, proof that Russia's war spirit is not wholly dead.

Food Ministry officials allow that domestic pastry may still be baked, since that kind of pastry tends to reduce the number of food consumers. Allied officers find fifteen hundred tons of potatoes hidden in Athens, which finally justifies the Salonika expedition. A Kingston man wears a hat band urging everyone to eat less bread, and crowds rush gratefully to the tea rooms to obey.

Punch, volume 152, dated May 9, 1917, opens with Charivaria. A Rome paper reports that Hindenburg has asked for all royal princes to be removed from the West Front. The plan of protecting them by moving the front further west has been abandoned.

The Vossische Zeitung calls the late Bissing a veritable angel of mercy, and the Kaiser wonders who started the scandal. Mr. Pretyman is quoted that Britain is back in the days when the merchant marine and the navy were one. The column's jokes keep circling the same point: official words and plain facts rarely meet.
punch-or-the-london-charivari-volume-153:
Charivaria opens volume 153 of Punch on August 1, 1917. A Frankfort paper discusses King Ferdinand's imperial aspirations under the title What Bulgaria Wants, ground nearly identical to an unpublished piece of the column's own called What Bulgaria Won't Get.

A cow that walked down sixteen stairs into a Willesden cellar is blamed on a false air-raid warning. Industrial unrest reporting from Scotland never mentions liquor restrictions, some thoughts being too poignant for utterance.
