An Austrian partial crisis is noted, with the feeling that one day something really serious will happen to that country.

Punch, volume 153, dated August 15, 1917, leads with Charivaria. Count Reventlow recalls the heroic days of 1914, when God gave Germany daily bread and a daily victory; the column suggests the Wolff Bureau deserves some credit for the victories.

Mr. Winston Churchill's car was lately run into by another coming the opposite way, which lacks the Antwerp spirit the Munitions Department expects. A testimonial is proposed for the people of Dundee, who returned Churchill to Parliament after a certain morning paper asked them not to. The Evening News asks what to do with the allotment harvest.

A cartoon opens Punch for August 22, 1917, in volume 153. A poultry keeper hears that defences at the front are sometimes disguised as hen houses. He disguises his hen house as a fort instead, and the enemy is stricken with panic.

Charivaria follows with dog statistics. Policemen bitten numbered eighty-eight in 1913 and forty-four in 1915; one explanation offered is that policemen taste worse than in rabbit-pie days. Heavy rain sprouts Essex corn in the ear, pleasing busy city men who fancy portable allotments. Feeling about the Stockholm Conference shifts, with Ramsay MacDonald proposed as a reprisal.

Charivaria fronts Punch dated August 29, 1917, in volume 153. Germany is a bankrupt concern, says the Daily Mail, and a denial is expected hourly from Herr Michaelis, Germany's official deceiver.

Sympathy goes to Admiral von Tirpitz, whose cure in Switzerland is off; his doctor advised a long sea voyage without adding how to carry it out. Patrons of German royal theatres who pay in gold can now have two seats for the price of one. The offer is less tempting than it sounds. The German who took two seats for one ticket is almost extinct.

Punch, volume 153, dated August 8, 1917, opens with Charivaria and a rebuke to doubt. The Weekly Dispatch remarks that War Office approval, in any amount, will not make hens lay. Such blows at confidence in the war's conduct are called deplorable.

A northern shell-factory workman is fined five pounds for fastening his trousers with iron nails, without explaining why he abandoned the rivets usual in the North. Charlie Chaplin has not joined the United States Army. His excuse is that Pemberton-Billing, a much funnier man, is not in khaki either.

Charivaria leads Punch dated December 12, 1917, in volume 153. Hamburg has a new Company for Oversea Enterprises. Any link with the German High Sea Fleet is firmly denied.

Isle of Wight rabbits fetch a guinea a dozen, though most are holding out for a war bonus before selling. A Newcastle man missing eleven months has turned up at home, excusing himself on the ground that the tea queue was rather a long one. Reports of a brewery workers' strike in the North include threats to down beer. Confirmation of torpedoed food ships is still awaited, in the column's driest manner.

Punch, volume 153, dated December 19, 1917, opens with Charivaria on the fall of Jerusalem. General Allenby has announced that all the holy places will be protected. The Kaiser is about to tell his Turkish subjects that the place is less holy than when he visited in 1898.

The leader of the Sinn Feiners is now stated to be an American citizen, a point unlikely to be pressed given friendly relations with the United States. Another long pamphlet on cheese has come from the Food Controller, whose department claims there is no longer any excuse on that subject.

Charivaria fronts the last number in this set of volume 153, dated December 26, 1917. Von Tirpitz calls victory a mere question of keeping cool. A long-suffering fatherland, the column notes, should manage that easily in winter.

Berlin's semi-official word is that Jerusalem was given up because Germany's friends wished no fighting on holy ground. The Sultan, by report, wired the Kaiser advising him to think of another story. America breaks records again, this time with a miniature said to measure sixty feet by nineteen. A provincial tribunal case begins the remaining items.

Punch, volume 153, dated December 5, 1917, opens with Charivaria and a ruling on rations. Mr. Justice Bray has announced that bigamy is rampant, and the Food Controller wishes it understood that no head of a family will draw a sugar ration for more than one wife.

An Evening News correspondent possesses a loaf baked by her husband's mother in 1821, which disposes of the belief that nobody anticipated the war except Mr. Blatchford. Lug-worms at Deal sell for five shillings a score as an agreeable substitute for macaroni. News from China follows in the same deadpan column.

Charivaria leads Punch for July 11, 1917, opening volume 153. Mrs. H. B. Irving told the National Baby Week Exhibition that a London baby runs more risk than a soldier in France. Middle age, the column notes, bars it from either perilous role.

London County Council tram tickets are now thinner, one of several means under study for giving passengers more room. A boy of sixteen sentenced for theft was found with over a thousand penny dreadfuls, and the commonplace sentence has disgusted him. Reports that Charles Chaplin would serve in the British Army at a shilling a day are denied.

Punch, volume 153, for July 18, 1917, opens with Charivaria. The Emperor of China is reported to have joined the Boy Scout movement, under the paper's spelling of the name.

The Kaiser's anxiety for peace now has an explanation. A Boston paper reports Charlie Chaplin on the point of joining the army for the Allies. A baker is fined ten shillings for selling war bread that was overweight, endangering his customers. German cigars are now made of cabbage or hay flavoured with strawberry leaves, stealing a march on British makers who insist on a flavour of tobacco.

Charivaria fronts Punch dated July 25, 1917, in volume 153. Not one morning paper advocated the appointment of Sir Eric Geddes as First Lord of the Admiralty, which the column calls a big scoop for the government.

Germany reports a shortage of paper yarns, the coarser varieties having been monopolised by the Imperial Government. A foolish rumour claims a music-hall comedian confessed he had never made a joke about the mess in Mesopotamia. With no sea serpent this year, a tope of thirty-nine pounds captured at Hastings fills the vacancy, to its captor's cost.

Mentioned in Despatches, a village tale, leads Punch for July 4, 1917, opening volume 153. The oldest inhabitant sits on a bench in the sun with the day's newspaper across his knees, telling the newest visitor about Billy.

Billy is mentioned in despatches by Sir Douglas Haig himself; without him, the old man asks, where would the army be? He came round the bend whistling, cheery rather than cocky, and always stopped anywhere if you held up your hand. Golfers ran up from the clubhouse and he waited, polite as any gentleman. Readers get a bus driver praised as a war hero, in dialect.

Charivaria opens Punch dated November 14, 1917, in volume 153, with a question: can there be a hidden brain in the Foreign Office? People are asking.

A German posing as a Swiss has been sentenced to six months' imprisonment. Police stated he was a spy and a dangerous character. The matter will be investigated further pending his escape. Three men at Old Street are charged with the pot of tea trick, in which the thief minds your tea while you fetch his ham sandwich, and the tea vanishes. Brandy consumption figures follow in the column's driest register.

Punch, volume 153, dated November 21, 1917, leads with Charivaria. New York has yielded a hidden store of sugar worth over a million pounds, thought to be the start of a hoard.

A contemporary says Lenin claims to stand for the leadership of Russia; the column answers that in Russia they do not stand for leadership, they rush for it with revolvers. Colonel House, newly arrived in England, calls this a time for action rather than talk. A sharp reply is looked for from the Food Controller's people. Restaurant keepers will stamp the price of beefsteaks clearly on the sole.

Charivaria fronts Punch dated November 28, 1917, in volume 153. A correspondent marvels that the Germans got no wind of the attack on the Hindenburg line. Silence from certain members of Parliament beforehand may have done its part.

An order fixes the composition of horse chaff, a measure blamed on the approach of the pantomime season. The Ministry of Food is anxious that Christmas plum puddings should not be kept long. A Young Patriots' League has formed to carry out Lord Rhondda's wishes at any cost to their patriotic stomachs. Winter rations loom behind it all.

Punch, the London humor weekly, dated November 7, 1917, in volume 153, opens as usual with Charivaria, its column of short jokes built from the week's news. Britain was deep in the First World War, and the column treats war strain, food rules, and German politics as fair game for dry, quick mockery.

One item notes that Chancellor Michaelis left office just after a Berlin paper praised him. Others joke about a man fined for feeding oats to a pleasure horse. A ratcatcher is granted sugar so rats would take poison. A rumor adds that a maker could earn a title by giving sugar to party funds.

Dated October 10, 1917, this issue of the London comic paper Punch, volume 153, leads with Charivaria, a run of brief jokes drawn from current headlines. The war sits behind nearly every line, yet the tone stays light, poking at clergy, courts, enemy cities, and famous names alike.

Colonel Roosevelt tells an interviewer he cannot be in France and America at once, and the column doubts he has really tried. A Berlin coal dealer is punished for rudeness, a Belfast woman is caught chewing bank notes, and George Moore's low view of Stevenson as a storyteller draws a pointed reply.

Volume 153 of Punch, the London Charivari, for October 17, 1917, begins with Charivaria, the magazine's weekly string of short, sharp jokes on public events. Printed in the third year of the Great War, the column mixes home-front food rules with jabs at the Kaiser and his government.

The German sailors' mutiny at Kiel is blamed on dread of another speech from the Kaiser. A Turkish poet's Shakespeare is teased, flour is banned from sausages, and Germany's new Pulp Commission draws a dry remark. Even the King of Siam's yacht, now hauling cargo, earns a closing joke.

For October 24, 1917, Punch offers its readers volume 153 and a Charivaria column packed with short jokes on wartime life in Britain. The humor weekly turns royal visits, army ranks, escaped submarines, and city honors into brief comic notes, each only a few lines long.

The Duke of Connaught is said to have braved two glasses of government ale at a factory canteen. Two German bankers face arrest in New York. Spain promises care over the escape of U23. The Premier's gold casket of London freedom prompts a rumor that it might hold tea instead.

Punch for October 3, 1917, volume 153, starts with Charivaria, where the London humor magazine turns the week's war news into a chain of short, dry jokes. German prisoners, sermons, Arctic travelers, and London cab fares all pass through the same mocking lens within a single page.

One joke denies that King Alfonso was asked to limit German prisoner escapes to Sundays. The Bishop of London's sermon is turned against young staff officers. Eskimos who had not heard of the war embarrass a newspaper's reach. The Kaiser, quoting his own speech, is called a forger of a high order.

Halloween 1917 finds Punch, volume 153, opening with Charivaria, its regular column of brief jokes on the news of the week. Food control, government building seizures, and escaped prisoners give the London weekly plenty to mock in the fourth autumn of the war.

The Ministry of Food rules that a doughnut is not a bun, calming Twickenham. London grocers ask for orders a week ahead. German escapees are caught with ease. A paper's piece called "The End of the World" is read as fear of Churchill gaining an air post. The Kaiser keeps Admiral von Capelle, to the column's pity.

September 12, 1917 brings volume 153 of Punch and a Charivaria column of quick jokes aimed at the war and at daily life in Britain. The London comic weekly mixes American troops, film stars, objectors, and giant vegetables into one short page of deadpan humor.

A German paper warns that American soldiers will be slowed by foreign tongues, and the column answers that Americans can shoot in any language. A man who refuses any part in the war plans a sharp letter to the War Office. Charlie Chaplin's new American status and a forty-three-pound marrow from the Isle of Wight close the page.

Volume 153 of the London Charivari, dated September 19, 1917, leads off with Charivaria, Punch's column of short jokes built from small news items. Wartime Britain supplies the targets: a peace conference, food prices, tube fares, and even a stolen church clock.

Rumors that the national anthem would gain a line about Scandinavian tricks are denied with a straight face. The Stockholm Conference is feared sunk without a trace, a Wimbledon church loses its clock, and a servant in the East asks what war everyone means. Undertakers' mutes form a union and, the column hopes, will strike for longer life.

Readers opening Punch for September 26, 1917, volume 153, meet Charivaria first, the column where the London weekly turns small news stories into short comic notes. War shortages and enemy royalty share space with a boy who ate far too much in Chatham.

Three bandits shot in Mexico without trial are declared, in jest, not legally shot at all. Butterflies under attack now travel in pairs for safety. A Chatham boy spends a pound note on cakes, fish and chips, fruit, and pop, then feels ill, while a Kingston potato shaped like the German Crown Prince earns the closing lines.

Punch dated September 5, 1917, volume 153, opens with Charivaria, a page of brief jokes on the war and on small events around Britain. The Kaiser, escaped prisoners, wet weather, and a shortage of matches all get the same calm, mocking treatment.

The Kaiser urges his fleet, safe at Wilhelmshaven, to stick to it, which the column finds easy advice from shore. A rumor that an escaped German fled dressed as Ramsay MacDonald is denied. A man accused of whistling for a cab pleads that the sound was his natural face, and smokers short of matches wait by fires for a light.
randolph-the-truth-about-lynching-its-ca: The Truth About Lynching is shown here by a single title page, its edges garbled in the scan. The page divides the pamphlet in two. Its Causes and Effects is by Asa Philip. His surname is cut off at the page edge. He was president of the Independent Political Council. He edited The Messenger. The Remedy is by Chandler Owen. Owen was executive secretary of the same council. He edited The Messenger too. The publisher is the Cosmo-Advocate Publishing Company, 2305 Seventh Avenue, New York.
reuchlin-de-arte-cabalistica-1517:
Johann Reuchlin founds Christian Kabbalah in De Arte Cabalistica, in Latin from 1517. The great humanist teaches Christians to read the Jewish mystics with respect. Hebrew letters hide, in his account, deep truths about God and Christ that Greek and Latin learning alone could never have found without the key.

Reuchlin risked his name to defend Jewish books from the flames. His stand made him the hero of the humanists' war against obscurantism. Erasmus and his circle rallied to the aging scholar's cause in print. The book brought Kabbalah into Renaissance thought for good, and it still marks the spot where two great traditions met in one mind.
ricardo-principles-1817:
David Ricardo was a London stockbroker who retired rich and turned to writing on money, rent, and trade. His Principles of Political Economy and Taxation, published in 1817, is the engine room of classical economics. Later thinkers from Marx to modern trade theorists built on its frame.

Ricardo argues that rent rises as farming is pushed onto poorer land, while wages and profit pull against each other. His best-known idea, comparative advantage, shows how two nations both gain when each makes what it makes best. The reasoning is dry and tight, and it still drives debate on trade.
robinson-merlin-1917:
Edwin Arlington Robinson turned to the Arthurian legends for Merlin, a long blank-verse poem published in 1917. Robinson had spent two decades writing about small-town failures in Maine. Here he tested his powers on the grandest story material in English tradition.

Robinson's Merlin is no stage magician but a weary, self-aware man who foresees the ruin of Camelot. He leaves Arthur's court for love with Vivian, knowing the escape cannot last. Around them the fellowship of the Round Table rots from within. The poem treats the legend as a mirror for a world sliding toward war, which readers in 1917 felt keenly. Merlin is Robinson's most ambitious single poem.
russell-finished-mystery-vol7-1917:
The Finished Mystery appeared in 1917, a year after Russell's death, as the seventh Studies in the Scriptures volume. Followers completed it from his notes, expounding Revelation, Ezekiel, and the Song of Solomon verse by verse. The church's leaders hailed it as the founder's posthumous gift to his people.

Instead it split the movement, and its publication fed the great schism of 1918. Governments also seized on its pages during wartime. The volume that was meant to crown the set became its most fought-over book, which makes it key reading on how the Bible Students divided.
russell-political-ideals-1917:
Political Ideals, published in 1917, gathers lectures Russell gave while Britain was at war and he was campaigning against it. Excluded from Cambridge for his pacifism, he turned to the question of how political life should be rebuilt after the war.

Russell argues that institutions should be judged by whether they free or stifle creative impulse. He sketches reforms in government, property, and education aimed at growth rather than obedience. The tone is hopeful against the evidence of the trenches. The lectures show Russell the public moralist forming, a role he would play for fifty years.
sacconi-summa-de-catharis-1717:
Rainier Sacconi had been a Cathar perfect for seventeen years before he turned Dominican and inquisitor. His Summa de Catharis, written around 1250, reports the sect from the inside. Martène and Durand printed the Latin in their Thesaurus Novus Anecdotorum in 1717. No closer witness to Cathar doctrine survives.

Sacconi maps the Cathar churches of Italy and France, their bishops, their rite of consolamentum, and their split over how the evil world was made. He counts their numbers and names their houses with an ex-member's exactness. His aim was to arm preachers against them, yet his facts outlived his cause. Scholars still start with Sacconi for what the Cathars actually taught.
simmel-grundfragen-der-soziologie-1917:
Georg Simmel published his Fundamental Questions of Sociology in German in 1917, late in a career spent mostly outside the university's inner circle. Sociology was still a young science without a settled subject. Simmel's little book asks what that subject really is, and answers with the clarity of a lifetime's thought.

His answer: sociology studies the forms of human association, the patterns by which people join, rule, compete, and cooperate. The same forms, the dyad, the triad, the stranger, recur in churches, armies, and markets alike. Content changes; the geometry of relations endures. The book is the Berlin master's late, brief statement of his life's theme. It remains the clearest short door into Simmel's work, the place where society's geometry is traced in a few bold lines.
sinclair-king-coal-1917:
Upton Sinclair published King Coal in 1917, drawing on the Colorado coal strike of 1913 and 1914 and the Ludlow Massacre that ended it. Sinclair had visited the strike zone, picketed in New York for the miners, and been arrested for his pains. The novel sends a rich man's son into the camps in disguise.

Hal Warner, a coal operator's heir, takes a job under a false name to learn the mines from inside. He finds company towns run like feudal estates: scrip pay, cheated weights, and guards against organizers. A mine disaster turns his education into action, and he joins the strike he came to observe. Sinclair builds his case like a prosecutor. King Coal is his novel of the mine wars, still the fullest fictional record of them.
slave-narratives-a-folk-history-of-slave: Slave Narratives gathers talks with former slaves into a folk history of slavery in the United States. The typed records were made by the Federal Writers' Project in 1936-1938 and put together by the Library of Congress project, with photos, at Washington in 1941. One part is Volume XII, the Ohio Narratives. Its list of those who spoke begins with Charles H. Anderson, Melissa Barden, Susan Bledsoe, Phoebe Bost, and Ben Brown.
state-of-the-union-addresses-pg5017:
Martin Van Buren gives four yearly addresses, from December 5, 1837, to December 5, 1840, parted by three stars. The first renews devout thanks to the Giver of All Good for his kind guard. On every side, Van Buren says, the country shows lasting favor, having risen by degrees from a few weak and held colonies to a thriving and strong band of states.

Calm rules at home, and all the seeds of national thriving are at hand. A sickness that for a time struck some rich parts of the Union has been kept in bounds and stopped in its deadly course. Trade skill and care are by degrees freeing folk from the money troubles that weighed on some. Sound laws and the country's vast stores have lent wise and timely aid to private work, and busy hands have in great part found their old gainful paths again.
symbola-avreae-mensae-dvodecim-nationvm-: Only the opening leaves are present here, and much of their type is garbled. A catalogue entry lists works of Michael Maier. Among them stands Symbola Aureae Mensae Duodecim Nationum, with engraved border, portrait, and plates, printed at Frankfort in 1617. His De Circulo Physico Quadrato of 1616 and Jocus Severus of 1617 stand beside it. A note credits the Getty Research Library. The book's own pages do not appear in readable form here.
tagore-nationalism-1917:
In Nationalism, published in 1917, Tagore prints lectures he gave in Japan and America during the First World War. He warns his hearers that nationalism, the worship of the nation as a machine of power, is a spiritual menace. The warning sounded strange while empires were at war.

Tagore argues that the modern state, built for gain and force, crushes the social and moral life of a people. He speaks to Japan, to America, and to his own India in turn, urging each toward a wider human loyalty. His critique of the modern state still reads as prophecy to many.
tales-and-novels-of-j-de-la-fontaine-vol:
Volume 17 of The Tales and Novels of J. de La Fontaine contains The Progress of Wit, The Sick Abbess, and The Truckers. The first of the three is less a story than a riddle the poet sets his readers, in praise of a certain play.

He calls it a diverting game. It resumes its fascinating sway by night or day. It delights the sex, fair, ugly, or sour. It is sweet at any hour and known everywhere to fame. He bids the reader guess its name. Its chief charm, he adds, is unknown to husbands, for it excels with the lover alone and needs no umpires. The Sick Abbess and The Truckers follow in tale form, turning to convent illness and to carriers cheated and cheating on the road.
the-bastonnais-tale-of-the-american-inva:
John Lesperance published a Canadian tale in Toronto in 1877, set during the American invasion of Canada in 1775 and 1776. Book one is called The Gathering of the Storm. Early chapters name blue lights, a chateau, cathedral square, and the receiving of despatches.

Pauline weeps, a beautiful rebel appears, and a hermit of Montmorenci enters the list. A casket, a spirit of a waterfall, and Three Rivers follow, mixing war with romance. Lovers meet, a round table gathers, and a noble reparation is promised. Headings for a spectral army and frightened doves close the first book's list on an eerie note.
the-caxtons-a-family-picture-volume-17:
Pisistratus pauses the story in Part XVII of The Caxtons, the family novel that is also his life. He narrates, as ever, in the first person. His father the scholar waits in the wings while the son addresses his audience directly, theater-style.

The narrator pauses the tale and speaks to his readers as if they sat in a theater between acts. He bids the audience settle, chat, and look about the house. Ladies in the boxes take up opera glasses, boys in the gallery sound the cat-call, and grave critics in the pit shake their heads at new actors. The aside treats long habit and the creed of youth with warm respect before the story resumes.
the-great-events-by-famous-historians-vo: Rossiter Johnson was editor-in-chief of The Great Events by Famous Historians. This record is Volume XVII. Only front matter is present here. It gives the title page and a contents list. The list opens with an outline narrative by Charles F. Horne. The pieces then run by year: the telegraph in 1844; the Corn Laws repeal and Neptune in 1846. It names the Mexican War and famine in Ireland for 1847. It names the Mormon migrations and the February Revolution in France for 1848.
the-great-round-world-and-what-is-going-: Dated March 4, 1897, this seventeenth number of The Great Round World and What Is Going On in It is a weekly newspaper for boys and girls. Only front matter is present here. It gives the masthead and the paper's prize competitions, open to subscribers only. Five prizes go to the best five commercial maps of the United States. Each prize is a book of the winner's choice, costing not over $2.50. Klemm's Relief Map is to be used, and one is sent free to any subscriber who competes.
the-history-of-don-quixote-volume-1-part:
Don Quixote, by Miguel de Cervantes, reaches Volume 1, Part 17 here, in John Ormsby's translation. Chapter fifty tells of the shrewd controversy Don Quixote and the canon held, with other incidents. The argument turns on books of chivalry and how they are judged.

A good joke, that, Don Quixote returns, when the worth of such books is doubted. He points out that the books were printed with the king's licence and with the approval of those who reviewed them, and read widely. The canon presses a learned case while the knight defends the romances that shaped his life. Talk replaces blows for this stretch of the road home.
the-merry-wives-of-windsor-pg1517: William Shakespeare's The Merry Wives of Windsor shows only its scene list and the first part of its cast here, so the play itself does not appear. The scenes move between Page's house, Ford's house, Doctor Caius's house, and the Garter Inn, ending in Windsor Park. The cast opens with the Host of the Garter Inn and Sir John Falstaff, followed by his page Robin and his followers Bardolph, Pistol, and Nym. Justice Shallow and his cousin Slender come next.
the-mirror-of-literature-amusement-and-i: Only the title page of Volume 13 is present for this record, so no issue or article appears here. The page, printed and published by J. Limbird at 143 Strand in 1829, is headed by a portrait of the late Sir Humphry Davy. Its contents promise original essays, historical narratives, biographical memoirs, sketches of society, and topographical descriptions. Novels and tales, anecdotes, poetry, discoveries in the arts and sciences, and useful domestic hints complete the list. A preface begins below, declining to be long in a season of ennui.

Number 477 of The Mirror of Literature, Amusement, and Instruction, dated Saturday, February 19, 1831, illustrates Mount St. Michael in Normandy. The mount, at the province's southern extremity, is one mass of granite, a fine specimen of the primary rock containing no remains of a former world. It carries celebrity in the chronicles of old France and England alike. Current politics add interest, the editors note.

The ex-minister Polignac will in all probability be exiled to this monastic spot, they predict. A pattern is confessed: Lulworth Castle, the Hotel de Ville, and the Palais Royal in the last volume, then Vincennes prison and Mount St. Michael in this one. Instead of catching manners as they rise, the magazine seems to watch crowns and ministers falling headlong. The mount's recent English visitor, a Mrs. whose name begins the next portion, awaits below. Readers get geology and revolution sharing one granite island.
the-queen-of-hearts-pg1917: Wilkie Collins organizes his tales as ten days of storytelling. Three brothers take turns as narrators. Owen tells of a siege at a black cottage. Griffith tells of a family secret and of Mad Monkton. He also tells of a biter bit. Morgan tells of a dream-woman and of a dead hand. Owen returns with a parson's scruple. Only the title pages and contents list are present here. The tales themselves do not appear. The list extends the shorter one in the companion record.
the-skin-game-a-tragi-comedy-pg2917: John Galsworthy's The Skin Game, a tragi-comedy, is presented here through its cast and scene plan. Hornblower is a man newly rich, with sons Charles and Rolf. Chloe, wife to Charles, has her own maid, Anna. The epigraph warns that who touches pitch shall be defiled. Act one is set in Hillcrist's study, the plan says. Act two moves to an auction room and Chloe's boudoir. No dialogue appears in the portion shown.
theoria-philosophiae-hermeticae-septem-t: Henricus Nollius, professor of medicine at the gymnasium at Steinfurt, explained a theory of hermetic philosophy in seven treatises. A damaged Latin title page lists them, starting with Verus Hermes and a gate of hermetic wisdom. Other tracts treat hermetic silence and axioms. Further headings promise the generation, regeneration, and renovation of natural things. Hermetic philosophy mixed medicine, alchemy, and nature study in this period. The title page shown here is garbled and stands alone, so Nollius's treatises themselves are not present.
tob-0117:
Organized Freemasonry dates its public life from James Anderson's Constitutions of 1723. The young Grand Lodge of England ordered the book, and Anderson, a Scottish minister, compiled it. Lodges across the world still treat it as their founding charter.

A legendary history runs from Adam through Solomon's temple to London, giving the craft an ancient pedigree. Then come the Charges, rules of conduct for Masons, and the Regulations for running lodges. Every later Masonic constitution descends from these pages. This entry draws on a checked pre-1930 edition. Few club rulebooks have ever mattered so much.
tob-10017:
Job is the eighteenth book in this King James ordering, and its author is unknown. Its central figure is a righteous man who loses family, wealth, and health in a single sweep of disaster. The story is told largely as poetry, in long speeches rather than plain narrative.

Job's friends insist his suffering must be punishment for some sin. Job rejects that answer and demands to plead his case before God. God finally speaks from a whirlwind, answering with questions about creation rather than an explanation. Few ancient books press the problem of undeserved pain so openly, or leave the sufferer still speaking back.
tob-10817:
Israel Abrahams walked through the whole of Jewish literature in Chapters on Jewish Literature, in short, readable chapters. Bible and Talmud come first, then medieval philosophy and poetry, and finally modern writers. Three thousand years of writing pass through one slim volume, with each stop chosen to highlight essentials.

Abrahams explains what the essential books are and why they matter, rather than merely listing titles. His map helps readers place a name like Maimonides or a form like Midrash in a living sequence. For students beginning Jewish studies, or general readers filling a gap, Abrahams remains a humane guide who assumes curiosity, not prior knowledge.
tob-4017:
Vasari crowns his history in volume three with the giants: Leonardo, Raphael, and above all Michelangelo, whom he worshipped as art's culmination. The volume runs to Vasari's own contemporaries, making the ending read like a victory lap for his age and city. Florence, in his telling, has led art back to life and beyond the ancients.

Many famous Renaissance legends survive only because Vasari recorded them, which makes the volume source and suspect at once. His Michelangelo material draws on personal acquaintance and devotion. Students still start here for the stories behind the works, then check them against documents Vasari never saw or chose not to use.
tob-4117:
Volume two of Bhishagratna's Sushruta Samhita turns from the operating room to the clinic. Sickness, fevers, and poisons fill its pages, with their causes, signs, and cures set out in the Ayurvedic manner. Bhishagratna finished the translation in 1911 from the Sanskrit.

Snakebite, madness, and diseases of eye and ear each get their regimen of herbs, oils, and diet. The physician's judgment matters as much as the drugs. Together the two volumes give Ayurveda's surgical classic in full English dress. Checked from the 1919 printing, book two completes a landmark: the Indian healer's handbook, whole at last.
twenty-two-goblins-ryder-1917:
Arthur W. Ryder translated Twenty-two Goblins in 1917, from Sivadasa's recension of the Vetala-Panchavimsati. King Vikrama carries a goblin-haunted corpse from a burning ground, and the vetala tells him tales on the road. Each tale ends in a riddle; if the king speaks the answer, the corpse flies back to its tree.

The frame forces the king to repeat his journey again and again, tale after tale. Sanskrit story craft shows at its cleverest here, mixing wit, horror, and moral puzzles. Ryder, a beloved Berkeley teacher, gave the cycle an English as crisp as its own riddles.
un-ga-res-17: House rules for the new General Assembly fill Resolution 17, passed on 29 January 1946. One fix bars the General Committee from deciding any question of politics. A new rule lets a member state with no seat on that committee sit in, without a vote, when its own request for a new agenda item is heard. A third change ends nominations under Rule 73.
un-ga-res-a-69-17: How the UN plans its work and spends its funds fills Resolution A/69/17, from the Assembly's sixty-ninth session. The text recalls a long chain of votes back to 1982 on programme planning and the budget. It recalls the mandate of the Committee for Programme and Coordination, the body that checks plans before money is set. Rules on planning, budgets, watch of work done, and tests of worth frame the whole system.
un-ga-res-united-nations-general-assembl: General Assembly Resolution 17 was adopted in January 1946. It made three small changes to the Assembly's provisional rules of procedure. One change added words barring a committee from deciding political questions. One let a member with no seat on the General Committee attend and speak. That applied when its own agenda request was heard. One barred nominations under rule 73. A further change let the Economic and Social Council call world conferences on trade, prices, and health.

Resolution 69/17 is the General Assembly's programme-planning decision for the 2016–2017 period. It backs the findings of the Committee for Programme and Coordination on United Nations performance in 2012–2013 and on the proposed strategic framework. It fixes the organization's priorities for 2016–2017. They are economic growth and sustainable development, peace and security, and development of Africa. They are human rights, humanitarian coordination, and justice and international law. They are disarmament, and drug control and counter-terrorism. The Secretary-General is told to build the next programme budget around those aims.
un-sc-res-117: Judge Hsu Mo of China died in June 1956, leaving a seat open at the International Court of Justice. On 6 September 1956 the Security Council set the election to fill the vacancy. The vote would take place during the General Assembly's eleventh session. The decision was taken without a formal vote. The text follows the standard wording of the court's statute. It does nothing beyond fixing the occasion for the election.
un-sc-res-1317: From the Council's official record comes the text numbered 1317, catalogued here at 2000. Behind each numbered text lies a meeting, a draft, and a vote, even when the final wording runs to a few lines. Read in sequence with its neighbours, it helps trace how Council practice grew across the postwar decades. No summary replaces it; the record itself is the content of the entry.
un-sc-res-1417:
United Nations Security Council Resolution 1417 deals with the Democratic Republic of the Congo and its long war. The Council adopted it on 14 June 2002. Talks among Congolese parties at Sun City had raised hopes, but killings in Kisangani that May shocked the Council. Foreign troops still held parts of the country.

The text extends the United Nations mission, called MONUC, until 30 June 2003. States are asked to fill the mission up to its full strength of 5,537 troops. The Council condemns the Kisangani killings and holds the rebel group in charge there to blame. It demands the full and fast withdrawal of all foreign forces from the Congo.
un-sc-res-1517:
Cyprus's peacekeeping force gained six more months in November 2003. On 24 November 2003 the Security Council extended UNFICYP until 15 June 2004. The government of Cyprus agreed the force should remain. The Secretary-General's report had called on the parties to address missing persons with urgency. That humanitarian issue ran alongside the military one. The Council restated its Cyprus resolutions, with 1251 of 1999 at their head.

Turkish Cypriot leaders and Turkish forces had to lift all limits on UNFICYP. The Council voiced concern at new breaches at Strovilia. It demanded the military position there as it stood before 30 June 2000. The force's freedom of movement was a standing sore point.
un-sc-res-1617:
Al-Qaida and Taliban sanctions are the subject of United Nations Security Council Resolution 1617, adopted on 29 July 2005. The threat had shifted since the first sanctions text in 1999. Groups used the internet for propaganda and recruitment. The Council wanted a clear test for who counts as linked to the networks.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council keeps the asset freeze, travel ban, and arms embargo on listed names. It defines being associated with the networks to cover funding, planning, arming, and recruiting for them. States must file a written case when they propose a name. Lost passports must be voided fast and shared through Interpol. The expert Monitoring Team is extended for seventeen months.
un-sc-res-17: How far a UN probe's powers reach was tested in Security Council Resolution 17, passed on 10 February 1947. The team sent to study the Greek border fight had asked the Council a point of law. The team wished to ask the Greek state to hold back the death penalty for men judged for acts of state. Does its writ allow such a plea? The Council's answer is no. The team may plead a stay only where a man's words as a witness would aid its own work.
un-sc-res-1717: Resolution 1717 is a Security Council decision preserved in official-record form, transcribed for this collection by English Wikisource. The fifteen members act as one body in such texts, whatever their private disagreements. The entry preserves the public result of that process: a single document, numbered and complete, whose words carry the Council's authority.
un-sc-res-1817: Kept under the number 1817, a formal Security Council decision survives in this collection in official-record form. The transcription comes from English Wikisource. Inside, the members' findings come first, in the preamble's careful clauses; their decisions follow in numbered order. The entry's completeness lets any later reader test summaries against the source itself.
un-sc-res-1917:
Resolution 1917 recorded the Council's decision on Afghanistan, adopted on 22 March 2010. The London Conference that January had set fresh goals under Afghan leadership. A Kabul conference was planned for later in the year. Taliban and Al-Qaida attacks still threatened civilians, aid workers, and Afghan forces.

The Council extends the assistance mission, called UNAMA, until 23 March 2011. The mission leads the civilian aid effort and backs Afghan ownership of the recovery. It will help prepare the 2010 parliamentary polls and support Afghan-led peace talks. The text ties security, honest government, and growth together. It also presses for stronger regional cooperation and better protection of civilians.
un-sc-res-2017:
When the Council met on 31 October 2011, it adopted Resolution 2017 on Libya after the fall of Muammar Gaddafi, days after the civil war ended. Weapons from Libyan stockpiles were spreading across the region, and the Council feared they would reach armed groups.

The text calls on Libya's new leaders to secure all arms and guard them with care. It singles out shoulder-fired missiles that can bring down aircraft. It urges work with the global chemical weapons body to destroy Libya's chemical stocks. A sanctions panel must study the threat and propose ways to keep the weapons contained.
un-sc-res-217: Resolution 217 of the Security Council reaches readers here as an official record text, catalogued under the year 1961. Behind each numbered text lies a meeting, a draft, and a vote, even when the final wording runs to a few lines. Read in sequence with its neighbours, it helps trace how Council practice grew across the postwar decades.
un-sc-res-317: Catalogue data places Resolution 317, a United Nations Security Council text, in the year 1972. The Council is the UN body charged with world peace and security, and it speaks formally through texts like this one. For students of the UN, the record offers the Council's language itself rather than a summary written later. The entry belongs to the library's DECLASSIFIED group of public official records.
un-sc-res-417:
United Nations Security Council Resolution 417 condemns South Africa's apartheid government for its violent crackdown on black citizens. The Council adopted the text on 31 October 1977. Reports told of torture of prisoners, deaths in detention, and bans on groups and newspapers.

The Council demands that the regime end its violence and free people jailed under security laws. It also demands an end to torture, to bans on the press, and to the Bantu education system. It asks governments to help victims, including students who fled the country. The Secretary-General had to report back by 17 February 1978.
un-sc-res-717:
Cambodia's settlement gained a United Nations advance team in October 1991. The Paris framework of August 1990 had been endorsed by resolution 668 (1990). Draft accords for a full settlement were now on the table. Prince Norodom Sihanouk had been elected chairman of the Supreme National Council. The Cambodian parties had declared a voluntary ceasefire and renounced foreign military aid.

The Council approved the Secretary-General's report of 30 September 1991. It decided to set up, under its authority, a United Nations Advance Mission in Cambodia, UNAMIC. The mission would deploy as soon as the Paris accords were signed. Its first tasks were to help the parties keep the ceasefire and to start mine awareness work. The Supreme National Council and the Cambodian parties were called to cooperate with the mission in full. The Council welcomed the plan to reconvene the Paris Conference at ministerial level.
un-sc-res-817: Preserved as Resolution 817, this Security Council text carries a 1993 date in the catalog record. A resolution may address a conflict, a court vacancy, a new member, or the running of the United Nations itself. Anyone studying UN practice can read the decision itself here, in the Wikisource transcription of the official record. The catalog places it in the DECLASSIFIED group of official public records.
un-sc-res-united-nations-security-counci:
The world court lost a senior judge in the summer of 1956. Judge Hsu Mo of China died on 28 June that year. His term on the bench still had years to run. Resolution 117, passed without a vote on 6 September 1956, set the way to fill his seat.

The Council chose the Assembly's next session for the vote. Judges there are picked by both big bodies at once. The eleventh session would host the ballot. Hsu Mo had served since the court's first days in 1946. He was a key figure in Chinese law. His death left one of the court's founding minds gone. The text is brief, a formal note of loss and a date for the cure.

Sierra Leone's peacekeeping mission gets only a few extra days in this brief text of 5 September 2000. UNAMSIL, the United Nations Mission in Sierra Leone, was backing a fragile peace process after years of civil war. In two short operative lines, the Council moved the mission's deadline to 20 September 2000. It also kept the country's situation under active review while it decided what should come next for the mission.

War in the Democratic Republic of the Congo is the setting for Resolution 1417, adopted on 14 June 2002. The UN Mission, MONUC, was still building toward its authorized strength. Killings and attacks in Kisangani in May had followed fighting there, and RCD-Goma held power in that city. The Inter-Congolese Dialogue at Sun City had made progress but produced no all-inclusive deal yet. Foreign forces were leaving, though slowly.

The Council extends MONUC until 30 June 2003 and calls on states to supply personnel up to the authorized 5,537. It holds RCD-Goma responsible for ending executions, rights abuses, and harassment in Kisangani and demands the city's demilitarization. It backs MONUC's work on disarming and sending home foreign fighters and its deployments to Kisangani and Kindu. It demands the total, speedy withdrawal of all foreign forces, with plans and timetables sent to MONUC. Reports are due at least every four months.

Cyprus's peacekeeping routine continued with Resolution 1517, adopted unanimously on 24 November 2003. The Secretary-General reported on 12 November about the UN operation. He urged both sides to address the fate of missing persons urgently. Cyprus's government agreed the UN force should stay past December. Conditions on the island left little choice.

Members extended UNFICYP's mandate until 15 June 2004. They demanded an end to all remaining restrictions on the force. Violations at Strovilia drew sharp concern. Turkish Cypriot forces had altered positions there since June 2000. The Council insisted the earlier military balance be restored. A report on implementation was due by 1 June 2004.

Resolution 1617 is a Security Council decision adopted on 29 July 2005. It renewed and tightened sanctions against Al-Qaida, the Taliban, and people and groups tied to them. It builds on the sanctions system first set up in resolution 1267 in 1999. That system was restated in several later resolutions.

Under its terms, all states must freeze the funds of listed persons. They must also bar their travel and block arms sales to them. The text spells out what counts as being associated with Al-Qaida or the Taliban. It asks states to give a statement of case when proposing names for the Consolidated List. It also extends the Monitoring Team that helps the sanctions committee, for seventeen more months.

A question from its own fact-finding commission in Greece is answered on 10 February 1947. The Commission of Investigation, created weeks earlier, had asked whether it could request Greece to postpone executions of people sentenced to death for political offences. The question reached the Council while the commission was working in the region.

The commission, the Council ruled, had no power to ask Greece, Albania, Bulgaria, or Yugoslavia to delay any execution. There was one narrow exception. If the commission had reason to believe that hearing a condemned person as a witness would help its inquiry, it could ask for a postponement on that ground alone. The Secretary-General was to pass this reading of the mandate to the commission.

Rwanda tribunal short-term judges are allowed to finish the cases they have begun, in this text of 13 October 2006. Eighteen ad litem judges had been elected in 2003 for four years ending in June 2007. Several were mid-trial in cases that would not end before their terms expired, and the Secretary-General had asked the Council to act.

The ad litem judges named in the text may keep serving past their terms until the cases they are assigned to are completed. One judge may also be assigned to a further case as needed. States are asked again to make sure their nationals serving as ad litem judges are released to sit for the tribunal, so its completion strategy is not held up by staffing gaps.

The chemical precursors that turn Afghan opium into heroin are targeted on 11 June 2008. Afghanistan's drug trade fed terrorism, organized crime, and money laundering. The key chemicals, above all acetic anhydride, are legal in normal trade but are smuggled into Afghanistan for drug making.

All states are called on to tighten cooperation against drug production and trafficking in Afghanistan, including stronger tracking of the world trade in precursor chemicals. Exporting states are urged to notify importing countries of every shipment of the relevant chemicals when asked, under the 1988 drug convention. The aim is to stop legal shipments being diverted into heroin production while keeping lawful trade moving.

Afghanistan's UN mission is renewed behind the London Conference agenda in Resolution 1917, adopted on 22 March 2010. The London Conference of 28 January 2010 had set priorities under Afghan ownership. A Kabul conference was planned for later in the year. Taliban and Al-Qaida violence, civilian casualties, and the narcotics trade remained severe.

The Council extends the United Nations Assistance Mission in Afghanistan, UNAMA, until 23 March 2011. UNAMA and the Special Representative continue to lead the international civilian effort. They co-chair the Joint Coordination and Monitoring Board to align donor support with Afghan priorities. They improve civil-military coordination with ISAF. They give good offices for Afghan-led reconciliation and reintegration within the sanctions framework. They support preparations for the 2010 national legislative elections. UNAMA must also help the government prepare the Kabul conference and the transition toward Afghan leadership on security, governance, and development.

Weapons spilling out of Libya after its 2011 war are the worry in Resolution 2017, adopted on 31 October 2011. Arms of all kinds, above all shoulder-fired surface-to-air missiles, were spreading across the region. The Council feared they could fuel attacks by groups such as Al-Qaida in the Islamic Maghreb and unsettle the Sahel. Libya's chemical weapons stocks also still had to be destroyed.

The Council calls on Libya's authorities to stop the spread of arms, keep them in safe custody, and meet the country's arms control duties. It calls on Libya to keep working with the Organization for the Prohibition of Chemical Weapons to destroy its chemical stocks. States in the region are asked to weigh steps against this flow. The Libya sanctions committee, with its Panel of Experts, must judge the threats this spread poses and report with plans to counter it and guard stockpiles and borders.

Southern Rhodesia's white minority rulers declared independence from Britain on their own in November 1965. Britain, the ruling power, treated the move as an act of rebellion. The Council adopted Resolution 217 on 20 November 1965 to answer the declaration.

The Council condemned the seizure of power by a racist settler minority. It said the declaration of independence had no legal validity. Britain was called on to crush the rebellion and end the minority regime at once. All states were told not to recognize the illegal authority. They had to cut off arms and military supplies. Economic ties had to be broken as well, including an embargo on oil and petroleum products.

Israeli forces had seized Syrian and Lebanese soldiers and security staff on Lebanese territory on 21 June 1972. An earlier resolution, passed that June, had already pressed for their release, without result. The Council returned to the matter in Resolution 317, adopted on 21 July 1972.

The Council reaffirmed the June resolution. It deplored the fact that the captured men had still not been freed. Work by the Council's president and by the Secretary-General had not secured their release. Israel was called on to return the men without delay. The president and the Secretary-General were also asked to make fresh efforts. Their task was to see the resolution carried out at last.

South Africa's crackdown on apartheid's opponents is condemned in Resolution 417, adopted on 31 October 1977. The Council noted reports of torture of political prisoners, deaths of detainees, and a wave of bans on people, groups, and news outlets since 19 October 1977. It recalled its 1976 condemnation of killings of African protesters, including schoolchildren in Soweto.

The Council strongly condemns the regime's mass violence and states its solidarity with those fighting apartheid. It demands an end to violence and repression. It demands freedom for everyone jailed under security laws or for opposing apartheid. It also demands a halt to killings in detention and torture. It also demands that bans on anti-apartheid groups and media be lifted. It demands that the Bantu education system end. It demands that majority rule based on justice and equality replace apartheid and the bantustan policy.

Cambodia's peace settlement takes a step forward in Resolution 717, adopted in 1991. Draft agreements for a full settlement were ready, built on a framework the Council had backed in Resolution 668. The Supreme National Council of Cambodia had chosen Prince Norodom Sihanouk as its chairman, backed a voluntary ceasefire, and asked for UN staff to be sent quickly.

The Council approves the Secretary-General's plan and decides to set up a United Nations Advance Mission in Cambodia as soon as the settlement papers are signed. The mission's members are to head to Cambodia right after the signing. The Council calls on the Cambodian parties to work with the mission and welcomes the plan to reopen the Paris Conference so ministers can sign the agreements.

A new state from the former Yugoslavia sought a United Nations seat in 1993, but its name stood in the way. The applicant met the tests for membership set out in Article 4 of the Charter. A dispute had arisen over the state's name, and it had to be settled for the sake of calm in the region. Resolution 817 was adopted on 7 April 1993.

The Council recommended to the General Assembly that the state be admitted. Inside the United Nations, it would be referred to for the time being as "the former Yugoslav Republic of Macedonia". That temporary name would hold for all United Nations purposes until the dispute was settled. The parties were urged to keep working with the co-chairmen of the peace conference on the former Yugoslavia. Their task was to reach a speedy settlement of the difference over the name.
wharton-summer-1917:
Edith Wharton published Summer in 1917, setting it in a poor Berkshire village she called North Dormer. Wharton usually wrote about rich New Yorkers. Here she turned to a young woman with almost nothing, and produced her boldest novel of female desire.

Charity Royall, adopted from a lawless mountain settlement, works in the village library and suffocates under her guardian's eye. A young architect, Lucius Harney, arrives to study old houses, and a summer love affair follows. Charity's awakening brings freedom and danger in equal parts, ending in pregnancy and hard choices. Wharton treats her heroine's longing without a hint of shame. The book shocked readers who expected safer fare from her.
whiston-astronomical-principles-religion:
William Whiston held Newton's chair at Cambridge and wrote on both science and faith. His Astronomical Principles of Religion came out in 1717. In it he read the Bible through the lens of the new astronomy of his day.

Whiston argued that a comet passing near Earth had caused the great Flood. He linked planets, comets, and scripture into one bold system of causes. The book mixes real skill in astronomy with deep trust in revealed truth. It shows an early clash, and an early truce, between Newton's cosmos and the Bible that shaped his age.
williams-al-que-quiere-1917:
William Carlos Williams was a doctor in Rutherford, New Jersey, who wrote poems between house calls. Al Que Quiere, published in 1917, is the book where his own voice first comes through clearly. Its Spanish title means roughly 'to him who wants it,' and the full title carries an exclamation point. The poems turn away from fancy European models toward plain American speech.

Williams writes about local people, streets, flowers, and small daily scenes around him. He favors short lines, sharp images, and the rhythms of talk he heard every day. Some pieces are tender, others wry or blunt. The book laid the ground for his lifelong project: a poetry built from American things, seen up close.
woodward-piltdown-fourth-note-1917:
Arthur Smith Woodward, keeper at the British Museum, gave this fourth note on the Piltdown gravel in 1917. Grafton Elliot Smith adds a part on the brain cast of the find. Piltdown man was then held a true dawn man of England by its chief backers.

The note tells of a new find spot, with parts of a second skull of the same kind. That 'Piltdown II' skull seemed to prove the first was no freak or chance mix. In truth both were fraud, and the note shows the hoax at its most safe and sure hour.
young-journal-of-discourses-vol17:
Volume XVII of the Journal of Discourses appeared at Liverpool in 1875, three years before Brigham Young's death. The stenographic record again holds his sermons beside those of his counsellors, the Twelve, and others. A church nearing thirty years in Utah speaks here with the weight of long habit.

Talks in this volume show leaders instructing a people many of whom were born into the faith. Doctrine is less argued than applied, fitted to farms, families, and towns. The year-by-year record gains value from such stretches, where the movement's settled voice can be heard plainly.
zimmermann-telegram-1917:
Arthur Zimmermann, Germany's foreign chief, sent his famed telegram in 1917. The secret offer invites Mexico to join a war on America. Texas and the Southwest are dangled as the prize for joining.

British codebreakers seize the message and pass it to Washington with care. American papers print it, and public fury sweeps the neutral nation. Within weeks, the United States declares war on Germany at last. One intercepted cable thus swings the whole Great War's balance. Few single messages in history have changed so much so fast for so many. Germany's bid for a second front collapsed the moment it leaked.
